# THE ARGUMENTS
## of the Books on the Harmony of the World.

**First,** the tenets of the Christian religion are taught through philosophical reasoning.
**Second,** the life, upbringing, and customs of Muhammad, the lawgiver of the Arabs, and his followers are handed down; finally, the Quran is examined from beginning to end <note>original: "à capite ad calcem," literally "from head to heel"</note> from the Arabic and refuted.
**Third,** what the entire world holds in common, both by human and divine law.
**Fourth,** by what skill false beliefs about God or the gods might be drawn toward the true one without civil unrest <note>original: "seditione"; Postel was deeply concerned with achieving religious unity without resorting to the violence seen in the religious wars of his time.</note>.

## TO THE CANDID READER.

I implore you, whoever you are, fair-minded Reader <note>In the 16th century, a "candid" or "fair-minded" reader was one who approached a text without prejudice.</note>, if you do not have the leisure to read through this entire book, at least skim chapters 3, 4, 7, 8, 10, 14, 20, 21, and 22. Or if even fewer are possible, read 3, 4, 20, and 21. For I do not hesitate to affirm this one thing without rashness: it will come to pass that whoever reads those chapters attentively with a spirit of learning rather than contradicting, will be able by reason not only to satisfy himself in difficult matters but also—provided they follow reason as their guide—
->to persuade others of the same, however much they are estranged from the truth.<-

<summary>This page outlines the four-part structure of Postel's work, which moves from philosophical theology to a critique of Islam and a search for universal laws. It includes a personal appeal to the reader to focus on specific chapters that demonstrate the rational power of his arguments.</summary>

# GUILLAUME POSTEL TO THE PRINCES
## AND GREAT NOBLES, THE PRESERVERS 
### *and Promoters of True Piety toward God, and to the* 
### *Fellowship of the entire Holy Church, Greeting.*

<image-desc>A large square historiated woodcut initial Q. Inside a circular frame, a figure is depicted in a reclining or seated pose within a landscape containing architectural elements.</image-desc>

**"What will this boaster produce worthy of such mouthing?"** <note>original: "QUID tanto dignū feret hic promissor hiatu?" This is a famous line from the Roman poet Horace’s *Ars Poetica* (line 138), mocking writers who promise more than they can deliver.</note> It pleases me, O Princes and most upright assemblies, to meet certain people with this verse of Horace, lest I be preempted. I do not doubt that as soon as they see the title of the work and the argument of the first book, they will say that one who promises such arduous and unheard-of things will perform them either with too little wisdom, or without sufficient holiness and perfection—since even in handling the smallest matters, powers that have not been well-weighed often fail. 

Besides the fact that the greatest matter in the whole world—one that could occupy everyone to the highest degree—is being undertaken by a man of slender learning, both reason and authority oppose such a treatment, making it less likely to be completed. When I endeavor to prove and confirm the principles of the Christian faith (already confirmed by men of the highest genius and by divine and human authority) using arguments that are not foreign to the teachings of the most excellent philosophers, I will seem to those people to contradict the opinion of Pope Saint Gregory the Great. For he left it written: **"Faith has no merit where human reason provides proof."** <note>original: "Fides nō habet meritum, ubi humana ratio præbet experimentum." A famous quote from Gregory's 26th Homily on the Gospels, often cited to argue that trying to "prove" religion undermines the virtue of believing without sight.</note> 

However, although something agreeable to reason could be offered against this <term>axiom</term> <note>A self-evident truth or established principle.</note>, it shall be enough to show that I do not depart from the common opinion received in the Church of Christ to this day. For those who are imbued with the sacred mysteries and are moved by the Spirit of God, faith does not need to be confirmed by reasons, as they are already sufficiently persuaded of it (though they ought primarily to persuade themselves of this one thing: that God, the author of reason, has not commanded or taught anything, however difficult or obscure, without a reason). 

Therefore, I have not undertaken this work to play the role of a "Christian Philosopher" among you. For what else would that be in this so learned an age—with disciplines partly revived and partly restored, with such illustrious geniuses and such a great abundance of learned men—than, according to the proverb, **"to bring owls to Athens"**? <note>original: "γλαῦκας εἰς ἀθῆνας." A Greek proverb meaning to do something redundant or useless, as Athens was already full of owls (the symbol of Athena/wisdom).</note> 

But for those who are strangers to our persuasion, and who in divine matters use their own authority (which differs from ours) and rely upon it, that reason must certainly be set forth which we believe flowed from God, the author of truth. For what end will there ever be to bickering and stubbornly defending one’s own views by simple authority, unless the reason of truth and falsehood makes a distinction and sits as a judge between the litigants? Therefore, it is permitted to me, since the cause of the nations wandering from the true goal of happiness... 

<meta>The text cuts off here at the catchword "scri", which likely begins the word "scribendi" or "scribam" on the next page.</meta>

<meta>This page continues Postel’s dedicatory letter. # LETTER

I shall write to convey, through reasons, those things which were instilled in us and convinced us along with our mother's milk. In the birth of Christ’s Church, it was done through miracles; now, in its old age, when piety is all but afflicted, we must act through reason. Truly, let it be permitted to act through reason among foreign nations by the authority of our own people. To be sure, many have persuaded themselves with certain flimsy arguments that those dogmas which are proved by us can never be demonstrated, because they are "elements" and indemonstrable principles, just as in geometry. <note>In traditional logic and geometry, "elements" or axioms are starting points that are accepted as true without proof. Postel is arguing against the idea that religious dogmas are like these axioms and cannot be logically explained to outsiders.</note>

Yet, if I may speak by their leave, they are wandering in error in this matter, while they think that the things they have convinced themselves of are known by nature equally to all men as they are known to themselves by indubitable faith. For if the things received by us from heaven had elements naturally common to all, the world would undoubtedly have agreed on them long ago, nor would there have been a need for revelation, just as there is no such need in mathematics. Indeed, a different law must be observed here. For just as divine providence gave to our minds a certain "nursery of reason" <note>Postel uses the phrase *rationis seminarium*, suggesting that humans are born with the "seeds" of logical thought planted by God.</note> by which we might arrive at the knowledge of things through cause or effect, so according to those principles which no one can deny, we can deal with natural and supernatural causes. We can persuade and demonstrate by inductions and <term>syllogisms</term> <note>A form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal).</note> so that, at least from their effects, the nature of divine things might be revealed—which not a few philosophers have done. 

Moreover, Paul also affirms that they <note>Referring to the pagans or those without scripture.</note> came to the knowledge of the Creator from the reasoning of the created world. Therefore, I have collected, explained, and enriched the reasons scattered among the philosophers, insofar as they approach the truth more closely; and, as if reclaiming them from unjust possessors, I have adapted them for the confirmation of our own beliefs. I have refuted in those same authors the things written and weakly proved by them, not infrequently based only on authority, or a desire for argument, or error—for "sometimes even good Homer nods." <note>original: "quandoque bonus dormitat Homerus." A famous line from the Roman poet Horace, suggesting that even the greatest experts and geniuses occasionally make mistakes.</note>

But what I have achieved in the whole work will be judged most especially by whoever reads attentively the chapters on the Trinity, on the creation of the world, on <term>separate substances</term> <note>A technical term in medieval philosophy referring to beings that exist without physical bodies, such as angels or the human soul after death.</note>, the immortality of souls, and the resurrection. I was led to this treatment for a twofold reason. For since I see that <term>letters</term> <note>Meaning literature, scholarship, or humanistic learning.</note>, the most excellent ornament of this mortal life, have been given to many in this time as if for the destruction of other men, or only for ostentation and conflict—yet it is truly the most blessed duty of this life to have dispelled those shadows from the minds of men which block the way of immortality—I thought it was part of my duty that, if I have tried to cultivate my mind with any learning until this day, I should use it to explain and persuade the truth to those minds occupied by the fog of falsehood. 

The second cause of the undertaken work was this: Since I see that by many men distinguished in the knowledge of both sacred and human disciplines, the truth has been affirmed and confirmed just as the false has been refuted, partly by reason and partly by authority; yet I see those brilliant works lying hidden among our own people who do not doubt the truth, I have decided [to share them] among...

<summary>Postel argues that while the early Church relied on miracles, the current age requires using reason and philosophy to demonstrate Christian truths to the world. He explains his method of reclaiming "scattered truths" from ancient philosophers to support doctrines like the Trinity and the immortality of the soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dedicatory letter of Guillaume Postel's *De Orbis Concordia* (On the Harmony of the World). Postel is explaining his methodology: using reason and his knowledge of languages to reconcile different faiths, specifically targeting the conversion of Muslims through logical persuasion and the translation of Christian texts into their own languages.</meta>

-># DEDICATORY<-

->### LETTER<-

...me, while I collect whatever proves the truth and disproves the false—both from the labors of others and from my own, albeit slender, industry—guided by reason, and permit this work to be examined by your most holy assembly, I shall translate this very work into the languages of those peoples against whose errors I write. I shall bring it to them and open it, so that they may either refute the objections raised against them and give satisfaction, or, having rejected what is false, embrace the truth. For I think that God Almighty entrusted and committed to me this proficiency in such diverse languages—modest though it be—as a <term>talent</term> <note>Postel refers to the Biblical "Parable of the Talents" (Matthew 25), where a servant is expected to invest the money given to him by his master to produce a "return" for the Kingdom of Heaven.</note>, so that some fruit might overflow from it to other men, for whom I was born. I hope that providence might at least grant courage, through this example of my own insignificance and superficial knowledge of all things, to men great and perfected in every kind of virtue and learning, so that they might execute in deed what I at least have held in my desires. 

Since this work requires a spirit not cast down by its greatness, yet stands in need of resources and the great help and favor of Princes and nobles, I nevertheless judged that it could be undertaken by me, however humble and entirely unequipped in terms of external fortune. I believe this because I hope I cannot easily be surpassed by anyone in a mind well-disposed toward persuading the truth and helping the <term>Christian Commonwealth</term> <note>original: *Remp. Christianam*. This refers to the collective body of Christian nations and peoples, seen as a single political and spiritual entity.</note>. As for the resources necessary for travel, if they are not provided from elsewhere, I will provide them from my own means. That is to say, I will ward off the laws of necessity by my own efforts; through abstinence, I will cut back even on useful things. I will struggle against hunger, thirst, and nakedness with patience, **so as even to live a life that is no life.** <note>original Greek: *ὥστε καὶ ἄβιον βίον ζῆν* (hōste kai abion bion zēn). This is a classical Greek idiom describing a life of such extreme hardship that it hardly counts as living.</note> If men are lacking, God, who gave the courage for this task, will not be lacking. 

Relying on the favor of **Jesus Christ**, I will undertake a journey to those cities where studies of the Arabic tongue flourish. I shall acquire a knowledge of that language—which is common to almost all of Africa and Asia—(if life remains a companion to prosperous health) to such an extent that I may translate my work *On the Harmony of the World* into it. I wish to communicate with those, and explain in familiar conversation, who are well-versed in philosophy and humane letters. For just as the common people of the Muslims, and those who have been formed only in superstitious belief, are most observant of the **Quran** <note>original: *Alcorani*</note> and most addicted to that belief, so those who have touched the Gospel or philosophy are most estranged from it. Therefore, not a few **Caliphs** <note>original: *Chaliphę*</note>, when building public schools, decreed that no one who was well-versed in philosophy or the Gospel should be admitted into them. <note>The Latin text *admittat* includes a terminal abbreviation mark indicating the passive form *admittatur* ("be admitted").</note> 

My second care will be that, being abundantly instructed in their literature and opinions, I may be able to be armed against them on all sides, and to provide our own men with weapons wrested away from the enemy to attack them. If truly by chance while traveling some Greek authors present themselves, but I am unable to purchase them (for which money is needed) or satisfy the scribes, I will at least point them out to **King Francis**, so that he may see to their transport into his famous **Library at Fontainebleau**, or to men who are wealthy and lovers of literature; lest such great treasures lie hidden any longer under barbarians.

<summary>Postel declares his intent to live in poverty and travel to the East to master Arabic, translate his work, and convert Muslims through rational debate. He also mentions his secondary mission to recover lost Greek manuscripts for the library of King Francis I.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dedicatory letter of Postel’s *De Orbis Concordia*. -># LETTER<-

<meta>catchword: -nus (completing "Ciceronianus" from the following page)</meta>

Indeed, the plan of the work I have undertaken is such that I wish to translate not only my own writings into the Arabic and Hebrew languages, but also the Holy Scriptures, and whatever else seems likely to restore light to blinded men. For I ask, what else is it but <term>fighting with shadows</term> <note>original Greek: σκιαμαχεῖν (*skiamachein*). A metaphor for fighting an imaginary opponent or engaging in a useless struggle because the "enemy" cannot see or understand the arguments being made.</note> to act against nations whose beliefs and dogmas differ from our own, unless they can hear, read, and understand in their own native languages the arguments being made against them? If I do not fully reach this mark, I will at least pave the way for our monks and professors of Holy Scripture by which they may prove their devotion to Christ. For those men falsely claim that the time for defending the Gospel at the risk of one's life has passed, so long as the knowledge of Christ and the truth is absent from any region of the world. Long ago, that foul and absurd belief <note>Postel refers here to Islam.</note> would have been exiled from the world if in every century there had been even a few individuals instructed in its literature who had warned Princes and engaged in debate with their learned men. But truly, since the <term>Alcoran</term> <note>The Quran.</note> was first accepted, scarcely one or two have written in Arabic to the Arabs against that impiety and destruction of nature.

Truly, just as I have dared to undertake a work far beyond my own strength, so have I completed it with such a meager supply of words and eloquence that it might seem like a superficial effort. For if I look to the great masters of eloquence, their leader <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and philosopher held as the absolute gold standard for Latin style during the Renaissance.</note> would say I immoderately abuse both my leisure and my letters, because I cannot express what I rightly feel in a polished way, nor am I able to entice and retain the reader with any delight of speech. But I shall appeal from him to you, Princes, and most holy assemblies; I shall consider it enough if the matters I treat bring light to an unadorned speech, rather than the reverse. A humble style of speaking, suited for logical demonstrations—such as I embrace, along with all those who treat the mysteries of nature—was never used by Cicero. Therefore, the explanation of natural things, of mathematics, and of <term>dialectics</term> <note>The art of investigating the truth of opinions; logic.</note>—disciplines most fit for demonstration—lack the brilliance of Latin literature in his work, except for those few places where he touched upon them sparingly. For in treating those subjects according to the rules of a discipline, the laws and richness of speech, the freedom to amplify, the flow of oratory, the "rouge" and seductive charms of words, and that great apparatus of eloquence which Cicero always used, would not have been able to reveal themselves sufficiently. 

I say this so that certain of our <term>old-childish</term> <note>original Greek: γεροντόπαιδες (*gerontopaides*). A derogatory term for older men who obsess over trivialities, like schoolboys.</note> chatterboxes and formula-mongers might not try to persuade us in their own way—hissing at everyone else who lacks their "proper" age—that only Cicero and a few others should be valued among the Latins. For they always have it on their lips that a work is not "good Latin" or worth reading if it does not breathe the phrasing of Cicero, or Caesar, or Livy; yet, at the greatest expense of their own lives, they can scarcely become even his "apes" <note>An "ape of Cicero" was a Renaissance insult for someone who mindlessly imitated Cicero’s style without having any original thoughts.</note>. Are there not, therefore, a thousand or more Latin authors who expressed the feelings of the mind so clearly in Latin fourteen hundred years ago that posterity might grasp what they wanted written? Certainly there are. But none of them is a "Ciceronian"...

<summary>Postel argues that converting non-Christians requires translating the Bible and rational arguments into their own languages, such as Arabic. He defends his "plain" writing style against Renaissance critics who insisted that all serious Latin must strictly imitate the style of Cicero.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the introductory letter (Epistola) of Guillaume Postel’s *De Orbis Terrae Concordia*. The previous page discussed the author’s plan to translate the Bible into Arabic to reach non-Christians; here he defends his unpolished writing style against critics who value rhetorical elegance over theological truth.</meta>

-># LETTER<-

...Ciceronian, or Caesarian. <note>original: *Ciceronianus, aut Caesarianus*. These terms refer to the strict Renaissance fashion of imitating only the prose styles of Marcus Tullius Cicero or Julius Caesar. Postel is arguing that content matters more than perfect Latin style.</note> Add to this that no art can make imitators so perfect that they are identical to the original authors—for every man has his own style and turn of phrase. 

But perhaps I am seeking a defense for my own laziness and lack of eloquence while I seem to dismiss those things which I neither care to achieve nor am able to. Yet the value of gold, gems, or <term>amber-gold</term> <note>original: *chrysoelectri*. A precious alloy of gold and silver, or possibly a reference to amber itself, used here to represent "high" literary style.</note> is not diminished by someone who says that silver, glass, and <term>copper</term> <note>original: *aeri Cyprio* ("Cyprian brass"). Since Cyprus was the primary ancient source of copper, the metal's name is actually derived from the island's name.</note> also have their own place in the Commonwealth. I condemn the backwards judgments of certain men who, while they grow old in the study of words, are—as Paul says—"always learning, and never arriving at a knowledge of the truth." <note>Postel quotes the Apostle Paul from 2 Timothy 3:7 to criticize humanists who care more about grammar than divine truth.</note> They seem born for this: to pluck at, abuse, nitpick, and belittle the labors of others. 

Truly, I have written in Latin well enough, if I have written truly enough. For such is the nature of truth that the less it is treated with the <term>artificial makeup</term> <note>original: *fuco*. Literally "seaweed dye" or "rouge," used metaphorically to describe deceptive or distracting rhetorical ornamentation.</note> of words, the more deeply it penetrates the minds of men. Otherwise, I easily disregard the judgment of slanderous men, as I seek no human glory or fame from this work. Indeed, I have intentionally left certain words in my writing for them to occupy themselves with criticizing; for such words are read in the sacred authors, and when new ideas are born, suitable words must be adapted to them. 

->Farewell.<-

<summary>In this conclusion to his preface, Postel defends his plain Latin style against humanist critics, arguing that the pursuit of truth is more important than the imitation of classical authors like Cicero. He asserts that new theological concepts require a flexible vocabulary rather than linguistic perfection.</summary>

# THE PROOF OF THE TRUE RELIGION, THAT IS,
## CHRISTIANITY, DRAWN FROM
### PHILOSOPHY, BOOK I.

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'E' depicts a scholar or theologian in his study, seated at a desk with an open book, pointing towards a window. The room is detailed with architectural vaults and bookshelves.</image-desc>

ALTHOUGH it is an arduous task, and one beyond human strength, to discuss things that do not fall under the senses—since even things that are admitted find a place among many with difficulty, many withhold their assent from the most manifest truths, and things usually perceived by the senses are only known only superficially—reason becomes ineffective for weighing all things, and most especially divine matters that are separated from this foul matter <note>original: "feculenta materia"; the author refers to the physical world of decay and change as opposed to the purity of the divine</note>. Nevertheless, spurred both by an eagerness to prove my efforts and a desire to achieve the highest good, I judge it better to test what human strength can do than to leave the matter unattempted through sloth or dejection of spirit; for the mere thought of pursuing this brings no small benefit to our mortal life. For while the mind is occupied in the contemplation of great things, even if it does not usually attain what it proposed for itself, yet while it is held by the zeal of pursuit and is entirely occupied in contemplation, it must necessarily be free from many troubles. Indeed, when the mind is carried so completely into the thought of a thing that it is plainly snatched away by the emotion itself, it happens that it does not even feel those troubles by which others are oppressed. Just as one who is intent on blood and vengeance does not feel the wounds he receives until he has settled down, because the emotion itself carries him away, so may he see and admire other forms of happiness only through a lattice <note>original: "per transennam"; a metaphor for seeing something partially or in passing</note>, like one who, having set his sights on the goal of true happiness, clearly looks at or cares for nothing else until he has reached it. 

Therefore, since I see that happiness is the goal of this life, which all things naturally desire, and that it has been dissected into various parts by various judgments—while one person proposes one part for himself, and another busies himself with attaining many parts—there is no one who does not desire solid happiness. By disputing about this happiness as the highest and most absolute that can be imagined, I have decided to treat the subject in such a way that from these sensible traces, shadows, and conjectures, I may come to knowledge, insofar as it is permitted for a soul shut in the prison-house of the body to reach it. I intend to demonstrate the divinity of the supreme deity and the creator of all things, so that by this labor (which meanwhile calls me away from other things), even as I try to satisfy myself, if the argument handed down can be of use to this age, I may indeed seem to have done a great service. 

To repeat this from a slightly higher summary, I judge that one must begin from the contemplation of all nature—not having dared to approach this without the favor and grace of Him whom we seek. Therefore, I pray and beseech Him with all my vows, that the knowledge of Him which He has deigned to open to us to this day through His mercy, through the holy scriptures and His son Jesus Christ, the God-man <note>original Greek: "θεάνθρωπον" (theanthropon); a theological term for Christ being both fully God and fully human</note>, He might permit and cause that same knowledge to pass for a little while into the power of reason, as if being vindicated by His own authority. As long as innocence lasted, ambition was banished, deceit did not creep into sacred places, and providence—the avenger of crimes and the worker of miracles—was present and revealed herself sufficiently to the world. Whatever sacred religion proclaimed in her name was accepted. But these dangerous times, which Peter foretold <note>A reference to the New Testament epistles (2 Peter or 2 Timothy) regarding the "perilous times" of the last days</note>, receive no sound doctrine; they mock authority, turn aside to fables, and recoil from all authority of antiquity so that they may follow their own dreams. I wish these arguments to be proposed so that they may be without excuse, and may be deservedly separated from the number of men if they do not listen to truth joined to reason. Furthermore, if this work is to be of use to others besides myself, I desire it to be written so that those who until this day are occupied by false authority may embrace the truth. Indeed, I do not so much pity the many who, after acknowledging the truth...

He announces his intent to prove the truths of Christianity through the study of nature and rational inquiry, rather than relying solely on scriptural authority, to combat the skepticism of his "dangerous times."</summary>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction to Guillaume Postel’s "De Orbis Terrae Concordia" (On the Harmony of the World), moving from the general difficulty of divine contemplation to a specific critique of the religious state of the world and the necessity of using reason for conversion.</meta>

->ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

They either attack the truth with words and deeds, or they completely reject it by their way of life. I am moved by the error and unhappiness of so many peoples who, although they are entirely absent from the truth and follow falsehoods, nevertheless omit nothing of those things which they are persuaded will lead to the highest happiness, so that they might finally attain it. For who would not weep that so many labors perish—that so many noble efforts die when vice is allowed in and accepted as virtue? It is as if the sweetest liquids were spoiled by the mixing in of wormwood <note>original: "absinthijs"; a bitter herb often used as a metaphor for sorrow or corruption</note>, and a life is never truly lived because it is constantly accompanied by death. One person claims for himself the opinion of Moses; another approves of Muhammad as the author of the law; to many, the foul image of a demon presents itself to be worshiped. Others are terrified by ghosts <note>original: "lemuribus"; in Roman mythology, these were the wandering and vengeful spirits of the dead</note> and perform sacred rites to them; whatever else is offered to the rest is held in the place of God. 

And meanwhile, the truth itself lies hidden among us; it remains concealed by our sloth, unknown by many names. Truly, because of our own way of living, even if there were those who would spontaneously submit to that law—which we prove and assert depends upon the highest happiness—they would be pulled in an entirely different direction. It seems unjust that the common actions of life should differ so much from holy prescriptions. The primary examples of this neglected belief are not to be sought from the common people, nor are they found only in lawless military service, nor do they show themselves only in the courts of princes; rather, they are by far the worst among the priests <note>original: "mystis"; literally those initiated into sacred mysteries, here referring to the clergy</note> themselves. 

A dreadful ambition and a grasping for empty fame twists those who are removed from the common noise and more splendid habits of human affairs. Pride and arrogance drive the wealthy off course. The middle classes, increased by the vices of their elders, think everything is permitted to them. In short, ignorance, vanity, and greed infect every order of society, so that those who answer to so holy a name—whom I wish were untouched—are very rare. Other nations leave no stone unturned to sow the seeds of their false persuasions wherever they can; they hunt for followers with gifts, entice them with friendship, compel them with authority, draw them in by force, and strive to join everyone to themselves by persuasion. But we, idle and sluggish, sleep deeply, considering it enough to possess the most noble thing for ourselves—like misers—without making any use of it. 

The third cause lies in the difficulty of the subject, which not infrequently rejects even the most excellent men. For although we may be well-disposed toward these matters, and faith itself is a gift of God—devoid of human reason and supported by divine authority—it ought to produce belief by itself. However, since that same authority offers itself everywhere, it seems that everyone has the same right unless you make a choice based on reason. For all people either seek God while they think they have Him, or they openly profess Him. The Jews, the Muslims <note>original: "Muhamedici"</note>, and the Indians <note>In the 16th century, "Indi" could refer broadly to people of the East or the newly contacted peoples of the Americas</note> either worship or acknowledge one Creator of heaven and earth; we do the same. 

Suppose there is a stranger who has never heard anything about God (whom you nevertheless think should be known by nature); it is certain that he will be in doubt as to which of all these he should believe, unless reason compels him to turn toward one side rather than the other. If authority alone makes the law, the reasoning of all will be equal, since there will be none. Surely no mortal would fail to highly approve of our prescriptions if he grasped everything from the very beginning. But since difficulty makes very many pagans, and indeed all Jews and Muslims, estranged from us, I judge that one must deal with them through reason—both in all things and especially in those matters which they cannot persuade themselves to believe. 

Such things are these: that not only must an injury be forgiven, but it must even be repaid with benefits in place of retaliation <note>original: "talionis"; the law of "an eye for an eye"</note>. This is something that must be done not only by one who embraces peace in this life, but by every Christian man. But what wonder if a Jew, a Turk, a Persian, or a Moor refuses to believe this, when we ourselves are accustomed to observe that sacred precept only with our lips? To others, we might even suggest that this principle—which is the basis and proof of a truly godly man—is not a command, but merely advice. Therefore, one must deal with the Jew and the Muslim by reasons, so that they may judge that forgiveness is entirely to be preferred over vengeance, except as it pertains to the punishment of the laws. Now, however, the Holy Trinity itself has made both the Moors and the followers of Moses estranged from Christ, because by no reason does it seem,

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Postel's masterwork, shifting from a lament over religious division to a formal outline of his three-book project. ### OF GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I. 3 ###

...it may be seen that the same and most simple thing is three, and vice versa. Although this is difficult to demonstrate and almost beyond human capability, I will nevertheless attempt to reveal it from the most sacred inner chambers of philosophy—insofar as reason can support authority—and to point it out by its traces, offering it to the sharp sight of the mind. <note>Postel is referring to the Christian doctrine of the Trinity, which he intends to prove through philosophical reasoning rather than just faith.</note> Regarding the necessity and the reason for the coming of Jesus Christ, if anything can be held which a seasoned judgment of human affairs can conceive and approve, I will make the attempt: although I must deal with those (I mean the followers of Moses and Muhammad) whom I might conquer by the authority of their own legislators. The immortality of souls will be proved in its proper place by a necessary argument agreeable to reason. The crowning achievement will be to use philosophical arguments against the philosophers themselves, and to show that the final outcome of this entire present life must lead toward the immortality of souls, the resurrection, eternal life, and the transformation of matter. For the greater part of the Jews are persuaded of this, and the Muslims <note>original: "Muhamedici"</note> read and believe it six hundred times in their Quran <note>original: "Alcorano"</note>. 

However, so that our persuasion might be armed on all sides against those who falsely claim the name of philosophy, we shall proceed from the causes of the world itself to the First Cause. We shall attempt to demonstrate and persuade that the world has its origin from God and must be referred back to that same end. All other things which do not seem at first glance to have self-evident principles—and therefore hardly deserve belief—will be handed down in this first book. In the second book, the life of Muhammad and the persuasion of the Quran will be presented and examined, and things yet unknown to us will be translated from their own writings. And lest anything be missing from this argument, I will subjoin in the third book those principles upon which all men of whatever persuasion agree—provided they are mature and cultivated—regarding both secular and sacred laws. In this way, I will not seem to have failed our people, even in this fractured state of affairs. For it is not enough to have asserted and demonstrated the truth itself, unless you also explain, defend, and clearly vindicate and assert it in whatever part it differs. Once I have taught from their own decrees what the Jews, the Moors <note>A term used historically for North African Muslims</note>, and the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnici"</note> ought to feel about their own persuasion, and by what reasons they might cross over to ours—having refuted their vain opinions and substituted our own—I will make an end of speaking, having noted and examined what serves the matter in every persuasion. Now, however, we must first deal briefly with the highest of things: namely, God and the world.

---

->ON THE WORLD AND GOD. CHAPTER I.<-

I do not think I should call into doubt whether there is only one world or many, or which is the most excellent: since among the leaders of philosophers, it is already thoroughly proven—as if by decrees received by the judgment of all—that there can be neither many nor different worlds. I judge that I should not use any further division before defining this.

For although I consider that I must proceed by reasons and demonstrations, yet because I judge the decrees of Aristotle, Galen, and Averroes <note>original: "Abenreis"; a 12th-century Islamic philosopher from Spain whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to Western thought</note> to stand in the place of reason for all, it is certain that their authority ought to be held as reason, since it is approved by everyone. Therefore, the "multiple worlds" introduced by Democritus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who proposed an infinite universe of atoms</note>—lest he seem to know nothing more than the rest—are exploded by these reasons. For absurdities would follow in both cause and effect: it would follow that there are multiple authors, either equal or unequal. If they were equal, they would be superfluous. If they were dissimilar, they would be in perpetual strife, which is repugnant to the First Cause. In the effect, however, or in matter, nothing would seem higher or lower; everything would collapse confusedly in every direction, and it would be a chaos rather than a distinction of worlds. By these and many other reasons, the greatest philosophers refuted the opinion of empty men born for trifles and contentions. Therefore, if anyone doubts that the world is one and finite, he is not to be counted among the seekers of truth. There was once another reason for doubting everything, based on two principal causes of the obscurity of things—

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD #

In the past, ancient thinkers were driven to call everything into doubt, not out of a desire for conflict, but out of a zeal for the truth. For although nature has made the signs of truth kindred to our own souls, difficulties have arisen—both from the things themselves and from the weakness of our senses—that prevent us from holding onto truth perpetually. This issue was debated among the greatest leaders of philosophy until they could grasp truth only as far as it can be conceived by human judgment. 

This period of obscurity and difficulty was followed by the stubbornness of certain men who were captivated by a desire for glory. Because they refused to accept things that are subject to reason, they willfully leaped away from the truth; they devised new ideas, forced them upon others, and asserted them—partly to seem as if they had discovered something original, and partly to avoid appearing to subscribe to someone else's opinion. This was the reason for searching for the truth for so long and following various opinions. For one man affirms that everything can be known; another withholds his assent from all things <note>This refers to the Academics and Pyrrhonists, ancient schools of Skepticism.</note>; a third makes everything doubtful. Some would even prefer to "strip off the human" <note>To cast aside human nature or common sense.</note> rather than prove that things manifest to the senses are as they appear; yet they themselves are forced to admit that they at least know this one thing: that they know nothing. This was the cause of the truth remaining hidden for so long.

Therefore, since those vain opinions have been hissed off the stage, and since we know that faith must be placed in the senses and in reason (which is, as it were, the eye of the mind), there is no reason for us to be moved from established and fixed demonstrations by the opinion of a few men who deny that reason exists within themselves. 

The **World**, therefore, is one, finite, and in every way most adorned <term>ornatissimum; Postel plays on the Latin word *mundus*, which means both "the world" and "neat" or "adorned," mirroring the Greek *cosmos*</term>. The root meaning of the word in all nations signifies this "adornment," and the reality itself reveals it. Whatever is adorned, however, must necessarily depend upon a cause, be ruled, and be set in motion; from this, it follows that the world is finite. For no power can contain the infinite. We assert, then, that the World is this "temple of nature," which encompasses everything subject to the senses. Whether some call it the "universe" or others "whatever this is," they differ in words, not in reality.

But since the rashness of "fortune" (I meant to say the rashness of the insane opinion that devised "fortune"), the continuous change of corruptible things, ignorance of the truth, and a lust for lying place fortune, chance, and I know not what other monsters in the causes of such a great mass—though no true philosopher allows this—and since some would cast God, the author of a work so great and truly worthy of Him, out of His own heaven with their words: we shall show in a few words that the world itself is ruled by the judgment of **Providence**. We shall then add a discussion on eternity: whether the world will be eternal in its form, or in the cause of its form, or even in its matter, or whether indeed both joined together will be an eternal nature. If one had to attend to and satisfy every objection of every person, one would linger longer on the side-issues than on the work itself. Therefore, leaving aside the question of whether the world is "animated" or "an animal," or whether it has a cause outside of itself (which will be treated in their proper places), I come to the demonstrations sought from the innermost parts of philosophy. 

I demonstrate that **God exists** in this way: from the contemplation and nature of truth; from the composition of all things; from motion; from distance; from order; from the perfection of good; from happiness; and from the purpose <note>original: "fine" (end/goal)</note> of all things.

### 1 ###

I believe it is confessed by all that **Truth** exists in the nature of things, and that it is manifold; for there is the "false," and that which is "falser than the false." That is "most true" in which the senses or the intellect of all people—but especially of the wise—do not hallucinate when weighing it. Its very assertion produces the greatest faith because it is "most so." For example: he who says there is light in the dim shadows of dawn touches upon the truth to some extent. He who asserts a greater light in a greater glow says something more true. He who speaks of the light of the moon is truer still. Finally, if one speaks of the light of the sun (as far as the sense of the eyes is concerned) as the "truest," he will undoubtedly not err. From this, it appears to us that what is most greatly and perfectly "being," and in which judgment cannot be deceived, is the "most true." 

Thus, the things commonly thought to be "most real" are actually "barely true." Things that are physical are merely present and dregs; those things that both exist and live are worthier and "truer." Even more worthy are those that also possess sense and life. Far truer are those to which intellect is added, infused into matter. But the **truest** things are those devoid of a body, which flourish and are powerful by intellect alone. Among these, that thing is the most worthy and most true, whose...

<meta>This page continues the opening of Book I, moving from a critique of ancient skepticism to the positive philosophical proofs for God's existence and nature. Postel focuses here on the soul's innate drive for truth and the physical evidence of motion in the universe as indicators of a First Mover.</meta>

->### WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK I. ###<-

**1** The soul runs through all things. Therefore, God Himself is truth, and the goal of all truth; He is more true to the degree that He exists more through Himself. For since these lower things do not exist of themselves, it is certain that they depend on a far truer principle. For the basis of all things—namely, *being*—exists in the cause of the most perfect perfection, which is entirely devoid of matter. Therefore, that supreme truth is sought not through the senses, like other things, but through deprivation <note>original: *priuationem*; in Scholastic philosophy, defining something by what it is not—the "way of negation."</note> and the removal of all other things. It is more desired than it is actually reached, though we know Him to truly exist (even if only from His effects). For the nature of our soul indicates this most clearly, as it never ceases from contemplation and the longing for truth, even if it has grasped all those things subject to the senses as far as they can be grasped. For Nature—and God Himself, the parent of Nature—would never have created the soul so greedy for further progress unless there were a set goal in which it might find rest: a goal which, by its immensity and the glory of being known, would satisfy that desire. For we see in other things, toward which we are moved to desire by objects either inward or outward, that we set a limit to our longing once we have attained them. Therefore, God is the truest and most perfect cause of all things, from whom all things come, through whom all things consist, and toward whom finally all things tend, whether mediately or immediately, as if toward their rest and happiness.

**2** The perfection and composition of all things also argue that there is a mind that adorns them all. For since all things consist of matter and form, and formless matter cannot by itself approach a form, nor can it subsist alone, it is certain that their bond depends on something else. For even if the celestial bodies lacked motion, they still consist of matter (of a fifth element <note>The "quintessence" or aether, thought to be the material of the heavens.</note> known by deprivation) and of the form that is seen. But who would believe that these moist things could be joined with the dry, or the hot with the humid, unless they coalesced into one by some supreme and powerful cause, and lasted only so long as they preserve that bond conceived by a spirit that penetrates all things? God, therefore, is everywhere. That was surely the reason why certain philosophers said the world was animate <note>Life-infused or possessing a soul.</note> and called God the "soul of the world," <note>original: *animā mundi*</note> wishing for an infinite power to be contained within a place. To refute their opinion (if they conceive of God as circumscribed by place), I will offer nothing other than what would follow: namely, that all things would be eternal if they were contained within the embrace of the substance of divinity. For the intellect assimilates all things to itself; since it is an eternal substance, it would animate all things eternally. Therefore, although He is supremely powerful and penetrates all things, He acts upon these lower things chiefly through the movements of the superior bodies in their order, while being Himself most remote from matter.

**3** I think no one is so stupid or stubborn as to doubt the motion of the world, in the manner of certain ancients, or to deny that anything moves, since the contrary is clear to the senses and to the eyes by experience. Whatever is moved is moved by something else, whether from generation to corruption, or the reverse, or in any direction or arrangement; for motion is manifold. Motion, as it is generally agreed, is a successive change according to place or state. Or more briefly, it is the action of a mover upon the thing moved. <margin>Aristotle, *Physics*, Book 3.</margin> Whatever things exist in the nature of things, consisting of some motion in act or in potentiality, are clearly moved. For heavy and light things, although they are at rest in the place of their repose, are nevertheless at rest only according to a "more or less"; they are born to tend toward that point as long as they are away from their true point of standing still. And it is certain that those things in which life also exists receive their motion from a vital principle. It is clear that whatever is moved receives its motion from elsewhere. For otherwise, if anything moved itself, it would be partly at rest and partly moved; then the whole itself, of which a certain part is at rest, could not be moved by reason of itself, but only by reason of a part; and if that moving part were at rest, the whole would be at rest. But when the rest of one thing depends on the rest of another, motion must also follow from that. Therefore, nothing is moved by itself, but from elsewhere. Beings are moved simply by an aptitude proceeding from the First Mover, and animate beings by the soul...

<meta>This page continues the logical progression from the existence of the soul to the philosophical proofs for God's existence. Having established that the soul seeks a supreme truth, Postel now employs Aristotelian physics and metaphysics—specifically the "Argument from Motion" and the "Four Causes"—to demonstrate that a First Mover and an Intelligent Designer are necessary to explain the universe.</meta>

### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD ###

...of the soul from a certain supreme mind. For unless motions were halted in some constant, perpetually immovable thing, and from there made their beginning, it would be necessary for all things to proceed into infinity, from which many inconveniences <note>In Scholastic logic, an "inconvenience" refers to a logical absurdity or a conclusion that contradicts known principles.</note> would follow. For everything that is moved must be divisible. And every divisible thing is finite, and would be moved and would move in a finite time. Therefore those infinite moving and moved things would be moved in a finite time, just as each thing is in a certain time: which is impossible. Therefore there is a certain first mover, who is also God, whom the Greeks—because His act runs through all things from a constant principle in Himself and bestows motion—call *theos* <note>original: θεὸν</note>. For they name Him thus from *theein* <note>original: ἐκ τοῦ θὲειν τὰ πάντα θὲειν</note>, from "eternal running" <note>Postel is citing a common classical etymology, found in Plato’s *Cratylus*, linking the word for God (*theos*) to the verb "to run" (*theein*), suggesting God is the ever-active source of motion.</note>. That it is impossible for movers to proceed into infinity is also clear from this reason: for among them there would be no first mover. But where there is no first mover, there is no motion: therefore nothing would be moved. It is necessary therefore, since there is motion, that there be one first mover; therefore, God exists.

**4** A demonstration is also made from moved things in this way. That which is born to be moved in the manner of an instrument must be moved by a primary and principal cause. And that this happens mutually to some extent, until we reach something first: which is the first mover. For otherwise the first inconveniences would follow. Corruptible things act by the power of the heavens; the heavens by the power of the first impeller: who is God Himself.

**5** The work itself is an argument for the skill of the craftsman. For although the things themselves demonstrate the author and cause by some slight indication, nevertheless by a comparison of all effects we can easily judge which was more excellent. For he who has built a house perfect in every detail <note>original: *omnibus numeris*; a Latin idiom for "complete" or "perfect."</note> must certainly be judged greater than one who has erected huts, dug out caves, or constructed cottages. For he who performs what is greater is also permitted to carry out what is lesser: but not the reverse. Therefore, the greater and more constant the order seen in things, the more skilled the craftsman must be judged. And yet, nothing more ornate, or of greater or more constant order, can be found than the world. Therefore, the world has a most prudent and wise cause: God. But when I speak of order and constancy, and argue that all things act most orderly, there will immediately arise those who assert that fortune, chance, or rashness preside over human affairs in the place of fate. You might heal these people with all the more difficulty, as they will more hardly recognize their own disease and its cause. Nevertheless, although I know they are moved to these objections more by a disease of the mind than by any nature of things, and I am persuaded they are driven by a lust for contending and resisting rather than a love of truth, I must nonetheless strive to deal with their reasons in a few words: not so that they themselves (who wish to be so persuaded) may return to their senses, but so that their poison does not creep into more people, their words must be refuted. According to the opinion of the Peripatetics <term>Followers of Aristotle, known for walking while they taught</term>, the genus of causes is manifold. For some are proximate, some remote; some open, others hidden; some antecedent, others consequent. We must deal here primarily with these. For to deal with the universal genus of causes would be another work. In the whole number of causes, therefore, it is accepted that there are four, which no natural thing can lack. For nothing that falls under the senses can be its own cause. There is, therefore, a primary cause, which is called the **efficient** cause, in the first place. Since it is confessed that all things consist of some matter, we will place the **material** cause in the second place. The third will be that which takes its name from the **form** <note>The "formal cause," or the internal design/essence of a thing.</note>. Truly, it is certain that all things act for the sake of an **end** <note>The "final cause," or the purpose for which a thing exists.</note>. For all other things would be present in vain, unless all things were made for the sake of some use. For example: before houses are made, it is necessary that builders and architects exist who are not unskilled, who conceive the thing in their mind before it happens. If resources, stones, mortar, beams, and the rest are lacking, nothing is made. But the work itself can be distinguished from anything else and made fit for use: otherwise the rest are present in vain, unless for the sake of the end of some utility. The two middle causes <note>Material and Formal</note> are proximate and joined to the thing. The extreme ones <note>Efficient and Final</note> are separate, and proceed from the mind of the craftsman or master. From which place it necessarily follows that all things exist by the cause of the first author, and his...

<meta>This page transitions from the metaphysical proof of God as the First Mover to an explanation of Aristotelian causality and a defense of Providence against the concepts of luck and blind chance.</meta>

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I #

<margin><image-desc>manicule pointing left</image-desc></margin> ...of that to whom the thing belongs. For it is certain that those things which are made are made for the sake of the Author. There are indeed, not rarely, several antecedent causes before the artificial or efficient cause; but one is necessarily supreme, for the sake of which the end <note>The "final cause" or purpose in Aristotelian philosophy.</note> exists. Thus we see that those things which are subject to the senses consist of matter and form, such as the elements, which it is certain have already necessarily coalesced from some cause, and exist for the sake of those things which are composed from them. For from the elements all things subject to change are born, and to them they return. From these, life is composed: things destitute of sense tend toward the use of living things; living things toward the use of intelligent beings; intelligence itself necessarily toward its own use, happiness, and the honor of the First Cause. While the First Cause, being blessed and happy in itself and needing nothing, draws all things to itself, it then grants them happiness and their highest goal. For the goal of separate substances <note>term for angels or pure intellects who exist without physical bodies</note> is in the contemplation of the First Cause, just as it is for a house and other things in the use of their master. If, however, insensible things were capable of any happiness, they would then at last enjoy the greatest joy when placed in their highest end. In these causes, therefore, there is as yet no fortune, nor any rashness <note>blind chance or randomness</note>. The entire order of nature, therefore, is most especially free of them.

But in causes, antiquity placed fate, fortune, and chance. It certainly did, but in these one may see fate itself, which some called *heimarmene* <note>original: ειμαρμένην</note> and others *hermon* <note>original: ερμόν</note>; which is nothing other than that eternal and once-prescribed order of things of which we have spoken. Even if we do not see its causes, it is nonetheless no less in order despite our ignorance. For our knowledge relates to the truth of causes no differently than the eyes of an owl relate to the sun. For the things most known to nature are most obscure to us, and vice versa. It remains to speak of fortune and chance.

This indeed chance and fortune have in common: that they are properly said to happen in those things which are not according to will, and they produce an effect different from the goal of the agent acting from deliberation. Thus they happen rarely and by accident. But they differ in that chance comes from elsewhere, while fortune comes from the agent. For example: I go to the city; it happens by a chance falling of a brick <note>original: 'lateris', a tile or brick</note> that I am injured and pulled away from my goal; or that I fail myself through negligence. The first accident is from chance, the second from fortune. Therefore the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> rightly placed the location for this monster of "fortune" in the soul—that is, in opinion—and said it was a quality of a noble life, for it is not customary in the order of nature. 

But because it frequently happens in those things which depend on human choice, and stands before the eyes of those men who rarely or never weigh the first and certain cause: therefore they perpetually set this fortune before their eyes, even though it is very far away. Thus they do not hesitate to assert with the greatest impiety that the world is ruled by fortune. Kings meditate on kingdoms, wealth, victories, glory, vanity, and fame; they apply themselves to any arts whatsoever so that they might achieve what they desire; and as if their will and choice imposed laws upon things, they do not fear to immediately ascribe everything to fate, fortune, or chance, unless things succeed according to their lust. While they follow their own dreams, they make themselves unhappy by their own laws, and they resolve to overthrow Providence. Someone meditates and imagines for himself priesthoods, dignities, and rewards on account of his merits; in which, if he is surpassed by anyone, you immediately hear: "There is no God, fortune rules." Just as if the whole nature of things were changed because of the forestalled lust of a most wicked scoundrel, by that one injury, because no one sets a limit to desire. This is the reason why you hear nothing else from the impious: "All things depend on chance and fortune." Oh, unbearable blindness! 

And yet, among the "speakers" (for so the philosophers call men believing in Providence from faith), this authority is held. For in Solomon <note>Ecclesiastes 9:11</note>, a worshiper of the Old Testament, this opinion is held: "There is one chance for all" (some translate "event," others "occurrence"): therefore their opinion is not to be rejected. Let them weigh in that passage what the subject is, what follows, what precedes, what the context is: it will be clear that he does not ascribe all corruptible things to chance, but to fate and the laws of ending, from which neither wealth, nor strength, nor wisdom provide exemption. Therefore that passage does nothing for the impious, who, having itching ears, twist everything to their own opinion. Like that most wicked scoundrel Pietro Pomponazzi <note>An Italian philosopher (1462–1525) often accused of heresy for his Aristotelian arguments against the immortality of the soul.</note>, for the sake of a certain...

<meta>This page continues the author's philosophical inquiry, moving from the physical and causal proofs of the divine to the moral and ethical proofs based on the nature of "the Good" and human happiness.</meta>

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD #

...had twisted authorities from Aristotle, Galen, and Ibn Sina <note>original: "Aben reisso"; refers to the Persian philosopher Avicenna (Ibn Sina), known in the Islamic world as "al-Shaykh al-Ra’is" or "The Supreme Master."</note> to test mortal minds. Oh, what times we live in! But we must move on to the remaining matters.

**6** That **good** and **evil** exist in nature—the former as a state of being <note>or "habit," a translation of the Latin *habitus*</note>, the latter as a privation of good and an annihilation—no learned person calls into doubt. There is, however, so great a difference among goods (not indeed in their essence, but in their increase and decrease) that they are impossible to grasp unless you divide and weigh them by their types. They are usually partitioned into a three-fold difference: they look either to the **soul** and its happiness, to the **use of the body**, or partly to both. These latter are called external things, or things of **fortune**. For although external things contribute nothing to the perfection of souls, yet while the mind is led by false images of glory and ambition and obeys the body, it seeks its instruments from external things and, so to speak, "leans upon a reed" <note>A common biblical and classical metaphor for a fragile or deceptive support.</note>. Since goods of whatever kind differ by "the more and the less" (as the Greeks say), it is certain that there are middle, lowest, and highest goods. Regarding those things that provide support for the body and for reputation—which they call external goods and goods of fortune—no limit or measure has yet been found in them that could satisfy anyone's greed or lust for possession. This most clearly reveals our ignorance of the Cause from which these things proceed. Nevertheless, I do not speak of this for the reason that no one, while pursuing these things, can strive toward the cause of true goods. 

That scoundrel, the destroyer of Asia, and the scourge of God, **Alexander**, was driven by such a desire that when he had not yet conquered and despoiled a twentieth part of the world, he was already contemplating other worlds to be subjugated by him. From this most unjust example, we nevertheless learn that what is most excellent is that which is most unified in supreme power; and from this, if one first commands his own passions, he will be the more excellent the more people he commands and gives laws to. Furthermore, in the goods of the soul, we feel from the eternity of those things which we acquire through contemplation that there is necessarily something **supreme** in which the soul must find its rest. For nature would never have given those "little sparks" <note>The *igniculi* or "seeds of light," a Stoic and Neoplatonic concept of innate divine ideas in the human mind.</note> to everyone unless there were something by which they could be satisfied. This is as necessary to the intellect as food is to the body. Therefore, nature draws us toward both parts, enticed by the elements: partly so that the body itself—which nature gave to us destitute in all respects—should not be endangered; and partly so that the soul, striving toward the knowledge of the **true and supreme good**, might at least recognize that the supreme good exists through the privation of it. If, therefore, there is a good, and something greater than a good, and a truth, and something truer than a truth—lest we proceed into infinity (a concept nature abhors except in the First Cause)—it is certain that there is one **fountain of good**, where those perfections with which the soul and body are adorned are most absolute and entirely free of matter. **God**, therefore, is the apex of the entire good; for otherwise, there would be neither an end nor any perfection in the nature of things, which is a conclusion that defies common sense.

**7** Indeed, the consideration of **happiness** confirms the preceding argument. For while one person places happiness in the body—and the more of it he enjoys, the greater the pleasure he is drenched in (though he pursues a shadow and a falsehood)—it is certain that there is some most excellent happiness of all, than which no greater can be felt. He who places the supreme good in the **contemplation of truth** is certainly led by the same impulse; for the more he attains what he follows, the less he satisfies himself, and meanwhile he enjoys both greater pleasure and greater desire. This makes it manifest that there is something supreme to which we can aspire in spirit, though we cannot reach it in this life. The same can hardly happen to him who enjoys the pleasures of the body and places his happiness in them. For besides the fact that the pleasures of the body enervate and effeminate the powers of the soul and lead it away from the contemplation of truth, they bring this evil with them: they are prone to turn bitter with weariness, unless they are made desirable by rare use. And from this it is clear that it is most characteristic of the soul to **contemplate** and to **hunt for the truth**. For that reason, it is drawn more and more by it every day, after it has once tasted it vividly, striving meanwhile toward its goal, namely the supreme happi- <note>The text breaks here; the catchword is "tem," for *felicitatem* (happiness).</note>

<summary>Postel argues that the hierarchy of goods—from bodily needs to intellectual contemplation—proves the existence of a Supreme Good (God) as the ultimate "fountain" of perfection. He contrasts the fleeting, bitter nature of physical pleasure with the soul's endless, divine hunger for truth.</summary>

...and God the Blessed. Although the following arguments depend on the force and inference of those above, yet because the hinge of all things turns upon this argument—which is for us the basis of all others—I shall add this as well, for the sake of better confirming the truth.

**8** The world was made either by itself, by art, by chance, or by providence. It cannot be by itself, since nothing creates itself. It cannot be by art, because the material would have to be taken from something else (even if art were capable of it), and thus some part would always remain unformed. Chance can do nothing there, because it does nothing with order or constancy. Yet all things, whether they will it or not, are ordered and constant in their species and natures. Therefore, the world is said to be ruled by fate <note>The author is likely reconciling the classical concept of *fatum* (fate) with Christian Providence.</note>, because it necessarily obeys the command of providence and cannot depart from its genus or species. Therefore, God is the author of the world, creating all things by His fate—that is, His command—nourishing them, and allowing them to be consumed and perish.

**9** **From the consensus of all nations.** Whatever is naturally implanted in all members of the same species cannot be false or a vain persuasion. Yet there is no nation which, even if it ignores what kind of God it ought to have, does not feel that a God must be believed in. Therefore, that which is naturally persuaded to all to some extent is true. Therefore, God exists.

**10** Judgment and intellect are the test for recognizing the truth; he who excels more in these judges and asserts things more truly. Yet it is not only the common people—upon whom even a false persuasion might be imposed—who think there is a God, but the most excellent of the philosophers affirm it through demonstrations. Therefore, He exists.

**11** Authority and the venerable majesty of the laws prove this by the decrees of antiquity. To these, histories, which are narrated or written by the testimony of many good men, teach the same.

**12** Furthermore, daily experiments <note>In this context, *experimenta* refers to lived experience or empirical observation.</note> should not be rejected; otherwise, nothing would be established or sacred among us. Yet by laws, histories, and experiences, it is established that there are **separate substances** <term>separate substances: in Renaissance philosophy, these are non-material beings like angels or demons that exist independently of physical bodies</term>; even the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note> dare to affirm this. But if they exist, there is a certain supreme power that presides over the multitude. Therefore, God exists, under whom angels and demons exist, and before whom they tremble and obey. We must now place the "colophon" <note>The finishing touch or final crowning argument.</note> upon these demonstrations: an argument that is most certain and relies on sensory demonstration.

**13** Although all the preceding arguments are necessary, yet because they become known more by the force of the mind than by the faculty of these senses, they cannot easily persuade those who are reluctant and who only agree to those things that fall under the senses. However, unless readers are skilled in mathematics—that is, in the first principles of demonstration—they will not grasp these things either. It is established from self-evident principles that escape no one's senses that **two straight lines do not enclose a surface.** Therefore, before a surface is enclosed, it is necessary at minimum for three straight lines to meet for the formation of the first figure consisting of straight lines: which is therefore called a **triangle**. From a single line drawn into an orb, or in any way other than a straight line, figures arise; so too from two lines, but other than the circle, such a figure is not called "regular," because it lacks rules. It is manifest to those experienced in geometric demonstration that from such a triangle—whether it be equilateral <note>original: "isopleuro"</note> or isosceles—the **five regular bodies** <note>Also known as the Platonic Solids: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note> are produced. These bodies, which themselves fall under the senses, were compared by antiquity to the five elements due to a certain very similar property. Nor was there any reason for Aristotle—an unfair judge of another's labor—to condemn Pythagoras for ignorance regarding those dogmas, as if he meant the forms of the elements were exactly identical to the forms of these bodies. He was not so foolish as to want to ascribe that round form of the elements to an angular and polygonal shape; for he was most skilled in the nature of things for his century, while the truth was still hidden in Greece. Aristotle certainly ought to have credited himself instead for being unable to grasp these noble dogmas unless he refined them by picking them from elsewhere—which he himself shows in his "drum-shaped" <note>original: "τῠμπᾰνοειδῆ" (tympanoeides), referring to a flat, drum-like shape.</note> earth...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument for a divinely ordered universe by moving from logical proofs to the mathematical and physical structure of reality. He specifically draws on the classical theory of "Platonic Solids" to show how the building blocks of matter (the elements) correspond to perfect geometric forms.</meta>

-># ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

...demonstrates <note>original: "strat," the conclusion of "demonstrat"</note>, where he deals with the winds. Therefore, just as we perceive through our very senses four elements in matter that is inherently perishable—fire, earth, air, and water—so too is there a fifth, from which the nature of the heavens and the stars is composed. Indeed (as Aristotle, the very "god of philosophers" <note>Aristotle was so revered in the Renaissance that he was often called the "god of philosophers" or simply "The Philosopher."</note>, would have it), even the origin of souls is derived from this fifth element. Aside from these five bodies, nothing can be found in the nature of things that presents itself to the senses, except as a composition of them. Thus, whether he be a mathematician or anyone else—even if he were to cut through the entire globe, smoothing it by carving, or attempting a thousand times to forge all metals and meltable things into other regular shapes with consistent parts—he could still form nothing entirely regular except for those five regular bodies <note>These are the "Platonic Solids": the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note>. From this it is clear that there is a plain affinity of form between these first principles, just as there is an affinity of number.

For this reason, antiquity rightly compared these bodies produced from the triangle to the five elements. When I reflect on this, I certainly know that the human intellect is capable of much on its own; yet I cannot believe that whoever first passed these truths down to posterity received them as anything other than a divine gift. Otherwise, such a person would have had to exceed our normal lifespan at least tenfold, even while constantly thinking and shaping forms. This is proven by the fact that if you were to ask even the most skilled craftsman to produce a single unique version of these mixed bases, he could not even complete the trial of one within ten whole years—which is evident in experiments. For many craftsmen have dared to attempt this, but after trying for a very long time, they finally came to their senses and acknowledged both the truth and their own rashness.

Now, we must very carefully weigh how well these shapes correspond to the nature of things. Just as the triangle is the smallest of all regular surfaces, so the smallest of all regular bodies is the **tetrahedron**—that is, a shape of four bases rising from equilateral triangles <note>original: "isopleuris," meaning equal-sided.</note>. There is no way you can admit any other surface into it. For if you add a square to the triangles, it will become a pentahedron (five-sided); if you add a pentagon, it becomes a heptahedron (seven-sided); if you add two squares, a third must necessarily be added along with two triangles to make a pentahedron. Thus, a smaller regular body cannot be given. For that reason, the ancients compared it to **fire**, which is the thinnest among the elements; unless there is matter in which it is fed or kept, it escapes the senses. However, when fire acts upon matter, the flames represent the pyramid of a tetrahedron quite well, as they stretch from a wider base to a sharp point.

But the primary consideration must be given to the bases. Because **earth** itself shares the quality of "dryness" with fire, they placed its symbol in the second spot: the **hexahedron** <note>original: "ἑξάεδρον"</note>. This is the most stable of all figures and serves as a base, just like a cube or a die <note>original: "tesserá"</note> having six sides; whichever side it falls on, it stands unmoved. Gamblers know this best. Furthermore, there is no doubt that a square consists of two opposing isosceles or equal-legged triangles. Therefore, the most stable shape is suited to earth, the base of all elements—not for the sake of the shape itself, but for its properties.

The **octahedron** is compared to **air** because it is far more prone to motion than earth, yet far duller in its action of heat than fire itself. Finally, they represented **water** with the **icosahedron** <note>original: "εἰκοσάεδρον"</note>, because it is well-suited for motion but has a very dull action. For although water is the source of moisture, air is actually much "moister" in its power. Unless water is moved or dissolved by the force of air and fire, it has no action at all; thus, water is more easily confined to a place. Air itself penetrates all things and dampens even stones and metals, which is evident in "sweating" and the contraction of things; for drops flow from solid and polished bodies. After great cold, when the moisture is released by the force of heat, stones and bronze columns often "sweat"—not because of water, which could not be admitted into solid bodies, but because of air, which by its thinness mixed itself into the bodies and then returned to a liquid state. This agrees with the three higher elements, in that the figures assigned to them rise immediately from triangles...

<summary>Postel explains the geometric foundations of the universe, linking the four elements (plus the quintessence) to the five Platonic solids, arguing that such perfect mathematical order proves divine revelation.</summary>
