<meta>This page continues the discussion of the five Platonic solids and their relationship to the elements and the heavens. The catchword "phiæ" on the previous page refers to "philosophiæ," which appears at the very end of this page's text.</meta>

# BOOK I BY GUILLAUME POSTEL <note>original: "G V L. POSTELLI LIB. I."</note>

...because of the greater speed of action and passion, with the earth mediating. For a square consists of two opposite isosceles triangles, as has been said; the earth, however, consists of six squares <note>In Platonic cosmology, the cube (six squares) represents the Element of Earth.</note>. But just as there are only five regular bodies by hypothesis, it is not permitted to progress beyond the pentagon for their formation. Thus, from twelve pentagons, a body with twelve bases is composed, which they call the **dodecahedron**, and they fit it to the heavens for this reason: just as the circumference of the heavens consists of 360 degrees, so the body consisting of twelve pentagons yields the same number. Indeed, each individual pentagon is made of five triangles, each of which in turn consists of six scalene triangles; this number, when multiplied by itself, produces the 360 degrees of the greatest circle. Therefore, I believe it happened that this number of degrees—though discovered by the **Chaldeans** <note>Ancient Babylonian astronomers and mathematicians</note> and by divine men (whoever they were) rather than human ones—has held its place throughout the entire world. For although the calculation of years has varied, it was necessary to preserve the year based on that number of degrees.

Now, therefore, it has been seen that the four elements and the **entelechy** <term>The "realization" or vital principle that makes a thing what it is; here used for the fifth element or soul.</term> correspond entirely with the five regular bodies. There remains a figure easily the prince of all in capacity, form, and motion, embracing all those others within itself. Even if it is not seen by the eyes, nevertheless, because it exists in the nature of things beyond those others, it also necessarily has its own archetype and image, with which it must agree in many things, if not in all, and which is God himself, corresponding to the **circle** as much as possible through all things. For the circle is born to be moved upward and downward at once; it proceeds forward and backward in a single action, and it encompasses whatever exists in other things and forms within a single opposition (such as motion and rest, and to speak once for all, everything) which consist of presence and not of privation. Everywhere it has a beginning, a middle, and an end; yet it has no beginning, middle, or end. Nothing can be added to or taken away from it without corruption, as is the case with other forms.

But it differs most from the other regular bodies in that their size can be grasped by a certain measure, and they can be reduced to the **squaring** <term>The "squaring of the circle" (quadratura circuli) is the ancient mathematical challenge of constructing a square with the same area as a given circle. Postel sees this as a boundary between human math and divine infinity.</term> by which all things can be measured. The squaring of the circle, however, will be perpetually knowable only in potential, nor can it be precisely measured by anyone. Thus the elements themselves and the celestial orbs have come within the grasp of counting, except for the line from the center; but no thought will ever be able to grasp the measure of the immense God, since there is no proportion between the finite and the infinite. Therefore, all other things can be called imperfect because, while their name remains the same, something can be added to or taken away from them. You can take nothing away from a circle, nor add to it, without destroying it.

Therefore, that first circle is most especially in accordance with unity—perfect, and least subject to matter. Even **Averroes** <note>original: "Aben reis," referring to the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd.</note>, the greatest seeker of truth according to the intellect, says that the substance of the orb has neither matter nor form; how true that may be, let him see. For concerning those things which we know through privation, such as all celestial things and the First Cause, we can assert nothing except from their effects. Certainly, Averroes would have been by far the most excellent of mortals if he had been willing to spend as much effort in proving the First Cause and the persuasion of God received throughout the world as he labored to uproot it from the minds of men. The cause of this was the most absurd persuasion regarding God left in writing by **Mohammed** (as will be clear in its proper place). Having been imbued with this from boyhood and diligently instructed in it—as is fitting for a leading man, such as he was—when he came to the knowledge of the truth, he did so not through the prescriptions of a foolish and wicked law, but by the guidance of reason. He burned with such a fire against that foolishness and imposture that he did not only take up arms against the religion under which he had long been a wretched captive and buried in the darkness of ignorance, but he attempted to overturn them all. He tried to thrust upon the world a certain fate and a most impotent God—that is, one destitute of the freedom of choice—for this one reason: because he saw many people approving the tenets of that persuasion, and especially a certain **Al-Ghazali** <note>original: "Gezelem." A Persian theologian who famously attacked philosophy; Averroes wrote his "Incoherence of the Incoherence" as a rebuttal to him.</note> who wrote against philosophy...

He critiques Averroes for allowing his hatred of Mohammed’s "absurd" theology to drive him toward a philosophy that denies God's free will.</summary>

tenets of **philosophy** <note>original: "philosophiæ"</note> to rise up, and it is absurd to try to persuade the world of a false persuasion regarding God. By these wretched opinions of men—who seek their own emotions rather than the truth—the world has been undermined, and truth has been taken from our eyes. Therefore, that God is God, blessed above all, whose image we see in the **sixth body** <note>In geometry, the sphere is the "sixth" figure that can perfectly enclose the five Platonic solids mentioned on the previous page.</note> which encompasses the other five, touching each one at its angles and covering them, or touching the middle lines of them all (if they could be made four times more powerful and larger); He is as distant from matter as light is from darkness. But I am the more fortunate because, through this ignorance, I shall continue to seek you at least until death and the end of this life's work. This is not unlike a **sculptor**, who achieves the form he conceived in his mind by removing everything in the stone, wood, or whatever material that is *not* what he seeks, and finally, at the end of his labor, he finds what he was looking for—the image itself. In the same way, one must strive with all his might until the end of human life, so that we may more ardently pursue that which we know most certainly exists from its effects, the less we are able to grasp it.

### ON THE QUALITIES OF GOD. CHAPTER II.

Before we come to the reasoning regarding the **Holy Trinity**, we must briefly provide a "shadowy" description of that Good which we have demonstrated in the preceding arguments to exist in the nature of things, so that it may be known as the apex, the end, and the beginning of all things. Since God is the beginning of all things and their end—as has been clear and will necessarily be made clear—His "being" and His "essence" are the same. For He is never in a state of **potentiality** <term>The capacity to become something else; Postel argues God is already "complete."</term>, but is a perennial **act** <term>Pure actuality or existence without any unfulfilled potential.</term>. Whatever instruments of virtue, justice, and any kind of goodness have been given to man, however many are sweetly received by human senses, and whatever allurements nature has offered to both body and soul, it is right that all these have their origin in Him. This is not as "feelings," "changes," or "passions" as they usually exist in bodies, but as the simplest dispositions, so innate to Him that despite that most simple nature, He has nothing outside Himself; rather, they are so "born-with" Him that they cannot exist separately. For otherwise, nothing here would be just, laudable, honorable, or good (even though these are qualities added to the soul), unless the root proceeded from Him—a root, however, that is itself devoid of "quality." In the same way, all motion would necessarily be in danger if that **Unmoved Mover** <term>An Aristotelian concept of God as the primary cause of all motion who does not Himself move.</term>, remaining unmoved in Himself, did not provide the beginning through an eternal act. And although He wills nothing else outside Himself, and cannot act contrary to how He acts (since nothing can be the cause of His will), He nevertheless must not be considered to lack **free will**. Indeed, since the freedom of the will is its own cause, it belongs to no one more than the First Cause, who does all things for His own sake—just as it is believed to be in "separate substances" <note>Angelic or purely spiritual beings.</note>. For instance, if there were a most just man who had never sinned and could not sin because of his inborn justice, we would still not believe him to be deprived of free will. Truly, no human comparison can be fashioned for God Himself from this lowest, elementary dross. For what can corruption have in common with immortality? In God, to **have** and to **be had** are the same; in Him, **acting** and **suffering** are equal (if indeed He were able to suffer). For we are permitted, due to our senses' incapacity, to use words known to us, even though in truth His "being" can never be expressed except through a certain riddle.

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.

...rightly <note>original: "rito," completing "merito" from the previous page</note> asserted our Paul, who indeed could never express what he had seen in his rapture, yet it was very far from the highest state of bliss. For this reason, the philosophers undeservedly attack us, as if we wished to attribute qualities and various actions and changes to the simplest goodness—they are surely poor judges of the condition of human affairs. I would ask them: what are the principles of all our knowledge—specifically that which does not depend on nature or the constitution of the species, but proceeds from learning? Is it not because of the weakness of our intellect that men need to reveal everything to one another through words, even in the easiest and most common matters? We are so ignorant of all things that unless a word is added, or reading in place of a word, we grasp nothing. Otherwise, the disciplines themselves, which are most perfect in the mind of the teacher, cannot pass into us except through some object of both the thing itself and the word. How much less—although there things are not seen in the same way as actions are seen here—can we, by the nature of our minds which judge everything by the senses and the magnitude of the matter, conceive so high a thought.

Therefore, when dealing with divine matters, we use words after the human manner, intervals of time, circumstances of things, and other means by which our senses can be moved, so that finally, by the argument of those things, we may come to a more sublime thought, which can only be reached by the mind and which itself cannot be explained in words. Nor are we **anthropomorphists** <note>Those who believe God has a human physical form.</note>, nor do we place any passions or new actions in God, since we know that all things depend upon and are established by eternal disposition. Therefore, when we use present words, it is because we cannot otherwise express and explain the notion of God. For even the greatest feeling, however much it explains itself and satisfies itself in many ways, remains unknown unless it brings itself forth by a word; and in these lower matters, even the most skilled know many things which they cannot explain at all. Let the most skilled philosopher give me a description of those men, or animals, or any matters, even the most familiar, which he knows; he certainly cannot reveal them except by words borrowed **metaphorically** <note>original: "μεταφορικῶς"</note> from elsewhere.

So it is with the knowledge of divine things that we have, whether from sacred scripture or conceived divinely: we can neither deliver it in words nor write it down, except in words accommodated to our sense and the use of things. For this reason, divine providence, pitying our errors, whenever it wished to open something of itself to this mortality (since inspiration itself is unreliable and akin to dreams unless you show it to be in you by miracles and unusual deeds), it manifested itself through the work of separate substances <note>A common philosophical term for angels or purely intellectual beings.</note>, even using voices uttered in the human manner, assuming a certain body very similar either to us or to some most innocent animal. And it willed that its angels should associate more familiarly with men, and most often opened those secrets concerning divine and human matters which could have been grasped or understood by no human wit. 

Hence, if anyone denies that those **Magi** <note>Ancient wise men or priests, often associated with the East.</note> and **Indians** <note>Referring to the gymnosophists or sages of India, often cited in Renaissance literature as possessors of ancient wisdom.</note> were in the greatest familiarity with marvelous bodies, he will reject the consensus of all men and cast off reason. But it happens to certain philosophers, and especially to **Averroes** <note>original: "Aben reisso," the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> himself, to **Galen** <note>The famous Greek physician whose works dominated medieval medicine.</note>, and sometimes to **Aristotle**, that they denied the existence in nature of things they themselves could not grasp in their minds, as if they knew everything. As if there were not far more things in our ignorance than in our knowledge—which we gather from perils. Let us run through all kinds of disciplines. What is not born of **induction** <note>original: "epagoge," the process of reasoning from specific instances to a general law.</note> or **paradigm** <note>original: "paradigmate," an example or pattern used for reasoning.</note>? From where were the first conclusions held, if not from experiences gradually converging into the same kind? Who doubts that the ages always progress? Shall we deny that nature has also left things for us to prove ourselves? There are indeed, there are far more things unknown than known. To this, that knowledge which we have of things is so blind, crippled, and mangled—except for certain common principles—that it is not the things themselves, but their...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument regarding the limitations of human reason. The previous page ended with the suggestion that divine truths cannot be fully explained by human language. This page picks up with the necessity of accepting certain truths on authority or faith before they can be fully understood, using scientific and historical examples as a parallel for religious belief.</meta>

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
## GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.

...we may know the surface; and far more things must be held from the opinions of authors than from logical demonstration. For otherwise, unless we first believed through things unknown and undemonstrated, there would undoubtedly be no place for science. Who would be willing to receive a student to be trained in the disciplines if, as long as he is not yet capable of understanding demonstrations, he would not agree to the axioms of his teacher? Who would immediately revoke his trust in a matter he received from his instructors for the sole reason that he does not yet grasp its underlying causes? Believe me, unless we attributed more to the consensus and judgment of men—and especially of experts—than to our own capacity, we would indeed withhold our agreement from almost all things. How many people are actually able to grasp the difficult demonstrations of Ptolemy’s *Great Construction* <note>original: "Magnæ constructionis Ptolemæi," referring to the *Almagest*, the definitive text on astronomy in the 16th century</note>? Almost no one, or very few. Yet there is no lover of truth so impudent that he would deny the earth is twenty-seven times the size of the moon, or that the sun exceeds the globe of earth and water by 166 times <note>These figures represent the standard scientific consensus of the era, prior to the widespread use of the telescope</note>. You might say the same of mathematics and numbers; it is clear that we ought not to deny that things exist simply because we are ignorant or incapable of understanding them, provided they are not contrary to the reason of the Creator. Therefore, philosophers ought to restrain their impudence and their lust for contradiction. If they would give credit to histories received by the judgment of all mortals, or at least by the consensus of the most outstanding men, and to the visible effects of things, they would follow us—we who have set before ourselves a goal far more certain than their own opinions.

But the lust for doubting, for overturning the ideas of others, and for substituting their own, has led them to such a state of unhappiness and madness that they have determined that the most laborious pursuits in nature are ultimately fruitless. They have suggested that labor should be undertaken for its own sake—meaning for the sake of hardships, thirst, hunger, and sleepless nights—while seeking nothing beyond the "hunting of a little glory" <note>original: "gloriolæ aucupium"</note>. They claim that virtue, science, and whatever things are most noble in human life are their own reward. It is no wonder, then, that the world has been weakened by so many sluggish men. For those who hear only the dogmas of such philosophers judge in this way: "For what purpose should I lead a life of such great hardship for the sake of virtue itself? Is it not just for a little glory, which cannot help the dead? Shall I live in perpetual care, labor, and misery for the sake of mere smoke?" It would be better, they think, to live as a dog or a horse and be held by no laws of conduct than to be always tortured for such an empty price and be utterly deprived of happiness. By this argument, we can conclude that these philosophers have been driven into a degenerate state of mind and toward destruction.

For although they knew that all things are done for the sake of a goal greater than the work itself, they "ran aground in the harbor" <note>A classical idiom meaning to fail just as success is in sight</note>. While they asserted that even the lowliest matters have their own meaningful ends, they established nothing but misery for the most excellent things in human life. They hunted for fame, but found only smoke. Therefore, no reward in this life is worthy of a thing as excellent as virtue itself. To those endowed with virtue is owed immortality and the unfading peak of the most excellent state: namely, the contemplation and society of God. This is because they desired most greatly to be like the Divinity through their kindness toward all men, piety toward God, and personal innocence.

Because the philosophers did not weigh these truths, their "hunting for fame" incited tyrants and desperate men to seek renown through "Herostratic crimes" <note>original: "facinoribus Herostraticis," referring to Herostratus, who burned the Temple of Artemis solely to ensure his name would be remembered</note>, striving to create a long-lasting memory of themselves. Meanwhile, wretched humanity fails to notice that fame left without any use for utility, honor, or justice—as soon as people are free to judge and speak without the presence of the tyrant—becomes infamy. Posterity recognizes that those mortals were so busy obeying a "great man" that they failed in all other things; they see public or private money squandered and scraped together from everywhere, spent rightly or wrongly for one single purpose: so that there might appear a building more fit for crows to inhabit than men, or some other such useless work. This is what we owe to the "distinguished" judgments of the philosophers. Therefore, a thing is not immediately false just because they refute it, nor is everything they assert necessarily true.

<summary>Postel argues that faith and the acceptance of expert authority are necessary for knowledge, comparing religious belief to the acceptance of complex astronomy. He critiques secular philosophers who view virtue as its own reward, arguing that without the hope of immortality and God, such a view leads to nihilism, vanity, and the "Herostratic" pursuit of empty fame.</summary>
<keywords>epistemology, Ptolemy, Almagest, virtue, immortality, Herostratus, fame vs. infamy, Guillaume Postel, 16th-century philosophy</keywords>

-># ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-
->## GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.<-

...stand, because a good part of them were expected to move toward repentance, even unto death; for this reason, they denied that there is a God, who would spare their impiety for so long. It is permitted for us, therefore, using words plucked from this mortality, to explain things about God that we otherwise cannot, and to describe matters as best as we are allowed, even if philosophers contend that such descriptions are inconsistent with the actual use of those terms. If we then proceed to speak of the qualities of God, we shall find these specific traits in him: power, wisdom, love, charity, and kindness, so that God himself has obtained the names of "Goodness," "Charity," and "Love" among the most learned writers. 

But let that divine Plato, the god of philosophers, come forward among the first. Although Aristotle—showing little gratitude toward his teacher—wished to oppose him in many things, he nevertheless judged that these opinions of Plato regarding God were most true and not to be trifled with. I say this regarding that most self-loving man <note>original: "φιλαυτοτάτῳ" (*philautotatō*), meaning extremely conceited or devoted to oneself</note> <note>Postel is here criticizing Aristotle for his perceived arrogance in diverging from his teacher, Plato</note>: because whatever he could pluck from his teacher, he ascribed to himself while suppressing Plato's name; yet those things which seemed open to doubt, he refuted while naming his source. Other things he seemed to approve through silence and by subscribing to them. Now, Socrates speaks of God in this way, in the *Theaetetus*:

> But it is entirely impossible for evils to be driven out from this world, O Theodorus. For there must always be something opposing the good, which it is not proper to attribute to God. Indeed, evil necessarily haunts this mortal nature and this lowest of places. Therefore, we must strive to flee from here as quickly as possible. But this flight is not to be understood as a change of location, but as an approach to God and the greatest possible likeness to him. Moreover, that likeness is possessed when one joins justice and innocence with prudence.

And a little later:

> In truth, we say this: God is never in any way unjust, but is as just as can possibly be; nor is anything more like him than when one of us becomes as just as possible.

That most excellent man <note>Socrates</note> attributes justice to God, and does not think he is adding a conflicting quality. Indeed, he calls God "the Good" frequently and in many places. In his book *The Republic*, he asserts that God is not only good, but the most excellent. In the *Timaeus*, he says that God created this world because of his goodness, which no good person begrudges to another. In the *Protagoras*, he says God is perfectly good—a quality with which no one can be gifted for long in this life. Furthermore, in both the *Theaetetus* and the second book of *The Republic*, he so strongly argues for God’s goodness that God cannot even be the author of evil. Therefore, he judges that Homer and the other poets should be expelled from his Republic, because by writing recklessly about God, they make him the author not only of misfortunes, but even of crimes. 

It is necessary, moreover, that love exists in God because he is the highest goodness. But that impious Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the *Natural History*</note> claimed that charity was the highest good; while he denies that God exists in nature (except as something immersed in matter), he affirms that God exists in human action.

> God is (he says) for a mortal, to help a mortal, and this is the path to eternal glory; this is the path the Roman nobles walked, etc.

He has surely mistaken the path, which is the journey toward God, for God himself—as if one were to substitute thirst for a drink, hunger for food, a house for a dwelling, or rest for labor. Nevertheless, he touched closely upon the nature of divinity. For charity consists in helping one's neighbor, as a brother born of the same father, God; not so much for the brother's sake as for the love of the father, and as a testimony of being a legitimate heir and companion. Furthermore, what he added—that this is the path to eternal glory—is agreeable. But as for what follows—"This is the path the Roman nobles walked"—if he were alive today, he would see how falsely he spoke. Those plagues of the whole world, tyrants driven by unquenchable greed, blood, the overturning of cities, the devastation of provinces, and the oppression and slaughter of men (for whose sake nature had created all other things), by ranging through and depopulating the entire world, they achieved a kind of immortality: they became more famous for the memory of their crimes than for their virtue (of which there was none or very little in them), and they have almost vanished from the positive memory of men. Instead, they gathered and carried to Rome the spoils of the entire world, the eternal seeds of civil discord, and an eternal mark of injustice from the plundered peoples. That is indeed a remarkable and distinguished "immortality"...

### ON THE MOST HOLY TRINITY AND THE TRI-
### une God. CHAPTER III.

This labor is undertaken chiefly for your sake, O Muhammadans <note>Muslims</note>, who have fallen away from God. For those who are led by the omnipotence of God from false and absurd persuasions into the true one far more easily receive all things usually said about Him; and the more difficult those things are, the more ardently they embrace them, seeking no reason for them. Even if reasons were demonstrated to such people, they could hardly grasp the logic. But you, who believe that you possess everything that must be believed because of your worship of one God, admit those things which are true with greater difficulty. But because I have learned—both from conversation with you and from books and the talk of many—that you greatly desire to understand those supreme mysteries of the Trinity, I wish these writings to be intended first for you, O leading men in your religion, and finally for the other nations of the world who are estranged from the truth. 

Pay attention, therefore, diligently. It has been sufficiently demonstrated above with necessary arguments that God is the one judge and moderator of this world. In Him, although there are no "qualities" <note>In medieval philosophy, God is considered "simple," meaning He is not made of parts or accidental qualities, but is His own essence</note>, nevertheless whatever is rightly held as a "good" is found most amply and perfectly as if in its own source. I now proceed to demonstrate in the following pages that He is one and three—containing the Trinity in unity and vice versa—and that the mind cannot in any way conceive an image of Him without the Trinity.

### THE FIRST DEMONSTRATION OF THE TRINITY.

<margin>These three properties of the divine nature are Power, Wisdom, and Love (or charity).</margin>
1 Since God is both the author and cause of all nature, He must be most powerful. For otherwise, nothing could have been made by His will. Yet, even if He were most powerful, if He lacked Wisdom—by which He might know, arrange, prepare, and preserve all things before they exist—then any amount of power would be of no use. Furthermore, although He were most powerful and most wise, as one who could do and know all things, yet unless Will and Love were present in Him toward the things themselves, so that He might create them for the sake of a certain end, neither power nor wisdom would accomplish anything. It was necessary, therefore, before anything...

<meta>This page continues the "First Demonstration" of the Trinity, following the previous page's introduction of God as the author of all things possessing Power, Wisdom, and Love.</meta>

GUILLAUME POSTEL'S BOOK I.

<margin>
Goodness is understood in three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. These are distinguished in this way: the Father generates, the Son is born (generated), and the Holy Spirit proceeds from both.
</margin>

...was led into being by God, that there was in Him power, wisdom, and love. Since, however, power is first in order—though not in time—it is ascribed to God the Father. Wisdom, because it proceeds from the highest power, is called the Son, a metaphor <note>original: "metaphora"</note> drawn from natural birth. But because benevolence or love proceeds from wisdom and power, it is called by the name of the Holy Spirit. These are not three gods, but one God. In power, the whole deity exists; in wisdom, likewise; similarly, in love, charity, and benevolence, the whole of God is present.

Just as when I think about something to be done, I revolve the whole matter in my mind before I begin; I also express the whole of it in a word, and I execute—or care for the execution of—the whole in the thing itself. And yet, these are not three separate things, but a single one, weighed by different reasons. Thus God is one: Father and Son (so called by analogy) and Holy Spirit; power, wisdom, love; His mind, the Word <note>referring to the "Logos," a term for the Son/Christ as the expression of God's mind</note> (also by analogy), and the Spirit; the whole divinity in each, and the whole is only one in all of them together.

### THE SECOND DEMONSTRATION.

2. The divine mind or intellect, as we have already taught, is most powerful. Indeed, the mind holds and creates the images and ideas of all things most perfectly within itself—which is also evident in this weak intellect of ours, for we conceive the likenesses of all sensible things. Since, therefore, the intellect of God is most powerful and infinite, and incomprehensible except to Himself, He also reflects the knowledge of Himself back into Himself, and sees it. There then arises in Him a "thinking intellect" and a "thought intellect," the latter being generated by the former. 

For there would be no happiness in God if He possessed ignorance of Himself within Himself. Since, therefore, that thinking intellect and the thought (or generated) intellect know each other mutually, this cannot happen without great delight, love, and glory. Thus one and the same God and "Mind of the World" is the intellect understanding itself, the intellect known by itself, and the love or delight proceeding from the knowledge of itself. Nor could He know Himself—in whom all things exist most perfectly as if in a mind and a stable essence—without that same great love and the eagerness of His knowledge overflowing into Him. 

Indeed, the whole divinity is in the thinking mind, the whole in the understood mind, and the whole in that love and glory. Therefore, the Platonists <note>Followers of the philosopher Plato</note> held, not without merit, that the "ideas" <note>The eternal, perfect forms or patterns of all things</note> of all species exist in the divine mind as if in their own proper subject. For nothing can exist in the nature of things unless it was in the divine mind when it was produced. Nor, in my judgment, can anything subsist unless it is preserved by that same force, just as in a living body there is no movement according to nature that does not proceed from the force of the soul; and if that soul had enough perfection, it would even know those things which are done in the body by its impulse. 

Just as, therefore, if I write anything to be brought forth, I think, speak, and write by one and the same action, yet I perform a single, very simple action: so God, knowing and thinking Himself from eternity, generates from Himself a Son proceeding from Him from eternity, and from both there also comes forth, by one and the same action, love—all of which are one Deity and three <term>hypostases</term> <note>A theological term for the three distinct persons of the one Divine Essence</note>.

### THE THIRD [DEMONSTRATION].

3. No one can deny that Providence also contains within itself a most perfect love, unless they deny that Reason itself exists within it. For God (as Plato says), since He is good, wills His benefit to be open most widely to all, because He loves all things. For we have said above that He loves all things in Himself. Hence that saying of Aristotle <note>The famous Greek philosopher</note>, approved by all nations: "The more common a good is, the more divine it is." It is certain, therefore, that this world is held together by love, and is dissolved by strife and hatred, as Empedocles <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who taught that Love and Strife were the two forces moving the universe</note> rightly says in his *Physics*. Therefore, the nature of love must be more diligently examined. In love or charity—which is God and the bond of all things—there must be a lover, a beloved, and the love itself; otherwise, it cannot even be called love in lower things. Therefore, God exists, by whose love all things that exist are sustained...

<summary>Postel argues for the reality of the Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) using philosophical analogies of human thought, speech, and action. -> ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD <-

...love most loving. Since indeed He loves all things most greatly in Himself (for in Him is life consisting of His love), He does so with the greatest unity of love. For as He is most perfect, so He unites most perfectly. Furthermore, since He is the highest love, within Him is the very equality of love (for otherwise He would love nothing, unless the equality of love represented itself to Him from within Himself) responding to the lover, so that there is in Him the lover and the beloved, from whom proceeds their common love. The loving friendship stands in the place of God the Father; the friendship by which all things flourish is the Son; and the love proceeding from the lover and the beloved is called the Holy Spirit. The whole of friendship is in the lover, the whole in the beloved or lovable one, and the whole is in the love; and yet there are not three friendships, but one friendship. For while God knows Himself in Himself, He loves Himself in the knowledge of Himself with a most uniting love (just as one who sees himself in a mirror loves himself most greatly, because he especially delights in his own form) and generates a beloved love, whom we call the Son of God. From these two proceeds the bond <note>original: "nexus"</note>, and these three things are one. 

It is just as water is one and the same—differing only by what comes before and what comes after—which runs from a source through a river into a pool. For from the source proceeds the channel, and from the source and the channel comes the pool. And to demonstrate this with a clearer example: a fountain returning the waters to itself and sending them out can be compared to God. Let the water spring up in one place and form a pool; finally, let it be soaked up again into the veins of the earth. It is one and the same water springing up, pooling, and receding, in which there is no "before" or "after." For it is one single thing that does this, if we observe carefully. We do almost nothing in which a single will, action, and "passion" <note>In this context, "passion" refers to the experience of receiving an action, the counterpart to "action."</note> do not run together. For example, if I strike a man with <unclear>one</unclear> act, my will, the blow, and his suffering of it run together as one. Human love also imitates the divine. For one cannot be loved unless there is a lover, a beloved, and a love proceeding from both; more on this later.

## THE FOURTH [DEMONSTRATION]

There is no one who doubts that there is multitude and number in the things of the universe. And yet, before all number and multitude, it is necessary that a most simple unity precedes them. For if that were taken away, number could not arise. Therefore, God is the most holy and primordial Unity. Among created things that differ in number, there is necessarily a certain inequality. For otherwise, all things would be one and the same. Furthermore, nothing is so similar to another, even under some specific appearance, that it does not differ in some way. Therefore, since there is difference and inequality among individual things, before the creation of all things there was Equality. For one cannot recognize inequality in a thing or in the mind unless one first knows the Equality by which to judge the unequal. Therefore, even before all things, there is Equality, which is also the one God, equal to Himself.

All things, insofar as they represent themselves to the perception of the senses, are separate. For no clear notion can be held regarding things that are confused. But before all separation, there precedes a bond <note>original: "nexus"</note> by which things are what they are. By nature, conjunction precedes separation, nor can one exist in the senses without the other. Therefore, that eternal bond is called God. Thus, although He is the most simple "One," He nevertheless also holds equality and connection within Himself. There is likeness and connection in unity; in the connection, there is equality and unity; and in equality—by which things are neither less nor greater—there are species and forms, and there is also connection and unity. These are three in one, and one in three, existing as one, neither confused nor separated.

## THE FIFTH [DEMONSTRATION]

Individual things—whether made by nature (that is, by God) or by art—usually testify to their author (as is commonly said) and bear his traces. Hence, the skill or lack of skill of craftsmen is usually discerned from their works. Since, therefore, all natural things are produced by God as the First Cause through the way of nature and craftsmanship, nature testifies to its author in this: that just as He is one, and yet possesses a trinity in persons such that He cannot be without it, so also individual natural compounds have His image so closely bound within them...

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.

...image, so that it cannot perish from it without the things themselves perishing. Just as, therefore, from the eternal power of God proceeds His eternal wisdom, and from both of these, benevolence and love toward Himself and created things; so also in individual things there is a fruitfulness or power of acting according to their nature, from which comes an inexhaustible progression of their action and virtue. This progression, through a love of acting, never ceases from its nature and, as it were, makes a selection <note>original: "delectum," implying a natural inclination or choice in where it acts</note> in its activity. 

For example: as long as pepper is pepper, it possesses an inexhaustible power of acting—that is, of heating or burning—from which proceeds that scorching or action, naturally loving to act. For as long as it is pepper, it can burn the tongue if it is rubbed; nor does that force ever fail it as long as it exists, but it moves forward and acts in its own way from the moment it begins, as if making a choice. For it acts upon sweaty skin rather than upon skin with closed pores, and upon flayed skin rather than whole skin, and upon the tongue suited for tasting rather than upon other parts of the body. 

Likewise, fire, no matter how small the quantity, has a tireless power, from which flows an unceasing progression of heating and burning, having its own selection and delight in acting. Thus, in the smallest spark there is such force that it could burn forests and the whole world; and it makes its choice with such delight and love of acting that it prefers straw and thin, dry bodies over wet and thick ones, choosing in such an order that it is never deceived. 

So it is in us: the vital, natural, and animal faculties act upon those things which are added to or taken from the body, such that nothing more powerful, nothing more fruitful and abundant, and nothing more prudent could seem possible. Thus are trees nourished, thus are animals preserved—the natures of all things exist with that holy Trinity giving life to all, so that when that force and image has perished in them, they are no more. The entire force of things is in power, the whole is in progression, and the whole is in choice and love; and yet they are not three things, but one, just as power, wisdom, and love are only one God.

### DEMONSTRATION FROM CREATED THINGS, 
-> and firstly from spirits and souls. <-

I see that no one doubts that man consists of body and soul. Let us speak first of his most excellent part; so that since it is especially one and simple—fleeing the senses of the body and accessible only through its effects—we may nevertheless see the image of God within it. The Soul, as it is called by a general term, is one, yet consists of three parts and properties: the vital life, the sensitive life, and the discerning life <note>original: "discretiva"</note>. Although some maintain that there is a soul in plants, having the faculties of attraction, retention, and expulsion. 

The life of brute animals consists of life, sense, and choice. The first acts while the second and third are at rest; from the first proceeds the second, and the third from both. When I grant "choice" to the brutes, I do not mean <term>free will</term> <note>original: "liberum arbitrium"</note> or intellect, but the knowledge of fleeing and seeking: without which faculty they could not prolong their life nor provide for themselves. These three parts are also common to humans. For by the vital life, one lives and is animated while sleeping. Sensation proceeds from that, and while it is at rest, one does not choose. Therefore, that choice proceeds from the vital and the sensitive, and not the other way around. 

But Reason, which is added to these, consists of intellect, reasoning, and <term>reminiscence</term> <note>reminiscence, or "reminiscentia," refers to the active search for a memory, distinguished from simple passive memory</note>. For in the brutes are found apprehension, thought, and memory; but that they should understand those things which are more remote from the senses of the body, or that they should reason and gather conclusions, or recall things through a process of discourse as a human does, is impossible. 

The Father is like apprehension, that is, the source. The Son—the progression from apprehension—is thought. The Spirit is memory itself, which proceeds from both faculties. In the same way, the reason, mind, or intellect, or spirit (for these differ in words, not in reality) produces reasoning and wisdom: these procreate reminiscence. For (as the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle</note> says) in this foul matter <note>referring to the physical body</note>, nothing can be found that is capable of understanding, gathering, and...

...and has a capacity for remembering. Certainly, we cannot act prudently without a likeness to that Divine image. For our will is frequently hindered, whereas nature is never, or only rarely, impeded.

### FROM BODIES.

7 Now, from the body itself, which is perceived by the senses, the arguments will be even more manifest. In the entire nature of things, no body can be found that is not both a single thing in itself and composed of "form" and "matter." Thus, Plato used to say that there were three principles of all things: matter, form, and God. Aristotle, opposing him as if he had thought up something brilliant, put "privation" <note>original: "privationem" — in Aristotelian philosophy, the absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present</note> in the place of God; let those who are led by reason, rather than mere authority, judge this well. Both would have spoken better and more appropriately had they said: form, matter, and Divine unity. Yet Plato is closer to the truth. Thus, the form itself, giving "being" to a thing, places the matter into existence; from these two proceeds the "composite" <note>the finished, whole object</note>. One cannot separate form from matter (or vice versa), nor the whole composite from its parts, except in the intellect. For if you separate them, the thing no longer exists. From this, the mystery of the holy Trinity and Unity is clear: how one is three, and three are one. Rightly, therefore, should that atheist Lucian and Julian the Apostate—those deserters of holy reason—be hissed away not only from our number but also from the number of philosophers, for they could never grasp such clear arguments, or refused to acknowledge them once known.

### FROM THE PARTS OF BODIES.

8 But perhaps matter, once dissolved from its composite and separated, or the parts inherent in the whole, do not possess this image of the Trinity within them. Let us consider this. Certainly, when a person dies, the most excellent forms—namely the spirit and the soul—depart; yet even the lifeless corpse consists of its own form and matter. It cannot be deprived of the unity of matter and form until it has lost its "principle of generation" (that is, its place/structure) and returned its parts to the elements. Plainly, the same must be felt regarding the parts of things, whether they are simple or composite: everywhere there is matter, form, and unity (or a bond). You may see this in a familiar example in the magnet <term>magnete: a lodestone, which was a source of great scientific and mystical wonder in the Renaissance</term>. That stone consists of one southern part and another northern part. If you touch and rub iron needles with it, one part will be forced to turn toward the north and the other toward the south. Cut whichever part you wish from the whole, and try to separate the southern part from the northern: you will never be able to. Cut a slice as thin as you like from any part, and in it will be both parts, just as in the whole, no matter which way you cut it. Thus, in all human things, the triune power of the Creator is most evident. For (as in the magnet) two different parts are so connected that their bond cannot be torn from them.

To such an extent does the power of Satan blind the wretched minds of men that they delight in their own miseries. But to...

...thing. No one denies that the sun itself is a body that acts as a center of light, nor that rays go out from it. For it is well established that the rays and the power of the light differ greatly, because while the rays spread out very widely, the body itself does not. Yet the effect—whether it be splendor, the ripening of crops, or whatever usefulness reaches us from it—also differs from the sun itself. Therefore, the center of the sun is like the Father, having all things in his power and eternally generating rays from himself; by both of these, everything in the heavens and the elements that is born to be moved, helped, or changed by his power is nourished. This is indeed a most clear example. First, the center or body, like the Father, has a Son—the ray—procreated from itself from eternity, in whom it places the power over all things, just as it has in itself. The effect itself is not "generated" <note>In Trinitarian theology, the Son is "begotten" (generated), while the Holy Spirit "proceeds" (is an effect or breath).</note>, but is seen proceeding from the body and the rays. It is therefore necessary to confess that the Archetype <term>archetypum: the original model or divine pattern</term> is of a similar nature and exists in a most simple hypostasis <term>hypostasi: a Greek term for the underlying reality or "person" of the Trinity</term>, since an example of it is never lacking.

### 10 FROM THE REASONING OF THE UNIVERSE.

No one among the most excellent philosophers denies that the heaven itself is moved by a power that is perpetually constant and stationary, and that it must necessarily obey and has no choice in how it is moved. From this, it is clear that the universe also consists of a triple hypostasis. For although the power, majesty, and action of God are diffused everywhere (otherwise needing no specific place), yet because of the excellence of His essence, He is properly said to be "above the heavens," where His greater and more noble operation is perceived. In the second place is the "middle world," namely the celestial region; the ancients called it "middle" because countless separate substances <note>A term often used for angels or celestial intelligences.</note> are established there, and from there the motion, action, and change of things flow down into the lower realms. Third is this corruptible world known to us, which is the most imperfect and dependent on the first and second. If we see this world as admirable, what should we judge regarding the excellence of the others? Unless we consider the forms mixed within it and the spirit that nourishes the things themselves, this world does not fully match the comparison. But if we look at the forms and the vital force, it fits in every way. It is as if the Father were the higher world, the Son the middle world (eternally generated by the Father), and the Holy Spirit the lower world, not generated, but proceeding. It has been sufficiently demonstrated by all parts of the universe that the Author must necessarily have within Himself a most perfect unity in trinity, and trinity in unity. But perhaps someone will object that while such a demonstration holds true for things governed by nature, human actions are exempt from this pattern. Yet surely, whatever things come from deliberation—however poorly weighed or useless—it is impossible for them to exist without a trinity necessarily being present from the very power of the thinking mind.

### 11 FROM THINGS MADE BY HUMAN INDUSTRY.

Whatever we ever attempt must proceed from the mind's knowledge, wisdom, and will. For unless I comprehend and have the capacity, how could I freely "will" anything? For to will and not be able is slavery, not freedom of choice. But before we come to the work itself, even outside the mind, there is a need for the craftsman, the tools, and the material. For without these, the work does not arise. In friendship, there is the lover, the beloved, and the love that is the bond between both. For the lover is not the beloved, nor vice versa; so too, the love that proceeds from both is not either one of them. This is also clear in neutral actions. As in a race, there is the action, the passion <note>In this context, "passion" refers to the state of being acted upon or the physical experience of the runner.</note>, and the connection between both, which is the race itself. Thus, it is less surprising when, in the Divine goodness, action and passion are the same thing—even though that most simple nature can suffer nothing. But we speak this way because it reflects back upon itself in all the most excellent ways, in a manner unknown to us.

...to establish: yet because human reason and intellect were forced to find a remedy for human affairs, it could not have happened otherwise than that the Holy Trinity itself provided the beginning. Even where things grew in false religions and those alienated from God, it formed an order in its own image. Thus, all magistrates were divided into three differences. For they manage the care of either souls, bodies, or external things: namely, priests, judges, and kings. In the first institution of Republics, these three "persons" were united in one. For when few people were gathered and the ambition for dominating others was unknown, the same man was priest, judge, and leader. Hearing legal causes based on sacred laws, and when necessity arose after the sacred rites were finished, he was a successful leader for his soldiers—defending his own people, not lusting after the goods of others. Finally, as affairs grew, three grades of men were introduced for each individual office. Since one person was unequal to the weight of sacred duties, having been made the superior, he established others in various places. If a dispute arose among them, so that they would not struggle too much by seeking justice from so far away, he willed there to be certain officials of "middle power," to whom he shared his authority as far as he wished. Thus, the total power began to exist in the highest, the total in all the middle ones, and the total in the lowest; and yet there are not three powers, but one power. The second rank uses its authority from the first, and the lower ranks from both the first and the middle. The same is seen in military affairs, regarding the king, the commanders, and the soldier; and likewise concerning judges: the highest authority, the middle, and the lowest. The whole is in each individual and the whole is in the total—a unity within a trinity. In short, there is nothing that does not represent that most holy property of the divinity. In all things, there is a beginning, a middle, and an end. In motions: upward/downward, forward/backward, right/left. For these do not differ except because they consist of impulse and three straight, transverse lines. The nourishment of things is drawn inward, outward, or from both sides. Time consists of past, present, and future. In geometry, no regular angular figure exists before three straight lines meet; in the composition of regular solid bodies, only three surfaces meet: the triangle, the square, and the pentagon. In summary, nothing is free from the mystery of that Triad <note>original: "triados." Postel uses the Greek term for the Trinity to emphasize its universal philosophical nature.</note>.

## THE TESTIMONY AND AUTHORITY OF THE PHILO-sophers concerning the Trinity.

13 Aristotle, the philosopher of truth, writes the following about the Trinity in the first book of *On the Heavens and the World*: "The science of nature," he says, "is mostly concerned with bodies, magnitudes, their properties, and motions, as well as with principles of the same substance. For of those things that consist by nature, some are bodies and magnitudes, others are the body and magnitude itself, and others are the principles of these. Therefore, the continuous is always divisible, but a body can be divided in every direction. Furthermore, magnitude can be divided into one part, as a line; into two, as a surface; and into three, as a body. Beyond this, there is no other magnitude, because all things are three, and the Trinity is everywhere." For as the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed numbers were the fundamental reality of the universe.</note> say, the universe and all things are limited by three. For the beginning, the middle, and the end hold the number of the universe. I understand this to be the number of the Trinity. Therefore, receiving this from nature as if it were her own laws, we use this number in sacred rites and give the names of numbers to it. For we do not say "all" for two, but "both"; however, for three, we say "all." And likewise in the eighth book of the *Physics*, he says that the world is ruled by three: the unmoved mover, the moved mover, and the moved non-mover <note>Aristotle's categories for how motion is transmitted. The "unmoved mover" is traditionally identified by theologians as God.</note>. This is as if he were saying: the uncreated Father generates the eternal Son, from whom and from the Father proceeds the Holy Spirit, in whom is the end of the divinity—if it is permitted to compare corruptible things to eternal ones, and finite to infinite. If I were to record everything regarding the Mind <note>original: "mente" - the Divine Intellect or Logos.</note> and the Parent that is found in Plotinus, Porphyry, Proclus, Maximus, Amelius, Iamblichus, Hermes Thrice-Great <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage.</note>, and their teacher Zoroaster, there would undoubtedly be no end. For in all ages, nothing has more thoroughly convinced learned men than that a "Mind" necessarily proceeds from the supreme Parent. Therefore...

<meta>This page transitions from Postel’s observations on human social structures to the intellectual history of the Trinity, arguing that ancient pagan philosophers like Plato and Pythagoras secretly understood the Triune nature of God but hid it in riddles or symbols. # WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK I.

Leaving behind their opinions and authorities regarding this mind, let us see what they thought of our Triad. *Plato*, the god of divine philosophers, opened it to the tyrant *Dionysius* with this riddle: "Regarding the king of all things, all things exist; all is for his sake, and he is the cause of all good things. Second things concern the second, and third things concern the third." Once *Porphyry* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who was often critical of Christianity but deeply influenced by its concepts.</note> had learned to explain these words from the *Christians*, he interpreted them as the Triune God: the first substance is the supreme God, the second is the maker of all things, and the third is the mind of the soul. Although that wretched man recognized these truths, it is a wonder he valued human glory so much that he recoiled from the very truth he was forced to admit; like *Maximus*, *Amelius*, and *Plotinus*, he took his ideas from our own people. 

Meanwhile, regarding *Amelius*, we must not omit the fact that when he read the *Gospel of John*, he immediately exclaimed at the very beginning: "May I perish," he said, "if that barbarian <note>Amelius, a Greek philosopher, refers to the Apostle John as a "barbarus" simply because he was not Greek.</note> has not briefly captured what *Plato* and *Heraclitus* taught regarding divine reason, the beginning, and the arrangement of things." There is no doubt that *Plato* would have produced far more regarding the Holy Trinity—which he had certainly learned from the prophets—had he not considered it a religious duty to keep secret the holy mysteries he had with difficulty obtained, keeping them for himself alone. He did not even wish to betray them to the tyrant from whom he had received great benefits. Thus, ambition destroyed the truth and expelled it from our fellowship. 

What would the great *Pythagoras* not have declared after seeing the *Gymnosophists* <note>Ancient Indian philosophers known for their asceticism and "nakedness."</note>, the *Magi*, the *Egyptians*, and those divine men the prophets, had he not wished to be admired for keeping such things silent? To avoid betraying the Holy Trinity, which he had read about in *Trismegistus* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of secret wisdom.</note>, he thrust upon his disciples the *tetractyn* (that is, the four-fold number), by which he hinted at the same truth, though covering it in veils. For he meant: Father, Son, Holy Spirit; God, Creator, Mind; Begotten, and the Soul of the World; God or Cause—all one thing. For this reason, the Greeks used to call those who were perfectly happy *trismakares* <note>original: τρισμάκαρες</note>, meaning "thrice-blessed," to whom nothing was lacking. They understood their gods to be fully worthy of this title. The Latins say "thrice-blessed" in the *Platonic* manner, and "four-times blessed" in the *Pythagorean* manner. 

The *Egyptian* sages, according to the witness of *Damascius the Platonist*, would acclaim the deity three times in their religious practice, and they had an altar dedicated to *Minerva* in whose temple this was written: "I am everything that has been, and is, and will be, and no mortal has yet uncovered or revealed my veil." <note>original: ἐγὼ εἰμὶ πᾶν τὸ γεγονὸς, καὶ ὂν, καὶ ἐσόμενον, καὶ τὸν ἐμὸν πέπλον οὐδείς πω τῶν θνητῶν ἀπεκάλυψεν</note> Those worthless Greek poets—*Orpheus*, *Linus*, *Homer*, and the rest—by dragging these truths down to their own gods and concealing their true sources, have shaken the world and made a path for all kinds of errors. But now we must come to the settled doctrines of the written religion.

# PROOF FROM THE OLD TESTAMENT
## and Kabbalah and Talmud.

These things were not only abolished by Christ himself, but even the prophets more than six hundred years before him already seemed to disapprove of them. In that Law, to put it briefly, God acted with Israel as the best teacher does with a very young student: because of the student's tender age and ignorance, the teacher permits the usual games along with the roots of discipline. 

Because, I say, that law is the first authority of God (existing in writing) in which He opened Himself to His servants, there will be no greater method than to confirm from that source, in reverse order, the things that have been proven from philosophy. I say "in reverse order," because even in the teaching of disciplines, authority comes before reason. Hence it is rightly written: *Unless you believe, you will not understand.* This applies not only to sacred matters, but also to human...

These men spoke with two tongues (so to speak) whenever they relied on the authority of Sacred Scripture. Therefore, they explained it only by word of mouth to their successors—men called to that duty based on the merit of their lives—and for that reason they called it **Kabbalah** <note>original: קבלה. Meaning "that which is received." Postel views this as a mystical tradition that mirrors Christian theology.</note>, because it was received by one from another.

Truly, that tradition contained the greatest mysteries and was very similar to our own **anagogical** sense <note>A method of spiritual interpretation that finds deeper, heavenly meanings behind literal text.</note>, by which we lead minds from corruptible things to the celestial. The other "tongue" was the interpretation common to all the learned, representing **allegory**, which was usually entrusted to writing and preserved. Thus, the anagogical ones were called **Kabbalists**, and much later, the allegorical ones were called **Talmudists**. But when Jesus Christ had come in the times of *Simeon*—whom not only the Gospel but also the Jews call "the Just and Holy"—then the teacher and lawgiver failed from Israel, and a foreign king <note>Referring to Herod the Great, an Edomite/Idumean, rather than a descendant of David.</note> gained control of affairs. Finally, as other opinions were added—as time brought forth those authors who were discovered—they wrote the first **Talmud** from the *Mishneh* and other sources, having gathered the Jews from everywhere to Jerusalem; they call it the *Jerusalem Talmud*, written more or less 300 years after the suffering of Christ. Subsequently, as other issues arose, they composed another *Talmud* about 70 years later, having gathered the Jews in Babylon, having summoned teachers from the whole world. They use that *Talmud* now. Many Kabbalistic traditions abound in it, yet they are also scattered separately in many volumes. Therefore, because the Jews use three authorities—the sacred, the mixed, and the human—I shall deal with them using those three, taking my beginning from the sacred.

Certainly, he wished to indicate a plurality of persons in the Godhead, and finally to gather that plurality into a unity. This happens throughout the entire course of Scripture; from this, you ought to recognize the most holy mystery, and that there are several properties in God. But someone will say: "It is according to the usage of the language to place that word in the plural with a singular verb." Therefore, it ought not to happen that the noun is placed in the plural while the subject verb is singular. In the creation of man it is said, *And God said [singular], Let us make [plural]*. Is that not an inconsistency? Certainly, the reason is the same: it is the intention of the prophet, wishing to indicate a plurality in God. ...unknown, whom he named **Jehovah** <note>original: יהוה</note>, that is, the "revealer of secrets," where he wrote many things about God and His son **the Messiah** <note>original: hamassiah</note>, but especially about the Trinity. Rabbi Nehemiah son of Hakana <note>A 1st-century sage to whom many early Kabbalistic works are attributed.</note> (who lived during the times of the consulship of Antoninus) <note>Likely referring to the legendary friendship between the Roman Emperor (Antoninus) and Rabbi Judah the Prince.</note> writes as follows in his letter to his son Hakana, which he calls the *Iggeret ha-Sod* or **Letter of Secrets** <note>original: אגרת הסוד</note>:

> Antoninus, the Roman consul, once asked our Holy Teacher <note>original: Rabenu haccados, referring to Judah the Prince, the redactor of the Mishnah.</note> to teach him about the truth of the properties of the names of four, twelve, and forty-two letters. He replied: "Since you desire to know the truth of the name of 4, 12, and 42 letters, know that these are divine mysteries which ought to remain hidden from men. However, because I see that you seek this out of a desire to learn and not for the sake of contradiction, I will reveal it. Know that God has no name of which we can have full knowledge, since His substance is His name, and vice versa. And just as we cannot have knowledge of His substance (for then we would be equal to Him), so we have no knowledge of His name. Nevertheless, His names are attributes. And because the 4-letter name is more peculiar to His works, it shows a notion of Him that is broader and more suitable to our understanding. From it proceed all other names. Therefore, this name **Jehovah** <note>original: יהוה</note> is called the **Expressed Name** <note>original: השם המפורש; a term for the Tetragrammaton which was considered too holy to pronounce.</note>—not that it is His substantial name, but only so far as we can grasp it. Truly, the names of twelve and forty-two letters are not single words where there are so many letters, but rather each one is composed of several words."

Nehemiah writes these things from the ancient Rabbi Judah <note>Postel is distinguishing this Judah from a later one killed by Hadrian.</note>; yet the Jews ascribe the works of others to him, as if he were the only one. Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>The famous philosopher Maimonides (1135–1204).</note>, who was more a lover of truth than you are now, writes clearly to the same effect in chapter 60 of the first part of the *Moreh* <note>original: Moreh Nevukhim, or "The Guide for the Perplexed."</note>, stating that all names are bestowed from God's effects, except for **Jehovah** <note>original: יהוה</note>. And a little later, Rabbi Eliezer says in his **Chapters** <note>original: פרקי (Pirkei); referring to the "Pirkei De-Rabbi Eliezer," a midrashic work.</note>:

> When the world had not yet been created, there was only the Blessed God and His name (he writes this regarding the passage in Zechariah chapter 14: *In that day the Lord will be one, and his name one*).

From this it should be noted that all these names of God are newly made, and were created after the world. This is certain, because they are named after the works of God discovered in the world. Therefore, if you consider God in Himself, His name is the **Expressed Name**, etc. These are most extensive arguments from the same Rabbi Moses. Likewise, from the time that Simeon the Just died, his brother priests ceased to bless the people with the 4-letter name, and blessed them with the 12-letter name. By these words of Moses [Maimonides], the "Letter of Secrets" is confirmed. But now, listen to the very secrets themselves, and return to your senses! Thus says our Holy Teacher:

> Observe the 4-letter name as it is written. For it is written thus: **יהוה** and it signifies God Himself generating. And because there cannot be a generator without a generated one, necessarily love must proceed from the generator to the generated, and vice versa; for otherwise He would not generate. If love did not proceed from the generated to the generator, and if the generated differed from the generator, there would be two substances. Therefore, we maintain that the generator and the generated are one substance; hence it is necessary that mutual love proceed from both. Therefore, from this **יהוה** is derived the 12-letter name. For it is **Father, Son, and Holy Spirit** <note>original: אב בן רוח הקודש</note>; thus there are twelve letters. Since, however, nothing is found in God which is not God, from the 12-letter name comes the 42-letter name, in this manner: **Father [is] God, Son [is] God, Holy Spirit [is] God, three as one, and one in three** <note>original: אב אלהים בן אלהים רוח הקודש שלשה כאחד אחד בשלשה</note>. These are the 42 letters which it is proper to hide until the righteous Messiah comes, our Righteous One. I have revealed them; now hide them.

So says that author. These things are likewise confirmed by Rabbi Moses the Egyptian in the book *Moreh*, first part, chapter 61, where he says this 12-letter name was not one, but two or three names; by which the holy fathers pronounced the name **Jehovah** as we now pronounce it through **Adonai** <note>original: אדני; meaning "Lord," used as a substitute for the Tetragrammaton.</note>. It was permitted for all to know this 12-letter name, but not **Jehovah**. But when men began to abuse that name, they also hid it on account of the wickedness of men.

There are countless similar examples among you which you yourselves cannot disprove, nor can you assert that they were fabricated by us.

Come now, O Hebrews, how does it happen that in your language—which you rightly believe was revealed and impressed by God through the authorship of **Adam**—how does it happen, I say, that there is no original word for the significance of any thing whatsoever that has more or fewer than three letters? Are these not the footprints of the Triune God, when one thing is signified and expressed by three? Otherwise, if it had been done by chance, there would surely be many other words. Truly, if there are any of four, five, or six letters, they are entirely foreign or doubled; this occurs in no other language. Therefore, your expression of all things is similar to the Triune God.

## THE OPINIONS OF THE MUSLIMS CONCERNING
### The Nature of God.

I will now deal briefly with you, O men who are eager for truth and in need of it, because I shall engage with you more familiarly and attentively in the proper place. For I know that after my proof of the Trinity and of God has been demonstrated by reason, strengthened by both human and divine authority, and supported by examples, there will be no place for doubt among you. Truly, because there are very many things in your law which run contrary to these things I have demonstrated concerning the Trinity, they seem to me to require examination, so that I may understand you, and you may understand me, and we may have common principles. I think it was done not without reason in the **Quran** <note>original: Alcorano</note>, even if he did not fully grasp it, that your **Muhammad** <note>original: Muhamedes</note> almost never speaks of God except in the plural voice, just as **Moses** does. For it is certain that God Himself, though most simple, possesses a certain number within Himself. Otherwise, this plural usage would almost never have occurred everywhere, unless by the deliberate intention of the founding Jews. Yet, what that plurality in God signifies for itself has never been handed down or explained. Rather, in all places Muhammad seems contrary to himself when he asserts that he spoke first of the unity of God, and that God has no partner, and that God does not beget, nor is He begotten. Your religion seems to have been written toward this target through the favor of **Nestorius** <note>A 5th-century bishop whose followers were accused of over-emphasizing the distinction between the human and divine natures of Christ; Postel suggests Islam was influenced by Nestorian "heresy."</note>, whose disciples had defected from us to you.

Let us therefore weigh certain sentences from the Quran where your prophet seems to contradict himself. For it is well established that he asserts one God. But in several places he also introduces the **Spirit of God**, through whom all things seem to be made. Thus, by your own lights, there is already a duality in divine matters. Let us see, therefore, from the text itself. It is written in the **Sura of the Table** <note>original: ſora Elmeide; Surah 5 (Al-Ma'idah) of the Quran.</note>, which is the fourth <note>Postel’s numbering of the Surahs often differs from modern standard editions.</note>, that God will call the prophets on the Day of Judgment, and among others will address **Jesus** thus: "Hear, O Jesus son of Mary, remember my favor toward you and your generation, because I formed you from the **Holy Spirit**, and you spoke to men in the cradle and in swaddling clothes, and that I taught you the Book, wisdom, and the law, etc." From this passage, we see that there is God and His Spirit. And likewise, toward the end of the **Sura of the Cow** <note>original: ſora Bacara; Surah 2 (Al-Baqarah).</note>, it is written: "We have distinguished these prophets in a certain order by the word of God, and we have established degrees among them, and we gave to Jesus son of Mary wisdom, and we formed him from the Holy Spirit, etc."

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

We have here God, the word of God, wisdom, and his spirit. A little earlier, he writes the same sentiment in the same words. For he says: **"And we gave Jesus the son of Mary wisdom, and we formed him from the holy spirit."** <note>Postel is quoting a Latin translation of the Quran (likely Sura 2:253 or 5:110). He interprets the Arabic *ruh al-qudus* (holy spirit) and *hikmah* (wisdom) through a Christian theological lens.</note> Here is God who gives, the wisdom which is given, and the holy spirit. But since God is one and most unified, and yet sends from himself wisdom (or the word) and the holy spirit, it is necessary—even according to your own prophet—to infer a trinity in unity and a unity in trinity, as we demonstrated from necessary principles at the beginning. 

For if there were only one single quality, nothing at all would come forth into being, unless, having been conceived by the Father through his wisdom—which he eternally generates—he had created all things in the spirit and the will. For as has been shown, you would imagine in vain unless you also knew and were wise; and you would think and know in vain unless you also willed. For it is necessary, as we have said, for all these to concur; just as our own intellect, unless it becomes three and one in the act of thinking, we shall never do anything from its movement. For it must think, know, and will before it produces an effect. 

Therefore, it is not right that you alone among mortals—O most excellent minds of the world, as long as you judge freely—it is not right, I say, to resist manifest reason and the proven truth of all wise men without cause, even if your own persuasion were to contradict it. But when you see that reason supports us in this matter, and admits and approves of God, his wisdom, and his spirit, how much more ought you to approach and <term>extend the hand of surrender</term> <note>original: "herbam porrigere" — a classical Latin idiom meaning to acknowledge defeat or yield the palm to a victor.</note> to the truth? 

A <term>Muslim</term> <note>original: "Muffulmanus."</note> will say: "Our law opposes this elsewhere, where it says that God does not beget, nor is he begotten, because he has no females, and because there are no male or female spirits in heaven." It is certain that God, in our human fashion and through the instruments of nature, neither begets nor is begotten. But as we have seen, it is so necessary for the Father to eternally generate the Son-Wisdom that the world itself could not otherwise stand. For the Son of God is not a corporeal thing, insofar as he is God, but a purely spiritual thing; this generation is a necessity. And so, both points will stand firm, as I shall reveal more fully in its proper place by explaining the life of Muhammad and your law. You see therefore—O <term>Followers of Muhammad</term> <note>original: "Mahumedici."</note>, whom I love the more because you were once a part of us that perished—that by both divine and human reason, by the authority of all philosophers, and of Moses, and of your own, our faith concerning the trinity is most true, and that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, the Word, and Wisdom: which he joined here to humanity for the sake of the salvation of all. But more on these things in their proper place.

## ON THE CREATION OF THE WORLD, AND WHETHER THE WORLD IS 
## from eternity. CHAPTER IV.

Thus far, the entire crowd of philosophers, of whatever sect they may be, has seemed to favor me. For all find it necessary to admit a cause for this universe—which is indeed corruptible in itself—from which, through which, and in which all things consist; otherwise, they must assert that the nature of things is nothing at all. But now I must declare war against the entire tribe of philosophers, and finally settle a peace with them. There is, above all, a great disagreement among everyone; if it could have happened from the nature of the matter, you would have seen here "as many opinions as there are men" regarding the constitution of the world. 

Truly, there could not be more than these five views. For as pertains to the universe, not a few—including those bound by the oath of greater authority—assert on both sides that it is eternal; that is, it had no beginning and will feel no end. It pleased others that it had an origin indeed, but will not perish. Some held that it was indeed eternal from eternity, but would finally fail bit by bit. We ascribe both origin and destruction to it from the will of the Mover. If there are any who attribute these same things to its own nature, I know not: certainly, if they exist, they are in great error and deprived of common sense, affirming that this order of things and so great a mass lacks a cause. To judge among all these is not without the greatest difficulty in the whole world; thus it seems to me as if some members of a prince's household...
