...of certain principles, they would argue about His majesty in such a way as if they were dealing with their own most well-known affairs. Through either ignorance and an inability to grasp His majesty, or even through contention and desire, they would cast Him down from His own empire by their own opinions, while they are either unable to protect His laws or even attempt to subvert them. It is certain that this nursery of discord was sown in the seat of truth by the adversary of the human mind <note>The "adversary" refers to the Devil or Satan.</note>, so that miserable men might perpetually remain here in an argument while seeking the truth, and might contend for glory: not so that they might beg for more votes for the truth, but so that they might thrust their own dreams upon posterity and testify by a wicked crime that they had lived. I do not deny that the love of truth has made many men perplexed, as has the zeal for searching out the truth; but a far greater number have been driven off course by lust. It is certain that we owe this to Greece (as we do many good things), so that even the most excellent thing might not lack its own plague. Those opinions must be examined more carefully, and they must not be settled in an irreligious manner. 

Regarding the opinion of the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for walking while teaching in the Lyceum.</note>, which is first in authority and position (because it has more people who approve and defend it as being more likely true), it must be spoken of in the last place, once reasons and authorities have been applied from both sides. **Plato** partly agrees with us; his axiom holds the second place. For, compelled by necessity, he knew that this **matter** had an origin, or at least was inferior to the **First Cause** by its posteriority. For whoever posits a cause (as all learned men do) will necessarily say that it differs from the effect; otherwise, the cause and the effect would be one and the same thing, which is repugnant to the senses. For nothing can produce itself. And furthermore, the very matter of the world would be a part of God, nor would the **cause** differ from the **thing caused**—which is altogether absurd. 

Therefore, Plato necessarily ascribed a **beginning** to the world. But as for his removing an **end** and **destruction** from it, he does not prove this by arguments or tricks taken from the common use of such things, but he affirms that this will happen by the favor of the Creator, because He is good, and He does not envy anyone His own goodness. For this reason, he likewise attributes this to separated and immaterial substances <note>Refers to angels or "intelligences."</note>, and says that they are mortal by their own nature, unless their life is prolonged by the will of the Creator through His own kindness. 

Truly, in my judgment, he did not hold a sufficiently diligent consideration regarding the nature of **demons** <note>In the classical sense, *daemones* were intermediate spirits, which Postel equates here with both good and bad angels.</note>, whom we call angels, both good and bad. For since they are purely immaterial forms, while the **First Cause** thrives and does not perish, it is impossible for them to perish. But he did this, in my judgment, not so much because of a falsely conceived opinion about those things, but because he considered it a religious duty not to subtract anything from the will and power of the Creator. That good man did not notice, as I judge (saving a better opinion <note>original: *salva meliori sententia* - a humble theological disclaimer</note>), what he himself often asserted: that **evil is non-being**, which is not made by the Creator, but happens on the part of matter through a privation of good and essence. 

And so he agrees with us, except for the **transformation** of matter, which we hold by religion will certainly happen. For although we grant a beginning to the world, we do not however admit its destruction, but rather its **transformation** <term>immutatio: a change in form or quality rather than a total annihilation of substance</term>, which both God and nature perform, and we affirm it will be entirely for the better, so that all corruption may be absent in the future. But concerning this, we both agree on the fact and the manner regarding the **beginning**; but regarding the **end**, we differ only in the manner, being equal in the reality of the thing. He believes in eternal corruption, while we believe in eternal **incorruption**, which is far more worthy of the majesty of the Creator. But if the philosophers, those lovers of truth, deny this to me, I shall necessarily wring it from their own principles in the Chapter on Transformation. Those who affirm that the world is corruptible only at its end, and that it is firm and constant from eternity until a certain period, agree on one hand with Aristotle, and on the other hand with us regarding the end, except that they introduce destruction in place of change and perfection. I shall bring both walls together with one trowel <note>A metaphorical expression meaning to harmonize or reconcile two opposing views simultaneously.</note> when the beginning is discussed. We hold that which the nature of things carries, as is already evident, and will be more widely evident. Just as they are entirely destitute of reason, so...

### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

Those who have arrived at such impudence and rashness do not even need a refutation, as they attribute to fortune and chance those things which are most constant and orderly. They affirm that atoms—with their little hooks <note>original: "cum suis uncinis." This refers to the Epicurean theory that atoms had physical hooks that allowed them to link together to form matter.</note>—are wiser than God and more noble than the whole of nature; they even attribute "choice" to these atoms, suggesting they can choose one another, connect themselves together, and generate things from that process. I am weary and ashamed of such an opinion. Should one even call them "men"? In their hunger for a bit of glory, they preferred to deny that reason existed within themselves rather than subscribe to the common sense and consensus of the rest of mortality. Nature brought forth such monsters so that we might not grow sluggish once the truth has been found.

Now I come to **Aristotle** and the disciples of his sect. Hey you, whoever you are, who thinks that assent should not be withheld from things that are manifest: pay attention. The **Cause**, which we all prove and affirm to preside over this world, necessarily preceded the **Effect**, at least in respect to time or by the logic of order. For whether a cause is antecedent or remote, or joined and nearby, it precedes the thing of which it is the cause. The **efficient** and **final** causes are prior in time; the **formal** and **material** causes precede their effects at least in the understanding. For although matter may pre-exist corruptible things, nevertheless, while the thing does not yet exist and before the matter is joined to it, it is not said to "pre-exist" that thing. 

But so there is no occasion for doubt, I am speaking here of the **efficient cause**, not the others, unless we also admit the likeness of the **formal cause**. Suppose, then, that the world is as continuous and eternal as you like; you must necessarily admit it is posterior to its cause—otherwise, you would call the world either the cause itself or a part of the cause, which is utterly absurd. For you know that the cause and the effect differ, and nothing can be called a cause except in respect to the thing caused. Furthermore, the cause would necessarily be creating itself in part if it were joined [to the effect]. All these things are clearly absurd, inconsistent, and impossible. Therefore, the world had a beginning, no matter how ancient you make it. 

I will not dwell on **Time** now, for I shall deal with it in its proper place. But whatever had a beginning (provided it consists of form and matter) is certain to experience ruin as far as its own nature is concerned. Aristotle proves this regarding lower and elemental matter. But it must also be understood regarding the **Heavens**. For in the heavens—whether **Aben reis** <note>This is a Latinized form of Ibn Rushd, known in the West as **Averroes**, the famous 12th-century Islamic philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> likes it or not—there is matter and form, a point Aristotle does not disprove. Therefore, by reason of its "body" (which, although not having form annexed to matter in the same way as these lower things), it is nonetheless necessary that it be apt for corruption and subject to a beginning because it is a body. 

This is also clear by reason of **Quantity**. For whatever things are bodies, because they are finite, they are of themselves subject to corruption, unless sustained by an infinite moving power. Yet that the heaven is finite is clear even to the eyes; it is demonstrated by the nature of a finite circle (that is, a body), and is established by its Greek etymology. For the Greek word for heaven is *Ouranos*, which means "the boundary of the things above" <note>original: "οὐρανὸς ὅρος τῶν ἄνω" (ouranos horos tōn anō). This is a folk etymology used by Plato in the *Cratylus* to suggest that the sky/heaven is the "limit" or "boundary" (*horos*) of the upper world.</note>, as **Plato** rightly says. Whatever is of such a kind is finite, and therefore corruptible. Indeed, the Philosopher <note>Standard medieval/Renaissance shorthand for Aristotle.</note> himself affirms this in the eighth book of the *Physics*, the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*, and the second book of *On the Heavens and the World*; Averroes also proves it in the third book of *On the Substance of the Orb*. **Alexander of Aphrodisias** <note>A celebrated commentator on Aristotle from the late 2nd century AD.</note> does not shrink from this opinion. 

Furthermore, whatever things possess **potential** are also of themselves subject to corruption, since nothing can be eternal of itself unless it is **pure act** <term>pure act: "actus purus," a theological concept describing God as complete, perfect, and unchanging, with no "potential" to become something else because He is already everything He can be.</term>. But here I have touched upon a knot more than **Gordian** <note>The Gordian Knot was an intricate knot in Greek legend that could not be untied; Alexander the Great eventually cut it with his sword.</note>, and one scarcely to be loosened even by Alexander’s sword. For the idea that God is "pure act" or "power" (philosophers understand "power" as the potential to act or not act, not as it pertains to the power of nature, for God is most powerful) creates a great difficulty. Therefore, the nature of God himself must be sought—not from the authority of the divine spirit, but from the prisons of the philosophers who restrict Him with bars and bolts—so that we might see, since other things are "necessary," whether it will be permitted (even through the faculties granted to God by the philosophers) for these same things to be called true, so that what is clear to the senses might also be established by reason. For the wretched...

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK 1

God, unless the philosophers allow him, would not even be able to reign according to his own judgment. Certainly, if he acts out of necessity within matter, and against his will, and cannot be moved except by an external object, then the impious have won: reason will surrender to them and give way. But the opinion of that man—who has seemed somewhat unjust and semi-impious toward the **First Cause** (which he attempted to bind to matter in the manner of form and soul)—**Averroes** <note>original: "Aben reis," referring to the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd.</note>, even grants to God by his own authority what we, according to reason, place in Him. And he concedes this purely to his adversary, whom he opposes more out of a zeal for disagreement than for the truth, namely **Al-Ghazali** <note>original: "Algezeli," referring to the 11th-century Persian theologian who famously critiqued philosophy.</note>. He does so in these words from the *Third Discussion of the Second Doubt*:

*It is clear therefore from these things,* he says, *that the argument of Al-Ghazali does not strike the philosophers. For they always judged that the action of God proceeds from knowledge, without a necessity driving him to act, either from himself or from some intrinsic thing; rather, he acts from pure goodness. And therefore he necessarily wills and chooses, in the most excellent mode of willing and choosing. For he never commits an error in those things, such as we act here in the world.* <note>original Latin quote: "Patet ergo ex istis... quale hic in mundo agimus." Postel is quoting Averroes's defense of the philosophers' view of God's free action.</note>

This is what he says. From this passage, I must take the following: since He has the will and the choice of acting, it is certain that He has it universally; that is, both in matter and in time (if He were subject to time, though He is far superior to it). Therefore, since He willed it, He acted, and in the manner that He willed. Consequently, it was not necessary for Him to act upon matter from eternity, even though He is <term>Pure Act</term> <note>Latin: *actus purus*. In Scholastic philosophy, this describes God as being fully realized, having no "potential" to become something else, because He is already perfect.</note>.

But you will say: if He is **Pure Act**, then He ought to have acted perpetually (even if you imagine Him being subject to time before there was motion or time, just to satisfy your own curiosity). I admit this. But I deny it in respect to **matter**. For if He could not act except with matter, He would be more powerless than the human soul or the "separate substances" <note>An Aristotelian term for celestial intelligences or angels.</note>. In what, then, did He act and rest for so long? In the contemplation of Himself, and in the wisdom that encompasses all future beings—in which His will was not forced to act according to the perfection and the **Idea** that He saw within Himself. 

For if He saw all things in Himself (as He certainly did), no perfection could be added to Him from matter produced into existence by His mind, just as He is not helped by it now. Otherwise, imperfection would complete perfection, which is contrary to reason. From this it is clear that by perpetual action He can act happily by Himself, even if the whole world were to perish; for His perfection does not depend on the world, but rather the other way around. Otherwise, you immerse Him in things and make Him subject to corruption if He requires matter. The world, therefore, is not from eternity, but has a beginning, as we have shown.

But you will say to me: "What was He doing in such a great eternity of self-contemplation?" Surely you are imagining a "time" for yourself where and when there is none. But let us pretend it exists; I am willing to grant it. Although He Himself ought to satisfy you in this regard by His singular wisdom (for certainly if that knowledge were necessary for the salvation of man—for whose sake He made all corruptible things when He willed—He would have opened and satisfied it), I will nevertheless attempt to satisfy you in this difficult matter with a certain fitting comparison. 

For you know that the principles of all arts must be taken without great inquiry and received as proven. If someone were to ask a teacher why fire is hot, snow is white, earth is dry, a line is a line, or a point is a point, he could say nothing else except that it is so, and it holds this from the **First Cause**. So in these questions concerning the simple **Highest Good**, one could not say anything else except that it is so. 

But pay attention, and test this in yourself. If there were some kingdom for you to both form and rule, or any other great matter to be undertaken (since those things would add nothing to your happiness except regarding your glory and the display of your virtue), could it not be that you would be held longer in the contemplation of it, with a pleasure that is supreme and plainly equal to the finished work? (If it were permitted to seek pleasure outside yourself). Could not that pleasure of thinking be drawn out even unto infinite ages? Finally, the work itself would be produced according to your judgment when the time seemed right—not for the convenience of the kingdom (which does not yet exist), but for your mere liberty.

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...and the decree according to your will? It is certain that we are daily held by similar pleasures and can be greatly affected by them, yet we postpone things until it seems right to us. For if the capacity to act fails us in many of our desires, that is our own fault and has nothing in common with God. For when wisdom and will are present in our minds, if the capacity is also there, we necessarily act. But God, acting in the **eternal Trinity** <term>eternal Trinity: The Christian doctrine of God as three persons (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) in one essence, existing and acting outside of the constraints of time.</term>, comprehending the nature of the forms of things through wisdom, also had will as a perpetual companion, by which he always willed things to exist. But since he had the free choice of time in which he wished them to be made, it was his prerogative to create when he willed that which he had been contemplating in himself with eternal meditation and joy, while in the meantime never lacking either the capacity or the will.

For there are also two ways of willing in us. We either will a thing simply, without any consideration of time, or we will it at such and such a time. But you, who are affected by the weariness of human affairs, tossed by the motion of the heavens, and moved by the cycles of birth and decay—measuring the condition of all things by the length of time calculated from the motion of the stars—you cannot weigh for yourself how, above and before motion, "a thousand years are as one day, and one day is as a thousand years," as **Peter** left written along with **David**. <note>original: "cum Dauide Petrus." This refers to 2 Peter 3:8 and Psalm 90:4, a standard theological defense for God's perspective on time.</note> Therefore, satisfy yourself with these reasons if you can, or seek better ones, and consider that your own perfection in deliberating on what is good is not greater than **divine providence**. Furthermore, one should not speak of a "new" will in God because he willed to produce the world at some pre-fixed time, since the divine will is not new; rather, things are born daily as new which he previously willed not to exist yet.

But you will object: "Why then did that God hide for so long?" You will say he suffered from either **laziness** <note>original: "socordia"</note> or **envy** <note>original: "invidia"</note>, because he kept such a magnificent thing in his mind for so long. It cannot be laziness, except where there is neglect and delay of a designated and necessary duty. Neither could exist in God. For things that did not yet exist could not bind him; no one could prescribe duties to him. Envy was not an obstacle, because nothing existed besides him. Yet, to share what you have immediately is a divine thing. For the more common a good is, the more divine it is. How much worldly things benefit us who possess them, and how eager he ought to have been to give and create, must be considered from these factors.

Indeed, a wide field opens up here. I proceed now with the comparison already begun concerning our capacity. When you think about that kingdom of yours and are happily fed by the knowledge of it, you are very often refreshed far more than by the work itself. If that work—which can make you neither better nor more perfect, and is prepared only for the sake of your honor and glory—consists of the labor and diligence of certain people who, while carrying out your work to please you and striving toward you as if toward their highest happiness, would have to undergo the greatest unhappiness through the difficulty of administration for their whole life, so that they could never be happy in the work itself—would your delay not be envy? Not at all.

Furthermore, those servants who are in your service, to be more attentive to the task, ought to be endowed with **freedom** <term>freedom: "libertate," here referring specifically to the philosophical concept of free will or the power of choice.</term>, so that they can act or not act. For he who acts without choice must be good or bad without his own merit or fault. And so, since you yourself would not be envious if you thus deferred gifts mixed with punishments for future subjects—especially since a future reward will be equal for all, even after hundreds of thousands of years, and those who refuse or ignore his rule would pay equal penalties—would you not want the blessed and most just Creator to have been in a worse condition while he deferred those punishments of life and those rewards for man which he disposed from eternity? Especially since there is no harm in the delay, whether he exhibited them later or sooner. See, therefore, that the Creator himself neither ceased from perpetual action even in the absence of the world, nor [did he act out of] laziness or envy...

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I

<meta>catchword: mus,</meta>

->...if he had labored for a day, since in human judgment, in which resides the power of discerning equity,<-
you would assert that you would have committed no sin by delaying in those two final matters, nor would you ever have ceased from the first action any longer than necessary, considering all things—which indeed it is certain a man can do for a long time. Acquiesce then, acquiesce to the **omnipotence of the Creator** <term>Creator: Postel uses the Latin "Conditor," meaning a founder or builder, emphasizing God as the architect of the universe.</term>, whose manifest signs and riddles we discern in our own minds and deliberations. 

Truly, to persist further in this example: how could it be that that Supreme Wisdom—from whom it was impossible for any future thing to be hidden—would want humans who were destined to decline toward future miseries and vices of their own accord, turning entirely from their freedom toward wickedness and acting against what was prescribed? How, I ask, could it be that He willed them to be created under such a condition? Would it not have been far better not to be created than to be made under a condition where one could perish and fall away entirely from the Creator? For it is better not to have been born than to have been born to perish miserably.

Attend diligently to which of these two men would be more perfect or more imperfect: the one who, out of fear of the ruin that necessarily accompanies matter (from which evil proceeds, rather than from the Author himself), would never attempt anything noble, lest the defect of matter would have to be restored too often? Or the one who, knowing the imperfection of matter, nonetheless established noble works, intending to restore them until all things achieved their end? It is clear that the latter is by far the most outstanding, courageous, strong, and good, who nonetheless performs noble deeds even though they must be constantly renewed and mended. It is established that the first man is cast down by small-mindedness, useless, abject, and as if he were nothing.

It was therefore far more excellent to have produced man—who is the **pinnacle and the target of the lower world**—even if he must be daily corrected and renewed, than to have left the world a desert out of fear of error and vice. Therefore, He both foresaw it and willed it. 

"But evil would not have been in the world if He had made matter perfect." Matter is not evil of itself, since all things made by the Best are "very good." <note>This is a reference to Genesis 1:31, where God sees that His creation is "very good."</note> But lest the first life in this world of dross be immortal, and the **free will** <term>free will: Postel uses "arbitrium," the legal and philosophical term for the power of making a decisive choice.</term> of man be taken away—who, if created without choice from the most perfect matter and a similar form, would have been unable to sin—God willed matter to be not evil, but fluid. He did this so that through the resistance of matter and form, the victory of great things might be achieved in difficulty, while in the meantime the entire mass of elements is purged, to be led at the end entirely beyond corruption, so that all things may obtain what is necessary for happiness in eternity.

That evil does not proceed from the Creator, nor from matter itself, you may easily learn from this: if you place water, clay, stones, or anything else good in itself into a well-constructed building, and it falls due to the injury of time, the fault is not yours, nor is it in the thing itself, but in the condition of things and in motion, which daily renews and corrupts lower things. For it is necessary that matter itself, being compliant to whatever forms, be daily cut apart, joined, and changed into various parts. 

From this, it happens by innumerable chances that the composite things themselves are weakened and affected; so much so that sometimes matter even seems victorious, covering certain forms in such a way that you do not easily recognize the individual, as in **monsters** <term>monsters: Postel uses "monstris" in the classical sense—not as "scary creatures," but as "marvels" or "signs" (from the Latin *monstrare*, to show) that deviate from the natural order.</term>. These are so named because they *show* (*monstrant*) something by their own truth. I believe the nature of things would lack these if we were moved by a just estimation of things to acknowledge and admire the benefits of God. For when common things become cheap to us, then we are moved by the rare; not indeed because rare things possess any more noble or greater nature than an ant, a small herb, or any other thing, but because of our negligence and contempt for common things. 

Whatever we are ignorant of, as soon as it appears—if it has an unusual life, mass, or property—we are struck dumb by it; and that which proceeds from our own ignorance, we often believe to be something new to nature and to the **omniscient Creator**. Yet I would think that those things which we do not know exceed in number, magnitude, and power unto infinity those things which were known even to the greatest philosopher of the whole world. Because that which I have never seen happen or exist...

<meta>catchword: ...judge</meta>

...judge that a thing immediately does not exist simply because it is not within our senses; yet we possess knowledge and disciplines gathered from experiments, as I said before. And because only one mode of generation and corruption <note>The natural cycle of birth and decay.</note> is known to us, another is not believed to exist, even though all these things are commingled by a **vital seed**. For this reason, various seeds and various species of living creatures emerge daily on land and in the sea. These appear new and like monsters to us for two reasons: either because they were created at the founding of the world but remained unknown to us, or because they spring forth from the putrefied parts of the elements—such as the many types of serpents in the sewers, small fry in marshy places, and many other things in the sea and innumerable ones upon the earth. For no one except the Creator alone knows the number of forms and those species which are able to come from potentiality into act. This is also evident from the fact that nature is obedient to human art; we see mixed species, differing from the primary species, produced daily by industry: **mules**, **ox-headed hybrids** <note>original: "bucephalos." Likely referring to specific cattle hybrids or creatures with ox-like features.</note>, and countless others which cannot propagate their own kind because they have fallen away from the divine form. Thus, we are compelled daily to beg from nature itself the animals, fruits, trees, and herbs for our use. Therefore, it is clear that those things which are least able to propagate themselves through their own kind have proceeded from the command of the Creator. Furthermore, the passions of causes—whether natural, manifest, or hidden, or those accustomed to happen by chance—are so varied that no mortal can comprehend them in his mind. 

Hence, the fact that we live in such blindness and are tossed up and down proceeds as much from ourselves as from external things; yet the Creator eventually turns everything to His own praise, except for our sins. Since sins are a **privation of the divine habit** <term>privation of the divine habit: A philosophical way of saying sin is the absence or "lack" of God's presence, rather than a thing God created.</term>, they do not harm God, but they wretchedly destroy us. O wretched man, who so abuses the free will that was meant for his salvation, and so departs from the boundaries of nature, that he alone rises up against his Author! All other things, which were created by God for his benefit, obey the laws of the Creator—though not without a **groan** <note>A reference to Romans 8:22, where the "whole creation groans" waiting for redemption.</note>, because they are driven by eternal motion and rotation almost in vain. For those things achieve their purpose while they assist man in dealing with this material world; but they do not reach their true and ultimate end when man, whose end was the knowledge and enjoyment of God, does not strive to attain his own purpose. Instead, he is accustomed to be a ruin to himself and others, to be captured by his own torments in this world, and to tire himself out preparing eternal punishment through his labors. 

**O wretched minds of men, O blind hearts!** <note>original: "O miseras hominum mentes, ô pectora cæca." A famous quote from the Roman poet Lucretius (De Rerum Natura), lamenting human ignorance.</note> It happens, therefore, to things lower than man and devoted to him, just as it would happen to stones and marble and any material fit for building if they were cut, hewn, and polished by eternal and tireless labors to be assembled into tall and magnificent houses—yet no one ever inhabited those houses for whose sake so many labors were undertaken, but they remained useless, never to be used. What groans do you think would come from the stones themselves, if they had sense and voice? What complaints? "Shall we be tortured thus forever? Shall we remain useless after such torments? Will there never be rest from this useless activity?" If he for whose sake the buildings exist were enjoying his purpose, it would be enough happiness for us; we would not bear these torments and agitations with grievance. But not only were we created in vain, we are also continually tortured after our creation because of you. O unhappy houses, in which our being perishes and our purpose is lost! 

Indeed, there is no doubt that this entire machine <note>The "machine of the world" or the universe.</note> would say the same things against a man who does not strive to reach his end, if there is any sense in nature. Truly, because the action of forms upon matter is well-ordered, we should not believe or say that there is an evil Author or evil matter because many evils seem to be born from it; for in truth, **nothing is evil in all of nature except sin.** All other things are to be placed among evils only by opinion, not by essence. But you will object: "What good can there be in serpents and every kind of most harmful animal?" If man could have had any benefits from them, he would have experienced them, or having experienced them...

<summary>Postel argues that "new" species arise from hidden divine seeds or spontaneous generation and explains that the suffering of the natural world (the "groaning" of creation) is caused by humanity's failure to pursue its divine purpose.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Postel’s philosophical defense of divine providence. On the previous page, he discussed the variety of species and how "monstrous" creatures are often just unknown or human-made hybrids. Here, he shifts to the problem of evil, arguing that what humans perceive as "bad"—such as venomous vipers, disease, or poverty—actually serves a greater good or acts as a necessary correction for the soul. He uses classical examples of decadence to show that wealth is only "good" if used by a virtuous person.</meta>

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK 1

...would remember those goods as much as the evils. Certainly, nothing has been created which, while remaining in its state of creation, does not easily and in many ways compensate for evils with goods. But that is not how it is seen. Ascribe this to yourself, and to your own laziness and ignorance, not to the things themselves. How many men can you name who have been bitten and killed by a viper? Very few indeed. But you may find six hundred thousand to whom an antidote derived from the viper has brought relief against other kinds of animals. If we had tried to hunt for the good things in creatures more diligently, surely nothing would be categorized as evil; rather, goodness would overcome the evil. Let us ascribe "evils" to ourselves, to our laziness and our opinions, not to the things themselves. If anything is truly evil, it must proceed from the **will** <note>original: "arbitrio." Here referring to the power of choice or free will.</note>. This, however, is absent from things, except in the case of man and the **separated substances** <note>A philosophical term for angels and demons, who lack physical bodies.</note>. 

But do you not call diseases, deaths, undeserved misfortunes, and the like—the categories of what they call "unhappiness"—evils? They certainly are, if they happen to a bad man; because for him, even the things that are not bad, but are considered good, are turned to his destruction. He uses them like diseases: just as a **dropsical man** <note>A person suffering from edema or "dropsy," where drinking water actually worsens the swelling.</note> is harmed by drink, a **plethoric man** <note>original: <term>πληθωρικὸς</term> (plethorikos); a person with an excess of bodily fluids or "humors" that causes illness.</note> by food, a greedy man by gold, a madman by a sword, or a tyrant by a kingdom. Therefore, the impious and unjust man ought to place nothing in the category of "goods," because in reality all things are evil to them—both those which are good and those which are bad. 

Others, for many reasons, hold as "good" the things that are usually considered "evils." First, death itself, which is judged the greatest of evils, is to them in the place of the highest good, and is daily longed for, so that they may depart from this change, seek peace, and live most happily. Because the impious are not persuaded of this, they think that which is the best is actually the worst. 

What should we judge concerning diseases? They are either a medicine for the body, or the soul, or both. How many kinds of disease do we see avoided by the prevention of another preceding and smaller illness? How many fevers consume those humors in us from which danger to the whole body would proceed? For what purpose are precautions, bloodlettings, cauterizations, fastings, and labors (all of which are called "evils") prescribed by wise physicians, if not so that you might flee worse things? If you see, even in the great blindness of human foresight, that disease is driven out by disease, and that by contracting smaller evils—either by our own fault or a fault of our constitution—the greatest ones are turned away and avoided, what will you judge concerning that **Divine Wisdom**? Is it not permitted for that Wisdom, like a parent, to use the switch to call her children back from error, and by a minimal affliction to drive away diseases contracted in both soul and body, and restore a lost man to himself? In truth, that which the impious are move to call "evil" may be the most excellent thing—not perhaps in itself, but as the cause of a greater good than the evil itself is. 

What shall I say of misfortunes, since here the "splendor of fortune" brings nothing besides its use? Just as we are equal in the chance of being born and dying, so we are equal in the use of things. Do you think it is worth nothing to act as a king when placed in a position of "distinguished fortune"? I approve the first part (the role/responsibility), but I disapprove the second (the "fortune"). For what do you call "distinguished fortune," unless it is the permission to devour more in one mouthful than a thousand men could in a day; and to compete in pomp and gluttony with **Sardanapalus**, **Heliogabalus**, **Cleopatra**, and monsters of that kind, born for the destruction of the state and of human affairs? <note>These figures were famous in the Renaissance as archetypes of extreme luxury, decadence, and moral failure.</note> If you are evil, then riches add to your disdain, pride, anger, insolence, and indeed a **swamp of evils** <note>original: "lernam," referring to the Lernean Hydra, a mythological monster signifying a source of endless, multiplying troubles.</note>: so that it would be far more useful for you to live in the lowest fortune. I am silent here about the sailors wandering the whole world, seeking servants for every luxury from every side, so that the lust of I-know-not-how-many wealthy men might be satisfied. For that reason, the poorer people throughout the whole world are plundered, from whose labors these things were produced. These are the "endowments" of splendor, these are the "successes": while in the meantime, that miserable man for whom these things are prepared never rests, as he tries to put a limit on his lust. 

"But," you say, "I do not wish to use wealth badly; I wish to help the needy; I am accustomed to distribute it to many." If so, what is lost to you if the task of distribution is committed to someone else? Surely the necessary use of things cannot be lacking. Therefore, misfortune cannot be among the "evils," since the use of all things is equal. If you are wicked and you lose things, it is deservedly so—either so that the things may be saved, or that you may recover your health, or both. For it is better for one who abuses things to have nothing. If you are good, you [ought] not [to think] that your distribution has been entrusted to another...

<summary>Postel argues that "evil" is a matter of perspective and human will rather than a flaw in creation. He contends that hardships like disease, death, and poverty are actually divine tools for spiritual and physical correction.</summary>

On the previous page, he argued that perceived evils are often human misconceptions or tools for spiritual correction. Here, he concludes that philosophical section by citing Plato and then begins a scientific (for the 16th century) proof of the world's beginning based on the transmutation and consumption of elements like air and fire. ->ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

you should not be troubled. If your health is only fair, you are in a sense twice as healthy due to your misfortune; for the **tool for sinning** <note>Postel suggests that physical impairments might prevent a person from committing physical sins.</note> is gone, while the tools for meeting your needs are not lacking. "I am struck in my body": the sooner you perish, the sooner you will be happy. "I am gradually consumed by a lack of things": you are all the dearer to God, who seeks out purified bodies along with souls. Therefore, unless you fail yourself, nothing should be categorized as "evil." For this reason, certain learned men have thought and affirmed that evil has no **subsistence** <note>original: "subſiſtentiam." In Platonic and Scholastic philosophy, evil is seen as a "privation" or a lack of good, rather than a thing that exists on its own.</note>. Indeed, since God is the author of things—not of "privation"—He cannot be the cause of evil. Rightly, therefore, did Plato (who is closest to the divine scriptures) write that God is not the author of evil. Since we have seen through many arguments that the world once did not exist, and that God is **pure act** <note>term: "pure act" (actus purus). A theological concept meaning God is fully realized and eternal, with no unfulfilled potential.</note>, yet free, and acting eternally in Himself without matter—neither lazy nor envious, but good through all things—it follows that He cannot be the author of evil, and that the nature of evil itself does not truly exist. It remains, then, for us to proceed to the confirmation of our argument.

### FROM THE CONTEMPLATION OF MATTER, AND FIRST, *it is proven from the nature of air that the world had a beginning.*

Although I believe I have already satisfied the requirements regarding the creation of the world by stating things that are partly necessary and partly consistent with reason (which cannot be logically refuted), I nevertheless think it should be confirmed by the following arguments. First, by considering the matter itself, which is plain to our eyes. For those things which are presented to the senses form a more powerful argument for the common people than those which are usually persuaded by reason alone. I say, therefore, that the world had a beginning and was not eternal; or, if it was not created all at once, it has more often been restored anew from its entirety—not just by the "renewal of the old" which the philosophers admit, but by the restoration and increase of matter itself. This I shall attempt to prove as follows. We see by a sensible argument that the elements are not only altered, but entirely perish through mutual action, with fire being the primary agent. The first argument will be from the **air**, which is usually consumed by fire. It was for this reason that **cupping glasses** <note>original: "cucurbitae," literally "gourds." These were bell-shaped glass vessels used by doctors to create a vacuum on the skin.</note> and **steam-balls** <note>term: "aeolipylae." An ancient pneumatic device, often a hollow sphere with pipes, used to demonstrate the power of steam or air pressure.</note> were invented by physicians and mechanics. For when fire is applied to the small amount of air held within the capacity of a cupping glass and the vessel is then sealed, the air is prohibited from escaping. Then, once that air is "devoured" and respiration is lacking, the enclosed fire dies. However much air it consumed, the nature of the fleshy body restores that amount—lest there be a **vacuum** <note>Postel refers to the ancient belief that "nature abhors a vacuum" (horror vacui).</note> within it—and thus occurs the attraction of moisture for "scarification" (as they call the process of drawing blood). That the air is almost entirely consumed is indicated by that force of attraction, which is so powerful and causes such pain that no greater force could be proven in the drawing action of forceps or any other instrument. To be sure, air can be compressed a little and forced by a heavy blast to occupy a smaller volume than its nature usually allows, as we prove with **medical cupping glasses** <note>original Greek: "σικυοις ιατρικοις" (sikuyois iatriois).</note>; by sucking the air out of them, some water is admitted, and by pressing it, it is sent out. However, that quantity is small and does not consume the substance. Fire, however, needs air so much to thrive that without the use of it, there is no fire except what is latent and potential. This is far more clearly evident in steam-balls. For the air in them is so entirely exhausted and destroyed that through a narrow hole and a tiny, barely passable pipe, they draw in as much water as the capacity of the body allows. For whatever air remains is extremely thin and very much like fire. Thus, it does not only consume the air but thins out the remainder so much that it occupies the space, unless a dense and cold body, such as water, approaches. If we can "touch with our finger" <note>An idiom meaning to experience something as an obvious, undeniable fact.</note> these things in daily experiments, do we doubt that the same thing happens in the rest of the air, and that much is consumed daily and replenished from watery matter as it gradually dissolves? That fire also needs air to act is proven by the fact that it is ignited when air is rushed and moved more violently toward it, and extinguished when air is removed. Therefore, flames are the "airy" parts resolved from water. Since these facts are established regarding the air, it is certain that it can be diminished and finally consumed, and from there, even the water and the earth. Therefore, the world would have failed long ago if it had existed from eternity; and there would have been a need [for a creator].

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.

...that it has been recreated quite often; yet no one would admit this. For if they deny that it was created even once, they will deny it all the more two or three times. But, they say, floods and great fires <note>original: "conflagrationes." Refers to the ancient philosophical idea of the world being purged by water or fire.</note> have purged it. Fire can indeed diminish things, but it cannot increase them; and the greater the fire, the more it diminishes. Water must either be multiplied from this nature, or created anew by the Creator: which alone can restore nothing, except for a certain amount of air.

### FROM EXPERIMENTS WITH WATER.

Nature must also be constrained here into a place where nothing can perish that escapes our senses, so that we may clearly see what matter undergoes when fire acts upon it—how it is altered, or whether it perishes. Let a certain quantity of water be placed in any vessel made of very solid material which admits no breathing out or leaking; and let this vessel be a distilling vessel, such as we call by the Arabic word **alenbíc** <term>alembic: a traditional distilling apparatus used in alchemy and early chemistry</term>, smeared on every side with strong clay so that no air may evaporate. Then, with fire applied beneath the vessel, let us ensure that what has fled from the fire distills into another vessel, also sealed and joined to the first so that no air escapes (even though uncompressed air does not seek the lowest points by its own motion). Then, when the water has distilled, we will see that not an eighth part remains. Therefore, the fire consumed the rest, since it could not have been consumed anywhere else but in the fire, nor could it have slipped into the lower vessel.

What of the fact that we experience the same thing daily in all boiling water, when all its parts are consumed? Must we not judge the same of the whole? For from that water which is raised into rains by the heat of the sun from the entire humid nature, it is certain that a part is consumed. This is proven by the single argument that its exhalation, which is raised on high, sometimes nourishes fires for a long time in the highest region of the air, from which various **impressions** <note>In Renaissance science, "impressions" referred to atmospheric phenomena like meteors, rainbows, and lightning.</note> are formed.

Indeed, that thick and putrid air is set on fire is evidenced by the miseries of our own bodies—as children can testify when they ignite foul flames from intestinal gas. Then, in that region of the air, one sees **comets**, **bothyni** <note>original: "bothyni." An Aristotelian term for a meteorological phenomenon resembling a pit or chasm in the sky.</note>, "beams," and countless other likenesses of things. From this come falling stars, and from this come lightning and flashes. Now, if the world were from eternity, it would have reached its end many times over.

Who does not know that from dry and burning wood, "watery tears" <note>sap or moisture</note> come out of the ends, followed by a watery and thick smoke, into whose place—once the thicker moisture is driven out—the flame immediately rushes, so that they succeed one another until the moisture has sweated out entirely. This was so thoroughly approved by many philosophers that they even affirmed (though falsely) that the stars themselves are nourished by an inferior exhalation.

This consumption and diminution of water is also seen in marshy places, where it rots and is consumed, and infects the air as if by dying, so that epidemic diseases crawl everywhere from there. It does not only perish, therefore, but does so at the expense of neighboring places. Springs vanish daily in higher places, and are found with difficulty in lower ones (though all waters naturally tend to find their level in the earth), which is a sign of diminution.

But no argument for the diminishing of waters and their daily consumption is more manifest than the fact that in many places there was once sea where there is now land; and deep water where it is now shallow. Aristotle confirms this with histories in his *Meteorology*. Indeed, I can enrich this with many examples. It is established by the elementary order that the globe of the earth naturally ought to have been surrounded on all sides by the nature of water, just like the other elements and the heavens, like the layers of eggs or onions wrapping around themselves; but it is certain that by the command of the Creator, the water receded, and not by any natural motion. For there is no "prudence" or foresight in the elements, nor could an unfeeling nature provide for the safety of living creatures.

The sea, therefore, once surrounded the whole globe, as you may see in all places. For there is no part of the earth where you cannot find the remains of all kinds of oysters (unless where the soil has rotted away), such as in the sands or in harder rocks. That surrounding was also present at the time of the **Flood** <note>original: "diluuij." Referring to the biblical Great Flood of Noah.</note>. Since that time, the earth has not been entirely enveloped. That the sea has been greatly diminished since that time, I shall prove with many histories. To me, indeed, in...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument regarding the gradual consumption and change of the physical world. On the previous page, he discussed the distillation of water to show its reduction; here, he turns to historical and geographical evidence to prove that the Earth is drying out and the sea levels are receding, contradicting the idea of a permanent, eternal world.</meta>

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
<meta>catchword: rum (of/the)</meta>

Aristotle admits as a proven fact that locations are altered; however, I shall demonstrate that they are also diminished. For now the whole world is open to us, from which we may draw a conjecture regarding the entire terrestrial globe. First, indeed, Homer testifies—and Aristotle records—that Egypt was once submerged by water; now it is partly drier than the water itself. It is evident to those people that the region of the Venetians, which they commonly call the Paduan and the Trevisan March, was once the sea. When you dig deep (even twenty miles from where the sea is now), fragments of sunken ships are found there; even in our own age, this was proven near the city of Antenor <note>original: "Antenoris urbem." This refers to Padua, which according to legend was founded by the Trojan prince Antenor.</note> when the bed for an aqueduct was being dug. This should not seem strange, since there is an eternal foundation of oak, alder, and many other woods, as some write hyperbolically. Unless the Venetians today took diligent care so that the channels were frequently cleaned to save the waterways and the city, the city of Venice would have been on dry land long ago. Ravenna, fifteen hundred years ago, was entirely similar to Venice, for it was possible to travel through it by bridges and small boats. Now, however, it stands nearly two miles from the sea—such is the power of human diligence. Venice, founded eleven hundred years ago and more, has avoided by its diligence what happened to the people of Ravenna in the same period of time. Ptolemy had diligently searched the Adriatic and Aegean seas; nevertheless, far more islands are seen in both than he, or Pliny (following Strabo), wrote about. From this, it is clear that the sea has subsided. In the lower coastal regions of Asia Minor, and likewise in Africa, the same has occurred.

And it is not only salt water in the sea that vanishes, but also marsh water. For many regions once uncultivated because of marshy ground are now inhabited, the waters having dried up. This is evident on the furthest shores of Gaul and Germany, where they turn toward the Ocean; the tides do not reach as far as they once did. In Greece itself, the arguments are the same. Mount Athos (except for the base of the Haemus mountains) was once surrounded by water; otherwise, if it had been as it is now, it would have been a promontory. No trench is seen there now, as everything has dried up. In the Peloponnese, there are very many signs of this. What was more famous than the kingdom of Tyndareus? Yet today, almost the entire peninsula is sterile, showing the very bones of the earth. What shall I say of the Argives and Mycenaeans, who showed that immense marshes dried up within a span of more or less four hundred years? The Maeotian Marsh <note>original: "Palus Maeotis." Known today as the Sea of Azov.</note> was so changed in sixty years during the time of Aristotle that it could only support ships much smaller than before; now, truly, it carries nothing but small boats, except along the channel of the river Tanais <note>The Don River.</note>.

Aristotle also grants that rivers are changed and dried up, which is certain. For in the third year before this one—that is, the year of Christ 1539—there was such a great heat in summer that many rivers in Gaul vanished, and all the water in wells sank by more than a cubit’s space. In some places, it sank by a **hexapeda** <term>hexapeda: a Roman unit of length equal to six feet</term> or a **decempeda** <term>decempeda: a ten-foot measuring rod</term>, which is a certain sign of the diminished quantity of the elements being consumed by fire. 

But they object: "We do not deny that it diminishes, but we affirm that it moves elsewhere, and that certain regions unknown to us are being flooded; just as we see the sea let in between the most famous parts of the world." I marvel at the impudence, or certainly the lazy negligence, of men who profess the knowledge of truth, yet are so accustomed to swear by the words of storytellers in certain matters that they despise the reason of things following them. If the sea was once admitted through the Pillars of Hercules <note>The Strait of Gibraltar.</note>, before it was admitted, where did the Ebro, the Rhône, the Po, the Danube, the Dnieper, the Don, the Phasis, the Thermodon, the Nile, and the Bagradas—all the greatest rivers—put their waters? One of these, the Danube, carries sixty navigable rivers with it; another, namely the Nile, runs from almost the winter tropic to our own. I say nothing of more than three hundred others, all navigable. Where, finally, did those waters go before that famous God "admitted" the sea? Hey you! Are you not ashamed of such silliness? Since all waters are necessarily positioned at a level <note>original: "ad libellam." Refers to a plumb-level or water-level used in surveying.</note> in their vicinity (for I am not ignorant that the globe is made of water and earth), how could it happen that that water did not fill the basin and the place where the sea was going...

He mocks the idea that the Mediterranean was once a dry basin before the Strait of Gibraltar opened, pointing out the impossibility of such a basin remaining empty given the flow of major rivers.</summary>

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK I.

...of the coming of that God, I believe from eternity He reserved that miracle for Himself: and the waters vanished against nature. O the vanity of **Greece**, O the madness of the philosophers who give credit to such trifles! I do not name them, lest they be noted for folly in this place. It was certainly necessary that the water always remained perfectly level <note>original: "ad libellam," meaning perfectly horizontal or according to a plumb line</note> by the command of the Creator. It is so far from being admitted from the **Ocean** into our sea <note>The Mediterranean</note> that, on the contrary, our sea overflows into the **Ocean**, and with such violence that from the **Propontis** <note>The Sea of Marmara</note> it drives mills of every kind with a most rapacious force.

This is the reason why the nature of the **Ocean’s** reciprocal tide is not seen in our sea—the source of so many disputes among philosophers. The force of our overflowing waters wards off the tides of the **Ocean**, preventing them from meeting except in the very straits. For at the **Columns of Hercules** <note>The Strait of Gibraltar</note> the tide is almost equal to the **Ocean**. Further inland, near **Spain** and the **Mauritanias** <note>The coastal regions of North Africa</note>, it gradually diminishes, so that the greatest tide at **Rome** and **Carthage** seems barely a foot and a half. In **Venice**, when the Adriatic wind blows, it is a little greater; otherwise, it usually rises barely half a foot. In the **Pontic Sea** <note>The Black Sea</note> and the **Propontis**, it is not even felt, except when the south winds blow in the **Propontis** and it rises by the thickness of a span <note>A "spithama," or the distance between the thumb and little finger, roughly 9 inches</note>.

Now, therefore, water is not admitted [into the Mediterranean], but is sent out. How could a falsehood persist so long? It is restored by the mixing of the other, replacing what might be lost from the fresh waters. Thus it is saltier at the mouth than in the recesses. Because of this, along the entire shore of the **Ocean**, water is dried into salt by the power of the sun, which does not happen inland beyond **Italy**. Yet it is established that water is sometimes admitted into the land. I do not deny that it is sent in by the force of a storm or the will of the Creator as a punishment for crimes, but if it happens by natural movement, it immediately recedes, as it seems, after a few years. For that quantity of water which has already been lost over so many thousands of years in our world—since the waters themselves, when calm and quiet from the agitation of winds, are set at a level—ought to overflow in a perpetual course, now these people, now those, so that nothing would be more familiar than a flood. Or at least in certain places, it would rise in a mound and exceed the level, neither of which is seen. Therefore, it is consumed.

You will say that floods do not recede immediately, for the island of **Atlantis**, once located before the **Columns of Hercules**, perished in a deluge. This is an excellent **Egyptian** fiction <note>original: "commentum," meaning a fabrication or invention</note>, and unworthy of what **Plato** left written in the *Critias* <note>Postel refers to the "Atlanticus," a common alternative title for Plato’s Critias</note> and the *Timaeus*—he who was otherwise quite far from the rashness of asserting falsehoods. As if, indeed, that which is no longer visited has perished, or perhaps never existed. 

But suppose it did exist, and that **Plato** spoke the truth to grant his fellow citizens an ancient origin. There is even today a very large continent, a part of the furthest end of **Asia** seeking the west through the antipodes from the east. It is certainly very wide, and beyond the memory of all literature (unless he understood this place), it was opened in our time by the efforts of the kings of **France**, **Portugal**, and **Spain**, and surveyed; and it did not perish. <note>Postel is arguing that the "New World" (America) discovered by European kings is actually the "Atlantis" mentioned by Plato, and is a continuation of Asia rather than a sunken island.</note> But it is necessary that the **Egyptian** fiction, or **Plato’s** authority, places it a little further from the straits of **Hercules**. Certainly, since it extends from pole to pole, it cannot fail to be set against the strait of our sea. Therefore, nothing was submerged there. 

Who would deny that certain cities are swallowed up, shaken by earthquakes, and finally enveloped by waters? Yet these things happen more frequently in low and humble places. Elsewhere, after a short interval of time, the waters recede into their bed, which even **Greek** trifling <note>original: "nugacitas," meaning nonsense or triviality</note> will not deny. For the floods that **Greece** imagined for itself, it devised in imitation of the divine flood [of Noah] about which it had heard. In every matter, **Greece** has been nothing but an ape of others' discoveries—and truly an ape, which is to say, a distorter. Therefore, it would have been necessary for that mass of water to immediately start floods elsewhere from that place, especially in our sea, which is not capable of containing such a mass. I am easily led to believe that divine providence (for otherwise it cannot happen by natural motion) punished those peoples with a deluge of waters—those who were to pervert the world with false opinions and become instruments of demons. But these things are enough to make it clear that the waters lost from here do not turn into floods, but are gradually consumed by exhalations, while they are dissolved into air; the air itself is the fuel for flaming fire. From which both by the air and by...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument against the "eternity of the world"—the Aristotelian idea that the universe has always existed in its current form. Having previously discussed the behavior of water, he now turns to the physical decay of the earth itself to prove it must have had a beginning.</meta>

ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

The nature of water makes it clear that the world has not existed from eternity; for if it had, it would have been consumed long ago.

### FROM THE CONTEMPLATION OF THE EARTH.

We perceive by our senses that the Earth is constantly perishing by the force of rains, and is being dragged elsewhere by the course of torrents and rivers, gradually vanishing until it is finally left behind like naked bones; those regions neighboring torrents and rivers serve as examples of this. For we see that something is eroded every year, a fact which even **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE) argued for an eternal universe, but acknowledged local changes like erosion.</note> himself does not deny. It would follow, then, that if these same actions had lasted from eternity, the earth would have perished many times over; and since it exists now, it must have been created anew. 

The philosophers do not wish to concede this based on this single argument because they cannot conceive in their minds what God Himself, who is *self-originated* <note>original: αὐτοφυής (*autophyēs*), meaning self-grown or existing by His own nature</note>, could have been doing hidden for so long in that eternal vastness before creation. Indeed, if they wished to be fair evaluators of the reason they claim to seek, they would find it far more difficult to conceive how the world itself—whose parts are utterly perishing—could persist for so long in the nature of things, than to conceive that the eternal Providence, happy in Himself and needing nothing, could have existed from eternity without this dross-filled matter. 

Come, let us learn by example, so that we may understand infinite things from finite ones. Suppose someone builds a sheepfold, a hut, a hovel <note>original: *mapale*, a term for a portable North African hut</note>, or anything else that is unstable by its material nature, and whose parts we see perishing every day with our own eyes. Because of the instability of the material, we would judge that the house has suffered since its beginning and could not last for even ten years. 

If someone then asserted that the house had already lasted for a full fifty years, because the one who built it is of an age where he could have built it that long ago, which would you more easily conceive? Since the author is free and was not forced to build it, is it easier to believe the house has lasted fifty years alongside its author, or that the author lived happily by himself for forty years without the house, and only then built that fragile dwelling? If you say you cannot grasp that reasoning, I shall appeal to the consensus and judgment of the whole world. 

But they burn so much with the desire to corrupt the truth that while they confess God in words and recognize Him in His works and effects, they deny His existence with all their effort, their writings, their words, and the very tenor of their lives. For if they acknowledged Him as omnipotent, most perfect, free, unconstrained, infinite, most happy, and as a perpetual act moving all things within Himself (whether they exist or not)—as they are forced to confess in words—they would never join this matter to Him as if it were necessary for His completion. For His happiness is the same before matter was created, and after it was created, and after it is changed and purified or released from action. They wish to add the mass of matter as a "perfection" to the Most Perfect. 

O stupid and blind men! How rightly our **Paul** <note>Saint Paul the Apostle</note>, who was conscious of the secrets of heaven, said: *Wishing to be wise, they became fools, and they vanished in their own thoughts, and their foolish heart was seized by madness.* For when they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God. Therefore *the wisdom of the flesh is death, an enemy to God.* <note>Postel is paraphrasing Romans 1:21-22 and Romans 8:6-7.</note>

Since, therefore, it is established that the earth itself gradually perishes, one must necessarily judge that eternity is lacking to it by its very nature. Otherwise, the mass of the four elements would have already vanished: the caves of the earth are constantly dripping water, vapors are daily extracted from the earth by the work of the sun, water turns into air, and air is consumed by fire (since the fuel and base of flames is present). Nothing would have remained long ago. 

But when I assert (as is plain to the senses) that the mountains themselves are gradually eroded and perish by the flow of waters and other injuries of time, and that the slopes are washed and wiped clean by rains, that circumcised <note>original: *recutitus*, a Latin term often used polemically to refer to Jewish writers, here Philo of Alexandria.</note> **Philo** will object to me. I wonder that he, though imbued with the decree of the Holy Law, should wish to depart from that decree because of these trifles which he ascribes to **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BCE), a successor to Aristotle. Philo discusses his views in 'On the Eternity of the World'.</note>. "It is true," he says, "that mountains are eroded and consumed; but meanwhile, by the force of fire enclosed in the earth, others are born as the fire attempts to break out. Thus they emerge as the fire exits, with the earth itself following the erupting fire." 

O invention worthy of Theophrastus! Thus they attribute their trifles to great authors when they wish to lie with impunity. Who would believe that so learned a disciple of Aristotle, whom Aristotle [left in charge] of the school...

# THE BOOK OF GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.

...chosen to govern the most excellent things, has he arrived at such impudence against his teacher’s decrees as to assert that the flow of the earth follows the motion of fire? Indeed, one can admit that a violent motion in the air drags another thing along with it—fire dragging fire, and perhaps water dragging water—to avoid a vacuum <note>original: *fuga vacui*, the "horror vacui" or belief that nature does not allow for empty space</note>. But who is so impudent as to think that the earth, which is solid and hard in body, suffers the same? Truly, let him have his opinions, the argument for his judgment. Mountains are accustomed to be dissolved daily by active fire, and everything to be broken; he claims [the earth] is born and consists from the same fire, even though active fire cannot exist except in matter, such as in sulfurous substances. We see this in Iceland, Sicily, Mount Vesuvius, and many parts of the world, where fire does not bind things together, but consumes them. That distinguished man could not discern the difference between potentiality and actuality <note>Postel is using the Aristotelian terms *potentia* and *actus* to distinguish between the capacity for something to happen and its physical reality</note>. There is indeed something of a spiritual fire mixed into the whole bond of earthly nature; through this, by restorations <note>original: *refudationibus*, referring to the cycling or "pouring back" of matter</note> and vegetation, all things are created in the earth with the spirit mediating. But as for that fire ever breaking out or applying such force [to move the earth], it is far from the case.

But I move to other things: **The invention of the arts.** For it is established both that the earth is consumed and that the objections of **Philo** <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Jewish philosopher who wrote on the eternity of the world</note> are frivolous. How does it happen that the invention of arts emerges daily, and that all things were not long ago either handed down by hand or produced in writings? Even necessary things are of new invention, created by men only recently deceased. Various types of crops emerge daily; species of fruits are seen through human ingenuity helping nature, and are added to natural power. What more? General floods (they will say) and conflagrations take away all memory of men. Then, everything must be repeated and learned anew from the first principles. Therefore, all would be equal to that power, and if there are those with greater genius, they would be more excellent.

How does it happen then that the **Greeks**—a race of men fortunately born, and to whom (as **Aristotle** wished it written) the best powers of heaven, soil, genius, and bodies were never lacking—did not find all those things which serve to enrich human life and nature long before other mortals, especially the **Athenians**? Why did religion, arts, and letters, previously unknown, reach the Greeks a thousand years after the "barbarians" (as they called the **Chaldeans**, and the **Magi**, **Egyptians**, **Prophets**, and that sort)? Whence did that opinion arise, that as many as were distinguished in Greece went to the barbarians for the sake of learning? This was observed in Athens 1,500 years ago, where that divine force of genius (which is surpassed by the barbarians) is taught and formed.

Therefore, since after the general flood of **Deucalion** (the name by which the Greeks changed the name of **Noah**, lest they seem to have drawn anything from foreigners), the condition of all men was equal—and since the barbarians are considered more unrefined than the Greek authors—how could it be that they possessed so many kinds of the greatest disciplines so much time before? <term>“Greeks, Greeks, you are always children, nor is there in you any ancient learning.”</term> <note>Postel quotes a famous passage from Plato's *Timaeus* where an Egyptian priest tells the Greek Solon that his people lack historical depth.</note> It was necessary, therefore, that those men were survivors of the flood, as the sacred scriptures hold, and that they received those disciplines from their ancestors; these were immediately cultivated and from there gradually diffused into the whole world over many subsequent centuries.

But those same people whose decrees must necessarily be believed [the Hebrews] handed down that the world had an origin, and that the sciences of divine things were given by the deity before their time. Posterity found the other arts, which were not as necessary for life, with necessity acting as the teacher. But those earlier people learned everything by the aids of things received from their fathers. From them afterwards the Greeks learned, and from them the Latins. Since, therefore, they had been survivors of the waters in **Asia**, they had certain knowledge of past events. Therefore the "humane arts," which the prior age (occupied with better, divine things) had not yet discovered, were still hidden at that time. Therefore, the world had a beginning. The philosophers must therefore subscribe to the sacred authority which handed these things down without added reason; these things must be true, seeing as reason, when laboriously sought, leads us there even against our will. But enough regarding the world for now. For where all things in it are seen to be corruptible and recent, it is established that it had an origin.

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

### THAT THE WORLD WAS CREATED FROM NOTHING. Chapter V.

Whoever admits that the world depends upon a cause, and that God is above the nature of all things, and is *self-sufficient*, *self-originated*, and *blessed* <note>original Greek: αὐταρκῆ (self-sufficient), αὐτοφυᾶ (self-produced), εὐδαίμονα (blessed)</note>—to put it in one word, blessed in every part—does not need to be persuaded that the world was brought into being from nothing. If, however, one must argue with someone who removes cause and providence from the universe, such a person is not moved by their own senses, nor does he admit necessary reason, nor does he approve the authority of any name or judgment, however great. He follows nothing but his own dreams; certainly, the effort would be wasted, like "beating the air." Therefore, so that some light may be added to the obscurity of the preceding matters, and so that the nature of truth may gradually reveal itself, we shall treat these things. For we shall confirm for good and pious men those things which have already been handed down, and we shall pave the way for what follows. So that this may be done more easily, all the causes of things must be recounted again.

There are, therefore, two kinds of causes and "co-causes." The **Primary** causes, without which the secondary cannot exist, are first the **Agent** (or Providence) and the **End** <note>The "End" refers to the *telos* or final purpose for which a thing exists</note>. The **Co-causes** are those so annexed to things that they can in no way exist without them: namely, **Matter** and **Form**. The metaphysician considers the first and second; the mathematician and the craftsman consider the second and third. Although, therefore, the secondary causes cannot exist without the effect of the primary ones, it is not always necessary for them to be joined. For although a house is not made without the mind and labor of a craftsman, nor except for the sake of some use, yet a constructed house can be destitute of the craftsman’s presence and remain uninhabited. However, unless there is a certain form of habitation, and made from some kind of matter, it is no longer a house.

Concerning the reason of the universe, the same must be judged: that there is one Craftsman, by whom matter is spread beneath the form itself for the sake of a certain end. If, therefore, there is a **First Mover** and a **Providence** of the universe, as there necessarily is, then He created all things from nothing. For if He held material that was already formed beforehand, He is not the **First Cause**. Since nothing exists without a cause, that matter—whether formed or unformed—would have to come from another cause, and that from another, and so on into infinity. Thus, there would be no First Cause, which is most absurd. But perhaps that matter originated from itself? Yet it is impossible for anything to create itself. It must be—if it is not from nothing—that it is from another, or from itself, or is a part of God and the First Cause. The first two are false, and therefore so is the third. For that "part of God" would then be creating itself, which is absurd; it would mean God makes matter, and that the most Simple Being is made divisible. Therefore, the matter and bulk of the world were fashioned from nothing.

Yet the mind does not grasp how something is made from nothing. It cannot grasp it because our knowledge is "nocturnal" <note>Postel uses a common medieval metaphor: human intellect is like an owl’s eyes, which are blinded by the bright sun of divine truth but see well in the "dim light" of material things</note>, proceeding from the things less known by nature (if indeed there is any difference in knowing) toward things better known to itself through material experiments. Accustomed to this globe of the world, the mind cannot grasp what it has not seen by example. However, from those things which daily reach our senses—and which we would never have believed before we saw them—we clearly recognize that if we compare the part unknown to us with the known, we know plainly nothing of the whole universe, if you look at the reason of the whole.

But we know the four principles from which all things come: namely, *that is a task for the powers above* <note>original: "is superis labor est," likely a variation on Virgil's "hic labor est," implying a task of divine difficulty</note>. For we know all things just like a man who, because he knew the elements of the alphabet of any language, would profess knowledge of all the sciences written in those characters. He could perhaps read all the syllables and words of the letters, but judge for yourselves what he would gain. So the philosophers, because they know that fire is hot and dry, earth is cold and dry, air is hot and moist, and water is cold and moist—as if reciting a natural history—they think they can know by what reason it is so, or how many species can come from it. First of all, they will never know the **why** <note>original Greek: τὸ διότι (to dioti), the underlying rational cause or "the wherefore"</note>, and they will never recognize it except through admiration of Providence; and if they do recognize it, it will happen in such a way that they conceive it in the mind but cannot explain it in words. The rest they will learn by the experiments of the senses. And they wonder if they do not grasp how that God—who in His goodness submitted these things to our eyes for His own honor and praise, and gave us the senses by which we might know them—could 

<meta>catchword: have [been able to]</meta>

<summary>Postel argues that the universe must have been created from nothing ("ex nihilo") by a First Cause, as any other explanation leads to an impossible infinite regress. He explains that human difficulty in grasping this concept stems from the limitations of our sensory-based intellect, which he compares to an owl's nocturnal vision.</summary>
