<meta>This page continues Postel’s metaphysical defense of creation. He is finishing a thought from the previous page regarding the ability of the Creator to produce something from nothing (ex nihilo), and then moves into an empirical illustration involving plant growth.</meta>

<header>WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK I.</header>

...could produce something from nothing. Although there is no example among lower things <note>The "lower things" refers to the physical, earthly realm as opposed to the divine</note> by which it can be shown to the senses that something is made from nothing, I will nevertheless provide an example that is as close to nature as possible. Take three thousand pounds—or any other weight—of fertile earth; soak it with water as much as you can before you weigh it, so that it is at its maximum state of heaviness, to which nothing of the same quantity and kind can be added to make it heavier. From this, make a "hanging garden" <note>A container or raised bed</note>, placing stone, metal, or any other body underneath it which will for a very long time prevent communication with other earth, and ensure that nothing perceptible is lost. Then, sow seeds—any kind of seed, but especially those of a luxuriant nature—in that garden, so that you may complete the experiment more quickly. Every year, collect the leaves, the stalks, and the fruits; weigh them, and you will certainly see that before many years have passed, you have taken a great part of the weight away from that garden. Weigh the watered soil again, just as before, and you will find nothing diminished in it. Consider, therefore, from where those fruits came to you, since nothing at all was lost from the earth. But you will say: "It proceeded from the air and the rains; it grew through the watering." It is certain that Moses did not without reason leave it written: *And the spirit of the Lord was carried over the waters* <note>original Latin: "Et spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas." A reference to Genesis 1:2.</note>. For although the <term>four elements</term> <note>Earth, Water, Air, and Fire—the classical building blocks of matter</note> concur in the generation of all things, nevertheless water claims such a large part for itself in everything that the work of the others, if compared to it, does not appear; and it carries matter from elsewhere through parts that escape the other senses. But if you give those things which grew for you (while the earth was not diminished) to fire—the purifier of all things—there is no doubt that there will be a large quantity of ash, especially if you planted trees or shrubs. Now, philosophers confess that ashes are "pure earth." For although the action of fire consumes the water and the air, and even if it diminishes the earth somewhat, it cannot destroy it entirely. See, then, from where that earth comes to you, since you blocked the path from neighboring earth and none of your own was lost. Certainly, you would say it was created from nothing, were we not dealing with the material part of the world. Enter into a reasoning from this example, O lover of truth and true wisdom, and place the whole nature of things before your eyes; you will see many things indeed created as if from nothing. Or at least, if they are not created from nothing, you will never grasp how a thick and sensible body creeps into the composition of nature. Do not, therefore—do not, out of your ignorance—attack God with your blasphemies or diminish His power, since it far surpasses those things which you know. For your "knowing" is merely reciting His works.

## THAT GOD CARES EVEN FOR
### particulars. Chapter VI.

Not a few philosophers, although they confess that <term>Providence</term> <note>Divine guidance or care</note> gives a beginning to human affairs, and even if they acknowledge it against their will, nevertheless remove it from the care of the universe. They believe that after things have been produced, God cares no more whether they preserve their being well or ill than a craftsman who, having finished a work, is then accustomed to neglect it. But this view is held with too little accurate consideration of things. For when we, by our art, apply a certain form to any matter, it remains by the strength of the matter, according to the nature of the thing, the place, and the time, so that there is no need for our industry in its principal parts. For it is not within our power to determine how long it can last, except when parts are usually changed by the injury of time and place. And when we restore something, we do so using matter taken from nature, which is destined to last in that work for a prescribed time. We, who are so <term>corruptible</term> <note>Subject to decay and change</note>, require rest, motion, and alterations; but since divine Providence is <term>pure act</term> <note>original Latin: "purus actus." A philosophical term meaning God is fully realized being, without potentiality or need for change</note>, never resting, without doubt an immense power—either mediated or immediate—always rests upon the matter itself. If the world consisted entirely of stone, or any thick matter which, even if it had no sensation, nevertheless participated in elementary matter, then once the parts of these bodies were bound together, it could remain for some time as far as the things...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument for a divinely ordered universe. Having used the example of plant growth to show how life seems to emerge from "nothing" (or rather, from the invisible power of God), he now describes the "Great Chain of Being"—the hierarchical structure of all created things—and moves into a philosophical defense of God's omniscience, citing both Greek and Islamic philosophers.</meta>

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
### BOOK I

...would be dissolved and remain at rest. However, beyond the fact that things lacking sensation are usually created gradually—some by addition, others by connection—so that we may everywhere recognize the traces of a divinity who is always active, He willed that far more perfect things should come forth into the light. These things serve as a sort of foundation, and He placed others upon them, until the fourth level was reached.

For certain things in the whole of nature are exceedingly coarse and devoid of life; these we say simply "exist" <note>Postel is using the philosophical distinction of "being" (esse) vs "living" (vivere)</note>, such as the elements themselves, stones, gems, metals, and other things which we see consist mostly of earth and water; these do not exist for their own sake. 

In the next rank are those things conceived from seeds which—by the power and presence of God and the seed previously sown—draw nourishment from those first elements. They live and rise up in a greater mass until they reach the cycle of their own nature and serve the following rank. 

This third rank, besides life, also possesses sensation and motion. It grows by that same power until it reaches the end of its life or usefulness. This end is not found within itself (for it is certain that things and their purposes are always different) but is found in the following rank, and attains its purpose in the greatest of all mortal things. 

This fourth step, embracing all four natures, exists with the stones, lives with the plants and animals, and feels with the sentient creatures: this is **Man**, the goal <note>original: "scopus," meaning the target or aim</note> of all nature. Since man could not have been created for his own sake, he must necessarily have his end in a more sublime level. Therefore, besides the soul common to other living creatures, he is endowed with an immortal intellect, by which he can frequently contemplate the heavens, the origin of souls, and God. His chief end in this life is mutual labor with other men as if they were brothers; in the future life, it is the knowledge of God and the perfect vision of all things within Him.

Thus, the "Efficient Cause" <note>The force or agent that brings something into being</note> of all things, creating all things for His own sake, then returns their purpose to them when man passes into and dwells within the recognition of his Creator. Does it seem possible that this order could endure, even in the smallest things or for a moment of an hour, unless that Moderator were perpetually present—preserving and binding forms into matter and caring for all things? Certainly, it is impossible. For dying nature would never be replaced unless a preserving form were always present, commanded to be there by the Creator. 

Therefore, because these things can never subsist by themselves if deprived of a ruler, **Plato** rightly said that they "are not." He asks at the beginning of the *Timaeus*: *“What is that which is always becoming and never is? And what is that which always is and never becomes?”* <note>original Latin: "Quid est quod semper nascitur, & nunquã est: aut quod nunquã nascitur, & semper est?" Postel is quoting a central tenet of Platonic metaphysics: physical things are always changing (becoming) and thus lack true "Being," whereas the divine is eternal and unchanging.</note> By those things which are "always becoming" and never subsist, he means these lower individual things which truly never exist by themselves. Forms, however, although they are never seen except in matter, are nevertheless always "being"; thus God is everywhere.

If there is a need for authorities to confirm these reasons, no philosopher from the entire body of the Gentiles <note>Non-Christian/Pagan philosophers</note> will be found wanting (except perhaps for the **Atomists** <note>original: "ἀτομόλογοι" (atomologoi), those who believe the world is made of random collisions of atoms</note> and the **Epicureans**), not even **Averroes** <note>original: "Aben reis" (Ibn Rushd). Postel considers him a difficult or "unjust" critic of divinity, yet still useful for his argument.</note>, who is as hostile to God as one can be. 

Therefore, we must see what he thinks regarding the knowledge of God. For unless God knew all things, and understood them all simultaneously and at once through a single act of knowledge, He could not have care for all things. Averroes speaks of this in many places, but most especially in his work against **Al-Ghazali** <note>original: "Algezelem." This refers to Averroes' "The Incoherence of the Incoherence," a rebuttal to Al-Ghazali's "The Incoherence of the Philosophers."</note>, from which I more gladly take authority because he is unwilling to grant even the most reasonable points to his opponent. In the sixth discussion, in the solution to the third object, he says: 

> "It is not impossible for a multitude of knowable things to be contained within the knowledge of God, which exists as one and the same. For the philosophers prove that God knows Himself, and furthermore, other changeable things." 

And a little later: 

> "Knowledge in God is **actual**; ours is **potential** and dependent on the object, which must not be admitted in God. However, the human intellect cannot be informed as to the *manner* of God's knowledge." 

And elsewhere: 

> "God's knowledge is neither universal nor particular, for we measure the quality of His knowledge by power, not by [human] science." 

But so that we may explain this difficulty a little more easily, we must first set forth the divisions of things as they are produced by causes, so that we may weigh—since God knows all things—of which things He is the **Author**, and of which He is the **Permitter**. In the universe, there are four "Efficient Causes": **Nature**, **Art**, **Fortune**, and **Divine Providence**. The first and the last are the same...

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.

...since nature itself possesses neither will nor motion on its own. Therefore, since things exist by nature, they demonstrate that they have God as their author and protector through every single detail in a perpetual order. Whatever occurs by fortune or outside of divine judgment—though with God himself permitting it—God also knows. Likewise, He knows those things done by us, whether good or evil, which I categorize as human skill and industry. Therefore, nothing can be placed in a state of being unknown to Him. 

But **Alexander** <note>original: "Alexander." Likely Alexander of Aphrodisias (c. 200 AD), a famous commentator on Aristotle who argued that God's providence only covers universal species, not individual "particular" people or events.</note> and those who, due to the perceived impropriety of it, wish to strip God of the knowledge of particulars, will object: if they make God know all things, they say it is an "impious" claim, because it would mean He sees so many impious crimes and yet turns a blind eye. A "fine" conclusion! <note>Postel is being sarcastic here.</note> If the servant of a prince should administer affairs poorly while the prince knows of it (whom anger—which God lacks—urges toward vengeance), would the prince not immediately take up arms against him and his associates for all those wicked acts? 

Is not the **freedom of choice** <term>libertas arbitrij</term> always present in that servant, so that he might be able to come to his senses and become better after his errors? Is it not just as metals, after they have contracted and then been cleansed of the **rust** <note>original: "rubiginem." Postel uses the cleaning of metal as a metaphor for the purification of the soul through suffering or discipline.</note> they have from the mines themselves, are more refined? Furthermore, since everyone overflows with and is driven by vices—stemming from the "disease" of both physical matter and habit—who would not rather wait for the **catastrophe** <note>original: "catastrophen." In classical drama, the 'catastrophe' is the final resolution or unraveling of the plot; Postel means the end of a person's life.</note> of life, so that he who persisted in acting wickedly until that point cannot be excused? 

Would these vengeances not be more praiseworthy in a good and honest man? How much more should this be approved in God, who is the height of gentleness and kindness? He cannot be impious or unjust simply because He sees, knows, and permits these things. For there will be a place for **rendering an account**; whether you believe it or not, you must undergo it. There you will know God not as unjust, but as most just. 

But this objection belongs to those who think God is unjust because they judge that the minds of men die after fate <note>meaning after death</note>, and they marvel that God has not exacted the punishments for their impiety. The fact that He sees things made by Himself and by nature is no obstacle, even though to our own recklessness certain things in them seem evil; nevertheless, it is certain that nothing is evil in them that cannot be compensated for many times over by its utility. 

In the first place, they will set down—I know for certain—that many human bodies are defective from birth, such as in their limbs, or even that they lack the use of their intellect. They will assert that this is unjust and that no utility is gained from it, and that great misery is inflicted upon the one having those defects; if God knows this, they say, He is unjust. 

But if God shows His power in one or two people, to show how He could also have formed *you*, if He had wished—and indeed the whole human race—what injustice does there seem to be to you, since nothing of **eternal happiness** is lost for that person, even if they have an unsuitable body? To others, a comparison with their own happiness is provided, along with innumerable other benefits. Indeed, it is the highest equity to be "unjust" in this way. 

Come now, is the **master of a household** <term>paterfamilias</term> unjust if, out of many servants of equal merit, he should according to his own judgment depress some to lowly tasks and elevate others? And if he uses one out of many as an example for the rest? Not at all; because by his own right he is permitted to allow that which seems evil in appearance, whenever a greater utility flows from it to the **whole flock**. 

We deny that this is just only because we are ignorant; and also because we remember the bad things but forget the benefits of God, if we have perhaps gained anything from the use, form, deformity, or nature of creatures. This cause has led many to deny that **providence** either exists or cares for human affairs. These are idle men, unskilled in the nature of things, who do not notice that it is not the case that no law or right is implanted in the souls of men by nature, or that there are no laws among men, simply because unjust judges overturn the laws or the crafty pervert the right by means of the law. 

For he would be plainly foolish who would conclude such a thing. Divine providence does not exact punishments in this world; it wishes to give deserved punishments when there is no longer a place for **repentance**. Otherwise, since all things were made for the sake of man, he would be nothing after this life, whether he acted well or ill after so many hardships. And since the lowest things have their own ends, shall the most excellent thing—the one second only to God in order—lack an end? It cannot be. Those things which happen by chance, since they come from the necessity of matter, are not "evil." Properly speaking, therefore, that which is evil comes from the **will** <note>original: "arbitrio"</note>, for the violation of which one must pay the

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...deserved punishments: thus wickedness is farthest removed from God, since that which they call "unjust" is actually the most illustrious property of the entire divinity. Furthermore, God does not preside over this moderation of particular things alone, but he also sends "separate substances" <note>original: "substantias separatas," a philosophical term for angels or purely spiritual beings that exist apart from physical matter</note> who are good to assist. However, he frequently permits evil ones to be present among men, kingdoms, and places; the ancients called these **Genii** <note>original: "Genios." In Roman religion, these were protective spirits or tutelary deities of a person or place.</note>. Concerning these, I will treat immediately after adding some authorities from the philosophers to prove my assumption. Aristotle, in the second book of *On Natural Things*, or *Physics* <note>original: "Naturalis auscultationis"</note>, says the following:

> In those things where there is some end, the earlier and later steps are performed for the sake of that end. Therefore, as a thing is meant to be, so it is born to be; and as it is usually made, so it is always made, unless something hinders it. It is made, however, for the sake of something. Therefore, it is born to be for the sake of this end. For if a house were among those things that occur by nature, it would be made in the same way as it is now made by art. But if those things which are of nature were made not only by nature but also by art, they would be made in the same way as they are born to be made. For one is the cause of the other, and art performs all those things which nature cannot, yet it nevertheless imitates nature. If, therefore, things made by art are for the sake of some purpose, it is certainly established that natural things are also made for the sake of some end.

And a little later:

> Just as art is sometimes frustrated in its end, so also is nature by the fault of the material; or rather, nature sometimes (though rarely) does not achieve its end, etc.

From these points I infer that an **efficient cause** <term>causa efficiens: the primary source of change or rest; the 'maker' of a thing</term> is required for created or artificial things for as long as it takes for them to receive their completion. Even all the parts of things which ought to be present for the completion of any thing must necessarily be known and adapted by the "acting cause" until the completed work arises; otherwise, nothing would ever be finished. Therefore, for as long as the construction of any work lasts, it is necessary for the artistic cause to be present, knowing, and completing the work. Since, therefore, the world is perpetually in motion and in action, and will not be "completed" until the very last human being of the world is born, has lived, and has acknowledged God, it is most certain—by these accepted premises—that God knows even the smallest particulars. 

For if He were to leave this work even once (which cannot happen), it would remain imperfect, since the parts that lead to its completion would not yet have been applied to it. And so, since its parts pass away at every moment, they have need of healing through "perpetual restoration and innovation" (as the philosophers say); but this cannot happen without a knowledge of all the parts. Truly, if so many errors and imperfections occur, how can it be that that most wise Judge, knowing all things, does not heal those imperfections? 

The reason is this: He created **Matter** <term>materia</term> to be a follower of **Forms** <term>forma: the internal principle that gives a thing its specific identity and characteristics</term>, as I have already said, but in such a way that it always carries the evidence of its own nature. For if He had made matter as perfect as the Form He generated (which He certainly could have done), He would have rendered it unsuited to be a "subject" <note>The underlying material that receives a shape</note>, and would have made every species created from it eternal. From this, all things would have been eternal and unique, just like the Forms themselves. Or, if by the will of the Creator other things not subject to corruption had been produced over time, then the elements would have been entirely solid bodies, gathered into a heap without mutual use or order; and once those were completed, God would have been "powerless" to create further. All of these things are unworthy of the Creator. 

It was necessary, therefore, to have left imperfection in matter until the world is purified. Therefore, that imperfection of matter—caused by the slowness or speed of motion and its own nature—causes it not always to be disposed to the Forms. This happens by no fault or ignorance of the Form or the Creator, but by the "flux" of matter and the concurrence of external causes; and since these are placed in the realm of chance, they cannot be numbered. From the preceding arguments, therefore, we hold that God knows and creates particulars, and that He tolerates and permits evils but is not their author. Nor is there one God who is the cause of good and another who is the cause of evil, as some have foolishly claimed <note>This refers to Manichaeism or similar dualistic heresies</note>, whom Aristotle hisses off the stage in the 3rd and 12th books of his *Metaphysics*. Furthermore, that which we categorize as "evil" is not truly evil unless it proceeds from human choice. For that a man must die who is destined to die at some time, or that houses will catch fire which are destined to fall at some time, and...

GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.

...that fortunes gathered over a long time should perish and be scattered, or that they will eventually cease to exist or perpetually change masters—all these things we falsely judge to be "evils." But the one who willfully and intentionally commits murder, sets fire to a home, kidnaps, rapes, plunders, and other such crimes: that person has truly sinned most gravely and committed an evil. He has fallen away from the Creator's favor, and unless he repents <note>original: "resipiscat," literally meaning to "recover one's senses" or "return to a right mind"</note>, he will pay eternal penalties. Therefore, nothing prevents God from knowing these things and tolerating them as if by looking the other way. For otherwise, as we have already said, because of the crafty tricks <note>original: "uaframenta"</note> of men, He would scarcely be worshiped by anyone in the world. For man is of such a depraved will that if God were to punish him every time he sinned, the human race would have vanished long ago. A ruler prefers to wait for improvement rather than to act with cruelty toward his subjects.

Nevertheless, God also permits the most grave punishments to be inflicted upon men—by the works of demons <note>original: "dæmonũ," referring here to spiritual agents of harm</note> who bring it about—firstly through ignorance of their own God, and then through diseases of the body, the devastation of kingdoms, the plundering of provinces, plagues, famines, and wars. No one should doubt that all these things are born from the merits <note>or "deserts," meaning what people have earned through their actions</note> of men. For God permits these things to happen so that we might return to the path of innocence; this is usually done only by those who are afflicted and divinely inspired, not by those who are fortunate.

### ON SEPARATE SUBSTANCES, OR
-> spirits, or Genies. CHAPTER VII. <-

In no matter has there been greater dispute, greater obscurity, or less agreement of opinions than when the discussion among philosophers turns to demons or separate substances <note>original: "substantijs separatis," a technical term in Scholastic philosophy for beings like angels who exist as pure intellect without physical bodies</note>. For our ignorance of unknown things tends to pull us in one direction, while various observable effects pull us in another. Therefore, this section must be reached and treated more diligently, precisely because it is more difficult. I will place the reasons in the first position; in the following order, I will rely on the authority of learned men; then, I will argue from the universal consensus of all nations. Finally, I will come to the effects and experiences, which are innumerable. If we can truly grasp anything regarding these higher substances, it will surely be far more pleasant than the greatest knowledge of lower things, as Aristotle says. For he says in the second book of *On the Heavens and the Earth*: "When we grasp certain celestial things through demonstration, it happens that we rejoice exceedingly." Even if these reasons do not fall under the senses, they will still be usefully received as if they were fully proven. Just as many things are proposed to be believed by the unskilled and by great men alike concerning God and other harmless matters—things which it is very helpful to believe—having been proven by the simple authority and consensus of men.

<margin>From reason.</margin>
1. Just as we have found the truth up to this point from the contemplation of all nature and the comparison of things and causes to one another, so it seems we must act here as well. Aristotle demonstrates it from the motion of the heaven in this way: Every motion that is unfailing in itself comes from a mover who is moved neither by itself nor by accident <note>term: "per accidens" - a philosophical concept meaning a property that is not essential to the thing's nature, like a person moving because the ship they are standing on is moving</note>. But there are many different motions in the heaven. Therefore, it is necessary that several movers be present for them. A body does not move unless moved by something else; this is proven by the logic of motion. However, an incorporeal mover joined to a body is moved "by accident" according to the motion of the body, as is evident regarding the soul. But in celestial motions, there is a need for movers who are devoid of both body and motion. Truly, those celestial motions are from some intellect; from which it is established that there are separate substances, at least equal in number to the heavens.

<margin>From the harmony and order of the world.</margin>
2. A higher nature touches the highest part of the lower nature with its own lowest part. Now, a nature endowed with intellect is superior to a corporeal one, and it is that which gives completion to all corporeal things in man. It is necessary, therefore, that just as a body endowed with intellect is the highest among bodies, so the soul joined to it must be the lowest in the category of intelligences—which is itself free from death. From the order of things, therefore, there are also other substances above it, even of many orders and powers.

<meta>This page continues Postel’s philosophical proofs for the existence of spiritual beings. Having established that God permits certain evils for a greater purpose, he now uses Aristotelian logic and the principle of cosmic "fullness" to argue that the universe must be populated by "separate substances"—beings we might call angels or spirits—who occupy the space between God and humanity.</meta>

->### ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD<-

3. If a composite thing results from any two elements, such that a difference in perfection is found in one of its simple parts, the same must hold true for the other. From this, it follows that something is "first" and less dependent on the rest; this is evident in the logic of physical bodies. For the foundation of bodies does not depend on others, but rather the opposite: thus, by analogy, we also find **separate substance** <note>original: "substantia separata," referring to beings that exist without physical bodies, such as angels or pure intellects</note> which exists through itself, and is distinguished into as many orders as there are types of bodies. Therefore, separate substances exist. They differ, however, by this comparison, even though they meet in their various grades of being. In divine matters, the further things are distant from the "First" <note>God</note>, the more they require Him for their own perfection.

The opposite occurs in physical things. For matter and form subsist in a contrary manner. It is possible for insensitive things to exist without life, sense, or intellect; life can exist without sense, and sense without intellect—but it does not work the other way around. Thus, in this case, that which is most excellent—Man—cannot subsist without the lower things. Our mind, which is now in the fourth grade of being and should by this logic be more perfect than the other separate substances, is (if one may assign a rank among equal substances) far inferior and most in need of the "First." 

However, when the order is reversed, all things agree. For just as nothing is created without the "being" of matter, nor can anything reach the highest point without it, so too there is no place for any substances without God, who is the most excellent and infinite among all **forms**. Just as the second grade of matter is worthier than the first, so the second intellect is inferior in nobility to the First. And again, just as things endowed with sense are nobler than the first and second grades of matter, so the third-ranking beings from God are less worthy than the second. Likewise, just as the highest things are the most worthy here, so the third beings from God (which are fourth in the overall order) are lesser. Therefore, the perfection of lower things is not by reason of their body, but by reason of their approach to the highest; similarly, for others, the cause of lesser nobility is their proximity to matter and lower things. 

From this, it follows that there is a "link" <note>original: "nexus"</note> between both in the middle, so that in the human body itself there is a most excellent form: the mind, which is derived from that **fifth nature** <note>original: "quinta natura," referring to the Aristotelian "quintessence" or ether, a celestial substance distinct from the four earthly elements</note>, as **Aristotle** says. This mind is able to act, reason, and gather thoughts by itself—a power denied to other living creatures made of the same elements. If this capacity for reason came from those earthly elements, then brute animals would necessarily use it too, which is seen in no case. But these matters are better discussed where we treat the **immortality of souls**. 

Therefore, just as there are grades of being here on earth, it is necessary that they exist there in the heavens as well. Consequently, between the mind and God, there are separate substances. If there were no intellects in that clear and translucent matter and vastness of the heavens (since all things consist of life and the praise and honor of God), it would certainly be absurd: why would God create so many kinds of animals in this "filthy" matter <note>referring to the heavy, decaying elements of Earth</note> for the sake of one man who praises God (if he is wise), yet leave the most remains of the most magnificent part of the world a total desert? That would be just as if someone, seeking praise from his works and wealth, wanted his most magnificent buildings to be entirely devoid of inhabitants, while wanting the ugly ones to be crowded and full. Since the end of all things is in God—namely, that He be recognized, praised, and loved (even though He does not need these things except by His own will)—it is certain that He left no place in the world empty of a "praiser." From this, our proposition is clear: there are most excellent spirits in the most excellent part of the world, where they assiduously praise God. Furthermore:

5. Whether there is one intellect or many, I do not wish to argue here against **Averroes** <note>original: "Abenreis," referring to the Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd, who famously argued for a single, universal human intellect</note>; I shall do that in its proper place regarding the immortality of souls. It is enough that, by the consensus of all philosophers, the intellect survives after death. It is separated from the body not by its substance, but by "accident" <note>meaning its connection to the body is a temporary circumstance, not its core nature</note>, and it survives. But that which exists "through itself" is prior to that which exists "by accident." Therefore, besides the human intellect, there are other separate substances subsisting through themselves. For this reason, the **creation of spirits** <note>original: "dæmonum procreatio," here meaning the generation of spiritual beings or "daemons" in the classical sense</note>, which exists through itself, was done before the mind that is joined to the body itself. Thus, the premise is proven.

6. Furthermore, substance can exist without quantity, but not the other way around. Substance is prior to all the most general categories in time, reason, and knowledge.

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.

But no corporeal substance exists without quantity. It is possible, therefore, for certain things in the category of substance to be devoid of a body. Furthermore, everything that is possible is found within the nature of things; otherwise, the universe would be imperfect. Moreover, in eternal things, there is no difference between *being* and *being able to be*. From this, it is established from that very possibility that substances exist even beyond God and the human soul. For God is the highest of such beings, and our soul is the lowest. It is necessary, therefore, for there to be intermediate beings that are possible, so that they may truly exist. I could proceed with even more reasons, but these will satisfy those seeking the truth in order to learn; as for those who seek only to argue, neither these nor any other reasons will ever be enough. Now, I must rely on authority.

7 While I am about to confirm these points by authority, I could certainly bring forward the philosophers of all nations with a single word to support me—those whose judgment has stood the test of posterity—were it not for a few stubborn dissenters. These men, in order to appear different from the rest, denied that there was any judgment within themselves. Among the Latins, if you exclude Pliny and Lucretius, no one will fail to subscribe to this view. Among the Greeks, it is no wonder there were many more, since the plague of the world flowed from there. They had Pyrrho of Elis, Sextus Empiricus, Lucian, Arcesilaus (though the latter seemed more modest, as he did not assert that the things he was ignorant of were false, but rather thought that one should withhold assent from things), Democritus, and their followers. For there has never been such a foolish type of opinion or deed that did not find a defender or witness among them. Contrary to the sense of the entire world, they wished to oppose the opinion regarding **separate substances** <note>original: "substantijs separatis," referring to immaterial beings like angels or celestial intelligences</note>. I judge them unworthy of refutation because they have recoiled from the opinion of everyone else. It is surely no wonder that those who claimed nothing could be perceived by our senses—and that everything we touch was created falsely and uselessly, and that the whole world consists of phantoms rather than substance—refused to support these views; they were not men, but illusions of men. They were forced to be ignorant of this one thing at least: that they did not even know themselves. 

Let us see what moved others to introduce an opinion so different from the consensus of the world. The abuse of all religions—namely, the greed of the priests—is the reason why people have less faith in those things held sacred. For this reason, many used to call the gods <term>pure givers of wealth</term> <note>original: ἁγνὸς πλουτοδότας (agnos ploutodotas)</note>, because those most innocent beings were used to provide a very rich profit for the sacrificers. Therefore, since that deception was seen almost everywhere, and they saw everything overflowing with impostures and perceived nothing of the truth beneath, they believed in nothing. This very thing renders some people estranged from our most holy persuasion; if they see the truth in one matter a hundred times, but feel that a single falsehood has crept in once, they will immediately abolish whatever faith they previously held for the sake of that one perception. It is established that this proceeds from the fact that they wish for things to be as they believe, and they judge with bias. This is how those Greeks and Latins felt about religions, illusions, and demons: because they were answered more frequently with slanted and obscure responses, as if issued by <term>the Oblique One</term> <note>original: λοξίᾳ (Loxia), an epithet for Apollo, the god of prophecy, referring to his notoriously ambiguous or "slanted" oracles</note>, those gods never truly appeared to them. 

Partly ignorance of things, partly deception, and partly the desire for thinking and devising differently, caused them to assert that no such substances exist. But let us dismiss those <term>followers of Democritus</term> <note>original: δημοκριτίζοντας (democritizontas), referring to atomists who believed only in physical matter</note> and pass on to the most certain judgments. Let the "Prince of Philosophers" <note>Aristotle</note> himself come forward, who says in Book 12 of <term>his works on nature</term> <note>original: τῶν περὶ τὰ φυσικὰ (ton peri ta physika); Postel is likely citing Aristotle's "Metaphysics," Book Lambda</note>, while investigating substances, that substance is divided universally into two parts: the sensible and corruptible, the sensible and eternal, and a third, the immobile. The second type <note>the sensible and eternal</note> cannot be understood except as referring to separate substances. Because a celestial body, insofar as it is a body, consists of form and matter, it is impossible for it to be eternal [on its own], as we have demonstrated before. What he calls "gods" more than once in the *Ethics* cannot be understood except as separate substances. Furthermore, by his authority already cited, it was clear that there are intelligences that move the celestial spheres. But it is most clear from his statement that "all things are in a way three," that there are separate substances. For after God, the first and unmoved cause remaining in Himself—who is the simplest unity and trinity—it is necessary that there also be the same...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...harmony of the three orders of <term>separate substances</term> <note>These are "separated" from matter—incorporeal spirits like angels or daemons.</note>, and those are also tripartite within themselves. Since this idea is not repugnant to reason and fits the natural order of things, it must certainly be believed and accepted as proven, especially since it is held through revelation and inspiration rather than mere logical proof. The supreme God is accustomed to governing these lower realms through the administration of those spiritual orders.

But I turn now to Plato. After he spoke concerning the divinity of the heavens and the stars in his *Timaeus*, he wrote: "To speak of other <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Greek tradition, *daemones* were intermediary spirits between gods and men, not necessarily evil "demons."</note> and to recount their origin is a task beyond our strength; we must believe what was handed down by the ancestors. For since they were descended from the gods, it is certain they knew their own progenitors, whom they passed down to posterity. It is indeed most absurd to deny the children of gods credit regarding their own parents, even if they speak without any demonstration, whether true or probable, as if their words must be obeyed as law." By this decree, he commands that what was anciently handed down by the ancestors regarding religion be ratified. 

And again, when he introduces the supreme God addressing the lower gods—that is, the daemons—he says: "Whatever is born is likewise corruptible. Therefore, since you were born, you are not indeed immortal by your own nature. Nevertheless, since my power is immense and superior to corruption, I do not wish you to be held by the laws of death, etc." 

In these words, we have three of the greatest authorities: Pythagoras, Plato, and Cicero, who were followed by an infinite crowd of most learned men: Plotinus, Iamblichus, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage.</note>, Amelius, Maximus Tyrius, Porphyry, Epictetus, Chalcidius, and Proclus. All of these asserted both that separate substances exist and that they are distinguished into good and evil kinds. Through a certain succession of teaching, Pherecydes received this from the Syrians and Chaldeans; Pythagoras from him; Plato from Pythagoras; Cicero from Plato; and posterity from them. 

It would be nothing other than a burden to the reader to bring forward what Orpheus, Homer, Hesiod, and Empedocles wrote of them; among the Latins, Virgil, Catullus, Valerius, Ovid, and Seneca would have to be examined almost in their entirety. Truly, however, one or two other passages of Plato ought to be brought forward. In the fifth book of *The Laws*, he affirms that when we are advancing in the highest happiness, each person is helped by a daemon who presides over them, as if meeting them on the way. In the *Apology of Socrates*, he proves that daemons are everywhere. In the *Cratylus*, he places them in a threefold category: heroes made from men, daemons, and gods—all of which are separate substances. 

I could indeed bring forward many things from Proclus now, but because he gathered and claimed for himself all that our <term>Dionysius the Areopagite</term> <note>Postel follows the Renaissance belief that the Neoplatonists stole their best ideas from early Christian writers like Dionysius.</note> handed down, I shall skip over him. For our own traditions are sufficiently proven to us. But before I come to the other authorities, I wish to bring forward what Plutarch—a man most skilled in both Latin and Greek learning—handed down, because it pertains much to the matter and confirms even what we have in writing from the sacred texts. Concerning the "loss of oracles," he writes thus: 

"Concerning the death of these (he means the daemons), I heard the account of a man who was neither unwise nor vain, the rhetorician Aemilianus, whom many of you have heard. His father was Epitherses, my fellow citizen and a teacher of grammar. He recounted that, when he was once sailing to Italy, he boarded a ship laden with various merchandise and a great multitude of people. As evening approached on a certain day, when they were near the Echinades islands, the wind died down and the ship was carried near the island of Paxos. While many were still awake and not a few were drinking—supper not yet being finished—a voice was heard from the island of Paxos, calling 'Thamus' once and then again, so that they wondered. Now, Thamus was the Egyptian pilot of the ship, and his name was unknown even to many of the passengers. Though the voice called once and then again, he remained silent; but at the third call, he responded to the caller. Then the voice, straining aloud, said whatever it was calling for:

> When you are near Palodes <note>original: "Quum fueris iuxta Palodes"</note> (a place not far from Corcyra), announce that the Great Pan is dead. <note>In Christian tradition, this famous story was interpreted as the moment the pagan spirits lost their power at the death of Christ.</note>

When these things were heard, Epitherses said they were driven into a stupor by great wonder, and began to debate in their minds whether they should do as commanded or care nothing more for it; but Thamus decided that it must be done."

## GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.

If there were a wind, they would sail past and neglect the matter; but if there were a calm and a tranquil sea, he was to say what he had been commanded. When they were in the region of Palodes <note>An island group near Epirus.</note>, the wind ceased entirely and the waves grew still. Therefore, from the prow, **Thamus** <note>An Egyptian pilot mentioned in Plutarch’s "On the Obsolescence of Oracles."</note> shouted toward the land, as he had heard: "Great Pan is dead." He had barely finished saying this when a great lamentation was heard, mixed with voices of wonder—not from one person, but from many. Just as if many men had been present, the rumor of it was immediately spread to Rome, so that **Thamus** was summoned by **Tiberius** <note>The Roman Emperor (reigned 14–37 AD), during whose rule Christ was crucified.</note>. Indeed, **Tiberius** believed this so firmly that he inquired of his learned men who this **Pan** might be. Those around him, being scholars, conjectured that he was the son of **Mercury** and **Penelope**. **Philip** (whom Plutarch introduces in this passage) also had witnesses of these events, which he had heard from **Aemilianus**. 

**Demetrius** also says (he is another person introduced by **Plutarch**, a native of **Britain**), that among the islands around **Britain**, many are deserted and scattered (they are called the **Orcades** <note>The Orkney Islands.</note>); some of these they named the islands of <term>daemons</term> <note>In this context, intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil.</note> and heroes. He himself, for the sake of observation and history, had sailed by the King’s command to the one nearest the desert islands, which did not have many inhabitants, but was considered sacrosanct and inviolable by the neighbors under the jurisdiction of the **Britons**. When he arrived there, he learned that a great confusion in the air had recently occurred, and many portents were seen there; the winds broke forth in blasts and fiery whirlwinds fell. The islanders said these signs signified that one of the great gods had passed away. 

These things **Plutarch** writes, which demonstrate a multifaceted experience of daemons and <term>separate substances</term> <note>Incorporeal spirits existing apart from physical matter.</note>. Furthermore, they clearly provide evidence of the death of **Jesus Christ**, at which time hell trembled, and the daemons were everywhere routed and afflicted. For this reason, they rightly had to flee and stir up the air. 

But we must not admit what **Plutarch** infers from this: that daemons are mortal. Indeed, who could doubt that those things were said of the Most High God, since from that place where the voice was made all the way to Rome is more than seventy thousand paces? And yet that power of the daemons roared throughout the entire world, even to the ends of the earth. For those agitations of the air caused by the daemons in the **British Isles**, according to **Demetrius’s** narration, had already begun earlier; and the daemons had already revealed that the Great God had died, because they had willed it so. But because that great <note>original: "πᾶν" (pan), meaning "All" or "Everything."</note> **Pan**, the arbiter of the universe, was dying in the body, they sensed their own upcoming defeat. But that souls and separate substances could die—that is foreign to their nature. Moreover, that **Pan**, the god of shepherds, had already died a thousand years before. 

Therefore, no stronger testimonies could be brought forward concerning the time of Christ’s death, nor concerning separate substances. The title <note>original: "τῶ παντὸς" (tō pantos), meaning "of the universe" or "of the all."</note> **of the All** certainly fits no one other than **Christ**, the moderator, restorer, and arbiter of all things. 

**Maximus Tyrius** <note>A 2nd-century Platonic philosopher.</note> in his *Sermons*, when he treats many things concerning separate substances drawn from the very nature of things, creates the greatest belief by this one thing: that he himself was once present at the **Tauric Chersonese** <note>The Crimean Peninsula.</note>, where he saw the manifest works of daemons, and beheld the heroes themselves sitting at the table of **Achilles**. And lest anyone should think it a fable, he wished to establish the reality of these specters by the most certain sense of his own eyes, and to hand it down in his writings for others to see. He is a man of distinguished judgment and erudition, whom you should not rightly distrust. 

The opinion of **Damascius the Platonist** <note>The last head of the Neoplatonist Academy in Athens.</note> will also greatly confirm this, which he left written in his books <note>original: "τῶν θεολογουμένων" (tōn theologoumenōn), meaning "On Theological Matters."</note> *On Divine Matters*. It goes like this: We can also grasp by certain arguments that there are many species of lives, and that there are innumerable vital illustrations of the one primary life existing and flowing from there into all living things. Likewise, many emanations proceed from one substance into all those things that exist. Why are many words needed? Since even **Iamblichus** <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> and those who flourished before him wrote that there are many substantial gods, but one "super-substantial" one who illuminates all the lower ones and grants them divinity; and although those lower ones are the most perfect unities...

### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...most perfect, yet they do not have this perfection from themselves, but receive it from the Highest. These are the words of **Damascius** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 458–538 AD) known as the last head of the School of Athens.</note>, which do not differ much from the sentiment of our own **Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a figure traditionally believed to be a convert of St. Paul, whose writings on the "Celestial Hierarchy" defined Christian angelology.</note>. Indeed, **Proclus** <note>A hugely influential Greek Neoplatonist (412–485 AD).</note> took everything from him to such an extent that he transcribed many things word-for-word while the works of **Dionysius** were still hidden. He did not wish to attribute these things to their true author because he knew him to be initiated into **Christ**, to whom he was hostile. He easily thought it would come to pass that Dionysius's works would perish, as the Christian state was not yet firmly established. To prevent them from becoming known, in the pagan manner and to confirm impious religions, he always calls "gods" those whom we call **angels**. He affirms three triads of them, so that there is clearly no difference except in name alone, as he strives to turn truth into a lie. In place of our vocabulary, so that his thefts would not be exposed, he used simple numbers. Thus, the first three orders for him are the <note>original: "noētoi"</note> **intelligible**, the <note>original: "noētoi kai noeroi"</note> **intelligible and intellectual**, and the <note>original: "noeroi monon"</note> **intellectual only**. These terms hardly have a suitable expression in Latin, unless you say those "endowed with mind," "comprehending with mind," and "comprehended by mind," and "comprehended by mind"—yet these cannot fully express the matter. For even though no lower species follows these, they are so powerful in intellect that nothing at all is hidden from them, except for the **First Being** <note>original: "יהוה" (YHWH)</note> **the LORD**, whom they indeed know, but do not comprehend. They are arranged in these three triads. In the first order are those whose names that impious man <note>Proclus</note> wished to shun: **Seraphim**, **Cherubim**, and **Thrones**, who purify, illuminate, and perfect all lower things. In the second are **Dominations**, **Virtues**, and **Powers**, who—having been purified, enlightened, and perfected by the highest order—similarly preside over the lower ones. For the **Principalities**, **Archangels**, and **Angels** are only purified, illuminated, 

<margin>Dionysius grants this function especially to angels, in *On the Celestial Hierarchy*.</margin>
and perfected. From these orders, **Providence** wished for individual counselors of divinity to be present for individual humans, so that the soul, having been placed in a body, might more easily overcome the stubbornness of matter. Furthermore, they prove that there are various kinds of evil beings opposed to these. **Plato** writes of this, religion receives it, and reason dictates it. For insofar as they are intelligences, it is certain that they possess free will. Hence they are called by **Plato**, the **Pythagoreans**, and all writers of ancient theology <note>original: "kakodaimones"</note> **evil demons**, because they abused that will and cannot return into favor with the **First Cause**, because they lack divine favor and help, from which they fell by their own choice. These oppose themselves to individual angels, and each acts at least around individual men, leading them away from the truth and forcing them, in their own manner, to misuse true happiness; many examples of these will be made clear. Nearly all who were **Platonists**, and men of the better schools, wished to call the good angels "gods," but the evil ones more frequently "demons." **Plato** himself did this first; for in the fifth book of the *Republic*, while he gives counsel on religion, he says that the difference ought to be taught to the common people themselves: which of those departing this life are <note>original: "daimonioi"</note> **demonic**, and which are <note>original: "theioi"</note> **divine**. Through these two terms, he explains two kinds of men departing from life: the good and the evil. In this, however, he erred: he posited that the souls of the wicked become demons. **Psellus**, in his book *On Demons*, will easily clarify the mind of **Plato**. And a certain **Chaldean**, he says, posits some demons as good and some as evil; but our pious discourse asserts that all are evil, because they sinned by their own will and exchanged goodness for wickedness. The reason the **Chaldeans** thought all were good was that they used the labor of evil demons for futile and vain things, since they could not have compelled the good ones. These apparitions, as **Hesiod** says, <note>original: "aera essamenoi pasan phoitōsin ep' aian"</note> **clothed in air, they wander over all the earth**, appearing wherever they wish on the lands. Therefore **Hermes**, or **Mercury Trismegistus**, asserts that there are no good demons. **Plato** calls them sometimes good, sometimes evil. Good more frequently, but evil in the third book of the *Republic*, where he says they are the <note>original: "goēteias kai apatēs aitias"</note> **authors of sorcery and deception**, which must be categorized among evil things. And **Porphyry**, in his books *On Abstinence*, says that the evil are contrary to the good, and are the authors of sorcery and evil desires...

This should be held as having even greater authority because he rises up against us and is unwilling to grant us even what is most fair. Indeed, testimony from an adversary is by far the strongest. Therefore, once those aerial pests were cast down from the celestial region, the world is agitated and tends toward ruin. Moreover, that they act in the air is confirmed even by the **Philosopher of Truth** <note>A common medieval and Renaissance title for Aristotle.</note> in his books of *Metaphysics*, where he says that these four bodies are substances, along with the living beings produced in them—namely, animals and **demons**—and their parts. Likewise, in the first book of *On the Soul*: "Someone might ask," he says, "for what reason the soul that is in the air is more immortal and better than that which is in living creatures?" Explaining this, **Simplicius** <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note> says: "It is much more excellent if it is supposed to be the genus of demons, which itself occasionally creeps into a body subject to passions." This is to be understood not as if it "creeps in" to provide form <note>In Aristotelian terms, the "form" is the soul or organizing principle of a living thing.</note>, but to torment and infect a body already possessing a soul. This happens so frequently—nothing is more common—as is evident from experience.

<margin>On which **Plutarch** <note>A Greek-Roman historian and philosopher (c. 46–120 AD).</note> wrote much in his book *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*.</margin>
Indeed, some were led by this reasoning: because they are seen in the air, and sometimes dwell in one place (often even for many centuries), and finally vanish and betake themselves elsewhere to destroy and drive men mad, the ancients thought they were mortal. **Hesiod** <note>One of the earliest Greek poets (c. 700 BC).</note> himself testifies to this when he says that the goddess nymphs fulfill ten lifetimes of the phoenix, a span which would extend to 9,720 years. Antiquity seemed to say the same thing when it called them **Hamadryad nymphs** <note>original: *nymphai hamadryadas*</note>, that is, Nymphs equal in age to the oak tree. These ideas are found to be false because these substances—whether pure or depraved—being of the simplest essence, cannot be corrupted in their essence. For they suffer nothing contrary to themselves. What then was the cause for antiquity to feel so variously about them, such that in no matter was there less agreement than in those "gods" who were made out of demons? It was the craftiness of the scoundrel <note>Satan</note>, drawing clouds over the minds of mortals so they might be held in perpetual error. To ensure nothing was firm or stable, he moved from one place to another, and with new crimes he enticed new men to himself, until he turned everyone away from the knowledge of the **First Cause** <note>A philosophical term for God as the ultimate origin of all things.</note> and thrust himself into the place of God through the statues of things, animals, and criminal men—until the one Truth, which alone could do so, blunted his efforts in a world initiated into the true sacred rites. Because of those changes, some thought they did not exist because they had not seen them; to others, they seemed to have died when they were merely absent from a place; to some, this one was true and that one false, so that nowhere was a lie more frequent than under the opinion of the **Author of Lies**. For what wonder is it that many have felt so variously about the most inconstant thing of all, when truth itself is called into doubt by many, no faith is given to the senses, the testimony of others is treated like a dream, and many hold the authority of the wise in the same regard as fools and children, being moved by no consensus of the world, while certain people wish their own judgment on things to be preferred to the whole universe? If they hallucinate in the most certain things, what wonder is it if they are deceived in dark and doubtful ones? But although those whom persistence drives sideways cannot be conquered by any arguments, I will nonetheless bring forward the consensus of all nations regarding this nature of substances, so that those who refuse to stand by the judgment of divine men and those skilled in all things might at least accept what our ancestors, taught by experience, believed.

For otherwise, something very similar would have been seen throughout all of human nature. It was certain that these powers were summoned by the will of wicked men so that harm might be brought upon other people. Hence that provision in the first chapters of the **Roman Laws**: <note>This refers to the Laws of the Twelve Tables, the foundation of Roman law.</note> *if anyone should enchant crops, or cause harm [by magic], let there be a penalty.* <note>original: "si quis fruges incantassit, læserit, pœna esto"</note> This very law was held as valid many centuries later and confirmed by other laws; otherwise, this would not have happened unless the events were real. I do not wish to touch upon how civil law treats these matters, lest I be too long-winded; those things are obvious to everyone. In religious law, how frequent is the mention and prohibition of these things! Truly, since laws do not belong to just one or two people, it is established that they are set down and approved by the consensus of all—both in all states and especially in a popular and democratic state, where nothing was held as valid without the vote of the entire community. It is necessary, therefore, that there were and are **separate substances** <term>separate substances: A philosophical term for beings that exist without physical bodies, such as angels or demons.</term> and malevolent ones, by whose work wicked men were undermining the **Commonwealth** <note>original: "Rempub.", abbreviation for Respublica</note> with unusual crimes. From that vice (since it was placed in the will of men to commit it or neglect it) laws were born, which would both prohibit witchcraft and establish punishments for those who dared to perpetrate such deeds. Indeed, of all opinions held concerning matters, nothing is as exactly weighed as the law, which is usually established not by a private person, nor by [mere] authority, nor by just anyone, but is weighed by the highest and wisest magistrate. I am speaking of those laws in which there is no dealing with the confirmation of a single person's authority, nor with swindling, nor the commercial trafficking of money—in which princes set laws for themselves by their own authority and compel even unwilling citizens to obey their decrees—but rather those laws concerning matters in which a remedy is sought for the diseases that have arisen in the Commonwealth. For the decrees of all administrations agree on this. To this is added that poets especially, historians, philosophers, and in short, those handling every kind of discipline, have made mention in their writings of **illusions**, **bewitchments**, **theurgy** <note>Theurgy is a form of "high magic" intended to invoke divine presence or spirits.</note>, **magic**, **geomancy** <note>Divination by earth or soil.</note>, **hydromancy** <note>Divination by water.</note>, **pyromancy** <note>Divination by fire.</note>, **aeromancy** <note>Divination by air or atmospheric phenomena.</note>, **divination by lots**, and **demons**, from whom all those things proceed. Surely this could never have happened unless the things existed for which names were invented and accepted by usage.

<margin>By the consensus of the common people and nations.</margin>

From this, it is established by the common consensus of all that the things themselves exist about which the words stand, and that **separate substances** gave origin to those things. They are, therefore, in the nature of things. In this matter, it could not happen that men bound by the most diverse human laws would agree, unless it were made known to everyone by nature and they recognized with certainty that the thing exists.

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I

Let us trust our own eyes. Therefore, I shall begin first with the history of the Romans. Where effects are seen, even if the cause remains hidden from us, it is nevertheless necessary for us to prioritize the cause over the effects themselves. For nothing creates itself. Is it not true that what presents itself to everyone’s eyes and moves by its own will must necessarily exist? Is it not written in the Roman annals that during the consulship of Lucius Scipio and Caius Norbanus <note>83 BCE, during the Roman Civil Wars.</note>, between Capua and the Volturnus river, the massive sound of standards and the horrific clashing of arms were heard? And lest these be thought merely errors of hearing, opposing battle lines clashing together also presented themselves to the eyes for several days. Nor was that enough; so that belief in the miracle might not be lacking from the senses of hearing and seeing, or be held as uncertain, the sense of touch was added. For to those investigating the miracle closely, the footprints of men and horses appeared; and—what could convince even an unbeliever—not only the grass but even the shrubs were found trampled. 

All these things were rightly shown by the demons whom the Romans worshipped; since they could not prevent the calamity, they could at least foretell the ruin they had begun and were fulfilling upon wicked men. For a hundred thousand men were lost at that time in the civil war and the proscriptions <note>The state-sanctioned murder or banishment of political enemies.</note> of Sulla and Marius. But perhaps those things, seen only once, do not prove that <term>immaterial substances</term> <note>Postel uses "substantiae separatae," a philosophical term for beings like angels or demons that exist without physical bodies.</note> exist. This must be confirmed by other examples. During the Antonine War, the same apparition was seen in Rome for a long time. When Pompey was killed in Egypt, the same clamor and crashing so terrified the people of Antioch that they twice rushed to arms at night. What could have been the cause of that roaring which seemed to be carried from the center of the earth into the sky during the consulship of Marcus Antony and Aulus Posthumus? 

Are these not your gods, O Romans? (I address you, while excepting the good ones). Even today, it is well known that in Italy there are and have been many men very similar to Pomponazzi <gloss>the atheist</gloss> <note>Pietro Pomponazzi (1462–1525) was a philosopher who controversially argued that the immortality of the soul could not be proven by reason alone.</note>, who argued that there are no immaterial substances, and who attempted—by perverting the sayings of the philosophers—to persuade the Supreme Pontiff, who was eager for novelty, of the mortality of souls. O Rome, how you are never without monsters! 

What of the serpents that glided into so many places and then immediately vanished? Are they not illusions and images very close to the foul demons? What of that fire, the herald of calamities, which was often seen to burn the earth and sky, and to be carried frequently from the west to the east and back again? Are these things done by natural and elemental labor? Certainly, if they proceeded from nature, they would be fixed and steady like everything else. There are innumerable things of this kind in the annals. I do not wish to touch upon the impostures of your false religion. For religions were introduced so craftily by you that after the work of men was added to them, nothing certain can be held. 

Although the history of the Pessinuntian Mother of the Gods <note>Cybele, whose cult was brought to Rome from Pessinus in 204 BCE.</note> and the Aesculapian serpent <note>The god of medicine, brought to Rome in the form of a snake to stop a plague.</note> seems to contain real events, they certainly could not have happened without the work of a demon. A "Cycnus" <note>Likely a reference to a miraculous or divine bird/swan mentioned in local lore.</note> could not be captured by the hands of men (even though it could be seen by everyone), even when a large circle of men surrounded it and watched it in the temple of Minerva. Therefore, although the ruses of Numa’s Egeria, the visions of Proculus regarding Romulus, and other tricks were prudently devised to hold the minds of the foolish multitude, not everything in religion was like that. 

A demon spoke frequently in statues, temples, and animals; it even occasionally brought destruction so that it might be worshipped. For two whole days in the closed temple of Juno, a deceiver imitated the voice of an infant so that the minds of the unrefined might be incited to worship. Why should I mention the injury inflicted on the Latin man because he had not immediately revealed to the Senate that the procession of the games usually held in the Circus Maximus was faulty? <note>Referring to the story of Titus Latinius, who was punished with illness until he reported a divine warning about the Roman Games.</note> What does the foul nature of the demon not fabricate? It commits crimes, and then, when it seems to care for the things it committed, it mocks and agitates the minds of men. If anyone wants more examples, let him read Julius Obsequens *On Prodigies* or Valerius Maximus *On Religion*; he will see miraculous evidence of immaterial substances. Although their form is not seen, it is certainly established that they exist from their effects. For...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

For those things happen either by human skill or by nature. For all natural things are fixed and accustomed to happen in one way; but those [supernatural] things are illusions and mockeries, proceeding from separate powers <note>Postel refers here to "separate substances," a philosophical term for spirits or demons that exist independently of physical bodies.</note>. All these things are established in the common experience of everyone, from which they have earned their credibility. In ancient times, they were seen frequently; but now they partly remain hidden, and partly have vanished from these regions. It is indeed well-known through the preaching of the Word of God, which we have through Christ and in Christ, that many ghosts have disappeared. However, it is certain that in sparsely inhabited and mountainous places, where preachers of the Gospel are rare, nothing is more common than sorcerers and evildoers; from whom innumerable disasters, calamities, and diseases proceed. When these people are caught, they themselves cannot deny it; many acknowledge their crimes of their own accord, and they free themselves from such a foul power, ending their lives through punishments without reluctance. If anyone does not agree with me, let him read what **Giovanni Francesco Pico**, Count of **Concordia**, wrote concerning these substances and their effects—both what he diligently observed himself and whatever he had read in literature <note>Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola (1469–1533), nephew of the famous humanist, wrote *Strix* (The Witch), an influential work on demonology and witchcraft.</note>. He did this so that he might try to persuade those stubborn men who otherwise believe very little—men who, like cattle, depend only on their physical senses—and to show that he had sweated diligently in revealing that obscurity of nature. Whoever reads that book which he titled *On Witches* <note>original: "de Strigibus"</note> will undoubtedly find himself satisfied in a marvelous way. I do not wish to bring into the open the art and the dire dangers of all those vanities which it is well known once flourished in **Toledo**, since they are very well known and proceeded from the "plague of the Moors" <note>Toledo, Spain, was historically famous as a legendary center for the study of magic and "the dark arts" in medieval European folklore, often associated with Arabic learning.</note>. Daily, near the slopes of the **Pyrenees** mountains, men infected with that blight are caught, and they are usually given over to the avenging flames. To whom in **France** is the **Gap** incident not known? The mountains pushed upward and forward, the vineyards moved from their places, the meadows, the trees—in short, the entire surface of the soil—testifies to the crime of unspeakable spirits. It became known to the most celebrated courts; the wretched owners of the lands, now beggars, point it out. Nothing is more recent than that miracle, and nothing is more certain.

<margin>Demons and their attendants also frequently play together.</margin>
I do not wish to bring into the open how many substances of this kind are removed from possessed bodies every year by the command of the Lord, both in many other places and especially at the **Column** in **Rome** <note>The "Holy Column" (Colonna Santa) in St. Peter's Basilica was traditionally believed to be the column Christ leaned against in the Temple, and it was a site famous for exorcisms.</note>. Let the sacred temple of **Philip the Sicilian** <note>Likely referring to a shrine associated with St. Philip of Agira, an early Christian exorcist saint in Sicily.</note> be visited; the very same thing will be seen. But these matters belong to us [Christians], and they are not likely to be believed by the impious, even if they were seen a thousand times.

<margin>Experience concerning foreign nations.</margin>
Now let us come to foreign nations, which lack the light of the Gospel. In no part of the world is there not a very great familiarity of certain people with those spirits. In many places, foul figures with airy bodies present themselves to the sight of everyone of their own accord. What is more familiar in **India** than enchanters? No ship sets sail lacking a man skilled in magic; so that if a loss should occur, or be caused by anyone else, as soon as he is asked, he shows the place in the waters and restores the items through divers. But you will say it is easy to lie about the Indians. Consult the **Portuguese**, who live familiarly among them, and they will confirm these things. Often, when asked, would they not take such men with them? The **French** who have gone there will assert the same. Read the *Itinerary* of **Varthema** <note>Ludovico di Varthema (c. 1470–1517) was an Italian traveler whose popular travelogue described the Middle East and India.</note> and of others who saw these things and wrote them down. But it is no wonder that where a demon is worshiped, he offers himself to the sight. Yet truly, it is even more marvelous that these things appear familiarly to peoples who are ignorant of all things. Those peoples who are in **America** at nearly the 50th degree (among whom **Magellan** lived familiarly for nearly 6 months while he was circumnavigating the globe) see ghosts of horrific demons, and they call them **Setebos** <note>The name Setebos was recorded by Magellan's chronicler, Pigafetta, as the name of a Patagonian deity; Shakespeare later used this name for Caliban's god in *The Tempest*.</note>. A barbarian giant captured by Magellan himself, when he could not do so with words, revealed their horrific likeness through signs and a drawing on this occasion: while they were waiting for a more favorable wind, they were busy trying to instill the principles of religion into that giant. Thus, when he began to cross himself with the sign of the cross in the manner of our people, he cried out "**Setebos**" with a horrific voice and horrific clamor, and he explained by signs as best he could that the demon had insulted him and would kill him if he continued to use that sign. ### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.
