Because of the familiarity of such a long period of time (for it lived with them for about eight months), it revealed the nature and infestation of demons to our people, and how, when a certain man was dying, a great crowd of dancing spirits was present. Read the *Itinerary of the World's Circuit*, written by **Antonio Pigafetta**, a man no less learned than he was diligent <note>Pigafetta was the chronicler who accompanied Ferdinand Magellan on the first circumnavigation of the globe (1519–1522).</note>. How much mockery they suffer under the equator in the New World from their own spirits (whom they call *zemes* <note>original: "zemos." These are the *cemí*, ancestral spirits or deities of the Taíno people in the Caribbean.</note>), unless where Christ has been heard of, is clear from many histories, if anyone reads the voyages to the West with care. 

Those lands joined to them toward the North, which were discovered by **Francis**, King of the French <note>King Francis I, who commissioned the voyages of Jacques Cartier to Canada.</note>, are usually disturbed in a wondrous way by these specters, so that the inhabitants cannot even rest. They call this kind *Cudiague*. Even when the sky is quite clear and there is a total lack of wind, the forests are so moved (for inhabitants are rare there, and everything is full of woods) and filled with cries that you would believe trees were being torn up by the roots. Yet you see nothing, which itself exceeds the powers of nature. For nature acts by a continuous, uninterrupted motion; those spirits act by their own will. 

Now who could count the things that happen in the North? In **Iceland**, which the ancients seem to have been ignorant of, the effects of "separate power" <note>Postel uses "separate power" to describe the agency of spirits who exist independently of physical bodies.</note> are so great that no one is able to recount them. Near the mountains burning with perpetual fires in the manner of Mount Etna, specters present themselves so frequently that nothing is more familiar; nor, until they vanish, would you believe they were specters. In the northern part of the island, there is a kind of ice from which pitiable groans are heard; if you try to carry even a small piece of it away, you waste your effort. For it eludes the senses once you touch it. 

Huge rocks, torn from mountains with violent force—which no human strength could move—are seen carried about in the air and moved from place to place; by what powers this happens, if not by an intellect, is not understood. These things agree with what Demetrius the Briton said about the islands nearest to Britain in the works of Plutarch. **Ziegler**, a man of singular knowledge of all things and absolute science of mathematics, reports this; the authors are **Johannes** and **Olaus**, the Gothic brothers <note>Johannes Magnus (1488–1544) and Olaus Magnus (1490–1557) were Swedish brothers and historians; Olaus's *History of the Northern Peoples* is a famous source for Nordic folklore.</note>, expelled from their own borders—the former a most distinguished Archbishop of Uppsala, the latter driven from his great possessions. 

Who indeed could count what happens in that part near and subject to the Pole, caused by "impure substances"? Sometimes for two days, sometimes three, even for a month, a specter offers itself as a servant; you do not recognize it for what it is until it disappears. Indeed, there is such familiarity with some people that it obeys the nods of many. Almost none of the **Lapps** <note>The indigenous Sámi people of northern Scandinavia, frequently associated with shamanism and magic in early modern literature.</note> is not powerful in magic incantations, so much so that they stop and sink ships if they see fit. The authors are **Ziegler** and the **Goths** already named; to whom is added the testimony of **Stella** and the ambassadors of the **Muscovites**. 

Therefore, wherever the power of the Gospel is not seen, there these plagues reign, and they come forth more frequently from caves and dens, as the ancients seem to have believed. This is why they used to say that the power of oracles—which they knew in truth existed in many places—proceeded from the earth itself; which is still evident in many places, and especially in gold mines, where one must go very deep into the earth. A most trustworthy man, **Johannes Agricola** <note>Postel likely refers to Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the author of *De Re Metallica*, though he writes "Johannes."</note>, tells in his book *On Metals* that the mines of **Bohemia**, which are the most famous in all Germany, have miracles from the frequency of demons, and that their nature is varied. For in some, there are malevolent ones who frequently suffocate and kill men; in others, they are even accustomed to prepare work of a different kind, so that when those whose task it is to follow the vein have left the place, they not infrequently find more dug out during the night of a feast day than they could have dug in a whole week. Concerning these various kinds, see the letter of **Trithemius**, the greatest investigator of magic, to the Emperor Maximilian.

For it is more than sufficiently established that there are "separate substances" <term>separate substances (substantiae separatae): a philosophical term for spirits, angels, or demons who exist without physical bodies.</term> in the nature of things, which is evident everywhere in houses and families. ### CHAPTER VIII. ON THE NATURE OF DEMONS AND ANGELS, and on magicians and prophets, and the difference between them.

Based on the preceding demonstration, philosophers are forced to admit that those natures we call "separate substances"—some call them demons, others gods, and there are those who call them angels—not only exist in the nature of things but also differ greatly in kind. Pythagoras called the evil ones *spirits of the underworld* <note>original: "καταχθονίως" (katachthonios).</note> and the good ones *gods* <note>original: "θεὸς" (theos).</note>, performing sacred rites to both: to the latter so they might be of benefit, and to the former so they might not do harm. The Romans also called the evil ones *Vaeioves* <note>Vejovis was an early Roman deity often interpreted as a "little Jove" or an "anti-Jupiter" associated with ill-fortune or the underworld.</note>, as if they were "adverse gods," and they were commonly known by another Greek name, *apotropaioi* <note>original: "ἀποτροπαίος," meaning "averters" or those who turn away evil.</note>. For now, I do not wish to enter into that arena of discussing "gods" in general who were born from human merits <note>Postel is referring to euhemerism—the ancient theory that the gods were originally human heroes who were deified after death.</note>; since these usually consist of opinion and imposture rather than the true nature of things, they should be dismissed to their proper place. We must deal with those who actually exist in the nature of things. 

Although no distinction among these natures is handed down among the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, whose philosophy dominated the medieval and Renaissance university system.</note>—who thought they were perfectly simple substances—it does not follow that they are not different just because they did not write about them. For many things were hidden from them which posterity has most clearly recognized and proved, as was handed down in the previous chapter. This nature must be considered from its very origin. Just as our own mind is endowed with the freedom of choice <term>freedom of choice (libertas arbitrii): the capacity to choose between different courses of action without being forced by necessity.</term> so that it acts in either direction—that is, from deliberation, not from necessity—so we must believe that those substances which are of a higher degree and devoid of bodies are also free. For otherwise, the most excellent gifts of essence and thought would be lacking in these most perfect natures, which is unacceptable. For nothing above this elemental mass of our world is oppressed by servitude; all things are free. 

Therefore, it is certain that they can both use and abuse their power and liberty. The laws themselves show that some have abused it and continue to abuse it daily, for they prohibit dealings with them as evil beings. Therefore, some are altogether evil and destructive, as has been shown. But since all things were created as "best" by God, and if any are evil, they become so through their own liberty or from the corruption and flux of matter, it is clear that they fell from the decree of divine goodness by their own choice, and perverted their excellent nature through this change. Thus, since philosophy cannot grasp these reasons, yet the facts clearly seem to exist in the nature of things, it must necessarily reach out its hand to religion. For in matters that are seen to exist by their effects, when the human eye cannot reach their nature through reason, one must acquiesce to divine revelation, which is not repugnant to the nature of things. 

After all the most excellent things (as far as the condition of the universe allowed) were established by the Prime Mover <note>A term for God derived from Aristotelian physics, meaning the first cause of all motion.</note>, and since in those natures which cannot admit bodily sins and which were the most excellent, a clear and human-harming wickedness is seen, it must be that they turned away from their beginning and nobility by some crime, and admitted into themselves the greatest vice—than which none is greater. From this (as is the nature of misery and envy), they strive to make humans like themselves and lost. But what was said from the beginning must be repeated here from a higher principle. It is conceded by all philosophers worthy of the name that this entire temple of nature, as far as the parts subject to the senses are concerned, was established for some cause and is preserved in existence; and man, indeed, was made for the sake of God. Since supreme happiness lies in knowledge, it is rightly believed that after this darkness, eternal life consists in knowing God. For otherwise, man (even if he enjoyed the most abundant use of these things) would be most unhappy if he lacked his goal after so many exhausted labors. And God would be hardly wise if He had willed to prepare so many great things for the sake of an eternal nothingness. He would surely be far inferior to spiders, who so diligently weave webs to hunt flies, if He had prepared such great and numerous things for the sake of a laborious life (and one more afflicted the better it is), yet willed it to be endowed only with present miseries. He would be not only unjust but inept.

He concludes that human life must have a divine purpose and an eternal end, otherwise God's creation would be less rational than a spider's web.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Postel’s philosophical defense of the divine order. He transitions from discussing the existence of spiritual beings to the moral obligation of "honor" that all creatures—human and angelic—owe to God, explaining the fall of the demons as an act of cosmic pride.</meta>

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK I.

It is contrary to human reason—which can be biased, unwise, or even malicious—to suggest that God could be unjust, imprudent, or evil; it is even less possible for such qualities to exist in the divine nature itself. Therefore, He created this entire universe, which is perceived by the sight of our eyes as much as by our intellect, for His own sake, and for the purpose of His recognition and honor. 

But since God Himself lacks nothing, is infinitely blessed, is the arbiter of the universe, and is so absolute that He cannot be made greater or happier by any addition of our own effort, what could we possibly believe that man and his mind could "return" to Him? What is within our power that could satisfy or delight Him? This is a harsh and difficult question, but one that must be resolved by looking at the practical experience of this life. 

The natural desire placed within every human being—the thing expected by all people from human works, according to both necessity and utility—is glory, honor, and renown. We see this naturally in every class of people; and the more powerful they are, and the less they lack in material things, the more they are seized by a hunger for praise and glory, and the more they seek after honors. To be sure, these honors do not add any "perfection" to such people, but they represent the loyalty and faith of the people beholden to them. By these "spurs of glory," people are incited to pursue virtue, which is otherwise difficult to achieve; ignited by these small sparks, they eventually undergo hardships for the sake of virtue voluntarily, and they return the reward of true praise to God. This is necessary because our own glory is fragile and fleeting; often, when we try to claim it for ourselves, we receive infamy in its place. 

It is manifest even in us—composed as we are of this fleeting matter—that honor must be referred back to the original causes of things, even if those causes do not "need" the glory for themselves. How much more, then, since we can honor, deserve, and know God through no other means, should we attribute all things to Him? We must refer the use of ourselves and of all external things back to Him from whom we received them. Thus, the **honor and knowledge of God is the ultimate goal of life**. 

Wretched mortality can prove itself to God in no other way than by placing itself in the position of a child, and all other humans in the position of siblings, and by acknowledging God as the Parent, to be loved, praised, celebrated, worshipped, and adored for these gifts. Total honor is therefore owed to God alone, the parent of all things, in exchange for the use of this life. Since we have no other gift by which He can be acknowledged, we must fear Him as the All-Powerful, love Him as the Supreme Good, worship Him as a Parent, and adore Him as the King of Kings. Certainly, we must acknowledge ourselves as guilty of ingratitude and violated faith if we do not return these things to Him. 

What punishment, then, shall we judge ourselves worthy of when we not only neglect to acknowledge Him, but even try to claim for ourselves the very things we owe to Him? Would not any prince justly sentence to the ultimate punishment a man who, despising his ruler, claimed the royal regalia and ornaments for himself—especially since it is by those very things that a ruler’s majesty is held sacred? 

This is also clear through the logic of <term>analogy</term> <note>Postel uses "analogia" to mean that the laws governing the physical world and human society reflect the laws governing the spiritual world.</note>. Since Holy Providence wishes for no "payment" from a creature except honor, love, and fear, it follows that even the <term>separate substances</term> <note>A philosophical term for angels and demons, who are "substances" existing without physical bodies.</note>—who behold and admire everything in the Creator without the help of a body—were brought into existence for this same duty of praise and honor, and were granted the ability to do so freely and not by force. 

Therefore, in this one thing only can they fail their Creator: if they attempt to claim for themselves what they most owe to Him. Because they are "simple intelligences" <note>Pure spirits without the complex, conflicting drives of a physical body.</note> lacking the assistance (or hindrance) of a body, they cannot sin in any other way as seriously as when they proudly claim for themselves what is owed to God. That the demons committed this very act must be admitted by reason and held as a tenet of religion. For when a great multitude of them saw the gifts given to them and the freedom they had been granted, they wished to attribute their own perfection to themselves. Thus they fell from their rank, were cast out of the heavenly region into the midst of these physical elements, and became wicked demons. 

In this realm, they are very frequently seen through their effects. They mingle with the lightning, they are wrapped in the winds, they disturb the seas, they obsess humans, they haunt houses, and they enchant, harm, or destroy crops—either by themselves or through the instruments of wicked people. They oppose the efforts of people striving toward piety, lest those people have the soul... <note>original: "animus," the catchword for the next page.</note>

<summary>Postel argues that the ultimate purpose of human and angelic existence is to return honor to God. He explains that demons were originally "separate substances" who fell from grace specifically by claiming divine glory for themselves, and they now express their malice by disturbing the natural world and human piety.</summary>

->### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

...the soul is more fortunate, which is able to approach heaven, from whence they <note>The fallen angels/demons.</note> are eternally exiled and have been cast down. Therefore, those demons who were created by God as a single kind have been divided into two parts: into <term>eudaimones</term> <note>original: εὐδαίμονας; well-disposed or "good" spirits</note> and <term>kakodaimones</term> <note>original: κακοδαίμονας; "evil" spirits</note>, whom we call good and bad angels. It is necessary to admit these things from what is conceded (since we see them by their effects) and to investigate their nature by the same reasoning. We see from the writings of *Proclus*, *Iamblichus*, *Hermes* <note>original: Mercurio; referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note>, and others, that there are indeed two kinds, and that the good are distinguished by a three-fold difference, taken three times <note>Meaning nine total orders.</note>. For there are nine orders of angels—or of "gods" as *Proclus* and *Porphyry* <note>Neoplatonic philosophers who sought to reconcile pagan polytheism with a hierarchical spiritual system.</note> call them—or, if we prefer, nine orders of good spirits. They teach that the first orders receive the light of the intellect from nowhere else but God; the second receive it from the first and pass it on to others; while the lower ones only receive it. In the same way, we must judge the opposite side, since spirits from all those orders fell through their own pride and, by denying honor to God, are now found in opposition. 

Furthermore, they are as much worse here as they were once in a more excellent condition <note>A common medieval theme: the higher the angel, the more terrible its fall.</note>. The mages themselves admit this, compelling individual kinds with specific names and rites. There are, therefore, nine orders of evil demons (if "order" can even exist in such ruined things) just as there are of angels. This fact did not escape *Virgil* in the 6th book of the *Aeneid*, when he says: *And the nine-fold Styx, flowing between, hems them in.* <note>Postel interprets Virgil’s description of the underworld river Styx as a metaphor for nine levels of demonic opposition.</note> For he says that nine orders of envy or hatred—that is, of demons—stand in the way of those who departed from life without the Emperor’s command, preventing them from escaping. For he who commits suicide, since he could not commit a more monstrous crime, is rightly believed to be possessed by the entire cohort. Although it has been sufficiently proven by demonstration that there are diverse kinds of demons—because their effects fall under our senses—yet concerning the good (whom they call gods, heroes, or spirits), let it be agreed among all. To confirm the recognition of the evil ones, I shall bring forward an ancient witness, *Hermes Trismegistus*, who flourished shortly after *Moses* and was regarded as a god. His words from the 9th dialogue of the *Pymander* <note>A foundational Hermetic text.</note> are as follows:

> The Mind conceives all notions: good ones indeed, whenever the seed is poured in by God; but the contrary ones, when seeds are cast into the soul by certain demons. Truly, no part of the lower world is destitute of the presence of evil demons. Finally, the demon, creeping into the human being, sows the seeds of its own operation; and the mind, sprinkled with these adulterous seeds and made pregnant, gives birth to adulteries, fornications, murders, parricides, sacrileges, thefts, impiety, the overthrow of cities, provinces, and kingdoms, plagues upon men, and all other evils, which are the works of nefarious demons.

So he says. *Iamblichus*, in his work *On the Mysteries*, says—according to both his own and *Porphyry’s* opinion—that the evil and lowest demons, being deprived of governance, are moved by passions. Otherwise, he calls the "separate substances" <note>Beings without physical bodies.</note> subject to the High God: plagues, Heroes, spirits, and souls. From this it is clear that demons, although they surpass our soul in intelligence, are nevertheless of two kinds. For it is established that some bind us to leadership over matter, while others pull us upward, snatching us toward celestial things more sublimely, or more lowly, according to their nature and ours, by various kinds of desire. Therefore, those who cause the noble nature of the soul to cling to flowing and decaying things (since its origin, nature, and end were implanted in it by the divine nature) cannot be anything but worthless and wicked. This is because the study of all laws, all efforts of religion, the prescriptions of philosophers, our natural inclination, the innate love in us for knowing the truth, and the natural thought of God all call us upward and away from earthly things. Therefore, those who wrote about magic and sacrifices handed down distinct orders of the inferior powers, just as they did for the superior. Hence our *Paul* rightly called them "the princes and rulers of this darkness" and "the powers of the world" with whom we have a struggle; who can be conquered by no other power than the "shield of faith." Just as the highest order of angels, who are called Cherubim, Seraphim, and Thrones, contemplate the inaccessible light and receive from it the purification...

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.

...sublimity, light, and the perfection of all good, happiness, and virtue, as well as of knowledge; so it is necessary that those who fell from that kind by their own choice must dwell in the deepest darkness, wickedness, unhappiness, vice, and ignorance of themselves. For a thing becomes so much worse as it has changed into the opposite from a more sublime nature. Finally, the same comparison claims its place even in the second and third ranks. Since every natural thing consists in action, it is necessary for these substances to act upon certain subjects, and thus to act upon mortal souls, either rightly or wrongly, according as they are of a good or wicked lot. Because they are moved by the good, with the power of the wicked driven away, they fare happily and are useful to the commonwealth. They recognize God everywhere and are masters of themselves. The opposite happens to those obsessed by the impure company of demons. For they do all things toward their own ruin, the overturning of their brothers and the public good, and the disgrace of God.

<margin>
These things are also in the book of the *Shepherd*, or *Concerning the Two Ways*. <note>A reference to *The Shepherd of Hermas*, a popular early Christian work that describes two angels—one of righteousness and one of wickedness—contending for the human heart.</note>
</margin>
But these things are common to the whole human race: to have two different companions throughout the whole time of life, by which the freedom of our soul is incited. For "he shall not be crowned, unless he has striven lawfully." <note>A quote from 2 Timothy 2:5.</note> It happens, indeed, even by a similarity of life, that more than one from the two orders are present to men themselves. And from this, many excel in divination, because, forsooth, the commerce of separate substances <note>Spiritual beings like angels or demons who exist without physical bodies.</note> familiarly insinuates itself into the soul, so that by known movements it may open those things which are above human faculty. Yet one must not sink into the opinion of Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>, who teaches that a body of this kind, by whose command admirable virtues are performed, no longer lives and acts by its own soul, but has life from a divine particle approaching it. For it is impossible for a man to be <term>informed</term> <note>original: informari; in the philosophical sense of a spirit becoming the "form" or animating principle of a human body.</note> by a demon. Hence no mage could ever raise the dead. A spirit often offers itself as a ghost; otherwise, it clings to the mind and there reveals future things. And so, in hope of our familiarity and of gaining our company, they perpetrate deeds surpassing human strength—good ones, if the inspiration was good, or the contrary, if evil. They differ in this: those who approach by divine movement, not by mere permission, can do all things because they adhere to the First Cause <note>God.</note>. The evil can do only those things which serve for ostentation, not likewise for the use or restoration of nature, unless when they have harmed or feigned. For whatever they commit, provided they have not taken away life, they are able to restore all those things; but life, neither taken away by them nor lost from elsewhere, are they able to return.

<margin>
Prophets and Sibyls.
</margin>
Those who are divinely inspired, or who have surpassed the human condition through angelic company, are called **prophets**, if they be men; if women, **Sibyls**. Those led by more wicked demons, if they have summoned them of their own accord, are usually called **mages** and **evildoers**. If they suffer them against their will, they are named by our people <term>energumenos</term> <note>original: energumeni; from the Greek for "those worked upon," used in the early Church for the possessed.</note>, because the demon carries out his works in them as if in instruments. Therefore, when he is admitted into one unwilling, he is accustomed to violently rack both body and soul. This kind is frequently seen and is expelled by exorcists by the power of the cross and the name of Christ.

<margin>
Exorcists were different in the primitive Church than certain rascals are today.
</margin>
The first kind <note>The divinely inspired.</note>, using a spirit familiarly on account of the innocence of their life, is not in fault, because they never command evil angels except so that they do not harm, and that in the name of God Most High. For an angel does not obey an angel except by the command and power of God. Therefore, prophets and divinely inspired men, in the name of God and by the ministry of angels, command the dire powers and compel them to do what is commanded. They use the work of the good, however, to heal both bodies and souls; not at all for trickery, unless when public utility demands it for the sake of the unfaithful, so that at last, unwillingly, they may be compelled to believe these things have proceeded from God. Men therefore have familiarity with separate substances either willingly and knowingly, or unwillingly and unknowingly. Those who are unknowing and unwilling, being compelled by the good, break out into words not premeditated by themselves, and some do this constantly, others occasionally, for some use of mortals.

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

...the divine power, and he foretold excellent things concerning all kingdoms and the coming Christ. I would not likewise believe that the holy prophets spoke what the Spirit dictated without understanding it in every detail, as <note>Montanus was a 2nd-century Christian who claimed that prophets were merely passive "pipes" through which the Holy Spirit spoke while they were in a trance.</note> Montanus falsely claimed. All holy men, knowing and willing, called upon and held as companions good angels who were heralds of many things. Therefore, those of all mortals are most unspeakable who, for the destruction of other men and for the sake of deceptions, summon foul powers. Since there have been many such people throughout the memory of all literature, I must bring forward a few into the open and compare them with the deeds of the prophets, so that the clear distinction between them may appear. No one was more famous than Simon the Samaritan <note>Commonly known as Simon Magus, a sorcerer mentioned in the Book of Acts who tried to buy the power of the Holy Spirit.</note>, who, on account of his unspeakable deeds, obtained a statue at Rome as if he were a god from Nero. Who has not read of Apollonius of Tyana? Who does not know that Apuleius labored—not in vain—under the infamy of magic and sorcery? Let us see what the famous deeds of these men were. Simon, by promising more than he could perform, mocked Nero with deceptions and frequently faked his own appearance. He made it so that various things appeared wherever he wished. A mountain seemed to be moved from its place by his work, and houses were overturned. He took care that news was brought from any part of the world, and that he appeared as a dog, or any other animal, though he was a man. But how do these things look toward the use of human life? There were also in our memory men appearing to others with a wolfish body <note>A reference to lycanthropy or "werewolves," which Postel attributes to demonic deception.</note>, accustomed to commit dire deeds, murders, and thefts by the authorship of a demon. This is frequent. When finally caught, they acknowledged their crimes, likewise having from the demon that which Simon professed. He seemed to fly in the air; yet he could never raise the dead, nor heal any man from disease. Greek vanity has handed down many things about Apollonius; but nothing is more "famous" than what they say: that he recognized demons, saw an Empusa <note>A shape-shifting female demon in Greek mythology.</note>, received news from the most remote parts of the world while events were happening, and understood the songs of birds. # GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I

...brought them to ruin, although more than 300,000 of them were devoted to him, having had their thumbs cut off <note>Postel refers to a legend concerning the followers of Bar Kokhba, a 2nd-century Jewish messianic figure, who supposedly cut off their own thumbs to prove their courage and loyalty.</note>, to protect that Messiah. From this it is clear enough how the false differs from the true. For if they had held their illusions by the authority of God, they would have foreseen the outcome, and could not have brought such great harm to their own people; instead, they would have sensed future evils beforehand, in the manner of the prophets. For Elijah and Elisha foretold the future, raised the dead, and multiplied the substances of things, so that a tiny bit of flour and oil sufficed for many people in abundance. Therefore the Spirit of God accompanied them and set them on fire to foretell the truth. 

But since the dreadful nature of the demon desires to be seen as a god, it has very frequently sought to deceive the simple-minded under the pretext of piety. And so, when the true light of divinity began to shine in Christ, an innumerable filth of impure men also arose, who by magical illusions dragged many into ruin so that they might resist the budding Gospel—no differently than the sorcerers <note>Referencing Jannes and Jambres, the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses in the Book of Exodus.</note> resisted Moses when he began to deliver the Law. For because the Jews saw, according to the predictions of the prophets, that the time of the true Messiah was pressing near, many peoples flocked to Judea from the whole world. Among these, impure men supported by the illusions of demons rose up; some called themselves prophets, others gods, and others the Messiah; with wicked phantoms they agitated the minds of men searching for the truth, and finally dragged them to ruin, such as Judas the Galilean, Theudas, a certain Egyptian, Elymas Bar-Jesus, the two Simons—one from Cyprus, the other the Samaritan—and innumerable others, as Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian whose works *The Jewish War* and *Antiquities of the Jews* are Postel's primary sources here.</note> says in more than one place. 

Magicians (he says) and robbers gathered together, bringing afflictions upon many; and calling them as if to liberty, they threatened present death to those who would bear the power of the Romans, so that they dragged even the reluctant into their own opinion. Simon the Samaritan had gathered up to 4,000 men, the Egyptian up to 30,000, and Bar Kokhba <note>original: "Barchozbae"</note> (as we have already said) shortly after Christ, gathered six million <note>original: "sexagesies centena milia." This is a massive rhetorical exaggeration common in early modern accounts of the Bar Kokhba revolt.</note>; while they all strove to tear down the power of the Romans, they dragged themselves into ruin. Festus finished off the Egyptian; Peter put Simon to flight in Caesarea, not with an iron sword but with the Word of God; Titus and Hadrian <note>The Roman Emperors who oversaw the destruction of Jerusalem (70 AD) and the final suppression of the Bar Kokhba revolt (135 AD), respectively.</note> finished the others. Famous deeds indeed! Those indeed are the arts and rewards of demons. 

Who would not notice how much a true prophet differs from the evil and false ones? Christ Jesus our Lord and God, having performed as many miracles for the benefit of men as the Father had first created in him and placed in the core of his being—did he bring any ruin upon his own people? If one man gathered four million <note>original: "quadragesies centena hominum milia"</note> for one wicked deed, what could Christ not do, by restoring whole men to life (which is indeed more difficult to our senses than creating them), by renewing whatever parts of them were broken, returning sight, hearing, feeling, speech, hands, and feet, freeing entire bodies from ill health, walking on the seas with a dry foot, and finally rising again? What crowds of men could he have gathered—he who, of his own accord, fed a multitude flocking to him even in desert places with heavenly bread multiplied by his power, to the number of four, five, and seven thousand men? —whom the Roman magistrate <margin>as did Pilate and Tiberius.</margin> admired for his innocence and approved? 

How much company and gathering do you think there was for him in cities and inhabited places, when such a great crowd flocked to him in the deserts? He could have moved entire provinces; if he had come to acquire human power (I know to whom and for what reason I am writing these things), one great argument for this is that when he entered Jerusalem—the most famous city of the whole East (as Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist who described Jerusalem as the most famous city of the East before its destruction.</note> says)—sitting on a little donkey amidst an infinite crowd, while innumerable people flocked from the whole world, and innumerable priests were in the most venerable Temple very intent on their sacred business, he was able to overturn their trade, throw down the tables of the money-changers, and disrupt the public use of the sacred forum, without the high priests even daring to mutter against him because of his holy deeds? O Christ Jesus, how great is your power and majesty!

### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

<meta>catchword: and by [his] vices</meta>

Ragged, filthy, needy, despised, alone, and poorest of all, you are able to overturn the force and majesty of laws with a single act. This is not, this is not a human power; behold, it is God, it is God. Thus you differ from lost men, and all the more so because in you dwells all the fullness of divinity <note>Postel alludes to Colossians 2:9, "For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily."</note>. You display both the office of a prophet and the majesty of God, while maintaining the form of a servant <note>A reference to Philippians 2:7, describing Christ’s humility.</note>. Satan knew this once he saw the effects of your work, and he employed his own ministers to become "apes of divine works" <note>original: "simiae divinorum operum." A common theological concept suggesting that the devil can only mimic, not create, true miracles.</note>, and finally to prepare a wicked vengeance for the nation. These same impious men—just as Egypt was never without the illusions of demons—opposed Moses, the prophet of God, and rose up with false powers against the true ones. But in the end, the inferior were conquered by their betters and yielded to the divine will, recognizing that the power of God is greater than that of demons. For Satan does not conquer himself, as it would be against nature for anything natural to rise up against itself. From these effects, it is clear enough which are evil and which are good spirits; from this, men who use "separate powers" <note>term: "separate powers" (potentiae separatae). This refers to spiritual intelligences or beings that exist independently of human matter, such as angels or demons.</note> that exceed human effort can be identified.

A wicked man or a demon, while playing tricks on the eyes with illusions, drives men mad with vain terrors, promises false and fleeting things, pursues vices, and persuades others toward virtue with a deceptive cunning; he approves of virtue in words, but condemns it by his deeds. By the permission of God, he sends in evils and plagues because of our crimes or as a trial. He wishes to be seen as a god, rejoices to be celebrated by the words of all, strives to be praised, desires and hunts for empires, and overturns human affairs so that he may finally possess his own desire. But if he is not allowed to achieve this, he seeks fame and immortality through illusions. 

<margin>The Ecclesiastical Histories report this regarding Peter.</margin> While Simon the Samaritan—the god of Nero and a "lid worthy of its pot" <note>original: "dignum patella operculum." A Latin proverb meaning two things are a perfect match, used here to say the tyrant Nero and the sorcerer Simon Magus deserved one another.</note>—strove to seek the heavens, he was cast down by divine power while Peter and Paul were praying, and shortly thereafter he resigned his unhappy soul to its possessor. All Rome is witness; Hegesippus is witness; Tertullian is witness; and Nero is witness, who for that reason executed Peter and Paul. While Simon desired to acquire eternal fame for himself, he instead achieved eternal death along with eternal infamy. What shall I say of Apollonius? <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century philosopher and miracle-worker often compared to Christ by pagan authors.</note> He preferred to lay hands on himself rather than fail to beg for a reputation of divinity. I will say nothing of the others, for a most unhappy catastrophe closed the final act of their play. 

There arose between the good and the bad a certain clever, shape-shifting kind of men. This was the sort that gave origin to false religions, faking and lying about divine conversations, while meanwhile devising tyrannies and violent empires. I will not speak of this now, but I shall when I treat the origins of all religions. We are forced by the effects to recognize the distinction between these separate powers, both in themselves and especially when men use their works. For the evil ones prepare and bring ruin both to themselves and to the spectators who believe them to be divine. The good, by their effect, direct both bodies and souls; then, they seek out, manage, and execute whatever they do for the safety of both. 

It is necessary for there to be most holy minds, which either command the evil spirits or are familiar with the good ones. For wisdom does not enter a malevolent soul <note>Reference to the Wisdom of Solomon 1:4.</note>, nor does any familiarity with divine spirits. Those who are willingly occupied by evil ones seem, in their words and signs, to be upright, and they fake virtue as much as they can. For they do not want to betray themselves immediately, not until they have baited men under the pretext of integrity and extorted their faith. And so, by forcing themselves upon people more frequently, they conquer them, and once they have conquered, they abuse them to their own and others' destruction. 

Through good powers, divine providence does not indeed create these lower things, but seems to rule them—even if, by its infinite virtue, it manages everything, even the smallest matter. By the command of God, the good spirits exhort us toward virtue and toward common and private utility through inspiration; the evil ones, by His permission, so that they may test us, dissuade us with false inspirations. When we pay too little attention to good exhortations, angels appearing in men show us the divine will and confirm it with signs. For no prophet was ever certain without a sign or a sure prediction of the truth. From this it follows that Muhammad is not a prophet, for he lacked both, and by [his] vices...

...and it overflowed with the greatest vices. These very beings (I mean humans and angels, as well as the commands of God) are opposed by unjust powers of their own accord, and they use wicked men as their instruments. From this, innumerable evils spring forth, though the causes themselves remain hidden. For the more pious someone is, the more ardently do the demons <note>The Latin *dæmones* here refers to fallen spirits or malevolent intelligences that Postel believes actively interfere in human morality.</note> press against him to prevent his progress. They lead him astray, either by swaying him with an unexamined opinion of the truth, or by turning him away through injuries to the soul or body—distracting him from all good things, and especially from true piety toward God, self-knowledge, and love for one's neighbor. No mortal who has ever attempted to look within himself <note>A reference to the Socratic "know thyself," which Postel integrates into Christian theology.</note> can deny that he is moved toward virtue itself by a certain natural impulse, yet he feels that the love of truth (which consists in the knowledge of oneself and of God) is not fully within his own power. However, although we possess free will <note>original: *liberum arbitrium*</note>, we are never able to carry out those desires so perfectly that we are not either deprived of the wish itself, or find much lacking for its perfect fulfillment. Therefore, I must say a few things regarding the nature of man.

## ON THE NATURE OF MAN. CHAPTER IX.

Even if a vast multitude of men now seems scattered throughout the entire world, and an innumerable number have inhabited the earth from the first man down to our own memory, yet no man can deny that all have flowed from a single beginning. Born of a single parent, they gradually moved into various regions. The philosopher Averroes <note>original: *Aben reis*. Postel refers to the Andalusian polymath Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), known in the West as Averroes, whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to medieval and Renaissance philosophy.</note> testifies that they share a single origin, saying that the entire generation depends on the first man. Thus, wherever nations are found, they name the lineage after the father, not the mother, for those who are reckoned into a particular family. For if they were not from the same first parent and a single beginning, one of two absurdities would undoubtedly follow: either God was superfluous, or there are multiple kinds of humans. For if He created many of the same form beyond the usual mode of nature, He would have spent His effort superfluously, since it could have been done otherwise through the order of nature. If, however, they were of different forms, that would be apparent; yet neither should be admitted. For there is but one form—namely, humanity itself <note>original: *humanitas*</note>—with which all are endowed, and no other forms have been seen. Indeed, God never wished to lead nature beyond its limits when she was capable of the task. It was enough to have created a man and a woman for natural propagation, and—having instilled in them the appetite for procreation—to have left the care of posterity to them, just as with all other living creatures. For just as in all other things produced by seed, unity necessarily precedes all number, so too must it be confessed in the human race: Unity exists before all number. For this reason, all are held by the same laws of nature; the same force of reason moves them, the same appetite incites them, and the same goal drives them. From this it is most evident that they are held by the same nature and composition of both soul and body, and are always connected by the same matter and form. For it does not happen that the figures and qualities assigned to specific forms are shaped by some other common form. If that were so, a confusion of all species would occur, and the order of things would be overturned.

Truly, someone will object that the Blemmyae <note>A legendary race of people described in antiquity as having no heads, with their eyes and mouths located on their chests.</note> lack heads; that some have the heads of dogs, others the snouts of swine; that some are half-goats and satyrs; or that there are "strap-feet" <note>original: *imantopodas* or *loripedes*. These were mythical beings with feet like leather thongs or who were said to crawl rather than walk.</note> and those of that sort. Since these appear to have human senses but a dissimilar shape, into what category do you think they should be referred? By experience itself you will learn (though I grant that many such stories are fables, and I do not believe those things handed down about Centaurs are true). If they speak, if they gather together, if they reason, if they remember, and if they are held by a sense of religion, do not doubt that they should be counted among men. Otherwise, it is certain they are an unknown genus of animal. It can happen, however, that the most perfect form and figure with which we were gifted by the Creator is changed; while lost men, through excessive license, take on the danger of various appearances, they may procreate various monsters <note>term: "monsters" (*monstra*). In early modern thought, a 'monster' was a biological marvel or warning, often seen as a sign of nature going astray or divine judgment.</note>, which then depart into a lost lineage and a dissimilar shape. This is also the work of unspeakable demons, who, having taken seed from elsewhere and placed it...

...in a natural place, and with proportionate heat, for certain species to take their beginning is not foreign to their nature. Furthermore, that nature itself can be altered by art <note>In this context, "art" refers to human intervention or cultural practices, as opposed to "nature" which is the innate biological order.</note> regarding physical form is something the very famous author Hippocrates discusses in his books *On Airs, Waters, and Places*, when speaking of the Long-heads <note>original: *macrocephali*. These were a group described by ancient writers whose heads were elongated, initially through binding infants' skulls, which Hippocrates claimed eventually became an inherited trait.</note>. For among them the opinion had become so strong that it was honorable to be born with an oblong head, that the care of midwives and physicians was used to shape the tender heads of newborn infants into an oblong form, until nature eventually began to imitate art, and children were born naturally with the same shape that had previously been fashioned by hand. This is a truly incredible thing, were it not known throughout the world and written of by such a distinguished man.

That there are some of cubit-height—and therefore called Pygmies—or others with a swinish snout, or with their heads sunken into their chests, narrow mouths, protruding or hooked noses, or even entirely noseless <note>original: *syrictę*. This likely refers to the Scyritae, a legendary race described by ancient geographers as having only holes for noses.</note>, could have happened through art subverting nature. This is just as modern industry has brought it about that fruits are born without seeds, though they possess a grace far inferior to natural ones. For they smell more of water than of the true nature of fruit. Thus, a variety of outward figure does nothing [to change the essence], provided that the nature of the form remains in the things themselves, and the innate power of reason flourishes. 

Our human race seems to have been composed with the best constitution, whether you look at the gifts of the soul or the body, and was happily equipped for choosing things to seek or avoid. This is because divine power had formed man with a most holy breath and adorned him with judgment and the prudence of choice, lest, while he wished to pursue those things which do not pertain to his proposed end, he should become the author of his own ruin. For alone among the natures of so many living creatures, man is a participant in reason and thought. By this alone he excels the beasts and is joined to God; through this he infers, argues, refutes, and concludes. 

If it were not for "self-love" <note>original: *philautia* (φιλαυτία)</note>, ignorance, contempt for the First Cause <note>Postel uses "First Cause" to refer to God as the origin of all existence.</note>, one's own rashness, and thoughtlessness—along with the depravation of customs and the variety of opinions taking their origin from those first principles—then all men would be as similar to one another in both reason and soul as any individual is to himself. From this it happens that while all good men, knowing that man was born for the sake of man, might be called gods to one another; conversely, one instructed by human opinions and worldly prudence is usually said to be a "wolf to man" <note>original: *homo homini lupus*. This famous proverb suggests that humans, when stripped of moral restraint, treat one another with the predatory cruelty of wolves.</note>. Thus, while in other kinds of living creatures no species rages against its own kind—for as the saying goes, all things live rightly within their own genus—for man alone, the greatest evils come from other men.

Whence we see that what was the most excellent of nature's gifts has become the most ruinous of all. Nor does man bring ruin only to others, but also (which is itself against nature) he rejoices in his own miseries, of which he both wishes to be seen as the craftsman and architect, and indeed truly is. For it happens to him from the use of natural things that the nobler his condition was from the Creator, the worse he has become through the depravity of his own will. The more delicate the body of a thing, the more its putrefaction corrupts the air. The sharpest vinegar comes from the finest wine without any art; a fall from the heights is more foul and greater than a fall from a meager fortune. The most foul smells come from the most delicate foods. 

O miserable man, who of your own accord cast yourself down, and have sought yourself outside of yourself for so long, becoming worse by the day! Therefore, antiquity, hinting at these things, established several "ages" of men according to the types of metals for which they were most inclined, while posterity was truly weakened. The first age was called Golden, and the second Silver, though both were lacking [the actual metals]. Hence Homer says: "And they themselves perished through their own blind folly" <note>original: οἱ δ' καὶ αὐτοὶ ταῖς ἀταθαλίαισιν ὄλοντο (Odyssey 1.7)</note>. And elsewhere: "For few sons are like their fathers; most are worse, and few are better than their fathers" <note>original: παῦροι γάρ τοι παῖδες ὅμοιοι πατρὶ πέλονται, οἱ πλείονες κακίως παῦροι δέ τε πατρὸς ἀρείως (Odyssey 2.276-7)</note>. Men, he says, are the makers of their own fortune. But if they receive some contagion or temperament from their parents at birth, as they certainly do (for it is the custom of nature for the noble to be born of the noble, and the fearful from the fearful), let no one wonder that men have long since arrived at such a point of wickedness that nothing can be added to it. Plato confirms these sentiments in the *Alcibiades*, even citing the verses of Homer:

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the corruption of human nature. Having previously described physical abnormalities, Postel now transitions to the moral and intellectual "diseases" that afflict the human soul and the mechanism by which corruption is transmitted despite the soul's divine origin.</meta>

->G V L . P O S T E L L I B . I . 67<-

"In vain," he says, "do mortals caught in evils blame the gods, since they are captured by their own miseries, and even willingly undergo evils heavier than death." Hence it is clear that some have entirely stripped off their own nature and put on a contrary one, so that they do not even feel their own unhappiness. Others, although they feel it and try to look within themselves, recognize the disease but cannot heal themselves. Glory carries them elsewhere, pleasure drives them off course, opinion besets them on all sides, and invincible necessity presses upon them. In all of these, reason is cast down from the citadel of the mind and, contrary to its own judgment, **yields the palm of victory** <note>original: "porrigit uictoribus herbam," a Roman idiom meaning to concede defeat or surrender by offering a handful of grass to the victor.</note> to the conquerors. Since that stupor or depravity of nature dwells in every mortal, and all agree in this, it must be that just as they had received right reason and most perfect judgment from the Creator in the first man, so also this noble gift was endangered in that same man. 

For just as all agree when the very roots show signs of disease, so unless light shines again from heaven, all agree in evil; so much so that those who know themselves do what they do not want <note>This is a likely reference to the Apostle Paul’s struggle in Romans 7:15: "For what I want to do I do not do, but what I hate I do."</note>. Others, even if they are carried away by depraved habit, still judge themselves to be doing wrong, yet do not stop. But they differ in this: though both go astray, the former sins unwillingly, the latter willingly. The reins of human **free will** <term>arbitrium: the faculty of choice or decision-making</term>, which was the most excellent thing in man, are so poorly managed that it cannot be restored to its original state at all, except by Him who was the first Creator. 

If, however, someone should say that this inclination toward the bad side and toward vanity—arising from free will—was intended for the sake of virtue (which is placed on a steep and difficult path), they would be saying something, but too little on the matter. For where there is pure freedom, there should be no reason more inclined to one side than the other. We see this ourselves when we choose between two goods without any inner conflict, or avoid a greater evil. For there, there is no compulsion or violent inclination that urges us because of vain opinion, small fame, or self-destructive pleasures. From this it is clear both that we are all depraved from a single origin, and that we are pressed by the power of demons. 

But how can it be that this plague, by which we are infected, reigns in all and creeps further day by day, since our soul is not transmitted by physical descent <note>original: "ex traduce." This refers to "traducianism," the belief that souls are generated by parents like the body. Postel argues here that while the body is inherited, the soul comes directly from God.</note>, but enters our bodies from heaven? And since from that soul free will usually arises, by which we are incited to noble deeds and flee their opposites? Truly nothing can be solved more easily than this question. Let us assume a certain common principle upon which both sides agree. Nature or art does nothing without an instrument so disposed as to be most fit for its functions; this, nature shows by certain laws. Nothing grows without the action of heat upon **radical** or accidental moisture <note>Postel uses the language of medieval medicine: "radical moisture" was thought to be the innate life-sustaining fluid of an organism, while heat was the active force of life.</note>. These are therefore the instruments without which nature can do nothing. 

But if these are out of proportion and depraved, excessive moisture will kill and cause rot; violent heat will burn and consume the moisture. If they are less than is proper, it is necessary that all things suffer from wasting away. This, however, is not to be ascribed to the impotence of nature, but to a defect of the matter and the instrument. For if the seed is worthless or faulty, even a well-disposed instrument will not act upon it. Just as an axe fit for splitting wood will not act upon stones or metals, so too it will not act upon those woods which <margin>† have diverted into the nature of stone.</margin> † have turned into stone, nor upon those that are flimsy and unstable. For it cannot split piles of hay, wool, cotton, and the like, which are not held together because of their softness. 

Three things, therefore, must be weighed in every action (so that nothing exists without the image and mystery of the **Trinity**): the agent, the instrument, and the **recipient** <term>recipient: original "patiens," the object or matter being acted upon by an agent.</term>. The last two must be arranged proportionally to the power of the agent. For if a most wise prince lacks a soldier, he achieves nothing; if an unfit soldier is present, the same is true. If a best leader and soldier are present, but victory cannot be had because of very high mountains, the strength and fortification of the place, or anything else, what, I ask, can he accomplish? Does he not therefore seem imperfect? The same reasoning applies to the craftsman, the axe, and the material. For...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument regarding the corruption of human nature. He argues that the soul itself remains a perfect, celestial entity, but its expression is limited or distorted by the "instrument" of the physical body—a concept rooted in the Aristotelian idea of the soul's different levels (vegetative, sensitive, and rational).</meta>

->ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

No one is considered imperfect simply because they cannot perform a task with a dull tool, or because they cannot cut through material that is harder than the instrument itself. Thus, what seemed to be an objection against us actually confirms our point most strongly. For since the mind is derived from a heavenly origin—or at least from a "fifth element" <note>The "fifth element" or quintessence was believed by ancient and medieval philosophers to be the incorruptible substance that makes up the heavens, distinct from the four earthly elements (earth, water, air, fire).</note> which has no contrary—it must be most perfect. And because it is perfect and celestial, it is present in the same way in everyone. From this, it is clear that the fault and the unfitness for receiving the mind's actions lies in our matter and our lineage <note>original: "traduce," referring to the transmission of nature or sin from parents to children.</note>. This fault is no common thing, as it almost forces us to act against our proposed goal (unless a restoring divine power is present); meanwhile, other animals seem to avoid what should be shunned and choose what should be sought more prudently than man himself. What animal anywhere has ever taken its own life through imprudence or vice? They set a limit to their nature out of necessity, not out of pleasure.

But, good God, how many men has gluttony killed, how many has drunkenness destroyed? How many has the pursuit of lust caused to live in a state of constant death? How many has the greed for possessions cast into immense labors and dangers? How many has the desire for revenge and the fulfillment of irrational will thrown into disgrace and a criminal death? What more can be said? Man fights against himself at every moment and seems to begrudge himself the happiness of living, while he arms himself with every skill for his own destruction. Therefore, this human lineage is most poorly affected, following so badly the things that are good for it, and so unskilled in its own future that while it thinks it is choosing a certain end, it brings ruin upon itself by those very choices. 

This has led to a situation where many, looking into themselves, have been taken from life by a weariness of living, while others have been led into despair by the regret of false efforts. This happens through no fault of the most excellent intellect or the reason placed within us, but through the stubbornness of the corrupted "human mass" <note>original: "massae humanę," a term often used in theology to describe the fallen state of humanity.</note>. Therefore, some judged it best not to be born, or to be abolished as quickly as possible, for this one fault: they were ignorant of the purpose for which God had created man. 

It also follows from our first principles that the intellect is not only unable to act upon corrupted matter, but also upon matter that is disturbed or not yet properly arranged. For suppose there is a skilled craftsman and an excellent tool, but the underlying matter is not ready to receive the action: if the proper position or resistance is lacking, the craftsman certainly cannot act. Just as a blacksmith cannot shape glowing iron in the mid-air without an anvil—and as long as this is the case, he cannot work according to his art—so it is with our body. Since the "vegetative" (or nutritive) life is what provides nourishment, and the "sensitive" life provides movement, if anything in the nourishment is done incorrectly, the senses must also act incorrectly. If the first level does not act at all, there is no place for the second to act. 

If the vital and sensitive parts within us are perverse, or not yet fully developed, the intellect will not act at all, or it will act only slightly and imperfectly. This is why the action of the mind does not appear clearly in children, the elderly, the delirious, or the foolish—not because the mind is absent, or because it is imperfect in itself, but because the instruments are corrupted. For since we consist of a vital soul, a sensitive soul, and an intellectual soul <note>Postel refers here to the "three souls" of traditional philosophy: the Vegetative (growth/nutrition), the Sensitive (movement/perception), and the Rational/Intellectual (thought/will).</note>, the second cannot act without the arrangement of the first, and the third cannot act without the operation of the other two. In the same proportion that the lower parts are made imperfect, the power of acting is lacking in the higher part. 

We see this same thing in various subjects. For some children, because of an excellent physical constitution, are immediately wiser than old men. If the intellect came to us only through habit and experience—as the atheists <note>original: "ἄθεοι" (atheoi)</note> claim—it would be impossible for such a noble gift to exist in a child who lacks experience of things. It cannot be denied, certainly, that through use our life becomes more obedient to the intellect, and is, as it were, tamed and civilized by reason itself. It is just as if a blade, through constant use in cutting, acted more readily upon the material, and the material itself, having been cut frequently, immediately admitted the sword from every side without a great effort from the one using it. So also we see that old men, through constant experience of things, are for the most part wiser than others. This is not because their intellect or reason increases (as is commonly said), but because their vital and animal lives have been made more fit and more obedient to the movements <note>original: "motibus" (the catchword from the previous page), referring to the impulses or motions of the soul.</note> of the mind.

<summary>Postel argues that human vice and irrationality stem not from a flawed soul, but from the "corrupted matter" of the body and the physical senses, which act as imperfect tools for the perfect, celestial intellect. He explains the levels of the soul—vital, sensitive, and intellectual—showing how the higher mind depends on the proper functioning of the lower physical faculties.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Postel's argument that the human soul is a perfect, celestial substance, while the physical body is merely its "instrument." He is responding to materialist views (like those often attributed to the physician Galen) which suggest that the soul dies when the body's physical balance is destroyed.</meta>

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.

...movements. Therefore, when the blood perishes in animals, life perishes and the soul departs, because the instrument of life has collapsed. And there is an answer that can be given to Galen <note>Galen (129–216 AD) was a prominent Greek physician and philosopher whose views on the relationship between the body's "temperament" and the soul were widely debated in the Renaissance.</note> when he questions Plato and all those who wish to argue for the immortality of souls, asking: "How is it that a human being perishes when the blood flows away?" 

Certainly, if Galen had wished to investigate the nature of the mind and the soul as deeply and diligently as he scrutinized the parts of the body, he would have undoubtedly seen that in his elementary matter <note>Matter composed of the four physical elements: earth, air, fire, and water.</note> there are no parts that have the power of judging, deliberating, and thinking about the purpose of things—and in short, of gathering and knowing all things, even those that are absent. He would have agreed with Aristotle and would have sided with antiquity rather than denying that reason exists within himself while striving to devise new theories. 

For if the reason and intellect within us are assumed to come from the elements, it must happen either by reason of matter or by reason of <term>temperament</term> <note>In ancient medicine, "temperament" refers to the specific balance or mixture of the four bodily humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determines a person's health and character.</note>. If from matter, then even all parts of the elements—stones and metals—would possess intelligence. If from temperament, then the closer brute animals approach the human mixture, the more they would possess reason. But this is seen in none of them. Therefore, both premises are false. It is established, therefore, that the intellect comes from elsewhere and enters into all men from heaven. 

But Galen will object again, citing Aristotle (if indeed he is the author of that foolish book *On Physiognomy* <note>original: "peri physiognomonias," a work once attributed to Aristotle that claims character can be judged by physical appearance.</note>): "The character of the soul follows the temperament of the body." Fine words. The <term>sensitive soul</term> <note>The "sensitive soul" was thought to be the part of the soul responsible for senses and emotions, shared by both humans and animals, as opposed to the "rational soul" unique to humans.</note> itself is affected by the passions of the body (as is clear in the books *On the Soul*), and as long as it is affected by its disturbed order, so long does it judge poorly or is affected in some other way. A drunk man, his brain filled with fumes, becomes either cheerful or sad according to the nature of his temperament and the circumstance. I admit it. But what happens to him is not unlike lamps, which are nourished by oil when applied moderately; but when that same oil is excessive or withdrawn, the light vanishes. 

An ape suffers the same as a man. Therefore, it is not the soul or reason itself that is affected, but in a body that is physically composed and depraved, it performs its function poorly—even according to Aristotle. Moreover, that there is something in us above those things that proceed from temperament is proven most strongly by the fact that we judge against the feelings of nature, even in the midst of passions. Unless this were done by a different nature, it could not possibly be done by the nature that is entirely affected. 

For it is established from its own nature that a single sphere is moved by a single motion, and cannot be carried in different directions by one action. Thus, no action of a single agent can occur unless the actor is intent upon that thing. And yet, being angry is different from judging that one should not be angry—which happens at one and the same moment. Therefore, these come from two principles that share nothing in common. For this reason, we are given precepts against anger and the movements of the sensitive soul; which, to this day, would have been done in vain by wise and learned men and by laws. For if we consisted only of that soul common to the beasts, we could not be healed by moral precepts. 

Whence it is necessary to admit that immortal souls, always consistent with themselves, act within us, and the imperfection of the action does not depend on them. It is established, therefore, that the human race is entirely depraved <note>Postel refers here to the "depravity" or physical corruption of the body as an instrument, rather than the soul itself.</note> in its physical state, but there is no vice of dullness, slowness, or imperfection in the soul itself. Although this is widely evident from what has gone before, even the most unskilled—let alone philosophers—will grasp it by considering the end and goal of man.

## ON THE GOAL OF MAN IN THIS LIFE,
## and how far it differs from the path of duty. CHAPTER X.

Not without reason did antiquity wish to celebrate the phrase "Know Thyself" <note>original: "gnothi sauton," the famous Delphic maxim.</note> so greatly and heap every kind of praise upon it. For from the knowledge of oneself proceeds the entire reason for duty; just as from ignorance and neglect flows unhappiness and a mountain of false opinions. But whoever said that, said it indeed; yet he neither taught nor provided the means by which we could achieve it. Whence, though everyone has had it in their mouth, in actual effect and the practice of life, either none or certainly very few—and those the most fortunate—have possessed it,

...except for those whom providence has shaped and restored anew. For since knowing truly and by demonstration is to know through the cause, no one could ever descend so deeply into themselves as to consider for what end they were truly made, unless they had first known their own causes. Or if perhaps some were able to know, no one was ever able to perform or manage it in such a way that they were not always many <term>parasangs</term> <note>A parasang is an ancient Persian unit of distance, roughly 3.5 miles. Postel uses it here metaphorically to mean being "leagues away" or "far off" from the truth.</note> away from the true mark. 

Let us therefore begin to know man from his causes themselves, and let us try not to seek ourselves outside of these rational principles. Quite ordinary things must be proposed by us here, yet without them, there is no room for greater matters; they are the starting point from which one may arrive at a great knowledge and demonstration of our present nature. As with all other natural things, there are four <term>causes</term> <note>Postel uses the Aristotelian framework of the Four Causes: Efficient (the creator), Material (the substance), Formal (the design/essence), and Final (the purpose).</note> of man: the primary cause, the two conjoined causes, and the final cause. 

It has already been shown in the preceding pages that all things were created, are ruled, and are preserved in existence by God as their author. Therefore, **Providence** is the **efficient cause** of man. He shares the "conjoined causes" with other composite things: **matter** and **form**. He shares matter with other physical things, while his form is distinct and suited specifically to his species. 

Now there remains the fourth cause, the most excellent of all, and the one without which the others would be in vain. For both art and nature are accustomed to do all things for the sake of a **final cause** (the end). Since in the whole of nature nothing is more excellent than God, it is certain that the end of man is God. If any impious person denies this to me, I shall force him either to admit it or to cast aside human reason entirely. Where things have different conditions, it is clear that their ends are also different; the ends of superior things are superior, and those of inferior things are inferior. 

Yet in this lower world, nothing is more excellent than man. Therefore, nothing can be more excellent than man's end. Since nothing is greater than God, it is clear that He is man’s end, so that He is the beginning and the end of all things—both the efficient and the final cause—just as man himself is the primary cause and final goal of his own actions. The comparison differs in this: God is the goal in His very nature; whereas for man, the goal of his works is, or ought to be, his own "utilities"—those things that serve to preserve life for himself and his kind. 

From these points, we can now define man: **Man is the most excellent living being of the whole world, endowed with intellect, soul, and body, and created for the sake of God.** 

With this established, we must see how he might best prove himself worthy of that final cause, and in what activities he might engage that are useful for reaching that goal. For any craftsman, while striving toward the completion of his work, is usually extremely attentive to what leads toward that end: first, to do everything that looks toward the goal; second, to avoid useless actions; and third, to commit nothing that fights against the utility or the beauty of the work. 

For a man would be justly condemned for ignorance and forced to repay his master's expenses and compensate for lost time if he were so mad as to not only fail to act usefully and honorably toward the set goal, but to waste labor, time, and resources—a waste that is not only useless but costly for himself, his master, and the project itself. It would be shameful and damaging to himself, unjust to his master, and destructive to the very thing that was meant to endure. 

Thus, man placed in this life, endowed with soul and body, must pay close attention to his goal, taking care not to fail in these ways. By knowing and reflecting upon himself, he must see that he does not try to pass off any "adulterated" work as legitimate before God. Reflect on how grave a sin it is when a person is not content with having wasted his efforts and done no good, but actually assumes the Lord is so mindless and sluggish that He either does not see these wrongs or, seeing them, does not disapprove and simply ignores them. Such a deed is no less than the crime of <term>lese-majesty</term> <note>original: "violatæ maiestatis." This refers to treason or an offense against the dignity of a sovereign.</note>. For anyone who believes and declares the Lord to be mindless, foolish, lacking in reason and judgment, or a supporter of evil works, effectively thinks there is no Lord at all. For one who is bound by no laws of justice or injustice can have no place in a commonwealth, either because he does not understand them...
