-># GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I<-

...or because it is not grasped or restrained. For to fools and those who are mentally incapacitated, the law and an injury are one and the same, because they grasp the reasoning of neither. To tyrants and the propagators of inequity, it pleases them to observe no distinction between these things. Therefore, he who willingly sins against God is rightly called guilty of treason against His Majesty <note original: "reus maiestatis eius">This refers to *crimen laesae maiestatis*, the legal concept of 'injured majesty' or high treason against a sovereign.</note>. 

But we must persist in the comparison of the artisan aiming at a mark <term>scopus</term> <note original: "scopus">From the Greek *skopos*, meaning a target or the mark one aims at in archery.</note>. For from this, a greater light will shine upon our treatment of the subject. Every artisan needs a body, a strong instrument, and material before he can undertake any work. In the same way, man has been granted those three things by God in this temple of nature so that he may work toward his end; and as often as he abuses them, he treats the Master who gave him this province with contempt and mockery. 

Those three instruments granted to man for action are: first, man himself, given to himself by God, consisting of such excellence that he cannot be weighed or compensated for by this entire lower world. For this mass encompassed by the heavens would have been made for man's sake in vain, unless the purpose of the work were more excellent than the work itself. Man is the goal of the material world, but God is the "mark" or target of man. 

The second thing, which should properly be called the instrument, are the goods of the soul, the body, and of fortune. With these, man acts upon "material"—that is, upon another human being. Meanwhile, he must observe this one rule: that while he uses the instrument, he does not imprudently cause harm to himself (for example, by the handle or any other part of the tool) without some greater gain. 

Therefore, all those things must necessarily be referred back to God, the giver and creditor of all these things, as if to a target. Whenever we wander away from Him by our own will, we lapse most gravely. This is easily seen by a single reason. If someone were to proceed to such a degree of impiety against a father that he not only despised and mocked him, but also rose up against his dignity and abandoned his prescribed duty—would he not be rightly condemned for ingratitude and be disinherited from his father’s estate? 

If an earthly father, who is merely the instrument for propagating the body, rightly exacts such a heavy punishment from an ungrateful, unjust, and lost son for the sole reason that the son despised, provoked, and harmed him—how much punishment do we think nearly all men deserve? For they neglect God, the author of the body, the soul, and all goods, and they sin in every single moment against His prescription, which is planted in all their minds so that there would be no room for ignorance or excuse. 

Truly, we ought to love God as a parent above all things, and love our fellow man as a brother—indeed as another child of God and as our very selves—preserving ourselves in the highest innocence as children of God. Instead, we neglect this so thoroughly that we not only fail to love God above all, but we prefer a prostitute, a coin, a most vain opinion, a bit of petty glory, or a pleasure over Him. We cancel and deny His prescriptions by our words or deeds as if they were counterfeit, and we even attempt to cast Him down from His seat. 

And the neighbor, whom we ought to hold in the place of a brother through love, and whom we ought to cherish and bind to us by doing good as a father does, we instead despoil of his possessions, his body, and his reputation. By whatever art we can, we busy ourselves with harming him. Yet in all these types of duties, nature had prescribed that we should most especially prove ourselves to God. 

What shall I say of ourselves? How many crimes does a man commit against himself? The soul given by the divinity, akin to the divine, and capable of virtues, we plunge into the abyss and whirlpool of every crime. We establish the body as a slave to all pleasures. We abuse the very things and the instrument with which we ought to provide equally for our brother and ourselves, leading to the ruin of both.

<margin>Human justice is nothing without grace.</margin>
And meanwhile, if it please the Lord, man thinks he can be "just" without God, the renewer of this corruption. O blasphemy! This is what "human justice" is: to pile up wealth by any art possible, and to care not for what is sufficient, but only that another does not become richer than you. What else do you see in a "most holy" man—at least as far as human laws allow—except that he is judged "best" simply because he abstains from evil? 

But this is exactly as if someone highly skilled in a certain craft—whose industry ought to be building houses for the whole neighborhood—were called the "best artisan" simply because he had done nothing evil to anyone with his tools. But what is the point of the art? What is the point of the instrument? What is the point of...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument regarding the purpose of human existence. On the previous page, he established that man is the goal of the physical world, but God is the ultimate target or "mark" for man. He now applies this to the use of physical and mental faculties.</meta>

-># ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

To what end is a strong and fit body? To what end is the power of the soul? For what purpose, finally, were all these things granted to man? Should a man be considered a good citizen if, while living in a city, he gathered a great heap of tools into his house every day, spoke most excellently about the work itself, and yet meanwhile—due to a lack of craftsmanship—allowed his materials to be neglected and ruined by wind and rain? Such a person would be not only a poor citizen, but utterly unworthy of dwelling in that city. 

And yet, in the meantime, we are not ashamed to gather wealth from every side as if we were to live forever. We heap up and bury immense weights of gold and silver, while countless poor people—spoiled either by our ancestors or recently by ourselves—are consumed by hunger, thirst, cold, and toil. We all judge these things to be unjust, yet no one amends them. Is it not the sign of a most depraved and utterly rotten nature to judge a thing and condemn it, yet fail to correct it? If you sin only against yourself, you do an intolerable injury to your Father, the author of your most worthy nature, and you destroy yourself. If you sin against your brother—that is, another human being—without cause, you deny that you are a son, that he is a brother, and that God is the Father. But who does not make a mockery of these things daily, not only by committing them, but by encouraging as many as possible to do the same? To arm our own people with cunning, to draw our inferiors into crime by our example, and our equals by our fellowship—this is truly considered "the work of virtue" by the world.

<margin>Against the Pelagians <note>original: "Contra Pelagiastros." The Pelagians were followers of the 5th-century monk Pelagius, who argued that human nature was not fundamentally corrupted by original sin and that humans could achieve goodness through their own will without divine grace. Postel strongly disagrees here.</note></margin>
And our petty philosophers, speaking of virtue, dare to affirm that human nature has no inherent flaw <note original: "labem">meaning a stain, defect, or ruin</note> within it. They do this because they think of virtue merely as words, just as they might think of a grove merely as a collection of wood. Beyond doubt, since even the most "perfect" man judges himself to have sinned against himself, his brother, and God, and neither cares to nor is able to amend himself, it follows that the perfection of man does not depend on man alone, and cannot be restored by him. For it is established—alas, it is established more than enough—that this foul mass <note original: "massam istam feculentam">Postel uses this strong language to describe human nature in its fallen state, corrupted by sin.</note> is entirely depraved, since it acknowledges judgment and guilt, yet no one can provide an absolute remedy. 

Whoever, therefore, looks deep within himself and weighs the "mark" <term>scopus</term> for which he was established by God, cannot help but cry out to divine providence and confess his own impiety, seeing how gravely he sins against it daily. He feels nothing in himself (even if he exerts all his strength) except his own condemnation, unless God helps him. But those who are truly moved by the divine power of God are entirely different from worldly people. They strive to turn everything to the glory of God; they commit nothing unworthy of the sons of God; they spend all their effort and wealth on others, not themselves. Through fasting, vigils, and labors, they willingly weary the body; they adorn their souls with virtues; they laugh at the splendor of material things and embrace insults. They mock the power of "fortune" (a hollow word) as having no sway over them, and they even undergo death willingly for the sake of persuading others of the truth and for the sake of their neighbor.

<margin>Contempt for death.</margin>
When many most famous philosophers saw such "imitators of Jesus Christ," they were amazed by the divine presence and the transformation of the men, and they voluntarily crossed over into their fellowship. For they said it was impossible for those who sought death with such cheerfulness to be evil men or criminals. For although there may be great constancy in a man throughout his life, whether in vice or in virtue, no mind is so great and lofty that it cannot be weakened and broken by the terror of a guilty conscience—unless, of course, he is conscious of no wrong, or if some human frailty has befallen him, he knows for certain that providence is favorable to him.

Yet, some wicked person might object to me here: "That God is unjust, who permits this plague to reign in nature and has placed a law in our souls that no one is able to observe." <note>This is a classic theological problem: if God is good, why is human nature so prone to sin? Postel addresses this "theodicy" in the following sentences.</note> Watch your words! Is a father or a friend unjust who gives gifts that I can use for either good or evil, simply because I abuse them? Is He unjust who confers so many and such great benefits upon us that the world itself, and all the people who ever were, are, or will be, would be unequal to acknowledging even the smallest benefit bestowed by God on a single person? Because the weight of our obligation is so great that it is impossible to fully satisfy it, should that which is supreme goodness be called "injustice"? To this is added the vice of our first parent <note>Adam</note> and our own vice, by which we daily provoke the God we ought to venerate. God gave what is best: the power of use and free will <note original: "ab usu & arbitrio">Referring to the freedom to choose how to act.</note>.

He defends God's goodness against those who claim it is unfair to be given a moral law that is impossible to perfectly follow without grace.</summary>

...judgment <note>original: "arbitrio"</note>. We lose this so completely that we do not even perceive that we have perished. There is no injustice in God, but rather in ourselves and in the very **mass of nature** <note>original: "naturae massa"; a term used by St. Augustine to describe humanity's collective state of sin after the Fall</note>. Returning then to our purpose, we must acknowledge that our common material is all but lost through descent <note>original: "ex traduce"; referring to the biological and spiritual inheritance of sin</note> from the first man. Though our soul is always present and capable of action, it no longer wishes to yield its stubbornness; therefore, to mend that material so it may act rightly and look toward its intended goal, there is a need for a **notable physician**, one who is not inferior to the Creator Himself.

->### ON THE NECESSITY OF THE PRESENCE OF GOD MADE FLESH<-
->### among men. CHAPTER XI.<-

God, the almighty and all-knowing, to whom future things are as well known as the present and the past, had a most perfect view of how man would lead his life—both in general and in every detail—before He even created him. Yet, even though He knew man would perish partly by his own doing and partly by the craft of the devil, He did not wish to desist from creating him. For it would have been a work of fear, weakness, small-mindedness, and folly to delay the creation simply because of that, when He could heal man just as easily as He could create him. 

Therefore, since the most wise God made all sensory things for the sake of man, and made man for the sake of his own salvation and happiness, for the benefit of other men, and for His own honor, He judged that corruption (which is inherent in things because of the nature of **matter** <term>materia: the physical substance or "clay" of the world which Postel views as prone to decay</term>) would necessarily affect man as well. I speak here of a corruption that is not common or similar to that found in other things. For the more excellent He fashioned man to be above all other living creatures, the more grave He foresaw his fall would be. Indeed, a fault is considered more serious when the one who commits it is wiser and of higher status. This is why brute animals do not sin—because they do not choose; and the fall of a king is more significant and visible than that of a private citizen. 

We have already satisfied the question of why God did not create man absolutely free from sin, or so good that he could not sin. This was permitted neither by the nature of matter nor by the power of **free will** <note>original: "arbitrium"</note>. For unless the nature of matter felt accidental corruption within itself, it would be as incorruptible as a pure form, and would have left no room for the many diverse forms of life we see. Furthermore, since the nature of "the Good" is blessed in every part, it cannot exist unless it is free. For he who does good unwillingly is not only a slave, but it is as if he did not do it at all. No opportunity for merit—which proceeds from liberty—can exist for one who acts well whether he wants to or not. Therefore, there was no way God could have created man with a better lot regarding this present life. 

If He created man (as has been gathered) and knew he would become unjust and evil through the depravity of nature (which is most true), then even from the eternal constitution of the world—I speak of the **uncreated world** existing eternally in the Divine Mind, within the Wisdom of the Son—it was necessary that He had already forethought a remedy for this ruin. This remedy He would send for man's restoration at the time when human wickedness appeared to have reached its peak. 

Since this depravity was greater the more noble and closer to God those men were whom it affected, an intolerable plague soon invaded everyone shortly after the world was founded (save for a few who had struggled to keep the knowledge of themselves and God). Many demons spread their works among the gatherings of those few men (for those two natures, human and demonic, had fallen by their own choice, as we have seen) and both sides used their faculties for evil. Therefore, while the knowledge of God the Creator was still fresh, and while men had—owing to their recent innocence of life—frequently enjoyed the sight of good angels, God did not use mere warnings toward these deplorable men. Instead, He commanded the element of water to return to its own order (from which it had receded at His command), and with a flood of waters, He consumed everyone except a very few. This was done not by some new plan or sudden change of will, as the philosophers say, but by eternal deliberation. And lest the trifles of the Greeks should seem barren...

...that they have devised nothing new, nor attributed anything to their own regions. They even claim a great fire <note>original: "conflagrationem"; referring to the Stoic belief in *ekpyrosis*, or a periodic destruction of the world by fire</note> was brought upon the world, a concept they took from sacred sources and applied to the Great Flood—but they lie without much wisdom. For the sun’s power was never granted to a lost man like **Phaethon** <note>In Greek myth, Phaethon attempted to drive the sun-chariot and nearly burned the Earth; Postel argues this is a distorted memory of divine judgment</note>, much less to a good man, that he might set the world ablaze due to human errors. Furthermore, if such a fire had occurred, they could not have remembered it, since no living animal can be rescued from fire; whereas we can meet the dangers of water, as they occur, by using ships. 

This is the divine order of things. When destruction began to spread once more—for among those who escaped the danger of the Flood, there was one not sufficiently upright <note>A reference to Ham, son of Noah</note> who was nonetheless saved for his father’s sake—God (the Blessed One) began to deal more mildly with the offspring born from that race, and He did not see fit to destroy them further. For even lightning bolts would not have sufficed if He had wished to pursue the sins of every person. 

Furthermore, those holy men who survived the Flood had received by hand from their ancestors knowledge of the ancient condition of things, as much as the divine goodness had revealed to the first parents of human nature, either through His own voice or through an angelic vision. These things were indeed believed by a few good men—those, specifically, who possessed the wisdom to strive to become better because of it, and to lead and benefit the rest. 

Yet, human ferocity could not be moved from its own path of destruction by those laws. For the **multitude** <note>original: "multitudo"; referring to the common masses or the "unthinking crowd"</note> and the pride of this world are of such a nature that if you share sacred things with them, they are neglected and become cheap through familiarity; but if you reveal nothing, they immediately begin to be carried headlong into vice, lawless and reckless. Therefore, there is a frequent need for repeated miracles, or for rare and new events, so that you may draw the multitude where you wish. 

Satan, understanding this, and wishing to be held as God, never left a stone unturned to offer himself in God’s place and to deceive under any appearance of good. God, therefore, having sent certain angels throughout the whole world, revealed what was to be expected regarding a future remedy, and what was to be done in future times (so far as it is permitted for man to know). Thus, He divinely inspired the **Sibyls** <note>Prophetic women of the ancient world whose verses were often interpreted by Christians as foretelling the coming of Christ</note>—women inspired by God at various times and in various provinces. All of them, but especially those who warned the **Gentiles** <note>original: "ethnicos"; non-Jewish peoples of antiquity</note> held captive by false religions, urged the recognition of the one God and spoke of the future change of kingdoms and the end of false religion. Their verses were most religiously collected and preserved, both by many others and by the Romans, in whose libraries they remained until the time of **Constantine** <note>The first Roman Emperor to convert to Christianity, who famously cited the Sibylline oracles</note>. 

But these things were of little use to lost men, who had grown deaf as if they lived at the **Catadupas** <note>The waterfalls of the Nile; ancient writers claimed the people living near them were deafened by the constant roar. Postel uses this as a metaphor for spiritual deafness</note>. Few were skilled in these matters; and those who opposed the efforts of demons and challenged false beliefs were rewarded with **hemlock** <note>A reference to the execution of Socrates, who was forced to drink hemlock for "introducing new gods"</note>. Thus, vice creeps in easily but can scarcely ever be torn out. 

Divine providence, therefore, wishing to leave nothing untried that pertained to the salvation of men, saw that the entire world was suffering from a most heavy disease. He did not wish to reshape the whole body at once—a mass foul with rot and struggling under its own weight—because the people could not all gather in one place of the world to hear God’s prescriptions, and they were accustomed to losing things that were rarely repeated. Instead, He chose a nation, as He had determined from eternity, to whom He might repeat, through the ministry of both angels and men, the written rules for living which He had intended to be naturally implanted in the minds of all. Thus, for those whom conscience did not move, the written words might refresh their memory of that which had perished within them. 

He chose, therefore, **Abraham** from the **Chaldean** race, to whom He might give the beginnings of the holy law. By God’s command, Abraham chose to live as an exile from the unspeakable **Babylonian** people, lest the contagion of a wicked religion bring a stain upon the fledgling belief. His progeny, imbued with holy precepts and persisting in them for 400 years, eventually found themselves in Egypt. At that time, **Moses** was sent, who claimed for God’s jurisdiction a vast number of people who had been contaminated by the fellowship of Egyptian religion and oppressed by a most heavy tyranny. 

God wished this to be accomplished in one nation, not in many, so that by the example of those men, at least the foreign nations might see that it is far more blessed to live under the empire of God than under that of demons. If He had wished to give it to other peoples (for the slanders of the impious must always be satisfied), He would have given either the same law or a different one. If the first, He would have acted in vain, since it could be propagated and handed down from one; if to all...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s explanation of divine pedagogy. Having previously described how God preserved humanity after the Flood, he now addresses the specific nature of the Mosaic Law. He argues that the Law was a transitional tool—a "schoolmaster"—designed to lead a stubborn and "child-like" people away from Egyptian paganism and toward true worship through temporary concessions and symbolic rituals.</meta>

## GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.

...the same in every province, it would have been superfluous, and the choice of accepting what was received from others would have been taken away; for that reason, they would have believed without merit. For there would have been a need for wonders and signs throughout the whole world to compel them. Furthermore, there would have been no difference between truth and falsehood, since a conflict between truth and falsehood must necessarily exist until the end of the world. If, however, He had given a different truth <note>original: "ueritatem"</note>, He would no longer be God. For in the nature of things, only one truth underlies everything. Therefore, nothing better could have been done than what was done. Moses, therefore, relying on divine power, confirmed the truth with wonders and signs.

<margin>Yet He most wisely provided for the unlearned in this way, so that in the shadows of ceremonies, the whole work of Christ and the formation of morals might be indicated.</margin>
Indeed, God prescribed such a law there, just as a skilled teacher is accustomed to doing for children who are coming to the "bitter roots" of learning. For if he immediately confronted a child coming to him with whatever domestic, corrupt, or undisciplined habits the child had, he would undoubtedly not be inviting him to school, but rather frightening him away as if from a slaughterhouse; nor could he imbue a stubborn nature with any principles of discipline. Thus the Blessed One, as if feigning not to notice, put up with many of their unnecessary works and vices, and established as law what He permitted for their tender age—an age unfit to grasp divine things. Such things include all kinds of sacrifices, vengeance, divorce, and many similar matters. For it is better to have a "half-evil" man <note>original: "semimalum hominem"; meaning someone who is partially reformed rather than entirely wicked</note> than to leave him altogether lost. Since there is a need for sacred ceremonies in every religion, both for the sake of all who are imperfect and for the sake of providing a sign, it is manifest that sacred days and rites must be established in certain places: not for the sake of God, who is everywhere and always present, but for our sake. Since we consist of both body and soul, we find it necessary to explain those things which are in the soul by means of some physical sign. For although deep meditation is more excellent than spoken prayer, the words of prayers must nevertheless be uttered by the mouth and accompanied by signs. Therefore, in order to lead their worship—which had been corrupted by the idolatry of the Egyptians—back toward divine honor, He commanded that all those things which were sacrificed to Egyptian idols should be sacrificed to Him. This was not for the sake of the smell (for as the royal prophet <note>King David</note> says in the person of God: *All living things are mine. If I were hungry, I would not ask you; I do not feed on flesh or blood* <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 50:10-13</note>), but rather to turn a bad form of worship into a good one. This is the same reason for the law of divorce. The injuries they were frequently accustomed to receiving in Egypt made them more prone to vengeance. For "patience, when injured too often, turns into fury." The commanded "thefts" of Egyptian vessels were justified because the rights of the afflicted people had not been upheld; it is indeed permitted, when ordinary law is denied, to pursue one's own property by any means, provided it can be done without public riot.

<margin>Epiphanius <note>Saint Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 315–403 AD), a Church Father who wrote extensively on biblical law and heresies</note> argues excellently regarding the right by which God commanded the Egyptians to be despoiled.</margin>
For if the laws do not help the State or a single assembly, one can justly pursue what is theirs from another by any skill. God permitted this to them as compensation for the injuries they had received, so that they would not be delayed when the opportunity came to pursue or reclaim what was theirs. The unleavened bread was nothing other than a way to ensure they would not forget the beginning of the divine favor. Therefore, there is no reason for the impious to say that God was the author of evil, or that He changed His mind. For it was not an evil thing to pursue one's own property; nor was it a change of mind to permit those things and establish them as if by law, without which He otherwise could not have offered and persuaded them of the best and holiest precepts while still preserving their freedom. For God does not wish to bring force upon the will <note>original: "arbitrio"; referring to free will</note>, except perhaps to a specific individual, so that from there they might pass from habit to acting freely. He wishes the proverb to have its place: *Break, rather than correct*, those things which have hardened into depravity; He does not want people to be lost. Although the Israelites were almost compelled by wonders and signs to receive the sacred law, we can nevertheless judge from ourselves what sort of people we would have been if we had stood in their place. We judge the vices of others easily, but we applaud our own. If those who beheld God present and were stirred daily by miracles were like that, what of the rest? How great was the impiety in the whole world, if even among the pious there was sin? Man acquiesces to God with such difficulty. We have been spectators of that kind, yet we are far inferior to the actors themselves. Furthermore, that Law, although it was bitter, nevertheless seems not unlike the rod of a schoolmaster. For it reveals vices by the punishments it inflicts, but it cannot substitute virtue in their place.

He justifies practices like animal sacrifice and the despoiling of the Egyptians as necessary legal and psychological steps in God's long-term plan for human salvation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument regarding the historical necessity of the Incarnation. Having established that the Mosaic Law was a "schoolmaster" for a child-like people, he now describes the progressive moral decay of both the Jews and the Gentiles (Romans and Greeks), arguing that humanity had reached such a state of corruption that only the direct intervention of God in human form could provide a remedy.</meta>

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD #

Thus the law of Moses, having been given, pointed out vice and, by pointing it out, increased it; but it was never able to take it away. For it struck frequently, but did not correct. But let us consider this: if those who had two laws—both that of nature and the restored law <note>The Mosaic Law, which Postel views as a restoration of natural law for a fallen people</note>—were wicked men, what should we judge of those who were lawless? The holy prophets succeeded Moses, sent by divine inspiration; they, noticing that the law was now entirely perverted and neglected, rebuked evil men and gradually lessened the reliance on ceremonies, showing that salvation was not in them, but in charity, piety, and self-knowledge. These [ceremonies] were indeed signs not to be neglected, provided their internal power was present; if it was absent, God was mocked by them, not worshiped. It finally happened that those who were under the law were the worst of all men, and in that respect even worse than the lawless nations, because they abused the best law as a cover and color for their crimes, and by their own traditions overturned the most sacred prescriptions. Therefore, when there was no longer any place for true piety, except in very few, and the demon <note>original: "dæmon"</note> was worshiped in the whole world, and man was perishing by his own hand <note>original: "suo marte," a Latin idiom meaning by one's own efforts or force</note>, and ambition, glory, pride, and the other plagues of the world had reached their peak: then, when there was no longer any room for lesser remedies, and divine and natural precepts had been trampled upon, the greatest evils required the greatest remedy. It was necessary for God Himself to come, not as a specter, but clothed in a body. For God’s threats, human efforts, and the art of angels had all become obsolete. From the humility and faith of Abraham—who as a youth could have seen Noah—the people who had been gifted the law gradually fell into such vice (after being frequently recalled to the path of truth by prophets, worn down by captivities and wars, and corrected more often) that nothing could clearly be added to their wickedness. Sin against God by that nation was all the more grave, and hope for repentance seemed less, because in addition to the crimes reigning everywhere among the Jews, a system of laws was established by impious sacred magistrates which both contradicted sacred things and paved and leveled a way to wickedness.

The laws of God had taught that God must be loved above all things, and parents honored and helped with resources. But through the greed of the scribes and Pharisees, having circumvented the words of the divine law with fraud, it had been determined on the contrary that no one was bound to support his parents—not even his father—whoever had bound his possessions to sacred uses with an annual gift <note>This refers to "Corban," a practice criticized by Jesus in Mark 7, where people avoided helping parents by claiming their money was dedicated to God</note>. The law of God sought the hearts of men, but the synagogue had burdened the people only with ceremonies, and those most heavy. In short, gold—as Isaiah already said in his own century six hundred years before—was entirely turned into dross <note>original: "scoriam"</note>.

Now, if we consider human affairs more diligently among foreigners, the Romans, descended from shepherds and thieves, had reached such magnitude that on account of those things which they had snatched from the whole world by robberies, slaughters, violence, and injustice, civil wars were now beginning at home; they were laboring under their own weight and degenerating into a monarchy from an aristocratic tyranny. The whole world, lying subject to their empire, suffered damage from pestilential men not only in their bodies, but also in their souls after their property was plundered. The affairs of Greece, once most flourishing, had either entirely perished or had now degenerated from virtue into vice. For those crafty wits <note>The Greeks</note> were devising and teaching the arts of pleasure for the splendor of the Romans, by which things ill-gotten might be even worse squandered. The disciplines which had once been for the greatest good of the Republic brought ruin and the trouble of learning without any fruit. Pythagoras, Plato, and Aristotle lay buried; Epicureans, followers of Arcesilaus <note>The Academic Skeptics</note>, Pyrrhonists, sophists, gluttons <note>original: "gastrimargi"</note>, and such plagues flourished; so that you would judge that whatever most excellent things God had given to men, all those had been turned toward human destruction rather than benefit. Therefore, no god was thought to exist, because he saw and endured those things. Satan moved in the widest mastery of affairs. The poor man languished under oppressions; the rich man contrived nothing but crimes with his ill-gotten gains. And meanwhile, that splendor of unhappy men swept the innocent into crimes. For if sin was not committed through violence and iniquity, it was yet done by the very abuse of things and the worst example (which almost always [follows] courtiers...

# THE FIRST BOOK OF GUILLAUME POSTEL #

[perfection was reached,] magistrates followed, leaving a plague behind them everywhere; so much so that in no part of the world was there ever rest, until Augustus—having dealt with his allies and rivals—brought long-lasting peace to Rome, under whom the Creator willed to send salvation to the world. Just as the Emperor had brought some rest to the weary bodies of men, so too Eternal Wisdom would come to provide eternal happiness to minds acknowledging the truth. For God, like a most pious father, willed that the one for whose sake He created all things <note>referring to humanity</note>, and who was created for His own sake, should not merely be brought up and then exposed like a wild beast, with no further concern for such a noble nature; but like a most wise physician, He willed to proceed gradually from the smallest remedies to the greater ones, so that He might leave no room for excuse. For if Jesus Christ, the Angel of Great Counsel <note>original: "magni consilii angelus," a title for the Messiah derived from the Septuagint version of Isaiah 9:6</note>, had come at the very first instance of wickedness, mortals could have said that there was no need for such a great remedy for their correction—that if some angel or prophet had come, they would have been ready to repent. Your Creator, O man, proved all things in order to lead you back to the way of truth. Through the works of the prophets and legislators, some progress was always made toward God. 

But since all men are children of God, it must be admitted that they are a care to the Father. For since it is known that God has care for particular things, even the smallest, how much more for men? Otherwise, He would be like one who takes care to preserve, transport, and raise into a structure stones, cement, lime, plaster, bricks, beams, and rafters <note>original: "canterios," meaning rafters or supports</note>, and so on, yet finally neglects the most perfect work itself and seems to hold it for nothing; no greater madness than this could ever exist. Therefore, such a thing applies neither to God nor to a prudent man. Man is something greater than the lower world; therefore, he is a care to God above all things, even more than the world is. For that celestial soul is deservedly to be preferred to all these things. 

Man indeed has need of two things so that he may return into favor with himself and with God. For it is necessary both to renew his nature and to have the capacity to use that renewed nature. For if you wish a captive to serve you, it will be necessary both to free him and to watch over him, lest he fall back into the same dangers. No angel or man can perform this work in a whole human being; thus it remains that it must be God’s work, if it has been repaired in anyone. But when it is demonstrated that these defects of nature have been repaired in a hundred million <note>original: "C milies centenis," an idiomatic way of expressing a vast, countless number</note> men, it will be established that it was the work of God. It is fitting in divine matters that their effects seem to receive proof from what follows. For example, if someone wished to gain the most certain faith that there were divine prophets—Moses, David, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the rest—he will not call them divine because they predicted Christ, but rather because of the coming of Christ, about whom they all prophesied and who bears testimony of them, they will most deserve belief in their divinity. 

In the same way, Christ himself, although he clearly testified to his divinity with every kind of miracle, nevertheless created much greater faith in himself through his members—the Apostles and martyrs—who, by his name alone, performed all the miracles that can fall within human perception. But we are called to greater miracles: how the Son of God received this stain of nature into himself without stain. This must be repeated by a higher method. God the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Deus optimus maximus," a superlative title Postel adopts from Roman tradition to describe the Christian God</note>, unless He had been Three and One, could not have brought things into being. For there was Mind endowed with Wisdom, led by Will and Love to the creation of the universe; without these qualities of the most simple Being, nothing at all could have been brought into existence. Therefore, in His Wisdom, or (as is better) through Wisdom in the Holy Spirit, He established all things—He from whom, through whom, and in whom are all things. For He could not have accomplished anything if He were ignorant or unwilling. That Wisdom of the Father is called the Son, the Word <note>original: "verbum," the Logos</note>, the Beginning, and by many other names. Therefore, just as the eternal God created all things through Wisdom, that is, the Son, so He willed all things to be restored through the same. And just as we are blind in the works of creation, so in the mystery of restoration—which is far more sublime in its value—we ought to dismiss our senses entirely and offer faith to the divine words. For since in our own mind...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD #
<meta>catchword: only</meta>

If we see that by no art can we comprehend the distinction of those properties that are within the soul—namely, **understanding** <note>original: "intelligentiæ"</note>, **reasoning**, and **recollection** <note>original: "reminiscentiæ"</note>—even if we certainly discover through arguments that they exist: how much less can we grasp that eternal and infinite nature and supernatural cause? We know within ourselves that the soul within us does not require a physical space, nor is it moved locally, except by accident when the body moves. Yet we see that in the blink of an eye it penetrates, traverses, and contemplates the whole world, and brings back to us the most perfect notions of things. From this it is clear that spirits, when released from the fellowship and prison of the body, immediately traverse all this matter of the sensible world, far more perfectly and freely than we do. For our soul is frequently called away from the contemplation of great things by these coarse senses of the body. Hence it happens that in sleep, when a release from the body seems to occur, revelations, divinations, and many forewarnings of events take place. How great, then, do we think is the power of that infinite divinity, to doubt whose power is to overturn the truth of all things?

Into the **immaculate virgin**, who was immune from the original stain of the rest of humanity by an eternal privilege, the **wisdom of God** <note>original: "sapientia Dei"</note> willed to descend, by the command of the Father and the guidance of the **Holy Spirit** <note>original: "spiritussancti"</note>. Thus the order of things demanded. For it was necessary that God fulfill all possible modes of generation. The first was without seed and without a vessel <note>that is, a womb</note> fit for generation <note>referring to the creation of Adam from clay</note>. The second is common to all nature, arising from seed cut off from a progenitor and placed within a vessel fit for generation. The third, being as it were a mixture of both, is closest to creation: coming from a vessel, indeed, but without seed sought from elsewhere. In this way it was necessary for **Christ** to be born. 

For just as it was most excellent and admirable to have created the first man by command alone, outside of nature's vessels, brought from clay into the temperament of flesh (which, because we see it was done, we must believe), so also it was most worthy of the **Creator** to make the first restoration similar to the creation. Thus, the generation of the **Restorer** <note>original: "instauratorẽ"</note> would be related partly to nature and partly to the work of divinity, just as was proper and peculiar to the God-Man. For it was fitting that the Restorer differ from those to be restored in his generation and origin, just as he did in his nature; and he needed not only to be distinguished by body and origin, but also to accommodate himself to us. 

For God could have visited us with a body brought from elsewhere (just as spectra <note>ghosts or apparitions</note> have often been seen); He could have used the common mode, or a partial one. If He had done the first, mortal stubbornness and impiety would not have believed that He had a real body. Many heretics have given proof of this fact, having dared to assert that He did not have a true body, but a phantastic <note>imaginary or illusory</note> one. If, however, He had been born in the common and vulgar way, He would never have been received; since He was barely accepted even when born of a virgin and made most famous by signs and miracles. 

Thus, a middle way had to be chosen for the **Mediator**, for many reasons. First, so that He would not wish to redeem us without our own flesh and the temperament He received; which He would have done if He had taken it from elsewhere. Second, so that He might indeed take flesh, but not receive the stain of depraved nature into Himself, which He had come to wipe away from the pious and those who would believe in Him. Third, so that He might be born as the God-Man by a generation different from others, yet most worthy of Him. Fourth, so that He might participate in the extremes of that generation, just as He joined two extremes in one subject. For as God, He descended into the virgin without seed by the guidance of the Holy Spirit; but as man, He willed to take from her a body like our own. Fifth, so that the highest dignity of divinity might correspond to a similar dignity in lower things; namely, that He who was God and immune from every stain might take flesh from a most innocent and pure virgin, with a mortal body as close to divinity as is possible. 

For although the common mode of generating was instituted by God in nature so that nature might be extended and propagated through it, nevertheless, conception and the sexual act cannot lack the stain of sin. All religions, even the false ones that are **apes of the true ones** <note>original: "uerarūq; simię," referring to pagan religions mimicking divine truths</note>, have naturally recognized this, since they require most holy supplications from virgins and in the highest...

-> ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD <-

...it is <note>original: "est," continuing the sentence from page 79</note>, that although more than 20,000 men arose in various regions, no illness or weakness remained wherever even the least of the Apostles and saints of Jesus Christ might be. Moses, Elijah, Elisha, and whoever else performed miracles, did them in the name of God. Jesus Christ alone acted in his own name, since he could do so by right. For he himself was, is, and shall be one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, of one substance. For that assumption of flesh in no way hindered the incomprehensible God from being entirely present where he was in the body, as well as in the administration of all nature.

<margin>The example of the sun especially pleased theologians.</margin>
For He who is contained by no place, and yet holds all things, cannot be hindered. I cannot marvel enough at the great blindness of men, that they dare to bring such things into question, when we see the most familiar examples in the smallest things—namely, that many things are entirely in one place and yet entirely in all and diverse places. Who would not admire the nature of scents, which, though they come from a single source, are nonetheless represented equally to the nostrils of all? The same must be judged regarding sounds to the ears, and likewise regarding the images of things striking the eyes of all: about rays of light stretched out into all parts of power, and about the same image seen in countless mirrors. All these things show that while a thing is in one place, it is not moved away from another. How much less could that omnipotent God, penetrating all things, be entirely circumscribed by a place? These things transcend local motion, nor should they be restricted by the laws of bodies. But if we see these things in objects that proceed from a body, how much greater must we consider that cause which is without a body, at whose nod the stars shine, the heavens are moved, the elements remain stable, living things live, sentient things feel, and rational things excel in intellect? Will He who makes others give birth (as the prophet, inspired by divine power, says) not be able to generate? <note>original: "Nónne quí párere facít... nõ poterít generare?" A reference to Isaiah 66:9, arguing that the Creator of reproduction is not bound by its usual limits.</note> He who made things to exist from nothing, will He not be able to make from something? Since He made the first man outside the **vessels of nature** <note>referring to the womb or natural reproductive organs</note>, which did not yet exist, could He not make it so that they are born not only in this way, but also in many other ways? For to God, it is the same to be born from seed or without seed. For as for our wanting to impose a law upon Him from common usage and the sense of things—what else is it, I ask, than wanting to confine infinite power within a finite place or limit? It was not necessary for divine power to be moved from its place (although it is understood to act more nobly in the heavenly region) in order to raise the form of our body to itself and join it to divinity. Come, let us take examples of such great power from things subject to the senses. What person unskilled in natural things would admit that fire is truly mixed with earth in every natural composite, and especially in those endowed with life, because this never falls under the senses? Yet nothing is more proven or more manifest to the philosopher. And yet fire is a body, but it does not fall under the senses. The Virgin was made pregnant by the work of the Holy Spirit, and in the natural manner she fulfilled the time of carrying in her womb. Christ was born as God-Man. Like other men, he drank, ate, and suffered the other needs of the body, lest—while the works of divinity were seen in him and the sufferings of the body were hidden—he should be said not to have been a man, but only God. ### V. ON NATURAL DESIRE ###

Nature or God gave no false desire for things to any kind of living creature. For although men (who alone in this corporeal world are able to sin) pursue many false things, they are not false insofar as they are in the use of things: but the falsity arises from a depraved impulse of choosing. For there is something in every single thing to be desired which is sought for its own sake, and which has the form of the Good. Truly, when the reason of laws, things, place, time, and persons is poorly observed, it causes us to choose (while we pursue the appearance of good) things that are diametrically opposed. All men are held by a **desire for divinity** <note>original: "cupídítate díuínítatís"</note>: in seeking which they err in this, that they wish to attain it before the proper time (namely, in this life), without their wish being sufficiently balanced with its proper end. <meta>This page continues Postel’s philosophical defense of the Incarnation. Having established that God's power is not limited by physical presence, he now argues that human nature requires a union with the divine to achieve its natural desire for eternal life, and that this union is the "finishing touch" of creation. The catchword "proprie-" at the bottom suggests the next page will begin with a discussion of the specific properties of the God-man or the circle.</meta>

Whatever is in this lower life is subject to change, ruin, oblivion, and corruption; but divinity is truly eternal. Thus, it can indeed be possessed, but not in these earthly realms. Since we are all held by a desire for this divinity, it is certain both that divinity exists and that it can be joined to humanity through divine favor—and humanity to it. Otherwise, nature (which usually does nothing in vain) would be mocking us with a false hope. Since man cannot achieve that divinity on his own, nor receive it from angels, it remains that he must receive it from God. For although a man could return to heaven in spirit—either through hope or in reality—by the gift and direction of the Creator, he could never be perfected in the flesh so as to achieve this by himself. Therefore, it was necessary for our flesh to be joined to God by the Creator’s gift, so that man could fully attain what nature gave him the desire for. For a man is neither just a soul nor just a body, but both together. Thus, God the Son of God was made man for this reason, at the moment it seemed right to Divine Providence. For just as nature did not immediately grant the best possible state to a creature, but rather it receives its fulfillment especially when it has become more mature, so God did not wish to bring the absolute remedy for Himself at the beginning, nor to repair the path to divinity for man—which had perished in Adam—until the proper time.

### FROM THE IMMENSE GOODNESS OF GOD.

The best and greatest God, out of His immense and supreme goodness, ought to have created a supreme and visible work—one greater than which could not be given or even imagined—and to do so in such a way that it would become clear and manifest to man (since He made all things for His own glory and honor). This work must be either uncreated, created, or consisting of both. He produced the uncreated Son from eternity, and created matter and form—either separately or together—from the mind where they were kept from eternity, when it pleased Him to build the world. There remained the third thing, the greatest and most noble of all: the God-man, God before the ages, man in time. In him, He made both extremes one, in whom the most absolute perfection would be joined to the greatest imperfection. Just as the sluggish and unfit earth is stirred into life by a fiery force hidden within compound things, so also our heaviness and weight might be liberated by the best and greatest God and drawn toward heaven. Before He placed the finishing touch <note>original: "colophonem," a Greek-derived term for the crowning completion of a work</note> upon mortal things (which find their end in man), He willed that all of human nature—like a single person progressing from small beginnings to greater things—should pass through each age. He willed that the recklessness of adolescence and youth should cool down—ages prone to every crime by their own lust and running the risk of error—until the age of stability <note>original: "consistentem aetatem," referring to the maturity of middle age</note> is reached, when one must especially come to one's senses and think about the future and death. Then the supreme Moderator Himself, pitying our errors, willed to be present—not in that invisible form which He always has, but in that form which would be clothed in our body. In this form, although the divinity (which cannot be seen by eyes) was not visible, He nevertheless testified by His works that the fullness of divinity dwelt within Him, and that He made our weak and corrupt nature truly happy by its ability to be joined to God.

> Grace be to you, Jesus Christ, who have taken upon yourself the stain of those who acknowledge you, and have made them children of God and your brothers, and have established them as co-heirs of the kingdom of God.

### FROM THE HARMONIC PERFECTION OF THE UNIVERSE.

The most perfect shape and the most similar to God is the circle, as I taught in the first chapter. Therefore, because equality is sprinkled in every direction from the center to the circumference, it agrees with the circle through power, but like the infinite with the finite. Every circle also agrees in form with the archetype. ...properties can a circle be understood or made) so, unless we understand in God an infinite power from which all things come, and a comprehension or knowledge—the **Word**—through which all things are made, and a love or will—a benevolence—proceeding from both, in which all things are established and flourish, we can conceive of no image of divine things. Therefore, just as we see the logic of a total unity within a trinity "squaring" or fitting perfectly through all things, it is also necessary that the method of composing and perfecting the world does not differ. For although God is without beginning, much like a circle that is already perfected, they agree most truly in this: that for the true completion of the whole, it is necessary to unite the lowest things with the highest, and the extremes with the extremes. The highest end is God, and the lowest is man; these are the two extremes: God the beginning, and man the end. 

Therefore, for the completion of this unity, it was necessary for man to obtain salvation by God being joined to man and becoming one: which was achieved in the nature of Jesus Christ. For just as in all things there is <term>theory</term> <note>original: θεωρία (*theōria*), meaning contemplation or abstract thought</note> or thought which exists prior to <term>practice</term> <note>original: πράξις (*praxis*), meaning action or implementation</note> no matter how much time passes; so from eternity the most holy Trinity—through power, will, and wisdom—drew the first lines of the universe in creation after eternal thought. Finally, coming to "practice" in the recreation <note>The "re-creation" or restoration of the world through Christ.</note> of the world, He truly joined the end to the beginning when He worked the salvation of the universe through the <term>God-man</term> <note>original: θεάνθρωπον (*theanthrōpon*), a theological term for Christ being both fully God and fully man</note>. 

In this way, Jesus, assuming human flesh for a double reason, wished to make man, in a sense, God. That occasion was twofold: the "fitting" and the "useful," from which "justice" arises. For where these are separated, truth perishes and justice is routed. It was **fitting**, for the sake of the harmony of the universe, for God to be joined to man; it was **useful** for man—who was lost by his own will and unable to rise by his own power—to be helped. The "fitting" aspect refers entirely to the Actor (God), while the "useful" refers entirely to the recipient (man). From these two, "Justice" was born as a mixture of both, by which rewards are given to the good and to those following the Restorer as much as they are able, while punishment is given to the wicked; otherwise, all praise goes to the Creator. 

Since no part of our duty should lack what is honorable or fitting, good or useful, and just, it is impossible that all men should know this naturally unless it was implanted by one principle common to all. Thus, it neither should nor could have happened that in the conjunction of God and man—the end and the beginning—these three elements did not concur for our necessary salvation. To ensure that the harmonic order of the universe was preserved and the truth of God fulfilled, it had to happen this way. For the truthful God, who established for all things below man their own true purposes (so that they could not be ignored or bypassed by any creature except through human negligence), also pre-ordained a purpose for man. Man is a <term>microcosm</term> <note>literally "small world" (*paruo mundo*); the idea that a human being reflects the structure of the entire universe</note>, far superior to material things. Through this purpose, man would become far superior to and happier than himself, and greater than the entire material world; yet he could not achieve this without that honorable, useful, and necessary connection between the true God who allows it and the needy man who requires it.

### FURTHERMORE, FROM THE WELL-BEING OF MAN, OR HIS LIBERATION.

We have taught above that man was created excellent by God, but brought upon himself by his own choice the evil in which he now delights. He is therefore oppressed by his own depraved nature. We have also seen that he is attacked by depraved angels and has become their slave to sin. For since those angels fell away from their own goodness, it is established that they changed their nature into its opposite. Therefore, instead of the angelic perfections—which consist of following God with charity and love, and praising and thanking Him for the sake of man—they adopted the opposites: through which they might blaspheme the Creator and rage enviously against mankind. 

Thus it is clear that man is oppressed by a double tyranny. To this was added the yoke of the **Mosaic Law** given to those of old. This law was given partly to restrain the rebellious and partly to stir up virtue through small physical rewards, yet it oppressed the more mature people of God with a heavy servitude. Since depraved man could not rise again by himself, much less drive away a foul power far stronger than himself, it was necessary for the Author of both to come in a different way than He did at the beginning, and to purge that nature within Himself which had conceived the stain. He did this so that He might bring the power of faith against the perverse enemy, and so the same Author of the law might lead the soul back to the spirit and the truth which...

**O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! The judgments of God are a profound abyss.** <note>A combined reference to Romans 11:33 and Psalm 36:6.</note> Since God created all things for His own praise, and created beings endowed with intellect or reason for the purpose of being perpetually happy in praising Him, He placed the angels (who excel in intellect) and men (who excel in reason) in the **power of their own counsel** <note>original: *in potestate consilij sui*, referring to free will or autonomy.</note>, as the Wise Man says: so that if they persisted in His praise, they would enjoy the happiness granted to them forever; but if they withdrew from their duty, He would lose nothing, while they would accumulate eternal misery and torments for themselves. For it is just that according to the logic of an infinite majesty having been offended, infinite torments are also imposed. Indeed, God is supremely just. Whether they sinned or not was the same to Him regarding the order of the universe, though not regarding the fault. For as much as was lost from the angelic nature, it was necessary for an equal amount of praising souls to be substituted. 

Adam, along with his posterity, could have been immortal if he had not abused his choice. Even the demon could have remained in his angelic order, in the praise of God, as he had been created good. Man sinned; the demon was cast down. The goodness of God wished to provide for man for a double reason: because the impulse of the flesh (though not as fragile then as it is now) and, moreover, the cunning of the demon, had solicited him toward defection. Therefore, so that the will of God might be completed while keeping free will intact, and so the place from which the evil angels fell might be filled, and lost salvation might be restored to man: it was necessary for that depraved flesh—which was all but destitute of free will due to immense desires—to be restored anew, and to be joined and united to the Creator. 

For this reason, there was a need for a Creator who, having assumed and joined a nature to Himself, might wash away the vice of man in Himself. He did this so that as many as would swear by His words and obey them in all things as far as they are able, could not only return to the condition of the first man (as if returning by **right of postliminy** <note>original: *postliminio*, a legal term referring to the restoration of rights to someone returning from exile or captivity</note>), but, as superiors and companions of angelic virtue, they might fill that place with blessed souls. Finally, they might even bring a solid and corporeal human nature there. 

Thus, the first arrangement of God achieves its end, with God Himself having been made man. For otherwise, neither could salvation be returned to man through man, nor would it have been possible to provide for all things except through the creative wisdom of God. Therefore, the fall of the angels was repaired by Christ, the **God-man**, and a dignity and happiness greater than that in the original creation was returned to our nature, which had collapsed so fundamentally. I could derive this same argument again from the "end" or purpose of man, if I had not already touched enough on both. For with the same bucket, as they say, **I have whitewashed both walls.** <note>A Latin proverb (*eadem fidelia duos parietes dealbare*) meaning to accomplish two goals with a single effort—here, explaining both the restoration of man and the replacement of angels.</note>

Therefore, so that God might restore the lost elect who wished to obey, He Himself came to the aid of the good, and to bring counsel to the wicked, so that by His help they might either repent or be most justly assigned to the most terrible punishments. Therefore (which should be a source of dread for us), there are no punishments of divine vengeance so immense imposed on any of the damned as those imposed on evil and faithless Christians. That man was created for the sake of something which easily surpasses the world in value is proven by the fact that the lower and visible world was made for his sake. Now, the end <note>The "end" (*finis*) here means the ultimate purpose or goal.</note> must be far more excellent than those things which exist for the sake of that end. For otherwise (as I frequently emphasize, and not without reason), the author of such a massive undertaking would be unwise and vain if—while other things act for the sake of a more excellent goal and as causes leading toward that goal—He had made man without any purpose at all. For there is nothing here that is, I will not say blessed in every part, but rather that is not utterly miserable. Therefore, man cannot and should not have been made for the sake of misery (for thus it pleases me to name those things which the world of foolish men places in the highest happiness, since even the best things here possess more affliction than joy), but for the sake of some greater happiness than can be felt, seen, heard, or thought in the whole world. And yet, such a thing is eternal and immense. It remains, therefore, that man was made by the eternal and immense God for the sake of eternal and immense happiness, and that he can and ought to attain it. But since in the first man—who of his own will fell away from such a goal—all posterity was deprived of its end because of sin and could not rise again to innocence by its own power, it was nonetheless impossible for God to be cheated of His own design. For how could a man who had destroyed himself satisfy a most just and infinite God, who had been infinitely offended, since man is a finite creature? Therefore, by no means could he have justly expiated a crime committed against God's infinite goodness, even if he had killed every individual man a hundred thousand times over with the harshest torments, unless He who was also infinite paid the penalty in the name of all, and led lost man back to the predetermined goal. It was necessary, therefore, for the Creator—the **Wisdom and Word of God**—to be joined to our body: so that He, who alone was able, knew how, and was willing, by undergoing a death heaped with unheard-of torments and insults, might satisfy the offended and most just Divinity, and especially provide for those who would strive to imitate Him according to their own strength. For although the fruit and the payment of the death of Jesus Christ is offered to all, and many, through the supreme mercy of God, are translated immediately from death to life and from sin to **justification** <term>Justification: The process by which a person is made righteous in God's eyes.</term>, nevertheless, according to the hidden judgment of God, unless one cooperates with Christ through good works and, as Paul says in **Colossians 1**, "fills up in his own flesh those things that are lacking in the sufferings of Christ," by wailing, mourning, fasting, giving alms, repenting, confessing, and performing other works of piety toward God, oneself, and one's neighbor, there is no doubt that Christ is so far from benefiting him (if he has had the opportunity since his baptism and the use of reason) that He will instead vehemently stand in his way to condemn and gravely accuse him. For it is most just that, just as for the sake of maintaining justice and for the sake of an infinite expiation the **God-man** <note>original: *homodeus*</note> Jesus Christ died for each and every person, so too everyone called into the freedom of the cross should imitate their leader with good works, whoever desires to be His soldier. ### FROM THE POWER OF GOD.

<margin>One must stand fast. Moreover, Paul speaks of himself as he does of all the members of Christ: who must be conformed to the Head through afflictions.</margin>Although the omniscient God foreknew that man would abuse his free will, He nevertheless did not cease from working toward man's salvation, so that He might show in his **restoration** <note>original: *instauratione*. Postel uses this term to describe the "renewal" or "repairing" of the fallen world.</note> an omnipotence no less great than that shown in creation. For He is just as powerful to restore lost man anew as He was to create him. Therefore, in no other thing could man more clearly see the power of God than in the fact that He hid, within a most humble and abject man, that very power which was equal to the creation of the world. Indeed, it belongs to a more powerful being to have led something through to its final end than merely to have ordained it toward that end. From this, the innumerable myriads of the followers of the holy Jesus produced such stupendous miracles after him—by attributing them to him—that that immense power shone forth almost more in them than in the master: which is an evidence of inexhaustible power and infinite grace.

### FROM WISDOM.

It likewise belongs to the Wisest Architect to assist collapsed things no differently than if they had remained eternal. Since man must be saved and led to infinite blessedness, this cannot be achieved except through a supreme and omnipotent wisdom, which knew how to cleanse vices and solidify broken parts just as skillfully as it once fitted them together in the **original state of nature** <note>original: *prima natura*, referring to humanity before the Fall.</note>. This the one God-man, Jesus, was able to do, wished to do, and was obligated to do.

### FROM CHARITY.

<margin>Faith in Christ, which is practiced in the sacred mysteries, brings blessedness.</margin>Charity, mercy, and love for the human condition had to join the highest things with the lowest in a similar way, so that man might reach his goal. For otherwise, the Author of charity would have seemed quite indifferent to humanity if he had not raised up a nature so collapsed, miserably lying down, and entirely perishing, when he alone had the power to do so. But He who was able, did indeed raise it up and cleanse it; and He daily joins it to Himself through the most holy **sacraments** <note>original: *sacrosanctis sacramentis*. Postel refers to these as "mysteries" in the margin, following the Greek tradition.</note>, so that once health has been received, man might strive to follow the examples of His goodness through his own diligent effort, using those sacraments by which our fragility is healed. From that goodness, whatever is good has flowed forth.

### FROM THE CONSIDERATION OF THE GRAVITY
### OF THE OFFENSE.

<margin>It is said of all: "He who despises you, despises me."</margin>Just as he who is greatest and most knowledgeable sins most gravely, so too does a subject sin more deeply the greater the power against which he commits the offense. For one ought to be punished more severely for an offense against a king than against a duke; against the High Pontiff than against a priest; or against a supreme judge than against a **petty judge** <note>original: *pedaneum*. A "judge of the foot," referring to lower-level magistrates who handled minor cases.</note>. Thus, the gravity of the crime is measured by the status of the person offended or harmed. Since God acts for a specific purpose, He made man the most excellent of living beings for the sake of the most excellent happiness. And because God is infinite, a sin committed against Him deserves an infinite punishment; for He is no less just than He is merciful. Yet, unless God had given to man that for which he was made, human nature would not have reached its target. It was therefore necessary that both **predestination** <note>God's prior plan for humanity's salvation.</note> be preserved and that justice and mercy be fulfilled. However, it is impossible for man to satisfy an infinite offense by his own strength. Yet it was necessary for human nature to pay the penalties worthy of the crime: thus it happened that infinite wisdom, truth, and mercy assumed human flesh and the whole of corrupt nature in the name of everyone. This was done so that, in an infinite person, He might pay the infinite penalty owed to the infinite gravity of the crime. Therefore, it was altogether necessary that the infinite God be incarnated and take upon Himself the debts of all men, paying them so absolutely that He forgives everything for one approaching baptism and undertaking penance—though for one living longer under the holy law, it is necessary to **cooperate** <note>original: *cooperari*. The theological concept that humans must work together with God's grace to achieve salvation.</note>. For he will not be crowned unless he has competed according to the rules.

DE ORBIS CONCORDIA

# FROM THE CONTEMPLATION OF THOSE
->things which are done by free will.<-

It is impossible by any reasoning that things done by different people—who agree in neither language, nor institution, nor customs—could coincide in the same way, unless the Principle upon which all things depend gave that agreement to all. Therefore, it follows that since such things occur among fleeting men in this way (as well as they possibly can), the Prime Mover also acts by these same laws in the ordering of the universe. For whatever proceeds from our own free choice is first conceived and stirred in the mind; then (as I have already taught above) it comes into a certain unfolding, appearing as a <term>ground plan <note>original: ἰχνογραφίαν (ichnographian) - a floor plan or map.</note></term> or an <term>elevation <note>original: ὀρθογραφίαν (orthographian) - a detailed architectural drawing showing a building's vertical height and proportions.</note></term>, and finally rises into a physical work; lastly, it offers use and reaches its purpose. It is truly fitting that in the thinking mind there should be power, knowledge, and the will or desire for the actual doing, even before it comes to the <term>diagram <note>original: διάγραμμα (diagramma) - a geometric drawing or outline.</note></term>. In the same way, Divine Providence, which made all things in the most excellent manner, functioned thus in the completion of the universe. For from eternity, weighing all future things in His mind, possessing and knowing all things as if present, being powerful, knowing, and willing to create all things in time, He drew the lines of creation for the sake of the happiness of free man—which was, as it were, an unfolding of His own power preserved in His mind. By gradually refining this work through human talent, cultivation, and laws—both divine and human—and by carving it out of raw matter, He finally rendered the work complete when Wisdom herself revealed herself. Thus, from the architectural plan, He constructed the building upon the foundations already laid: namely, man absolved from his guilt. Furthermore, this most magnificent building is being completed day by day by the work of the Holy Spirit, until it reaches the consummation of this current state of corruption; and finally, after that corruption, man—for whose sake all things exist, just as he exists for the sake of God—obtains his final end. Just as the work of creation is attributed to the Father, and the restoration or redemption to the Son (or Wisdom), the building up—which consists in charity—is usually attributed to the Holy Spirit. Finally, the end or purpose belongs properly to the entire Trinity, no differently than the Eternal Mind was an inseparable Trinity and Unity from the very beginning. In a similar way (though thought, unfolding, and the work itself—as well as power, wisdom, and desire, love, or will—cannot and should not be confused or separated, as they are stirred in the mind before being enacted by us), we say that the thing devised and sketched in the mind is the work of Power, its unfolding is the work of Wisdom, and its actual effect is the work of the Will. But because we are temporary beings, we cannot individually increase a thing for so long that we might coincide with the works of the Holy Spirit. Truly, in the beginning and the end—in the thought which brings great pleasure, and in the use and final purpose—all three properties stand together, enjoying their own happiness in the divine manner. In the first place, God the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit (or Power through Wisdom in the Will or Love of helping), revealed His footprints in the creation of the world. But a much greater faith had to be established—and was indeed established—when the Wisdom of God, the Word, or the Son, showed Himself under the garment of our flesh, and placed the <term>finishing touch <note>original: colophonem - literally a 'colophon,' the final stroke or crowning completion of a work.</note></term> upon the "little world" <note>Postel refers to man as the "microcosm" or "little world," reflecting the whole universe in miniature.</note>, its matter being entirely purified. Indeed, the Redemption is a greater work in its effect than the Creation. Since, therefore, this is most worthy of God, necessary for man, consistent with natural harmony, handed down by the prophets and holy men, believed through sacred dogma, and in every way agreeable to reason, it must be held—even at the risk of one's life—that Jesus Christ is God-man, necessarily incarnated for our salvation and the salvation of all believers.
