### FROM THE NATURE OF THE GOOD.

It is a matter most certain by the consensus not only of philosophy, but of the entire world: the more common a good is, the more divine it is. By this proverb, or sentiment, it appears that God communicates Himself to the greatest degree in whatever ways are possible. Truly, He can communicate Himself in four ways: by presence, by power, by union of essence, and by union of person. He is present everywhere. The force of His power, however, is seen diffused and sprinkled even into the smallest things. For nothing lacks a miracle, or a thing to be wondered at, however hidden: which itself does not come from matter. Union occurs in the persons essentially <note>This refers to the internal life of the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit sharing one essence.</note>. There remains the fourth communication: which ought not to happen with the good angels, for they have not sinned; nor with the evil ones, because they cannot repent; nor with beings lower than man, which lack all sin and do not need duration. It is necessary, therefore, that the union of the divine person occur with man, so that He may lead him back to happiness. Therefore, it was necessary for Christ to become the <term>God-man <note>original: θεάνθρωπον (theanthrōpon)</note></term>. Otherwise, God would have begrudged us one of His communications: which is not to be admitted. By these reasons, it was altogether necessary that at some time God should be seen joined to man. Even if this were not necessary, nor predicted by angels, Sibyls, prophets, and even by demons who were forced to confess it: nevertheless, Christ sufficiently showed in himself that God was joined to human fragility in him. For the resurrection of Christ alone is seen to be—and truly is—as much greater than creation as eternity is more excellent than corruption. For we are born to die: but he lives never to die. But since the followers of Muhammad disagree with us concerning his death, although they do so against the consensus of the whole world; nevertheless, I judge that they should be persuaded by those external testimonies, lest they say we have fabricated these things.

## ON THE DEATH OF JESUS CHRIST THE SON OF GOD
### *& Mary, external testimonies. CHAPTER XII.*

Since it is certain that all things whatsoever we hope for and have from Christ depend upon the death of Jesus Christ, we would believe the rest in vain unless we preached and believed that he took up our infirmities in his own body and fixed them to the cross. For to believe other things about him not only does not help, but even harms us greatly. Therefore, since Muhammad—not at all ignorant of our religion or the Jewish religion—knew this goal set before us, he wished to attribute all other things to him, even greater things than have been handed down to us in writing, but he takes away his divinity and death, in which the hinge of our salvation turns. He did not indeed think what he wrote was true, but he did it so that, by removing Christ’s merit and purpose, he might seize a prophetic tyranny for himself: which things will be revealed most extensively in his life in its proper place. I will deal with him in few words in this place. If you do not wish to believe the Gospel, O follower of Muhammad, I will produce other most certain witnesses, very different from us and entirely contrary. From the heathens: Pilate, who had judged Jesus; Abgarus, who had not yet believed in him; Tiberius, Hadrian, the Roman Senate, the accounts of all the gentiles, Phlegon, Lucian, Pliny, Plutarch, and others: from the Jews, indeed, both all of them then, and six hundred places in those books with which they attempted to provoke him, and also from the Talmud. Pilate himself, after he had seen that he had risen, then wrote this letter about him to Tiberius Caesar.

> Pontius Pilate to Tiberius Caesar, greetings. It happened recently (as I myself later proved) that the Jews afflicted themselves and their nation with a cruel punishment. For when it had been promised to their fathers that God would send them a holy man, who should be called their king...

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

<note>original: "DE ORBIS CONCORDIA"</note>

...would be cared for, and born of a virgin, and that He was the God of the Hebrews. Having sent this man <note>referring to Jesus</note> to me in Judea by faith, they had seen Him restore light to the blind, cleanse lepers, cure the paralyzed, expel demons from men, and even raise the dead. He commanded the winds, walked with dry feet upon the waters of the sea, and performed many similar wonders. While all the common people of the Jews called Him the Son of God, the leaders of the Jews, moved by envy, seized Him and handed Him over to me. Crafting one lie after another, they affirmed that He was a magician and acted against their law. Believing this to be the case, I had Him scourged and handed Him over to their will. They truly crucified Him and set guards over Him. Nevertheless, while my soldiers diligently guarded the tomb, He rose on the third day. 

Because of this, the fury of the Jews flared up to such an extent that they gave money to my soldiers, wishing to buy their silence on the matter and make them say that the body had been stolen by His disciples. The result was that the matter was spread more and more by the soldiers. For they both testified that He had risen and affirmed that their silence on the matter had been bought with money. I thought these things should be written to you for this reason: so that you would not be persuaded otherwise by the slanders of the Jews. Farewell. 

This letter <note>This refers to the "Report of Pilate to Tiberius," a document widely circulated in the Middle Ages and Renaissance, though modern scholars consider it apocryphal.</note> rests upon the transcription of two witnesses and authorities. For it was first extracted from the Roman archives by Hegesippus <note>A name often associated with a 4th-century Latin adaptation of Josephus's histories.</note> in the 120th year after the birth of Christ, and was translated into Latin by Ambrose, the Bishop of Milan, who acted as Hegesippus's interpreter. Surely, he would not have wanted it translated unless its reliability had already been proven by the faith of all. Tertullian, who lived very close to the times of the Apostles, mentions it and brings its testimony against the Romans, because they knew it had been extracted from the Emperor's archives and that copies remained there. 

Justin Martyr says the same: he adds that Tiberius, having been informed of these things, wanted Christ to have a place among the gods of Rome. The Senate refused to agree to this for the reason that they had not been written to first regarding the matter. For there was a law in Rome that it was not permitted for anyone to be held among the gods without the consultation and will of the Senate. It is no wonder that the Romans, seduced by the plagues of worthless gods and their own fickleness of magistrates, were unwilling to receive even the truth. 

Now from these things it is clear that Christ suffered. There also exists a letter from Abgar <note>Referring to the Legend of King Abgar of Edessa, who was said to have corresponded with Jesus.</note> held and translated from his archives, with the people of Edessa themselves confirming it by their conversion to the religion. Mention is made of the resurrection of Christ in that letter, which death necessarily had to follow. Tiberius and the Senate learned of His death when the matter of receiving Him was discussed. All the religions of the heathens were overturned; they so dreaded the death of Christ that no oracle could be given wherever one person was marked with the cross of Christ. In the <term>hieroglyphic notes</term> <note>Postel, like many Renaissance scholars, believed Egyptian hieroglyphs contained mystical Christian truths.</note> of the Egyptians, the cross was the symbol of eternal life.

See then, Muhammad, how these things could have happened under the cross of a common and mercenary man, such as Simon of Cyrene <note>A reference to the Islamic view, often interpreted by Westerners at the time, that Simon of Cyrene was transformed to look like Jesus and was crucified in His place.</note>. But you say it was disgraceful for a man most dear to God to die in such a way. There is no disgrace in death—far less in a necessary death. Titus used to say, as Josephus witnesses, that he was not the cause of such great bloodshed, but rather it was divine vengeance. For in the first Jewish war, twenty times one hundred thousand <note>2,000,000</note> men died. Of those taken from the walls of Jerusalem, eleven times one hundred thousand <note>1,100,000</note> perished through purification; 90,000 were sold off at a very cheap price. These things are not for the death or vengeance of a mere man. You may bring forward Moses, Elijah, and David, or anyone else, even Abraham himself. Trajan slaughtered a slightly smaller crowd rebelling in Mesopotamia. In Betara—which they call Biter in the Talmud—under Bar Kokhba <note>The leader of the second major Jewish revolt against Rome (132–136 AD).</note>, Hadrian killed forty times one hundred thousand <note>4,000,000</note> men in vengeance for the death and the selling of Christ. Truly, he afflicted ten of their foremost learned and distinguished men with unheard-of punishments because they had favored Bar Kokhba and were the sons of those who had sold Christ. Because of this, the fast of the ten men is still observed among the Jews today. Porphyry, a declared enemy of our religion, confesses that after the death of Jesus Christ, no more oracles could be obtained. Plutarch confirms the same when he says that in his century, scarcely two oracles remained. Which happened...

# BOOK I OF GUILLAUME POSTEL

...from which time that voice was heard near Paxos: "Great Pan is dead," <note>This refers to a famous story recorded by Plutarch where a divine voice announced the death of the "Great Pan" during the reign of Tiberius, often interpreted by Christian writers as a sign of the end of the pagan era upon the death of Christ.</note> of which I spoke above. For that voice occurred under Tiberius. Pliny mentions the greatest earthquake, astounding beyond human memory, which happened under Tiberius at the time Christ was dying. He also mentions examples of those who were seen to have risen after burial. This cannot be understood as referring to anyone other than Christ, and to those who were raised by His Apostles and saints in all places. Indeed, the Apostles performed all their miracles through the power of the suffering Christ and His cross, which proves that He truly suffered. 

All nations used to throw this suffering in our teeth as a reproach—not only the Jews, who call Christ nothing other than *thalui* <note>original: "thalui"; a Latinization of the Hebrew *talui* (תלוי), meaning "the hanged one," a common derogatory term for Jesus in medieval Jewish polemics</note>, that is, the hanged or crucified one. Lucian <note>Lucian of Samosata, a 2nd-century Greek satirist</note>, in his work *The Passing of Peregrinus*, calls Him "the crucified one" more than once. All these, O followers of Muhammad <note>original: "Muhamedici"</note>, are external witnesses, and they are contrary to us in all other matters. Therefore, I wonder that you, O damned seducer <note>Postel is addressing Muhammad directly here, a common rhetorical device in 16th-century polemics</note>, dared to deviate from such manifest truth. But the truth was that you had to rule, which could not have happened if the truth had been accepted. 

An eclipse against the laws of nature revealed His death to the Romans. Phlegon <note>Phlegon of Tralles, a Greek chronicler</note> and Dionysius the Areopagite wrote of it. I could have also brought forward Josephus, Philo, and Hegesippus as witnesses, as well as Talmudic traditions and innumerable other testimonies. But these are more than enough for a matter about which no one ever doubted, which was carried out in the presence of a multitude of four hundred thousand people. Have you ever seen one person substituted for another who was destined for death? For justice never allows anyone who has been accused and caught to escape until they are either punished or set free. Truly, arguments must be brought forward in this place, as in the previous ones. It has been demonstrated that man, perishing by his own will, could not rise from his vice without the presence of God; and by many necessary arguments, it was required that human nature be joined to God to recover the perfection it had lost. Furthermore, by the miracles and the resurrection of Christ, it is impossible that He was merely a man or only a prophet (which will be made even clearer later). It remains to be seen whether His death and resurrection were as necessary as they truly were.

### WHY CHRIST, AS GOD-MAN, SUFFERED IN OUR HUMANITY
->joined to God, and how necessarily. CHAPTER XIII.<-

**F**or man, who fell into misery from his natural origin, to truly be able to return to his lost innocence, the necessary assistance of God was required. This was accomplished through Christ, by reason of man's necessity—whom God wished to help through His own liberality and mercy—and for the sake of happiness, so that man might finally achieve what he perpetually desires. It was also for the sake of God’s power and goodness, so that He might establish a work of thought as infinite as His infinite power, and entirely open and communicate the greatness of His riches to us. 

It remains, therefore, to be seen what He primarily took upon Himself in our name, and by what skill He washed away such a great vice. Since He took on a vessel in someone’s name, it is certain that if He bound Himself entirely in that person's name, He ought to provide for everything—except for the guilt—which depends on that person and their fortunes. For although one may pay the penalties for things committed by another, the guilt is always understood to be absent from them. This is exactly how we must judge the God-man <term>theanthropos; from the Greek 'theos' (God) and 'anthropos' (man)</term> Jesus Christ, who in our name bound Himself to the divinity and, in a certain way, to Himself. For all the imperfections we had contracted through our lineage <note>original: "ex traduce"; a theological term referring to the transmission of original sin through biological descent</note>, the seed, and the work of Satan—all these He took upon Himself, except for guilt (to which He who committed no sin could not be subject). Similarly, He wished to take all human conditions into His own nature, so that He might restore man entirely to his own nature and freedom, or as close to it as possible. To understand this better, we must go back a little further, namely to the nature of the first man. He whom we call Adam according to the sacred oracles (let the philosophers call him what they will, for they must admit that one first man was made), he, I say, had received a constitution from God, the Best and Greatest, by which...

...none more excellent, none more free. For, established at the very peak of all visible nature—which the Greeks therefore called the **microcosm** <note>original: *mikrokosmon* (μικρόκοσμον), meaning "small world." This is the philosophical idea that a human being is a miniature reflection of the entire universe, containing all its elements within themselves</note>—as a sort of summary of the highest and lowest created natures, it was necessary that he possess within himself whatever excellence was implanted by the Creator. Truly, it must be admitted that he possessed the highest degree of freedom in all of nature, than which nothing can certainly be greater. We even see great traces of this freedom in those who, through divine inspiration, have "descended into themselves" <note>This refers to the practice of self-reflection or looking inward to find the divine spark or reason</note>, and in others, certain faint glimmers. For everything drives into slavery the man who does not depend upon God and himself, but rather is tossed about by the whims of fortune’s opinion and by things placed in the recklessness of chance. Such a man is actually so far from being free (as all philosophers admit) that he carries around with him the foulest of masters, infinite in number, from whose tyranny human effort cannot be rescued; so far, indeed, are we removed from that remarkable condition of the first man. 

Placed in that noble constitution, the most happy Adam (as much as is possible on earth) was able to die by his own means, yet by the favor of God he could have been eternal. God did not wish to grant him that favor under such a condition that he would be forced to accept it, lest by imposing that necessity He should take away his **free will** <note>original: *arbitrium*, the capacity to choose between different courses of action</note>. For it was placed within his power to follow the divine prescriptions, either by obeying commands or by not committing forbidden acts. Indeed, unless it were placed within your freedom to do either of the two, you could not be free. Therefore, since he was free and could act through sin against the law of prescribed reason, he was able to be both mortal and non-mortal. 

Furthermore, out of His immense goodness, we must believe that he received from God his Maker a certain law—not one by which he (who had not yet sinned) would be coerced, but by which he (who was capable of wandering) would be directed. It is more certain than certainty itself that God gave him everything pertaining to human happiness. If he observed these prescriptions, he would be happy and eternal; if he violated them, he would eventually depart this life, overwhelmed by countless calamities. That he possessed a more majestic body than we do now, and a life that was nearly immortal of its own accord, is argued by the fact that even after the corruption of nature, they lived for nearly a thousand years before the Flood. This is established not only by our own sacred writings and those passed down by Moses, but also by the testimony of foreigners. Valerius Maximus <note>A 1st-century Roman author known for his collection of historical anecdotes</note>, quoting Xenophon, records that a king of the Latins lived for 800 years, and his father for 600. To these he adds Dando, who lived 500 years, and Litorius Epius, who lived 300. Berosus and Hellanicus <note>Ancient historians from Babylon and Greece, respectively</note> write that many men before the Flood enjoyed very long lives.

<margin>Josephus mentions these in his *Antiquities* <note>Referring to *Antiquities of the Jews* by Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note>.</margin>
The lives, deeds, and arts of these earlier people are attested to by two columns that survived the Flood. These were still visible in the land of Syria fifteen hundred years ago; one was made of brick and the other of bronze, so that they might withstand the injuries of the heavens and the elements. Who has not read that the lives of the Seres <note>An ancient name for the people of China</note>, the Macrobii <note>A legendary people mentioned by Herodotus as living in Ethiopia and having extreme longevity</note>, the Ethiopians, and the famous Pandoran peoples were three times longer than our own? 

Lest it be less surprising that the Almighty God gave this to the first man and his descendants, even human art has progressed to this point. Who has not heard it reported and read that not long before our own age, a certain **John of the Times** <note>original: *Johannes de Temporibus*, a legendary figure said to have been a squire to Charlemagne and to have lived for over 300 years</note> lived for 300 years (and was thus named for the ages he saw)? Certainly, that lifespan, increased through frugality and moderation, is much more wonderful than that ancient longevity; for in that former age, nature did not labor under as many corruptions as it does now. 

Lest public trust should fail (though it does not occur to me now which Pope was reigning), certain Bulls are kept at Rome by which a certain German wished to testify to posterity that, by a certain chance, he had lived for 500 years. This is how he tells his story: he was once captured by pirates and sold to a certain petty ruler in Arabia. Many years later, when the ruler of another territory sent ambassadors to greet his master, he sent as a gift a certain medicine by which, as he said, life could be prolonged for many years. Since the King did not wish to test the medicine on himself (as tyrants suspect all things), he ordered the German captive to try it. The result was that after five hundred years, or a little less, he came to Rome and wished this to be publicly signified by a papal diploma. A noblewoman in England (whom they say is from Tormeriacus), while she was intent on hunting, happened by chance upon an alabaster jar full of ointment; having been anointed with it, a peasant remained safe for 300 years

-> THE FIRST BOOK OF GUILLAUME POSTEL <-

...he remained unharmed, except for the soles of his feet (which he had not anointed), where he suffered pain. <note>original: "nō unxerat." This is likely a reference to a mythological or historical figure like Achilles, who had a single vulnerable spot because it was not treated with a magical substance.</note> There are many such examples in which, if we marvel at the skill involved, we must consider what should be judged concerning the power of nature and of God. Lucian wrote in his work *On Long-livers* <note>original: "Lucianus de Macrobijs." Lucian of Samosata was a 2nd-century satirist; "Macrobii" refers to a text attributed to him discussing people who lived exceptionally long lives.</note> that many lived for nearly two hundred years. Truly, however, there is no example so memorable as that of Artephius the Mage (of whom Roger Bacon wrote), who, while traveling the world, studying his art, writing about it, and practicing the art of healing, managed to reach the age of one thousand and twenty-five years—a fact he left recorded in his writings on magical experiments. Yet truly, no one can surpass those boundaries of time in which our first parent lived, except with extreme difficulty. From these things it is clear: if Adam lived so long after nature had been corrupted—specifically 930 years—what might have been possible with the help of God?

To return to the matter at hand, the condition of the first man was to be **able to die and able not to die.** <note>original: "posse mori & posse non mori." This is a standard theological distinction regarding human mortality before the Fall.</note> However, after nature was corrupted, infecting us all, his condition became to be **able to die and unable not to die.** <note>original: "posse mori, & nō posse nō mori." This describes the state of "total depravity" or inherited mortality after original sin.</note> But in the nature restored by Christ, the condition is to be **able not to die and unable to die**; <note>original: "posse nō mori, & nō posse mori." This refers to the state of the blessed in the afterlife.</note> this comes from grace, not from nature.

Therefore, since the God-man Christ took on our flesh and established himself as a guarantor <note>original: "vadem." A legal term for someone who posts bail or takes on someone else's debt.</note> for man before God the Father, he took upon himself the aforementioned conditions of the flesh. For if you look at his divinity, which had joined itself to a body, he was able by its power not to die. But if you look at our necessity and his immense goodness, it was entirely necessary for him to die. Finally, that same flesh, having been raised, confirmed the third state.

And likewise: he shared with innocent man a first immunity from sin, but he took from corrupted man the punishment and other defects; and from the third condition—which belongs to those who have given their names to him—he took the fullness of grace. This grace is indeed greatest in the saints, but it does not yet appear to be complete in them. The fourth state is that of the blessed and of divinity: to be unable to sin and unable to stop the contemplation of God. For the very humanity of Christ the God exists in admiration of the divinity joined to it.

It is also established that he had, and continues to have, two wills. The human will felt our calamities and fled from death; the divine will was entirely the opposite. For "he was offered up because he himself willed it." <note>A reference to Isaiah 53:7 in the Latin Vulgate: "oblatus est quia ipse voluit."</note> Therefore, his death for us was so necessary—so that he might pay the penalties owed by us in his own body—that otherwise his coming would have been entirely in vain. For it would have been rightly impossible for any human or angelic power to make satisfaction to God for our sins. From his fullness, therefore, we have all received; otherwise, his presence would not have helped us, unless he had restored the original purification in the name of our flesh, which had been cleansed.

But if he purified us through baptism, as is customarily done in his blood, why did he not entirely restore our original freedom? And why does a person who has been "dipped" <note>original: "intinctus," a synonym for baptized.</note> still produce another person through the persistence of women? <note>Postel is asking why baptized parents still have children born with original sin.</note> There is a very familiar example in human affairs. When a bud is grafted into an ignoble and wild trunk, the patterns of the graft <note>original: "Insitę gemmæ emblemata." He uses the metaphor of "emblematics" or grafting a superior branch onto a wild tree.</note> cause the fruit to differ from the trunk and to follow the nature of the graft entirely, with the former nature being, as it were, dead and abolished. Thus, those fruits do not reflect the first nature, but the nature of the added graft, as long as they are in use.

However, if the seeds from that best fruit are then committed to the best earth, they do not produce a tree similar to the grafted branch, but return entirely to the first, wild nature. So it is also in a Christian man. If he is baptized and produces fruits worthy of repentance, they are accepted by God and are good. But if his offspring are not washed by sacred baptism, without doubt whatever he produces is wild and dependent upon the vice of the first nature.

There is another far more excellent reason why it was necessary for Christ to suffer for man (and not merely to act as a prophet and then be snatched into heaven for fear of death, as Muhammad wishes to persuade people), <note>Postel is refuting the Islamic view (Docetism) that Jesus did not actually die on the cross but was replaced or taken up by God.</note> and why he had to pay whatever cause of sin was owed. We shall persist in our example of the legal guarantee. For man, miserably lost and indulging himself to his own destruction like a man with dropsy, <note>term: <term>dropsy</term> (Latin: *hydrops*), a historical medical term for edema or swelling. In theology, it was often used as a metaphor for greed or sin, where the "thirst" for the thing only makes the "swelling" of the soul worse.</note> no human satisfaction—God being so just—nor even the work of all mortals could reconcile him to God; indeed, all would have perished most miserably. Therefore, the thing to which man was most liable and held bound was death. There is no more grievous punishment in this life, and it is twofold: of both body and soul. Regarding which I shall speak...

<header># ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD</header>

...when the immortality of souls is discussed. To those who rightly estimate the human condition, it will seem that man’s obligation toward God is so great that it exceeds the strength of the entire world. For even if there were a hundred worlds equal to this one, inhabited by countless men, they could not justly repay the benefit bestowed upon a single human being. Who can consider the vastness of the heavens and the world? All this was prepared for the benefit of man. Who can count all those things born from these elements? They are under human dominion. Who can conceive in his mind the gifts of the body—sense, movement, life, sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch—or the use of things that man employs for utility and necessity? Who would not marvel and be utterly stunned if he more closely observed the gifts of the soul? And man was able to repay these things: naturally. But if, having neglected them, he has even acted against them, what punishment do you judge him worthy of? What son would not be marked with the brand of an ungrateful soul—even one upon whom a father had bestowed the smallest part of similar benefits—if he did not acknowledge, praise, and extol the giver? How much punishment would he deserve if he even brought war against his own father and, finally, destroyed himself willingly and knowingly? From these points, it can most clearly be seen how beholden man is to divine providence and how guilty he is on every side. Thus, nothing milder could be owed to him for his conduct than death, proscription, and perpetual exile from that Father against whom he had committed such unspeakable acts; he wished to destroy himself, kill all his brothers, and drive his father from his own seat, and as far as it was in his power, he did so. Therefore, that vessel of ours, the infinite Son of God <note>Postel uses the term "vessel" (original: *vas*) to refer to Christ as the container of divinity or the representative of humanity.</note>, infinite ways greater than the world, when he took up the name of man, had to pay the greatest debt. He therefore underwent death—and not a common one, but one unheard of, heaped with every kind of punishment—after which he wished to impart eternal salvation to those believing in him. For having been raised and having entered heaven, he opened heaven to us who are grafted into his trunk <note>A continuation of the botanical metaphor from the previous page, where humanity is "grafted" onto the divine life of Christ.</note>, so that we might produce the new fruits of a new life in certain hope. The same demonstration comes from the reason of His supreme goodness. For it is characteristic of that goodness to be widely open, and to employ the highest mercy and inexplicable charity. But no one can have greater charity than when he lays down his life for his friends. Therefore, Christ died for us, the just for the unjust. If you had any knowledge of antiquity or faith in the Old Testament (which Muhammad <note>original: "Muhamedes"</note> nevertheless urged should be consulted in many places in doubtful matters), you would recognize in countless passages that the coming of Christ as God among men, and that he would suffer the ultimate things from his own people, was foretold. Therefore, dearest brothers, whoever does not believe in the death and divinity of Christ is condemned, if he has heard of it. Alas, through the lust and the greed for ruling of a single man, you have perished and are condemned, because you are outside the way of salvation. Countless thousands of men have perished through the false persuasion of one man. Your wicked princes, the heirs of a deceitful man, keep you in those shadows through the works of cunning men, lest you come to the light of true knowledge. How can it be that any of you believes in the resurrection—though it is written often in the Quran <note>original: "Alcorano"</note>—when no one among you has provided proof of it? But we have, besides the faith handed down to us, also a leader who had to suffer death to provide proof of it. We also have Mary and John the Evangelist, <margin>Great authors record that both the divine Virgin and John fell asleep.</margin> <note>The margin note refers to the "Dormition" (falling asleep), a tradition that Mary and John did not suffer a typical death but passed into heaven.</note> who, like Enoch and Elijah, sought heaven in the body. It is therefore familiar for us to hope for the resurrection, but for you, it is a joke. For if anyone weighs the life of many, and especially of your magistrates, nothing is more greedy than they, and nothing more cruel than the soldier. From this it appears that they believe in nothing after this life, except in words alone. For otherwise, they would put a limit on their plundering.

### ON THE PROOF AND CONFIRMATION OF THE DIVINITY
#### Of Christ from his works, and the death of the disciples and martyrs. CHAPTER XIV.

Although in human affairs nothing can produce greater faith in things than their first comprehension; nevertheless, because of forgetfulness, varying opinions, and doubts...

-># GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK 1<-

<page-num>93</page-num>

Through doubt and negligence, **posterity** <term>posterity: future generations</term> gradually falls away from the understanding and belief in things once proven, unless there is a certain diligence in demonstrating and repeating them—whether this is done through human, divine, or a mixture of powers. Oblivion occurs for many reasons, but most especially due to the constant change of circumstances and the negligence of our ancestors. Humanity itself, daily joining and changing the form of diverse matter, nourishes those brought into life and consumes those it has raised. In this same way, it weakens their opinions and knowledge, even though the remedy of literature may provide a cure for this. While a province is overturned by war, sacred beliefs perish, and evil or new ones creep in; they spread all the more widely and easily the more absurd and alien to reason they are. Thus it happens that things received from fathers or ancestors are scattered among only a few if they are good, but among everyone if they are evil. For, due to the vice of our depraved nature, our sluggishness, and the works suggested by demons, **falsehood** itself rules almost the entire lower world. Truth has always resided among a very few. And because the smaller part always follows the larger and worse part, truth finds no place; or if it does find a place—since no one can truly fight against reason—it is praised in words but outlawed in deeds.

But let us deal with an example: What greater persuasion or truer belief could ever be held regarding a **divine man** than that held regarding **Moses**, when he drew his people to him with portents and miracles, and forced a tyrant to lose a great part of his empire? This matter was conducted in a gathering of six hundred thousand men capable of bearing arms. Nevertheless, a few months later—after so many wonders, after the present light of divinity (even while it was still present!)—they began to doubt whether they could be saved by God when they were trapped between the sea and the army of Pharaoh. He confirmed the preceding events by divinely opening the **Red Sea**; once they had crossed between walls of water, their enemies were killed to a man, suffocated by the water returning to its place. 

A few days after the crossing of the sea and these first miracles, because of a slight thirst, everyone doubted the power of God. He wished this power to be manifested not by providing water naturally from wells, but from an entirely sterile place. From a completely rocky mountain, He provided such an abundance that it could not have been matched by a most wide river. Not much later, when they suffered any kind of lack, they asserted that God was not powerful enough to give them food; to these, the **manna** sent from heaven persuaded them otherwise. Finally, they began to complain about wanting a cooked meal. Moses saw to it that there was such an abundance of meat sent from heaven that there was enough for everyone equally, both the poor and the rich. For God is no **respecter of persons** <note>original: "acceptor personarum"; meaning God shows no favoritism or partiality based on status.</note>. Yet God gave His gifts in such a way that, meanwhile, a great multitude died to persuade the rest that they should neither doubt divine power nor detract from His greatness. 

Now, though the multitude was satisfied in all things, they forgot the **Creator** and demanded an Egyptian god be made for them. Because of this, a great punishment was necessary, so that no one would dare to mutter against God any longer. But just as we seek out adversity by our own efforts <note>original: "nostro Marte"</note> during prosperous times and perish willingly, factious men began to pour out against Moses what they did not dare to vomit against God. Since they did not dare to say what they turned over in their minds for fear of death—namely, "Who appointed God over us?" <note>Postel highlights that by rejecting the appointed leader, the rebels were implicitly questioning God's own authority.</note>—they rose up against the most pious leader and the public order. They said there was no reason why he should be obeyed, and that there were many in that gathering who could provide what Moses provided. Therefore, they claimed it was also permitted for them, or at least for a part of the multitude, to preside over sacred matters. 

Moses, whose speech a little while before had softened the anger of the Creator, perceived this. After it seemed so to them, he permitted them to act according to their own lust. He suggested they separate themselves from the gathering of all others as if they were holier, take up their incense and censers, and burn the sacred fires; in this way, God would show whether that arrangement pleased Him. The factious men withdrew, gathered together, and burned the incense. It is a marvel to tell, and a horrible thing to have happened: the **earth gaping open** consumed them alive. See what posterity does, even in the presence of such things (so far as they can be perceived by man)...

He concludes with the rebellion of Korah, where the earth swallowed those who challenged divinely appointed authority.</summary>

<page-num>94</page-num>

(as much as is possible for man) with the miracles of the leader being open and evident by God’s hand, that same generation hardly believes; indeed, that very nation which deals with him daily disparages him. After his death, however, much clearer signs following the faith were shown to the successors of Moses. Therefore, as I said at the beginning of the chapter, that first knowledge was by far the greatest and most certain, so that the character of Moses might be known. But when the future events which he had foretold are seen to have come to pass, then at last that persuasion is confirmed and, as it were, renewed.

The leader succeeding him <note>Joshua</note> performed the same feat in the bed of the Jordan River, having implored God, as Moses did in the sea. An innumerable multitude crosses the dry bed of the river on foot; he places a stone monument <note>original: "molem," referring to the twelve stones set up in the Jordan</note> in the middle as a sign of the event. But these things are not enough. There was a need for signs that would be open not only to the chosen people but would also manifest themselves to the entire world. The sun is halted while Joshua <note>original: "Iosue"</note> pursues the enemies of the faith with the people of God, and it makes that day much longer than all others. The Persian is a witness, who left this written in his celestial records; lying Greece is a witness, falsely attributing this miracle to Phaëton <note>Phaëton: In Greek myth, a youth who drove the sun-chariot too close to the earth; Postel argues this myth is a distorted memory of Joshua's miracle</note>. 

How much less wonderful it would have been for the Greeks to have believed such a thing—since they were then unrefined in all matters and attributed divine power to a well-known scoundrel—had not that unrefined opinion had its own witnesses even among men of a more learned age. Indeed, there was no lie in Greece so impudent that it lacked some credit and a witness. That standing still of the sun, which occurred with the whole world in agreement and was seen, was thought by the Greeks to be a conflagration. But the author of that story was worthy of Greek cruelty, and poetry gave its support to the tale. Also held in the highest wonder throughout the whole world was the retreat of the sun performed under Hezekiah <note>original: "Ezechia"</note>, which was entrusted to the records of the Persians; this perhaps gave the origin of another "conflagration" story among the Greeks. 

Is it any wonder that the timelines do not agree? Secular literature <term>Secular literature: original "Literæ humaniores," referring to human history and classical studies as opposed to divine scripture</term> among the Greeks had nothing certain six hundred years before Christ. For Homer, although he was a little earlier in age (living around the time of Solomon), nevertheless contains nothing of history to which you might deservedly grant credit. Herodotus, four hundred years later than him, hardly deserves credit even in Greece. For deeds performed long ago in other kingdoms arrived there only after they had grown old elsewhere, carried only by rumor and gaining strength by the length of the journey. The Latins <note>the Romans</note>, indeed, had received the use of the alphabet <term>elementorum: literally "the elements," referring to the letters of the alphabet</term> only a little before that time.

But lest I digress further, from the innumerable deeds of his successors performed by divine will, Moses earned the most weighty credibility, until that man came whom he himself had foretold would come, and about whom the innumerable oracles of the holy prophets had predicted. Then Moses ceased to be the primary focus as a new light arose: Jesus Christ, God born as a man. Even though He had earned sufficiently great authority and faith—for there was no miracle of His (unless He willed otherwise) that was not performed in the sight of at least a thousand people, and that in various places and regions—nonetheless, His authority began to be far greatest when, by the invocation of His name alone, or even by the sign of the cross alone, all His disciples miraculously performed all the same things He performed in His own name; and if the occasion presented itself, even far greater ones. 

Thus, they demonstrated the divinity of their teacher not by predictions of the future or prophecies in the manner of the ancients (for after the divine remedy, none remains, nor can anything foreign enter into the place of truth unless it be false), but by the presence of divinity, they showed that nothing is difficult or impossible for God. They healed every kind of disease; they restored life and soul to dead bodies, even those kept for a longer time, which life they preserved for many years afterward. They drove demons from the body. In short, nothing was difficult for them; they could do all things in Him who strengthened them, Jesus Christ. 

Although Muhammad <note>original: "Muhamedes"</note> wished to diminish this through the whole course of his persuasion, nevertheless he was forced to admit it in more than one place, perhaps so that by mixing something of truth with his falsehoods, he might entice simple Christians with those flatteries—Christians who had themselves seen and read of the miracles. For he says that men dressed in white garments (by whom he means the Apostles) performed miracles; and he proposes a parable about them in the Sura of Jesus <note>original: "Sora iessu"; likely referring to the Quranic chapters discussing the disciples of Jesus</note>. But there is no need for that witness, except so that the unhappy followers of Muhammad [might...]

He concludes that the miracles of Jesus and the Apostles provide the ultimate proof of divinity, which even Muhammad was forced to acknowledge.</summary>

-># GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I<-

<page-num>95</page-num>

...is said to return to God. Come, O true lovers of truth, let us weigh all things more diligently and compare the opinions of the world with the works of the faithful who believe in Christ, and let us see men who are truly transformed. This world (I mean this mass of humanity depending on the whim of fortune), what crimes does it not commit? What fraud does it not devise? What tragedies does it not incite? What law is so sacred and inviolable that the world does not pervert it for the sake of acquiring wealth, favor, or a bit of vainglory? A man rushes into a thousand perils while he thinks he is securing peace for himself, whether by right or wrong; and while he seeks means for a longer life, he perpetually has, carries, and summons death as his companion. 

However, a man once truly devoted to Christ—both in soul and by evident signs—so that he commits nothing unworthy of divine goodness, and so that he might offer to men those things by which they may obtain salvation, first denies himself, casts off his own lusts, and takes no care for his own body. Whatever he has, he desires it to be provided for others, not himself; he covets no one’s property; he gives his own to all; he prays for his enemies, cherishes them with kindness, and breaks them with patience; he would rather accept death than commit a crime. In short, he denies himself and all his own things rather than act against law and equity. 

Although many Pagans <note>original: "ethnici," referring to non-Christian Greek and Roman philosophers</note> left this sentiment in writing, none however confirmed it with their deeds. Aristotle left it written, and Plato approved it: that it is better to die than to act against virtue. Horace depicted the "good man" as one who fears a disgrace worse than death. Truly, those are but words; these [the Christians'] are deeds. Whom can you give me from the world who would prefer to die rather than commit a crime? Yet all confessed it was better to do so. Therefore, every one of them was acting against his conscience and condemning himself. Their nature was so depraved under Satan that they saw their own judgment in the knowledge of the good, but found no remedy. 

To a truly pious Christian, however, committing such a harsh and iniquitous deed seems so unthinkable that many hundreds of thousands have perished for the sake of asserting the truth and repudiating the false. They were most prepared for death out of fear of sin; and so that a greater power of divinity might be seen, even infants <note>referring to young children or the "Holy Innocents"</note> rushed to death voluntarily and stubbornly, lest they should eventually perish by sin—they who were entirely ignorant of sin, having been moved to happiness by the Holy Spirit even before the age of discretion. When the princes of the world saw this, driven by the furies of Satan, they knew they could inflict a more grievous punishment on girls and virgins if they gave them to the pimp rather than to the lion <note>original: "lenoni, quàm leoni." This is a famous quote from Tertullian, meaning the martyrs feared the loss of chastity in a brothel more than being eaten by wild beasts</note>, as Tertullian says. For no wild beasts dared to touch those sacred bodies unless the one being offered was willing. 

That constancy, clinging to the souls of Christians against the judgment of the whole world, proves that in truth God alone has transformed the minds of those men, and it shows a present reward for the future life. For how else could it happen that they were so entirely different from the minds of other men and the senses of corrupt opinions? Since they were composed of the same elements and soul as the rest, how, I ask, could it happen unless that transformation proceeded from God the author? For He alone knows how to alter the nature which He composed; nor is there any reason for tyrants and executioners to say that there is such great power in magic. For the least of the Christians could overcome every kind of magician with the sign of the cross. 

<margin>In the *Apologeticus*, chapter 1</margin> Furthermore, as Tertullian says in truly golden words: Nature has imbued every evil with either fear or shame. Criminals, in short, delight in hiding; they avoid appearing; they tremble when caught; they deny when accused; they do not easily or always confess even to an enemy. Certainly, when condemned, they mourn; they turn the impulses of an evil mind against themselves; they impute it to fate or the stars; they do not want the deed to be their own, because they acknowledge it as evil. But what is similar for Christians? No one is ashamed, no one repents, unless it be that they were not Christians sooner. If one is branded, he glories; if accused, he does not defend himself. When questioned, he confesses even voluntarily; when condemned, he gives thanks. What kind of "evil" is this, which lacks the fear, shame, evasiveness, repentance, and lamentation of a criminal evil? What kind of evil is this, for which the defendant rejoices, whose accusation is a prayer, and whose punishment is happiness? These are the words of Tertullian.

<header>ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD</header>

<margin>The pious who today believe in the Gospel in Germany and in other regions do not despise true miracles, such as those performed by the apostles in the name of Christ, and those which God often performed in memory of the martyrs to bear witness to their holiness and true religion. But these same people attribute lying signs to the operation of the devil, of the kind that occurred among the heathens and occur today among the Turks. Paul attributed such things to the Antichrist, as did Augustine in the 20th book of *The City of God* <note>original: "De Civitate Dei"</note>.</margin>

When I consider these things, I cannot help but be moved by indignation that certain pestilent men—world-burners, plagues, far worse than Muhammad <note>original: "Mahumeto"</note> himself, worse than tyrants, and worse even than Satan—have dared to attribute divine miracles to the devil, even though they were performed through the invocation of the name of Christ and God. O unheard-of plague! O poison from which the ruin of the whole world proceeds! O plague worse than the Antichrist himself! It was not enough for them to have overturned the sacred and public orders, to have cast fire into the midst of Christendom, to have trampled the most holy sacraments underfoot, to have torn the Gospel apart, and to have overturned the decrees of the apostles; they must also say that he was a most foul demon, he under whom hell trembled, and whom Satan himself with his legions was forced a thousand times to confess as God. For what else is it, I ask, to trample Christ underfoot, to call Him a demon, and to deny that He is God, than to assert that while His holy name is invoked, while His holy martyrs struggle in prayer to implore healing, an evil demon is working the miracles?

Truly, he rightly does not believe the saints can do anything who believes their souls are mortal, or at least that they do not exist in the nature of things until the Day of Judgment. For that is what the "sleep" <note>This refers to "Soul Sleep" or Psychopannychia, the belief that the soul sleeps between death and resurrection—a view Postel attributes to some radical reformers.</note> means to those who falsely boast today that they are so imbued with the Gospel.

These are the seedbeds of a most imprudent man, an overturner of the divine order. From this have arisen the Anabaptists, the Catabaptists <note>original: "Catabaptistæ," a derogatory term for those who "baptize against" or re-baptize.</note>, and those Jews who are apostates from Christ. For as many as this opinion has shaped here, they are now almost all either impious, or, while speaking frequently of the Gospel, they differ not at all from Epicureans <note>Followers of Epicurus, often used in this period as a slur for materialists or atheists who lived only for pleasure.</note> in their lives and from lawless men. But more on these elsewhere.

We must return to the propagation of the Gospel. How many rhetoricians, even those of the highest eloquence, could have persuaded anyone by the most absolute art of speaking of that which the rude fishermen, ignorant of all letters, persuaded the world: that a man fixed to a cross was God? And this among the most refined listeners, adorned with every kind of literature, while both letters and worldly fortunes were flourishing and brought to their peak? It was certainly no human work to have not only conquered dejected, wealthy, prudent, refined, and polished men, but also to have drawn so many into their opinion that they would even undergo death voluntarily and of their own accord for the name of Jesus.

The more the matter was alien to human sense, the more "living" it was. The lack of skill in the men persuaded more easily than rhetorical trickery. Truly, those works and a life full of God created by far the greatest faith.

Nothing was done in secret. While the most celebrated empire of the whole world [Rome] flourished, so much so that nothing could be added to it and it was already laboring under its own weight; when the disciplines refined by the Greeks had now reached their summit among the Latins; in short, when nature, art, and fortune seemed to have competed for power—God willed through the "foolishness of preaching" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 1:21.</note> to save those who believe.

The knowledge of all doctrines yielded the palm <note>original: "herbam porrexit," an idiom meaning to admit defeat.</note> to rustic simplicity; the recklessness of fortune gradually gave way to nakedness, and all care for the body to neglect. Hence the conflict was all the more grave: while Satan exercised dominion in his own followers, the truth remained victorious through patience.

O, if only I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths, so that I could at least sketch these things in outline! Satan yielded unwillingly; the empire of the world yielded. False religion, the more it was packed with human efforts the more false it was, was sunk; and through humility and patience, the power of the world yielded to Christ—not that power joined to the recklessness of fortune, but that which resisted the truth.

Princes, just like commoners, recognized that they differed in no condition from other men: that they owed everything to God, and to men as brothers. The wolf dwelt with the lamb <note>A reference to the prophecy of peace in Isaiah 11:6.</note>; the greatest tyrant, moved by the virtue of the Gospel, ceased to exercise tyranny over the lambs and began to hold all subjects in the place of a brother. In short, Christ made all things one among his own.

But if today there are no such Christians, it is the fault of the men and the time, not of the faith. For men have perverted all things; yet God has never ceased to reveal Himself to the world through the preachers of the Gospel with miracles, as long as they were open to all, and for some, the miracles live on; and today...

-># WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK I. 91<-

where in a part of the world recently opened to us <note>Postel likely refers here to the Americas or "New World," where Jesuit and other missions were reporting rapid conversions accompanied by what they described as signs and wonders.</note> an entry for the Gospel has been made, it is common for this to occur even with following miracles and signs in the name of Jesus Christ. By all these things, the truth of the Gospel is most strongly confirmed, as is the divinity of Christ and his presence among his own; which, unless he were God and had truly suffered, could not happen. But if the power of Jesus Christ was admirable in that alteration of the minds and opinions of his followers, and most especially in the constancy of the martyrs and the performing of miracles, it was by far greatest in the transmission of the Gospel, about which a few things must be said.

### ON THE CERTAIN FAITH AND AUTHORITY
### of the Gospel. CHAPTER XV.

Since Christ was in such nakedness <note>In this context, "nakedness" refers to extreme poverty and a lack of worldly possessions.</note> of all things that he did not possess even as much of the earth for the rest of his body as wild beasts have in their burrows <note>A reference to Matthew 8:20: "Foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay his head."</note>, and of such simplicity and gentleness that he yielded nothing to the most innocent children, and finally of such wisdom and prudence that he could be surpassed by no one: whom the magistrates of the Jews thought entirely unworthy even of their company because of his meager circumstances and his neglect of himself, but whom, on the other hand, those unskilled in worldly affairs—driven by his miracles and teaching because they never asserted anything contrary to the senses of the soul—judged to be either God or the greatest of prophets; how did it happen that without any force, without the disguise of human wisdom, in those places where he lived his life, his persuasion was accepted within thirty years, unless those very things which he had done and taught were impressed upon people without any addition, and were confirmed by the miracles of those preaching them? How could it happen that things which seemed so different in a man should so unite into one that the same meanings of doctrine resulted and became uniform, and were approved by all (except for the unspeakable magistrate who resisted for the sake of retaining human power) as the things he had done and taught in his life? The Gospel is a divine work. For immediately after his death it was written and preached by Matthew; whom Luke followed shortly after, a man most skilled in human affairs; not much later Mark followed, a disciple of Peter; to all of whom John added the finishing touch <note>original: "colophonem," a Greek-derived term meaning a crowning touch or finishing stroke.</note>. Nor did only these men write, but up to fourteen others had reported in writing what they had seen, and explained more broadly what had been omitted by others. All these things were preached not only to foreign nations, but first in those places where he had lived; where, although many Hebrew magistrates resisted his divinity, nevertheless, because the events had happened exactly as they were written and reported, no one was ever able to deny anything; which is an argument of indubitable faith. For if those men, who were entirely destitute of human authority and even hated for their neglect of splendor or glory, had been found to have read, written, or recited anything false, who would not have immediately accused them of lying? Who would not have hissed them off the stage? Indeed, so far was Christ from wishing to embrace human protection in the beginning of his religion, that even if any such thing were added, he would not want it approved.

<margin>
Luke in Acts 1 <note>This likely refers to the prologue of the Gospel of Luke rather than Acts, where Luke mentions many have undertaken to compile a narrative.</note> signifies that many attempted to weave together the Gospel history, but did not excel.
</margin>

His most holy church, in which he reigns present, when it saw such a multitude of Gospel writers, decreed that the number should be immediately reduced to the four which it uses now, both for the sake of removing human persuasion, and because the holy prophet had foretold that four living creatures, to which they correspond in likeness, would be sufficient for praising the Creator. Ezekiel in the first chapter, while he paints the image of divinity in spiritual coverings, intended this to be signified. Moreover, that he wished human reasonings to be removed from the persuasion of the Gospel is most apparent in the works of Clement, the disciple of Peter and companion of the apostles, and also the supreme pontiff after Peter. For when the church saw that he had written many things about Peter (whose work he also promises in the *Acts*), and had confirmed them with human reasons, and had pierced through the gentiles with the highest eloquence and their own persuasions, the church did not want that book among the sacred and

<margin>
I do not believe the author is speaking of the printed Clement, but of his authentic <note>Latin: *germanis*. In this context, it refers to "genuine" or "original" works associated with Clement of Rome, rather than works in the German language.</note> books, which are said to be preserved in the libraries of Italy. Indeed, Scripture does not anxiously use the rigid forms of logical arguments; however, all its points consist of the most solid reasons.
</margin>

...be numbered among the canonical books, lest, since Christ himself makes a way for himself by his own authority and miracles, he should seem to need human support. For it was necessary that the simple minds of the first Christians be imbued with assent <note>In 16th-century theology, "assent" is the act of the mind accepting a truth as certain, even before it fully understands the "why" behind it.</note>, not with complex reasons, before they could grasp the logic of those things which they believed; just as is usually done with the basic lessons taught to children, so that they may one day arrive at greater degrees of learning. Certainly, the whole world possesses nothing more learned than the work of Clement <note>Postel refers to Clement of Rome, an early Church Father whose writings were often cited by those seeking to harmonize faith and reason.</note>, as far as the reasons for those things he treated are concerned. For he entirely sets forth and confirms our doctrines, while destroying and refuting foreign ones.

But that the Church held this view—that she did not wish to rely on human reasons—is seen everywhere in our books. For, to say nothing of the others, what is more wonderful than the Gospel of John? Who explains the greatness of divinity more deeply? Even the greatest philosophers admit that whatever Plato and others ever handed down about divine matters is comprised in that Gospel in a very few words; and yet, John adds no formal logical reason. The same is to be judged of Paul. For if you except one or two places, he never fights with human reasons, but, as he himself says, by the "showing of faith and power in Christ Jesus."

What then shall we say? Why did so many most holy authors have need of reasons? Many centuries later they were forced to fight with both authority and reason, because philosophers, heathens, Jews, and heretics had arisen and armed themselves against us. Since those people attacked us with reasons, they had to be slaughtered by their own sword <note>A common metaphor in Renaissance polemics: using the opponent's own logic (the "sword" of philosophy) to defeat them.</note>. Otherwise, if their authorities were not excerpted from others or borrowed from us, they would have undoubtedly turned the collision of viewpoints and the explanation of nature into their own cause, and corrupted them by twisting the truth. 

Reason had to be applied, therefore, for that cause, and especially so that the reasons for things might be gradually instilled and opened to a "grown-up" world now capable of more solid education—at least as far as the measure of human intellect allows and the condition of things permits. For Christ considered it enough to have acted entirely in the role of a teacher during his mortal life. Since he was most lowly, most unknown, and was to be received in a way that contradicted human judgment, he did not want human works to be the proof of him, lest anyone could claim that his influence was increased by human art or industry. He wanted "little ones," who can only grasp small things, to give their assent to the basic elements of letters, the joining of syllables, and the connection of parts, before we reached the full knowledge of those things preserved in the great monuments of literature. 

However, for a well-educated disciple who is worthy of the best teacher, it is permitted to search for the reasons of things through themselves (provided it is done soberly). Yet this must be done such that if he does not grasp everything, he does not think it is otherwise just because he cannot conceive the scale of such great matters. He should meanwhile trust in those things he has found to be most true, based on the authority of the teacher he once believed. For such is the thinness of our weakness, and such is the obscurity of even the smallest things, that if we want to create certainty of knowledge for ourselves based only on our own tiny understanding, we would undoubtedly admit that we are most ignorant of that which we once thought we knew best. 

Indeed, if we compare that small particle of nature which we believe we understand with the massive volume of what is unknown, we will undoubtedly feel that our knowledge is like the proportion of a giant <note>In the sense of something unnaturally large and overwhelming.</note> or a millet seed compared to the entire universe. To start from the greatest things: we conceive of all Heavenly things and those spiritual intellects whose effects we see here only by "privation" rather than by "habit" <note>A scholastic distinction: "privation" means we know what they are *not* (e.g., God is not finite), while "habit" would mean knowing their essence directly, which Postel argues is impossible for humans.</note>. As for lower things, even those which we have before our eyes daily are scarcely perceived by us except on the surface, and only insofar as they are useful to us; otherwise, they remain superficial. And those things we do know, we know through "demonstration" <term>demonstration: a formal logical or mathematical proof</term> only after we have first given our assent. For he who has not first accepted the basic concept—such as what a straight line is, or a triangle—simply because it *is*, will never be able to grasp a logical proof. God truly made it so that we easily agree with all these first principles. Knowing all these things, our Paul, who was inspired by God <note>original: θεόπνευστος (theopneustos)</note>, said: I do not think myself...

<summary>Postel argues that the Gospel’s lack of formal philosophical reasoning is a sign of its divine authority, intended to foster faith first. He explains that while the Church eventually used reason to defeat heretics, human intellect is too limited to grasp the universe without first assenting to divine truth.</summary>

<header># BOOK I OF GUILLAUME POSTEL</header>

<sig>i 2</sig>

...among you, except **Jesus Christ and him crucified** <note>original: *Inter uos scire pręter Iesum Christū, & eum crucifixū*. Postel is quoting the Apostle Paul from 1 Corinthians 2:2.</note>: just as if a philosopher were to say, “nothing is so certain to me as that there are four elements”; or a geometer, “I know nothing more certain than the line and the point.” Furthermore, it brings by far the greatest faith and authority to the **Gospel**, and proves the divinity of its author, that it even persuaded people of those things which clash diametrically with commonly accepted human reasoning. Nor does it contradict the reasoning of the wise or the just. For many philosophers have attempted to defend its reasoning against common sense, and the just have approved them. Truly, however, what they taught could never be persuasive for a twofold reason. First, because they lived one way—that is, badly—and taught another—that is, well. Second, because that divine spirit, the fuel of divine persuasion, was far removed from those men who taught these things neither out of care for honoring God, nor from a desire to amend their own lives, but for the sake of ostentation and catching a bit of glory from men. Otherwise, if the spirit of God had been present, even if their life had not entirely corresponded, they would undoubtedly have persuaded anyone in such a way that the listener would have been satisfied with nothing before proving it with works. For even many wicked men have taught in the name of **Jesus Christ** and performed miracles: by which it is most clearly seen that those miracles and words proceed not from man, but from divine power and order. Those precepts, which are more foreign to the sense of the common crowd, are of this sort: To love all men equally as

<margin>“</margin>brothers and children of God: and to admit even the loss of one’s own life rather than
<margin>“</margin>neglect this command: To accept injury with a calm mind: To pray well for
<margin>“</margin>**enemies**: To neglect vengeance and leave it to God: And that the assertion of truth
<margin>“</margin>and the action of virtue be preferred to parents, fortunes, safety, and life: To rush
<margin>“</margin>voluntarily and of one’s own accord into dangers, provided that both truth and the safety of man are preserved. Let **Demosthenes**, **Cicero**, **Aeschines**, or **Hortensius** <note>Postel lists the greatest orators of Greece (Demosthenes, Aeschines) and Rome (Cicero, Hortensius) to show that even the peak of human eloquence cannot achieve what the Gospel did.</note> approach to persuade these things; let these lights of both languages <note>referring to Greek and Latin</note> propose these things, let them argue with reasons, let them catch goodwill, let them creep into minds with insinuations, make them attentive, teachable, and well-disposed, and let them apply whatever other machinery of deceptive eloquence there is: if they should so persuade that there is anyone who, captured by their allurements, undergoes these things voluntarily and testifies to them with works, then **truth will yield the palm** <note>original: *herbam porriget ueritas*. This is a classical idiom meaning to admit defeat.</note>. But while fishermen, destitute of all things and especially lacking in eloquence, propose these things, they are believed. Since it is not they themselves who persuade, but that divine spirit—who knows how to soften the hearts of all and turn them in any direction—it prepared attention and goodwill for their speech in those chosen for itself. Where certainly anything is not placed within the highest art, it is surely not possible for that to happen when it cannot be achieved by a lower one. Since, however, it is seen to happen, it is established that it happens not by human art or industry, but clearly by divine power. Indeed, as many as gave their names to **Christ** at the birth of the **Gospel**, they were not persuaded of only one or another of these precepts, but whoever was a **Christian** held, believed, taught, and confirmed all of them in their entirety through their work. But the impious man will say: "those unlearned men of yours persuaded those similar to themselves and the unlearned. They drew no learned man to their opinion." Although it would be no wonder if our persuasion had, at first glance, none adorned with human disciplines and various kinds of doctrines (which are accustomed to infuse a great vanity in evil men through the opinion of bit of glory): since those precepts, which external life uses more frequently and which are smeared with pretense, depend on the decrees of certain philosophers who are such only as far as the **cloak and the beard** <note>original: *pallio & barba tenus*. A common ancient critique of "fake" philosophers who wore the traditional dress and beard but lacked the actual wisdom.</note>. Truly, however many the love of truth—not the love of popular favor—drew to the love of wisdom, our religion had them all as followers, if they heard concerning it. And so that it may be clear, I will produce a few out of many into the open. I do not wish to touch upon how many men of great name from the Jewish nation, placed at the highest peak of magistracies and dignities, preferred to be shamefully expelled from their senate than to fall away from **Christ**, such as **Nicodemus**, **Gamaliel**, and **Joseph of Arimathea**. Yet what was the highest knowledge of human letters among the Jews? What refinement? It was surely greatest, even by the argument that...

<header>### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD</header>

No one among the learned was considered to be such who was not quite well-versed in the knowledge of Greek literature; and this has been the case since the times of Alexander. For who would not marvel that a few years after him, seventy-two elders could be drawn from a single Jerusalem Senate and led to King Ptolemy for the interpretation of the Law? <note>This refers to the legendary origins of the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, reportedly commissioned by Ptolemy II Philadelphus in the 3rd century BCE.</note> Was not Aristobulus most eloquent? Philo, among the Jews, could be compared to Plato. Josephus, that most famous historian, sufficiently revealed how great the knowledge of humane letters was among the Jews, as he yields nothing to the Greeks in eloquence and culture.

The Jews, therefore, were not ignorant of human affairs. Why, then, did they not all come to Christ? Wealth, magistracies, glory, honor, smoke, and the popular breeze <note>original: *fumus, aura popularis*. A classical idiom referring to the fleeting and empty nature of public fame and political favor.</note>—all of which had to be either abandoned or counted as nothing—stood in the way. Lest this itself seem strange regarding the Jews, it has a place in every nation and province. For as many as either frequent the courts of princes or perform the duties of magistrates (if you except a few) are so far from wanting to receive even the slightest harm for the sake of the truth, that they hold nothing sacred or holy, provided they can benefit themselves or their own, and acquire the "smoke of honors." That is the disease of the world.

From his very eloquence, you will see that Luke was most skilled in the Greek language. Furthermore, from his professional practice, it is certain that he must have read philosophy diligently; otherwise, he could not have been a physician. I do not speak of Paul, who came [to Christ] by compulsion after many injuries inflicted upon our people. From their writings, **Paul**, **Dionysius the Areopagite**, **Ignatius**, and **Hierotheus** seem to be the highest Platonists. Why should I mention **Aquila**, **Apollos**, and **Timothy**, of the Jewish race? The more learned they were, the more quickly they flocked to our side. What is more learned than **Hegesippus**? What is greater than the younger **Philo**? They busied themselves with proving our faith by their lives and writings.

**Meletius**, **Justin**, **Quadratus**, **Aristides**, **Melito**, **Theophilus**, **Modestus**, **Tatian**, **Musanus**, **Bardesanes**, **Apollinaris**, **Miltiades**, **Apollonius**, and innumerable others, both Greek and Latin, no less eloquent than wise, all wrote for our religion to the Roman emperors against false persuasions. They did not only wish to approve of our teachings and live by their rule, but departing from the emperors' households or intimacy, friendship, and fortunes, they even dared to attack with writings the emperors themselves who were most hostile to us, to uncover for them the vanity of false persuasion, to introduce our own, and finally to die for its assertion. 

If anyone wishes to convince himself of the erudition that was in **Clement**, let him read his *Recognitions* (as **Rufinus** translated them, although I think the translator fell quite far from the majesty of the author); he will see nonetheless that the whole circle of disciplines was most familiar to him. The works of **Justin** are extant; the same may be judged of them. Who would not marvel that a Roman senator voluntarily preferred the cross to the *trabea* <note>original: *trabeæ*. The *trabea* was a ceremonial toga with purple stripes, worn by high-ranking Roman officials and senators as a mark of status.</note>? Let **Tertullian** be read. **Cyril**, **Lactantius**, **Victorinus**, **Arnobius**, **Origen**, and **Basil** are extant—all of whom lived for a very long time among the pagans. Whoever reads them will see that they knew nothing of Aristotle or Plato that they had not weighed far more diligently; and yet they preferred the doctrine and cross of Christ to vain opinions and reasonings.

I do not wish to dwell longer on these. I could fill as much paper with the names of men famous in every kind of literature as I could smear with writings: who, having disregarded the vanity of human philosophy, so embraced the divine that they wished to confirm it by the bitterest death and by unheard-of and innumerable torments. If anyone should object that they were neither great men, nor enriched with great honors and fortunes: I care nothing for what their condition was; whether it was a meager or a splendid fortune matters not. We see the poor seeking wealth and resources with all their effort, by which they might try to drive away the laws of necessity; we see the rich leave no stone unturned so that an addition might be made from anywhere. What they were before (as I said) matters not. It is certain that they preferred [the faith] to both hope and a splendid fortune, things which not even their enemies dared to hope for. Truly, how can it be, that the ineffable...
