--- Page 113 ---
<meta>This page continues Postel’s discussion on the spiritual hurdles that prevent people from embracing the truth. Having previously mentioned how the "smoke of honors" and worldly prestige blinded the learned Jews and Greeks, he now addresses why the laws of God appear so difficult and contrary to human nature.</meta>

->**WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK I.**<-

Why would that Creator establish laws so abhorrent to our senses? Since they ought to be of use to humans, not to angels or some perfect nature, the reason is obvious: it is so that while we see that those things which proceed from Him cannot be anything but most just, we might also recognize ourselves in them. We feel ourselves to be so depraved and drawn away from the laws of nature that nothing is more bitter to us than a holy sweetness, nothing more turbulent than peace, and we think nothing worse, more profane, more iniquitous, or more foul than things that are good, holy, just, and honorable. Above all, this is so that we may confess—even when we have done everything within our power—that we are "useless servants." <note>A reference to Luke 17:10: "So likewise ye, when ye shall have been done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants."</note> Feeling ourselves powerless to fulfill those precepts, we must attribute to God the Author even those things which were done by us with His help. For He gave us to ourselves, He vitalizes us within ourselves, He supplies the instruments by which we may act well, and He offers the material in which we can exercise our efforts.

The Divine and Evangelical law differs far from human laws in many other ways, but most especially in its beginning and its end. For human laws remove—or rather, they busily try to remove with threats—vices from the Republic after they have emerged. But God, the best and greatest, meets even the "tinder" and the root of sin. For example, regarding homicide, human law will say: *He who knowingly and willingly kills a man shall be punished by death.* But the Divine law says: *If anyone says to his brother "raca," he shall be liable to judgment.* <note>original: *racca*. From the Aramaic *reka*, an insult meaning "empty-headed" or "worthless" (Matthew 5:22).</note> *Love your enemies.* Why such a deep-seated beginning? Because if hatred, enmity, complaints, anger, contentions, and <term>self-love</term> <note>original: *philautía*. A Greek term for excessive self-regard, often viewed by theologians as the root of all sin.</note> did not come first, there would have been no place for the result. Remedies must be applied to the head. Where there is perpetual love, there can never be malice, nor a wound, nor death. 

How then does the same God seem different from Himself? For in the Old Testament He said only, *Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not commit adultery,* etc. But in the New, as if a greater prudence had been added to Him, He says: *Whosoever hates his brother is a murderer.* (1 John 3). And: *Whosoever looks upon a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.* What do these things mean? He wished to treat the Israelite people (as we have already said) in the manner of a wise <term>pedagogue</term>. <note>A reference to the Greco-Roman "paidagogos," a tutor who supervised a child's conduct. Postel draws on Galatians 3:24, where the Law of Moses is described as a pedagogue leading the people toward Christ.</note> Therefore, because of the hardness of their hearts, He gave those laws—which were indeed divine, but not much harsher than civil laws—so that through the Law, which leads nothing to perfection, they might eventually come as "half-evil" rather than "entirely evil" to the law of the Gospel. The Gospel itself requires a man not only to be good in outward signs, but also most pure in his interior mind. For whoever is such a person, dwelling within himself, can commit absolutely none of the more serious crimes. For this reason, the Law of the Gospel is rightly called "Grace"; the other is named with the title of "Law" because, like the laws God gave to other nations through natural impulse, it established a man as "civilly good." The prophets, understanding this many years before Christ, busied themselves with reducing all legal matters to the purity of the heart. Therefore, the Gospel alone bears witness to its Author as the searcher of hearts, uprooting the origins and fuels of crimes. Truly, those few laws which the world does not approve of—or if it does approve, confirms only in words—must be weighed individually to see how much utility they would cause in this life if they were kept.

***

## ON THE MORE DIFFICULT PRECEPTS 
### OF THE GOSPEL. CHAPTER XVI.

For many reasons, the laws of Christ seem unbearable to ruined men; truly, for no greater reason than that they suffer from innumerable vices of the mind and body. Whoever burns with bile, and is accustomed to frequently provoke it and make it sharper at the slightest occasion, judges it impossible not to seek revenge. He who rushes headlong into <term>lust</term> <note>original: *Venerem*. Literally "Venus," the Roman goddess of love, used here as a metonym for sexual desire or promiscuity.</note> and seeks fuels everywhere to incite his libido, cannot bear this precept: *He who looks at a woman to lust after her,* etc. If anyone is held by the pursuit of glory and "smoke," <note>original: *fumo*. A common metaphor in Renaissance Latin for the empty, fleeting nature of fame and public reputation.</note> you will never persuade him that he who is least and most abject is the greatest of all, and most dear and closest to God.

He contrasts the Old Testament's civil-like focus with the Gospel's requirement for total internal purity, which he calls the Law of Grace.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument regarding the human resistance to divine law. Having established that God’s laws seem "bitter" or "difficult" because of human corruption, he now examines how specific vices—avarice, ambition, and lust—distort human judgment and lead to the creation of false laws, specifically targeting the origins of Islam and the behavior of European nobility.</meta>

### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

For anyone who would maintain such things <note>referring to the humble Christian virtues mentioned on the previous page</note> would seem to trample upon the splendor of empires, magistracies, and all dignities. He who labors under avarice will never be able to persuade himself that "it is better to give than to receive" <note>original: "melius esse dare, quàm accipere"; a reference to Acts 20:35</note>; that all things are to be bestowed freely (even to an enemy); and finally, that no reward for a benefit should be demanded back. So it is in all other matters: as each person is inclined, so he judges against those things which do not serve his lust.

But whom does the fire of glory not drive off course? Whom does ambition not torture and kill? For whom is pleasure not a familiar disease? Whom does the madness of revenge not drive insane? Over whom does wrath not exercise a tyranny? From whom does the thirst for possessing not seek punishment? Nor does a single man suffer the dominion of only one or two vices, but such are the defects of nature: that if any one of them once creeps in and occupies the whole man, it immediately summons all the others like <term>satraps</term> <note>originally provincial governors in the ancient Persian Empire; here used to mean subordinate henchmen or tyrants</note> and ministers of tyranny. O miserable man, you who suffer these things for one fault—that you are ignorant of your own self!

It would truly be more tolerable if each person were weighed down by his own vices and perished for himself alone. But the more one is pressed by them, the more he busies himself with transferring them into others; so that what seemed to be a vice in him now becomes praiseworthy through the fellowship of all those committing the same, because he has many associates and colleagues in his opinion—as if he burns any less who burns with many others! Thence vice rushes into the name of virtue and occupies its seat: from this, the names of virtue are indeed splendidly brought forth, praised, and extolled in this mortal life, but in practice, vice is exercised.

Under the pretext of the holy laws of the Gospel (because they seemed too difficult for men ruined in mind and body), Muhammad introduced his own persuasion, fighting diametrically against Christ; for no mortal was ever more deceptive, or more stirred up to revenge, or finally, more ruined by a <note>original: "colluvie"</note> cesspool of all vices. For he used to boast that in one hour he could satisfy fifteen of his wives along with his handmaidens. Those whom he held most dear as friends, if they offended him by even a single nod, he would finish off while they were sleeping in bed. Therefore, he said his law was a "middle way" between the Old and New Testaments, and he adorned it with "distinguished deeds" of this sort.

It was not enough for him, therefore, to perish so that he might reign; but because the vices in him were being criticized, lest they be seen as vices, he passed laws almost daily so that the same things would be permitted to everyone as were to himself. Revenge, which he exercised most willingly, he wanted thus confirmed by law: asserting that he is damned who has not immediately compensated an injury with an injury. Thus, in his entire law, so that he might patronize his own vices, he established laws favorable to his own crimes—which will be made clear in the account of his life and doctrine.

Princes, courtiers, and men placed at the highest peak of affairs do almost the same thing everywhere. For although they do not pass a law permitting the license of crimes, yet while they serve as the example, they are ashamed, being conscious of their own guilt, to prohibit in others what they themselves commit. Thus it happens that from where justice ought to flow unto humans, a blight and plague creeps into everyone, for this one reason: that they do not obey the most holy laws of Christ.

If, for example, while they are dealing with revenge, they would set this before themselves: first, that they are acting against the law of God; second, that it is necessary to bring a stain upon nature; that whoever pursues revenge is pressed by infinite fires; that he who thirsts for a neighbor's blood must perish, either himself, the other, or both; that he will involve his family and parents along with his adversaries; that he can be conquered with the greatest disgrace, or conquer without glory; and that he destroys a man and removes nature itself, which was the cause of life and duration. 

Who, considering all these things, would not lead himself far better to flee so many evils and conquer an adversary with patience, rather than undergo so many dangers of his own accord for the sake of a trivial opinion? Especially since, once the crime is committed, he will bring back hatred from many, disgrace from the good, and from a very few—and those being flatterers and enemies under the forged name of friendship—he will bring back glory. I remain silent about the eternal repentance for the deed, the eternal <term>Erinnyes</term> <note>The Furies of Greek and Roman mythology, who personified vengeance and hounded the guilty</note>, and the neglect of God. For all these things must seem trivial to him who, for the sake of a very slight opinion, rushes of his own accord into death...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s critique of human nature and vice. Following the previous page's discussion on how vices like avarice and ambition enslave the human soul, Postel now focuses specifically on the "madness of revenge" and the false sense of "honor" that drives men to violence despite divine and civil laws.</meta>

<header>WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK 1</header>

<sig>i 4</sig>

falls. But someone says, "If I suffer an injury with impunity, I will only invite a wicked man to do more by my patience." He can be restrained by laws: go before a judge. But because you share a part in the crime, and perhaps you even provoked the one you now wish dead, you prefer to decide the matter by your own whim rather than by what is fair and good. If, by a balanced injury against the other, you could recover your health or the things you say you lost through him, it would indeed be justified; if he took your foot, and his would be useful to you in place of your lost one, you would want to take it from him: and so in similar cases. That would at least be something. But since you gain nothing else from vengeance except the fact that you aim a disgrace at him, it is a wonder why you are so insane. You cry out that he is a worthless and shameful man because he caused a man loss. But do you not see that when you desire to inflict loss upon him, you take those same crimes upon yourself? For you are causing loss to a man. "But he did it first," you say. He will say the same about you afterward. Thus, the cause of vengeance will be an eternal hell, both in this life and in the one to come. Vengeance belongs to God alone <note>original: "Vindicta Dei solius est"; a reference to the biblical principle in Romans 12:19 and Deuteronomy 32:35</note>. He who carries it out in his own name denies God, whom he does not believe to be just or able to return rewards according to merits. However, to carry out vengeance in a public name, or for the sake of the afflicted and the needy who require help—if the matter cannot be settled otherwise—that vengeance is indeed most just. But no one cares for this kind; everyone seeks the former. Someone will say: "This has been given by nature to all living creatures, that they may protect themselves and their own." It is indeed established by nature for all creatures that lack law to finish off or hunt down their enemies. But for man, whom reason commands and who governs himself with judgment—who, after his first impulses, looks into himself, for whom laws are established and judges appointed, and for whom a path to compensation for injury lies open—it is not the same as with oxen, horses, or lions, who rage against their own kind. For civil laws prohibit this in vain if a man must act simply because something is rooted in his animal nature. Those impulses must be governed by reason: otherwise, he must necessarily rush into all other dangers and deny that God exists by pursuing vengeance. We wish to snatch everything away from God and ascribe it to ourselves. It is no different than if there were many brothers in one family born of the same father, and one, having received an injury from another, wanted to pay it back and take away the father's authority and judgment in assessing it, seizing it for himself; even though it is established by the common proverb, "Everyone is blind in their own cause" <note>original: "Omnes in propria causa cæcutire"</note>. 

But the opinion has become so strong: "If I do not take revenge, I am not noble, I am not spirited, I will not be considered a good and brave soldier." If playing the soldier means killing a brother or a companion; if it is noble to approve in yourself what you condemn in another, then so be it. Why are you a slave to the eyes and judgments of others? What does fame or the judgment of another matter to you, provided you feel you have done nothing unworthy of yourself? You cannot be changed by another's judgment. Be good: though they may judge you evil as much as they wish, you do not become worse; but if you are otherwise, take care to correct what they disapprove of. If they see a deserter in war, or someone soft and remiss toward the enemy, or someone refusing commands, then naturally a concern for fame and honor must be had. But smoke and fame change nothing in the reality of things. That opinion tortures us for this reason: that we have and believe in neither God as a father and just judge, nor man as a brother. From here comes the root of all evils: hatred; so that nothing is holier or truer than that saying of John:

> He who hates his brother is a murderer. <note>original: "Qui odit fratrem suum, homicida est"; 1 John 3:15</note>

Now it is clear enough with how much advantage this miserable mortal state might submit to the divine precept in forgiving an injury, and in how many calamities those who think, speak, and act to the contrary are involved. A perpetual heat scorches their hearts, and a continuous fear curdles their blood. For he who wishes to be held as formidable by another must also be touched by dread. How much happier is he who breaks anger with a soft response, conquers hardness with patience, makes a friend out of an enemy through a kindness, accepts peace in place of war, and, to put it in a single word, attempts to reconcile a brother to himself by every kind of duty? There is also in these laws a difference from the civil laws and the <term>Mosaic judgment</term> <note>original: "Mosaica sententia"; referring to the Law of Moses (lex talionis) which Postel is contrasting with the internal Christian ethics of the heart</note>. For political laws, after the first impulses of the mind, forbid a man from pursuing injuries by his own whim. But whether he loves or holds hatred,

<meta>catchword: of the treasury</meta>

as they are unable to do, so they neither prescribe nor care for it. The Israelite way <note>Refers to the Law of Moses or the Old Covenant as understood in the 16th century.</note> allows an enemy to be held in hatred, and commands the same for the reasons we have reported above. But the precept of Christ—which commands his followers to live together like angels in the highest bond of peace—ordains not only that an injury must be forgiven and vengeance left to God, but also that the highest friendship must be maintained with an adversary. One should so conquer him through kindness that, whether he wishes to or not, he may look within himself and confess himself most unjust for having repaid good things with evil. *If your enemy is hungry,* says Paul, *feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink. For in doing so, you will heap coals of fire upon his head.* <note>original: "Si efurierit... inimicus tuus, ciba illum... carbones ignis super caput eius"; a quote from Romans 12:20, citing Proverbs 25:21-22.</note> By this reasoning, he understands that the fire of charity will necessarily steal into him in such a way that he begins to see himself for what he is. Christ is not satisfied if we depend on outward signs, whether in avoiding vice or in conferring a benefit. He demands the strengths of the soul; if these are lacking, the labor is in vain. Loving and doing good must come from the soul; retreating from evil must come from the soul. He who busies himself with winning over an enemy through benefits is seen to be very much like God. For although men are accustomed to provoking God at every moment and turning point of time—striving to do so, blaspheming, neglecting Him, some denying Him by their deeds and others even by their words—He nevertheless bestows benefits upon all equally. Therefore, whoever wishes to prove himself most truly a son of such a Father must clearly do the same toward all brothers; both toward everyone in general, and especially toward those of the household of faith. For a son ought not to be in a better condition than his father. That Father not only does not punish, but He heaps the greatest gifts upon them, and often the greater the gifts, the worse the people are—so that, at least bound by those gifts, they might either acknowledge so great a giver or deservedly perish as ingrates. On the other hand, because His own people are already His, He leads them back to Himself through afflictions, lest they become like the wicked, puffed up by prosperity. These people ought to give everything to their brothers because they know God as their common father; the others pile up in heaps what God has given because, as if "emancipated" <note>A legal term referring to children released from paternal control; here meaning those who act as if they have no father or communal responsibility.</note>, they act outside the fraternal fellowship. Therefore, he who loves God the Father above all things, and his neighbor as himself, will undoubtedly have no concern for parents or possessions, provided he is joined to the Author of all things. *This is eternal life: that they may know You, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent.* <note>original: "Haec est uita aeterna, ut te noscant uerū Deū, & quem misisti Iesum Christū"; quoting John 17:3.</note> To make this happen, one must leave everything behind in order to possess yourself. The philosophers have tasted these sentiments in whatever way they could, but in such a way that they taught only with words, not with deeds, as I said before. Therefore, no one ever wished to suffer even the slightest loss for the sake of keeping a precept of Plato or Aristotle, because they denied in their lives the very laws they set down. Certainly, Plato, in his community of goods, wished to incline toward brotherhood; but meanwhile, because he did not know how to distinguish what ought to be common and what private, he established a brothel, not a Republic. <note>Postel critiques Plato’s *Republic*, specifically the proposal for a community of wives, which many Christian commentators viewed as immoral.</note> But at this point the world will raise an outcry: since laziness and the impulse to inflict injury are innate in the greater part of men, if we endure all things and give away all things, we open the doors to idleness and invite injury upon ourselves. Oh, if only those who object to such things could have seen, at one time in the most uncultivated and desert places of Egypt, more than three hundred thousand men to whom no law could prescribe anything! There was no one who was not very wealthy, even though they all lived by gain and the labor of their hands. Riches flowed there from the whole world, where none grew; in the cities, there were as many communal dwellings <note>original: "κοινόβια" (koinobia); the root of the word 'cenobite,' referring to monks living in community.</note> as there were houses. Why should I mention the life of the Apostles, and the innumerable multitude following them everywhere on earth? It has often been seen, by the diligence and example of a single good bishop, that while a famine was distressing the whole world, with the greatest charity, no one in his jurisdiction felt it at all.

<margin>Among sincere brothers, a community of goods would have a place</margin>
It was not that the crops were more abundant there than elsewhere, but that they were less private. Each person strove to put his own goods forward for the common use; there was an equal abundance for all, and no penury. He who had spent his own goods first received from others, and meanwhile, nothing was lost to the public treasury. For Satan is accustomed to object this against the perfection of the Gospel: "If there are not some who are very wealthy, it will not be possible for..."

Consideration must be had for the time and the circumstances; yet in such a way that we think nothing more happy could ever happen to mortals than if those things prescribed in the Gospel—which the world does not want to acknowledge in its deeds—were entirely observed.

### ON THE DIFFERENCE IN ORIGIN BETWEEN THE PERSUASION OF CHRIST AND FALSE RELIGIONS. CHAPTER XVII.

Although these matters have been treated extensively, it nevertheless seemed good to touch upon them briefly in this place as well, for a greater confirmation of Christ's divinity: specifically, by what arts the plagues of wicked scoundrels <note>Postel refers here to founders of other religions or heretical movements who he believes tricked people.</note> have forced themselves upon the ignorance of men, and in what way Christ revealed himself to the world in such a short time. 

In order that we may weigh these things, we must examine the conditions of human affairs, so that we may perceive what is according to nature and what is against it. No student of philosophy can deny that every created thing has within itself a certain hidden drive for self-preservation. From this, it appears that individual things—as much as nature itself allows—desire a certain duration and immortality, if it were possible, and seek out all aids by which they may achieve it. Even those things which lack both sense and life, but consist of a simple essence, are nevertheless usually bound by such a link that they are not broken apart except with difficulty. For what does not fight back with sense and choice resists by the hardness and stubbornness of its body. Hence, we see that those things which tend toward the preservation of things are most in accordance with nature. 

For if the Creator willed this care to be the duty of all, it is most certain that they also desire to endure as long as possible. Hence, all corruptible things, although they cannot avoid corruption, nevertheless fear it most. Therefore, whatever things bring about corruption are those that most oppose nature and resist the will of the Creator. This applies to all things, but especially to those that tend toward the destruction of men—particularly if that harm proceeds from a person's choice and deliberation. For things that do not act by their own will, but spread a common danger or a destructive action to their surroundings—such as corruptions of the air, the water, and other things which, from the imperfection of nature, bring sickness to human bodies—act indeed outside the will of the Creator, but not against it, as He permits it; such things do not deserve our indignation. 

Similarly, the harms caused by wild beasts and all living creatures are beyond blame, since the intent to inflict injury is absent. Therefore, only that destruction which proceeds from evil demons and men is finally condemned, and is rightly said to be armed against God and nature. It is certain, then, that all wars undertaken anywhere (except for two causes) are against God and nature, because they bring destruction to human nature and a stain upon the things prepared for its salvation, contrary to the order of the whole world. 

In truth, those two causes for war are to be proved by the example of our own nature. For since nature has granted that all living things, and especially man, should protect themselves and their property, and since whatever things do harm and bring destruction are either internal or external, war is just against both types of enemies. Those things which are lower than man never suffer from internal discord, because they never fight with themselves; for they lack judgment and reason. Man, however, carries an enemy about at home or faces one from without. Since he suffers from a thousand monsters of vice as if from a domestic rebellion, he must first take care to drive that filth from his home and restrain it, before...

...before he can attack any enemies of the body. Other animals experience only external enemies because they can only be endangered in their bodies; but because man consists of both soul and body, he suffers from enemies of both. Therefore, no mortal will ever be permitted to blunt the strength of an external enemy unless he has first driven out the enemy within his own home <note>The "domestic enemy" refers to internal vices or spiritual failings.</note>. For he is unable to bear two powers at once. In the same way, any gathering of men—whether a commonwealth or a kingdom—can be undermined by a double enemy: the internal and the external. If a certain part of that multitude, which agreed to the laws and swore by the words of the living law, were to rise up against its fellow citizens <term>municipes; members of the same community or town</term>, or plot their ruin by any craft, it would undoubtedly be better to cut off the rotten limb—unless it could be healed by some other medicine—than to allow it to bring destruction to the rest of the body’s parts. Anyone should be considered an external enemy who threatens you, your people, or those you are able to defend, or who uses things to the dishonor of God and the injury of his neighbor and himself. For whoever does injury to the living and true God must be held as the most ruinous enemy to all. For human affairs are so arranged that they ought to be used, not abused. He who uses them for the destruction of nature and does not repent should be slaughtered in a most just war: lest he not only bring destruction upon himself but also infect others with his contagion. All other wars waged to this day were wicked, committed by aggressors against the majesty of God and the preservation of nature. For there is no doubt that they were undertaken out of a lust for ruling and possessing, a desire for glory and ambition, and a greed for fame—as were almost all the wars of the Romans—and were waged for the destruction of nature, the punishment of mortal crimes, and in direct opposition to the majesty of divine goodness. They were like Furies <note>original: "Erinnyes"; in Greek mythology, the Furies were deities of vengeance and retribution.</note> sent by Satan into the world, so that the God whom human iniquity acknowledged might have His daily blessings exploited.

->Now, therefore, let us come to the point: how the tyrants of the world, after the human race was undermined and despoiled of its fortunes, thrust themselves into the place of divinity.<-

<margin>Diodorus writes that he was cut into 26 parts by his brother Typhon; see Plutarch's *On Osiris and Isis*.</margin>
After the most famous parts of the world had been traversed and devastated, and his own people nearly killed by labor and taxes, Osiris was regarded as a god in Egypt—claiming descent from Jupiter the Greatest. This was achieved by bribing the priests with money (through the work of his wife, Isis); these priests placed the parts of the tyrant, which had been torn apart by his relatives, into statues, and displayed them in many places as if they were a whole body. The multitude, ignorant of these matters, began to worship him—partly struck by the terror of the injuries they had received, and partly moved by the novelty of the thing—even though he deserved to be considered the destroyer of the world. Hercules made a path for his own divinity by the sword. Mars was famous for his spoils; Neptune was a pirate; and all this occurred when there was the greatest ignorance and rudeness among men. And yet those "renowned" deities were barely worshipped in a few places (if you look at the whole world), and even for those, force, trickery, gold, and eloquence had paved the way.

When the world had matured and was cultivated with every kind of discipline, nakedness, simplicity, and patience offered themselves; and within a hundred years, Jesus Christ began to be worshipped and acknowledged throughout the entire world: among the Chinese <note>original: "Seras"; the Seres were the people of East Asia, known to the West primarily through the silk trade.</note>, Indians, Bactrians, Scythians, Sogdians, Parthians, Persians, Assyrians, Africans, all the Ethiopians, Libyans, Greeks, Romans, Germans, Franks, Spaniards, and to say it once, in the whole circle of the earth.

<margin>For there were 12 Apostles and 70 disciples.</margin>
And among such varied religions, He was preached by a little more than eighty men, who were ignorant of human literature and skilled from infancy only in the Syriac tongue <note>original: "linguae Syriacae"; Postel refers here to Aramaic, the vernacular language of Judea.</note>, which was not very widely known.

This fact surpasses all human power. It was necessary, therefore, for God, the author of the Gospel, to be present everywhere, to have taught the languages of various peoples, and to have performed the duty of a perfect orator everywhere in the world at the same time.

For since a decade is hardly enough to confirm any opinion and instill it into the minds of all or the most prominent people (which is most evident in the way the decrees of princes are approved and received), how could it be that they left the doctrine of Christ in more cities and places than they could have even traveled through or surveyed?

# BOOK I BY GUILLAUME POSTEL

Indeed, it was then that it truly appeared: *It is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit who speaks in you.* And *I am with you even until the end of the age; do not be afraid.* <note>Postel is quoting Matthew 10:20 and 28:20 to show that the Apostles were divinely inspired.</note> Simple men—yet so prudent that no one could deceive them—men who were outsiders, naked, poor, and of foreign tongue, rose up against the cunning, the eloquent, the natives, and those overflowing with luxury. And what is most significant: they rose against the vices of the most powerful. That they grew through death or in even greater numbers—who would believe such things could have happened, unless he saw that they had indeed been done? Oh God, how wonderful are your works! Oh, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God; how incomprehensible are your judgments, O Lord!

<margin>This was the King of the Persians, a persecutor of the church and enemy of the Emperor Heraclius. <note>Refers to Chosroës II, the Sasanian king whose wars with the Byzantine Emperor Heraclius exhausted both empires just before the Arab conquests.</note></margin>

<margin>† There is a chapter about him in the Quran.</margin>

But Muhammad will rise up in this place and say that his religion was immediately received into all of Africa, Egypt, and Syria. It is true: this happened within a hundred years of his death. But any most wicked tyrant is permitted the same. For a little before him (about a decade or so), Chosroës had begun to seize far more territory without any religion at all. The same has been done quite often by desperate robbers. This is how empires have begun. For he opened a way with the sword; he vented his rage upon the peasants. Once their fortunes were consumed, a great multitude was incited to plunder alongside Muhammad. Villages were pillaged, rage was turned against the cities, everyone was attacked, and such license was given to anyone that whatever he seized was his own, † with a **fifth part** given to the prophet. <term>khums; a practice in early Islamic law where one-fifth of war spoils were reserved for the leader or the community treasury</term> What tyranny has not arisen and been confirmed in this way?

But he will say to me, "I was permitted by my prophecy what was permitted to Moses: he killed enemies and waged war." But you differ greatly in your method. Moses fought against enemies for the sake of preserving his citizens; he wished for the enemies of God and desperate men—whose remnants even brought ruin to religion—to be finished off and entirely killed. Muhammad destroyed his own citizens to a man; he rose up against his own people; he took life from the rest with the blood of others; he killed the best men and those most devoted to religion, on the sole pretext that there were some idolaters in Mecca. Let the fair-minded reader weigh, by comparing the prophet and the impostor, and the just and unjust war, and finally by the reasoning of the law, what the difference is between this prophet and the others. He will easily recognize by what things the world has been polished. Such crimes are far from divine mercy **at all times**. <note>original: "διὰ παντός"</note>

For so far is it from the war Muhammad waged having any just occasion, that it was in every respect most ruinous. For having incited sedition, prepared by a hand of desperate men and those destitute of hope, and having received no injury, he overthrew the Republic in which he had been educated. He plundered and consumed the most illustrious fortunes of the citizens. He kindled such a fire in his fatherland that thirty successors after him perished by the sword in mutual sedition, seeking one another’s lives.

But more on those things shortly. Let us proceed to judge the religion of Jesus Christ by its works and power. Satan enters with false persuasions through the sword, blood, fire, gold, deceit, eloquence, and imposture. Christ offers himself through patience, death, charity, poverty, simplicity, and the naked truth. Those other forces bring violence to bodies, things, and fortunes. Our faith brings freedom to souls and eternal riches; it despises those that are fleeting. Whatever those others desire, this faith leaves behind of its own accord if no one takes it. Those others hunt for, cherish, and protect revenge, glory, riches, and pleasures with all their arts; this faith earns its enemies' favor through kindness, flees glory, rejoices in poverty, and curses and puts to flight pleasures as if they were capital diseases of the soul—barely joining with them even out of necessity. Those others claim the name of "Science" for themselves; this faith, under the highest wisdom, everywhere professes and acknowledges ignorance. This faith ascribes all things to God, hangs upon him, and holds him in the place of a father; those others seek all things from the splendor of fortune and think they possess everything by their own industry. They sell themselves through eloquence; this faith is recommended by its "infancy" <note>Referring to the "speechless" simplicity of the humble or the "infancy" of the early church's plain language.</note>. And to grasp in a few words: by whatever arts the world is ruled, this faith fights against them diametrically. Thus we may clearly recognize that it does not consist of human help, but is established by divine power. And it is of such perfection that it finds a place among the few, as has been confessed even by its enemies.

> Good men are rare indeed, scarcely as many as the gates of Thebes, or the mouths of the wealthy Nile. <note>original: "Rari quippe boni, uix totidem quot Thebarũ portæ, aut dītis hoſtia Nili." This is a quote from the Roman satirist Juvenal (Satire 13), used by Postel to illustrate that true virtue is exceptionally rare.</note>

Not even all who take his name today are to be considered among his true followers. For He asks for the soul, not for external things—except insofar as what is carried in the heart is revealed through outward signs. Just as in the beginning of all things, the Greatest Power [the Father] created the world through the Wisdom of the Son without the aid of any pre-existing matter, and gave it to man through supreme kindness rather than any merit of his own; so too did the Son of God, Jesus Christ, wish to fulfill the renewal of man without the assistance of any external power. He did this so that human ability could attribute nothing to itself in this matter, but might rather wonder at it forever, as it is beyond human comprehension. For just as we know by nature that man is born, made by God, and propagated, because it is so—though we do not grasp *how* it happens—so also we know that men are divinely driven by the God-man Jesus Christ to conquer the pride and arrogance of the world through a contempt for worldly things. Yet, we cannot fully grasp how this is done. For to willingly undergo evils—at least what the common opinion of mortals calls "evils"—and to despise everything except God and virtue, is certainly not something achieved by human strength alone. This is the power of the Gospel: the distinction between truth and falsehood, and a firm, constant peace even amidst torments.

### ON THE EXCELLENCE OF THE MYSTERIES
#### *instituted by Jesus Christ, through which his divinity is also most clearly revealed.*
#### CHAPTER XVIII.

<margin>See Dionysius on the ecclesiastical hierarchy, also on the celestial hierarchy. <note>Postel refers to the writings of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential 5th-century theologian who described the ranks of angels and the Church as a reflection of divine order.</note></margin>
To establish a certain faith in his power among mortals, Christ—having been raised in body and soul to heaven—promised gifts and, as it were, <term>treasures</term> <note>original: κειμήλια (*keimelia*), a Greek term for precious heirlooms or stored treasures.</note> to all his followers, which he provided ten days later. Not only were the disciples themselves adorned with these gifts, but they also passed them on to whomever they wished, rendering those people endowed with the exact same faculty as those who had first received them. This is the grace of the Holy Spirit, which taught various languages, granted power over all kinds of diseases of both soul and body, and established the sacred orders through which the sacred mysteries [sacraments] would be handed down in succession, confirming the faith already received. Through those sacred mysteries we perceive that, although Jesus dwells bodily in heaven, he nevertheless moves among us in such a way that he is never absent. For just as it is not enough for Nature, by God’s favor, to have produced all living and sentient things unless she also preserves and cares for what has been produced until they reach the end of their lives—otherwise it would be better not to have produced them at all—so too was it not enough for Jesus Christ to have sent out his disciples well-formed and armed against the arts of the devil, unless he also daily refreshed, strengthened, and vitalized their strength with heavenly nourishment. For such is the weakness of our nature that we would immediately fall away from the most excellent heights unless we were continually helped by divine power. Those who have been imbued with these sacred mysteries and have received from Jesus the power to confer them upon others are divided into a threefold distinction: Bishops, priests, and ministers. These men confer sacred gifts upon all those of lower rank. The <term>Pontiff</term> <note>Here referring to the Bishop.</note> holds the place closest to God and perfects the priest and the ministers, while the priest perfects those below him. Indeed, such great power has always been seen in that highest order—even if the man himself does not live up to the dignity of the office—that all separate powers yield to him, and divine powers assent when he performs the duties of his order. For demons are very frequently cast out of possessed bodies by men whose lives are not sufficiently praiseworthy; from this it is clear that this is done not by the man, but by the divinity present in the office. The sacred order of bishops and priests receives those approaching Christ with the holy washing [Baptism]; the bishop alone imposes hands and confirms the faith received. He imposes penance on those who have fallen and confess their errors; through the holy mystical body of Christ they are led back into the unity of the Church. <margin>Miracles of the Eucharist</margin> In this [the Eucharist], the divine power is so present that many in the beginning of the nascent Church who partook with "unwashed hands," as the saying goes, perished immediately; others were seized by the gravest diseases, and not a few...

For many others, as a proof of their faith, what appeared to be bread to some was truly flesh to them. Even today, one possessed by a demon is forced to prostrate before the sacred <term>synaxis</term> <note>original: "sacram synaxim" - a Greek term for the gathering of the faithful or the Eucharist itself</note> and acknowledge Christ. Finally, those about to die are anointed, and those who are to live together are bound by a sacrament; thus, our entire life returns daily into grace with Him through Christ’s frequent remedies, provided that repentance accompanies our past life. 

What you might admire even more is that the princes of many nations, from the time they received Christ (even though they received their anointing for the administration of a kingdom, not for holy orders), are celebrated for unheard-of miracles. This is not achieved through pagan arts, as the <term>Marsi and Psylli</term> <note>Ancient tribes famous in Roman literature for their supposed immunity to snake venom and power over serpents.</note> acted against serpents, but through their sovereign dignity. The Kings of France cure countless thousands of people of the <term>scrofulous disease</term> <note>Also known as "The King's Evil" (tuberculosis of the neck), which medieval and early modern kings were believed to heal by touch.</note> merely by touch and by invoking the name of Christ. The Kings of Britain were accustomed to healing the "falling sickness" <note>Epilepsy.</note> even from a distance by the giving of rings. The Roman Emperor holds a similar privilege, which I understand many others have also been accustomed to use. From this, it is clear that what Christ, the Truth itself, said is most true: *I am with you even unto the end of the age.* For in actual fact, He confirms this daily even now.

<margin>
The gift of Christ’s healing is bestowed upon whomever [He chooses].
</margin>

# THAT NO ONE HAS ATTAINED, OR CAN
-> attain happiness, unless the Gospel’s precept is observed. <-
### CHAPTER XIX.

When we speak of happiness, I believe it must be understood that I do not mean the kind perceived through bodily pleasures, nor that which is sought from chance circumstances outside our power, nor that which relies on the pursuit of glory and popular favor, nor that which <term>Epicurus</term> <note>The Greek philosopher who defined the highest good as "ataraxia" (freedom from fear and pain).</note> places in the absence of pain; for none of these can be pure. True and divine happiness is, of necessity, free from evil and misery. For if you measure happiness by the use of the body, you cannot attain it, because everything that affects the bodily senses is tempered with the greatest distress. For beyond the troubles of acquiring such things, they become cheap through constant use, turn into loathing, and wound our desires, because the capacity to enjoy is overtaken by the will. 

Suppose you have placed your highest good in the matters of Venus <note>Sexual love or lust.</note>: if the capacity is there, the body is undermined, strength is exhausted, nature is worn out, and pleasure turns bitter. If the opportunity is lacking, you burn entirely, you itch all over, all because of that one vice—because you have welcomed a cruel tyrant into your friendship. Or gorge yourself on delicacies of every kind: what else do you do but hasten disease? You may drench yourself in perfumes, but unless you change them daily, they no longer affect the sense; they become common through constant use, and all things long desired eventually wear out. Therefore, that cannot be happiness. 

Now, if you hold those things which are not within your power to be happiness, what else are you doing but killing yourself with a perpetual vow of greed? For those things help you, as <term>Horace</term> says, *as a painted panel helps a man with sore eyes, or a warm wrap helps the gout.* <note>original: "ut lippum pictæ tabulę, fomenta podagram" - from Horace’s Epistles 1.2.52, suggesting that luxuries are useless to those who are "spiritually ill."</note> For whether you desire or fear, what does it matter? If, whatever you see, you are either better or worse than your hope, do you not grow numb in eyes, mind, and body? You must do and suffer many things you do not want, and few things that please you, if you must depend on the necessity of fortune. 

"But glory nourishes me," you say. What an extraordinary reward for immense labors: a tiny rumor started by a few rustics or ignorant people. If you do not live up to it, it is a disgrace; if you earn the votes of the many, you acquire envy rather than praise. How many do you see who are more famous for their crimes and villainies than for their virtues? How often do rewards follow deeds? For it is placed outside of ourselves, what others judge of us. If they are well-disposed, you do not need their praise; if they are ill-disposed, they will belittle your deeds with slanders or bury them with silence. If they are strangers, what is their opinion to you? Since they cannot report back to you, they will praise the deeds, but will not know the author. Suppose you could earn praise from everyone: what does it contribute? If you are absent, will you [be nourished by it?]

->### ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD<-

...[you] enjoy? <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing a verb from the previous page.</note> Even if it helps: how long will fame endure, when even the passage of a single year buries the most illustrious deeds? In the meantime, consider at what cost you pursue it. You must abandon yourself entirely, and you are entirely deprived of your most holy liberty. You are clothed in another’s desire, not your own; you must serve the eyes, ears, and palate of others, and experience the servitude of all for the sake of the greatest vanity.

Come now, whoever seeks true pleasure, set before yourself **Osiris**, **Alexander**, **Caesar**, **Xerxes**, **Hannibal**, and whatever other greater monsters this mortality has produced; how does fame help them now? Where is their posterity? Where are their illustrious deeds? And meanwhile, as they ascribed to themselves glory, fame, and honor—which belong to God alone—what did they not suffer? What disaster did they not bring upon the world? You cannot be greater than they were; and yet they are nothing. If you propose to yourself a life free from pain <term>indolentiam</term> <note>Postel uses the Latin term "indolentia" to mean a state of being undisturbed by pain or passion, a concept borrowed from Stoic and Epicurean philosophy.</note> in this life, you will never be able to achieve it. Nevertheless, however false those names for happiness may be, there must be something true in the nature of things, of which those are but shadows and dreams. Since the nature of the mind <term>animi</term> <note>The Latin "animus" refers to the rational mind or soul, distinguished from "anima," the life-force.</note> survives us (for whatever things are considered "good" must belong either to the mind, the body, or to fortune), it is necessary to place true happiness in that mind. Happiness, therefore, is the action of a mind acting freely—namely, the contemplation of its own God and of nature, and the looking down upon great things that are subject to fortune. Whoever, therefore, is oppressed by any desire placed outside of our own judgment, and outside of what is just and honest, cannot be happy. Certainly, no will can be free unless it has the power to match its desire. For whoever wants what he cannot do is oppressed: he who is oppressed serves as a slave. What then should be done? If the desire should not precede our ability, must we become sluggish? Should nothing be hoped for? We must not be sluggish. Those things that are placed within our power are to be hoped for. Thus, every effort must proceed from us in such a way that, in external matters, an entirely contrary outcome is expected. If a matter turns out prosperously, let it be more pleasant for being unhoped for; if adverse, let it not crush us, as if it had been foreseen long before. Let us be after the manner of our **Paul**, *as having everything, yet truly possessing nothing*, <note>original: "tanquam omnia habentes, nihil vero possidentes" - a reference to 2 Corinthians 6:10.</note> or vice versa. Since, therefore, no action can be held or performed without a goal, and a certain goal cannot be sought from uncertain things, it is necessary that the end be proposed elsewhere. For a cause acts for the sake of an end, whatever it does out of deliberation. God, therefore, the neighbor as another man, and the actor himself, are the end and goal of human action. For a truly free man does all things either for the sake of divine honor, or for the sake of the utility and salvation of his neighbor, or by reason of preserving innocence within himself. Furthermore, he is accustomed to always follow what reason persuades, and never to assent to lusts.

In truth, whoever lives in this way (if any man ever could), if divine inspiration does this for anyone, he is a **Christian**. For whoever knew that Wisdom of the Father <note>original: "sapientia Patris" - a traditional title for Jesus Christ.</note> before He came among men, and had glorified it as God, was saved by His mercy; just as it must still be held and hoped for those who have not yet heard of Christ.

But he who knows Him, however justly he may live, unless he believes that he will achieve salvation through Him, is altogether lost: since those who act well out of a love for what is just, also ascribe their justice to God, without whom they can do nothing.

It cannot be, therefore, that he who depends on human affairs is ever happy. For he does not act happily who is deprived of his desire. But to be deprived of God never happens, except to one who is willing.

Therefore, whatever we do, if we do it for His praise and honor as if for a common father, it is certain that we act happily; and we should not expect the vain and fleeting rewards of immense labors, but the most certain and immortal ones. We hope that we shall attain all these things in the wisdom of God, **Jesus Christ**, God and man, and we believe it more certainly than certainty itself. Since nothing in this dreg of mortality <note>original: "fece mortalitatis" - a common Renaissance metaphor for the physical world or the corruption of earthly life.</note> is worthy of virtue—than which nothing is greater—virtue can be gifted with no other reward for its merits than God and immortality. Therefore, we must discuss the immortality of souls.

### WILLIAM POSTEL’S BOOK I ON THE IMMORTALITY OF SOULS, PROOFS. CHAPTER XX.

k 2
<meta>catchword: professor.</meta>

<margin>1. Reasoning from the final purpose. <note>original: "Ratio á fine"</note></margin>
That all things are led by a desire for the good, that there are various kinds of goods, and that there exists in the nature of things a certain highest and entirely blessed state in which the pinnacle of happiness is placed—this is a truth proven both by the consensus of all philosophers and the decrees of true religion, and it is confirmed throughout this entire work.

For since every agent <term>agens</term> <note>In the philosophical language of the time, an "agent" is anything that performs an action or causes a change.</note> (excepting those acting by mere chance), whether natural or artificial, acts for the sake of an end or purpose, it is manifest that the Highest Agent—than whom none more excellent can be granted—also acts for the sake of the most excellent purpose. Therefore, although there may be various acts, and intermediate or inferior ends established by Him, it is clear that they all strive toward the highest end and become, as it were, appendages to it; even if they are not present in that highest end itself, it is enough that they preceded the work as instruments.

The goal of the **First Agent** and the highest happiness are clearly one and the same.

For the highest good of any action exists first in the mind. And since the "end" is the final cause to be realized, it must also be the first thing in the soul's intention. But that which was first in the mind of the Creator was the final purpose, and that purpose was immortal and most like unto Himself; from this it is established that the highest good is immortality.

Furthermore, since whatever exists in this inferior world, subject to the senses, has been prepared for the use of man as if for its best purpose, it is necessary that man—as the most excellent part of this lower world—should attain a purpose worthy of himself and most excellent, both in this life and the life to come: here, virtue, than which nothing better can be given; there, immortality, than which nothing greater can be granted. Truly, we see that some men do partially attain that second-to-last end <note>meaning virtue in this life</note>; but as for the ultimate end, since men do not yet attain the highest good while in the body, it must be that they attain it as immortal souls.

Therefore, it is necessary to posit and believe in the immortal nature of souls. Otherwise, nothing would have been made for the sake of a purpose, unless that which is most excellent also possessed a final purpose.

But some impious person, a **Lucretian** philosopher <note>A follower of the Roman poet Lucretius, who argued for a materialist world where the soul dies with the body.</note>, will object: "Virtue itself is the end, bringing its own reward to itself." Ha! You there, listen closely: you are providing me with the very weapons with which I shall pierce you. Virtue consists in action.

You must admit this, or you shall become a mere stone. I proceed.

Every action, however, is a certain kind of motion. Moreover, every motion naturally tends toward rest, as if toward its final purpose. Therefore, since virtue never rests (but is always active), it cannot be its own purpose or reward.

From this it follows—against you and that lost **Satan** who introduced this idea to remove God as the ultimate purpose from the minds of men—that an eternal and highest end, namely good and rest, is necessarily owed to the action of virtue.

For you will not deny that the highest things are made for the sake of the highest purpose, unless you wish to strip yourself of your humanity.

Nothing, truly, is prior to virtue. Therefore, no reward greater than it can even be imagined.

And just as no one has yet, by himself, carried the full circle of all virtues within the body due to the magnitude of the task, so too has no one been able to comprehend the reward of virtue in the mind due to its excellence.

Truly, I shall not depart from this place before I reveal the arts of that foul demon, which he uses to fascinate men—even those of the highest reputation. These effects will betray their author. Since that most excellent plague <note>Postel refers to the Devil as a "most excellent plague" to acknowledge his high but corrupted intelligence.</note> had perceived through his intellect that the study, love, and admiration of virtue had been implanted by divine providence in the souls of every individual, and since he realized he could not uproot such a seedbed from the soil of the Creator, he approached from another direction and crept into the citadel through tunnels. He offered a fraud covered in the mask of integrity, a poisoned cake smeared with honey: he began to praise virtue, to extol it to the heavens, and to babble of nothing else. He affirmed it to be so great that it should be believed to be, in truth, the supreme good. Thus, while he praises the skill of archery, he removes the **target** <note>original: "album," the white bullseye of a target.</note>; meanwhile, the man does not notice—having been won over by the goodwill and insinuation of the scoundrel—that he is merely beating the air and gains not a shred of progress.

For it happens that he who, without a target, has done nothing but shoot arrows throughout his entire life, is on the last day of his life just as unskilled in that art as he was on the first day he claimed to be its **professor**.

<summary>Postel argues that human virtue is a form of motion that must naturally lead to a final "end" of rest and immortality in God. He critiques the Epicurean view that virtue is its own reward, calling it a demonic deception that removes the ultimate "target" of human existence.</summary>

### BOOK I, PAGE 112

...professor. Indeed, lest this reasoning should seem to carry too little weight, [the Adversary] has armed men of singular biting wit with these weapons—arguments which, disguised by the strength of eloquence and a display of words, might lie hidden from men. Pyrrho of Elis <note>The founder of Greek Skepticism</note>, Sextus Empiricus, Epicurus, Democritus, and their followers (and whatever such pests Greece produced, as it produced very many): and among the many who held these views among the Romans, Pliny and Lucretius dared to set them down in writing. To these very men, as if to gods, not a few courtiers and the "half-learned" <term>scioli</term> <note>Literally "know-it-alls" or those with superficial knowledge</note> of our own time subscribe today. They desire nothing more in their prayers than to draw many others into their own opinion, despising the authority, reason, and judgment of the whole world.

Thence it has happened that **fortitude of mind**—which was given to endure the accidents of fortune and to moderate the necessities of nature—has been turned into the ruin of nature itself. To overturn as many cities as possible, to kill myriads of men, to provoke everyone, to yield to no one, and to willfully seek out, summon, and love excuses for inflicting injury: these are the deeds of a counterfeit virtue <note>original: "suppositæ uirtutis"</note>. 

Meanwhile, that "excellent athlete of fortitude," who knows not how to suffer anything from anyone, and who would rather die (as he says) than serve another, feeds and bears at home as many tyrants as he has desires. A mistress, money, food, drink, clothing, and honor drive him up and down; whatever can happen to a man becomes a plague, a tyrant, and a master to a diseased soul. Yet the wretched man, tossed about so miserably, does not realize that a trick has been played on him. He does not feel the blows because he has rotted away with ulcers; his foul flesh has lost all sensation, nor does it feel anything other than the fact that it is flesh—if indeed it even feels that. O wretchedly baited and depraved man, whose very knowledge is his condemnation, unless he receives from the Creator that sense, motion, and life which was entirely lost.

**Friendship** tending toward God used to cherish all those seen to be needy and destitute. The "friendship of the world," however, is to rush into crime, to steal, to deceive, and to leave nothing unattempted so that wealth may be prepared from anywhere—all out of love for oneself, one's children, and one's kin. They do this because they claim "preparing wealth is a virtue," and because "virtue is its own reward," for whoever provides for himself in this way denies that God exists.

**Charity of God** <note>original: "Charitas Dei"</note> means being in the place of a father to one's brothers; but our charity is to look out for our own relatives, friends, and ourselves, while overturning justice. **Piety toward God** is to worship, love, revere, and fear Him from the soul; our piety is to lie about our faith in God with words, signs, and pretense, carrying "a fox within a clever breast" <note>A classical idiom meaning to hide a cunning or deceitful heart behind a fair face</note>, because virtue is believed to be its own reward and God is denied.

In sum, that famous commendation of virtue—so notable that it is believed the greatest of things—has caused man, lacking a goal, to never be able to aim at the mark. The mark is not truly removed, but it has been taken from our eyes, with illusions placed before us so that we cannot see it. This plague certainly cannot proceed entirely from a soul corrupted by its commerce with a foul body; for by his own judgment, a man would not condemn himself if he were entirely evil. Therefore, it is necessary that Satan claims the largest part for himself.

**Virtue**, therefore, is **not its own reward**. For in the entire nature of things, nothing would be unhappier or more miserable than man himself if his greatest labor and most difficult work were his only reward. It would surely have been better if God had placed man—whom He made the highest thing in the whole world after the heavenly beings—at the very bottom in the order of stones, rather than gifting him with such a "reward" in which he would be tortured until his very last breath with no future state to follow. 

But they reply: "Virtue has a reward outside itself. For we do not say simply that it is its own reward; it has praise, honor, fame, and celebrity." 

O "worthy" rewards! That a thing surpassing all worldly matters should be compensated by the lowest things and a breeze lighter than air (if it even reaches the man). O excellent judgments! O remarkable estimation of things! 

It remains, therefore, that the virtue which consists in the true worship of God, in supreme charity toward one's neighbor, and in one's own supreme innocence and equity—since it is the summit of all human actions—must also be adorned with the greatest reward in all of nature. And since that virtue proceeds primarily from the soul, and not from the body (which is dragged along unwillingly), that soul must be **immortal**. And just as in stirring up the power of virtue (if there was need for action)...

He denounces the corruption of fortitude and piety into self-serving vices disguised as noble traits.</summary>

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I
### PAGE 113

...the soul existed before the body) it preceded the body by many intervals; so it is necessary in receiving a reward that it should precede, until the Creator restores the body to it for a common reward or punishment. But against these things the courtiers will reply (I do not attack the good ones) — I meant to say the impious: Why then did God give such a thirst for glory, such a greed for praise and honor, and such a zeal for acquiring fame? I answer in a few words: Because by its own nature, the human soul is ignorant and unskilled in all things; before it knew the world, it would never be animated toward great things unless it were pricked and excited by certain stings. 

<margin>2. From the cause of virtue.</margin> 

The soul, detained in the foul prison of the body, would not approach the conduct of affairs, of which it is ignorant. **As kind teachers give little cookies to boys, so that they might wish to learn their first elements** <note>Postel is quoting the Roman poet Horace: "pueris dant crustula blandi doctores." It is a classic metaphor for using small rewards to encourage learning.</note>; so God incites us with those little rewards, not so that those "cookies" should forever be the rewards of letters and doctrines, but so that, excited by them, we might pursue the virtue of equity out of love, and pursue letters for their own sake and out of zeal for the teacher, and carry out our father’s commands so that we may please him. Lest there be any cause of ignorance for us, or any pretext for laziness, God rouses us from sleep with those little rewards; not so that, as adults, we should act out of a desire for a prize or fear of punishment, but so that we might perform His commands out of the highest love for Him. 

Whatever things are natural must be consistent and endure. But because God is eternal, immense, and the best, therefore praise is fitting for Him alone, not for fragile and mortal man. **Therefore, leaving the walnuts behind** <note>A Latin idiom meaning "leaving childhood behind," as walnuts were used by Roman children for games, similar to marbles.</note>, we must come to serious matters. We must not always act as if in childhood. What we began to do when invited by a prize from an unknown Giver must finally be cared for diligently—not so that we take account of the reward, but so that we strive to prove ourselves to the Giver and the Arbiter of victory. Those rewards, such as fame, honor, and celebrity, follow the unwilling and flee the one who chases them. No one descends into the arena for the sake of a prize unless he has earned the voices and votes of the judges; for otherwise, he could attain more things with far less expense. No one contending in a contest would not prefer the votes of the arbiters to any prizes whatsoever. It can happen that he who is led by a prize relies on corruption. He who is approved by the judgment of all, and especially by the Giver, has obtained the fullest victory. Those things which we desire but neglect will come to us of their own accord if we study to prove ourselves to the supreme Arbiter of nature. 

We know this by these arguments: for since the Father of Truth must be revealed among mortals, if anything has been approved by a lighter judgment, no matter how the victor has hunted for prizes, the trickery will gradually reveal itself, and the hidden truth will emerge. That noble "father of the gods," **Jupiter**, teaches this by his adulteries; although he had begged for divinity at first glance through the voices of the common people, yet the lapse of time testified that even among his own worshippers he had committed one hundred and twenty adulteries. Finally, he appeared to posterity as a parricide, a fratricide, a robber, and most celebrated by every title of infamy. I do not touch upon the others, since the judgment is the same for those of lower rank, and the descendants are worthy of that father. 

But who would not admire our own people—abject men, hated by all evils, like the refuse of the world—who preferred to die rather than ascribe even the smallest bit of praise to themselves? Thus they seem to have ascended into heaven with favors they did not seek, and to have opened the eternal happiness of blessed souls with eternal fame, so that they flourish with praise that will never die. What is the cause? Honors were despised and trampled upon so that solid and true honor—namely, divine honor—might appear to men. They wished to bestow benefits on all, and to bring evil upon no one, not even those who had harmed them. By constant testimonies even after death, they provided an argument for the divinity joined to them. For at the tombs and memorials of the martyrs, innumerable and unheard-of kinds of miracles have been performed. Glory follows the unwilling; infamy marks a falsely sought fame. To the latter, their shames have joined praise to happiness; to the former, their splendor has degenerated into eternal punishment and infamy. 

But having refuted these vain opinions, it has now been sufficiently demonstrated by two very strong arguments that souls are necessarily immortal: namely, by the reasoning of the **End** <term>Final Cause</term>, and of the whole order, and from the **Cause of Virtue**. Therefore, we must pass on to other matters.

<margin>3. From the nature of the human mind.</margin>
3. The nature of the soul, the intellect, the reason, or the human mind—for it is well-established that a philosopher should not argue over words as long as the underlying realities are understood—would reveal its own immortality from its very substance, even if it were not proven from any other source. I believe that no one relying on their sense of reason can doubt that there is a certain power in human nature that other types of living creatures lack—except for Pomponazzi <note>original: "Pomponatium." Pietro Pomponazzi (1462–1525) was a controversial Italian philosopher who argued that the immortality of the soul could not be proven by reason, only by faith.</note> and his followers. It is certain that this can be argued through many proofs, drawn both from authority and from reason. Truly, I shall place the authorities of Aristotle, the prince of philosophers, in the first position—both for the sake of asserting the truth and for refuting and exposing the vanity and impiety of that man. Thus, it is written in the first book of *On the Soul*: **The intellect, however, seems to be a certain substance, and it is not corrupted.** <note>original: "Intellectus autem videtur esse substantia quaedam, & non corrumpi." Aristotle, *De Anima*, Book I.</note> For it would be corrupted primarily by the decay of old age. The philosopher left us to conclude that, since the intellect flourishes most when the body is decaying, it must be of a different nature than the body. He adds a little later: **Indeed, understanding and contemplation are sometimes dulled when something else inside the body is corrupted (as in illness and drunkenness), but the intellect itself is free from passions.** <note>The term "passions" here refers to "passio" or being acted upon/undergoing change, rather than just emotions.</note> Reasoning, loving, and hating are not its own affections, but belong to that which possesses it—that is, the animated body, insofar as it possesses the intellect. Therefore, when this body or composite is corrupted, the intellect neither remembers nor loves. For those things did not belong to it, but to the whole composite. But the mind or intellect is something more divine and free from passions; therefore, it is not moved. In that passage, he argues against the definition of Plato, who defines the soul as moving itself. For if it were moved, it would be acted upon. It is clearly evident that, in his opinion, our immortal intellect, soul, or mind is of a different nature from bodies and is immortal. As for the fact that it is not moved, it differs in this way from the soul that gives form to the body. For "to be moved" happens to it only by accident. Furthermore, we feel within ourselves that the intellect is not moved into action [through physical motion], since we can revolve any notions and reasons of things in the mind in an instant. This is just as light rays act instantly on every part of their power without local movement, or as the eye conceives the images of things in an instant. These three things are most substantial, and yet they are not bodies.

Truly, in the second book of the same treatise, the same Philosopher, after the partition of the nature of living things into the nutritive, the sensitive, the intellective, and the motive, adds: **Concerning the mind and the contemplative faculty, it is not yet clear. For it seems to be another genus of soul, which alone is separated, just as the eternal is from the corruptible.** <note>Aristotle, *De Anima*, Book II, 413b.</note> There, all the interpreters agree—even Averroes <note>original: "Aben reis," a Latinization of Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), the influential Andalusian Muslim philosopher known as "The Commentator" on Aristotle.</note>—that this nature of the soul is superior, more noble, and entirely immortal. And yet that "good" man, Pomponazzi (if it please the gods!), in order to pervert that sentence by which he was being strangled, tries to anticipate the mind of the author by reading it as a question. O Italy, you even nourish such monsters of men, who are not satisfied with being impious themselves unless they also serve their poison to everyone else! With this destruction, they penetrate into the courts of princes, and there they promise impunity for crimes where those crimes are daily practiced in their works. A little later, at the end of the fourth chapter of the same book, as the Latin scholars note, he says: **Wherever there is reasoning, all the lower functions must also be present, but not the other way around. However, there is another rule regarding the intellect or the contemplative mind.** From these words, Averroes and the other interpreters infer that it is a more divine genus, and least of all subject to matter and corruption. There are many other authorities in Aristotle, but these are sufficient. Plato, Cicero, and men of the better schools of thought <note>original: "melioris haereseos." Here "heresy" is used in the classical sense of a philosophical sect or "choice of life."</note> wished to persuade us of nothing else than that souls are immortal. In this they disagree: for some posit that they are entirely free from passions, as Aristotle and Averroes seem to want; others hold that they have an aptitude for the bodies in which they lived and a memory of things done in them—which are the views of Plato and our own, and they are the truest. Otherwise, many absurdities would follow: that souls are a part of God; that there is only one soul for all; and that there is neither justice nor injustice...

He fiercely critiques the skeptic Pomponazzi for distorting these classical texts and warns that denying individual immortality leads to moral and theological ruin.</summary>
