# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK I.
### PAGE 115

...to be: neither that there are punishments in the future, nor rewards. All of these ideas conflict with the reason and goodness of the Creator. It should be enough to have turned that nature, sought from Aristotle, against such impious men. But the quality of the soul must be sought from elsewhere. For Aristotle said it was not sufficiently understood by him, except to say that it exists and is unlike lower things.

<margin>From the nature of substance.</margin>
4. Regarding the nature of substance, one can argue as follows: Whatever things participate in the same principles and have all their matter in common, those things ought also to agree in their composite form. For example: All things produced from the four elements have—according to their kinds—being, living, and sensing in common. Whatever possesses the first possesses all that follows in turn, and so on through the third and fourth levels. For it is certain that those things in which they agree arose from the same principles. But since in man there is the faculty of contemplating, collecting thoughts, and remembering, it must be held as more certain than certainty itself that this power depends on something other than the elements. For if that force were found in the elementary nature or the harmonious composition of the body, it would surely be seen in lower creatures as well, proportionate to their rank, or at least by some slight sign. Yet there is no such thing in lower creatures. Therefore, the intellect does not come from lower matter. It remains, then, that it comes from the highest. But all things above the moon are eternal; therefore the mind also is immortal. Truly, I had already gathered these points against Galen <note>original: "Galenum." Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD) was a Greek physician and philosopher whose views on the soul's dependence on the body's temperament were often debated.</note>. Lest he should say that minds arose divinely—and thus make it seem that God performs the labor of creating every single day—Aristotle did not trace them all the way back to heaven. Instead, he taught that they glide down into lower things from a fifth element, which they call <term>entelechy</term> <note>original: "entelechiam." A term Postel uses here to refer to the soul as a non-material "actuality" or "form" that gives life to the body.</note>. It is enough to have gained this admission from him. For Aristotle hardly admitted spiritual things and separate substances, except insofar as he knew them almost through the physical senses. Certainly, the mind must be held to have a supreme origin. And since that origin is eternal from this point forward, it follows that minds must also be immortal.

<margin>From the equity and justice of God.</margin>
5. Furthermore, since supreme equity and justice must necessarily be admitted to exist in God (for unless He were just and good, He would not be God), He must also have a subject for Himself upon whom to exercise that power. For it is necessary both to possess justice and to exercise it. Otherwise, that which is never in action exists in vain. Justice, truly, is spoken of in respect to error and sin. For if there were no sinning, there would be nothing to judge. Only those things that possess the power of choice can sin. For those things that do not act against the judgment of reason or sense do not sin. Therefore, only the demon <note>Postel refers here to fallen spiritual beings or the devil.</note> and man are capable of committing sin. For only God, the demon, and man possess choice <note>original: "arbitrium," referring to free will or the capacity for moral decision-making.</note>. The demon sinned once, so that he might be damned; but men sin daily. Therefore, it is the work of a most just action that they be punished and also gifted with a reward. But since our bodies rot away here on earth, no punishment can be inflicted upon them after death. It remains, then, that the mind survives, in which God may exercise the action of His justice. For if men did not undergo punishment and reward, God would undoubtedly be wicked—a God who would grant such impunity for crimes to the impious, to robbers, tyrants, assassins, and those infected with every stain of wickedness. He would be cherishing them in the course of this present life with such prosperity that they would be all the happier the more they were destructive to nature. This line of reasoning (because God seems to them to be either non-existent or to neglect human affairs) drives many to rush into crime with loose reins. But one must conclude at this point: either the world made itself without an author, or the mind is immortal. Yet it is clear that God is the author of the world. Therefore, He takes vengeance on the impious. For if the mind is mortal, God does not exist. For he who posits an unjust God effectively removes Him entirely. If He punishes, some <term>pretender to philosophy</term> <note>original: "philosophaster." A derogatory term for a superficial or false philosopher.</note> will say, then He is moved by passions. I will respond with a comparison, showing how even a human can take punishment without being moved by emotion. Imagine a master of a house presiding over a vast family, who has spoken his laws to them thus: "whoever moves into such or such a place, unless he repents, let him perish." Can not all those in that assembly, in the presence of the master, transgress and plunge themselves into ruin and the abyss, even without any change in the master's mind? For it is so established by eternal law, and there is no need for a new decree to be made.

How much easier are these things for the highest good? For whoever exempts himself from divine laws binds himself to the perverse power of demons. Indeed, they are the torturers of those whom they lure to themselves with flatteries. God certainly did not create them as evil, nor in this state at the beginning, so that no injustice would be done to anyone. Yet He knew it would come to pass that there would be no lack of <note>original: "sannæ & nebulones"</note> buffoons and scoundrels: by whose labor the wicked spirits of men would pay their penalties. Just as it is now among men, even if no injustice is intended, there are nonetheless never lacking those depraved individuals who bring ruin to others; God does not procure or incite this, but permits it. This is because He placed man, as the Wise Man says, <note>A reference to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 15:14, a common proof-text for free will in the Renaissance.</note> in the hand of his own counsel, and He wishes no force to be applied to our free will. For he who does good unwillingly, and does not acquire the habit of acting from the soul, is just as bad as a wicked man. Therefore, God exacts punishment from the wicked, yet He is not moved by passions in doing so. Furthermore, the souls upon whom justice is exercised are immortal. For otherwise God, who is <term>pure act<note>The philosophical concept that God is fully realized being without potential for change or non-existence.</note></term>, would act in potentiality only according to justice; which is not to be granted.

<margin>From the reasoning of the nature of the universe.</margin>
6. The Philosopher <note>Aristotle, often cited simply as "the Philosopher" in Scholastic writing.</note> says: "that because of which each thing is such, is itself more such"—it is understood. Whether the world is posited as eternal or temporary, since it was made for the sake of man, God, the most wise author of both, must give the greatest duration—indeed, eternity—to man, for whose sake the world is either eternal or of the greatest duration. For since the world and the things within it have their duration for the sake of man, it is necessary that man be "most such" in that regard, that is, most durable. But the greatest durability is eternity. It is necessary, therefore, both that the souls of men be eternal, and also that they eventually receive their bodies back, so that the whole man, lasting forever in eternal happiness, may make use of an eternal and purified world. Therefore the soul is eternal, lest the end be inferior to those things which exist for the sake of that end, and lest that thing be "less such" for whose sake all other things are "more such."

<margin>From the wisdom of God.</margin>
7. In a similar way, the eternity of souls is proven by this reasoning. For a wise person orders a good toward a good, and the best toward the best. God ordered all the goods of the world toward a good, that is, toward the end of man; but the best thing, that is, man—the most excellent part of the corruptible world—He established for the best thing, which is eternal happiness, than which nothing better can be imagined. Therefore it follows that souls are eternal, so that by lasting forever, they may attain the best end. For otherwise God would be accused of the greatest imprudence, having made that which is most excellent so vanishing that it would be the most degraded and miserable of all living creatures—namely, man.

<margin>From the omnipotence, goodness, and will of God.</margin>
8. The omnipotent goodness of God wills that those things which are most excellent should have the greatest participation in the highest good. For just as a good is more divine the more common it is: so one endowed with the greatest good has no higher priority than to communicate his good as much as possible to capable natures. Earthly princes and magnates and the wealthy show off their masks <note>likely referring to their outward displays of status or "personas"</note> not by sharing, but by hunting for glory and empty air from the admiration of fools. God, however, communicates not masks, but Himself, most powerfully and eternally to human minds capable of the highest good. Therefore, after this life filled with miseries, He preserves eternal souls for Himself for eternal rewards, whether they be good or evil. Furthermore, He does not wish other things lower than man to be capable of that highest good; for they have their end in this: that they assist man by his use of them. But in eternity, when the soul shall rule over the bodies, the use of these things will not be necessary, as corruption will have ceased.

<margin>From the nature of sin.</margin>
9. We have said in the preceding sections, when we were treating the necessity of the divine incarnation, that a sin is more serious the greater the one against whom it is committed is held to be. This is clear enough. Hence, so that man might attain the end for which he was created (and which he had lost of his own accord), it was necessary for an infinite redeemer, greater than the world, the <term>theanthropon<note>From the Greek 'theanthropos,' meaning God-Man; referring to Christ.</note></term>, to satisfy the infinite sins of all and the infinite penalty of even a single sin. But since this miserable mortality daily heaps sins upon sins, an infinite offense...

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK 1
### PAGE 117

...offense that no one can wash away except through the death of Christ and faith in His mercy, it is necessary—according to the laws of divine justice—that the impious be afflicted with eternal punishments. Conversely, it is necessary that those upon whom God has had mercy, and who have striven to earn His favor through good works and prove themselves to Him, be blessed with eternal joys. This is so that the benefit performed for the sake of the infinite God may be followed by a joy that is both most just and granted by the highest goodness. This cannot happen unless the souls of men survive, who through their own free will were able to act well or poorly. Therefore, it follows necessarily—both because of the cause of God and the sin committed against Him, as well as because of His most severe justice—that the soul is immortal for either punishment or reward. Indeed, the wicked are justly punished, while infinite goodness comes to the aid of the good. Since His justice and mercy are eternal, the soul must also be eternal in the future, so that there is a subject in which these attributes may act forever, whether in punishing or in blessing.

<margin>From the properties of the divinity.</margin>
10 I think no one is so mad or impious as to be able to deny that eternity exists in God. Truly, whatever things are most perfect, since they exist in God in the most perfect way, are also co-eternal with the divinity. Therefore, not only are the primary attributes of the <term>Persons<note>Referring to the three persons of the Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note></term>—namely power, wisdom, love, will, or charity—destined to exist in God after the refined matter of this world has passed away, but also mercy and truth. Neither Plato, nor Aristotle, nor their followers would deny that God possesses compassion within Himself without any imperfect emotion. Since, therefore, those two properties are eternal, it is necessary that they act eternally upon some subject created from matter; for they cannot exist in vain. For this reason, it is necessary that the souls of men survive after death not only for a time (as I taught before) because of the scales of divine equity, but also that they endure forever. And not only those souls, but the **solid man** <note>Postel refers here to the "whole person," implying the eventual resurrection and union of body and soul.</note> as well, in whom both mercy and truth (or justice) may operate. Therefore, etc.

<margin>From the perfection of the universe.</margin>
11 The entire mass of nature consists of a certain harmonic and concordant perfection, as I said especially in the chapter on the Trinity. For all things consist of matter, form, and the composite of both. Therefore, whatever is found to have extremes must also have a "middle" that participates in both. Consequently, since it is established that there are <term>separate substances<note>In Scholastic philosophy, "separate substances" usually refers to angels or celestial intelligences—beings that have form but no physical matter.</note></term> which are eternal (though they are created) because they do not contain opposites within themselves nor this fluid and corruptible matter, it is necessary that there be some "middle" which is partly eternal by nature and partly corruptible. This is indeed human nature, which agrees with the <term>demons<note>In the classical sense: "daimons" or spirits, not necessarily evil ones.</note></term> in the immortality of the soul, and with the beasts in the body. Therefore, the most beautiful part of man, namely the soul, is immortal.

<margin>From the perfection of the soul.</margin>
12 Mortality or corruption occurs through motion and the power of the heavens acting by the command of the Creator. It therefore corrupts only those things upon which it can act. For a less noble thing does not act upon a more noble thing. Yet the heavens, although they possess "being" or (if one prefers) "living" as well, nevertheless differ greatly from the nobility of the soul, which is above sense and physical life. Hence, the soul cannot be subject to the actions of the heavens. Therefore it was said by the astronomers: *A wise man shall rule the stars.* <note>original: "Sapiens dominabitur astris." A popular medieval and Renaissance maxim suggesting that human reason and will are not bound by astrological influence.</note> Since, therefore, the soul neither has an opposite in its composition nor can be dissolved by the heavens, it must be eternal. These points are drawn from St. Jeremiah and Thomas Aquinas.

<margin>From the reasoning of its action.</margin>
13 Whatever is received into something is received according to the manner of that in which it resides. For example, the forms of things in the <term>possible intellect<note>A term from Aristotelian psychology referring to the capacity of the human mind to receive and become all things through knowledge.</note></term> are entirely intelligible, just as the intellect is immaterial. Since they are thus immaterial in act, they must be incorruptible; therefore, the intellect is as well. But since that possible intellect is a part of our soul, it is necessary that the soul be immortal at least to that extent. For the <term>agent intellect<note>The active power of the mind that "illuminates" sensory data to create universal concepts.</note></term> is the light of the soul.

<margin>From the mode of acting.</margin>
14 Nothing can be destroyed by that in which its perfection consists. For example, the perfection of fire is to act vehemently through heat or light. From this it follows that it cannot be destroyed by the action of heat and light. Thus, since the perfection of the soul in this life is its [contemplation?] from the body...

...withdrawal into contemplation (for it is perfected all the more as it considers through the sciences things that are immaterial and most distant from the body), it is necessary that when it is separated by death, it be most ready and immortal for contemplating and knowing. For, in this life, the companionship of the body seems to stand in its way.

<margin>From a comparison of power.</margin>
15 Everyone admits that the efficient cause is nobler than the effect. But the <term>potential intellect<note>Original: "intellectus possibilis." In Aristotelian philosophy, this is the part of the human mind that has the capacity to receive and understand abstract concepts.</note></term> makes things actually intelligible, which are by nature immaterial and eternal. Therefore, it follows that since the intellect is nobler than these things, it must be immortal. For insofar as they are intelligible, they are eternal; but the intellect itself, in which they exist as if in a subject, must be immortal to the greatest degree.

<margin>From the consideration of the soul’s substance.</margin>
16 Though some may wish—and it is granted to them—that our soul consists of matter and form because of the intellect and the will, this does not mean it is not incorruptible. For corruption does not exist where no "contrary" is found in the composition. <note>In ancient physics, things "corrupt" or break down because they are made of opposing elements (like hot and cold). Since the soul deals with abstract ideas that don't fight each other, Postel argues it cannot break down.</note> For generation and corruption proceed from contraries to contraries. Therefore, the heavens are not corrupted by nature because they lack the matter subject to corruption. In the soul, however, the notions of all things are conceived without contrariety, since by its own knowledge it makes the learning of them the same. Therefore, it follows that souls, surviving death, always remain vigorous.

<margin>From the difference between the soul and lower things.</margin>
17 The specific action or operation of a thing follows its specific nature. Furthermore, the soul’s own action is to understand and to will, which it shares with angels and blessed substances entirely devoid of bodies; and thus it acts more according to its nature the more it is removed from the body. For this reason, divinations, forewarnings, and prophecies happen either in dreams, or in ecstasy, or by a movement of the mind. Since understanding belongs to an eternal nature, souls must especially be such, and they must excel in understanding all the more as they are more withdrawn from bodily things. Hence it happens that no mortal fails to naturally admire those who exercise virtues most removed from the use of the body. For life is more perfect the more it is according to the intellect and the less it is according to the body. It is therefore clearly established that the nature of souls is eternal, having nothing in common with these lower things, and that it employs its functions more intensely the more it is led away from the nature of lower and material things through knowledge. You may refer these points to <term>Thomas<note>Likely referring to Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential medieval theologian.</note></term> and <term>Jeremiah the Sicilian<note>Original: "Hieremias Siculus." Likely referring to Girolamo Siculus, a 16th-century monk and scholar known to Postel.</note></term>.

<margin>From the supreme desire of the human soul.</margin>
18 It has already been demonstrated above that all men are naturally held by a desire for immortality and endurance. This could not happen at all unless the soul were able to achieve it—either by its own industry, or by another's, or partly both, in whatever way possible. For nature is not accustomed to stir up any movements in a species without it also being established within that species that a fulfillment should follow. Since man undergoes even the most difficult things for the sake of that end—as if for rest and the highest good—it is manifest that he looks toward immortality. Otherwise, it would follow that nature does something in vain, which must not be admitted. For if someone should say that this desire is born in some from pride, vanity, or the opinions of "great men," and that the lowest people are not held by such an expectation, the opposite will be clearly established by experience. For common people take up almost every vow and bind themselves by every religion so that they may enter into a kinship with God; yet they are moved by very little outside opinion. Indeed, the great men differ from them most in this: because they try to seize immortality in this life through images, noise, ostentation, pomp, and rare deeds, and attempt to cast God down from His own heaven. Those who almost never achieve it rightly do violence to themselves so that they may at least appear to have wished for it. The lowest, however, rely on hope and humility. Truly, all tend toward the same goal: while the former walk a royal path, the proud seek shortcuts through the twists and rough places of the road. The soul is therefore immortal, so that it may attain by the grace of Christ what nature taught it to desire. Truly, these things are more than enough. For whatever else could be added would be more of a burden than a benefit. From the justice of divine providence, then, from the nature of the soul, from the ends of things, from the reward of virtue, from the nature of action, from natural motion, and from the reason of the universe,

# THE BOOK OF GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.

...of the universe, based on the authority of all the most excellent philosophers and for the other reasons already stated, the soul is immortal. I have not thought it necessary to demonstrate that the universal judgment of all things must necessarily occur, because unless it were to come, God does not exist; and if God exists, it must come. For since He exists, He must be just. And if He is just, since nothing escapes Him, He will judge all people.

## ON THE RESURRECTION. CHAPTER 21.

Divine goodness was not satisfied merely to give essence to things, unless it also conferred "well-being"—and a kind of well-being than which no better can be given according to that species. This may be seen in all of nature below humanity. For all living creatures, which were provided for the use of man, because they achieve their end and highest happiness in him, therefore possess the summit of their happiness here in this world. This is most clearly evident from the fact that no sign could ever be taken from any living creature that it was held by any desire other than for this present life. From this it follows that when they have lived and brought utility to man, they have attained their end and highest good in all things. For nature would otherwise have given them some motion and appetite for greater things if they lacked anything further. Nature did not do so. Therefore, their well-being is simply life and sensation. 

If we begin with the admiration of the smallest of all living creatures, who would not be stunned—indeed, deprived of sense—rather than grasp that power by which they live, thus concentrated and brought from matter to form? Who does not see Providence present in all things? All things take care of themselves and their offspring. They know what they must avoid and what they must seek for the preservation of life. In short, they are weighed down by no troubles. For it is clear they are affected by the sensation of sadness and pleasure, but they do not think about being affected, nor do they recognize it. They certainly suffer everything, and with pain equal to human feelings; but truly it is not an "evil" for them, because they do not understand it to be evil. 

For although they flee harmful things, they do so spontaneously and by the guidance of their nature, not by thought and intellect. Otherwise, they would have gathered together and risen up in arms against the men who use and abuse their labor. And so they are slaughtered and killed in the middle of their flocks, with no knowledge of another's misfortune or their own. For they are not affected by a sense of past events, except as long as the object or its action is fresh. For they have memory, as we have said, but not recollection <note>Original: "reminiscentiam." In the philosophy of the time, memory is the passive storage of images, while recollection is the active, human ability to search through those images to find a specific past event.</note>, nor are they driven by any judgment of future things, unless the object is also imminent. 

In distinguishing all these things, the Creator wished them to have a far more certain and acute sense, and one seemingly far more perfect than in humans. For as much as God wished to make them heedless of the future or more forgetful of the past, so much more keen did He make them toward present things, so that they might be moved most sharply by present objects. Therefore a dog, who does not think he has an enemy when the enemy is absent (though an animal attacking almost all living things must have many enemies), if an adversary approaches the arena, he is so powerful in scent that he immediately betrays it with a bark and looks out for himself by strength or flight. 

They perceive things from the object presented, but they do not "recognize" them, nor do they weigh their nature. Moreover, though they all suffer bodily calamities, they do not judge themselves to be suffering. Thus they come closest to the "indolence" <note>Original: "indolentiam." Here referring to the Epicurean concept of *aponia*, or the total absence of physical pain and mental distress.</note> of Epicurus. Nor are they for that reason deprived of their happiness and highest good. They are therefore in their proper end and goal when they have lived, because they lived so that man might use them. For if man abuses them, they do not live or profit him at all, but rather he perishes—just as a man with dropsy <note>A condition of fluid swelling, now called edema.</note> is harmed by drink, a plethoric <note>Someone suffering from an excess of bodily fluids, like blood.</note> man by food, a learned show-off by his own arrogance, or a madman by a sword—the things themselves having no vice within them. 

Now, if anyone should look at how much industry the Creator wove into them and armed them against enemies and all dangers, who would not fail for wonder? He clothed all things with the hardest skin: these with hair, those with bristles, fleeces, or shaggy coats.

<summary>Postel argues that while animals possess superior physical senses and instinct, they lack the human intellect's ability to reflect on suffering or the past, achieving their "well-being" entirely within this life. This serves as a philosophical backdrop to his upcoming defense of human resurrection and divine justice.</summary>

Scales are given to fish, feathers and plumage to birds. He <note>Meaning the Creator</note> granted shells to snails, and sometimes fourfold bark to trees. Yet to man, who is destined to rule over all other living creatures, He conferred nothing but nakedness in all things and the greatest weakness. Who could deny that those other creatures have achieved an excellent end in this life, when they are more fortunate than the man set over them in at least this one respect: that they are not burdened by opinions? If no other life were to follow, the prince of all living beings would surely become the most miserable of all. I do not see what could be thought of as more absurd than this. For if those creatures were made for the sake of an end, then man, for whose sake they exist, must also achieve an end. Since they possess their "best state" <note>original: "optimum esse," a technical term for a thing reaching its highest potential or "well-being"</note> while they live for the benefit of man, it remains certain that man also, by the very nature of the Creator, must be destined to achieve a certain "best state." Otherwise, the "end" <note>The final purpose or goal (humanity)</note> would be in a worse condition than the things leading to that end <note>The resources of nature</note>, which is against all reason and the order of things.

2 Furthermore, as we have seen, the better a person is in this life, the more unhappy they are. Therefore, they do not possess their highest good here. For we have seen that they pursue this good through the soul, which is by far the most excellent part of man. However, since the well-being of a thing does not belong to a part alone, but to the whole, it is necessary that the solid body of the human being—which never experienced true well-being—be raised up, joined to the soul, and gifted with immortality. Therefore, there will eventually be a resurrection. This is also evident from divine equity <note>original: "aequitate," meaning fairness or justice</note>.

3 For since justice requires that souls be immortal so they may receive the rewards for how they handled their free will, and since they did not act well or poorly alone without the body consenting and carrying out the work, it is also entirely necessary that bodies be present with the souls at some time. The human being must be restored so that they may also receive what is proper to the body. For, as has been said, the soul is not the human being, nor is the body the human being, but the body joined together with the soul composes the human being. Therefore, it is necessary for the body to be raised from the earth and for the resurrection of the solid human being to occur at some point. Otherwise, one would have to admit that there is injustice in God—which is a sin even to imagine.

4 The logic of order also suggests the same. For it is characteristic of God’s wisdom to make all things perfectly ordered. Now, "form" <note>The soul</note> is ordered toward "matter" <note>The body</note>, just as matter is toward form. Furthermore, it has already been shown above that man was born for a happiness far greater than the human mind can conceive. Moreover, since it is clear that the nature of souls is eternal, it follows necessarily—for the sake of maintaining order in the universe—that the form designed for matter, and vice versa according to their suitability, be united once again. This allows them to share the reward of their common work. The very same body that was once joined to the soul (when the soul gave it life through a vital connection) must feel the rewards for its merits. Indeed, one must especially avoid the impiety—for it should not even be called a heresy—of those who claim that it is not the same body which exists now that will be raised, but a new one, not subject to corruption or deformity. By this claim, God is denied, for such injustice is attributed to Him that He would reward what did not labor; or else He is called so powerless that He cannot make this currently imperfect body perfect in all its parts at the resurrection. If you take away rewards for merits, you deny God. If you give them, but not based on merit, you do the same. Since actions belong to the whole person <note>original: "suppositorum," referring to the individual person as a whole entity</note>, not just a part, the rewards also pertain to the whole, not to a part—to the same being, not to a different one. It remains, therefore, to conclude that for the sake of order and divine decree, our same soul, restored again after its sleep, and that same body which exists now, brought back to the highest perfection and the fullness of the "age of Christ" <note>A reference to Ephesians 4:13, implying the resurrected will reach a perfected maturity modeled on Christ</note>, shall be joined together once again for good or evil rewards and live forever.

As demonstrated above, a person endowed with virtue is worthy of the most excellent reward. God cannot but will the most perfect things; yet dissolution <note>The breaking down of the body in death</note> is a greater imperfection than restoration. From this, it follows that He wills all things to be most perfect. Furthermore, no one should doubt that He is able to act just as He wills. For just as He brought together parts—which were known only to Himself before they were joined—into a composite whole, so too can He gather them again once they have been scattered. If we were to deny this power in God, He would appear more powerless than many craftsmen, who, by taking up the parts of a composition, restore many things. The difference here is that for God, the elements cannot perish; whereas for the craftsman, corruption <note>Decay or rust of materials</note> is an obstacle. Therefore, since He both wills it and is able, and since He is most excellent, it is necessary that the whole, solid man will exist eternally, and that the body be raised and reunited once more with the soul. Thus, the resurrection of the dead man shall come to pass.

<margin>Methodius also beautifully resolves this objection in his *Sermon on the Resurrection* found in the works of Epiphanius.</margin>

However, two slanders of the impious must be addressed here. For if God wills all things to be most excellent and immortal, they will say: "Therefore, an immortal ox would be better than a mortal one; thus, it too shall rise." I respond: God indeed wills all things which are made for an "end" <note>A final purpose or goal</note> and for the sake of God, for He is the beginning and the end. Therefore, whatever things contribute toward that end are necessary. But when the necessity ceases, the things themselves must cease. In this life, because of necessities and uses, all living animals were necessary for man; but since the resurrected man will not be subject to such necessity, he will have no need for other animals. For then, man shall neither drink nor eat, nor shall he procreate. Indeed, all transformation of matter will cease. Since God and nature do nothing in vain, and since there will then be no need for those animals, they will not exist in the nature of things. Man, however—the commander of lower things, created for the sake of praising, knowing, and loving God because of the created world—will be the only one necessary from the lower order of things, being abundantly happy in the knowledge of God without any use of corruptible things.

Another objection is this: "It is impossible, if there is a resurrection, for all men to rise. For countless people have become the dinner of Thyestes and the banquets of Tantalus." <note>Thyestes and Tantalus are figures from Greek mythology associated with cannibalism; Postel uses them as a shorthand for the problem of one human body consuming another.</note> Everywhere on earth there have been man-eaters; they exist even today in many parts of the world. The Scythians gave banquets for their own [dead], their bodies containing the very funeral lamentation for them. All those who were devoured became parts of those who ate them; therefore, the first will lack what the others have taken. For if those who were devoured are made whole, the devourers will be incomplete, and vice versa. These are the arguments of the adversaries, to which I respond briefly. The nature of daily food teaches us that a part so thin is joined to the nourished bodies from what is taken inside, that after many months, scarcely any addition seems to have been made. Since we cast off the greatest and more corpulent part as waste and dregs, the part that remains in the body is seen to be very small. Even if the body has already reached its full growth, it is certain that as much of its own substance flows away as is added; this is something neither philosophers nor physicians will deny. For it is well known that nature requires drink and food because of the <term>flux of substance</term> <note>original: "fluorem substantiae," the idea that the body is constantly losing and replacing its physical matter</note>, to use a truly appropriate term. Indeed, our body is everywhere fluid and "breathable" <note>permeable or porous</note>, as Hippocrates says; by continuous action it loses something, which must be restored by food. Therefore, one body does not enter entirely into another body, but something very thin and familiar to the parts is added—only as much as is lost from elsewhere, and nothing more. Bodies are also whole in themselves without the addition of food, and can naturally last many days in that state, especially for those accustomed to it. Indeed, there appear many examples of men who lived for many years without any use of food or drink, and without the rejection of waste. Charles de Bovelles <note>A French Renaissance philosopher and mathematician</note> mentions in his letters a certain man who lived up to twelve years in perfect health without food or drink, even though antiquity wrote that the seventh day of fasting was fatal to man. Thus, these conditions are entirely contrary to one another, just as are the things for whose sake they were acquired. # ON THE TRANSFORMATION OF MATTER
## which must necessarily occur. CHAPTER XXII.

It is most clearly evident in all things, and established by the judgment and authority of all philosophers, that God wills to preserve the same order—one that is similar to Himself in every part—throughout the whole of nature. In the entire use of things, the *end* <note>The goal or purpose</note> differs from that which *tends toward the end*. Furthermore, there can be no doubt that the end is by far the most excellent thing in both nature and art. For if it were not the case that the things which are the goal were better than the things used to reach that goal, then everything would be done in vain, and nothing would act according to order and deliberation. For it would be plainly foolish and entirely lacking in mind to consume action in vain, reporting nothing back from it except the action itself and spontaneous labor—or if anything more, something worse, or plainly equal and similar. Since all such things are most absurd, they are rejected by the order of things, by common sense, and by authority. Therefore, one action cannot simply be the cause of a near-identical action or motion.

It follows, therefore—as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> left in his writings and as our senses teach us—that all motion occurs for the sake of rest. Since, however, all things here are in some way in motion, it is certain and necessary that rest will one day come to all things. Aristotle does not hesitate to concede this regarding the elements; indeed, he affirms it. Motion shall therefore one day stand still in eternal rest and peace, without any movement. For when these fleeting things perish, or cease to act and be acted upon, there will be no need for the celestial motion which is the cause of the generation, corruption, and alteration of these things. But since matter can never be entirely banished from its own nature, and since rest is necessary at some future time, it is necessary that this matter be transformed. For as long as it remains as it is now, it must be subject to <term>passions</term> <note>original: "passionibus"; in this context, it refers to being "acted upon" or undergoing physical change and decay</note>. If actions and motions are to cease, as is necessary, it follows that matter will also become free from corruption and most excellent, becoming very similar to "incorruptible form." This is what holy men and divinely inspired people have affirmed through oracles.

We cannot truly know what the "optimum" state of that matter will be—that which survives the universal conflagration—because we lack any example of it. However, to those considering the diverse kinds and perfections of gems, and how they are naturally prized by all people even though their true power remains hidden, it might come to mind that there will be a certain affinity between the mass of the elements and these gems. Not that they will be exactly like them, but (as the diamond is a single proof) they will yield to no power. For the "goat’s blood" will then be lacking, even if matter becomes diamond-like <note>A reference to the ancient belief, recorded by Pliny the Elder, that a diamond (adamas) was so hard it could only be broken if first soaked in the warm blood of a goat. Postel suggests the new matter will be even more invincible.</note>. Who would not admire pyropes, carbuncles, hyacinths, balaustias, and garnets? <note>Historical names for various red, blue, and orange precious stones</note> What man would not be turned to mental stupor by that translucent green of the emerald? Who can grasp the clarity and solidity of the diamond? And yet, although these are the highest things among us, they seem to be scarcely a shadow or a dream of the things to come. For just as nothing more perfect and incomprehensible than God Himself and the First Cause can be given, so nothing is more incomprehensible than His highest effect and effort. He wished to scatter small fragments and rudiments of this perfection in this nature—not so that they might adorn the harlots of princes, or...

...that immortal desires might be awakened in us: but rather that they might sweep us away into the admiration and contemplation of future things. But because nothing can be perfect unless the dregs, the slag, and all waste products are consumed, therefore fire—the tester of even the most perfected things—will offer its services to the Creator and will purify all things. It seems to approach this task gradually, through both art and nature. Gold, well-refined by fire, represents certain images of the most perfected earth, just as the diamond represents the most perfected water. For these two cannot be simply dissolved by fire unless you mix in <term>pharmaca</term> <note>original: "pharmaca"; here referring to chemical reagents or fluxes used in metallurgy and alchemy to lower melting points or assist in separation</note>. There are, therefore, three "times" of the Creator that correspond to His power, and which are in some way similar to these times of ours established under the conditions of motion. For among us, there is the past, the present, and the future. The **past** is infinite with respect to the "instant" <note>The infinitesimal moment of the now</note>, which can never truly be grasped. The **present** seems to be within our power, but in truth, we can do nothing in it before it has already passed away. In the **future** alone is happiness found. 

With God, there was **Eternity** without matter. The **Present** and the "instant"—which, with respect to the past, is something almost imperceptible—is the time of matter subject to birth and decay; this is the duration of the world. The **Future** will be eternal, featuring the true enjoyment of matter brought to perfection and immunity from corruption. All our own actions provide evidence for this model. For all effects have a past time in the mind, a present time in the work, and a future time in the enjoyment of the result. Since these qualities exist within us and are our most excellent traits, it is certain that we possess them following the example of the Divinity. For nature has an analogy both with itself and with art <note>In this context, "art" refers to human skill and technology</note>.

The end of all arts is rest; therefore, rest is also the end of created nature. God—who is most happy in Himself and to whom no matter or creation could add any perfection—created all these lower things for the sake of man. He created man for the sake of divine honor and contemplation (in which lies the highest happiness). Thus, from this state of corruption and constant labor—where the best people are tested and refined as if by tortures—He might finally lead them into that happiness which is eternal and most like God. May He deign to lead us there by His mercy.

By these arguments drawn from the storehouse of reason, it seemed fit to hand down those decrees which Truth itself—God in God the Son—opened to the world. He willed these to be believed by His own authority without the need for additional reasons, so that the impiety now arising and reigning in the whole world might be countered. ## CHAP. XXIII.

It has been handed down and believed by authority that God, existing from eternity, is **Three and One**. For He possesses Power, Wisdom, and Will, which we call "persons" or attributes of persons. We call the first, who from eternity generates Wisdom from Himself, the **Father**; the second we call the **Son**; and the **Will** proceeding from Power and Wisdom we name the **Holy Spirit**. By Him, through Him, and in Him the world was created, consisting of both corporeal substance and that which is devoid of body—which we call the **visible** and the **invisible**. 

By "invisible," we understand separate substances <note>i.e., spiritual beings or angels</note>, both those who are good and confirmed in goodness, and those who were depraved by their own will and bring destruction to men. We believe all visible things were made for the sake of man, but man was made for the sake of God and himself: so that by glorifying God, he might be immortal. We believe that God takes care of human affairs, even the smallest. I judge that no one who possesses any experience of affairs or is well-versed in the records of history is ignorant of how great a stain the unrestrained desire for ruling has brought upon the world to this day, how much loss the laziness and luxury of many has brought among mortals, and how great a plague arises daily from the vain contention of those who neglect and ruin their own affairs at home while seeking out foreign things that are hardly beneficial. For after empires either arise or are long preserved and increased for the sake of profit and lust rather than the welfare of the people, it happens not infrequently—even though at first glance the causes may seem most just—that wars have brought no less misery to the victors than to the vanquished, leaving behind an equal sense of unhappiness for both peoples. Truly, with divine providence so permitting because of human wickedness growing with age—since man has preferred to be ruled by another’s will rather than his own, and to follow another man as a leader rather than reason—the world has never been free from being worn down by wars. This is the punishment for neglected duty. This is the down-payment <note>original: "arra"; a pledge or earnest money</note> of eternal punishment for the wicked and for those who depend only on this mask of human affairs; but for the pious, it is a sign of benefit from God, who calls His own back to Himself through calamities. # ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
<meta>catchword: which</meta>

...points <note>original: "principia"; referring back to the "principal points" of doctrine mentioned at the end of the previous page</note> that introduce changes in both affairs and opinions: so that, however unhealthily war presents itself to those whom it oppresses, it may bring a more fortunate condition of affairs to the survivors. Furthermore, the worship, customs, beliefs, literature, and laws of the victors are often accustomed to leave the conquered with a utility far greater than they had before the victory. Thus it happened that although the Romans and Greeks—whose empires were the most widely extended and famous after those of the East—carried off victory from the whole world known to us in former times, drove off plunder, and not infrequently used their victory most cruelly; nevertheless, they left behind nurseries and the practice of laws and customs more closely related to nature everywhere as compensation for the loss sustained. 

Certainly, other types of changes, such as those that occurred because of the Scythians and barbarians, almost more frequently and utterly uprooted whatever ornament both these two nations <note>The Greeks and Romans</note> had contributed to letters and customs. Therefore, the incursions of the Barbarians are most hostile to nature, and as if entirely armed for its destruction. However, they have this much less evil in them: that as much as they bring more immediate slaughter to human bodies, they bring that much less harm to souls. For, placing the goods of the body in the highest degree of happiness, they bring neither many nor perverse laws; but rather, when affairs are settled and they are breathing again after war, when they consider what happiness and leisure the conquered peoples used to enjoy under their own laws, they embrace those laws. 

This is shown by the many incursions of the Scythians and Goths into both Asia and Europe, the attacks of the Huns, Heruli, Alani, Saxons, Normans, Vandals, and Lombards, and their fixed settlements everywhere in Europe. For all of them accepted the laws from the conquered, both because of their utility and because of their own ignorance of literature and disciplines. Other empires, therefore, have this quality: either they bring laws and culture to the conquered in place of plunder and victory, or they inflict a blight only on bodies, but do not likewise inflict the blindness of some foul superstition upon souls. 

But the one Arabic rabble <note>original: "Arabica colluuies"; a pejorative term used by the author to describe the early Islamic conquests</note> brought such a foul slaughter to both bodies and souls in almost the whole world that, whatever plagues the world had ever experienced before, it ought to consider those as happiness if it uses a just comparison of things. For besides the fact that an impious belief persuades them that nothing is more excellent, and no way to happiness is more direct, than if one slaughters as many mortals as there are who disagree with their dogma, this wretchedly tossed-about nation—captured by darkness greater than that of the Cimmerians <note>A mythical people described by Homer as living in perpetual mist and darkness; here used to mean extreme intellectual or spiritual blindness</note>—nourishes, fosters, protects, and cherishes a perpetual nursery of plunderers even among its own people under the name of "soldiers of God," who have sworn by his words. 

Since, therefore, God created man (for whose sake all other things exist) for the sake of duration, laws, empires, and all types of magistrates should primarily have a plan for preserving his life for as long as possible; those moderating the reins of the republic should seek out, accumulate, and preserve all supports of both body and soul from every side for his sake. But this one law of a treacherous tyrant <note>A polemical reference to the Prophet Muhammad</note>, arising and armed by the authority of the Furies <note>In Greek mythology, deities of vengeance; here used to imply demonic inspiration</note> against the majesty of God, the safety of human nature, the salvation of souls and bodies, and public peace, has brought such slaughter to mortals and such ruin to all things (except for pleasure and vice) that it truly can and ought to be called the "Desolation of the World"; as something that never permits either its own people to enjoy peace nor outsiders to enjoy quiet. 

Egypt once had twenty thousand cities; now it has barely ten municipalities and six cities. More than ten thousand cities once adorned both parts of Asia; now barely two hundred remain. All things are wasted and overgrown with briars and thorns because of the Nomads <note>The author likely refers to the Saracen or Ottoman forces</note> enrolled as soldiers for religion. With how many follies it has entangled the souls of those devoted to it will become clear throughout the course of this book, especially in the examination of the <term>Alcoranus</term> <note>The Quran</note>; finally, when I have uncovered how crudely it sensed and decreed concerning God, demons, and natural things, I will show in a few words how great are the calamities to which those are subject who live under the <term>Muhammedan</term> <note>Islamic or Ottoman</note> empire anywhere in the world. Since, therefore, it is established by the decrees of all that wars and changes of things are introduced by the permission of Providence as a punishment for crimes: it is certainly necessary that...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument from Book II regarding the rise and fall of empires. Having previously discussed the civilizing influence of the Greeks and Romans as a form of divine providence, he now pivots to the "bitter" side of providence: war and conquest as divine punishment for the sins of a people.</meta>

-># BOOK II OF GUILLAUME POSTEL<-

...which are most bitter, are prepared for the sake of avenging even the greatest crimes. Nor am I at all delayed by the fact that many say there are fixed cycles <note>original: "períodos"</note> of events, joined to the recklessness of fortune and the lust of wicked men, from which wars are accustomed to arise. For if they admit that the world has a cause and is ruled by providence (otherwise I do not deal with the "Followers of Fortune" <note>likely referring to Epicureans or those who believe the world is governed by chance</note>), they can never deny—since He has a singular care for creating and preserving individuals—that He has a far greater concern for preserving a multitude, whether in a city, a province, or any kingdom. For unless He restrained this massive world with eternal commands, all things would immediately burn with wars. 

To return to the matter: the greater the transgressions, the greater the punishments God allows to be inflicted, not only on those who committed the transgressions, but also on their descendants and those connected by trade, so that through the inflicted punishments they may learn either not to commit similar crimes or to expiate those already committed. I could not easily say with what crimes the peoples formerly alienated from the law of God most provoked Him, since, destitute of the divine law, they labored most foully under every vice. Indeed, they rushed into mutual slaughter daily. But I shall provide evidence for my statement from the Sacred Scriptures, running through a few examples. Because they were depraved and not corrected by their father, Hophni and Phinehas <note>The sons of Eli the priest; their corruption led to Israel's defeat, as recorded in 1 Samuel 4</note> caused the entire army of the people of God to be slaughtered by the Philistines. For a crime is considered more grievous the greater the status of the one who sins. The expiation of David’s sin suggests the same. The Babylonian captivity avenged the long-abandoned God, since even the priests and princes had turned to worshiping Baal. 

But because no crime more monstrous could ever be committed than the killing of Jesus Christ, the God-man, by his own people: so too was no slaughter ever made so memorable as that under Titus and Hadrian in the land of Judea, in which, in two expeditions, sixty times one hundred thousand <note>6,000,000</note> men were slaughtered to a man. Indeed, the remnants of the Jewish people have been in captivity everywhere on earth from that time, according to the prediction of Christ. Many innocent people are killed daily through slanders; but for the God-man to have been killed by His own priests—those who professed the preservation of His law—is a crime more monstrous than any punishment.

What, indeed, is more holy than a faithful and perfect Christian, to whom all nature is subject by the power of piety in the name of Jesus? Certainly nothing. Therefore, he who sins under such a holy law sins more gravely than any other mortal. For *the servant who knows the will of his master and does not do it shall be beaten with many lashes* <note>A reference to Luke 12:47</note>. Antiquity did not remain silent on the fact that the most savage persecutions arose against Christians because already many, initiated into the sacred mysteries, were behaving with little holiness, while others were even acting impiously under the most sacred title of innocence. 

And so, to come to the point, I am led by conjecture to believe that, on account of the monstrous crimes of false Christians, **this plague of the law of Muhammad** was sent into the world, so that those who impiously abused the most holy law might feel God as an avenger in a perpetually raging pestilence. And so that posterity might no longer struggle and sin in luxury, glory, and contention, the administration of temporal affairs was permitted to this emerging tyranny. Jerusalem, where the first patriarchs of our holy religion resided, fell into the power of the enemy with no effort. Not long after, Alexandria and Antioch were taken away, even though Christians had previously held the power of the magistracy there peacefully for over three hundred years; indeed, the local populations there had already given their names to Christ six hundred years prior. Unless a certain monstrosity of crimes and an abuse of things that had come from piety—a nation once most dear to God being intent on luxury and gluttony—had driven God’s favor away from the Christian world, it could not have happened that a naked barbarity of all things, powerful only in numbers, would have reported victory over those peoples who, even without arms, were formidable in the whole world. The Emperor Heraclius, most unworthy of the name, was competing in luxury and inert idleness with the most profligate of men when this faction <note>Referring to the rise of Islam in the 7th century</note> began to arise in Arabia. The Roman Pontiff was not satisfied to neglect the regions of the Eastern religion—though he held the first place among the patriarchs in councils—unless he also ambitiously sought that name of "Pope,"

...out of hatred for which such great fires are kindled, he sought after the title so that he who was the greatest, and desired to be so, might be called by it, as if by *antonomasia* <note>original: "αντωνομασίαν"; a rhetorical term where a title or epithet is used instead of a proper name, such as calling the Bishop of Rome simply 'The Pope'</note>. Truly, all priests before him were called thus: as can be seen from the letters of Jerome, Augustine, and other Latin authors, and likewise from the common title for sacred dignity in the Greek church. For it calls its priests "Papas" <note>original: "Papas"; the word 'Pope' is derived from the Greek 'pappas', an affectionate term for father, originally used for many bishops</note>. Perhaps so majestic a name came from heaven, or perhaps from Jupiter Papa, who was worshipped by the Bithynians <note>an ancient people of Asia Minor</note> with pure hands and without any ritual, according to an ancient erroneous rite. I do not labor much over where the name originated. Phocas granted its use to Boniface IV <note>Pope from 608–615 AD</note>. 

But it is helpful to examine the cause of this disease a little more broadly, so that at least after the limbs of the whole Christian body have been so deeply consumed by the neglect—or the malice and ignorance—of the doctors of that time, we may look out for ourselves and, according to the proverb, "become wise like the Phrygians" <note>original: "Phrygicè sapiamus"; a Latin proverb referring to those who only learn a lesson after suffering a disaster</note> even if late, and be helped by the danger of others. To make the beginning of such a great calamity clearer, I shall first describe the condition of the Empire’s affairs, and then follow with the matters of the sacred magistrates. 

Pope Gregory was a man of remarkable piety and learning, such that he still holds the fourth place among the holy doctors of the Church because of his writings. His papacy fell during the time of Emperor Maurice, who confirmed Gregory in the papal seat under the most unfavorable conditions, even though Gregory resisted and even secretly refused such a burden of honor and duty through letters. Perhaps that man, so devoted to a solitary life, seemed suitable to the Emperor—someone to whom he could entrust the cares of such great business and the dangers of the looming Lombard wars, and whom he could laugh at or attack with insults at will. In other matters, however, Maurice is said to have held the Christian faith faithfully enough. 

Therefore, on a double occasion after he had been in power for some time, he alienated the minds of the Italian people from himself: first, because he provoked that most holy man [Gregory] with insults, mocking him even in public; and second, because Maurice neglected the very care that Gregory undertook no less diligently than any soldier or general, holding many cities in loyalty to the Empire, not without danger to his own life. Moved by these hatreds against him, the soldiers declared a common soldier [Phocas] to be Emperor. Warned by an oracle, Maurice attempted to flee at night, but was captured at Chalcedon, brought back to the New Rome <note>Constantinople</note>, and beheaded. 

It is believed this faction was stirred up by Heraclian, a man of great authority in that city, so that he might give the Empire to a friendly soldier who relied on no confidence of noble birth, which he could later hand over to his son Heraclius once Phocas was removed. For such is the nature of ambition: under the appearance of piety, it rushes into deceptions as if through underground tunnels <note>original: "cuniculos"; implying stealthy or undermining maneuvers</note>, and exposes to danger and envy those whose welfare it pretends to consult. Having removed the patricians and men of the opposing faction, as is common in military coups, Phocas held the Empire for about eight years. During that whole time, the entire East was in upheaval. The Persians not only revolted against the Empire but broke into Roman territory and the borders of Asia Minor, threatening Africa and Egypt. The primary care of military affairs was given to Heraclian and his son-in-law Priscus; they met the enemy from Africa and Egypt, and the hostile onset was endured rather than repelled. Meanwhile, various factions arose from the sacred order in Constantinople.

...pious deeds, as if he were about to confront the enemy, though the matter had first been excellently prepared for betrayal. Certain chosen leaders were sent ahead into Greece: Priscus, his son-in-law, and Heraclius, his son. This was done so that, having seized the opportunity upon the arrival of the younger Heraclius with his forces, they might immediately strike down Phocas <note>Phocas was the Byzantine Emperor from 602–610 AD, known for his cruelty; he was overthrown by Heraclius</note>. Thus, by the same arts with which he had gained the empire, he lost it. And so, Heraclius was hailed as Emperor by the soldiers, who had already been bribed by his father's distributions. At the beginning of his reign, a great weight of war loomed. For at that time, it was not a matter of expanding the empire, but of thinking how to ward off the enemy from the very hearths of the home <note>original: "penatibus"; the Penates were Roman household gods, here symbolizing the heart of the empire</note>. That war had already begun in the times of Maurice <note>Emperor Maurice, reigned 582–602 AD</note>, and it is the primary cause of today’s calamity. After the enemies had been broken in several battles, the Emperor dissolved entirely into sloth and luxury, until the enemy—who previously had not rushed into the neighboring borders of Greece—subjugated all of Egypt and Africa. He became so maddened by such great power that he refused to grant peace to Heraclius, even though it was offered at any price. On one side, this most insolent enemy was pressing hard; on the other stood the disgrace of our religion: the wood on which Christ hung <note>the True Cross</note>, which had been kept in the hands of the enemies for ten years since the fall of Jerusalem. Truly, the nobles began to press him most vehemently; they begged, they entreated, and they added threats to their prayers—that if he did not act, both the nobles and the soldiers would seek a leader for themselves who would run to their aid in such a great <insert>in</insert> crisis of affairs. Compelled and stirred up, not so much by a sense of duty or fear as by a desire that no mark of infamy should graze him (for the great, the more contaminated their lives are, the more they tend to make a show of virtue and flee the mark of infamy), he undertook the task. He took up the war, having prepared a massive army. Terrified by the movement of this army beyond all expectation, Chosroes <note>Chosroes II, King of the Sassanid Persian Empire</note> dropped his insolence and fled. Leaving the place near Azotus where he had decided to join battle, he retreated in fear across the Euphrates to his own lands, consuming the crops with fire wherever he went to strip his adversary of the ability to follow. Heraclius pressed on not at all sluggishly (as men often burn for rare and unusual things); he overturned and devastated everything. He invaded Mesopotamia and dislodged and routed the leader Salbarum, who held defenses at the River Saron. He was succeeded by another named Says with the full strength of the army. A doubtful and day-long battle was joined with him, until, as victory was inclining toward the Persians toward evening, God, the best and greatest, willed to help His own. For suddenly such a crashing of the air arose, with such a horrifying noise and such a dark cloud of hail and rain striking the faces of the Persians, that the astonished Persians were slaughtered almost to total destruction. Though Chosroes repaired his strength, the attempt was no more successful. Heraclius had hired for that expedition the forces of certain Arabs already raiding that part of the world in the name of Muhammad. This circumstance, it seems to me, was a great step toward those things which followed afterward. Heraclius, as victor, brought back twenty-seven military standards of the enemy along with the life-giving Cross. But Syrochius <note>Kavad II, also known as Siroes</note>, the eldest of the sons of Chosroes, because he had been passed over by his father (who had made the younger son, Medarses, a partner in the remaining empire), entered into a treaty with Heraclius and removed both his father and brother so that he might possess the kingdom. He barely survived his father by a year, leaving the reins of power to his son Adheser <note>Ardashir III</note>. After him, Hormisdas <note>Yazdegerd III, the last Sassanid king, though Postel calls him Hormisdas</note> was substituted. Coming out against him, the armies of Muhammad took from him both the empire and his life, and they thrust upon their countrymen the frenzied beliefs of their persuasion, to be believed under penalty of death. This was the end of the Persian state. Heraclius, in triumph, brought the wood of our redemption back to Jerusalem. He restored the patriarch Zacharias <note>Patriarch of Jerusalem from 609–632 AD</note>, who had been a companion to the exiled Wood for all fourteen years, to his see. After the customary supplications were held, he departed from Aelia <note>Aelia Capitolina, the Roman name for Jerusalem</note>. However, as if no enemy remained for him in the whole world, once he had established the salary for the Arabian soldiers there (whose labor he had used), he dismissed the Roman army far from its homeland. He left it in Syria, prone to plundering and wandering; from this not a few of the dregs of all the robbers joined the prince Muhammad...

He gave a clear proof of his lust by taking his sister’s daughter in the place of a wife. But as misfortune follows misfortune, having squandered the public money on luxury, he was unable to satisfy the foreign soldiers according to their agreement. Angered by this, and further insulted by the quaestors <note>The Roman officials in charge of the treasury and payments</note>, the Arabian soldiers took up arms against the empire. In a few years, by laying waste to Syria and Egypt, they captured and plundered the most famous cities of western Syria—*Damascus*, *Antioch*, and *Aelia Capitolina*, which is *Jerusalem*—and through the fear of death, they persuaded many to accept their false beliefs. 

Such were the beginnings of these pestilential affairs. The Emperor had been warned by an oracle, when consulting divine sources, to beware of a circumcised race, for a great evil threatened the empire from them. But he interpreted the oracle as referring to the Jews, whom he thought were the only ones circumcised, and he forced them all throughout the empire to undergo baptism. However, the matter was heading elsewhere: specifically toward the *Muslims* <note>original: "Muhamedicos"</note>, who also observe circumcision. This event, along with the recovery of the Cross <note>Heraclius famously recovered the True Cross from the Persians in 628, an act that initially made him a hero of Christendom</note>, was why he was considered a very good man—he who deceived the world with a false appearance. He even corresponded with neighboring princes, urging them likewise to force the Jews into the faith of Jesus Christ. 

That century was entirely full of disease. No region in the whole habitable world was free from its own upheaval. *Italy* was so agitated by the *Goths*, *Lombards*, and *Arians* <note>Followers of Arianism, a belief that Christ was not co-eternal with God the Father, which had been declared heretical</note> that almost no city was without factions. Almost everywhere there were two bishops: one Catholic, the other Arian. *Sisebut*, King of the Visigoths in Spain, stripped the Romans of all their garrisons. In Gaul (I do not know if it happened before or from that time), *Theodebert* was removed by his brothers *Clotaire* and *Theoderic*. These men were, as their names indicate, more akin to the savagery of the Goths than to the refinement of the Gauls, which was known to everyone. 

I certainly believe this beginning of misfortune flowed from the Emperor's foul alliance with the enemy of Christ, and it first fell back upon the head of the allied empire itself. For no one has ever given their trust to the *Muslim* filth <note>original: "colluuiēi Muhamedicæ"; Postel uses a very strong word meaning dregs or a collection of refuse to describe the early Islamic conquests</note> without immediately paying the penalty to that same nation. Let the especially unlucky dealings of *Heraclius* serve as proof of history. In the second place, let those compared among themselves come forward. 

A little later, when the Persian Empire was occupied, the *Turks*—then an ignoble people living near the Caspian Sea—were summoned by a Persian prince named Muhammad <note>This refers to a local leader, not the Prophet</note> against *Imraël*, the Caliph of Babylon. When they arrived, having immediately defeated the enemy and plundered his part of the kingdom, they seized the empire from those who had summoned them and have held it almost to this day. The same thing happened when an alliance was formed with the administrators of Egypt: they ruled there until the *Circassians*, who are also called *Mamluks*, took mastery over their lords, having been brought in from elsewhere as mercenaries. 

*Roderic*, King of the Goths in Spain, by raping the daughter of *Julian*, the Roman governor in Mauritania, caused the father, overcome by grief, to summon a countless swarm of that wicked nation into alliance. He gave them the power to cross into Spain to avenge the crime committed against his daughter. The result was that the king was killed, and within three years almost all of Spain fell into their power; from there, they could never be dislodged until the times of Emperor Frederick III. Julian paid the price for his lack of foresight regarding that treacherous nation, losing both his province and his life. I do not wish to mention at what cost they were invited into Italy during the time of the factions of *Frederick Barbarossa* and *Pope Alexander III*. Certainly, no one has ever experienced the help or favor of that nation except to their own great harm. Let the Emperor of *Trebizond* provide proof, having been killed by his ally. Let the Egyptian Sultans bear witness, [who were killed] by their servants...

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK II.

...were most frequently cut down. Now the Empire of Constantinople pays the price for its madness, because the Palaeologi <note>The final dynasty of the Byzantine Empire (1259–1453). Postel is looking back from his own time to explain their eventual fall</note> preferred to call upon the enemy of Christianity <note>The Ottoman Turks</note> for help against their own neighbors and kin, rather than settle with them peacefully and without bloodshed under some fair law. He made a treaty with that nation through the King of Hungary, making a Voivode—that is, a governor—and a petty king out of Wallachia in Moesia. If I wished to pursue all such unfortunate treaties, the day would fail me. I return to my purpose: namely, what the condition of affairs was in the Church of Christ when the destructive dogma of the Quran <note>original: Alcorani</note> gained strength.

We have seen the dispute that arose concerning the primacy in the time of Phocas <note>Byzantine Emperor, r. 602–610</note> between the Eastern and Western Church, but for far different reasons. For John <note>John the Faster, Patriarch of Constantinople</note> had long contended for authority and the claiming of the title [of Universal Patriarch]. On the other hand, Saint Gregory <note>Pope Gregory I, "The Great"</note>, though he sat in that see which by the consensus of the whole Church was established as the first, said that such an ambitious title should be recognized by no mortal. As a sign of this, he was the first to take the humble title "Servant of the servants of God" <note>original: Servus servorum Dei</note>. 

Since this altercation had arisen long ago, even from the times of Maurice and Gregory, Phocas (as I have said), for the sake of entering into friendship with Boniface IV, brought it about that the Pantheon <note>original: πάνθεον, meaning "of all gods"</note>—that is, the temple of all gods built in Rome during the time of the false religion, the work of Marcus Agrippa—should be dedicated to the memory of the Virgin Mother and all the other saints. Furthermore, he decreed that the Roman Pontiff should use the title of "Pope" <note>original: Papae</note>, and that the Roman Church should have primary authority over all churches. Although the Roman Church had held this authority by the consensus of all the faithful until that day, because no one had brought a lawsuit regarding it, the power of the Emperor had not yet been used for decrees on that matter. 

Thus, what the most holy pontiff <margin>† Gregory the Great.</margin> had striven with the greatest zeal to defend—that neither he nor any other should seize such a title—was immediately after his death dragged in a direction he did not wish. For between him and Boniface IV, the see was occupied for only two years by two men. The first of these was Sabinian, a worthless man and most unjust toward Gregory, who sat for 17 months; the other was Boniface III, who sat for seven. Sabinian was a factious man who, having stirred up infamy against the holy pontiff Gregory out of extreme envy for his integrity, had obtained the papacy by capturing the favor of the people through evil arts. 

Since he could not vent his hatred on the body of that most holy man, he wished to abolish his works by a wicked edict, ordaining that no one should keep them in their home. Indeed, he agitated the people against Gregory for one reason: that he had supposedly cast down various statues of the ancients and ornaments of the city. This was completely false, for Gregory had removed nothing other than idols and the remnants of old superstition. 

When, during a time of extreme food shortage <note>original: annonae charitate</note>, Sabinian was urged by the people to imitate the holy man Gregory through alms, he added calumny upon calumny, saying that Gregory had exhausted the entire treasury of the church so that there was nothing left to give out. Yet, there was in the Lateran Basilica <note>The cathedral church of Rome and the official seat of the Pope</note> a very great amount of gold intended for conversion to pious uses. 

For when Severinus was created Pope by the people and clergy according to custom 29 years later, and had to be confirmed by the Exarch of Ravenna <note>The Byzantine governor of Italy</note> in the name of Heraclius, the Exarch Isaac—wishing to gain favor with an Emperor who was short on cash (as pleasure-seekers always are) and to look out for himself—declared that he would not approve the people's vote unless the power of the Lateran treasury was granted to him in the name of the Emperor. Compelled, the Pope—who was otherwise a good man—assented. The sacred money was partly sent to the Emperor, partly given to the soldiers, and partly went to Isaac. 

The holy pontiff Gregory had fled from the proud title, but another snatched it up. Gregory had gathered funds through piety to be used for pious purposes; his wicked successor [Sabinian], by hoarding them during a time of total scarcity so that he might one day devour them, left those same funds for a successor shortly after, to serve as the price for a sacred office. Due to factions, the entire state of the Eastern Church then began to totter. The Bishop of Constantinople took the title of "Patriarch" <note>original: Patriarchae</note> by his own authority, from which a plague arose.
