arisen, there were immediately as many opinions as there were heads. For there were many Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father</note>, and not a <margin>Nestorius</margin> few were imbued with the error of Nestorius <note>Nestorius taught that Christ had two distinct natures (divine and human) that were loosely joined, rather than being one person</note>. The faction of the Monothelites <note>A 7th-century heresy claiming Christ had two natures but only one will</note> had even occupied the citadel of the Empire. This makes me willingly agree with the opinion of those who claim that Muhammad was aided by a certain monk named Sergius; that is, he wanted to persuade people throughout the entire Quran <note>original: Alcorano</note> that there were no other good Christians than those who, in the manner of Nestorius, did not acknowledge the divinity in Christ. Therefore, even today there are many Christians in the Eastern parts, but they are nearly all related to that dogma. When Geber <note>Likely Jabir ibn Aflah, a 12th-century astronomer whose "Almagest" (astronomical treatise) Postel cites for its cultural data</note>, in his *Almagest*, relates the annals of famous peoples, he describes the festivals of the Nestorians and Jacobites <note>A West Syriac Christian denomination</note>, both of whom favored Muhammad. They have many things unknown or unusual to the Roman Church, such as the feast of Christ’s baptism, the appearance of the cross in heaven, the crown, the ears of grain, the grapes, and such things. These things paved the way for that impious persuasion, while we either snore away, devoted to luxury, or bring evil upon our own heads because of others and through hatred, preferring that both sides perish rather than, setting aside ambition, preserving the bond of peace in union according to the instruction of Paul.

We have now paid the penalty for that crime for nearly 950 years. Hence I am easily led to believe that no less a crime committed by us than by them from that time has turned the mercy of divine goodness away from the prosperity of the Christian state, so that our dross may be burned away to the quick, just as it is in the Eastern and Greek Church. For our gold, as the prophet said, has turned into dross. Certainly, if we wish to weigh matters according to the standard of their own principles, there is no condition today—however holy it appears in the Christian order—in which the most "perfect" person of this age approaches the perfection of those who were once considered barely honest. Suppose there are some: they will certainly be so few in number that you would find as many as "the gates of Thebes or the mouths of the wealthy Nile" <note>A reference to a satire by the Roman poet Juvenal, meaning "extremely few"</note>. What else is the monastic order today (if you except those who entered at a mature age of their own accord) than a refuge for the disinherited? Certainly, unless God had left us a seed, we would be like Sodom and not unlike Gomorrah. From the four mendicant orders <note>The Franciscans, Dominicans, Carmelites, and Augustinians</note> there have always been many men of singular learning, whose work has compensated for the negligence of many parish priests. From this it clearly appears that although those men are only human and struggle with their own imperfections, the simplicity of life in monasticism is most excellent. For if you look at those who gave their names to Benedict, Bernard, and the others for the sake of a stricter profession—through nearly ninety distinctions—you would scarcely find one in a hundred in any century who practiced anything worthy of a man besides **wine-drinking** <note>original Greek: οἰνοποτίαν (oinopotian)</note>. For if they just live by the common standard of the vulgar crowd, they think that is truly excellent.

But good God, how much does this way of life differ from the condition of the ancient age? I do not wish to run through every single order. For everywhere so many things unworthy of their office present themselves that I judge it better to cover them in silence than to stir them up. Until this day, the Greatest and Best God has indulged us, perhaps in the hope that we might repent and leave behind this more-than-Sybaritic <note>Sybaris was an ancient Greek city famous for its extreme luxury and decadence</note> luxury. Now the axe is laid to the root. The same thing threatens us that happened to the whole East. Come then, dearest brothers! Since it is not permitted to princes—due to their many preoccupations—to turn this plague away from the lands, let us run to meet it, let us set ourselves against it for the name of Jesus Christ; let us sharpen the swords of reason against the impious nation, ready to strike at the first opportunity. Are we not ashamed that only a single corner of dominion in Europe is left to Christ? What account of our sloth are we going to give to God, that no one opposes such a great calamity? Certainly many martyrs, most famous for miracles after their deaths, teach us that this cause is most pleasing to Christ. For many, daily opposing themselves...

[adheren]ts to a perverted dogma, they restore health after death to those who approach their tombs in the name of Christ. Do we think that Christ will fail His own? He who brought it to pass that the tongues of African bishops, which had been cut off by the Arians <note>The Arians were followers of Arius, who denied the full divinity of Christ; during the 5th-century Vandal persecution in North Africa, several bishops reportedly continued to speak after their tongues were removed.</note>, were reborn as proclaimers of the truth? Why is this foolish and trivial opinion held as a most sacred decree among many: that the time of martyrs has passed? As if indeed the opportunity to prove oneself to Christ, even at the risk of one's life, were ever lacking. If the ungodly and those for whom the knowledge of the First Cause <note>A philosophical term for God</note> is foreign were to be lacking, there are still heretics, the impious deeds of princes, and the wickedness of evil tyrants. Even if both the ungodly and heretics are absent, there will never be a lack of affairs in the world in which a soul relying on God might exercise itself in rebuking them and become a witness for God. I do not wish to bring forward examples of the first [martyrs], since countless myriads of martyrs speak for themselves.

The rebuking of Herod brought death to John the Baptist. The bold criticism of the Emperor Valens <note>A 4th-century Roman Emperor who supported Arianism</note> would have brought death to Basil the Great <note>One of the "Cappadocian Fathers" of the early church</note> if providence had permitted it, but instead it brought exile. How many times did John Chrysostom <note>Known as "Golden-Mouthed," a famous early church preacher</note> oppose the Empress Eudoxia when she was infected by the Arian heresy: he suffered exile twice because of it. Thomas of Canterbury <note>Thomas Becket, who was murdered in his cathedral in 1170</note>, killed for the preservation of the liberty of the Church, afterward shone with miracles. All these things show that in nothing ought we more to prove ourselves to God than in persuading and asserting the truth.

A richer harvest was never offered to Christians since the death of Christ than now. For what difference does it make whether a man has never known the truth, or has forgotten it? The whole world is in greater darkness than when Christ sent workers into the vineyard. Certainly, just as no superstitious plague among the nations was ever more monstrous than the Muhammadan one, so nothing can be done in the name of the Savior that is more pleasing than to resist it with all one's strength. Angelus the Sicilian <note>A 13th-century Carmelite saint</note>, gloriously preaching Christ to the Moors, ended his life by the sword after long imprisonments. Five Franciscan martyrs, Berard and his companions, were beheaded for that same reason in Morocco <note>original: Mauritania</note>, becoming glorious through miracles immediately from the moment of death. Anthony, who is called "of Padua" from his place of burial, had made trial of this matter in his youth; but with the business unfinished, he was forced to return because of his ignorance of the language.

Only the Arabic language is needed, besides the capacity for engaging with the enemies of Christ, which opens the way for one who will travel through almost the entire world. For no language, as far as the memory of literature records, has ever occupied so much of the earth. The two Moroccos <note>The Roman provinces of Mauretania Tingitana and Mauretania Caesariensis</note>, Numidia, Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, the Arabias, Syria, Asia Minor, the Armenias, Mesopotamia, Assyria, Persia, Parthia, Aria, Gedrosia <note>Ancient regions corresponding to parts of modern Iran, Afghanistan, and Pakistan</note>, and the greater part of India embrace it for the sake of that ruinous dogma. The Clementine Decree <note>A decree from the Council of Vienne (1312) ordering the creation of language chairs in major universities</note> concerning teachers had commanded that the primary Universities ought to have two teachers of it, so that every age might have men suitable for uprooting that persuasion from the minds of men. It has not yet been done.

I have now laid for you, as far as was possible through my meager abilities, the foundations of that learning by printing a grammar. I possess a huge collection of books in this language, considering its rarity. But that which can make you most ready and equipped in every part is the refutation of that insane dogma. Indeed, I have undertaken that work—not like those who before me attempted the same task from a Latin version, or (to speak more accurately) a perversion <note>original: inuerſione</note> of the Quran <note>original: Alcorani</note>, but from the Arabic copies themselves. Come then, O dearest brothers, especially you who profess a contempt for the world: help me, both with work and prayers. Follow a leader, even if he is not skilled enough. Even the greatest geniuses began as novices. From these beginnings, by proving ourselves to Christ, we shall proceed to <insert>greater things</insert>. Thus it will happen that the zeal of Princes will be excited toward this cause and they will apply themselves to this care. A small flame has not rarely stirred up the greatest fires. "If you will not be healthy," as Horace <note>A Roman poet; the quote suggests that if one does not take care of their health while well, they will be forced to deal with the much harder task of curing a disease (dropsy) later</note> says, "you will care for yourself when dropsical." Thus God has ordained that after He has waited a long time for us to repent, He drags us along against our will; and those things which we use for our destruction, luxury, and pride, He transfers elsewhere, so that we may receive affliction from them, but no pleasure.

That immense tyrant Muhammad <note>Mehmed II, the Ottoman Sultan who conquered Constantinople in 1453</note>, who captured Constantinople, is said to have remarked when he saw the heaps of wealth with which the Patriarchate overflowed in its finery and pomp, and viewed the books of accounts: "O impious men, this shall fall upon your own heads. You, by abusing such copious wealth against the prescription of your own law <note>The Gospel/Christian teachings</note>, have hastened your own ruin. I shall see to it that posterity pays the penalty for your sin. This money shall go to the soldier who afflicts Christian affairs." Without delay, he ordered those riches to be gathered into a single treasury, from which it was permitted only to take enough for military expeditions against the enemies of the Muslim religion, and for the use of the poor, pilgrims, and those thin-pressed men who are engaged in the study of letters. In this quarter, sixty thousand gold pieces are spent annually in the name of alms. Once, that treasury was exhausted by Sultan Selim <note>Selim I, reigned 1512–1520</note>, the father of the currently reigning Suleiman <note>Suleiman the Magnificent</note>, contrary to the decree of his grandfather, when he was hastening to the Persian war at Chaldiran <note>original: "Chalderandagis"; a major battle in 1514 where the Ottomans defeated the Safavid Persians</note>. Thus the Patriarch heaped eternal slaughter upon his descendants.

Truly, the lower orders of that Church were no more fortunate. For whatever was owed to the churches, whether through tithes or other revenue, all of it passed to the soldier. So it is no wonder that those Princes abound in an eternal and copious supply of soldiers. For in the place of a dead man, another is immediately substituted, not unlike the way curates are replaced here. Unless we find a remedy in time, the same fate hangs over us. Indeed, it is customary for a victor to leave to any nation the free use of its own religion, albeit in extreme poverty; but the Emperor’s edict daily leads away the youth from Christian parents throughout the entire empire to be enrolled in the military after some years of training <note>Postel is describing the "Devshirme" system, where Christian boys were taken to be trained as Janissaries</note>; and finally, what is worst of all, they are made to swear by the words of the Quran, having denied Christ. And do these things not move us?

When orders of various religions <note>referring to monastic orders</note> arose among us with a certain fervor, at first the highest piety flourished in them, and they turned away the wrath of the Divinity through pious prayers so that it would not rage against other mortals; but gradually, as that "good strife" <note>A reference to Hesiod's *Works and Days*, where he distinguishes between bad strife (war) and good strife (healthy competition and hard work)</note> (as Hesiod calls it) cooled down, they returned to the old pursuits common to mortals, and began to differ from the rest little beyond their external dress. Therefore, for various reasons, one part of the Church approved only a single order, because it saw that all things are corrupted with time; another part substituted better ones for those that were corrupted.

strength, so that as many as possible might embrace it; nor did it succeed unhappily. For the brightest lights of the world taught that this way of life pleased Christ. We must not delay after the manner of heretics and the impious. For they say that the Muslims should not be resisted, because they have been sent by God to punish our iniquities. Others say that Christ’s empire should be left to Christ, so that he may protect it himself. But God is not accustomed to do anything without human will when it can be done by it. It is necessary for those who are his, if they wish to enjoy his happiness, to strive with all the effort of body and soul so that his doctrine may spread as widely as possible. 

If the tenets of that perverse dogma begin to be uprooted in just one place, the whole mass will collapse with no effort. Once the princes realize that their empires can be maintained under the doctrine of Christ, they will easily yield, and we shall report a victory more memorable than any that has ever been or ever shall be. May God grant it.

Therefore, they immediately resort to punishments if anyone says even one word against the Quran or its tenets. Those who cast themselves into this path will "possess their souls in patience." They will be conquered by miracles. Christ will be present, if once they undertake to engage in the battle armed with faith...

# AN EXPOSITION AND REFUTATION 
## of the Muhammedan Persuasion. The Life of Muhammad, the Lawgiver of the Arabs.
### CHAPTER I.

Since many and various points present themselves regarding the arts by which Muhammad was raised to the height of power, I have decided to describe his life using certain arguments and themes—in the manner of Suetonius in his *Lives of the Caesars* <note>Suetonius was a Roman historian known for his detailed, thematic biographies of emperors</note>—so that these facts may be more easily understood and preserved in memory. In this way, related matters can be more easily gathered, and once collected, they will allow the reader to explain things that are otherwise unpleasant to read or hear without any boredom. 

Therefore, in the first place, I will pass down the following: from what kind of family he was born, by what arts he was educated, what his character and mind were like, which supporters he used in promoting his sacred laws, what means he used to acquire power, with whom he contracted alliances, how many wives he married, and finally, through which expeditions he acquired the legacy he left to the descendants of the Koreish <note>The Quraysh, the ruling tribal group of Mecca to which Muhammad belonged</note>. I will also record what fate he met and where he was buried. Then, using the same method, I will examine the Quran, reducing it to common places <term>common places: a rhetorical method of organizing arguments by standard themes or topics</term> to show what he wanted treated, what he took from the Old Testament, what from the New, what errors were admitted in them, and what things are uniquely his own. Finally, I will discuss which authors those who have sworn by his words use to supplement the Quran. Lastly, I will speak of the succession of his power. But now, I set to the task.

## FROM WHICH PARENTS 
### Muhammad was born. CHAPTER II.

<meta>This page continues Postel’s biographical critique of Muhammad. Having previously discussed the strategic necessity of understanding Islamic scripture to better refute it, he now turns to the earthly origins of the Prophet, attempting to undermine his status by emphasizing his "ignoble" family, his poverty, and the conflicting accounts of his early life among his followers.</meta>

# GUILLAUME POSTEL BOOK II #

Let us learn what supports the man being described was able to use, whether for the path of virtue or vice; and so let us discern what he owes to his ancestors and what he achieved by his own industry. It is handed down that Muhammad's ancestors were citizens of the city of Mecca in Arabia, belonging to an ignoble family. They called them the Quraysh <note>original: "Choreissos"</note>, a people devoted to transporting merchandise from Persia, Syria, and Egypt into Arabia. He was born to a father named Abdallah ibn Abd al-Muttalib <note>original: "Hebdalla mutalibo"</note>, a man (as they would have it) rich and opulent, and to a mother named Amina <note>original: "Imina"</note>. They were pagans <note>original: "ethnicis"</note> and citizens of Mecca, as some have left in writing. Others, however, say he was born in Yathrib <note>original: "Ietriba," the ancient name for Medina</note>, which some call Jesrabam. The more common opinion among them is that he arose in Mecca.

Indeed, he is written to be descended from those whose efforts the later Caliphs <note>original: "Chaliphę," the political-religious successors to Muhammad</note> used in delivering their persuasion. For Yathrib is called *Medina alnabi*, that is, the City of the Prophet, because he was born and buried there. Others affirm it was called so only because of his residence and burial. This obscurity of his origin comes from the fact that he had seven men in the closest familiarity who were accomplices to the whole fable for a decade; others opposed these men out of envy and wrote certain Chronicles of his life that were entirely different from their version. These first seven are: Asr son of Amr, and another of the same name son of Ketir, Umar, Humayran, Al-Ansar, Awn, and Nafi. Theirs is the more common and primary opinion. For they are even said to be participants in the law of the Quran <note>original: "Alcorani"</note> and were admitted into partnership by the prophet; though when asked about this law more often, they themselves affirmed they knew nothing. The more recent writers opposed them—instructed by the following Caliphs—such as Abu Zayd, Ibn Abdallah, Muhammad son of Ezra, Al-Fadl son of Ja'far, Abu Umar son of Zayd, and countless others, in order to give greater authority to the smaller city in which he was buried.

Nor indeed were they satisfied to have defected from the first witnesses; they even devised two genealogies with fabricated names: one from Adam through Ishmael, with a certain light passing from the men into the women until it reached his father; the other, conversely, tracing from Muhammad back to Adam. And lest they seem to have told too few lies, they used the testimony of a single servant-girl named Halimah <note>original: "Halimæ"</note> (who had raised the orphan), claiming that his mother gave birth without pain, and they devised many other things worthy of such authors.

Wherever he was born, it is agreed by everyone’s calculation that he was posthumous <note>born after the death of his father</note>. It is handed down that his mother died two years—or as others wish, four years—after his birth. Received into the guardianship of his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib <note>original: "Abdumutalibi"</note> and the care of Halimah, a poor woman from the province of Banu Sa'd <note>original: "Venizat"</note>, he was raised quite meagerly, as may be seen from many things. For he himself confesses about himself in the Quran, saying:

> You were poor, and you were enriched; you were an orphan, and you were gathered in. <note>original: "Pauper eras, & es ditatus, pupillus eras, & es collectus." A reference to Surah 93 (Ad-Duha)</note>

Furthermore, he had the domestic care of camels in the house of a certain relative, until, already grown according to the custom of his ancestors, he began to drive pack camels (by which whatever merchandise there is, is usually carried in those regions) back and forth from Arabia into neighboring regions. All of these facts cannot be arguments for a noble or powerful family, if we look at things as they are usually judged among us. I say these things so that, having carefully weighed the man's origin, we may see where he first made his step toward power. It may be, however, that the paternal wealth was so narrow that it barely sufficed for him and his brothers, of whom he was the twelfth. If it were relevant, I would publish their names. But it is of no help to know anything else about them, except that it is clear they were his most bitter enemies on account of his imposture—except for two, who passed from the worship of idols to his foolish nonsense. Furthermore, he killed the rest. Such was the charity of the man for his kin,

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD #

### ON THE INHABITANTS OF MECCA, AND ###
#### the opportunities Muhammad possessed. ####
### CHAPTER III. ###

Even if these things do not seem to fit the argument—that when speaking of a man’s life, one should speak of the place—nevertheless, because the consideration of both place and time contributes greatly to discerning the events themselves, I believe I must speak of the condition of the men who lived in Mecca at the time Muhammad was born before I proceed further. Mecca is a commercial hub <note>original: "emporium"</note> situated in the western part of *Arabia Felix* <note>“Happy Arabia,” the fertile southern region of the peninsula</note>, about a hundred miles distant from the shores of the Arabian Gulf, which we are accustomed to calling the Red Sea in sacred scripture. Whatever spices exist in the region of Sheba <note>original: "Sabaea"</note> are usually brought there because of the frequent trade of all nations. The people are of very corrupt morals, who count nothing as good except the pleasures of the body. It happens in such places, due to the constant crowd of diverse inhabitants who change daily, that various types of religious rites are also held; thus, every nation finds even those ancestral gods they hold anywhere in the world represented in a large and crowded marketplace. The principal part of the men living there, when Muhammad was studying how to stir up a revolution <note>original: "rebus nouis studeret"</note>, served idols called Ellet and Aluza <note>Al-Lat and Al-Uzza, two of the three chief goddesses of pre-Islamic Mecca</note> (some maintain these were Pallas and Venus). The Jews observed the Mosaic temples. Certain Jacobite and Nestorian Christians <note>Middle Eastern Christian sects often viewed as heretical by the Roman Church</note> had their own sacred rites. But by far the largest part of the pagans was accustomed to gather for the sake of religious rites in a certain temple located in the middle of the city. Those who wrote of Muhammad’s deeds, in order to trace the authority of their religion back to the highest principles, claim that this temple—where the tower called the *Alquibla* <note>The Qibla or Kaaba</note> is located—had already been built from the time of Ishmael,

<margin>This is Kedar <note>original: "Cedar"</note>, the son of Ishmael, whom others call Kaidru.</margin>
and that the sacred rite was established by Abraham, Ishmael, and Kedar <note>original: "Cahidaro"</note> his son. Wishing to provide proof for this matter, they add that Kedar, so that the idol <note>the sacred stone</note> would not be ignored, placed a marble stone in that part of the tower, so that anyone who could not enter the temple due to his business might at least worship upon seeing the sign. Meanwhile, those "good" historians do not notice that while they seek antiquity for the prophetic lineage, they establish the leaders of that lineage as the authors of idolatry. Furthermore, these liars have poor memories; for elsewhere, in the *Hazear* <note>likely referring to a Sira or biographical source</note>, they say he was born from a most just and religious people. Yet he himself confesses that he was in manifest error and worshiped those idols, and it is written in the *Suna* <note>the Sunnah, the body of traditional social and legal custom</note> that he confessed to worshiping them; thus does the lie contradict itself. Lest the ancestral rite be entirely abolished, even today they worship that stone in memory of their fathers. Indeed, they say that in that city, or nearby, Abraham wished to sacrifice his son; and therefore they observe very many ceremonies during the pilgrimages, which last four months, as if they had been instituted there by Abraham. Among these, none is more frequent than the slaughtering of many sheep in memory of that ram which Abraham sacrificed in place of his son. But we shall speak of these in their proper place. Now we must come to his upbringing.

### ON THE YOUTH OF MUHAMMAD. ###
### CHAPTER IV. ###

Those distinguished historians of whom we made mention recite certain things worthy of their authors, based on the testimony of Halima, the nurse of this prophet. For they say he was born circumcised—lest they should not start lying soon enough. They claim that when he was born, angels cast the prince of demons into the sea, from which he barely emerged after forty days; they tell six hundred such absurd, ridiculous, and old wives' tales that it is shameful to read them. But from these, let others who enjoy such things learn the rest. When he was born, every kind <note>original: "genus"</note> of bird gathered,

The winds contended that they could do it much better from scents collected from all sides. The clouds contradicted both, affirming that they could nourish him with the sweetness of all the waters. Thus, no care was left for the angels. But God restrained those who were quarreling, saying that he ought to be nourished by the care of humans. Halima <note>Muhammad's foster mother and nurse according to Islamic tradition</note> narrated these and many other innumerable things; however, she had not yet arrived at that point. For according to those people, he was born in Yathrib <note>original: "Iesrab"; the pre-Islamic name for Medina</note>: from where his mother was forced by hunger to seek Mecca, because of the famine and poverty distressing the whole region. Thus, the entire faith of the Quran <note>original: "Alcorani"</note>, or at least of the book *Al-Shifa* <note>original: "Haffear"; likely referring to the famous biography of the Prophet by Qadi Ayyad</note>, which is of equal authority, depends on the report of Halima. 

But, O sensible readers, hear this miracle with a calm mind, and learn all things from this one instance. When, having been born on a certain day, he had gone to the shepherds' folds at about five years of age, he reported that he had been snatched away by an angel (having now reached forty years of age, he devised this and called Halima as a witness) and, led apart from the others, was disemboweled by the same angel with a razor <note>original: "nouacula"</note>. The angel, having extracted the heart from the body, split it down the middle, cut out a certain black particle from it, and immediately replaced it and restored him to health. He told the prophet that the particle which the devil uses to tempt men had been taken away from him. You have the story, you see it; judge for yourselves concerning him. 

I find nothing further passed down until the 15th year of his age, when he was given over to the care of camels. Meanwhile, however, the thinness of his fortune, or the rudeness of his entire nation, is proven by the fact that he knew neither letters nor how to swim. I would easily believe, however, that through constant conversation with boys trained in various cultures, he heard certain trifles regarding individual religions; and finally, when he had grown up, he recalled those things to memory and applied them to his own craft. For frequent Jews were able to catch the boy's attention, so that they might then especially make one proselyte twice as bad as themselves. Regarding his mind and the form of his body, since nothing has been passed down, I can judge nothing except from the effects. For I find nothing written except by those chroniclers of the Caliphs <note>original: "Chaliphorum"</note>, who make him more beautiful than the angels. That he was of a strong body is argued by his lustfulness, for he would enter twelve women in one hour; and he himself used to say that he had the strength of forty men in his loins. In mind, he was certainly most desirous of revenge. But I have nothing found for certain regarding him up to his 25th year, nor what he may have done.

## BY WHAT PRINCIPLE HE PASSED TO A ##
### MORE SPLENDID FORTUNE. CHAPTER V. ###

Given, as has been said, in the fifteenth year of his age to the care of camels in the family of one of his relatives, he traveled back and forth for the sake of merchandise, and observed the various rites of men as the opportunity of the place allowed. For that place was an equal distance from Babylon in Assyria, from Egypt, and from the most famous city of the entire East (as long as things were prosperous), Jerusalem. Imbued with that <term>versatility</term> <note>original Greek: "πολυτροπία" (polytropia); a term often used of Odysseus, meaning wily, many-sided, or cunning</note> and shrewdness, he already began to meditate on greatness. This addition of luck came to him: that on account of his bodily strength, Khadija <note>original: "Hadeiaga"</note>, a rich and very powerful woman who had married his relative whose affairs he was managing, was seized by love for him and used him in a clandestine habit as often as was permitted. 

From this it happened that, the wretched husband having been removed—not without suspicion of poison—the slave married the mistress as his wife and obtained ample resources. Such is the power of a woman's lust. Not long after Khadija <note>Postel uses the variant "Hadisam" here</note> began to live as a family with her new husband Muhammad, she perceived that the man was violently seized by the <term>falling sickness</term> <note>original: "morbo comitiali"; epilepsy</note>. This he had previously cautiously concealed, and she had been ignorant of it. Khadija then began to feel repentance for the deed; and yet there was no room for divorce on this most just occasion, before that scoundrel published a law allowing it on any occasion...

She <note>Khadija, Muhammad's wife</note> began then to complain vehemently about her lot, and to accuse the man of perfidy for having so deceived her, never having revealed this during their previous intimacy. She threw his former poverty in his teeth, turned the names of "chattel" and "servant" into a reproach, condemned his wickedness, cried out that she was miserable, and blamed her fortune. He, for his part, pretended it was something new—that he had never experienced anything like it before—and did not try to hide it, claiming it would be very short-lived as it had only happened once or twice. Meanwhile, moved by great mental distress, he began to meditate on what reasoning he could use to soothe his wife’s mind and what pretext he could bring forward for the disease. 

Therefore, since he was a wine-drinker as well as a womanizer (for wine and Venus <note>The Roman goddess of love, used here as a metaphor for lust</note> go hand in hand), he began to use drunkenness as a pretext. He claimed that the vapors of the wine occupied his brain too violently, and from this these fits occurred; he argued it happened daily of necessity, just as he was forced to drink his fill by the conditions and customs of his life. The woman, being quite unsuspicious, began to be led toward that opinion, and she begged the man vehemently, entreating him by their love to use wine a little more modestly so that the disease might gradually be driven away; otherwise, she feared it might take deeper root. The shifting scoundrel <note>original: "uersipellis nebulo," literally a "skin-changing rascal"</note> obeyed her; he abstained from wine and gradually withdrew himself from that particular pleasure, lest he lose the wealth and power by which he had already begun to be very influential as a master. For he knew he would never be allowed to use such great wealth at his own whim unless his wife permitted it. 

Meanwhile, many years slipped by while the credulous woman waited for the disease to end. Thus, having become abstemious, Muhammad returned into his wife’s favor and became master of the fortunes. Then, he devised another—and much more excellent—fabrication for excusing the disease, one which could hardly be resisted (since he knew the old excuse would no longer work). He claimed it had been revealed to him by the angel **Gabriel** that this passion had distressed him so much because he was not attending to the gift of **prophecy** to which he had been appointed by God. 

And so he began to weave a certain marvelous tale. For the whole day, and not rarely at night, he would withdraw from human company, entering a cave not far from the city daily for many hours. There, as he said, he practiced fasts, endured divine conversations, and felt frequent ecstasies, until he drew not only the woman into this opinion of his sanctity, but also many powerful men. These men were ignorant of all things, especially divine matters, and were almost all *suphehe* <note>original: "suphehę"; from the Arabic *sufahā’*, meaning fools or ignorant people</note> as he calls them—that is, stupid and unrefined. 

The woman, although she was almost drawn into this opinion, still knew the man "inside and out" <note>original: "intus & in cute," a Latin idiom from the satirist Persius meaning to know someone's true character</note> and could hardly persuade herself that there was no fraud underlying this "prophecy." For she frequently objected that an angel did not seem "good" if he tortured a man to the point of spasms, apoplexy, foaming at the mouth, and full-body sweats; surely he could communicate divine things at a lower cost. Furthermore, she argued that if he were truly a prophet and a friend of God and the angels, he could obtain from them the favor of not appearing at such unseasonable hours: so that they might stop seizing him while he was sleeping, at the table, just finishing a meal, in the very act of intercourse, or similar occupations. But when she saw the matter proceed even to the point of madness, she said it was the work of the devil and not of God, which upset him greatly. 

Nevertheless, with trifles and responses given as if from God while he was in his spasms, he eluded the woman’s objections as best he could rather than actually answering them. I believe he had heard—or perhaps had seen (as prophetic seers survived in many places)—those seized by fury giving divine responses. He knew this was an ancient kind of imposture; he knew many had been mocked by such tricks. Furthermore, he had perhaps heard of the meetings with the gods claimed by **Lycurgus**, **Solon**, **Zamolxis**, and **Numa** <note>Postel lists legendary ancient lawmakers who claimed divine inspiration: Lycurgus (Sparta), Solon (Athens), Zamolxis (Thrace), and Numa Pompilius (Rome).</note>. Following their example, he chose to enter the cave for so long, hoping that eventually he would succeed in persuading them. In this, however, he seems to have behaved with little prudence, because he revealed those tricks to certain accomplices of his attempt, from which afterwards, by revealing and betraying itself...

He frequently satisfies these critics in the Quran <note>original: *Alcorano*</note> with responses from angels, and affirms by oath that he has invented nothing. At last, through those distressful illnesses, he managed to appear far holier in public opinion than he actually was, especially when returning from his cave. For those who did not know his life and domestic habits admired him, believing he had met with the gods and was so afflicted by fasting and piety that he suffered such states. Finally, he would add some dream or vision to keep his spectators attentive. Thus, from the 35th year of his life to the 45th, he gradually hunted for a supreme reputation for piety out of a physical defect. And so that God might not seem to be sought from too far away, he constructed a sacred place at home where he held nightly meetings with his followers; he would recite and chant various trifles until a very large gathering of Jews and citizens was formed there. Indeed, he drew many into his way of thinking more easily because he spoke frequently of one God, calling him powerful, wise, just, merciful, and the creator of heaven and earth. He rose up against ethnic <note>pagan</note> religion, claiming that idols could do nothing—they could not see or hear—that they were demons, and that those who believed in them were damned, for God had created all things, and other such things. With these arguments, he enticed the minds of the Jews and terrified the idolaters and citizens of Mecca, so that a good part of them favored him.

## BY WHAT SUPPORTERS HE GATHERED ##
## POWER. CHAPTER VI. ##

A great multitude of Jews, who in every land are searching for their Messiah, were living in Mecca. When they saw that this man said things consistent with their own Law, and was affected in a way beyond the custom of other men, they—thinking no insanity or disease lay beneath it—joined themselves to the man. They began to approve of his decrees all the more easily because he established ceremonies almost entirely at the discretion of the Rabbis. For he agreed with them on frequent ablutions <note>ritual washings</note>; he even prayed for a long time facing the Temple of Jerusalem, which looks to the north from that direction. This continued until the Jews sensed they were being deceived and recognized the tricks of a man aspiring to tyranny—a man who was otherwise plainly insane and raving. For his disease progressed to the point that he barely enjoyed a lucid interval once every many days. 

Wishing to excuse this defect, the authors of the book *Al-Shifa* <note>original: *Assiffai*, a famous biography of Muhammad by Qadi Ayyad</note> say that the prophet so weakened himself with fasts and vigils that his senses failed him, and he was rendered astonished by God, so that he believed he constantly heard a voice calling him, yet when he turned, he saw no one. Frequently telling this to his wife Khadija <note>original: *Hadisæ*</note>, she judged these to be the crafts not of an angel, but of a foul demon, and she considered her husband plainly foolish and out of his mind. He was seized with such grief over this that he wished to throw himself headlong out of a window, preferring to die rather than be seen as a fool. But such an extraordinary prophecy deceived the woman; he claimed that Gabriel was immediately present and said to him: "O Muhammad, God greets you, and through me He wishes it to be signified to you that you shall be the prophet and the most perfect of all creatures." These things are in their own books; by which these wretched people do not see that their own authors are cutting each other's throats. For how could he be a prophet destined from eternity, endowed with light, born circumcised, visited by angels, disemboweled <note>referring to the legendary cleansing of Muhammad's heart by angels</note>, and suffer similar things, when before the fortieth year of his life he had not received word from an angel that he would be a prophet? This book entirely invalidates the chronicle *Al-Fajr* <note>original: *Alfear*</note>, which they approve of most highly. But I return to the Jews. Thinking he would be the Messiah, they joined the man; they instituted sacred rites, and even established an affinity with...

They provided him with secretaries <note>In the original Latin, *homines à secretis*</note> whom they believed to be most excellent, men who were capable of adding to or subtracting from the law themselves. The first of these, named Abdallah ben Salem <note>Abdullah ibn Salam, a historical Jewish convert to Islam, here portrayed by Postel as a deceptive influence</note>, worked with him for seven years. However, wanting to test both the law and the legislator, as he daily recorded the things the impostor dreamed up, he would completely change the rhythms and the rhyming endings <note>original: *finales homophonias*</note> with which the "rhythmic law" <note>Referring to the Quran, which is written in rhymed prose known as *Saj'*</note> abounds. When the prophet recited what he had dictated, he did not notice the secretary’s trickery at all. Consequently, this man left the prophet and returned to Judaism; he became the cause of a great Jewish defection after he exposed the man’s cunning and his profound ignorance. He used to say that such a wicked scoundrel could not possibly be gifted with divine inspiration.

He was succeeded by another Jew who, after testing him for three years, experienced exactly the same thing. For this reason, he urged all the other Jews to defect; they gradually fell away and, having been wretchedly misled, almost all of them returned to their former institutions. For just as they had very easily sworn by his words, they very easily departed—a people greedy for new things who will give their faith to any tyrant, provided he is called a Prophet or a Messiah. The cause of such an easy transition was already clear to them. For the circumcision given to Muhammad by them (which is the starting point for both faiths) and almost everything he had previously learned from various conversations agreed very much with Jewish practices. For he gave nothing else to be written in his books except those things which, having been learned at various times through social interaction, seemed partly consistent with the Law. Or, if he had heard something in a recent conversation, he would save it for another day and enrich it with fables and commentaries so that he would not seem to be claiming the ideas of others as his own.

For about ten or twelve years, therefore, he had Jewish followers from across Arabia (at least those whom his fame had reached). He seemed to satisfy them in many respects. For while he falsely claimed to be the greatest and the last of the prophets, they hoped their Messiah would give laws in the Hebrew language; they frequently objected to why he did not write in another language. To these two arguments he responds: that they would clearly object to the same thing if he wrote in another tongue; and finally, that it was necessary for the Arabs to have their own law written in Arabic. The Egyptians asked that he write in Egyptian; the Persians that he write in Persian.

After the Jews defected—from whom, as from others, he had squeezed much money under the name of <term>alzache</term> <note>Zakat, the Islamic practice of almsgiving or tithing</note>, that is, tithes—he first despoiled the wealthy of their fortunes in the name of religion, and then crushed them all in eleven expeditions, as will be said regarding the war. Meanwhile, seeing that he had gathered great strength from that Jewish addition, and wanting to draw people of other persuasions to his own opinion by any skill, he put forth a divine decree: that any Christian or Jewish slave who wished to become a <term>Mussulman</term> <note>Muslim. Postel notes that Europeans usually translated this word as "Saracen"</note> would be free, even against the will of their masters. He began this with his own slave whom he had at home, named Zeidus <note>Zayd ibn Harithah, Muhammad’s adopted son and former slave</note>, and a very large crowd of fugitives from everywhere followed him.

He did this with the trick of seeing that the reins of power were held by the pagans <note>original: *ethnici*</note>, while the Christians and Jews, as worshippers of one God and strangers to idols, were being pressed with many troubles by impious judges and were mostly harassed by captivities. Those Christians were either Jacobites, or Nestorians <note>Two major Eastern Christian denominations that were prominent in the Middle East during the 7th century</note>, or infected by various heresies. Therefore, in the fortieth year of his life, when his power now appeared formidable, he began to emerge from his house and hiding places and publicly declare himself a prophet. He claimed that the angel Gabriel had divinely brought him the law that year, which would teach men about the unity of God, and which would be a middle path between the Old and New Testaments—a law that would preserve all religions, and one which everyone ought to swear to follow. By this law, it is taught that God is one, that He cares for all things, produces them, and nourishes them, and concerning the im- [pious]...

that He would take vengeance on the wicked and grant rewards to the good; that there would be a future judgment of all men and a resurrection, along with similar precepts gathered from the Old and New Testaments. To establish faith in this persuasion, he gave certain small books to his followers to be recited, sung, and learned by heart; eventually, he would take them all back and hide them away in specific chests and small boxes, from which place he never drew them out again. Thus, if he were asked either to give them out again or to write them down, he would refer them to those seven men in whom, he said, the whole *Quran* <note>original: *Alcoranum*</note> resided. When these men were asked, they would say they knew nothing. When he was earnestly asked by them (for he held them as his most intimate friends) to speak it forth again, he would say that the devil had induced them to forget it. When they began to conceive an adverse opinion of him because of this, he would change his story, saying that God and Gabriel took it from his memory for the purpose of putting better things in its place. But when they demanded the publication of all the "miracles"—for that is what they call all the verses <note>original: *periodos*; Postel notes that Muslims consider the literary quality of the Quranic verses to be a miracle</note> of the *Quran*—lest his ignorance and tricks be exposed to everyone, he would say that God did not wish it to be published before all the precepts had come down from heaven. Thus, while he was living, nothing of that law was publicly released; instead, everything was preserved for posterity in many small boxes, and much was gnawed away by mice—would that it had all been so. But I return to the story. To those seven men was also added Abu Bakr <note>original: *Hubecharus*</note>, a most powerful citizen of Mecca, who abandoned the worship of idols and whose daughter Muhammad married. He was followed by Umar ibn al-Khattab <note>original: *Homar alhatabus*</note>, likewise almost the leading man of the city, who immediately also became a son-in-law to Muhammad. Likewise Hamza <note>original: *Hamzaus Alabezus*</note> and Ali <note>original: *Haly Butelibus*</note>, his kinsmen; and all were made "circumcised ones" <note>original: *appellae*; a classical Latin term for Jews, used here to suggest they adopted Jewish-style rites</note> on the same day and gave their names to the prophet. Therefore, he was increased by their favors (for they were very influential among the citizens), the law was publicly preached, and a sedition arose. For the idolaters judged that these men, greedy for novelty, should be removed from their midst, and that this false prophet, driven by demons, should be killed. Nine of his brothers offered themselves as leaders to that opposing faction; and in truth, unless he had been regarded as if he were insane and a fool, he would have been killed. However, that highest sense of equity restrained them, as they judged it a shameful thing to do away with a man who was mad and foolish. And so, the spirits of the multitude gradually subsided, but the persuasion began to creep further abroad, insinuating itself partly openly and partly in secret, up until the 53rd year of his life—specifically 13 years from the publicizing of the persuasion. But when he saw that he was not free to debate the changing of religion in Mecca, he took some companions—namely Abu Bakr, his nephew Ali, and a certain Zayd <note>original: *Zeido*</note>—and betook himself to the neighboring city of *Echeheph* <note>likely Ta’if</note>, where he publicly professed the name of prophet. From there, moving back and forth, now returning to Mecca, now wandering through the villages and neighboring provinces, he disseminated his teachings to the unrefined and rustic multitude for an entire decade. And he carried out the business in such a way that there was almost no house in which he did not have a follower. After the decade had passed, when he was in *Alabach*, a place in Arabia, sixty men who were robbers and greedy for new things joined him. They said that the Quran should no longer be preached in secret in the most famous place in all Arabia where the prophet was born, but that the religion of God ought to be introduced publicly and by the lead of the sword. The prophet agreed; he followed them, and they rushed into the tower of *Al-Qibla* <note>The Kaaba in Mecca</note> (of which I have already spoken), threw down the sacred objects of the idols, and put the worshippers to flight; they killed anyone who opposed their attempts. Once the temple was occupied, the prophecy was recited and heard until, a riot having been stirred up, Muhammad was driven from the place. Nor were they satisfied with having cast the seditious man out of the sacred place; they were even going to burn his house down, had he not fled. Seeking safety in flight, he went to the city of Yathrib <note>original: *Ietribam*; modern Medina</note>, which lies toward the northern part of Arabia Felix, a journey of three days from Mecca. There he spent about three years—or as others say, six—wandering with his companions in the neighboring regions.

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD #

... until, having gathered a larger force, he attacked the city of Mecca with great strength and captured it, plundering its citizens of all their fortunes. This period, which flowed from his exile to his return, the Arabs call the *Hijra* <note>original: *alhigera*; the migration of Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE, marking the start of the Islamic calendar</note>, that is, "the exile," and they calculate their accounts of time from this first year. For although he had already been a "prophet" thirteen years earlier, nevertheless the true time and beginning of the law was when his persuasion was introduced into Mecca, the idol was cast down, and the tower <note>likely referring to the Kaaba</note> was demolished and rebuilt. The leader of the expedition was Achmar <note>likely a reference to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab or a similar early commander</note>, who with drawn sword was the first to make a way for that law. He was followed by many others, but especially by those who had sworn an oath to the words of the prophet before the exile. For they too had been driven out because of their faction. The fortunes of all the other citizens were made common to these men, with a fifth part reserved in the name of the prophet.

There is a great deal of discord among their authors regarding in which year of the exile he gained possession of Mecca, which leads me to believe it was captured and lost several times. For some say in the second year, some the third, others the fourth, and thus by doubting they arrive as far as the eighth year, in which he established sacred and profane <note>meaning "secular" or "civil"</note> magistrates in the city. In the thirteenth day of the month of Ramadan, Mu'adh <note>original: *Moadus*</note> was therefore appointed governor of the city in the name of the prophet, to ensure the recently established sacred rites were observed. Meanwhile, while he [Muhammad] besieged the neighboring city of Cambichum, lest any movement arise in Mecca, he sent Abu Bakr <note>original: *Vbecharum*</note> there, whom we have mentioned, and entrusted the care of the republic to him. Among other things, he was to take care that no one be admitted into the city except the initiated; those who wished to receive the law were admitted on that condition. He also saw to it that the prophet's treasury was supplied so that there would be enough for the expeditions.

Matters were confirmed for him in this way. Great ease was also added to his affairs. For when he traveled through the countrysides, villages, and villas, he was so hostile regarding that law that those who did not give tribute or their names to the "persuasion" were endangered in both fortune and body; those who believed and joined him enjoyed immunity (except for what was paid to the treasury). By these arts, it happened that a great multitude of people came to him daily. Fear urged some; others feigned repentance; countless plunderers and those harassing their neighbors joined him, and many of those were most desperate men. Thus, in a very short time, a great army coalesced, and the dregs of society increased to such an immense degree that he not infrequently complains in the *Quran* <note>original: *Alcorano*</note> that there are more followers than is proper, and that they come for the sake of a living rather than for the sake of fighting.

Thus, neither under him nor without him was anything safe. By these arts, by these allies, and in this manner, he prepared his power. But we must deal with a few of his followers whose doctrine he used. The authors of the *Suras* <note>original: *Assuar*; Postel refers to the chapters of the Quran or chronicles associated with them</note> mention two Christian men who lived in his vicinity, hiring out their services to a certain sword-maker. It is believed he used their company when he was writing the Meccan chapters—that is, the sections of the *Quran* written in Mecca. For they had certain very small principles of the New Testament, which he wrote into various places, though expanded indeed with innumerable fables. More than once in the *Quran* he excuses this crime: saying that he had no teacher, and that the text is so elegantly composed that in the whole world nothing similar could be written except by God.

How many Jews he had as advisors has now become sufficiently clear. Certain men of our own religion, living close to those centuries, left it written that a certain fugitive monk named Sergius, corrupted by the vice of **Nestorius** <margin>Of Nestorius</margin> <note>Nestorius was a 5th-century bishop whose controversial views on Christ's nature led to his exile; Postel links this "heresy" to the origins of Islam</note>, betook himself there when he was being prosecuted in Constantinople for violating our religion. It is said he made the man [Muhammad] a semi-Christian, and by the persuasion of the Jews induced him to delete many things written against Christ. I more willingly lend credit to this narrative because those Christians who write these things were of the highest authority, and wrote at almost the same time and were similarly learned; hence, it is not to be believed that they raised false objections. However, their histories do not mention him, so far as I have read, nor does any work of a refined man in

->WITH WHOM HE JOINED IN AFFINITY.<-
->CHAPTER VII.<-

Such was the lustfulness of this impostor that he seems to have wanted nothing more from his friends than women, if any appeared of a more elegant form. The first was she who has already been mentioned, whom they call Hadijah <note>original: *Hadeiam*; Muhammad’s first wife</note>, the witness to the whole story, by whose wealth he acquired power. Besides her, when he reached the height of affairs, he took fifteen other wives, or at least eleven, and as many concubines as he wished, whom he boasted of entering in a single hour. He claimed that no bull could enter more cows in one day than he, by "prophetic virtue," could work upon women. Of his immoderate lust, there is no clearer example than that he took Aisha <note>original: *Assam*; referring to Muhammad’s wife Aisha</note>, daughter of Abu Bakr <note>original: *Vbechari*</note>, when she was eight years old; having accepted her as his betrothed, and respecting neither the laws of nature nor the tender age of the infant, as soon as he saw the beauty of the maiden, he loosened the girdle of Venus <note>a classical metaphor for the consummation of marriage</note>, in a "prophetic" manner indeed.

But while I wish to touch upon his vices, I am drawn away in so many different directions that I do not know where to begin, for I am overwhelmed by the mass of them. Therefore, the end of his life must be concluded. Finally, the crimes of this wicked man must be treated in certain places and arguments. Having put Abu Bakr in charge of Mecca, as we said, he conquered the neighboring regions with a formidable army and ordered them to obey the laws, and forced incursions as far as Persia, Syria, and Egypt with his spread power. He also relied on the power of the petty kings of Armenia, who laid waste to neighboring territories with incursions into the borders of Coele-Syria. 

But the greatest opportunity of all, it seems to me, was given to him to increase his power by our own error and sluggishness. For I am easily led to believe that, because of the monstrous crimes usually committed by many of ours under the pretext of piety, this plague undermined the minds of all and was raised up by Satan, with God's permission, as a punishment for crimes. Thus I am easily persuaded that even an ungodly soldiery was not lacking to him, deserting from our side. The wound was then fresh; the Church, having barely expelled the pus, had come into the hope of a cure. Barely breathing after the "monsters" of the Arians, Nestorians, Eunomians, Ebionites, Pelagians, Donatists <note>various groups declared heretical by the early Church</note>, and six hundred such types, it had just first gathered its breath. Hardly any were legitimately confirmed in the outer regions when, before the scar had even closed, this plague arose, into which whatever ruin and error had ever been devised flowed together, as if into the Augean stable <note>original: *Augiæ stabulum*; a reference to the Greek myth of a stable filled with enormous amounts of filth</note> and a sewer. 

To this (as if Satan had done too little by weakening minds), the sluggishness of Emperor Heraclius brought the greatest loss of all fortunes. For while he hunts by day and wenches by night, plays at dice, makes a trial of the art of Apicius <note>original: *Apitij*; refers to Marcus Gavius Apicius, a Roman gourmet, implying the Emperor was focused on gluttony</note>, effeminates the whole mass of the empire by his example, remits the duties of the soldiers, and squanders the treasury among whores, adulterers, flatterers, and triflers—to say it briefly, since he carried all his counsels in a single head, about 600 years after the suffering of Christ...

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD #

...Chosroes, the King of the Persians, attacked Syria, Egypt, Africa, and the other provinces of the Empire that were left without protection. He conquered them and proceeded from Babylon all the way to the Mauritanias <note>Modern-day Morocco and Algeria</note> with no one resisting him. His son attacked Thrace from the north. Yet, the Emperor <note>Heraclius, reigned 610–641 AD</note> was not roused from his lethargy until his nobles threatened that unless he showed himself a man, they would look elsewhere for a leader. They claimed the Empire was finished unless help arrived within a few days, and that a "bought peace" should not be expected at home, which the barbarian would not even sell from as far away as Carthage. To this was added a great shame pressing upon the Christian name: with Jerusalem overturned, the most holy Cross of Jesus Christ had fallen into the hands of enemies. They warned that God would be the avenger of their laziness unless they were roused to quench the fire consuming the world. They argued that great empires are permitted by God specifically so that we might subdue the proud and aid the oppressed.

Moved by these words, the Emperor gathered the largest army he could, destroyed the forces of Chosroes' son, and, relying on this recent victory, approached the very heart of the barbarian empire. Crossing Mesopotamia, he sought out Chaldea. Struck by this unexpected movement, the barbarian abandoned Africa and returned home at a most rapid pace; he who a little while ago was thinking of imposing laws upon the world was now forced to be anxious for his own altars and hearths. As he was returning with a massive force, Heraclius met him, overthrew the enemy, recovered the Cross, and dictated laws to the vanquished, which he obeyed. Thus, Heraclius, exulting with the sacred gift <note>The True Cross</note>, sought Jerusalem, and having restored the temple, he replaced the sign of our redemption. 

When these things were finished, now exhausted—as if he had traveled the entire circuit of the world itself and no enemy remained in the whole world—he dismissed his soldiers in the middle of Syria, far from their homes. These men, reduced to the utmost poverty by the scarcity of resources, were forced to harass those they had come to preserve. A soldier driven to desperation looks not for those he can help, but for those he can harm. Every wicked and audacious man becomes a most approved leader to desperate men. Aided by these wandering soldiers, it seems to me that Muhammad <note>original: *Muhamedes*</note> acquired such great power. For it could not have happened without the help of veteran and trained soldiers that "naked Arabs" <note>A common European trope of the period, underestimating the tactical skill of the early Arab armies</note> could conquer I know not how many well-fortified cities in Syria, Persia, and Egypt. 

A greater ease was added to this: when the rumor of the Imperial army was heard, everything was filled with trembling. Strengths were broken, affairs were afflicted, and the Roman magistrates were removed. Chosroes could not substitute his own men for them, nor did the Emperor, given over to sluggishness and idleness, care to restore them. All these things seem to me to have provided Muhammad a great opportunity for attempting a revolution. However the matter stands, he gained possession of Arabia and its borders. To make the soldiers more spirited, there was frequent reading of the Quran <note>original: *Alcorani*</note>. Pilgrimages were also frequently made. He wrote three chapters in the Quran concerning military law: that he who is killed in the war of God <note> Jihad </note> will be entirely happy. He claimed the dead wish to return to life only so that they might die again. He taught that all things belong to the faithful soldiers and the prophet; as for others who refuse to believe, they must either be killed, driven into slavery, or at least have their goods plundered. 

Three times he set out on a journey with an army, approaching the temple of Mecca <note>original: *Mechae*</note> and performing those sacred rites which were accustomed to be done by the ancestors. For as he was a "shrewd shifter" <note>original: *versipellis*, literally "one who changes skin," implying a deceitful or crafty person</note>, he borrowed certain ceremonies from the Jews as long as he could retain their support. Yet, so that he might also retain the Gentiles through ceremonies, he took care to perform the same things around the tower of Alquibla <note>Referring to the Kaaba or the direction of prayer</note> in the name of God that had been customary to do in honor of idols. Furthermore, from the time he became an exile—either because he did not dare to, out of a conscience of his evil deeds (and indeed he rightly feared ambushes), or because he did not want to live in Mecca among a people aware of his crimes and madness—he went to the city of Yathrib <note>original: *Iefrab*; modern Medina</note>, which had been destroyed a little before by the incursions of robbers and was inhabited by a few Jews. There he remained when he was at home, having cast out from his possession (even before Mecca was conquered) a ward who was the son of a certain smith...

...from his rival, whose house, estates, and courtyard he occupied. Once his seat was established there, he saw to it that a **mosque** <note>original: "Mesgedam", from the Arabic *masjid*</note> was built, in which the **Quran** would be read. He died in that same city in the 63rd year of his age, seized so violently by his **falling sickness** <note>original: "fontico morbo"; Renaissance authors frequently attributed Muhammad's visions to epilepsy</note> that, with his muscles contracted, all his limbs seemed to take on a circular shape, especially the fingers. From this, certain "excellent" interpreters of his signs even interpreted that it was permitted for his followers to engage in **unnatural vice** <note>original: "præpostero scelere"; a polemical reference to sodomy</note>. Therefore, those among them who are insane and most like the Prophet, and who satisfy their lust with all animals, are believed to be the holiest. Furthermore, that he was also driven by a demon—besides being charged against him two hundred times, as he never fails to repeat in the Quran—was also demonstrated by the catastrophe of his life's end. 

For if he had devised his impostures entirely with human cunning and prudence, he would never have predicted that he would **rise again on the third day**; rather, he would have taken care to vanish immediately in the manner of the ancient gods. But by his own command, his body was exposed in the open air for three days in expectation of the resurrection, until the stench drove everyone away. The corpse was thrown out of the city during a riot, and all the common people, having been deceived, returned to their former rites until they were brought back by the "hereditary soldier" <note>likely referring to Abu Bakr, the first Caliph</note>, whom they call the "Soldier of God," and were forced to pay tribute. For **Abu Bakr** <note>original: "Vbecharus"</note>, who succeeded him, said that he had left a large sum of money in his will for the soldiers who would confirm the religion. By this plague of robbers, all of **Arabia** and **Syria**, and even all of **Africa**, is afflicted today; so much so that no one can ever travel there safely unless they are in a **caravan**, as they call it—that is, in such a large company that they cannot be terrified by raids. For any robber or most desperate man is allowed to call himself a "soldier of God" and seize everyone’s property. Every year, the most powerful Prince of the Turks <note>The Ottoman Sultan</note> is forced to give pay to 60,000 of these men so that they do not harass the farmers or infect the cultivated provinces. 

The Prophet's corpse, having been cast out of the city, was cared for by his close relatives **Ali**, and **Zayd**, and several others, who saw to its burial; they embalmed it and placed it in a certain crypt in the **Mosque of Yathrib** <note>original: "Mesgeda Iezrab"; Yathrib is the ancient name for Medina</note>, and not in the temple of **Mecca**, as is commonly rumored. Thus, every year, when Mecca is visited for the sake of pilgrimage, one must first go to **Medina Alnabi** <note>The City of the Prophet</note>, that is, to the city of the prophet, Yathrib, where the body is kept. Finally, for the memory of the sacrifice of **Abraham**, they visit Mecca, where they also fulfill vows in two places: in the city at the **Al-Qibla** tower, and on a certain mountain nearby where they throw stones behind them, by which they are persuaded the demon is put to flight. I will recount his military expeditions when I speak of the origin of the empire.

### ON THE MIRACLES OF MUHAMMAD, CHAPTER VIII ###

Prudent philosophers, when they consider by what reason men give their assent to absurd things placed outside the laws of reason, usually first inquire by what deed they were persuaded. They can certainly be satisfied by many reasons. Muhammad, after he had publicly turned his hidden illness into a reputation for holiness, did not try to join himself to men skilled in affairs, but to the artisans in the cities and the rude and stupid people in the fields, all of whom he laughed at even while catching them with trifles. He calls them the **Fools** <note>original: "Supheha", from the Arabic *sufaha’*</note> and the **Arabs** <note>original: "Ahrab", referring here to Bedouins</note>—simpletons and rustics—whom he nevertheless used first for carrying out raids from ambushes and then for waging just wars. With their help, he despoiled parents of their fortunes because they would not subscribe to his absurd nonsense. He broke, plundered, and despoiled the rebelling Jews and subdued his enemies. 

The second reason is the folly and supine ignorance of all the common people, who, without any discussion, receive and approve whatever is said, and all the more so the more absurd it is. From this, one may gather the absurdity of these follies. For even the rustics themselves laughed at him, calling him sometimes a "poet" (that is, a mere writer of rhymes), sometimes an "impostor," and sometimes a "demoni-

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD #

...robber, <note>original: "latro"; this catchword connects to the previous page's description of Muhammad's followers as bandits.</note> naming him with titles of this kind. He greatly concealed their gullibility—a charge leveled against them a hundred times—and claimed instead that there was a disease in their souls. The reason they followed the man was that, besides the reasons I brought up earlier, he also promised to make them exempt from the **royal treasury** <note>original: "fisco"; referring to the state tax system of the Byzantine and Persian empires</note>. For since they were oppressed by the whims of petty rulers—and there are no common people who do not necessarily give something to the treasury—the poor wretches thought that liberty and tax-exemption would immediately arrive from heaven. 

Therefore, even when he was pressing them most heavily, he always had this on his lips: "Follow the prophet, follow those who do not ask a reward from you, and who are favored." Enticed by that expectation, and driven by both fear and hope, they all abandoned their own princes or republics.

There was also another, and more urgent reason. Since no nation in the whole world is softer, more effeminate, or more prone to lust than that race, he wanted to applaud the vices of all. For when the plurality of wives was charged against him—which was not allowed by the law of the land, where sometimes one wife had twelve husbands—he said it was permitted for the **Prophet** <note>original: "Machometus"</note> to take them in whatever number he wished. And for that reason, he said God had spoken, so that private citizens might have four, or as many as they could support and rule, who could be divorced and taken back according to certain laws. 

Furthermore, when he was charged with illicit intercourse with maidservants and female slaves against the law of the land, he sanctioned it as if by divine law, so that it was likewise permitted to anyone. For he said that the slaves themselves are a man's money: and therefore, as if the soil in the maidservants were **arable** <note>Postel is using a metaphor common in polemical literature to describe sexual access to slaves</note>. If anyone had committed any most shameful vice, provided he was a **Muslim** <note>original: "Mussulman"</note>, and was washed, he would be clean, and God would be favorable to the "faithful" (for so he calls his own in the Arabic tongue, whom we call **Saracens** <note>original: "Saracenos"</note>, a term unknown in their own literature). 

He did indeed institute a **forty-day fast** <note>original: "Quadragesimam"; referring to the month of Ramadan</note>. But lest it be too burdensome, and as if God were the God of the day and not the night, he wanted the nighttime gluttony to compensate until dawn. In short, whatever was pleasing to lust, the belly, or shameful parts, he wanted to permit to all as if with God as the author. It is no wonder that men devoted to luxury were enticed by these opportunities. 

Yet, the far greatest cunning and trickery of the scoundrel was added to this. Since he called himself a prophet, his followers would object: "All the holy prophets were most famous for miracles; therefore, you should show some specimen of divine familiarity, show some miracle, and we will follow you." If he were pressed, he would say that he was not God, that miracles belonged to God alone, and that he was only a forewarner and a preacher. There were others who said both. He would reply that God did not want him to perform miracles because in previous times they had been rejected and slandered: or lest they believe him to be God and worship him, he ought to do nothing else than remind them of miracles, and of the **Book of God** <note>original: "libri Dei"; Postel notes that Muhammad uses this term to refer to natural and man-made things as signs of the Creator</note>, and speak words about the Day of Judgment, and of **Paradise**, and **Hell**. 

Furthermore, as often as he dealt with Paradise, he suited himself to the character of the listener. For in six hundred places he asserted that his followers would experience all the pleasures of the body. But when he saw that nevertheless there were many whom he could not satisfy with these tricks and trifles unless he produced something unusual when they discussed miracles, he also professed that he had performed many miracles through his words. From their number, O wise reader, as God may love you, weigh these carefully. For he said that he had done so much: and if he had done it, judge how worthy it would be of a divine man.

The first I have already recounted: when he was five years old, he was disemboweled by the angel **Gabriel**, and his heart being torn out, a **black portion** <note>original: "particula nigra"; a reference to the Islamic tradition of the *Inshirah al-Sadr* (the opening of the chest to remove the "portion of Satan")</note> was removed, by which men are tempted, and then it was replaced. He saw it, felt it, and told his nurse; she believed him and recounted it to great men, who wrote it down. See whether a man can judge this to be happening to himself, even if it were done: and if it were done, weigh the effect and the witness of the miracle. How was he not afterwards tempted by the devil, when for his whole life he was occupied by him, a **robber**...

<summary>Postel argues that Muhammad gained followers by promising tax exemptions and religious sanction for polygamy and sensuality, while avoiding the demand for miracles by claiming to be a simple "warner." He begins to critique the specific miracle of Muhammad's heart being purified by the angel Gabriel.</summary>

Postel aims to use these stories to illustrate what he considers to be the absurdity of the faith.</meta>
