...robber, fratricide, a stirrer of rebellion, an impostor, treacherous, lustful, and so on. Hear another [tale], reader, and restrain your laughter if you can. For I certainly cannot. Since on a certain day he was wandering alone (for all these things were done while he was existing and present alone) and he wished to relieve his bowels <note>original: "cacare"; Postel uses crude language here to mock the dignity of the event</note>—let there be honor to your ears, but words similar to the deeds are appropriate here—his head was being scorched by the heat of the sun. He therefore commanded that the trees which he saw should provide shade for him while he was purging his body. Immediately, they were torn up by the roots and came running to him, and they provided shade for the "prophetic defecation"; indeed, once the defecation was completed, they sought out their original places again. Is this not a great miracle, and worthy of such a prophet? It certainly is. And lest you think I have made this up, this is written in the books of the **Sunnah** <note>original: "Suneh"; the body of traditional social and legal custom and practice of the Islamic community</note>, which is of almost greater authority than the **Quran** <note>original: "Alcoranũ"</note> itself—as are the following stories.

The third [miracle] is not dissimilar. For when he was sixteen years old and was given to **Khadija** <note>original: "Hadegę"; Muhammad’s first wife</note> to care for her camels, he says that when he was alone and his head was greatly scorched by the sun's heat, a cloud immediately appeared at his command. Walking with him all day, it protected him from the injuries of the sun. Judge for yourself this arbitrary movement of the clouds.

I come to the fourth. When he was in the cave to elude the opinion that he suffered from a disease <note>Postel refers to the polemical claim that Muhammad’s revelations were actually epileptic seizures</note>, Gabriel came to him and brought him that Law <note>The Quran</note>, which, as we shall see, perished having been issued almost piece by piece over twenty-three years.

In the fifth miracle, the rocks, mountains, trees, and birds spoke to him as he returned from the cave after he had heard Gabriel. By this trick, he even wished to elude the beginning of his madness, since he perceived himself being called from all sides. This was also presented to Khadija.

The sixth is altogether memorable. When a certain **Abu Jahl** <note>original: "Bugellinus"; likely a Latinization of Abu Jahl, a prominent Meccan opponent of Muhammad in traditional accounts</note>, his kinsman, always rejected those trifles which he was preaching, he finally said: "If you perform that miracle which I am thinking of, O Muhammad, I shall become a **Muslim** <note>original: "Musfulman"</note>." To him he replied, "I will do it; only tell me what it is." The other said, "Make it so that the moon descends from heaven and is divided into two equal parts; let one half enter through your sleeves, the right into the right and the left into the left; finally, let it emerge whole from your chest and return to heaven." Having been asked, he does it: the moon is split, enters the sleeves, and returns solid from his chest. Yet that man refuses to believe, but says it is a manifest incantation. There you have a miracle! The moon—the twenty-seventh part of the earth, serving the whole world—without anyone noticing except for two men, enters a man's sleeves. These things are clearly worthy of both the author and those who believe them.

Listen patiently, kind reader: I shall add two more. When on a certain day he was making a journey alone, a tree trunk was in the middle of the road, and the prophet had to turn aside a little to the side of the path; lest he should have to do so, the trunk was split down the middle, giving place to the prophet as he passed through, and then immediately it closed itself back up of its own accord. 

Another: When he had been banished, on the night he was to depart, a palm trunk in the middle of his house, which had been watered by him, wept at the prophet's departure. All the Muslims who were called saw this. 

When his adversaries were waiting for him as he fled, lying in wait in a certain place, lest he should be seen, he placed ash upon the heads of the horses, and he was not seen by his enemies. He used to narrate that these things were done for him and by him.

But why do we suffer a penury of miracles, when all the "periods" of the Quran are called **Ayat** <note>original: "Aiet"; meaning "verses" or "signs/miracles"</note>, that is, miracles? Was not Gabriel present for twenty-three whole years, giving fragments of the law? Was it not a great miracle when his primary women had caught him even in adultery—after he had ten times sworn oaths of fidelity—and Gabriel brought a law by which it was permitted to the prophet to do whatever he pleased? And that the prophet ought not to depend on women, for he would have others from elsewhere if these were unwilling to stay? What is more distinguished than the miracle by which God gave to the prophet the wife of **Zayd** <note>original: "Zeidi"</note>, his own servant, and announced that he should divorce her, since no one ought to have a wife who pleased the prophet? Are these not truly divine miracles? 

Recover your senses, O wretched ones, recover your senses, and finally acknowledge the imposture committed against you. The remaining miracles will be noted as we run through the individual **Surahs** <note>original: "Asuar"; the chapters of the Quran</note>, that is, the canticles...

<header>ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD</header>

...and the psalms of the Quran. But lest the memory of by far the most famous of all miracles should escape me (for I had almost forgotten it), since enough of them present themselves in the Quran, I wish to add this one below.

In Chapter or **Surah** <note>original: "fora"; Postel’s term for the chapters of the Quran</note> 16 of the Quran, which is called *Banu Israel*, that is, the Children of Israel, it is written thus: "Glory be to Him who transported His servant by night from the Sacred Temple, that is, of Mecca, to the Furthest Temple, that is, the holy place of Jerusalem." <note>original: "Sobhan illedi asrai bihe bdihi leilan min elmesgedi ilharani, illai mesgedi elacza"; this is the opening verse of Surah 17, which Postel numbers as 16</note>. On this passage the interpreters agree, and it is supported by the **Sunnah** <note>original: "Hassear & Suneh"; referencing the Sira (biography) and Hadith traditions</note>, that it refers to a certain great and immense miracle. Hear then a narration worthy of Apollo <note>A classical reference meaning a story so grand or strange it requires divine inspiration—or, ironically, a tall tale</note>. On a certain night, when he was sleeping deeply around the third hour before dawn, he was roused by a great blow and rose from the lodging of his wife **Aisha** <note>original: "Hasse"</note> in **Medina** <note>original: "Almedina"</note>, which is also called **Yathrib** <note>original: "Iefrab"</note>. Immediately, having opened the door, he sees Gabriel in the public street with 70 snow-white wings, and with an animal called **Alborach** <note>The Buraq, the celestial steed of the prophets</note>, which was also pure white. Gabriel said to him: "Come, Muhammad, I will show you the secrets of heaven; mount Alborach." But Alborach, having the form of a donkey, said: "I will never allow him to mount me." Gabriel said: "Permit it; Muhammad is the greatest of creatures, and he will make it so that you are the happiest of animals, because you shall be the first to enter paradise." 

Taken up, he is carried to Jerusalem. On this journey there were two women who called out to Muhammad, whom the angel forbade him to answer. For it would have happened that if he had answered the first, all **Muslims** <note>original: "Mussulmani"</note> would have been Jews, for she was the one who had spread the law of the Jews; and if he had answered the second, they would have been Christians. In the temple, he met all the prophets, who asked that he might pray for them, which he did in the **Mihrab** <note>original: "Machrib"; likely referring to the prayer niche or the inner sanctum</note>, that is, the Holy of Holies. Finally, upon leaving the temple, a ladder was offered from the temple gate all the way to the highest heaven. They climbed it, and from there the prophet reported these things: In the first heaven, which was made of silver and from which stars hang by golden chains, was Adam, who commended himself to Muhammad's prayers. There were all kinds of living creatures there, with angels praying for the earthly animals. There was a rooster there larger than the whole world, which, when it crows, causes the earthly roosters to crow. In the second heaven, which was of gold, was Noah. In the third, made of precious stone, was Abraham. In the fourth, made of emerald, was Moses; and finally **Yahya** <note>original: "Iachie"</note>, that is, John the Baptist. All of these prayed that Muhammad would intercede for them before God. In the seventh heaven, he found Christ, whom Muhammad asked to pray for *him*. 

Thus Muhammad approached God, within a bow-shot <note>original: "iactum balistæ"; a reference to Quran 53:9 describing the closeness of the divine encounter</note>, as he says in a certain **Surah** called *The Star* <note>original: "Negium", i.e., An-Najm</note>; and he asserts that he fabricated nothing, even when everyone laughed at him. There he spoke with God familiarly and obtained certain gifts, which I will add immediately. This is the sum of the matter and the major points. For if I wished to hand down how many absurdities are there, and the angels who have 700,000,000 heads, and to follow similar trifles in detail, a very large book of nonsense would certainly be made of it. And he found those who would believe these things! He confirmed that vision to his followers by the privileges granted to him by God, which I subjoin: First, that he should be the first of all men. Second, that he should be the most honored of all the sons of Adam. Third, that he should be called the general redeemer. Fourth, that he should know all languages, though he barely knew one. 

Fifth, that all the spoils of war or plunder should be his. This "miraculous" power alienated not a few from the sect. Now I must move on from miracles to other things. For I have indicated enough of these so that it may become known with what stupid judgment he must have been possessed to thrust these things forward, and how crude were those who received them. But the most stupid of all are those who wished to commit them to writing. There are six hundred similar things in the **Sunnah**. The book on the doctrine of the prophet, the Chronicles, and the **traditions** <note>original: "mashod"; likely referring to the *Ma'thud* or *Mashhad*, collections of witnessed reports</note>—in short, 700 approved books—teem with these absurdities.

## CONCERNING THE CEREMONIES
### instituted by MUHAMMAD. CHAPTER IX.

Although these matters seem to have little weight in refuting falsehood, and little to do with our specific purpose, they nevertheless seem worth touching upon for many reasons. For the common people and the unrefined are most easily captured by those forms of worship which are external; and, like **larger apes** <note>A common 16th-century metaphor for those who imitate outward actions without understanding their inner meaning</note>, they are more easily led into that which they understand the least. I shall therefore touch upon these rituals, not in their full extent—for that would be an endless undertaking—but insofar as they are common to all, and insofar as Muhammad wished to differ from us, even though he sought the examples for all these things from our own traditions.

I believe I can quite aptly begin with marriage, since it is there that the beginning of a human being lies. In this, Muhammad wished to agree with neither the Jews nor the Christians. For neither of those groups marries without the blessing of a priest. He, however, assigns or divorces a wife by the authority of a **Qadi** <note>original: "Cadhi"; an Islamic judge</note>, that is, a judge. All men marry, except for certain holy men and those devoted to religion; yet even these, if they wish, are permitted to draw back from their profession.

A child, once born, is raised by the mother or a nurse, according to the state of their fortune and the self-restraint of the man. For they are not accustomed to have intercourse with pregnant women. On this account, the interpreters of the law say that many wives are permitted. In the 14th year of his age, just like **Ishmael** <note>The son of Abraham, regarded as the ancestor of the Arabs; the Bible describes him being circumcised as a teenager rather than an infant</note>, the boy is circumcised, so that they do not coincide with the Jews on the eighth day. Otherwise, they say that one is purified and saved by daily washings—even if overtaken by death—lest they coincide with the Christians in having only a single baptism.

Indeed, almost everything among them consists in washings. For before the daily prayers, the soiled limbs—the face, hands, and arms along with the legs—are washed. At the Friday prayer, the whole body is washed. After passing urine, or gas, or semen, or any other waste, it is necessary to wash. Therefore, both women and men are frequently in the baths, and especially on Fridays.

In prayer, the **Muslim** <note>original: "Mussulmanus"</note> differs from the Jew. For those who follow the Mosaic law pray for the most part once a day, or twice on a solemn day. Christians pray seven times; the Muhammadans pray five times: before dawn, at noon, at the third hour after noon, at the evening hour, and at the first watch of the night.

The sacred day in the week for the Jew is the Sabbath; for the Christian it is the first day, which they call the Lord's Day; for the Muhammadan it is Friday. They have a "Septuagesima" <note>A Christian liturgical period preceding Lent; Postel uses it here to categorize the Islamic fasting period</note> in their greater fast, while Christians have Lent in their lesser; the Muhammadans observe this for thirty days <note>A reference to the month of Ramadan</note>. Jews and Christians eat food only once and at a single hour; the Muslim grants the entire night to his belly after the fast.

Christians pray toward the East because of Jerusalem; Jews pray toward the West for a certain reason; Muslims pray toward the South because of **Mecca**. For from **Yathrib** <note>original: "Iefrab"</note>, which is **Medina** <note>original: "Medinat alnabi", meaning 'City of the Prophet'</note>, Mecca lies toward the South. Christians have a solar year, the Hebrews a mixed one, and the Moors <note>A term often used by Postel to refer to Muslims in general</note> a lunar one. Thus their **Passover** <note>original: "pascha"; here referring to the Eid festival</note> happens at any time of the year, during which they forgive one another with a kiss of the hands; Christians do so with a word and communion, and Jews with unleavened bread.

Christians are carried out for burial at the feet; two others at the head. The corpse of a Jew sits; the Muhammadan lies in a spacious place, while the Christian lies in a narrow one. The Jew prays for the deceased; the Muslim prays and eats with the poor; the Christian prays and bestows alms.

For pilgrimages, the four months immediately before and after the **festival** <note>original: "behiram"; likely referring to Eid al-Adha</note>, that is, the Passover, are designated. Passover recalls for the Jews the crossing of the Red Sea; for the Christian, the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ, the Man-God; among the Arabs, it marks the origin of the law. Thus, while he took the greatest care not to agree with other religions, he enticed those **simpletons** <note>original: "supheha"; from the Arabic 'sufaha' meaning fools or the ignorant</note> and the unskilled, who were the beginning of the first multitude. But now we must come to the law,

->and to their prescriptions: so that we may see upon what authorities,<-
->and by what petitions, these things rest.<-

<meta>This page continues Postel’s polemical examination of the foundations of Islam. # CONCERNING THE QURAN, THE SUNNAH, AND OTHER
## books of the Muslims, and their approval.
### CHAPTER X.

We have already sufficiently shown how, for the sake of deceiving his wife Khadija, and because of his **falling sickness** <note>original: "morbi sontici"; a term often used in this period to refer to epilepsy. Christian polemicists frequently attributed Muhammad's visions to epileptic seizures</note>, Muhammad used to enter a cave and report dreams as if they were divine responses. It is accepted among them that he received the whole law in a single night; although elsewhere he contradicts himself, saying that he received it little by little. Moreover, if he received it at Mecca, as it is written, then a large part of it must (according to their own logic) be false. For a great portion was written in Medina, as is evident from the titles of the chapters—especially those pertaining to plunder, theft, and the laws of war. Therefore, it cannot be entirely divine if it is said to have been received in Mecca. If, however, that Gabriel gave it on that "fortunate day" in Yathrib <note>original: "Iezrab"; the pre-Islamic name for Medina</note> (for many disagree as to where it is said to have been given), then the greatest part of it is not from him, for it was written in Mecca, and thus not given by Gabriel. Furthermore, if it is said to have been given bit by bit and in fragments, then it contains a frequent lie within itself: namely, that it was received in a single night or day. But however the matter stands, it was not published while he was alive, lest its truth be called into question. Indeed, those small books, after they were taken down by a scribe and committed to memory by certain people, he used to hide away in various small chests, sometimes in holes in the walls, or elsewhere; from which places they were later collected and repeated when the Law was compiled. 

Truly, he promulgated two kinds of precepts and laws: either general laws or special privileges. He granted privileges only to himself, while imposing laws on everyone else. But before I proceed from this point, I wish to touch upon certain laws granted specifically to him, so that from these, the rest may be judged. It was decreed that all **Muslims** <note>original: "Mussulmanos"</note> must be content with at most four wives, with the exception of the Prophet. For him, it was permitted to take as many as he pleased. I shall indicate those places by examining the **Quran** <note>original: "Alcoranũ"</note> from which these meanings are drawn.

Secondly: whereas all Muslims are permitted by law to allow their abandoned or divorced wives to marry any other man, and the women themselves may choose other husbands for themselves, he did not wish this to be permitted for his own wives. This was so that, since he held them well or ill at his whim by his prophetic authority, those who had come from great parents and wealthy families with a huge dowry could not leave the Prophet. Thus, he even willed that they should not take other husbands even after his death.

<margin>Surah 143.</margin>
The third privilege: whereas the **Moors** <note>Postel uses "Mauri" as a general term for Muslims</note> must, out of fairness, distribute both the use of property and physical availability equally among three or four wives, or however many they have; otherwise, a wife may seek a trial before a judge and a bill of divorce, from which an innumerable harvest of lawsuits arises among the Muslims. Yet that law did not prescribe such things for the Prophet; for he loved and enriched those he wished, and left those he did not. For he was most vehemently infatuated with that one I mentioned above, whom he took at eight years of age, the daughter of **Abu Bakr** <note>original: "Vbechari"</note> (who reigned after him), named **Aisha** <note>original: "Axam"</note>, and with **Hafsa** <note>original: "Haiezan"</note>, the daughter of **Umar** <note>original: "Homari"</note>. For although he had thirteen others besides them, he slept with these two more frequently. Whereupon the others complained vehemently. He therefore suppressed them with his usual oracle, which nevertheless became suspect even to the women. For they used to say that God was quite obedient to the Prophet, since He would immediately give him laws to suit his pleasures. The law stated that the Prophet ought not to care for the words and objections of women; that whatever he wished regarding them was permitted to him. But they especially marveled at the indulgence of that God when, after neglected oaths and frequent perjuries, and after the man had been caught in adultery with a Jewish girl given to him as a gift by **Bahira** <note>original: "Baheira"; Postel refers here to a legendary figure in Christian polemics, a monk who supposedly assisted Muhammad, though here he is oddly called a "King of the Jacobites"</note>, King of the Jacobites, he even spoke familiarly with the Prophet. For since he could not keep faith with his wives because of the Jewish girl's elegance and his own impatience of love, he published that somewhat obscure law a few days later: because...

<meta>catchword: maxi-</meta>

<summary>Postel critiques the Quran's compilation and its internal contradictions regarding its revelation. He highlights "privileges" Muhammad allegedly claimed for himself regarding polygamy and marriage to distinguish his conduct from the laws imposed on his followers.</summary>
<keywords>Quran, Sunnah, Muhammad, Mecca, Medina, Aisha, Abu Bakr, polygamy, Islamic law, polemic</keywords>

--- Page 165 ---
<meta>This page continues Postel’s critique of the Quran's origins. He moves from discussing Muhammad's personal "privileges" regarding marriage to the historical process of how the Quran was compiled under the third Caliph, Uthman, emphasizing what he views as the text's fragmented and contradictory nature.</meta>

The aforementioned wives were greatly amazed and fell silent. Thus, a fourth privilege was born: that the Prophet himself could have women given to him as if they were legitimate wives, without a marriage contract <note>original: "dotali instrumento"</note> or the presence of a judge.

Fifthly, while it is permitted for no one else to have another man’s wife, not everyone was held by this law <note>Postel implies Muhammad exempted himself from the universal prohibition against adultery or taking another's spouse</note>. For no one was supposed to keep those wives who pleased the Prophet. Hence, under the guise of law, he would compel husbands through oracles, prayers, threats, or lashings to give a bill of divorce <note>original: "libellum repudij"</note> to wives whom he would immediately marry. These are the laws the Prophet wished to use for himself. Although there are countless similar examples, one may judge the character of the lawmaker from these.

After the death of Muhammad <note>original: "Muhamede"</note>, power was first seized to restrain the masses by Abu Bakr <note>original: "Vbecharus"</note>, Umar <note>original: "Homarus"</note>, and his kinsman Ali <note>original: "Halys"</note>—all of whom were fathers-in-law to the Prophet—though they eventually began to turn against one another. However, through the force of the will's persuasion and sheer power, Abu Bakr proved superior and took control of affairs. Second in power was Umar, who was also intent on maintaining his hold over the multitude. 

Third in line was Uthman <note>original: "Odmanus"</note>. When he saw that the people could not be kept in their duty by arms alone, he decided to compile the law—which until then lay hidden and was only preached by some from hearsay and memory, such that there seemed to be as many laws as there were men. He determined to collect it from everywhere, whether from oral tradition or from writings, and bind it into a single volume from which alone authority should be sought. 

Thus, first at Mecca <note>original: "Mechæ"</note> and then in Medina <note>original: "Medinat alnabi"; literally "The City of the Prophet"</note>, he opened the Prophet’s writings and set his scribes to the task of reducing those various scraps, as they presented themselves, into one whole. The prophecies, which were in themselves mangled, crippled, and partly gnawed by mice <note>original: "soricibus erosis"</note> or obliterated by the ravages of time—having been placed at various times in small chests or in holes in walls—were recovered. They were turned into chapters <note>original: "capita"</note> with various names, connected in such a way that there is no logical "before" or "after"; indeed, they fit together just as well even if their positions are rearranged. For nothing is connected throughout the whole work. 

Furthermore, because many fragments were pulled from holes in walls, it has turned into a religious practice: whenever Muslims <note>original: "Mussulmani"</note> find any Arabic writing at home, on the road, or anywhere else, they place it in the cracks of walls like a fragment of the holy law; once placed, they kiss it so that their law does not perish. Those fragments found in the house and chests of Aisha <note>original: "Axæ"; Muhammad's youngest wife</note> (for she, as I said, was the chief of the women and the one he trusted with everything) were arranged into *Surahs* <note>original: "Sorat"</note> or *Assuar* [chapters]. Those gathered from Medina were called *Mediniet*; those collected from Mecca were called *Mechiet*: that is, Medinan or Meccan chapters, songs, psalms, or prophecies, according to where they were written. 

The whole work, which was much larger then than it is today, was called the *Alcoran* <note>the Quran</note>, meaning a "collection" or "reading." Because it is divided into various chapters, it is also called by another name, *Alphurcan* <note>Al-Furqan, meaning "The Criterion"</note>. The *Assuar*, or chapters, were called "songs" and "psalms" because they were usually read and sung. Individual sentences are called *Aiet* <note>Ayat</note>, which is to say, "miracles." And because in those verses almost everything contradicts and destroys itself, later generations called some *Muhquemat* <note>Muhkamat</note>, meaning "judging" or those whose opinion stands, and others *Gair muhquemat* <note>Ghair Muhkamat</note>, meaning "non-judging" <note>This refers to the Islamic distinction between clear, decisive verses and ambiguous ones</note>. 

They are, moreover, of two kinds: for some are called *Naceh* <note>Nasikh</note>, that is, "positive" [abrogating], and others *Mansoh* <note>Mansukh</note>, that is, the "revocation" [abrogated] of the first ones. This was done (not at that time, but by the cunning of more recent men) by the Caliphs <note>original: "Chaliphis"</note> and the Jurists <note>original: "Alphachijs"; from the Arabic 'Faqih'</note> so that their religious persuasion would not utterly perish. When the religion was fresh, however, and the law should have been held as most certain and consistent, there was absolutely no one who agreed with another on it. Uthman first took care to summon the elders and any survivors of those seven men with whom the Prophet had been so familiar that he said the law had been entrusted even to those seven. They all claimed they had nothing certain; or if some did have something, each claimed his own version was the best and true, and the rest false. Others affirmed the opposite. Furthermore, as is usual in new developments,

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

There were many others who also claimed the entirety of the prophecy for themselves, in order to seize the people’s attention and take possession of the wealth of the various factions. After the others were suppressed, Uthman <note>original: "Odmani"</note> held the greatest authority. Yet even then, that law could not satisfy everyone. For more than two hundred completely different versions of the Quran <note>original: "Alcorana"</note> had been written, with every individual possessing their own book; they saw that the successors themselves held their power by virtue of this text. Some, following the twelve successors of Muhammad, removed many things from Uthman’s edition—subtracting more than two hundred sentences from the first chapter and substituting I know not how many others. Led by this example, many began to do the same, so that prophetic faith was clearly vanishing.

Disturbed by this matter, the Babylonian Caliph <note>The term "Caliph" refers to the civil and religious leader of the Islamic community; Postel calls him "Babylonian" likely referring to the Eastern seat of power, though he notes the capital was first in Arabia</note>—for the first seats of power were fixed there after Arabia—acting as the arbiter of the law (for those first successors joined both sacred and profane power to themselves), called a council in Damascus. Some call him Merwan, son of Al-Hassan, others call him Abu Bakr <note>Postel is likely conflating several historical figures here in his attempt to describe the later Umayyad or Abbasid efforts at codification</note>. He decreed that whoever was a learned follower of that religion should come to the council and bring as many copies of the books treating the law as they possessed. He spent great sums on this matter, buying up all the collected books and enclosing them in one place. Along with those books, he gathered six men who were the most skilled in that persuasion: Muslim, Bukhari <note>original: "Buheirum"</note>, Buhorus, Al-Nasa'i <note>original: "Annecenum"</note>, Al-Tirmidhi <note>original: "Atermundum"</note>, and Abu Dawood <note>original: "Daudem"</note>.

The task was committed to them to gather from that entire mass of books a treatment of the law, its origin, and its progress into six volumes, such that each man individually completed the whole work. This work precedes the Quran in authority and is held in greater faith in doubtful matters. Therefore it is called the *Sunnah* <note>original: "Suneh"</note>, that is, the law, much like a *deuterosis* <note>original: "δευτέρωσις"; a Greek term meaning "repetition" or "second law," often used by Christian writers to describe the Jewish Mishnah</note>. Those sentences which these six men collected from both the Qurans and their interpreters, they fortified with four levels of authority. 

For if anything was reported by the disciples of Muhammad and by Aisha <note>original: "Axa"</note>, his more beloved wife and the one privy to his stories, it is placed in the first rank as if it were most true, and judgment is rendered according to it. In the second rank is the sole authority of the other wives, which is called a weaker testimony. In the third is placed the accounts of the doctors <note>learned scholars</note> who lived at that time. In the last and lower authority are those doctors who lived since the time of the Prophet. When the work was finished, the remaining books from which they had made their selections—amounting to two hundred camel loads—were sunk in the nearby river. It was forbidden for anyone to use any books other than the *Sunnah* and the Quran. Thus, all writers are accustomed to cite from that book in this way: "Such a one, from such a one, from such a one, from such a one... he had it from Aisha, or from the Prophet, or from any other of his familiars." This is their faith.

But immediately after the council, which was gathered in or about the hundredth year after the death of the Prophet, that manifold opinion of the six authors birthed even greater doubts. A few years later, the care of the matter was committed to four primary men, that they might collect the institutes of religion from those sources into "commonplaces," with each man treating the whole individually. 

The first of these is called Malik <note>original: "Melichus"</note>, whose decrees are approved by the desert Arabs, Egyptians, Africans, and Spaniards. The second was named Al-Shafi'i <note>original: "Saphihius"</note>, whom those in Baghdad and Mecca follow. Ibn Hanbal <note>original: "Hannibal"</note> is heard in Persia, Assyria, and Armenia. Abu Hanifa <note>original: "Abahanipha"</note> is followed by the Syrians and Alexandrians. Thus, among the Muhammadans, there have arisen not just seventy nations or "sects," as they call them, but as many as there are provinces obeying these trifles. From both books of the doctors and the *Sunnah* emerged one volume which he calls *Anwar* <note>original: "Anuar"</note>, that is, "The Flowers," where someone attempted to collect something consistent for himself out of them all. There is also an innumerable multitude of other books, such that there are 700 volumes whose sayings command faith. But of primary authority is the *Chronicle of Hasyar*, the book *Ariscele*, the book *Mashool*, and the *Chronicles of Kings*. From these, the deeds, doctrine, and character of the Prophet can be sought, from which these things were excerpted. There are, furthermore, certain interpreters of the Quran approved by all,

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Quran’s organization and moves into a thematic summary of its contents. While the previous page focused on the historical struggle to standardize the text under leaders like Uthman and the Caliphs in Damascus, Postel now examines the specific theological claims and the "scope" of the book as he understood it in the 16th century.</meta>

Buhatias, Butzemamin, Mahinud of Mecca, and I know not how many others, divide the Quran <note>original: "Alcoranum"</note> itself into various chapters, according to the reason and usage of different regions. For it is divided one way in Africa, Egypt, and Spain, and another way in Arabia. In some versions there are *Asuar*—that is, chapters—numbering 211, contained in four books. In the first of these there are 5; in the second, 12; the third has 19. The remainder are in the fourth, namely 85; for the final chapters are merely two or three verses long. Others claim there are 112, as I have in my **African copy**. In the **Asiatic copy** there seem to be three fewer. But these details are of no consequence. We must weigh what the book contains: namely, what is its own, what is taken from us, what is against us, and what is against itself.

## WHAT THE PURPOSE AND SUMMARY 
### of the Quran is. CHAPTER XI.

In the beginning, during his withdrawal into the cave, it seems (as we have already said) that Muhammad <note>original: "Muhamedes"</note> greatly favored the Jews, until they deserted him; then, indeed, he began to act against them. Likewise, he seems to have been well-disposed toward Christians; and in truth he would have been, if he had known any others than the **Nestorians** <note>A sect of early Christians whose views on the nature of Christ were often the primary version of Christianity encountered by early Muslims</note>. For he could not immediately find a middle path until, having compared the power of both peoples, he established his own position. For if he had entirely imitated the Jews, the glory would have been ascribed to Moses; if he had subscribed to the Christians, Christ would have completely overshadowed him as a mere man. Yet, lest he seem to lack ancient authority, he said that he followed and taught the **Law of Abraham**. As he says in the *Sura* <note>original: "fora"</note> of *Ionus*—that is, Jonah: "This Quran was not made without God, but it rests upon certain authority between the Old and New Testament." While, therefore, he seems throughout the whole work to teach the worship of one God and to condemn idols, he rises up diametrically against Christ, against whom Muhammad seems to have written the Quran. However, as often as he names him (except in two or three places), he attributes all the highest things to him, except for his divinity and his death. Yet in almost every sentence he says he is not God, that he created nothing, that he does not help, and six hundred other blasphemies. 

The compendium and summary of that book is of this sort: That God is only one, the creator of heaven and earth, and of all things that are in them. That He created man from mud, then from cartilage, then from flesh, and then breathed of His spirit into him. That He created angels and demons: the former from heaven <note>or "light"</note>, the latter from fire. That the devil was unwilling to worship Adam when commanded, and was therefore damned. That He sent many prophets to foretell the calamities that would come upon those who did not believe. Also, that he himself is a prophet who must be believed, lest the unbelieving perish; and those who called him a liar will feel the punishment. That there is a hell prepared for unbelievers; a voice will come from heaven with a shout, with a trumpet, and with a drum, and the dead will rise again and receive their own bodies. That the wicked in hell will devour poison, sulfur, and the fruits of the **Zacon tree** <note>The Zaqqum tree, described in the Quran as growing in the center of Hell</note>; that that <margin>† For food. Unless perhaps it signifies the place of the damned. *That is, prayers.</margin> dwelling place is evil. 

That God is wise, just, good, and honored, and will do injury to no one, but will repay each person. That the good who gave alms, performed **assala** <note>Postel’s transliteration of "As-Salah," the Islamic ritual prayers</note> and good deeds, and paid tithes, will be in paradises in which there are rivers of milk, honey, and wine, and all kinds of fruits. There are **catamites** <note>Postel uses the term "catamyti" to describe the "Ghilman" or "immortal youths" mentioned in the Quran as cupbearers</note> acting as wine-pourers, adorned in multi-colored garments, who will give a certain powder to those who are saved. And there will be very beautiful women with large blue eyes, who for fifty years will engage in a single act of love and remain always virgins. Pillows are placed there where the saved may sit together and converse with one another and with the angels. You will find each of these sentiments at least six hundred times in the Quran. And meanwhile, while he inculcates these things in almost every sentence, he stuffs everything with blasphemies and follies against the teachings of Moses and Jesus Christ...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

Indeed, having received just grievances against the idolatry of the Meccans, he [Muhammad] almost always has in his mouth: "And they took gods besides God, and there is no god besides God, and they make a partner for God," that is, they adore idols. He claims that God placed an obstacle before the eyes of many so they would not see him, and that all are in manifest error. By all these things, he targets both Christ and his followers, as well as Allat <note>original: "Ellet"</note> and Al-Uzza <note>original: "Aluza"</note> and their worshipers in Mecca. He did this with such cunning that if others threw the accusation back at him, he could say he meant it about different people, and vice versa. I would gather more here in this place, if I did not wish to examine everything in the Quran while running through it.

The demon who was created good, he [Muhammad] claims was created evil by God; and thus he denies God when he makes him the author of evil. He makes the same demon a listener, witness, and preacher of the Quran, and finally even a Muslim <note>original: "Musfulmanum"</note>. He attaches a thousand fables to Noah’s ark; and in the book of his doctrine, dung, a mouse, a pig, an elephant, and six hundred trifles are joined to this history. ### THE QURAN CHAPTER BY CHAPTER, OR
#### *The Surahs <note>original: "Afuar," a likely corruption of the Arabic "As-suwar."</note>, an Examination.* CHAPTER XIII.

Imitating the custom of many who wrote on this hodgepodge of nonsense before me, I would have attempted to gather the notable lapses of the man in specific places, were it not for two reasons especially that I decided to run through everything. For as many as have written against this man have busied themselves with collecting errors of the same kind into specific categories; among these, Riccoldus <note>Riccoldo da Monte di Croce (c. 1243–1320), a Dominican missionary whose work was a primary source for European knowledge of Islam.</note> holds the first rank, who wrote in Latin, and whose book Demetrius Cydonius translated into Greek; and Joannes Andreas the Moor <note>Juan Andrés, a former imam from Xàtiva who converted to Christianity in 1487 and wrote "Confusion of the Muhammadan Sect."</note>, finally led to our faith by the Divine Spirit, both of whom were skilled in the Arabic language. But the most skilled of all in the law, traditions, and the language in which he had been instructed by his ancestors was the *Alphachius* <note>original: "Alphachius," from the Arabic "Al-Faqih," meaning a jurist or scholar of Islamic law.</note>—that is, the supreme interpreter and priest—than whom surely no one has written more learnedly. Dionysius the Carthusian and Cardinal Cusanus <note>Nicholas of Cusa, author of "Cribratio Alkorani" (Sifting the Quran).</note> also wrote, as did many others, but they were unskilled in that language. Hence, I see no room left for me to gather the errors by topic. The other reason is that since the Quran is a kind of solid lie and a continuous imposture, it cannot be gathered into topics by anything other than itself.

And yet, O follower of Muhammad, after you approve these things, it is necessary that you also do them. What it says first—that there is no flaw, doubt, or blemish in this book—is false. For it contains nine thousand lies and innumerable contradictions, than which nothing is more foul, as will be made clear and is already known. Whence it cannot be a "direction" for those who fear. For everyone feared you, O Muhammad, as a tyrannical prophet; yet they were not directed by you, but destroyed. Among the Jews, however lost they may be, there is still no physician <note>Postel likely suggests that Muhammad's "remedies" or laws add nothing of value even to the "broken" Jewish faith.</note>. Therefore you add nothing to them. As for believing in what you say was sent into you from heaven: no one could believe it, since you performed no signs <note>miracles</note>, you labored most filthily under every vice, and you drove people by force. Yet all the true prophets were famous for the innocence of their lives, for miracles, and for certain predictions of the future. What the truth once handed down must remain fixed. But those who were sent before you, since they are from God—if you contradict them, your words are false. # WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK II

You ought to receive the Law of Moses as good, true, and heavenly-sent news; you must believe it is entirely from God, or else you must say from the very threshold that there is a lie in the Alcoran <note>The Quran</note>. Thus, our laws are from God, while yours were invented by a demonic author; our truths do not need the testimony of an impostor. Here certainly, as often elsewhere, he [Muhammad] said one thing and thought another: while he draws everyone to himself, he seems to approve the opinions of all in order to catch unrefined listeners; he gradually instills his own ideas and overturns the best and most accepted ones. It had been confirmed for many centuries and by miracles that the first laws <note>The Mosaic and Christian laws</note> were sent from heaven; but desiring to protect himself with their authority, you frequently insert your own ideas into them. "Such was a Prophet, and sent by God; such and such a person, and that other one, predicted thus, and so it happened; therefore Muhammad is a prophet." It is just as if someone were to conclude: the garment is white, the tunic is white, the breastplate is white, therefore the cap must also be white, since they all agree in covering the body. They believed in a future life before all others—indeed, you learned it from them when you were an idolater, both from the law and your parents, which you yourself admit. 

It follows: <margin>“</margin> "But the impious, whether you <margin>“</margin> announce it to them or do not announce it, will not believe, for God has firmly set a seal <margin>“</margin> upon their hearts, and upon their hearing, and a darkness over their sight; therefore they shall have <margin>“</margin> the greatest punishment." By the word "impious," you now primarily target your fellow citizens of Mecca <note>original: "Mechenses"</note> to win over our people <note>Christians</note> and the Jews; but later you hurl the word *Chaphirorum* <note>original: "Chaphirorum," from the Arabic "Kafir," meaning disbelievers or infidels</note>—that is, "the impious"—at us, as if we do not have a God. Finally, you say that God placed an obstacle before the senses of men so that they cannot repent through preaching: what else is this but pushing men into vice by taking away their freedom, even while you wish to terrify them? You establish God as unjust, one who punishes those whom He does not wish—or does not permit—to be good. 

He adds: <margin>“</margin> "Furthermore, some men say: <margin>“</margin> 'We believe in God and the Day of Judgment' (or the last day), 'and yet they do not believe, but <margin>“</margin> they mock God. But those who believe and do not mock, except in their own souls, <margin>“</margin> shall in no way profit; there is a disease in their hearts, and God increases the disease, <margin>“</margin> and they have the greatest punishment, because they accuse us of lying; and when it is said <margin>“</margin> to them, "Do not corrupt the earth," they say, "Indeed, we are good." Are they not themselves <margin>“</margin> the corrupters? Therefore they shall not profit.'" 

Do you see how, after he seemed to rightfully attack the idolaters themselves, he then accuses others who were of honest faith (suppose they were good Jews or Nestorian <note>A branch of Eastern Christianity common in the Near East during the Middle Ages</note> Christians, for a choice must be made among many evils) and tries to convert them entirely to his own opinion? He says all believe wrongly who do not believe him. But he continues to be impious toward God when he says that God adds evils to our evils. Thus you warn in vain if God is the author of evil. 

I proceed to the rest, and in these few words I wish to show the lack of skill of the Latin translator <note>Postel is likely critiquing the 12th-century translation by Robert of Ketton, which was the standard Latin version in his time</note>, and I will show how recklessly the old versions are trusted for the purpose of refuting them. Meanwhile, I do not want to omit what is widely evident from his tyranny in the following words. For unless he had already used violence against them, they would never have professed one thing with their mouths and another in their hearts for a matter so vain and futile. Those people, miserably killed and harassed by slaughter and plunder, were practicing dissimulation <note>The act of hiding one's true beliefs, known in Islamic law as "Taqiyya"</note> to avoid suffering worse fates. He called this a "disease of the heart"—the fact that they uttered one thing with their mouth while being driven elsewhere by the judgment of their conscience out of fear. 

He says afterward: <margin>“</margin> <margin>“</margin> "But when it is said to them, 'Believe as the great men do,' they say, 'We believe as the <margin>“</margin> *Supheha*' (that is, the simple and unrefined). Are they not unrefined? And therefore they do not understand." What do these words mean: "Believe as men do" (for so he calls *elnaas* <note>original: "al-nas," the Arabic word for "the people"</note>, meaning cultured and civilized men)? He brings an example to the unrefined from these "great men" who had joined him for the sake of plunder and obtaining power, such as *Vbecharus* <note>Abu Bakr, the first Caliph</note> and *Homarus* <note>Umar, the second Caliph</note> and others. Thus the common people, when these things were thrown at them, said they preferred to follow the unrefined and uncultured multitude rather than the faction of a few powerful men. # WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK II
### ->ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

...when a power was already eager to emerge. Let us compare, using this art of teaching, the condition of this law. When Moses led out the people of God, he did not say, "Believe because this man is noble, or because that man believes," but rather, "Believe because God wills it so; if you doubt this matter, I am prepared to show that God acts through me with unheard-of miracles." And he proved it with signs. So did Elijah, and so did Jesus Christ. 

All heretics, however, creep in by another method, since they seek glory for themselves and not for God. They raise certain grievances. They point out the vices of men placed in high dignities and then persuade the unlearned multitude that those vices belong not to the men, but to their rank <note>original: "ordinis" – referring to the social or ecclesiastical order</note>. Therefore, they say the ranks themselves are evil and must not be tolerated. In the meantime, the wretched common people—who do not know how to discern between the rank and the person ordained to it—are tossed about and follow these impostors who are greedy for revolution. Even if they press their point most urgently, if their novelty is not disapproved by some prominent person's judgment, they claim it is approved by "great men" whose judgment is sincere. By pretending there is already a great fellowship of believers, they gather crowds and rise up against all others—whom they call "impious"—for the sake of persuasion. Meanwhile, they invade the wealth and fortunes of better and more steadfast men. In this way, heretics have dragged multitudes to destruction; in this way, they have incited factions within Republics.

In this same way, Muhammad persuaded the Meccans <note>original: "Mechensib"</note> by highlighting the disadvantages of false religion and by the authority of the great. But a certain *Alphachius* <term>Al-Faqih: a scholar or jurist of Islamic law</term> will object: "Did he not most justly oppose the vain worship of idols?" If someone exchanges very bad things for things that are merely bad, it is the work of an imprudent man. Certainly, nothing is more displeasing to God than the worship of idols. Yet, to worship one God has nothing evil in it. If God is worshiped well, nothing is more excellent. But if He is worshiped badly, and if the greatest vices are covered up under His name, it is far better to be ignorant of Him and be led by natural law <note>original: "praescripto naturali" – the innate sense of right and wrong</note> than to blaspheme Him once He is known and "worship" Him with crimes. 

For as our Evangelist Jesus Christ says: "The servant who knows the will of the master and does not do it will receive many punishments; he who does not know and does not do it, fewer." <note>A reference to Luke 12:47-48</note> For two reasons, it would have been better for the Meccans to have remained idolaters than to become Muhammadans <note>Muslims</note>. First, because among those who are ignorant of the true God, if any were a good person by the guidance of nature, even if he had not heard of Christ, he could be saved; whereas no Muhammadan can be, or ever could have been saved, unless he returns to Christ.

The second reason is also clear. For if you preach Christ to idolaters, they easily believe and embrace the true faith; but Muhammadans even persecute and kill Christians. Therefore, Muhammad taught badly and from a bad beginning, since even the faith of rustic pagans was less evil. Pagans easily believe the Gospel; and if they had perished, they alone would have perished. But all of Africa and the largest part of Asia have perished under the plague of Muhammad.

Furthermore, when they 
> are caught <note>or "meet together"; referring to Quran 2:14</note>, those who have believed say, "We believe"; and when they have withdrawn to their demons <note>their leaders or false gods</note>, they say, "We are with you, certainly we were only mocking." God will mock them and will make them obstinate; they will persist in their stubbornness. These are the ones who thought that darkness is the right direction, and by no means will any relief <note>original: "respiratio"</note> remain for them, and they will not be guided. Their example is like the example of one who once kindled a light, but there is no splendor around him. God withdrew their light and left them in darkness so they might not see.

They are a deaf, mute, and blind people, yet they do not return to their senses. He <note>Muhammad/the Quran</note> acts against them by terrifying them, and proceeds to take away the judgment of truth from the men themselves, making God the author of their wickedness. If God takes away the light, who could believe? Therefore, it must be that these followers have believed in the light of the devil, since as Muslims <note>original: "Mussulmani"</note> they are without the light of God. For if they are deaf, blind, and mute, and have no judgment to recognize the light, it follows they are led into their belief by something else—not by God, who took away the light so they might not see—therefore, they are led by the devil, which is the truth.

It follows:

...will rise. And if God willed, He would take away and remove their hearing and their sight, for God is powerful over all things. These matters look toward the same end as those mentioned above. For he hammers into those rustics <note>Postel frequently refers to the early followers of Islam as "rustics" to imply they were uneducated and easily deceived.</note> things that Christians hold as most certain, though they are not similar in quality. But I shall proceed a little further.

> "Ho there, you people! Serve your Lord, who created you and those who were before you, if perhaps you might fear [Him]. Who placed the earth for you as a floor and a seat, but the heaven as a high building, and sends down water from heaven, and brings forth with it fruits for your abundance. And do not set up a likeness to God, and you shall be wise."

All these things were believed by us long before, and much better, and sufficient caution was taken regarding idols <note>original: "simulachris"</note>. However, he always uses an ambiguous word when he speaks of a "partner" <note>Postel refers to the Arabic concept of *shirk*, or associating partners with God.</note>, so that he may direct it against idols, images, and Christ. He adds:

> "And if you are in doubt (now God speaks, so that it seems a common word of God and of Muhammad, which happens throughout the book) concerning that which we have instilled from heaven upon our servant, come with a Surah <note>original: "Sora"; a chapter of the Quran</note>, that is, with a certain chapter or Psalm similar to this, and call your witnesses besides God, if you are truthful."

Now he openly rises up against us; those whom he had said a little earlier had received books from heaven, he now says do not have even one chapter among them that can be compared to this one, or by which this matter could be contested. When he speaks of himself, he makes God the speaker for the sake of causing terror; and those whom he calls our "witnesses" besides God, he understands to be Christ. Therefore, what I said from the beginning is most evident: while he pretends to act against idolaters, he rushes with his whole force against us. For what "chapter" could the idolaters have brought forth, who held their worship from custom rather than from law? For among the Pagans, although their worship was false, nevertheless, if it was confirmed by law, that law did not go out publicly. Furthermore, I sufficiently revealed the divinity of Christ in the first book, and how He must necessarily be believed to be God, even by human reasons, if anyone lacks faith. He adds:

> "But if you have not done it—and you shall not do it—then fear the fire, which itself shall pierce through men and stones, which is promised to the impious."

He wishes to cast the terror of those things which we believe before them, if he is not heeded. He continues:

> "Announce to those who have believed and done good works, that they have paradises, beneath which rivers flow, so that they may inherit riches from its fruits. They said: 'This is what was promised to us for our abundance before,' and they were given similar things in that paradise, and they have in it most beautiful spouses, commendable to all, and they are in it sitting and conversing. Nor will God allow anything similar to be proposed, whether around or above; and certainly those who believed understand what is true from their Lord."

This is that noble paradise of Epicureans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Epicurus, often used as a slur for those who seek physical pleasure above all else.</note> and of pigs, most worthy of its author, who is most like a brute animal. 

> "Spirits before the resurrection eat and sleep together in paradises:"

but once their bodies are received, since there will be no further generation or corruption, effort will be given to gluttony and to Venus <note>The Roman goddess of love, here used to mean sexual lust.</note>. Those things which in this mortality are sought out of necessity or for the pleasures of the body shall be in use in immortality—where the total happiness should consist in contemplating God (which even here is customary among the most perfect). These are the very things that here block the path to happiness! For no one is more unhappy than a slave to the belly and to Venus. Having abandoned the most holy scriptures, which treat true and absolute happiness soberly and rationally, these were the things most worthy to be introduced to rustic and sedentary <note>original: "sellularijs" – common laborers or those who sit at stalls.</note> Arabs; indeed, nothing occurs more frequently than these paradises. Truly, at the end of the passage, where he says:

> "Those who believed, what is true from their Lord:"

he means his own "truth," in believing which his followers will have such paradises. But the impious will say, "What does God mean by this parable?" Many go astray with it, and many are directed with it: and they by no means go astray with it, except the corrupt. Here he calls the Quran a "parable." # ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
### BOOK II

...[if the most] excellent of men were with the lawgiver: what does that Law of God mean to itself, in which there are many wicked and many upright? As if they were to say, "If it is of God, men ought not to become evil by His decree," he satisfies them. "They are not," he says, "evil, except those who are evil." This is a most excellent demonstration!—as if to say: wine is nothing but wine, and a sword is nothing but a sword, and so on. 

,, But those who introduce falsehood and defect, God later deprives of certainty, and they cut off what 
,, God commanded in [the law] itself; they shall be burned and corrupted on the earth, and they are damned. 

He uses these threats lest his own writings, which he was disseminating in little books, be corrupted, and so that they might be held as divine. This is despite the fact that for seven years he did not detect the deception <note>original: "fucum"; literally a dye or pretense, referring to a legend that Muhammad's scribes altered the revelations without his knowledge.</note> practiced on him by a scribe who changed everything at his own whim; he only realized it after the impostor left him and incited others to defection. For this reason, because the man had exposed his fraud, Muhammad saw to it that he was murdered while sleeping. By this example, all Muslims—and especially their princes—treat their enemies as if such an act were lawful. 

,, When you have become ungodly toward God, then you will be made dead, and He will give you life; 
,, finally He will make you die, then later He will give you life, and then finally to Him you will return. 

These are mere scare tactics <note>original: "terriculamenta"</note> to prevent anyone from deserting his law. It follows: 

<margin>k</margin> ,, It is He who created for you whatever is in the whole earth; 
,, finally He ascended to the heavens, and leveled them into seven heavens, and He is wise in every thing. 

Here he depicts God as moving by local motion and being finite, which would therefore make Him corruptible. Furthermore, he inverts the order of things; for things prior in dignity should precede in creation—except for man, who is the end-goal of the lower matter enclosed within the world. Therefore Moses said, *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth* <note>original: "In principio creauit Deus cœlum et terram"</note>: the heaven and celestial things as causes in the first place, and elementary things as effects in the second. This is not because He created those first and these later by a successive motion, but because in the intellectual arrangement, He created simultaneously those things thus understood, which could not have been grasped by us otherwise unless they had been written in this way. Then he says: 

,, And when He said to the angels, "I am placing a prefect <term>caliph</term> on the earth," they said, "Will You 
,, place in it one who will be corrupted in it and shed blood? 
,, But we will praise You with Your renown and sanctify You." He said, "I know what you do not know." 
,, And He taught Adam all the names, and their breadth or accidents, above the angels. And He said, 
,, "Call out"—that is, celebrate me in heaven—"if you are truthful." And they said, "We praise You, 
,, nor do we have knowledge except what You have taught us: for You are the wise judge." 

All these things are dreams written nowhere else, tending toward this goal: that he might elude with fabulous dreams that which the sacrosanct Trinity had said—"Let us make man in our likeness and image" <note>original: "faciamus hominem ad similitudinem & imaginem nostram"</note>. (We must speak of God in this way, for otherwise we cannot express the concepts of the Divine Mind). 

Furthermore, the word *Pheseda* <note>Postel refers to the Arabic *fasād*, meaning corruption or mischief.</note>, which he used for "corruption," does not only signify that necessary natural corruption opposed to generation, but is everywhere understood as the corruption of sin. By this meaning, if he accepts God as the author of evil, he acts as we have seen above and denies that He is God. He clearly establishes that the angels and God are evil, since they willed for a man who is a murderer to be produced. Even Abenreis <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the famous Andalusian philosopher.</note> is a stranger to such impiety. O, you prophet of Satan and instrument of the devil! For God created nothing evil. It follows: 

,, He said, "Hey, Adam, call them by their names." And when he called them by their names, He said, 
,, "Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth, and I know what 
,, you reveal and what you hide?" 

You see how he joins together disjointed and abrupt things, since he does not say what Adam is calling. This is a mangled emblem taken from the biblical account of the naming of the living creatures and things. He adds: 

,, And when we said to the angels, "Adore Adam," 
,, and they adored him, except for the devil, who grew proud and was among the ungodly. 

Consider, O wise reader, the God of Muhammad: an author of evil, unjust, a murderer (for he who is the cause is at fault), and an idolater—for the blessed God wills to be worshipped above all...

From this, he wanted to thrust himself into the position of the Messiah for a people waiting in expectation and eager for new things. For once they were caught, he thought it would be easy to use them as a step to catch the rest. If, however, the Quran confirms the Law of Moses, it ought not to contradict it, which it does in many things. Cover and hide " the truth, and you will be wise. " In this place, he openly betrays himself, while he persuades them to hide the truth—which is exactly what he did, thrusting forward all manner of falsehoods. This passage needs no refutation. Then: "Keep watch over prayers in our manner, pay the " tithes, obey along with your parents, speak to men with innocence, purify " your souls, and read the book, if by any means you may understand. "The direction of God," he says, "is nothing but direction." What does this imply? A stone is nothing but a stone, a man is nothing but a man, there is no God except God, or besides God. It implies nothing at all, and yet he wanted the initiation into his sect to be confirmed by this formula: *la alla illa alla* <note>original: *la alla illa alla*; Postel's transcription of the Arabic *Lā ilāha illā llāh*, "There is no god but God."</note>, there is no God but God, or besides God—as if anyone proves anything this way, or produces a connected understanding of things by saying the same thing twice. The Jew and the Christian believe these things: that the direction of God is nothing but the direction of God, and there is no God but God. But for the sake of enticing the common people, he used this indefinite term: and when the great and the learned assented to the general truth, later using the same word among the unlearned, he substituted his own personal persuasion for that which is common to all, and drew the simple-minded to *hudan* <note>original: *hudan*; Arabic for "guidance."</note>, that is, "direction": for he managed to have the Quran itself called by this name. Thus, offering wormwood <note>Wormwood is a bitter herb, used here as a metaphor for poisonous or false teaching.</note> disguised with honey, and thrusting forward something that is partly true and partly plausible, you bring forth innumerable lies and impieties.

But now I come to the title and pretext of your law. After he [Muhammad] causes many fables to be brought forward concerning Abraham with Ishmael, and the building of the house of idolatry, the *Al-Qibla* <term>Al-Qibla: Postel refers here to the Kaaba in Mecca, the direction toward which Muslims pray.</term> of Mecca (as if Abraham had ever been in Arabia!), and [after] praying for the posterity of Ishmael, he adds in his [Abraham's] name:

<margin>cc</margin>
> Our Lord, make us Muslims (that is, the faithful) to you, and from our generation a people faithful
<margin>cc</margin>
> to you, and show us our place of refuge <note>Original: "asylum," referring to the rites of the Hajj pilgrimage.</note>, and turn toward us; for you are the Relenting and
<margin>cc</margin>
> the Merciful. Our Lord, promise among them a prophet from that nation who may read
<margin>cc</margin>
> your miracles <note>Original: "miracula," here translating the Arabic 'ayat' or 'signs.'</note> among them, and teach them the book and wisdom, and make them innocent;
<margin>cc</margin>
> for you are the venerable wise one.

He makes himself out to be the one promised by the Ishmaelites, so that he may do those things which he says he does. However, since all these things are foreign to the ancient Scriptures, they have no need of refutation, because they are empty lies. In another place, he says it was commanded to him afterward that he should be the "first Muslim," even though here he makes Abraham a Muslim. Yet the holy prophets who came after Moses never withdrew even a hair's breadth <note>Original: "latum unguem," literally 'a broad fingernail,' a Latin idiom for the smallest possible distance.</note> from the sacred prescription, although they were most famous for their revelations.

There exist writings approved not only by the Jews, but received by the Nestorians, Jacobites, and Armenians <note>Eastern Christian denominations that Postel notes as maintaining consistent scriptural traditions.</note>, and transcribed by the Latins, Greeks, and Illyrians, where they all entirely agree; yet they contain nothing of these trifles which you bring forward. Nor can they be corrupt, since they agree across countless myriads scattered throughout the whole world. Consult even those versions which the Arabs have: you will find nothing of those trifles and dreams which you, an impostor, have offered, but rather the complete opposite. For in the sacred texts it is held:

> Cast out the bondwoman and her son; for the son of the bondwoman shall not be an heir with the son of the free woman, but in Isaac shall your seed be called. <note>A quotation from Genesis 21:10-12, emphasizing the biblical lineage through Isaac rather than Ishmael.</note>

You see that these words work against you, and that the promise of the Prophet, in whom all nations were to be blessed, is not through Ishmael, but through Isaac. These things were sent from heaven by God, which you cannot deny; therefore yours are false, and from the devil, not from God. Nor can your law be that of Abraham, which is entirely contrary to his blessings, even though you take your authority from him.

Let the Muslims consider the origin of their law. There were three kinds of men where Muhammad preached: Idolaters, Jews, and Christians. He did not have these things from the idolaters, who did not possess them; therefore they flowed either from the Jews or the Christians, or from revelation. How could it have happened that as soon as you began to emerge and preach against the truth, everyone with one voice would have refuted you for lying—unless the copies of the world were so corrupted in themselves as to oppose you, even when you were scarcely known in a small corner of the world? Therefore, you gave false things that fought against the truth. "But," you say, "it was so revealed to me by God"—or rather by the devil. It cannot be from God, because every truth harmonizes with truth, and God does not change. It follows, therefore, that you had these commentaries from the devil. Though your followers may deny that you had him as a companion, this one fact will work against them: that he persuaded a most miserable liar to do this.

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD
### BOOK II.

...so that he believed he could rise again on the third day after death, no differently than Simon the Samaritan <note>Postel refers to Simon Magus, a practitioner of magic mentioned in the New Testament (Acts 8) and later legends, who allegedly claimed he would rise from the dead to prove his divinity.</note>. From this, that insane and wicked man [Muhammad] did not blush to believe it; he even provided in his will that his resurrection should be expected for three days, keeping his corpse—which, as I noted above, drove away all spectators with its stench. These things were in the ancient histories, but they were wiped out by your first Caliphs <note>original: *Chalephis*; early leaders of the Islamic community after Muhammad.</note> for the sake of maintaining the empire. Partly by your cunning, O Muhammad, and partly by the devil's, you have perished, and an innumerable multitude of men has perished, and perishes daily. Finally, he joins together certain dialogues of the patriarchs, which, although they seem plausible, are not to be believed because they are not in the Holy Scriptures. For one could imagine and add everything in the same manner.

"When indeed those patriarchs said: 'Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided,' say: 'But the law of Abraham is light, and it does not set up idols.'" Although he calls both [faiths] good, he nevertheless imagines one that was never written, which he calls the Law of Abraham. If he approved of it because it did not make idols or "partners" <note>A reference to the Islamic concept of *Shirk*, or associating partners with God.</note>, the Jews did the same; therefore, he ought to have been, and remained, a Jew. But a little later he explains himself: "Say, we believe in God, and in that which He instilled in us, and what He instilled in Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and in the tribes (of the sons of Israel), and in what was given to Moses and Christ, and what was given to the prophets by their Lord: we do not differ from them in even one thing, and we are faithful to Him." How does he profess everything, he who clearly has nothing? And [does he do] this for the sake of drawing a multitude after him?

Now he believes in the law of Abraham only, now in the law of all, now in the law of none, so that nothing is more inconsistent than these sayings. If you subscribe to all, you must receive the sayings of all; if you contravene them, you are necessarily a liar. He trifles at greater length with these same follies so that he may catch all men. Finally, having turned toward the *Al-Qibla* <term>Al-Qibla: The direction of prayer toward the Kaaba in Mecca, which Postel describes here as a "tower."</term> (that tower about which I spoke in the chapter on Mecca), he says similar things about adoration in all respects. But where he deals with pilgrimage, toward the *Masjid al-Haram* <note>original: *Mesgidam Elharam*; the Sacred Mosque in Mecca.</note> (that is, the Meccan one), he says that those who are killed in sedition and "the way of God" <note>Postel’s interpretation of *Jihad* or religious struggle.</note> ought not to be called dead, but living. What an utterly <unclear>base</unclear> man, who for his own lust and dreams wanted everything filled with slaughter, and did not value the life of men at even a hair's breadth! In this matter, he has excellent imitators in the Muhammadan princes, who, if they have an abundance of men, pave the way for the second ranks with the first ranks, with living bodies thrust into ditches or marshes and trampled underfoot. A little later he says: "Whoever shall contradict these things which are said by the prophet, the curse of God and His angel and of men be upon him," so that he may terrify in his usual manner. Finally, when he says that God created ships, he lies; for they are not of nature, but of art. There follows the prohibition of feasts: "Nothing is prohibited to you except carrion, and blood, and the flesh of the pig, and that which was killed without God," that is, without invocation. If you approve the laws of all, nothing ought to have been prohibited to you, for nothing created by God is evil. But you wanted to appear as a Jew so that you might retain those who were deserting. Moses prohibited certain things because of the stubbornness of the people, some because of the vice of the region, and some for the memory of the Creator. Leprosy was a great struggle in Egypt, to which disease the pig is a susceptible animal; but in other regions, not at all. Indeed, it is in very healthy use even under the equator. Other [rules] were so that whenever they killed anything, they could remember the divine precept. He says afterward: "It matters not whether they turn toward the East or toward the West in prayers, provided they do good, pay tithes, and do not contravene the prophet, nor the angels, nor the prophets; all will be saved." He gives salvation to all laws again, and says it matters not where you face when you pray, so that the Jews, agreeing with the Christians, might come to him. Regarding vengeance: "O you who have believed, it is written to you concerning the retribution of killing: the free for the free, the slave...
