"I am the servant of God; God has given me a book, and made me a prophet, and made me blessed; I fear [God] since I was made [a prophet], and He commanded me to perform prayers and give tithes as long as I remain alive, and to honor my mother; and He did not make me arrogant or troublesome. Peace be upon the day I was born, the day I shall die, and the day I shall remain alive." 
<note>Original: "seruus Dei, dedit mihi Deus librum..." Postel is quoting Surah Maryam (19:30–33), where the infant Jesus speaks from the cradle to defend his mother’s honor.</note>
This is Jesus, son of Mary, the word of truth, about whom they doubt. God has not taken a son—praise be to Him! He [Muhammad] fabricated all these things for the sake of his own "final period." I have already demonstrated many times that it is impossible for God to create or restore anything except through the Son; He creates all things in the Son as God, and restores all things in the Son as the <term>God-man</term> <note>original: θεανθρώπω (theanthropō)</note>, which I proved at length in the previous book. 

But the individual lies offered by the Prophet through the <term>Spatharians</term> <note>Postel likely refers to the *Spatharioi* or informants/guards from whom he believes Muhammad received corrupted traditions.</note> must be shaken out. When did Mary ever withdraw from her parents, since the Gospels never speak of it? Here is one lie already. Indeed, she was carefully educated partly in the Temple and partly with her parents until the coming of the Holy Spirit and until she was wed to Joseph. The custom of veiling virgins had not yet come into use among the Jews, which is why this was also made up. He [Muhammad] says the Holy Spirit was sent instead of an angel so that he might seem to make him a creature—impiously indeed—though it happened by an angel being sent. If he makes the Holy Spirit a messenger, no one can discern the truth. Furthermore, she did not leave her home from the time she conceived until they went to Bethlehem to register their names.

Where is that palm tree trunk? 
<note>In the Quran (19:23), Mary gives birth under a withered palm tree that miraculously provides dates.</note> 
The Muslims, pious toward our people, say that this palm tree came back to life and lasted until our own memory. We do not need lying miracles; we have the account written differently, we receive it, and we believe it. The claims that she desired death, and that the infant spoke to her, etc., are fabrications—granted to us, as it were, so that by believing them, we might deny God. Where was he commanded concerning prayers and tithes? These are all lies of the Spatharians and of a dreamer. Now, who does not see that the Spatharians imposed upon this prophet an error of 1,500 years? For Mary the mother of Christ is very far removed from Mary [Miriam] the sister of Moses and Aaron; and this, if it pleases the gods, is "not a lie"! May the man perish miserably with his trifles. 
<note>Postel is pointing out a famous chronological crux where the Quran refers to Mary as the "sister of Aaron," which Christian polemicists interpreted as a confusion with the biblical Miriam.</note>

To the rest: He was not satisfied to say that demons are made of fire, and that they were created evil and stupid, unless he also made them mortal. For he says that on the day of judgment they will die and finally return to life—a lie than which none is more false. For since they lack a body and can be nothing other than spirits, why would they die? Since they do not have corruptible matter to be purged, that would happen in vain, which never occurs with God as the author.
<margin>19. Theh.</margin> <note>Likely a reference to Surah 19 (Maryam).</note>

In reciting the history of Moses, he adds fabrications everywhere with his commentaries: now he says he was raised by his sister, now by the wife of Pharaoh, whereas the sacred records have it as the daughter. He sets the time of Passover as the moment when the magicians came against Moses, even though Passover did not yet exist, for it was instituted after the crossing of the Red Sea. Moses, as if having the legal right over the province, says he will hang the magicians from the trunk of a palm tree with their hands cut off. Furthermore, he calls Aaron a "Samaritan"—for what reason, I do not know. 
<note>Postel refers to the Quranic character "al-Samiri" involved in the Golden Calf incident, arguing this is a chronological impossibility as Samaritans did not exist then.</note> 
Finally, Moses seizes him by the hair and beard. Moreover, he [Muhammad] does not wish to publish the Quran until he completes it—which was never done before his death, as I have already said—lest he be proved false. Finally, he says a demon showed Adam the tree of life, as if God had not shown it. As a punishment for impiety, he says God will raise the impious blind. Lastly, while he snatched things from everyone by right or wrong, he says he seeks no reward, in order to cover his vices. He says things contrary to his deeds, etc.
<margin>20. Prophets.</margin> <note>Likely a reference to Surah 21 (Al-Anbiya/The Prophets).</note>

He heaps up ravings, weaving fables in his usual manner to elude those who said that he, a man similar to others and distinguished by no prophecy, had fabricated and dreamed these things. He concludes that there were other prophets before him, and therefore he is one himself. He claims the *Alcoran* and *Alphuran* <term>The Criterion/Al-Furqan</term> were given to Moses and Abraham, which we have previously shown to be false. He fabricates fables about David and Solomon. He claims God taught them judgment concerning a vineyard and sheep, through which...

...[with the] translation of the emperors that he had these things, for nothing is intact. He wishes, I think, to speak of the admonition of Nathan, and the proposal of the two men, one of whom had ninety-nine sheep, and from the one who had only one, he took it away, etc. <note>original: "Natanis admonitione... de duorum hominum..." Postel refers to the parable Nathan told King David in 2 Samuel 12, which appears in a modified form in the Quran (Surah Sad 38:21–25).</note> Regarding the vineyard, I know not from where he dreamed it up. That power over the winds and demons was granted to Solomon, I do not recall in the sacred records <note>the Bible</note>, much less the craft of a blacksmith. He numbers Enoch, Job, and others alongside Ishmael, so that by this association the impious one might appear pious. 21. **Elhegh** <term>Al-Hajj: The Islamic pilgrimage to Mecca</term>, is that pilgrimage, usually performed during four months in the year at Mecca, in memory of Abraham and his sacrifice. Therefore, he instituted certain things there conforming to idolatry; and he is, so to speak, the same everywhere. It has already been refuted that Abraham was ever in that "Ancient House" <note>The Kaaba</note>. Therefore, I shall not linger on these forbidden things. **Muminine** <term>Mu'minin: The Arabic term for "Believers" or the faithful</term>, that is, the faithful. 22.

Because he [Muhammad] had been caught in adultery by his wives with a young Jewish girl, whom Baheyras <note>Postel refers to the monk Bahira, whom Christian polemicists claimed was Muhammad's secret teacher.</note> had given to him, and he had committed perjury—having sworn a promise to his wives under the name of God—he therefore sets down a law here, by which the same thing is permitted to all his followers as to himself. This was done so that the vice might not be seen in him if it were permitted in everyone, as if a hundred thousand men sinning is less of a crime than one man alone. For if it is an unjust thing to commit adultery and not to render the debt owed to a wife—which nature itself has taught—it certainly could not be made lawful by the law and promise of this "prophet." I wish now to explain this deed a little more extensively, so that all may weigh what is contained in this "Chapter of the Faithful" and look deeply into this "faithfulness." For this chapter, and the one following, will greatly reveal this prophet to us. I begin the matter more deeply, from the very start.

When this prophet began to travel through the neighboring countryside and villages of Mecca for the sake of preaching—having already contracted kinships with great citizens and being accompanied by a large crowd—he won over and reconciled the neighboring minor rulers to himself as best he could, either through love or terror. Among others, there was a certain man on the borders of Arabia named Baheyras, who presided over a flock of heretical **Jacobites** <term>A West Syrian Miaphysite Christian denomination</term>. Since he was otherwise hostile to the rest of the Christians, if any were nearby, he considered nothing more important than that "like should be joined with like," so that according to the proverb, "similar lips might have similar lettuce" <note>A Latin proverb meaning 'like attracts like' or 'two of a kind'.</note>. An heretic cherishes and embraces an heretic and an impious man. To Bahyras fled all the lost souls and those accused of violating religion. Muhammad, indeed, summoned to himself a dross of all the lost souls and those eager for revolution. Among other gifts with which this prophet was presented—one most accommodating to a man, although fifty years old—Bahyras selects a girl of elegant beauty, fifteen years of age, Marina by name, of the Jewish religion, and gives her as a gift to Muhammad as a <term>memorial</term> <note>original: μνημόσυνον (mnēmosynon)</note> of their treaty. Once she was received, the master immediately began to fall miserably in love with her, even though he had taken as wives three or four very wealthy Jewish women and daughters of the more famous citizens of Mecca, up to fifteen in number, as I have said. For a long time, the girl attempted to protect her modesty; at last, partly by her master's command, partly by prayers and bribes, she yielded to the prophet's favors. But the matter did not succeed happily or "prophetically." For the two most noble and beloved wives he had, Hassa, the daughter of Vbecharus <note>Aisha, daughter of Abu Bakr</note>, and Hafeza, the daughter of Humarus <note>Hafsa, daughter of Umar</note>, caught the man with the young girl and rebuked him sharply. They threatened that they would complain to their parents, petition the judges for a divorce, and defame him among all the believers. Terrified by these things, the prophet, a suppliant with tears, threw himself at the knees of his wives. He swore he would never commit such a thing in the future; he had done it overcome by the violence of love. He invoked God, the law, and an angel as a witness to his oath: if he ever committed such a thing again, he would fear no punishment. He was urged by a greater fear of them than of others because he had obtained very large riches through their dowries and the great favor of their parents; all of which he would lose if they left the man. The women, being not at all wicked, accepted his oaths...

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK II.

They spare the man, but only on the condition that if he should commit such a thing even once more afterward, he should hope for no further mercy: they declared it would be the end for both the man and his law, and they would betray and ruin everything. For some days he masters his lust, held back by religion—or rather by the fear of the women—but finally, committing the same deed, he is caught by them again. They depart, defame him, and betray as much as they knew of his secret mysteries: that the man is an impostor, impure, driven by demons and furies, who fakes divine conversations and takes from other laws everything good that he possesses; there is nothing of the scoundrel’s tricks they do not publish abroad. By these events he was led almost to total despair: until, coming to his senses, in order to retain the spirit of the multitude, he proposes this law, which is at the beginning of this Surah:

> "Blessed," he says, "are the faithful who are fearful in their prayers, and who withdraw from deception, and who act purely, and who guard their private parts, except with their wives or what their faith has acquired—that is, among slaves. For they are without blame, or not to be blamed." <note>Postel provides a Latin translation of the opening verses of Surah Al-Mu'minun (23:1-6). He interprets the Arabic phrase regarding "those whom your right hands possess" as a license for sexual license born of Muhammad's own scandals.</note>

This is the law, and this is the cause. Blessed are they who rush into crime and wickedness in the manner of the prophet, who do not only lie with their wives, but also with slaves of any kind. For he writes indefinitely, nor is the handmaid under the <term>necessity</term> <note>original Greek: $\alpha\nu\alpha\gamma\kappa\eta$ (ananke), meaning a binding constraint</note> of the law, but *eu ma melecheta aimanuchum*, that is, "or what your faith has acquired" <note>original: "eu ma melecheta aimanuchum," Postel’s transliteration of the Arabic 'aw mā malakat aymānukum,' usually translated as 'what your right hands possess.'</note>—namely, what the crowd of the faithful has seized, profited from, or acquired under the pretext of faith, in which number are male captives and servants no less than female servants and handmaids. Unless he had understood it thus, he could have used the word *amah* <note>original: "amet," referring to the Hebrew/Semitic word for a female slave</note>, which signifies a handmaid specifically. But he wished to establish an expansive law, in which not only a recently committed crime might be permitted, but—what is the worst of all—it might be granted and made praiseworthy for everyone. 

O men captive in your senses! Do deceitful interpreters so mock you that you do not understand these things were written with an evil demon as the author? This law confirms those things I mentioned above concerning <term>pederasty</term> <note>Postel uses this term polemically to argue that the Quranic allowance for "what your right hands possess" was interpreted by some as a license for all forms of sexual behavior.</note>. For this purpose was that law devised: so that all things might be permitted under its name which otherwise are prohibited by divine, natural, and established law. An extraordinary faith indeed, and worthy of its author! I will not say how foul this author is in his writing; he typically uses specific words for the hidden and reproductive parts of nature in men, women, and beasts alike, and for the filthy and sought-after actions themselves. But it is no wonder: since he willingly and knowingly suffered the adulteries of even his own wives, from which one may detect proof of a degraded mind, born only for frauds and deceptions. 

Therefore, having ensnared followers with such a sweet and benevolent law, they <note>the followers</note> not only pardoned what the prophet had now made lawful with God as the author, but they even blamed his wives for having rebuked in the prophet that which was so pleasant and good. Their parents, having calmed the women’s minds, even persuaded the wives to return to the prophet’s house and to obey him in all things; for it had been divinely revealed to him that what they had thought was a sin was not a sin. The astonished women said nothing else to their parents except that this prophet must be a very great friend of God, whom God loved so much that He complied with all his desires. **Vbecharus** <note>Abu Bakr</note> and **Homarus** <note>Umar ibn al-Khattab</note>, and others who were in on the story, imposed silence on the wives—not because they cared for Muhammad or his nonsense, but because the matter seemed to pertain most of all to them. For when they gave the wealthiest and most beautiful virgins as wives to this mad and criminal impostor prophet, it was done so that, once his power was established, his affairs might pass to them after the prophet's death. Therefore, the scandal was more easily suppressed, with only a few understanding the tricks, and those people especially pretending to believe, so that at last the common folk and that rustic crowd—seeing that the powerful were not moved by the scandal but seemed to believe the revelations—willingly acquiesced and did not desert him. Indeed, from that time on, it was very frequently objected against him even

For they do not consider, he claims, that they might more quickly obtain wealth and children from his path—as if that were true, or as if those things were the reward for the good in this life. Truly, he held back the superstitious, the ignorant, and those forgetful of past events—who use no comparison of facts—with ambiguous and uncertain promises, as if they would be happier under one tyrant than another. The scoundrel <note>original Latin: *nebulo*</note> knew that wretched men, pressed by calamities and frequent injury and plundering, are refreshed more by even a small breathing-space than they were by great wealth before their afflictions. ### Elnor, that is, The Light; 23. Written at Medina. <note>Postel refers to Surah 24, "An-Nur" (The Light). Although he numbers it 23 here, it is the 24th Surah of the Quran. He characterizes its contents as "smoke" rather than "light."</note>

Just as we saw the kind of "faithfulness" in the "head of the faithful," so we shall see the kind of "light" in that smoke of his. For just as the man’s wickedness was clear in the preceding chapter, so also in this one it will manifest itself and shed light upon its author. He says:
> » "We have sent down a Surah <note>original: *Sora*</note>, and we have explained it, and we have sent
> » down in it miracles of wisdom, if perhaps you might remember. Let the fornicatress and the fornicator 
> » each be struck with 100 blows: and let no mercy seize you for them in the law of God, if you 
> » believe in God and the Last Day; and let some of the faithful be present at their punishment."

Let the fornicator not contract marriage, etc. These things refer back to the reasoning of the crimes committed above: that God therefore permitted many wives, concubines, and catamites <note>a historical term for a younger male partner</note> so that adulteries would not be committed; and if anyone should commit them, the punishments would be such as are described here. And yet, before this law, there was a paternal custom and habit that a man should not know any other woman besides his wife, not even a slave-girl. For it would not have been a fault if it had already been permitted before. Truly, the law he established, he never kept. For Aisha <note>original: *Assa*</note>, the daughter of Abu Bakr <note>original: *Vbecharí*</note>, whom he held most dear, was even publicly accustomed to many lovers. For this reason, he was warned by many to at least divorce her; they said it was utterly disgraceful for the primary woman of the Prophet to act so publicly as a prostitute. To these people he said nothing else than that she was his most beloved, and therefore he would not divorce her. The cowardly scoundrel placed no honor before his eyes, provided he could seize power. When he took her as a wife—born, as I said, eight years prior—and tasted of her, he "sold his power," as Plautus says, and "possessed a dowry, not a wife." <note>Postel quotes a Roman comedy to suggest Muhammad married for political gain and influence through Abu Bakr, rather than for a proper marriage.</note> And yet the "sacrosanct" faith of the Quran, and the exposition of prophetic deeds, depends on the report of a public prostitute, a wife, and the daughter of a tyrant; nor is anything more holy than that faith. For its opinion is called *hadith sahih* <note>original: *dhache tzahh*</note>, which means "this is certain and complete." Thus, that which would not be admitted as testimony in secular judgments due to infamy, brings authority to the divine law. The great crime of that prostitute excited the greatest discord among the successors, from which the faction of Ali <note>original: *Halí*</note> and Abu Bakr began, through which many myriads of men perished, and thirty Caliphs were consequently killed.
> » "Truly," he says, "those who accuse chaste women and do not come with four witnesses, let them be 
> » struck with 80 lashes."

As if it were easy to have four men at home for testimony! Therefore the lawmaker wishes to seem skilled and to depart from both laws <note>referring to Jewish and Christian law</note>. In truth, these things were not established for the sake of women, but for the sake of the Prophet and his wives. For by the same law that it is not permitted for a man to falsely accuse his wife of adultery without the proof of four witnesses, it was likewise not permitted for the wives of the Prophet—who did not have four witnesses—to accuse him of adultery, as if...

Since the law had already been established, everything tends toward this: although it is permitted by law to deal with female slaves <note>original: *mācipijs*</note>, so that if by chance he were caught with any other woman, he could not be accused. Certainly any impious, unjust, or guilty person becomes pious, just, and innocent in words while being pressured; and if the pressure continues, he becomes so in deeds. See how he makes a way for perjuries while he places proof in an oath, since nothing is more common than an oath among Muslims <note>original: *Mussulmanos*</note>. And meanwhile, the matter comes to nothing while the woman denies the charges with contrary oaths, so that the judge's time is wasted in vain. But I come to other things that are relevant. <margin>«</margin>Have you not heard the opinion of believing men and women, good among themselves, when they said, "This is a manifest fiction"? <margin>«</margin>Did they not come to him with four witnesses? You see the mysteries betrayed; therefore he wants his wives and household to be held by the law now established, after they had opened the secrets. Adultery does not trouble him so badly—which has already begun to be made legitimate by the preceding law—as much as the fact that they had called the law a fiction and a trick <note>original: *stropham*</note>. For the followers deservedly believed them, as if they were privy to prophetic secrets; whence he bears it most troublesome, and would want them to have proved with four witnesses that it is a fiction, when it was already plain to "the bleary-eyed and the barbers" <note>A Latin idiom, *lippis et tonsoribus*, meaning "everyone knows it" or "it's common gossip."</note>. For already it has been objected to him a hundred times before, and he did not demand four witnesses; but to be betrayed by one's own household is an argument for the truth. Therefore, the need for four witnesses. I continue. <margin>«</margin>And when you were disparaging it with your tongues, <margin>«</margin>and saying with your mouth that in which you have no knowledge, and you thought it a light thing which in the sight of God is great. <margin>«</margin>Rather, when you heard it, you ought to have said of it, "Let this not happen to us, that we should speak of this; far be it, this is a great sin." 

How can it be that this prophet so fears the tongues of his household and friends? (For so he calls the *muminīn* and *muminet* <term>believing men and believing women</term>). Does he want his affairs to be so religiously observed and admired that it is not even permitted to speak of them? He must surely be more wicked than any robbers or any lost souls, he for whom all his household are a source of fear. How is it that, if he is a prophet of God, he does not send divine fire upon the seditious like another Moses? Why does he not doom them like Dathan and Abiram, or punish them with leprosy like Miriam the sister? It was not necessary for Moses to repeat so many times, "I am the prophet of God," as if there were nothing else in his law. It was not necessary to reiterate a thousand times, "they say you are inventing these things," "you are driven by a demon," "you are mad," and other vices. For no such suspicion fell upon Moses and the prophets. Whence, since so many types of wickedness were being thrown at you by the voices of everyone, it could not be that you were innocent. For "the voice of the people" in exposing crimes "is the voice of God." You will never find in any of the true prophets that he asserted such things about himself three or four times. They held it sufficient to have brought forth the divine message, whether the listeners believed or did not believe. But you wanted to join the Jews, or the Christians, or the pagans to yourself. Therefore, because of your crimes and vices, [the truth is] open to all...

->The Furqan, Chapter 24<- <note>original: "Alphurcan 24" — Postel uses "Al-Furqan" (The Criterion) as a title for the Quran or its chapters.</note>

He begins immediately with blasphemies against God and Christ, claiming that God did not beget. I have already proven to this most frequent plague that it is entirely impossible for anything in the whole nature of things to subsist, unless God from eternity created a son from himself. Among all nations it is agreed that there is one infinite first cause, which, although it is most powerful, unless it is also most wise and benevolent, can create nothing at all. Nor is it enough to have used such wisdom in the first creation of things, unless, insofar as this life lasts—that is, generation and corruption—that same wisdom disposes, rules, and preserves in being whatever things exist in the nature of things. That wisdom we call the Son of God and the Word <note>original: "verbū"</note>. In power is the whole divinity, in wisdom the whole divinity, in benevolence the whole divinity; yet there are not three divinities, but one divinity. Just as in the thought of a thing the whole thing is present, and in the word and explanation the whole thing is present, and in the completion of the work the whole thing is present; yet they are not three, but one thing. For the sake of those men whom this plague has fascinated, I frequently hammer this in, so that they may cease from blasphemy against God and His Christ. Christ, therefore, the son of Mary, is the wisdom of the Father, begotten from eternity. But when it seemed good to the divinity, Wisdom itself joined our flesh to itself from a virgin, and God was made man; against whom this lost scoundrel rose up for the sake of obtaining power. But the truth of the Lord remains forever. Finally, he brings up the objections usually made against him: that it is a fiction, and that others provided him assistance. ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...a certain Nestorian hermit <note>Postel refers here to the monk Bahira, also known as Sergius, who in medieval Christian polemics was often claimed to be the secret author of the Quran.</note>, who narrated to him many things, but most notably the history of the 7 sleepers <note>original: "historiam 7. dormientiū"; referring to the Legend of the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus, which appears in Surah 18 (The Cave).</note> to provide evidence for the manifest faith of the resurrection. And for him, Gabriel was in Medina, just as the Jews were in Mecca. In those histories of the prophets which the Caliph <note>original: "Chaliphas"</note> submerged in the river, it was also noted shortly before the death of Muhammad <note>original: "Muhamedis"</note> that the Jews wanted to elevate Ali <note>original: "Halim"</note>, this prophet's nephew <note>Ali was actually Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, but early modern writers often confused these familial relations.</note>, a very young man, to the rank of prophet. While Ali incautiously sought a cave suitable for his faction, he found Muhammad in the cavern with the Nestorian monk, and so what everyone suspected became clear: that he sought a teacher from elsewhere rather than from an angelic spirit. Therefore, the scoundrel feared in a wondrous way lest his tricks be revealed. He busied himself with winning over the young man with great gifts, yet he could not prevent the matter from being betrayed; he countered this in this place and many others by bringing nothing but divine threats, saying it was injurious for anyone to say such things. Thus the deception revealed itself. About Sergius the Nestorian, it was common knowledge to everyone. Truly all those things have been erased from their histories, and they cannot be proven except through the commentaries of the Sunnah <note>original: "Suneh"; the body of traditional social and legal custom and practice of the Islamic community.</note>. He proceeds to threaten those who said he was nothing but insane, those who daily, evening and morning, received from elsewhere the things he dictated. If he had an angel, he ought to see to it that he no longer lived off others. Finally, as if he were a prophet, he says it is no wonder if he and the Quran <note>original: "Alcorano"</note> are opposed, for all prophets had adversaries. But if someone is a prophet simply because he has adversaries, then thieves, murderers, plunderers, the impious, sorcerers, and other wicked men are among the prophets; for they all have the good, the laws, and the judges as bitter and hostile enemies, as those against whom they plot destruction. Thus, no one denies that Muhammad was a prophet in that sense. Indeed, he left this confirmed by many arguments. The rest are the usual repetitions.

### 25. Sigra, Poetry. <note>original: "Sigra, poësis"; "Sigra" is Postel's transliteration of "Surah." He is referring to Surah 26, "Ash-Shu'ara" (The Poets).</note>

Since he mixes nothing but falsehoods with truths, joining many lies to the histories of the Old Testament, as well as the fables of old Arabian women, and recites the usual miracles and blasphemies already refuted above, I write nothing further in this place.

### 26. The Ant. <note>original: "Formica"; referring to Surah 27, "An-Naml" (The Ants).</note>

He patronizes himself and applauds his own vices when he makes Moses seek fire from a bush with a staff and calls God to himself without fear. 
> For my messengers are none but 
> those who have sinned; then if they have turned back, God is merciful and pious. <note>A summary of Quran 27:10–11.</note>

For although he was most defiled by every stain of vice, he nevertheless claimed God was favorable and familiar to him, and that vices did not stand in the way of piety and prophecy. Then he joins a lie to the sacred history, saying that Moses came to Pharaoh with 8 miracles, though he said nine before, and in both there is a lie, since there are ten <note>Postel is comparing the Quranic "Nine Signs" of Moses with the biblical Ten Plagues of Egypt.</note>. Then, inventing a fable about Solomon, he says: 
> And Solomon succeeded David, 
> and said: "O men, we have been taught the speech of birds, and we have been gifted with 
> everything, for this is a signal blessing." And the cohorts of 
> demons, and men, and birds were called by Solomon, and they assembled until they came to the river 
> of the ant. An ant said: "O ants, enter into your dwellings lest 
> Solomon and his cohorts seize you, and they will not spare you." And a cry was raised by 
> their voices, and he said: "Teach me to praise You for Your favor, with which You have benefited 
> me and my father, that I may do good," etc. <note>A translation of Quran 27:16–19.</note>

Who could bear to hear these absurdities? But these are nothing compared to the hoopoe bird <note>original: "upupa"; a bird that acts as a messenger for Solomon in Islamic tradition.</note>, and its conversation, and its embassy and preaching. Let anyone who wishes see those absurdities with which he mocks God and men. Nothing more insane or delirious can be found; and yet this law is supposedly from God and divine. I am silent about the horrendous absurdities concerning the throne, the Queen of Sheba, and the service of demons—all of which were directed toward woman-

In truth, I believe nothing could have been proposed to this man to which he would not have given an answer—a privilege granted only to fools and the mad.

### 27.

It is false that Moses was thrown into the sea; they sent him into the River Nile to be killed. There he was taken up by Pharaoh’s daughter and raised; here [in the Quran] it says by his wife, and previously by his sister: so far does nothing lack a lie in this man. What does he not falsely attach to sacred history? Concerning Pharaoh, Haman <note>Postel is pointing out a perceived chronological error: Haman is a figure from the Persian period in the Bible (Book of Esther), but appears in the Quran as an official of the Egyptian Pharaoh.</note>, and the key to the treasures which forty men could not move—this history must be sought elsewhere from the book of *Hafsiar* <note>original: "libro Hafsiar"; likely referring to a "Tafsir" or Quranic commentary.</note>, along with Al-Buraq <note>The celestial steed of Muhammad’s Night Journey.</note> and Gabriel. At the end of this chapter, he cuts the throats of his own chronographers, who trace a "light" from Adam down to him and say the prophet was born circumcised. For if he were a prophet from birth, how is it that he did not know for so long, such that until the 40th year of his age he did not feel or know himself to be a prophet? Indeed, he himself confesses that at one time he did not think so. "Say," he says, "my Creator knows who is guided and who is in manifest error." <margin>cc</margin> "And you did not hope that the book would be delivered to you, except by the mercy of your Lord; therefore do not be exalted over the blasphemers." <margin>cc</margin> In this place, he pretends to spare the idolaters <margin>cc</margin> among whom he had been educated, imbued, and initiated. But he did not think it would happen that the later Caliphs would one day make him so great; nor did they sufficiently notice what he confessed about himself.

### 28. The Spider. <note>Refers to Surah 29, "Al-Ankabut" (The Spider).</note>

There is nothing more worthy of the author in this chapter than his promise of a future resurrection for all living things, so that not only animals but even inanimate creatures shall be eternal. For the word *chelec* <note>original: "chelec"; referring to the Arabic "khalk" (creation/creature).</note> is general to all created things. Concerning brute animals, this is written as an article of faith in the book *Tezchere elimam* <note>Likely referring to "Tadhkirat al-Imam," a theological treatise.</note> among the reasons of faith. If miracles are with God alone, and some prophets had them, they were close to God. But since you [Muhammad] have none, you are a stranger to God. Therefore, the miracles of the wolves, the Buraq, the tree trunks, the moon, and the heart were not true but false, since you are not God. I skip several chapters here, very similar to the others, so that I may come to more noteworthy things: to Surah 32 <note>Though Postel writes 32, the margin and context indicate Surah 33, "Al-Ahzab" (The Confederates).</note>, which opens to us many remarkable deeds of the prophet.

<margin>The Confederates.</margin> First, it must be seen how he violently fell upon the property and inheritances of others in Medina and expelled the Jews and other inhabitants, so that they were forced to seek help from their tribesmen; this is hinted at in these words: "Remember when the double-hearted <note>A term Postel uses for "hypocrites" (Munafiqun).</note> said, and those in whose hearts was a disease: <margin>cc</margin> 'His Apostle promises nothing but losses and inconveniences'; and remember when some citizens of Yathrib <note>original: "Ietribæ"; the pre-Islamic name for Medina.</note> said: 'There is no place for you, go back'; and some of them asked leave of the prophet, saying, 'Our houses are in ruins,' though they were not desolate, <margin>cc</margin> but they wished to flee," etc. <margin>cc</margin> By these words and those following, he claimed he had a right to their property because they would not submit to his persuasion. For when he had begun this fable in Mecca with the Jews for ten years, and they had rejected the open deceit, and when he had to go into exile in the 50th year of his life or thereabouts, he expelled the miserable Jews and Christians living in Yathrib <note>original: "Iezrab"</note> from their homes on the pretext that there was "a disease in their hearts." Such was the equity of the prophet. Those miserable Jews were indeed persuading many followers to leave the prophet and return to their own people so they would not be crushed by the crowd; when he sensed this, his "prophetic equity" raged even more fiercely. ...he stripped the people of all their fortunes in the same city; now nothing is enough for him. At first it was enough for him to have occupied a place in which to act according to his whim; now he wishes to establish a permanent seat. But he leaves the greatest proof of his cruelty, both in many places and in that one shortly after. And when we approach, you see them as if dead, tormented by fear; but when we depart, they sharpen their tongues to criticize you.

What else would happen when a tyrant arrives? In his presence everything is like the image of death, nor is it permitted to judge freely until he has departed. But that sense of "equity" must be examined. *Some of them you shall kill, others you shall take captive, and you shall occupy their possessions, their goods, and the land which you had never entered, because God is powerful over all things.* <note>Postel is paraphrasing Surah Al-Ahzab (33:26-27), which refers to the conquest of the Banu Qurayza.</note> That is to say, Muhammad is a most cruel plunderer, who under the name of God commits every possible crime. But a cohort of women had to be led along with the prophet, and governed by the terror of the deity, so that everything might be permitted to the prophet both at home and abroad. 

But I had forgotten a most beautiful and truly "prophetic" passage, which though it is not in the African manuscript, is found in others. *And if you do not acknowledge your fathers or your brothers in faith and your wealth, it is not necessary for you to worry about that in which you sin; and therefore let not your hearts doubt, since God is merciful and kind to the prophet; those are the faithful, etc.* <note>Postel interprets various Quranic verses (likely 33:4-5 and 9:23) as a mandate to prioritize the "Prophet" over biological family.</note> This is so that it might be permitted for his followers to rage most "justly" against their parents, and to kill fathers and brothers; it is enough to use the ignorance of the name of "faith" as a pretext. And God is favorable to the prophet, for whose sake these things are done. Since he had declared war on his brothers, and had already killed some, he wanted—on account of this new faith—that not even fathers should be recognized by their sons, but rather that fathers, brothers, relatives, and kin should be finished off. O, how far these things are from Christian piety! 

I return to the women. *O prophet, say to your wives: if they love this world and reach for its splendor, I will give them life and many delights.* <note>Refers to Surah 33:28, the "Verse of Choice" given to Muhammad's wives.</note> This, and the following verse, pertains to those rich women who had left the man, and were very wealthy citizens of Mecca. To them, therefore, he promises what he forbids to others: so that it may be plainly said of him, "whatever pleases him is permitted." He adds frightening threats, saying they are worthy of double punishment if they do not comply; for in this context, that is what it means to sin. Otherwise, there is a great reward from God if they obey. God spares the messenger more if he kills his parents than he spares other men. *If the wives do not obey, they are worthy of double punishment; a fine sort of equity.*

I had already said before (something I have been able to note quite often) that God makes Muhammad His partner. It is established, he says, as a precept from God and from His prophet, that there is no believer without the faithful. <note>original: "non sit fidelis sine fideli"</note> Does he not strive to make his authority equal to the divine, while he wishes to be considered a partner and participant in the divine command? How often he hammers home: *Hear God and his prophet, obey God and his legate, those who do not believe in God and his legate*, etc. Is this not a participation in divine power? Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets used to say, "Hear the word of God" only—not "of God and the prophet," like this scoundrel <note>original: "nebulo"; a term of deep contempt.</note>. For those men sought nothing for themselves of wealth, honor, or favor, like this false prophet; and therefore they were satisfied to reveal the impulse of the divine spirit. Since this man had nothing from God or right judgment except what was begged from elsewhere, he never fails to join himself to God and hammer it into the gullible crowd. Such is the nature of falsehood: it never fails to commend and thrust itself forward more ardently and frequently the less it approaches the truth. For while it occupies the mind with frequent self-commendations, it removes and eludes the opportunity for examination, lest it be recognized. But the continuous discourse in several verses must be heard. *Let there not be,* he says, *a believer without the faithful, since God and his prophet have established a precept; if their precept is good for you, then he who turns away from God and his prophet already wanders in manifest error.* These points pertain to the same end as above: that he may share power with God. 

But concerning Zeid <note>Refers to Zayd ibn Harithah, Muhammad’s adopted son; the text likely transitions here to the controversy surrounding Muhammad's marriage to Zayd's former wife, Zaynab bint Jahsh.</note>:

Having previously attacked Muhammad’s military actions as mere plunder, Postel now focuses on a specific Quranic passage (Surah Al-Ahzab) to argue that Muhammad’s personal desires—specifically regarding his marriage to the wife of his adopted son, Zayd—were the true source of what he claims are "divine" laws.</meta>

## WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK II.

> And when you said to him whom God has blessed, and whom you also have blessed: "Keep your wife for yourself and fear God," and you hide within yourself what God is revealing, and you fear men, while God is more worthy of fear. And when Zayd <note>Postel uses the Latin *Zeidus* for Zayd ibn Harithah, Muhammad's adopted son.</note> had fulfilled his desire for her, We joined her to you in marriage. Let there be no scandal among the believers concerning the wives of their servants, when they have fulfilled their desire for them, and let the command of the Lord be done. Let there be no scandal upon the prophet in that which God said: "He has the power of the law." God was in those who passed away before, and the command of God is most powerful. Among those to whom the prophecy of God arrived, they all fear Him; he fears no one but God, and it is enough to gain favor with God. Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but he is the prophet of God, the seal of the prophets, and God is wise in all things.

Oh, how great are the mysteries that lie hidden here! From nearly his childhood, Muhammad had kept the servant Zayd in his house, to whom—as the first to be initiated as a Muslim <note>original: *Mussulman*</note>—he gave freedom, not without great promises. A few years later, already enriched by the spoils taken from his followers, and because Zayd managed the household affairs quite faithfully, Muhammad gave him his own kinswoman <note>This refers to Zaynab bint Jahsh, Muhammad's cousin.</note> in marriage, with whom Zayd lived for some years, loving her exceedingly. 

However, while the "prophetic people" were staying in Medina and Muhammad began to exercise kingship, he was seized by love for this kinswoman, the wife of his most faithful servant. Thus, approaching the house and not finding the husband, he said to the woman (as it is written in the book *Hassiar* <note>original: *Hassiar*. This likely refers to the *Sira* or *Siyar*, the traditional biographies of the Prophet.</note>) that Zayd had chosen the best "hinge for his door." He commanded the woman—who did not understand those words—to tell her husband. 

When Zayd heard this, immediately (as one who had long known the man's mind and knew how to interpret ambiguous prophetic sayings) he said: "The 'hinge' in the prophet's word means my wife, and the 'door' is my house. He meant to signify that I have a wife of elegant form, and that I ought to leave her so that she might go to the prophet. Such is the nature of the man: unless you do his bidding immediately, he is accustomed to compel you with more abundant force and death." 

Both dissolved into tears. Without delay, a prophecy arrived ordering Zayd to divorce his wife. He had to obey instantly; he left the house, and the next day she married the prophet, who already had twelve wives. This is the course of the "prophetic" history; this is its meaning. But a great scandal arose from this matter, because he had been so unjust as to take another's wife, and so wicked as to marry a kinswoman, whom he had forbidden to others by different laws. 

Now the text must be examined more closely. He reproaches the servant at the beginning for the benefits received from himself and from God—that is, from the spoils of war. For Zayd led many raids against the merchants with which they besieged Mecca <note>original: *Mecham*</note> from all sides, where he became wealthy. When Muhammad saw that everyone’s offense was intense, he told Zayd that he had ordered him to keep his wife, even though he had forced him to divorce her. 

But since Zayd did not dare to even mutter in his presence, yet complained in his absence of the injury inflicted, Muhammad says to him while he remains silent and approves the deed out of fear: "He hides something within himself, but God will reveal it." That is to say, if he hears anything of that matter, it is all over for the man; he will die by the authority of God. And that he should not fear men, but God—that is, the fury and insane prophetic rage of Muhammad. 

Then finally he places into law what he committed—that is, that the same thing is permitted to anyone over their household and subjects as was permitted to him: namely, after they have forced a wretched subject to divorce his wives so they may marry them immediately, they say that after they have fulfilled their will with them, there is no scandal for the master, or for the one who compels the servant to marry her through fear of death; and because God said it, it is done. Thus from his crimes were born laws by which others were allowed the same things as he. They took many women because he had many; female servants and handmaids are permitted to all without fault because that had been turned into a fault for the prophet; male favorites <note>original: *catamitti*. In Postel's polemical context, this is a hostile accusation regarding the Prophet's companions or household.</note> are legitimate because they pleased the prophet. To enter bru...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s polemic against the character of Muhammad and the legal precedents established in the Quran. Following the previous page’s discussion of Muhammad’s marriage to Zaynab (the former wife of his servant Zayd), Postel argues that this act established a dangerous precedent where personal desire is masqueraded as divine law.</meta>

By that same law, it is permitted to plunder everything and to lie in wait for the lives of all; it has been made lawful for everyone, once the name of "faith" is brought forward. Because it was permitted to the prophet, it is considered honorable to marry the woman left behind by a forced servant, simply because the prophet approved of it. O blind men! How can you bear such impieties, let alone ascribe them to God and comment upon them so seriously? But I proceed.

> "There is no scandal for the prophet in that which God commanded." <note>Postel is quoting Quran 33:38.</note>

But God commands whatever is pleasing to him [Muhammad]; therefore, whatever is pleasing is lawful—this is his law. It is true that the command of God was powerful among the ancients [the biblical patriarchs], as they excelled in signs, miracles, wonders, and the foretelling of events. But it was not powerful for despoiling citizens of their fortunes, nor for killing brothers and parents, nor for bringing back dreams and lies from caves, nor for hostilely invading foreign lands, nor for bestial acts, nor for oppressing servants, nor for overturning all sins and committing other atrocities which I shudder to mention. In these and similar things, you have made the most powerful "command" of your God. It is certain that your God is different from the God of the whole world. The God of nature sometimes permits adversity to happen to man; however, the God of Muhammad commands and approves whatever tends toward the ruin of nature. But let us hear the status of this prophet. To whom...

> "...prophecy reaches, everyone fears him, and he fears no one." <note>A paraphrased reference to the authority granted to Muhammad in the Quranic text.</note>

O, the patience of wretched men! Whether the prophet rushes into what is right or wrong, whether he subverts the sacred or the profane, or brings ruin to everyone, he fears nothing. What bloodthirsty tyrant could have devised a more convenient law for himself? Because of the impious deeds he has committed, Muhammad fears no one, even though he has inflicted six hundred injuries. From this, it is clear that he did not follow laws, he who wished to be the lawmaker for everyone. For if he had any spark of humanity within him, he ought at least to have feared offending mankind; but in truth, he fears no one but God. Yet, does not he who commits impious crimes and claims to fear God lie? Does he not, by his very deeds, affirm that there is no God?

But he spares the prophet more than others, as was said before. A sin is usually considered more grievous depending on how great the sinner is held to be. Muhammad wants to be the greatest of all, and yet to sin in nothing, even while he transgresses against God, nature, and man. It is enough for him to "gain favor" with God. A plunderer, a thief, a robber, a tyrant—so long as he takes in the name of God, all things belong to him. In this way, O Muslims <note>original: *Mussulmani*</note>, were your original riches acquired. What follows is a little more obscure:

> "Muhammad is not the father of any of your men." <note>Quran 33:40.</note>

He wanted to suggest by this that blood relationship was no obstacle to him marrying a kinswoman. For as long as she was not the wife of a biological son, he could take her by his law as if she were legitimate. Therefore, what he had said before—"He is not the father of your men"—meant that he may take your wives in marriage whenever he pleases. "He is indeed the seal of the prophets," <note>A translation of the Arabic term *Khatam an-Nabiyyin*.</note> that is, the completion, after whom there will be none. There will be people like you as long as the world lasts; but no true prophets ought to have come for 600 years before you. For the end of the Law and the prophecy was Christ Jesus, the God-man, who was the true Seal of the Prophets. For God would have acted in vain and foolishly if, after sending the highest remedy of all [Christ], He had reserved for Himself another lesser one. Indeed, the greatest of the prophets, as even Muhammad admits, was Jesus Christ. After the greatest remedy has been applied to human affairs, there can be no place for a lesser one. For if a stone column bears its burden with difficulty, how can that same burden be supported by a mere stake or a pole?

You are not the "seal" of prophets, Muhammad, but a seal of evils. There are others like you still to come until the end of the world, until the most wicked and last of the Antichrists comes, for whom you have paved the way by admitting every kind of pleasure and vice into religion. He indeed will surpass you, because he will confirm his power with lying signs—a power that will last all the shorter for the violence with which it breaks forth. But God is truly wise in all things, and powerful against you...

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK II.

...to defer the final punishment until the Day of Judgment. As for the rest:

"Worship God morning and evening; it is he who prays for you, and his angels, so that he may lead you out of darkness into light." <note>Postel is quoting Quran 33:42–43. The Latin translation he used translated the Arabic *sallā*—meaning to bless or bestow grace—literally as *orare*, "to pray."</note> It is certainly strange to think whom God could pray to, unless he prays to himself. If we are speaking of God insofar as he is God, nothing more foolish can be imagined. If a spirit compelled you, even against your will—just as it did Saul and Caiaphas—to utter this concerning Christ (against whom you write), I praise the spirit, not you. <note>In the Bible, King Saul and the High Priest Caiaphas are depicted as prophesying truths by divine compulsion despite their personal failings. Postel suggests Muhammad might have accidentally stumbled onto a truth about Christ's intercession.</note> For we truly have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, both God and man, who is also the atonement for our sins. This same sentiment is repeated more than once so that it may be understood. Certainly, you understand God as praying to himself, along with his angels, for the conjunction teaches this.

Although I am ashamed of such absurdities, those "privileges" must also be added, which he granted to himself by his own authority, contrary to the rules set for others. "O Prophet," he says, "we give you the power to dismiss your wives once you have given them their dower; and also female servants, once you have given the reward from those things which God has bestowed upon you; and the daughters of your paternal uncle, and the daughters of your paternal aunt, and the daughters of your maternal uncle, and the daughters of your maternal aunt, who travel with you <note>Original: *peregrinantur tecum*, referring to the *Hijra* or migration to Medina.</note>; and faithful women, if they give themselves to the prophet, if the prophet wishes them to be joined to him—this is a good thing for you, beyond the other believers. Now we know what we have established among them concerning wives and handmaids or slaves, so that there may be no offense against you by anyone on that account, since God is pious and favorable. You shall join to yourself and embrace whom you wish, and whom you desire from those whom you have set free, and this is not prohibited to you; whatever is allowed, if you are pleasing in their eyes, and they are not saddened, and if they accept what you give to all of them. It is not granted to you to exchange wives—that is, to have parents and the wives of others along with your own. But if their beauty pleases you, apart from the handmaids, God is pious. O you who believe, do not enter the houses of the prophet unless it is permitted to you for eating, and without staring at the vessels. But when you are called, enter; and when you have eaten, depart; and do not recount what was done or the events that took place, for the prophet bears these things with difficulty and is bashful before you, but God is not bashful about the truth." <note>Postel is paraphrasing Quran 33:50–53, which discusses the Prophet’s marriage privileges and the etiquette for guests in his home.</note>

The meaning here is abundant. The very law he had laid down for others—that it was not permitted to divorce without just cause—he exempts himself from, both for many reasons and on account of parents. For that scoundrel <note>Original: *nebulo*, a term for a worthless person or rascal.</note> was of such "charity" that he would drive away all parents because he had no use for them, since he could have any women he liked as wives even without a marriage contract. Furthermore, while he wanted others to be bound to treat their wives with equal law, he himself approves, summons, or repudiates whomever he wants, treating them according to his whim; he wishes to be bound by no law whatsoever. If they accept gifts, if they smile, they are immediately the legitimate wives of the prophet. Nor should he suffer scandal for anything he commits, because "God is merciful and pious."

Furthermore, because he was committing crimes of every kind at home—abusing whomever he wished, whether catamites <note>Original: *catamittis*, referring to young boys kept for sexual purposes; a common but historically unsubstantiated polemical accusation against Muhammad in this period.</note>, handmaids, or wives, arranged according to various dispositions (which I cannot decently describe)—he did not want anyone to enter his house unless invited to the table. And even when invited, he did not want them to look at the cups and furniture, because the plunder of the Arabian world was to be seen in his possession. Moreover, he wanted silence to be observed there, because by the occasion of the things they saw there, his wives were compelled to tell of the man's wicked deeds, which troubled the man greatly. Therefore, he makes God the author and vindicator of these laws. Judge the prophetic deeds, and evaluate the author! The ancients were quite stupid in accepting the false religions of robbers and lost men, but there has not been a more wicked or more foolish man since the creation of the world. From this it appears with how much blood he urged these things, and how many thousands of men he killed to persuade them. But I wonder how he could terrify those who were members of his own household with these trifles. Truly, even those of the household obeyed...

Here, he moves to the political and military suppression of dissent in Medina, mocking the Quranic accounts of Solomon and the nature of angels, while arguing that Islam’s primary goal is to diminish the divinity of Christ.</meta>

-># ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

...[he] was suppressing them with bloody edicts. Hear the decree: 
> "If those in whose hearts is a disease do not withdraw from the city, and if they persist in spreading rumors in the city, they are cursed. Wherever they are found, seize them and kill them." <note>Postel is quoting Quran 33:60–61. He interprets "disease in the heart" not as a lack of faith, but as a political label used to justify the seizure of property.</note>

Because women had shortly before exposed his tricks, and everything had been made public, he therefore threatens death if anyone even whispers. On that pretext, whomever he saw was wealthy or lived in a fine house, he would say there was a "disease" in that person's heart. Thus, unless they sought safety by fleeing and abandoning their possessions—especially the Jews, whom he calls the authors of these stories and plots—they were killed. And truly, they were justly afflicted and despoiled of their goods in that place; for out of envy toward Jesus Christ, they had helped this plague <note>By "plague," Postel refers to Muhammad/Islam.</note> reach a position where it could seize power. Thus, they are utterly oppressed by these and similar laws.

### 33.

It shames me to relate the things found in chapter 33 <note>Postel refers here to stories often associated with Solomon in the Quran, specifically in Surah 27 (The Ants) and Surah 34 (Sheba).</note> concerning the demons of Solomon, their works, and the winds. They are all similar to his stories about hoopoes, birds, and ants. Certainly, if some very senile old woman were to recite such things in that manner, she could not keep even infants or nursemaids listening. And yet, if it pleases the gods <note>original: "si dijs placet" — a sarcastic Latin idiom meaning "heaven help us" or "believe it or not."</note>, these things are supposedly from God. The interpreters of these trifles are not ashamed, but linger over them as if they were serious matters. Finally, he quietly babbles blasphemies against Christ and urges the lowly to believe, following the example of the rich. But, as he says, they often lacked the knowledge that the magnates possessed, because the elites were skilled in the "story" which the poor did not know but were coming to accept. Therefore, he now calls both groups by their proper names. The poor he calls <term>mutzehiphune</term> <note>original: "mutzehiphune" from the Arabic *mustad'afun*, meaning the oppressed or those deemed weak.</note>, that is, the afflicted and the weak; the rich he calls <term>mustecberine</term> <note>original: "mustecberine" from the Arabic *mustakbirun*, meaning the arrogant or those who grow proud.</note>, that is, the proud and haughty. For his "magnates" were people who, a little while before, had been commoners, those registered by head-count only, cobblers, and sedentary craftsmen. By the company of such men, joined with a few wealthy men from Mecca, he increased and prepared his power. A man who was recently poor and has become enriched by a shortcut can hardly be restrained by any laws; therefore, he is usually proud.

### 34. Angels, or the Creator.

> "Praise be to God, the creator of heaven and earth," he says, "who made the angels as messengers [apostles], endowed with two, three, or four wings; he adds to creation what he wills, etc." <note>Postel is quoting the beginning of Surah 35, though he labels it as 34.</note>

What nonsense he offers at the beginning, he who says that angels were once "apostles" or "prophets." For the word <term>rossol</term> <note>original: "rossol" from the Arabic *rasul*, meaning messenger or apostle.</note> signifies both. To what people, then, did they announce it, or what law did they give? We read that three angels visited Abraham, but they neither gave a law, nor did they have such a variety of wings. Truly, these things point elsewhere: for in the narration of the journey and the riding of <term>Alborac</term> <note>original: "Alborac" refers to the *Buraq*, the winged steed that carried Muhammad during the Night Journey.</note>, it is said that Gabriel had 70 wings, and that he saw infinite thousands of other angels having more, and being a hundred thousand times larger than the world. And so, to appear as if he had seen angels, he proposed this mystery of wings. Yet, in the Holy Scriptures, whenever the appearances of angels have presented themselves to human senses, no mention is made of their wings. The "rowing of wings" is attributed to bodies only because one sees that nothing can be carried through the air without that effort. But for spirits devoid of a body, no wings are needed, except so that we may accommodate divine things to the weakness of our senses, since in this body we can conceive of nothing except through examples and physical objects. All these inferior things fight against Christ. For by the persuasion of his Jewish instructors, he intended nothing else in the whole Quran than to extinguish the glory of Christ, the <term>theanthropos</term> <note>original: "θεανθρωπου" (theanthroupos), meaning the "God-man."</note>. To make it seem as if he does this under a greater pretext, he refers all natural things to God as the author, as if we denied that. He does this so that Christ may appear to have created nothing, even though without Him nothing was made, nor could have been made. For God, although most powerful, created nothing without the Word and Wisdom—which Solomon celebrated so greatly in the Proverbs. I marvel that the Jews are so captured in their minds that they read those things daily and never understand them. But concerning that same Word or Wisdom...

->## WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK II<-

...that Christ is the principle and the Son [of God], I proved by many reasons in the first book. For whatever notable miracles Christ performed, he did so in his own name (as I have often said), which belongs to God alone. As many miracles as were performed by the disciples and the saints, they were done in that same name. All those who followed him and used his instructions were completely transformed and made unlike other men: a transformation that only God can perform. But in the name of Christ, all these things were done, as if by the power of the Word <note>original: "ui uerbi"</note>—through which the concept of my mind is opened to me—whatever supreme things I might undertake, do, or complete, I would do in the name of both thought and action. For a thing is the same in its conception or thought, the same in the explanation of the word, and the same in the execution of the work. The Devil could not have pulled the human race back to himself in any other way except under the pretext of the glory of God, as if the glory ascribed to the Son of God were contrary to the divine glory; whereas in truth, the glory of God never appeared until Christ joined it to a human body.

In this chapter, I will not speak of the "blessed" and usual paradise, in which there are rivers of wine, milk, and honey, as well as fruits, silken garments, golden necklaces, gems, food, drink, sexual intercourse, and other instruments of bodily pleasure. For Muhammad became a prophet for no other reason than to be able to obtain, in this life, that paradise born from plunder and blood. But I have often wondered why God did not fear drunkenness in paradise more than in this world. The reason is ready at hand: Muhammad’s head will not ache, because they will drink their fill of it and not get drunk; they will be active in abundance, and the virgins will always be ready <note>Postel is mocking the Quranic descriptions of a carnal afterlife found in Surahs like 55 and 56.</note>. O great joys! O happy pigs who will live again! O happy rewards! This is the goal of the law received by that man. And are you not ashamed, O Muslims <note>original: "Mussulmani"</note>? Are you so lacking in common sense that you are more senseless than many brute animals? For by the silent sense of nature, the beasts cry out against your law. The faith and conjugal love of the turtledove, the modesty of the camel, the cleanliness of the elephant, the kisses of the wood-pigeons, and six hundred other examples condemn you before God.

<margin>35.</margin>
From here to the end of the book, he swears most frequently, so that the unrefined—who thought he held some concern for perjury—might finally believe what they saw to be false, being conquered and bound by the Prophet's oaths, just as they had previously begun to believe through fears, torments, spoils, and deceptions. Indeed, how much he valued faith is indicated by his breaking of conjugal faith with all his wives. He swore an oath before Hafsa and Aisha <note>original: "Hassam & Hafezam"</note> and immediately neglected and broke it for the sake of a mistress <note>Postel refers to the affair with Maria the Copt and the subsequent revelation of Surah 66.</note>. The covenant struck with the Jews was afterwards made so void that he destroyed almost all of them. He broke the laws that nature gave to the conscience and by which we bargain with her, while he ordered and saw to the slaughter of brothers, parents, citizens, and friends. Therefore, those were utterly seized in mind who, after God had been neglected, after human nature had been cast off, and after disaster had been brought upon everyone, thought he would have any regard for an oath. 

Therefore, in this place, he swears by the "Wise Quran" <note>A reference to the opening of Surah 36, "Ya-Sin."</note>, as if wisdom were something outside the soul. He truly wants to be followed by the example of the Apostles—for by joining together all the prophets, both false and true, he had previously crammed them in to the point of loathing—whom they rejected in Antioch when they were sent by God. Thus it says:

> And he set forth a parable for them: the citizens of the city, when the messengers came to it. When We sent to them two, they called them liars, and We increased the number with a third; and they said, "We are messengers to you." They said, "What are you but men like us? God has granted you nothing from heaven, and you are doing nothing but lying." They said, "Our Lord knows that we are destined for you, and nothing pertains to us except manifest preaching," etc. <note>This is Postel's translation of Quran 36:13–17.</note>

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...the people of Antioch <note>Postel is referencing a story found in Islamic tradition and Quran 36:13–27, often interpreted by commentators as referring to the city of Antioch.</note> refused to listen, until they healed a wealthy man named Abibaianus <note>Habib al-Najjar, known as "Habib the Carpenter" in Islamic tradition.</note> after he had believed in Christ. He immediately began to cry out in the whole city, "Listen to those who do not ask a reward from you, and who are guided." Whereupon the king, being moved to anger, killed the man and thrust the two Apostles into prison. This continued until Paul arrived; he asked the king if he might see them and learn what law they were teaching, acting as if he did not know them. When they had come out, a girl was brought to them who had been blind from birth, whom Peter immediately healed, along with a boy. Furthermore, that girl was the daughter of the prince. Then the people of Antioch were converted to Christ. These are the accounts of the interpreter Buhatias <note>likely al-Baydawi, a famous Quranic commentator.</note> and Hamahsseri <note>likely al-Zamakhshari, another influential commentator.</note> on this passage. Because the people had rejected the messengers and wanted to stone them, Muhammad began to make his own followers act similarly, so they would not refuse to hear and receive the prophet of God, since they had rejected those and all other prophets—as if he were already an Apostle or a prophet himself. With these inducements, he began to ensnare the miserable peasants and force himself upon them.

In the following chapters, he interposes the same sacraments, the same paradises with chaste women—that is, virgins—with whom they will spend fifty years in the ecstasy of Venus <note>original: "ecstasi Veneris," meaning sexual ecstasy.</note>; he describes hell with its poison and the tree of Zaqqum <note>original: "zaconiij." The Zaqqum is a cursed tree in Islamic eschatology whose fruit resembles devils' heads.</note>, etc. He repeats the stories of the winds and demons obeying the beck and call of Solomon, and six hundred other fables. Indeed, the chapters become shorter as they approach the end, so that the final ones are only a few lines long. Therefore, one should not linger over them as much as over the first ones, since we have touched upon the chief points of these matters in the earlier sections. I have opened these up to our curious countrymen, as it is right to know these things when one is about to speak on these follies. I will pluck a few things here and there until the end, if any seem relevant to the matter. I shall be more diligent in the Arabic edition.

In chapter 41 <note>This refers to Surah Fussilat, though Postel’s numbering varies from modern standards.</note>, which the Westerners call *Sori* and the Easterners call *Eschec* <note>Likely "Sura" and "As-Sajda" or similar phonetic renderings.</note>, there are certain things to be noted, one of which I have already noted above: namely, that God created spouses for us from the brutes <note>original: "ex brutis." This is a polemical misinterpretation of the Arabic word "azwajan," which means "pairs" or "mates," usually referring to humans or livestock in a general sense of creation.</note>, whose use He permits. It was not enough for this prophet, having violated the faith of his first marriage, to have brought in other women over the one who had raised him to power, or to have made fourteen other concubines lawful; or to have either divorced or married any woman he pleased without a dowry instrument, according to his whim; or that he had use of all women in all places; or that he had abused catamites with burning pederasty—unless he also granted to his "saints" sexual intercourse with brutes. All these things are worthy of the author, the prophet of the Arabs. Even if commentators veil these things with "honorable" interpretations, as I have said, the most "holy" Muslims nevertheless show how they are to be understood by mounting she-asses, camels, or any living creatures in the middle of the marketplace. We can assert this because we have seen it. In Tunis, nothing is more common; the same is proven in Syria. From where would such a powerful reputation for holiness proceed, such that you should admire such men, unless from the prescription of your 
<margin>,,</margin> law? I know, you explain *wamin al-an'ami azwajan* <note>original: "uemín elanhamí ezuagían"</note> as "and of the cattle, pairs," meaning females for the propagation of the species. But why did the prophet join females from the brutes with human females, when he is there speaking of carnal copula? If you deny the text, I shall appeal to the facts. Finally, he concedes our scriptures and those of the Jews as holy and proceeding from God, so that he seems to profess all those things—which he has already done quite often to ensnare our people. I take this from a crafty adversary and infer this: since our scriptures are from God, are prior, are holy, and are such that if we observed them, we would be most happy in the present life (as Muhammad says), then they must be the best and must be kept. And whatever contradicts them must necessarily be false. But since the Quran contradicts them more than a thousand times, it cannot be from God. For since it was written entirely against the Gospel, let no one doubt that it was produced with the Devil as its author.

<margin>,,</margin> He also here contradicts the precept of Christ when he says that one who is provoked ought to take revenge, otherwise he is impious. This is the cause of your scripture: when someone had offended this prophet even by suspicion alone, unless he had immediately taken revenge or killed him, he would have been among the damned, as he says.

## GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK II

Oh, how far those things are from that holy patience of Christ and his followers. Christ suffered all things; Muhammad undermined all things, even when provoked by no injury. Christ and his followers gave all, if they had anything; this man plundered all. Christ heals all; Muhammad harms all. Christ grants all to his enemies; Muhammad does not even spare his brothers. Thus do the shadows differ from the light.

<margin>" " "</margin>
He says in the following chapter that he plundered the goods of those among whom he lived for the purpose of dividing them among his followers and promoting certain individuals to ranks of dignity. What else would a robber do for his companions? He seizes the property of others so that he may bestow it upon others, and finally, for the sake of establishing power—however unjust the cause—it is necessary to appoint certain ranks of dignity and office. What can this be, if not the height of iniquity? To what end are laws, if such things are permitted? What do republics and the gatherings of men offer, if whatever is pleasing is thus permitted? So that when someone is stronger, he is immediately considered more just. These things are indeed permitted to princes against enemies, because enemies are to be restrained by such civil punishment. But who would not shudder to ascribe these things to God—things which he committed against citizens, against friends, against brothers, against the weak and afflicted, and against those who did not deserve it? "That is the law of God," he says. God has spoken; that is to say, let the will stand for the reason. <note>Postel is paraphrasing the Latin legal maxim *sit pro ratione voluntas*—"let my will stand in place of reason"—to criticize Muhammad’s justification for his actions.</note>

->34. *Dukhan*, that is, Smoke.<- <note>Refers to Surah 44 of the Quran, *Ad-Dukhan*.</note>

<margin>" "</margin>
Through the clear book, he says, we sent it down on a blessed night. He rightly says "at night," because no one saw it. Before the eyes of all, with everyone seeing the wonders on the mountain peak and hearing the thunder and voices scarcely tolerable to the ear, the law was given to Moses; but to you, it was given by night and in a cave. This is the ancient fiction of crafty men, which hates the light and seeks double shadows: of the night and of the cave. But tell me, in what place and what book was received? If at Mecca, as I have already said, the chapters from Medina are not sacred; if at Medina, the Meccan chapters are false. If you received the whole book at once, why could it not be completed in all twenty-three years? If it was whole, why did you not publish it? If only a part, why does it not stand out and get marked as a compendium of the whole, like the Tablets of Moses? It is entirely contradictory that the book was given in a single night, and yet given bit by bit daily to his followers, and composed according to the occasions of events. To this, since you frequently say that you have placed in that book matters concerning all things: those things which you did place, you did not have from God. Those are old wives' delusions, worthy of both the author and the believers.

->Chapter 46.<- <note>Refers to Surah 46, *Al-Ahqaf*.</note>

<margin>" " " " "</margin>
Many things are to be noted by us here; he betrays himself in almost every verse. When it is objected against him that it is a fiction, he denies it with an oath: "If I have fabricated it," he says, "may I have nothing from God." <note>original: "nil mihi sit Dei"</note> As if that scoundrel <term>nebulo (scoundrel)</term> believed God existed—he who has abused His name in the whole book and made Him the author of idolatry, homicide, fratricide, lying, theft, adultery, and whatever vices there are or ever were. I do not know what else this is than to deny God himself. Say, he says, "I am not the first of the prophets, nor do I know what will become of me or of you." <note>Postel is quoting Quran 46:9.</note> Certainly you are not the first, nor the last: because among them you are nothing. For what is false is a privation of the true. But it is most marvelous to wonder how it can be that the "universal redeemer," the "seal of the prophets," who saw God in the ninth heaven, who is the most perfect of creatures, who is on familiar terms with angels, who fulfills all laws—now knows not what the future holds for him, when God, loving him so much, did not render him secure regarding his own salvation. It is surely to be believed that his familiarity with God was not as great as was said, if he does not know whether he is on the path of salvation or damnation. Our Paul knew that neither death, nor life, nor things above, nor things below could separate him from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus. <note>A reference to Romans 8:38–39.</note> Never did any of the prophets doubt what would become of them.
