...who would not recognize this as a devil’s invention <note>original: "commentum diaboli"</note> (if it is true, and not rather a dream)? For God never does evil, far be it from him to act like a charlatan <term>circulator</term><note>An itinerant performer or "snake-oil salesman" who creates problems just to "cure" them.</note>—He heals evils, for to do otherwise would be most unjust. Who else would so violently stir the gut of a prince that he would not go to his usual retreats, and would call for his chamberlains who never sleep? Is this not the art of a demon, dragging a man toward impiety and nourishing a wicked and lost crowd of men? The devil frequently sends evils which he also cannot take away or cure; and if he does "cure" them after letting them in, he only appears to have conferred a benefit—much like a thief who, when he has not destroyed something he had the power to destroy, expects thanks. 

Who would deny that those scoundrels possess magic arts, since they had so maddened Muhammad <note>Mehmed II, known as "The Conqueror"</note> the Besieger <note>original Greek: "πολιορκητῶ" (poliorkētō)</note> with wicked spells? Though he was otherwise a most prudent prince, he was led by their illusions to trust them entirely. Seeing this, the Prince of the Tartars <note>Likely referring to a rival leader or an internal faction from the East.</note> plotted with these lost men so that, once admitted into the prince’s bedchamber, they would kill him and behead him. He promised that if they did this, he would hand over the reins of power to them, keeping only the title of Emperor. Money was counted out for this purpose, and a day was set. It would have been done, had they not been caught a day earlier and paid the penalty worthy of their crime. From then on, the prince raged against that whole class of people with such severity that, while he lived, none of them were ever seen in the court without the risk of their lives.

A similar thing nearly happened to Bayezid I. For a man on the road, seeking alms while hiding a sword, nearly cut down that generous prince while he was looking for something to give the scoundrel; the violence of the blow left the prince's horse half-dead. Let a prince see what a nefarious religion dares against private citizens, if princes with their bodyguards do not take care.

But enough of these things. Now we must see how inheritances are divided among the sons of the wealthy. It is clear enough what kind of friendship must exist between brothers conceived by different mothers, since even among the fathers there is such a great scarcity of charity toward their sons. Is it any wonder there is much less from parents and relatives? They think those who are worthless to both father and brothers are of no concern to them. This is why it is no surprise that the *Akinjis*, the *Azaps*, the *Garips* <term>Acangios, asaplaros, caripos</term><note>Postel lists various classes of Ottoman soldiers: the Akinji (scouts/light cavalry), Azaps (irregular infantry), and Garips (foreign or poor cavalry).</note> and other common soldiers are held in such low esteem by the princes. Not infrequently, the front line is trampled by those following behind, and in times of great danger, they are laid down like a bridge or pavement for the army to cross over. Thus, a human life is not valued as much as a beast's, for their law persuades them that "to die in the Way of God is best." The laws for dividing the family estate <note>original: "Leges herciscundae familiae," a reference to Roman inheritance law.</note>—specifying what portion a man who can claim a share of the inheritance may leave to his brothers and parents—are written in the blood of brothers. For as far as it can be done, if a prince is like Muhammad, he sees to it that everyone else is removed from the way so that he alone may preserve the inheritance. 

Now, as briefly as the argument requires, I shall bring down the histories of the Muslims <note>original: "Mussulmanorum"</note> from the expeditions of Muhammad to our own times. Once the practice of this governance is known, the wretchedness of the law will become most apparent. For just as the virtue of the Law of Moses is known from the lives and deeds of those who reigned after him, and the virtue of Christ’s law from the lives of Christians, so too from the Caliphs <note>original: "Chalisphis"</note> who took power after Muhammad, we may judge whether he left behind happiness or misery.

### THE AFFAIRS OF THOSE PEOPLES WHO GAVE THEIR NAMES TO MUHAMMAD. CHAPTER XX.

Just as no nation has ever brought greater slaughter upon the world, more savagely put virtue to flight, or introduced more wicked vices, so too has no nation ever shown less care or concern for its own history. For unless religion is joined to their deeds, they preserve hardly any historical monument worth reading.

### BOOK II BY GUILLAUME POSTEL

This <note>the lack of reliable historical writing</note> has occurred not so much through a neglect of literature as through the constant change of tyrannies. For when the soldiery is perpetually eager for revolution, the prince looks only to his own safety, and the lowly priests <note>original: "sacrificuli"</note>—who are estranged from the affairs of the court and war—either go into hiding or are plundered. In such a state, there can be no place for men of distinguished talent who are trained in the arts of both war and peace; yet these are the only men who can judge and write about history in an uncorrupt and sincere manner. 

Consequently, they have no historians; and if they do have any, because their books contain such monstrous crimes, they do not hand them over or trust them even to their own people until fifty years after a life has ended. They permit only the administrators of religion to handle them, who are by then so practiced in "prudence" that they can cover up those immense vices with silence. For it has happened that many people, after reading through the **Book of Kings** or the **Book of the Caliphs** <note>Likely referring to Islamic historical chronicles like those of Al-Tabari</note>, have recoiled from that impiety. What else does this suggest, other than that a tyrannical power—acquired through the greatest crime, increased by even greater ones, and preserved by the greatest of all—is being presented as divine? Does it not show that virtue is being manufactured out of the most foul vices?

I have not been granted access to that book, nor does it matter much to reveal to the Latins <note>Western Christians</note> those crimes which could not possibly be beneficial and might certainly be infectious. It would be enough if these things were made known to everyone in the Arabic edition, so that the secrets which have miserably deluded the common people might finally reveal themselves. In contrast, all the books of the Old and New Testaments are available to everyone; they do not fear a censor. If any human failing happened to either the prophets or the princes, the sacred authors are not ashamed to confess that those men were liable to sin. This is because if one or two improbable deeds are contained within them, there are, in compensation, innumerable good deeds by which readers might be incited to virtue. 

In the Muhammadan system, the opposite is true, as is evident from their secrecy. For there is scarcely any image of virtue to be found there, but many monstrous crimes. But we must now come to the expeditions of the prophet, so that this "prophetic virtue" may be more easily assessed. In the **Books of Hasiar** <term>Al-Siyar</term><note>Biographies or records of the military campaigns of Muhammad.</note>, it is recorded that Muhammad waged eighteen wars: eleven against the Jews, and the rest against the people of Mecca, the King of the Persians, the Romans <note>The Byzantines</note>, and neighboring cities. 

As we have said, for ten whole years he increased his power by using the influence of the Jews as if he were a new Messiah, winning over the wealth of many rich and influential men. From Mecca, he gained both sons-in-law and supporters: Abu Bakr, Umar, Ali <note>original: "Vbecharum, Humarum, Alim"</note>, and many others of lesser name. From other places in Arabia, he gained Uthman, Talhah, Zayd (distinct from the servant), Abd al-Rahman <note>original: "Odmanum, Thalhanum, Zeidum... Abdorachmanum"</note>, and many others whom it is no loss to history, men, or reputation to leave unmentioned. Relying on their wealth, families, and alliances, he subdued as many cities near Mecca as possible. Whatever lay within many miles of Mecca he claimed for himself, drawing the inhabitants in by persuasion until a great number had coalesced—some fearing his power and cruelty, and others following him of their own accord in search of plunder. 

Then, finally, he established his royal seat in Yathrib <note>original: "Ietriba," known today as Medina</note>, having driven out the Jews. These Jews, seeking help from their neighbors, were broken in many battles and raids. Those unhelpful and lying authors of the Chronicles report that the cause of the Jewish war was that seventy Jews sought the house of the prophet’s father with swords dipped in poison. They claim the Jews wanted to kill him because of his "prophetic light," fearing that such a great prophet was about to arise. For this reason, they say, the son <note>Muhammad</note> was cruel toward them. 

Meanwhile, those "good" historians do not see that they are contradicting their own prophet, who in countless places accuses the Jews of breaking treaties. Because of this, he not only permits but commands anyone to kill them with impunity as infidels who carry "a disease in their hearts." This was not without divine vengeance, so that they might pay the penalty to the very tyrant they themselves had fostered. Indeed, the mind of that prophet was incited to begin these revolutions by a certain astronomer <note>or astrologer</note> who predicted changes in religions and kingdoms (as that race of impostors is always talking nonsense about something unusual). Muhammad used this man as his guide and consultant for many years. For he helped him...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s polemical history of the origins of Islam. Having previously argued that the lack of reliable Eastern history is due to tyranny and the suppression of truth, he now begins a detailed, critical account of Muhammad’s early military activities in Medina, portraying them as banditry rather than divine mission.</meta>

-># ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

He <note>Muhammad</note> was not a little successful when he lied to the unlearned people and put forward ambiguous dreams. In order to begin his apprenticeship in the art of plundering, Muhammad attacked his own kinsmen. For when he had established his seat at Medina, he sent Hamza, the son of Abdelmelechi <note>Hamza ibn Abdul-Muttalib, Muhammad's uncle</note>, with thirty mules and some foot soldiers to lie in ambush in the Homensian forest <note>Likely referring to the coastal region of Al-Is or Sif al-Bahr</note>. This was on the route from Mecca to Syria. Their goal was to watch for a company of the Quraish <note>original: "Coraissorum," the ruling tribe of Mecca and Muhammad’s own kin</note>—his own relatives—who were loaded with merchandise. They were to slaughter the men, seize everything, and bring it to the "prophet." 

But the success was far different than expected. For Hamza fell upon a company of a hundred men led by a certain Angelus <note>Possibly a corruption of a name like Abu Jahl, or a sarcastic reference</note>, who was more warlike than Hamza. The raiders fled and returned to the prophet empty-handed and scattered. They informed him that he had sent them there with very little prophetic foresight or prudence. Indeed, God seemed to be "sleeping" as far as the prophet was concerned; nor did that famous Gabriel <note>The Archangel believed to have delivered the Quran</note> seem prudent enough, having persuaded the prophet to invest his first expenses so unsuccessfully. 

Nevertheless, Muhammad did not wish to desist from his undertakings. Entrusting the care of his raiding to other leaders, he sent a crowd twice as large to blockade the same road under the leadership of Heguida <note>Likely Ubaydah ibn al-Harith</note>. However, a certain petty king named Abo Zípharus <note>Abu Sufyan, the Meccan leader</note> struck him down severely and put him to flight. Few messengers returned from that expedition. A third expedition sent for the same purpose was frustrated by the Quraish who passed by in the meantime; therefore Zeidus <note>Zayd ibn Harithah</note>, the third leader, returned home with nothing accomplished. Never were other prophets so frequently deceived, because they undertook all things with God as their leader. 

Therefore, when he saw that the business conducted through his generals was not succeeding, he himself went to the place of ambush to plunder the wealth of his kinsmen. A man named Muhazamus resisted him strongly and routed the crowd of bandits; neither the prophet's angel nor any deputy was there to help him. Again, since he was of a most hostile mind toward his kinsmen and greedy to divert their wealth, he proceeded to another place which they called Barathum <note>Likely a reference to Badr</note>, where he was likewise broken by Umar, the son of Halaphus. On a third attempt, he did encounter adversaries, but they were far superior in strength. Thus, the first six expeditions perished miserably. 

But in the meantime, neither he nor his followers were doing nothing. For they were accustomed to live "prophetically" anywhere in the world, following the law that if you did not give to them, they would take it themselves. If anyone opposed their crimes and was a member of the household, he was killed by treachery; if he was an outsider, Muhammad promised a paradise of pleasure to whoever would kill him and anyone else who did not comply with the prophet. 

At last, such a large crowd of desperate men and looters flocked to him that he had the roads blockaded on all sides. Consequently, a large company of his Quraish kinsmen, along with their goods and many camels, were intercepted by twelve men under the leadership of Abdasta <note>Perhaps Al-Abbas or a related figure</note>. By these riches, he was not a little increased, and from then on, he began to be much more favored and formidable. 

Having gathered great power, he was also significantly enriched by the plundering of the inheritance of the Jews <note>original: "Iudæorum"</note>. For because they had first sworn by his words and then, except for a few, defected from him, their defection was more useful to him than their alliance. From allies, he received something in the name of tithes over a ten-year period; but from those who defected, he seized their entire estates and fortunes under the pretext of neglected religion. 

And as they are, and have always been since the death of Christ, hated by all—whether Pagans <note>original: "ethnici"</note> or Christians—every nation, while obeying the "prophetic" command in despoiling the Jews, also delighted to vent the hatred of their race. This remains even now, in every land, a great and notable testimony to the wicked impiety of that race, since they are in a worse condition among Pagans and Muslims <note>original: "Muslimunos"</note> than among Christians, and are everywhere destitute of their own magistracy. 

Muhammad, therefore, having driven off plunder from all of Arabia, enriched by the spoils of his kinsmen and stuffed with the money of the Jews, appeared as an equal to the most powerful men. His friendship began to be sought and courted by neighboring petty kings.

Therefore, accompanied by a great number of supporters, he broke the nobility of Mecca in a valley very close to the city, shortly before he took possession of the city itself; we have mentioned this matter in the Quran <note>original: "Alcorano"</note>. Once the city was captured, nothing stood in his way: neighboring cities either surrendered themselves or began to pay tribute. In this way, he who a little while before had been a beggar was made a tyrant, all the more formidable because he appeared everywhere more cruel.

The petty rulers of Arabia Petraea <note>A Roman province encompassing the Sinai, Negev, and Jordan</note> and those who belonged to the Persian sphere sought help from the King of the Persians, whose forces had been worn down a little earlier by the Emperor Heraclius. He gave what assistance he could and approached the Arabias. There, with his soldiers broken and weary from the road, and in a ruined region suffering from hunger and thirst, he was broken and put to flight; he returned home in a state of trepidation with a few men. I do not find it recorded in writing who that man was. I suspect, however, that it was the son of Khosrow <note>original: "Chosrois"</note>, who had been the author of the slaughter of his father and brother. For the timing suggests it. Having gained this victory, the soldiers became more spirited; persuaded by religion, they boldly invaded Persia, Chaldea, Syria, and Egypt, and with their incursions in all places, that power began to be formidable. I believe that certain remnants of the army which Heraclius had left in Syria were overwhelmed, perhaps under the leadership of some who had defected to him. For in the Quran there is one chapter <note>Surah 30</note> which has the title *Rom*, that is, the Romans or the Greeks (for today the Greeks are called *Romaei*, that is, Romans); it begins, "The Romans have been defeated." <note>original: "Victi sunt Romani"</note> But in what place, they do not say. However the matter may stand, shortly after his death, Abu Bakr <note>original: "Vbecharus"</note> had gathered sixty thousand horsemen, besides countless infantry. He <note>Muhammad</note> left his power to Abu Bakr and Umar <note>original: "Homaro"</note>, but Abu Bakr, being superior, took possession and increased the dominion as far as the Armenias, leaving only the coasts of Syria and some of the stronger and more fortified cities. For between Palestine and Mesopotamia, because of the boundaries of the Persian empire and kingdom, all things were subject to incursions, and there, the stronger party had the greater right to those matters by force. There were also some from the lowest rank of power raised to great and illustrious fortune by Muhammad, of whom the chief ones were Ubayd <note>original: "Vxeitus"</note>, Ammar <note>original: "Achmarus"</note>—under whose leadership he had entered Mecca—Abu Ubaidah <note>original: "Abubardas"</note>, Zayd <note>original: "Zeidus"</note>, and Ali the Elder <note>original: "Halis senior"</note>. For Muhammad's grandson <note>likely referring to Hasan or Husayn</note> was still unsuited for handling affairs. These men, with those I named above, were able to give the reins of power to whomever they wished, a practice which has lasted among the Caliphs <note>original: "Chaliphas"</note> down to our own times. Since things badly gained slip away badly, after he <note>Abu Bakr</note> had reigned only two years and undertook the dangers of restraining the multitude defecting from that dire and nefarious religion, he was killed by his necessary associate and familiar friend, Umar. Umar increased the power for ten years and studied to keep the people in check partly by war, partly by religion. For when he saw that although many did not refuse his command, they nevertheless laughed at the Quran, and there were as many opinions about it as there were men, he began to collect fragments, summaries, and books of it from wherever possible into one. But while he reigned longer than his successor wished, he was cut down, and Uthman <note>original: "Odmamanus"</note> succeeded in his place. He, with affairs a little more settled, began to seek out from the household of the Prophet those things preserved by writing as well as by hearing, and to collect them into one. The first authority (as I noted while speaking of the origin of the Sunnah <note>original: "Sunae"</note>) was from Aisha <note>original: "Assa"</note>, the daughter of Abu Bakr—that notorious harlot. For she was privy to the whole fable. Therefore, in the resolutions after various doubts, her opinion is stood by, etc., in order as has been noted. Thus, under him, the Quran first began to be published in that version which was preserved both at Mecca and Medina for some years afterward. But there arose a great license in asserting that book, for no one after that failed to pretend a truer and better edition: not for the sake of the book, which everyone knew was most foolish, but so that by it they might restrain the delirious common people. For by the reputation of the book, it was born, increased, and preserved

But when he had reigned for twelve years <note>Postel refers here to Uthman ibn Affan, the third Caliph (r. 644–656 AD), whose assassination sparked the first Islamic civil war.</note>, a faction was stirred up by Ali <note>original: "Hali"</note>, and as a crowd rushed upon him, he was slain. His corpse (just as the Prophet’s) was cast outside the city as a mockery of their religion and their prophet. For the crowd, to whom Ali had revealed the "fable," said it remained to be seen whether this new author of the Quran <note>original: "Alcorani"</note> would rise again on the third day, like a prophet; for his corpse had also been kept for three days until it reached an intolerable stench.

Ali reigned for fourteen years <note>Postel's chronology here conflates various periods; Ali's actual reign as Caliph was about five years.</note>, not without great difficulty and seditions; he held onto power with more pain because he had revealed the tricks of this false persuasion to a portion of the soldiers. For his repentance was almost too late for him to find a remedy in it. There was another seed of dissension dating back to the prophet himself. For since Ali foresaw that Abu Bakr <note>original: "Vbecharus"</note> would reign after Muhammad, and therefore everything would be permitted to that harlot Aisha <note>original: "Assæ"</note>, his daughter and the wife of the prophet—because favor and affairs depended on his power and favor—very grave enmities arose between them. These enmities reigned for many centuries afterward, and they were especially made public under Ali. Those of Abu Bakr's party were called the Quraysh <note>original: "Choraissi"</note>, although they hardly belonged to the prophetic nation. Those who followed the side of Ali took their name from him. 

The Moors say that this Ali penetrated into Africa as far as the province of Cyrene, where a temple was built in his memory, which they call Kairouan <note>original: "Caroan"</note>. To this place, for the sake of pilgrimage, people flock from all over Africa no differently than they do to Mecca and Medina. From that place, it happened that companies of merchants and pilgrims are called *Caroana*, or Caravans <note>original: "Carauana"</note>; this is because there is such a vast multitude of desperate men in Africa that it is nowhere safe to travel by land except in the largest of crowds. I cannot, however, bring myself to agree with the opinion that he crossed over from the Arabias that far, leaving Egypt behind his back. For the Caliphs <note>original: "Chaliphæ"</note> were not established in Egypt before the hundredth year after Muhammad's death. However, both points could stand: that he gained possession of Egypt long before the seat of the Caliph was transferred and established there. For in the 130th year of the Hijra <note>original: "Alhigeræ"</note>—that is, the "Exile"—the Mauritanias were already being shaken by the incursions of these pests; and it was the thirty-sixth year from the expulsion or <term>ostracism</term> <note>original Greek: "ὀστρακισμῷ", referring to the Hijra as a political exile</note> when Ali was finished off. 

A little before Ali's death, Hashim <note>original: "Haschemus," likely referring to the rise of the Hashemite or Umayyad factions</note> was created prince, not in the prophetic city of Yathrib <note>original: "Ietriba," the old name for Medina</note>, but in Raqqa <note>original: "Aracha"</note>, from which he set out with a large force and besieged Yathrib, and killed Ali, whom many nevertheless write was his father. After nine years were completed, leaving his post and his life, he left the empire to Muawiya <note>original: "Moalbio"</note>. This man overran Syria and occupied Damascus; he was the most bitter enemy of the Christians, though otherwise, as they write, he conducted himself laudably among his own people. He was most suited for plunder under the prophet; therefore, the prophet portended dominion for him. When he was removed in the manner of the others, Yazid <note>original: "Ieudus"</note> received the kingdom, and by the same end, thirty Caliphs, without any interruption, were butchered by factions and wretched slaughter, so that they might leave the "virtue" of their law to be judged by posterity. 

If they had left this life by a natural death, or honorably sought it among enemies, it could be said that it is common to princes, so that "no tyrant goes down to Pluto's house by a dry death" <note>A reference to Juvenal's *Satires*, suggesting that tyrants rarely die peacefully without bloodshed.</note>. But if we consider any most unhappy state, arising from the most savage tyranny (as almost all empires are), and compare it with this one, without doubt the most miserable people will be extremely happy when compared to these. Lycurgus gave laws by pretending to have a conversation with a deity, yet those laws brought safety to the Republic and destruction to no one. The laws of Solon, Zaleucus, Zamolxis, and Charondas <note>Famous lawgivers of Greek and Barbarian antiquity.</note> brought the highest health to the states that used them. But this raving persuasion brought a plague to the fields, calamity to the harvests, misery to men, ruin to the world, dullness to the minds, and finally brought to its own princes the kind of death that the author deserved—yet no one noticed. The Caesars seized tyranny over the Republic, and out of the first ones, except for a few (perhaps fifteen), they died from the seditions of veteran soldiers. The others from that time either died manfully in war, or at home among their own...

ended their days honorably. These [the early Caliphs] perished at the hands of their sons, parents, subjects, citizens, and friends. Now, if we compare those judges and kings who succeeded Moses—none of whom, over the course of eight hundred years, failed to die or pass away most honorably—with these men, it will then be seen how much the divine law differs from a lying and demonic one. I do not even bring forward the piety, innocence, and charity of our own people <note>The Christians</note> to oppose them, though compared to those most unhappy men, our people seem most happy; for the distinction between them is wider than that between light and darkness. For the sake of persuading and asserting the truth, for avoiding vice, and for preserving true piety toward God, the followers of Christ for nearly three hundred years voluntarily suffered death filled with every kind of torture and punishment. For if they had wished only to say this one phrase, "I am not a Christian," or "Christ is not God," they would have been acquitted and advanced with great honors. 

But some Muslim <note>original: "Mussulmanus"</note> will object to me: "Our soldiers and the followers of the prophet also die courageously for the sake of preserving and promoting our religion." They do indeed die, I know, and many even throw themselves into dangers of their own accord, so that they might meet death after killing some among the enemy. Truly, how much these things they commit differ from true piety—and from a man who believes that an account of his deeds must be rendered to God—can be weighed from their manner of living. For the soldier honors the prophet with every kind of pleasure; even those who are considered very pious offer sacrifices of stewed meats and a more refined gluttony to their divine beings and their dead. To have killed a man, to have plundered the property of others, and to have brought a stain upon one's own body and soul—provided the pretext of religion is present—the soldier considers a matter of glory. With this "Lerna" <note>An allusion to the Lernaean Hydra, meaning a swamp or vast heap of crimes.</note> of crimes, he believes he is most dear to God and hastens voluntarily to those paradises which the prophet promised, so that he might contemplate for himself in a future life those supreme and eternal pleasures which he cannot obtain here. It is just as if a bull, rushing into the heat of passion <note>original: "in Venerem," literally "into Venus" or lust.</note>, while seeking his rival with his horns, should perish in the conflict of his pleasure. Christian martyrs, most famous for their miracles, refuse no punishments so that they may worship God above all things, preserve themselves worthy of God the Father, and save their fellow man just as their own body and soul. Your men, while armed for the destruction of nature, rush headlong into death. 

Truly, this Arabic power was immediately split into various parts in its hundredth year. Once factions had been created by the leaders, some were dispersed to the East, some to the North, and others to the West. After Egypt was occupied and "liberated" (as he pretended) from the Roman official who held it, a Caliph <note>original: "Chaliphos"</note> was established in Babylon <note>Postel likely means Baghdad, often associated with ancient Babylon in this period.</note>. Those who sought Assyria were called by the native word *Benchi*, that is, "lords." In Africa, they chose to call them Sultans, Sheriffs <note>original: "Seraphos," likely referring to the Sharifian dynasties.</note>, and Maulas <note>original: "Maulas," likely *Mawla* or *Moulay*.</note>, that is, the powerful, the wealthy, and the protectors. The title common to all was *Emir* and *Emir al-muminin* <note>original: "emir elmumin"</note>, that is, "Commander," and "Commander of the Faithful." Some of our people call them *Miramommelines* <note>original: "Miramome limos"</note> and falsely think these are proper names. For it was the distinguished title of a prince, especially an African one, as is evident even from their coins. For they were inscribed in such a way, as I have found in very ancient money coined eight hundred years ago: "Joseph, Commander of the Faithful, son of the Commander of the Faithful, son of the Commander of the Faithful," back to the great-great-grandfathers. 

Because those regions were lost through the sluggishness of the most cowardly Emperor Heraclius, it was very easy for them to retain what they had occupied since no one resisted. For Constantine IV <note>Byzantine Emperor, r. 668–685 AD.</note>, the fourth of that name, was forced to confirm a peace with the petty king of Damascus. Far more things would have to be brought forward by me here if I wished to relate their histories exactly. But I consider it enough to note the main points, to weigh their outcomes, and to reveal how they gained power. They gained possession of Persia within the hundredth year from the *Hijra* <note>original: "Alhigera," the migration of Muhammad in 622 AD, marking the start of the Islamic calendar.</note> or exile; perhaps the opportunity was offered there because, shortly before, having refuted their foolish persuasion, the King and Queen of the Persians had received holy baptism and had come to Constantinople in the time of Constantine IV. For when a certain petty king named Mohammed and Imrael, the King of Persia, had sought the forces of the Scythians <note>Postel uses "Scythians" as a broad term for the Turkic and nomadic peoples of the East</note> under the leadership of Mucaletus the *benco*—that is, the Lord—they were contending for that empire, but were driven out by the newcomer. Eventually, they turned their forces, along with the remnants of the Scythians wandering throughout Asia, toward the West. Having subdued Asia Minor and the Armenians, they even dared, under the leadership of Suleiman, to attack and besiege Constantinople, and to overrun Thrace and the neighboring provinces. 

But after three years had passed, they were driven from the siege by a plague and forced to return to their own seats. At that same time (as that plague, like a scourge of God, was distressing the world), they rushed into Sicily and Campania, and held Sicily for several years. In Africa, matters succeeded according to their desires, except when Abd al-Malik, the Commander of the Faithful <note>original: "Abdemelichus emirus elmumin"</note>, was broken by John, the Master of the Soldiers, acting under Justinian II. 

But because of the faction of Leontius and the Patriarch Callinicus, Justinian was deprived of his empire and his nose <note>A common Byzantine punishment called *rhinokopia*, meant to disqualify a person from ruling by making them physically "imperfect"</note>, and sent into exile. Thus, he could not pursue the matters so happily begun, as the tyrant Leontius seized the empire. Yet the injury inflicted upon that most excellent emperor did not go unavenged. For Apsimar, elected emperor by the army, stripped Leontius of both his nose and his empire, and committed him to life in prison. 

Thus the Moors and Muslims lost a most formidable adversary in Justinian. For ten years earlier, Amurath <note>Likely a reference to an Umayyad leader such as Mu'awiya or Abd al-Malik, though the name is latinized here</note> had reached an agreement with him: having restored Africa and Libya, he was to pay to the empire one thousand gold coins, one servant, and one horse every single day for the whole decade, on account of the other provinces he occupied. Therefore, the fire that was nearly extinguished was revived under Leontius—who wasted the treasury among harlots and abused it to win favor (as is the custom of tyrants)—and it spread far more savagely than before. 

For they progressed as far as the borders of Mauritania. There, while Julian was acting as governor in the name of the empire, a dreadful and foul opportunity presented itself, involving Roderic, the King of the Goths, who was then ruling the Spains. For while the most beautiful daughter of Julian was staying with the King's wife to acquire refinement in manners and character, the foul and shameful King committed violence against the maiden. Some say he could not obtain permission from her father to take her as his wife, and so sinned out of the vehemence of his love. However that may be, the father Julian, moved by a righteous grief over the injury to his daughter, summoned a massive force of neighboring Muslims and provided them leadership into the Spains against Roderic. They crossed the strait, invaded, plundered, killed Roderic, and established their kingdom, subjugating all of Spain within three years. 

Not long afterward, Julian was crushed by them. For such is their "faith" toward their friends: they immediately eliminate those whose assistance they have used. I do not see what could be judged as further removed from humanity than this. To be sure, a prince may sometimes do this justly if the one who helped him had acquired formidable power; but to rage against a defenseless friend is truly a fight against the law of humanity. 

Not long after the conquest of Spain, another occasion arose for invading the Gauls. For Eudo, the Prince of Aquitaine, being unequal in strength to the kings of Gaul with whom he was waging war, invited that wretched dregs <note>original: "colluuiem" – a derogatory term meaning "scum" or "wash-water"</note> into the Gauls. They immediately showed the man what sort of reinforcements he had summoned. For every city from the ridge of the Pyrenean mountains to the borders of the Poitevins and the people of Tours was plundered and overthrown, so that nowhere among the nations has a greater devastation been seen or heard than that through which the Muslim army proceeds. 

Whence Eudo, like the proverbially late-wise Phrygian <note>original: "Phryx & sero sapiens" – an ancient proverb referring to those who only learn through disaster</note>, established a peace with Charles Martel, who was then wielding the scepters of the kingdom. With the combined forces of the Gallic and Aquitainian armies, he struck down three hundred and seventy-five thousand in a single day alongside Martel. The rest, who were staying in Narbonne, Toulouse, Salses, and other places under Eudo's jurisdiction on account of the treaty they had made, were proscribed. Thus, ten years after it had been called in, that dregs was driven out from Gaul. They occupied the Spains from the year of Christ 730 until 1400 or thereabouts. ## GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK II.

20. In twenty years, they finished off fifteen of their own leaders; nor did they cease from their usual slaughter until a certain Alhatabus <note>Possibly a reference to a local ruler or Al-Hattab; Postel often Latinizes Arabic names phonetically</note>, lest the same fate befall him as the others, removed three hundred nobles from their midst, and thus reigned for a longer time. But perhaps it turned out more happily for the others. One may judge this by the primary power. The most flourishing wealth of the Saracens <note>A medieval term for Muslims, especially those of the Levant and North Africa</note>, as they are called, was always in Egypt; therefore, it is likely that the example of the lesser powers depends on the primary power. I shall therefore touch upon their affairs summarily, and as much as pertains to the matter. Because (as I have noted before) they fear that their crimes will be seen and known by posterity, they neither care to commit them to writing, nor do they wish to publish what has been recorded. In Egypt, although the rule was varied and entirely different matters were possessed by the Caliph <note>original: "Chalipha"</note>—that is, the high priest, upon whom the authority of the law depends—nevertheless, until another of equal power opposed him in Baghdad <note>original: "Bagdeti"</note> in Chaldea, the other provinces always wished the supreme decision in doubtful matters to depend on his opinion. This was not due to the authority of the law, but for the sake of order, even though his dignity always seemed greater and more sublime than the rest, because the first successors of Muhammad <note>original: "Muhamedis"</note> exercised both sacred and profane authority, and fixed their seat there before power became divided. Therefore, since I have been able to obtain nothing concerning sacred matters except through the memory and reports of more recent writings, I shall speak of the profane authority, which is called that of the Sultans and Mamluks. For when this nation acquires new seats, it wishes to abolish all monuments of those who came before, not only among foreign nations, but among their own, so that they may appear to be the first produced in the world and the first rulers. For this reason, they even change proper names, so that you do not recognize your own in their writings: Saul is called *Talot*, Goliath *Galot*, David *Dauud*, Solomon *Suleiman*, Job *Aiub*, Moses *Musa*, Jesus *Isa*, John *Iachie*, and many other names are produced in inverted forms. They do the same with the names of provinces and cities. Mesopotamia is called *Merdin* and *Chorassan*, Armenia *Erminly*, Cilicia *Caramanly*, Galatia *Othmanty*, Asia *Natolda*, Greece *Romly*, Mysia *Bogdan*, Constantinople is called *Stambol*, Adrianople *Ederne*, and Pera is called *Calata*. And thus they hasten to abolish not only the things themselves, but the memory of them handed down in writing, entirely neglecting the literature of others.

<margin>The affairs of the Mamluks.</margin>

The affairs of the Mamluks <note>original: "Mamluchorum"; elite slave-soldiers who rose to rule Egypt and Syria</note> are as follows. When frequent incursions were made into Asia and Europe by the northern subject peoples two hundred years ago, a certain tribe belonging to the region of the Maeotis and the Pontic Sea—formerly called the Cercetae, and now the Circassians—having created a leader from among themselves and leaving behind only that portion of their people for whom the land was sufficient, sought the Armenias and came to the borders of northern Syria, and began to be formidable. Since that soldiery had no fixed seats, they began to serve for pay among their neighbors. From this it happened that a great addition of that nation was made to the Sultan of Egypt, and those Circassians were like the slaves of the prince, as the name implies. For *Mamluk* <note>original: "Mamluch"</note> signifies a royal slave, a word derived from *Melich* <note>the Arabic "Malik"</note>, that is, from "king." Taking the opportunity, since that nation never failed in Egypt after their first hiring, they finished off the proper prince and elected one from among themselves to preside over all, and to rule by certain laws approved among them. The first in the memory of men was Cahith bencus <note>Likely Sultan Qaitbay (r. 1468–1496); Postel interprets "Bey" or "Ben" as "lord"</note>, that is, Lord Cahith, who dictated laws to the Egyptians from the Circassians. Before him, the rule had been held by Sultans for nearly four hundred years, not without the help of the Circassians. For from the time they made their first incursion into Asia, they were sold annually from the remnants by the neighboring Tartars, and especially by those who are Muslims. For the Circassians who live near the Cimmerian mountains gave their names to Christ and were initiated in the Greek rite. After Cahith bencus, who reigned for thirty-three years, a great faction arose. For two leaders of the Mamluks began to contend among themselves for the empire: one was called Campsous <note>Qansuh al-Ghawri</note>, the other Acbardinus...

Campfous <note>original: "Campfous," referring to Qansuh al-Ghawri, the penultimate Mamluk Sultan</note>, whose name was Qansuh, in order to more easily turn the minds of everyone toward himself, with difficulty persuaded the dying Caitho <note>Qaitbay, the long-reigning Sultan of Egypt who died in 1496</note> to order that his fifteen-year-old son should reign after him. The father hardly complied with this because he knew the customs of his people and had clear sight of where things were heading. For he saw that in the future, once the son was killed, Campfous would seize the tyranny. Nor did this deceive him; for before the youth had spent two years in the kingdom—not without the blood of citizens and nobles—the fraud was uncovered while he attempted to remove them with a poisoned banquet, and he was judged an enemy and killed. 

With hostilities finally out in the open, Akberdi <note>original: "Acbardinus"</note> and Campfous clashed; Akberdi was bound and shortly thereafter ended his days. Campfous <note>original: "Chamzaus"</note> reigned, and as a reward for his favor, he created Tuman Bay <note>original: "Tomumbencus"</note> as <term>Emir-chebir: from the Arabic 'Amir al-Kabir', meaning the Great Commander or Commander-in-Chief of the army</term>, as if you were to say the prefect of the palace and the military, because he had slaughtered the young Muhammad <note>the son of Qaitbay</note> to please the nobles. Meanwhile, Janbalat <note>original: "Iambellatus"</note>, the emir of Damascene Syria, did not approve of the election of Qansuh and prepared for war. Qansuh, though not without suspicion of what would later happen, but because he could do no other, gave the task of breaking Janbalat’s forces to Tuman Bay. They set out, held a parley, reached an agreement, and Qansuh was betrayed and driven from the kingdom. He fled to the citadel of Alexandria, where he was besieged, caught, and thrown into prison, having not yet completed twenty months in his reign. 

Janbalat was created and crowned Sultan; but while he preyed upon everyone's property, he fell into the hatred of the Circassians <note>The "Cerceticorum," the ethnic group that formed the ruling Mamluk elite</note>, was captured, and strangled. Tuman Bay, succeeding him, was no more humane, but began to vent his rage more moderately at the start. By assessing every house in Cairo <note>original: "Alcahiri"</note> for tax, he demanded six months' rent, and immediately as much again, and finally ten months' rent. He proscribed, killed, and plundered foreigners, Christians, and Jews, and distributed their assets such that unless any merchant paid exactly what the Sultan valued them at, he would be slaughtered and his goods assigned to the tyrant. And because he did not spare even the leading men in these matters, he was besieged and fled the palace through tunnels, until on the fortieth day he was found by the associates of Janbalat, betrayed, and killed. Such is the state of those men who live under the law of Muhammad. All things are similar among them, since none of those princes believe that there is a God. By the consensus of all—though he was very unwilling and feared the danger—Qansuh al-Ghawri <note>original: "Chamzaus Chaurus"</note> was elected and reigned for a longer time, until he died, crushed in the middle of Syria by Sultan Selim <note>Selim I, the Ottoman Sultan</note>, the father of Suleiman. This was the end of it.

It is no wonder for a tyrant to rage against a tyrant. But for a brother to rage against brothers—that is truly something we, who are ignorant of those plagues, usually find marvelous. For no petty king, as I have learned from many places among the barbarians themselves in Africa, reigns without the blood of brothers or kinsmen. Muley Muhammad <note>original: "Maule Muhamedes"</note>, who now commands in Tunis, and to whom the Emperor Charles <note>Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, who restored Muley Hassan's son to the throne in 1535</note> restored the empire after Hayreddin Barbarossa <note>original: "Hairadino Aenobarbo," the famous Ottoman corsair and admiral</note>—a Greek man and pirate—was driven out, began his reign with the blood of **17** brothers and as many kinsmen. This is not usually considered a vice among them, because even the law, by which they seem to mock God, does not prohibit it. For Muhammad advised in the Quran <note>original: "Alcorano"</note> that in the "Way of God" no account should be held for a son, a father, or a brother, much less for anyone else. Everyone, while they strive for power, says that they are in the "Way of God." Thus, all things are permitted to them, since nothing is considered a vice. What shall I say of the "Scourge of God" Demirly <note>Timur or Tamerlane, the Central Asian conqueror</note>, whom we call Tamerlane? Was there ever a more iron-hearted man than that Muslim? He was well named: when throngs of infants, virgins, and priests approached him after his edicts, he trampled them like mud. For he did not value a human being more than a stone or a fungus. Perhaps the affairs of the Turks are better; let us see.

...[from which] this empire emerged: and through the laziness, envy, and factionalism of the Greek emperors, it arrived at its current peak of power. The eleventh of their emperors, Suleiman <note>original: "Suleimanus," referring to Suleiman the Magnificent, r. 1520–1566</note>, now holds the state; a man certainly (for that nation) of the highest humanity and equity. While his son Bayezid <note>original: "Bayazetes"</note> followed his father's European undertakings more intently, the wrath of God arose in Asia—Tamerlane <note>the Central Asian conqueror Timur</note>; when Bayezid opposed him with unequal force, he was captured by him and, bound in golden chains, was led around in a cage as a spectacle until he ended his days in Syria from exhaustion. His successor, Murad II <note>original: "Hamurathes secundus"</note>, added all of Thrace and the Peloponnese to the empire, along with many other provinces. 

Mehmed II <note>original: "Mahmetes secundus," the Conqueror</note>, along with many other places, captured and plundered Constantinople: and after many most remarkable deeds, he handed the kingdom to his son Bayezid II <note>original: "Baiazeto"</note>. The latter, born more for peace and the study of philosophy than for war, died after being removed by poison by his son Selim <note>original: "Selimo"</note>. Thus, through Selim, affairs came to Suleiman. This is the summary of events, and this is the order. This history has been written copiously by many, and for that reason I do not linger upon it, since it is not my purpose to speak of the origin or progress of things, or of famous deeds. 

I run through in a few words the arts by which they obtained their empires. Bayezid I, so that he might reign more safely, killed his brother Suleiman. Orhan, the son of Celebi, was suppressed by his uncle Musa <note>original: "Moſe"</note>; but Musa was suppressed by Mehmed, Orhan's brother. The second Mehmed, having killed his brother, enjoyed the empire more safely. But nothing is more famous than Selim, who, having killed his father and his brothers and relatives, would even have removed his own legitimate son (unless the most prudent mother of the now-reigning Suleiman had forewarned the youth), lest the same thing that he had done to his father should happen to himself. These are the "benefits" of the Muhammadan law <note>Postel uses the phrase "Beneficia sunt legis Muhamediis" sarcastically to critique Islamic legal and social structures</note>. Let the <term>Muslims: original "Mussulmani"</term> read the histories of the Christians; they will see what a difference there is between the laws of Christ and those of the devil. 

I say nothing of the wearing down of the subjects. The world, in the memory of literature, was never in such vast desolation as it is under the Muhammadan law, and will be, unless it is resisted. Formerly, the Romans received more taxes from Egypt alone than the King of the <term>Turks: original "Tur-charum," a hybrid of Turk and Khan</term> now receives from all of Asia and his entire empire; and yet the affairs of the peoples were most flourishing, even after an annual extraction of fifteen million, as we call it. Certainly, double that was commanded of Asia and paid. Today, money is exacted from all common people even to the skin and soul, and yet the sum does not reach even a quarter of that great number. Because of the foul extractions of princes who have nothing of God before their eyes, the <term>Nomads: Postel refers to the Bedouin or migratory tribes</term> in all of Africa—a most excellent province of the world when it is cultivated—likewise in Egypt and Arabia, prefer to become wanderers rather than be exposed to the lust and plunder of others while they till the fields. If I am imagining anything, there are most wealthy witnesses, both those who are worn down by innumerable exactions and those who professedly swoop down upon the fortunes of others. Therefore, the desolation of the world can be called the Muhammadan law, rather than the law of God, who wishes to nourish all things and for them to live peacefully, and to endure for a very long time by proving Himself to them.

### THE FIRST ENCOUNTER WITH MUSLIMS NOW

->translated into Arabic by the author, the title of which in Arabic is: *A Compendium of All Doctrines Required for Human Excellence.* It contains a brief proof of the Trinity, praises of Jesus Christ and the Gospel drawn from the Quran, and the principal errors of that persuasion.<-

In the name of the merciful and pious God. <note>This opening mimics the "Basmala," the traditional Islamic invocation "In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate."</note> Praise be to God, the most powerful, wisest, and best King of the Ages, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things; and peace be upon those who are comforted by Him and those who seek Him in truth; and may the leniency of God, and peace, and mercy be upon all men. Amen.

Before every thing, there preceded a cause, or causes for it, since no thing creates itself. Therefore, before all things is the most high God, powerful over all. The sublime God created this orb and world for His own praise, for the utility of mankind, and for both together. These three are one single end, or the "final cause" <term>final cause: the ultimate purpose or goal for which a thing exists</term> of the world. Man was created for the praise of God, for his own innocence and purity, and for the love of his neighbor. It is necessary that these three be present in every good work, as one thing: since it is not possible for a work to be good without these three.

Every thing is either by the hand of God, or by the wisdom and will of men, or by the power of fortune.

In the power of God, immediately, are all things, but especially eternity and essence, the heavens, the stars, change, motion, rest, the natural order, and the four natures—namely fire, air, water, and earth—and those things which are born from them. Man, however, with prudence and reason, discovers the roots and principles of non-natural things, and through his handling of them, sets them forth in science and art. From "chance," however, are those things that happen which have no likeness to the work of God or of men: such as fortuitous events and non-natural or divine accidents. And every thing which has no cause in nature—and in short, all the disturbances of this life and its unhappiness—he calls the work of fortune. However, the aim and end of God is to lead man, with faith and certainty, toward his own necessity, the utility of necessary things, and into the knowledge of himself and the acknowledgement of God; so that from there, faith may be given to men, that man may become holy with virtue and the love of the supreme good, and that after this life he may know the cause of all things in the most high God. However, the point at which a man ought to aim is to comfort other men who are afflicted and pressed by necessity, to help the rich and the poor, to harm no one, and to live as the precepts of divine and human law command him: and to dwell in this world as if in an inn, as one for whom the world is a single city, if he is wise. Fortune has no aim, since it acts nothing by will.

Every work has a likeness to its author. But since in every simple natural thing there is an image of the Trinity, it is necessary that in God, who created all things, there be a Trinity. For nothing can be the same one thing in all things unless it is in their creator. Therefore, in what follows, it will be seen that it is not possible for us to understand the most high God without the Trinity. We shall begin, therefore, from the definition of God. God is the first cause of all nature, moving all things, commanding all things; He is power, wisdom, and love, which acts in the universe just as the soul and the intellect act in the human body, stirring all motions as He wills. Man, however, carries out his works with will and judgment (unless he is under compulsion); his intellect penetrates into every thing except God. And for this reason, the Greeks call him a <term>microcosm</term> <note>original Greek: "μικρόκοσμον", meaning "little world"</note>, because in him is an example of both God and of lower matter. For man lives in matter with the plants, feels with the animals, and understands and reasons with the angels and spiritual substances...

# THESE ARE EXCERPTS FROM CHAPTER III. ON THE
# Harmony of the World. *A demonstration of the trinity in the divine nature.*

It cannot come to pass that anything is made without power. However, although God is powerful, He does nothing without wisdom. Truly, after power and wisdom, it is necessary that love or desire, or will, be present. Therefore, God is powerful, wise, and benevolent toward all things before He creates them. Thus power, wisdom, and love are one God. Power is the first person or subsistence <term>subsistence: a philosophical term for an individual existence or "person" within the divine essence</term>, and therefore it is that which Christians call God the Father. But because wisdom is generated from that power from eternity, without which nothing would be created, they call it the Son of God and His Word. and because love and will toward the creation of things proceed from both, they name it the Holy Spirit. Properly, the Father is powerful, the Son is wise, and the Holy Spirit is loving—one God. They are one thing in their essence: all power is in wisdom and love, all wisdom is in power and love, and all love is in wisdom and power; just as an inheritance in the mind, in a legal book, and in its physical location is only one thing. For they do not speak of three gods, but of one God: powerful, wise, and benevolent. Just as in every labor or work there is thought, speech, and operation <note>original: "cogitatio, locutio, & operatio"</note>, and yet there are not three works, but one work; so power, wisdom, and benevolence, though they are different things, are one God and not three. Since power, force, or strength are properties of the Beginning (that is, the Father); while wisdom, or science, or knowledge are properties of the Second (that is, the Son); and the will, or love toward things for the sake of an end, is the property of the End (that is, the Holy Spirit), therefore in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, just as there is only one divinity, so power, wisdom, and love are one. Just as in every work thought is the property of the Beginning, the word or explanation is the property of the Middle (between thought and art), and the operation holds the property of the End and completion; yet in every work, thought, explanation, and operation are only one thing. In this way, Christians do not think nor assert that there are three gods, but that God is one in trinity and triune in unity—unity in trinity, trinity in unity in the One. Nor can the intellect grasp God without power, wisdom, and love.

God is an intellect and a mind powerful over all beings. And therefore, since He understands all beings in His essence, it is necessary that He knows and understands Himself and His own substance within Himself. For unless He knew His substance within Himself, He would not be omnipotent. Therefore it is necessary that God be the thinking intellect <note>original: "intellectus intelligens"</note> and the understood mind <note>original: "mens intellecta"</note>. But because of this knowledge of Himself, He has love and joy, since without the knowledge of one's own good no one rejoices, and with the knowledge of one's own virtue every man rejoices. God, therefore, according to His knowledge, rejoices in Himself more than all men. For that reason, there is in God the thinking intellect, the understood mind, and love or joy as one thing. The thinking mind is the Father, the understood mind is the Son, and the joy is the Holy Spirit. The Father is in His Son, the Son is in His Father, and the Spirit or love is in the Father and the Son as one thing; substance in substance, or thing in thing, person in person, having nothing prior or posterior except in the order of naming and understanding; in which persons there is no confusion, nor separation.

Just as in the dominion of the world there is a trinity in unity in every single virtue (for nothing happens without God, heaven, and matter), so in the administration of individual kingdoms it is fitting that there be a trinity in unity, even though the leadership or administration is one, which has priests or pontiffs, and a king...

and judges, and it is one power or force: a power that is spiritual, corporal, and intermediate. Priests are like the servants of the Most High God in spiritual matters, kings in corporal matters, and judges in both, acting as the hands of both. Furthermore, this administration is one: for kings do not rule without the servants of God (or religion), nor do priests rule without a princedom, nor do these two accomplish anything without equity and judges. Therefore, there is one power in a trinity. Nor is it possible for power to exist for a long time without this trinity. These are necessary for the preservation of peace, just as power, wisdom, and love are necessary to God. For this reason, in every good work, it is necessary that there be an equity of the heart—both human (or civil and social) and judicial (or coercive). For equity is not that which thinks of evil, or does it, or opposes the law. Therefore, since good in this world cannot be held and preserved without a trinity, it is necessary that God—the fountain of good, from whose goodness those goods were given to man—possess most perfectly within Himself a trinity, whose image is never absent.

Similarly, in natural virtue <note>original: "uirtute naturali," referring here to the "power" or "inherent properties" of nature</note> there is unity in trinity, and trinity in unity, as I have said. There is a superior virtue, an inferior virtue, and an intermediate one. The highest virtue is in spiritual natures: first in the Most High God, and secondly in the angels and the citizens of paradise; the intermediate virtue is in the heavens and the stars; and from both of these comes the third, the elemental virtue, in which every body acts and suffers <term>suffers: in a philosophical sense, this means "to be acted upon" or to receive an impression, rather than feeling pain</term>. Yet these are one virtue, because nature is only one.

Likewise, in every natural body there is trinity in unity, and vice versa. For in every body there is a persistence of power, a progress from that power, and a love or "choice" during the act. We see this in fire: its force or power lies in its persistence to burn, its action or operation proceeds from that power, and it acts upon a thin, slight, and dry body rather than a dense, hard, and moist one; thus we see in it a certain thing in the manner of a choice <note>Postel is arguing that even "inanimate" things like fire show a "preference" or "will" (choice) by reacting differently to different materials</note>. Indeed, these things are one force; for a thing cannot act without power, nor does it act at all without the progress of action, nor does it act except upon a body that is disposed and chosen for it. In the same way, pepper burns the tongue more than the skin through its perpetual acting; nor does it cease to act until it perishes or lacks a body fit to feel the action. The same must be judged of other things. For example, in the sun there is the solar body (its center), its light, and its virtue: and these three are one in the sun. And while it acts, these three are one from one sun.

Moreover, in every body there is matter and form, and the composite of both. These three are one body, nor is it possible for any thing to be made from matter without this trinity in unity. Form gives being to the thing, matter bears and sustains it, and the composite holds both; yet one is not the other.

In the dimension of every body there is a trinity in unity; before any quantity can be known, there is length, breadth, and depth. For without these, no measure will be known. In motion there is time—in the past, the future, and the present—nor can any one of these be known without the others. In every operation there is the agent, the instrument, and the patient <note>the "patient" is the object being acted upon</note>. Every work is made by an agent, by matter, and by the operation itself. Yet the whole is in the power of the agent, the whole in the matter, and the whole in the work: and yet there are not three works, but one. This is the image of God.

Similarly, in spiritual nature there is unity in trinity: either a spirit exists without a body, or endowed with one, or in an intermediate condition. The first is in God, angels, and demons, for they have no body. The second is in the elements, and in that which merely exists, or that which exists and lives, or that which exists, lives, and feels. For all life endowed with matter exists in these three. For the lower spirit is in every thing, and properly in living creatures destitute of intellect. But the third and intermediate, which is sometimes in the body, sometimes...

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK II. ###

is taught outwardly, it is the soul or the intellect of man, in which there is a trinity in unity, and vice versa. For in the human soul, there is a gathering of the senses, recollection, and memory, and it is impossible for these to be separated from one another; for the whole soul is present in sense and apprehension, the whole in gathering or thought, and the whole in recollection. This is the image of the Most High God. The entire spirit of lower nature is found in the faculty of loving, attracting, and preserving; it is only one in the whole, and one in every part, and that is the image of God. So too in the natural, vital, and animal faculties <note>In 16th-century physiology, the "natural faculty" (centered in the liver) governed nutrition; the "vital" (heart) governed heat and life-force; and the "animal" (brain) governed movement and thought.</note>; just as in the souls of brute animals there is apprehension, imagination, and memory: these three are one soul, which cannot be conceived without them. In all knowledge, there is opinion (or imagination), doubt, and truth. For first we hold an opinion about unknown things; if they are in the middle, we doubt; finally, through proof, we come to the truth. The whole mind is in the one, and the whole is in each individual part. Life is either purely natural (or vegetative), or sensitive, or intellectual along with the body: the second does not exist without the first, nor the third without the first two, yet life is one. It proceeds, however, from the heart, lungs, and brain, through the veins, arteries, and nerves, which mutually compose a single harmony; without the first elements, there is no place for the second. This is the image of God, who preserves all things in a trinity.

The tradition of every doctrine that comes into operation is not possible without logical contemplation and operation, as I taught above. The whole matter lies in contemplation, the whole in reason (or rational expression), and the whole in the work itself. Therefore, in all of nature, we see the pattern and the footprint of the Trinity which is in the Most High God, since He is the all-powerful Author over all things, who gave us this world in which His image resides, so that we might know Him and the good He has bestowed upon us, and that we might praise Him forever. Therefore, God generated from His power the wisdom and knowledge of all things, through which He created everything in love <note>original: "charitate," often translated as "charity" or "divine love"</note>. Thus, before anything was created, God generated His Son, whom the prophets called the Word of God <note>original: "uerbũ Dei"</note>, using a likeness that can be understood by us. Just as we speak after we have thought, so after the power of God, we understand His Son as the Word, like a son of the mind. They also called Him Wisdom, because it follows immediately after Power. From both, truly, the Holy Spirit proceeds in eternity: these three are one God—powerful, wise, loving, glorious, the judge, and the King of Kings. He gave His law to Adam, the first of men, and wrote it in his heart; but Adam did not keep it. After grace was lost through disobedience, the natural law lasted for two thousand years; finally, God gave the written law nearly five hundred years after the promise to Abraham, and He entrusted it to His servant Moses to instruct the children of Israel, who were indeed a hard and stiff-necked <note>original: "ceruicosos," literally "thick-necked," a biblical term for stubbornness</note> people under a semi-perfect law. 

But after men were able to recognize that there is no salvation for a lost and sinful man except in God and through God, when it pleased God, He gave His Word through His Spirit to take on a human body. Because men were entirely evil and no longer believed in divine inspirations, they needed to see a single body in which the divinity resided. He took on flesh in the Virgin Mary through the Holy Spirit, as the angel announced—just as when one man makes a concept known to another through a word, and that man conceives it in his mind; for he does not conceive the word itself, but the notion that the word carries. In this way, the Virgin did not conceive the Holy Spirit sent from God the Father, but by means of the Spirit, she conceived the Wisdom and Word of God, which indeed came for the direction of all men. That Word and Wisdom is Jesus Christ, the Son of God, born of the Father before all ages and conceived in time from the Virgin, and made man so that He might bring light to other men. He exists as both God and man, the only one who can restore all men, just as He created everyone as one in the beginning. To Him be praise in heaven and on earth forever. Now, indeed, we shall write His praises from the book of the Quran <note>original: "Alcorani"</note>.

# THE PRAISES OF JESUS CHRIST,
->In the Quran, in Surah Baqarah, <note>Latin: *Sora Bacara*. Postel refers to the second chapter of the Quran, which he calls the first after the opening prayer.</note> that is, the first chapter.<-

God said: "And we gave Jesus the son of Mary wisdom, and we formed him from the Holy Spirit." Thus says Muhammad. He who possesses the wisdom of God, and is born or formed from the Holy Spirit, must necessarily be God, and the Son of God. For even if we did not believe him to be God, he is still loftier than other men, greater than all the prophets, and more worthy of belief.

->And a little later:<-

God says: "And we ordained these prophets among themselves. For God spoke to some, and he raised some of them by degrees. And we gave Jesus the son of Mary wisdom, and we formed him from the Holy Spirit." Although Muhammad writes elsewhere that wisdom was given to the prophets, no one could possess it in its solid completeness except him who was conceived from the Holy Spirit, and who is God, and light from light. The prophets were participants in it; he is solid wisdom and divinity itself.

->In Surah Al-Imran, <note>Latin: *sora Humram*. Modern Surah 3.</note> that is, of Joachim, which is the second.<-

Hannah, the wife of Joachim, said of Mary her daughter: "I have called her Mary, and I defend her and her offspring from the ruinous demon." From this passage, it appears that those two <note>Referring to Mary and Jesus.</note> did not sin, for to be defended from the devil is to not sin.

->And later:<-

"O Mary," (says the angel) "behold, God brings you the good news of his word from himself, whose name is Christ Jesus, son of Mary, to whom the faces of the present and future world shall turn; he is among those who are near <note>To God.</note>, and he shall speak to men in the cradle and in swaddling clothes, and he shall be an excellent man." Thus says the Quran. The Word of God is the most high God himself, so called because just as we do not understand anything from another man without a word or explanation, so we do not conceive of God’s power without his own explanation, word, and wisdom—which is also God. Therefore, God is not without his word or wisdom. Nor are they for that reason two or three gods, but one God, who is in no single place, yet is in every place. For God is not a body, but is free from body and matter. We do not call Jesus "God" according to his body, but according to his divinity; for the power of God and his wisdom are one thing. Just as our own word is the "son" of our thought, and there is nothing else in the word except what was in the thought (whether true or false), for thought, word, and the thing itself are one single thing—even though the whole thing was and is in the thought, and whole in the word, and whole in itself.

->And a little later:<-

"And God taught him (Christ) the book and wisdom, the law and the gospel, and established him as a prophet to the children of Israel. 'I have now come to you,' (Christ says in the same place) 'with miracles from your Lord. I create for you out of clay the figures of birds, and I breathe into them, and they become birds by the permission of God; I heal scabs <note>original: *psoras*</note> and leprosies, and I bring the dead to life, by the command or permission of God.'" The title of "Creator" and "Raiser of the Dead," performed without prayers, belongs properly to God alone. Regarding the creation of birds, this is a miracle from the Savior's infancy. <note>This story appears in the Quran and the apocryphal "Infancy Gospel of Thomas," but not the canonical Bible.</note> Furthermore, when Jesus raised the dead, he raised them by simple command, with no prayers poured out, to show that he was God, the arbiter of nature. The apostles, however, raised countless thousands in the name of Jesus and his cross. But miracles can only be done in the name of God. Since, therefore, all kinds of miracles were done in the name of Jesus through the sign of the cross, it follows that he is God. Though we do not find in the Gospel (except that he groaned over Lazarus) that he invoked his Father to raise the dead, it is not surprising, because he himself...

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK II.

...and the Father are one God. But according to the fact that he was man, he raised the dead by the command and power of his divinity. For according to his divinity, these would not be "miracles," because all things are very easy for God. Indeed, we have already seen above that the substance of the Father and the Son is one, and the "command of God" in Jesus is the divine will, since in Jesus there is a will with God and a will with man, which are two wills. Therefore, when he performed miracles as a man, he did them with divine command; and when he did them as God, he then did them by his own command and will. For these two wills differed in that one subject, just as the will of nature and the will of grace differ in us: for by one we do evil, and by the other we will the good.

->In Surah an-Nisa, <note>Latin: *Sora nesæ*. This refers to the fourth chapter of the Quran, "The Women." Postel numbers it as the 3rd chapter.</note> that is, "The Women," toward the end of the third section.<-

>O you who are endowed with the Book <note>Postel notes: "sometimes he understands us and the Jews by this name, and sometimes he understands idolaters and naturalists by the term, because they follow the dictates of nature."</note>, do not be puffed up in your own judgment, and do not say anything about God except the truth. Jesus Christ, the son of Mary, is nothing but a prophet of God, and His Word, which He sent into Mary, and a spirit from Him. Believe therefore in God and His prophet, and do not say "three."

We have already seen this in the Quran: that it is not possible for God to exist without a Trinity; therefore it is necessary that God be three-in-one and one-in-three. And the Messiah is God and man, both a prophet and the Word of God, and His Son—not insofar as he is man, but insofar as he is God, from God, and wisdom from power. For we do not say that he is a carnal son of God through the emission of seed; far be it. But we say that he is an intellectual and spiritual Son, who descended into the womb of the Virgin Mary and was made man, with the Holy Spirit coming upon the Virgin Mary. 

That he was something other than merely a man is clear from these arguments: He demonstrated this in the miracles performed in his own name alone. His true disciples and followers performed the same and even greater things in his name. He rose again with no one praying for him. He transformed his followers and made them different from worldly people. For other men are either evil, or they wish for the good but do not do it, or they do less and more imperfectly than they would wish. Only true Christians have surpassed in their works those good things that were ever able to be written by the philosophers. They did not fear death, but craved it. They held the pleasures of the body in hatred, contrary to the common nature of men; from which it is established that they were changed by his words and sacraments with divine power. For this cannot be done by man. For God alone, who knows nature because he made it, can likewise change and amend it. Men and prophets can do nothing else but speak and forewarn; God alone gives perfection. 

But you, O Muslims <note>Latin: *Mussulmani*.</note>, you say the Gospel is too perfect, and therefore you place the Quran above it. If Christ was the greatest of the prophets, then he gave the highest law, and the most perfect, and therefore the one necessary for salvation. For this reason, there are so few even among us who are truly good, because few obey the Gospel.

And those who opposed said that this was manifest incantation. And when I revealed to the Apostles: 'Believe in me and my messenger,' they said: 'We believe, and be yourself a witness, for we are faithful Muslims <note>Latin: *Mussulmin*.</note>.'"

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

Christians do not deny that whatever the Messiah possesses, he has from his Father. For he himself says in many places in the Gospel, "I have received all things from my Father." <note>original Latin: *omnia accepi a patre meo*. This reflects the Christian doctrine of the "eternal generation" of the Son, where the Son is equal to the Father but receives his divine nature from Him.</note> But it does not follow from this that he is not God: just as it does not follow, when a thing exists in the mind, in the word, and in the work, that it is not equally in all three. The word is received from the mind, and the thing is perfected in both; and yet they are not three separate things, but one.

->And a little later regarding the sacrament of the altar, which is therefore read in the great Behiram, <note>Postel uses the term *Behiram*, likely referring to the Islamic *Bayram* (festival), but he equates it here with the Christian Passover or Easter (*Paschate*).</note> that is, the Passover, when they are reconciled.<-

Thus he [Muhammad] wanted to pervert the Gospel, referring solely to God what belongs to Christ as God-man. These and the following things are nowhere in the whole Gospel, and besides, why would God object to what He knows is not so? These are manifest lies with which the Quran teems.

### In Surah Maryam, that is, Mary. <note>Referring to Chapter 19 of the Quran.</note>

All prophets were men like us, and they sinned, and therefore they could not be truly "blessed." But Jesus, since he was a sent prophet and God, was blessed in this world—I understand this to mean without stain and sin. For only sin makes a person evil, miserable, and unhappy.

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK II

...to those among them who believed, their reward. <note>Postel is concluding a thought from the previous page regarding the rewards of faith.</note> Since Christ came from God with the Gospel, and in it there is guidance and faith for those who fear God, it contains no fault, and therefore it is not corrupted, even if evil and perverse men do not observe it.
