Therefore, he who does not believe that which the Gospel uniquely intends to persuade—namely, that Jesus is above all most holy men, that he is God, the Son of God and of the Virgin, and that he died for the justice of all men and rose from the dead—has no mercy from God, nor eternal life. However, he who does not know the Gospel and does good can be saved in the name of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; but he who has heard of Jesus and the Gospel and does not believe in him faces a great punishment.

->ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD.<-

...he was conceived by the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, performed miracles in his infancy and throughout his life, and raised the dead by his own power alone, without even invoking God <note>Postel emphasizes "without invoking God" to argue that Jesus acted as God himself, rather than as a mere prophet who asks God for a miracle.</note>. He gave power to his own followers so that, in his name and by the sign of his cross, they might do the same as he did, and even greater things, so that they might all despise the world and desire death for the sake of the truth. Although they received injuries from all, they nevertheless loved everyone and bestowed benefits—gifts which cannot be given to men except by God. He is nearest to God through his humanity, the judge of all, dwelling with the good, and capable of killing all in the blink of an eye. And how can others be preferred to him? How then can his law be abandoned for another <note>Referring to the Islamic law or Sharia.</note>, which considers the pleasure of the body, shared with the beasts, to be the highest good? He who does not go to God through him is damned. For since God confers all things upon us through his wisdom, and that is his way of showing favor to men, it is necessary that we return to him by that same way; otherwise, we shall not arrive there.

### Praise of the Gospel, in Surah Al-Baqarah. <note>original: "Sora Bacara." This refers to the second chapter of the Quran.</note>

And they said: "Be Jews or Christians, and you shall be guided." Say: "Nay, but the law of Abraham is mild, and he was no idolater." Say: "We believe in God, and in that which was sent down to us, and to Abraham, and Ishmael, Isaac, and Jacob, and to the tribes, and that which was given to Moses and Jesus and the prophets from their Lord; we make no distinction between them." <note>Postel is paraphrasing Surah 2:135-136.</note> But why should we not distinguish between the true and the false, between that which is from God and that which is not from God? Why did God give us intellect and free will, if not so that we might understand what is true and what is false? He who speaks a falsehood fears that his word might be examined; therefore, if it can be judged, he does not permit it. But he who speaks the truth rejoices that everyone should know it and debate it, so that it may be better understood. If, therefore, all the prophets—Abraham, Moses, the tribe of David, Christ—agree with one another, they are true; therefore, if anyone does not agree with them and differs, he cannot be true. In this way, a distinction must be made. Two thousand three hundred years before Muhammad <term>Muhamedes</term> came, the law of Moses was as it is now; and six hundred years before, the Gospel and the "new law" or "law of grace" existed, as it is found in the languages of all nations. In no place in either the Old or New Testament is it written that Abraham was ever in Mecca <term>Mecha</term>, or that he sacrificed there; rather, the contrary is true. In no place is it written that anything of the law was given to Ishmael, except for circumcision. For he was expelled from his father's house, an outcast and an idolater, who took an Egyptian wife devoted to the cult of idols. This is contrary to the Quran <term>Alcorano</term>, which is founded upon the faithfulness of Ishmael and the sacrifice of Abraham <note>Islamic tradition holds that it was Ishmael, not Isaac, whom Abraham nearly sacrificed, and that they rebuilt the Kaaba in Mecca together.</note>.

Mustapha <note>A title for Muhammad meaning "the Chosen."</note> Muhammad says in Surah An-Nisa <note>original: "Sora nesæ." <margin>An appeal to the Muslim princes.</margin>
Come now, O princes, keep the earthly power now acquired and confirmed for you, and receive the truth of Jesus Christ. Since he [Muhammad] sought that power unjustly through fabrications, you will possess it justly if you swear by the words of Jesus Christ; all people will follow you. See to it that the Gospel is read in your provinces, and let it be debated alongside the Quran with reason, and you will see a victory without blood. Let the Suras <note>original: "Sorae." The chapters of the Quran.</note> of the Quran be brought forth with the chapters of the Gospel, as the *Furqan* <note>original: "Alphurcan." From the Arabic "Al-Furqan" (The Criterion), another name for the Quran.</note> often says; if it wins, all will become Muslims. All Christians can read the Quran, and it is read everywhere; but no one can believe it, because it seems to us entirely written against God and nature. By debating both, the truth will emerge.

That the Gospel is the truest and to be preferred above every law is clear from these reasons. Prophets and holy men, along with the Sibyls <note>Ancient prophetic women whom Renaissance Christians believed had foretold the coming of Christ to the pagans.</note>, predicted with one voice in different places concerning Jesus and his Gospel; no one predicted Muhammad. Christians in the most distant parts of the whole world agree on what we hold concerning Christ, just as the prophets had agreed before; this could not happen unless God illuminated the minds of the holy. You, currently under Muhammad, were destined to be divided into seventy nations <note>A reference to the *hadith* of the 73 sects, suggesting that only one group among Muslims would find salvation.</note>, of which only one is to be saved.

Our sacred books were received early and discussed in freedom, in councils, and in the highest wisdom, without any force. The Quran, on the contrary, was thrust upon the unwilling through fear of death or the confiscation of goods by force. By teaching gently and suffering all things, the Apostles taught the law of Christ. Soldiers, robbers, and tyrants persuaded the unskilled and the rustic of your law by force—laws which even many of you would struggle against daily if it were allowed. But because of the danger to your lives, it is not permitted. The truth of the Gospel does not seek corners <note>original: "non quaerit angulos." A Latin idiom meaning the truth does not need to hide in shadows or act in secret.</note>; it may be discussed publicly and privately. Our law teaches that in this life there is no happiness for the body; it places everything in the love of God, charity for one’s neighbor, and one's own innocence. It harms no one and helps whom it can. Yours promises and expects a paradise for itself through carnal and bodily pleasures shared with the beasts. Furthermore, it invades the property of others by force in the name of religion, and thinks nothing holier than having killed a man, while in our law nothing is more hateful. 

In addition to these things, what was holier than Jesus Christ and his followers who handed down the Gospels to us? They would have preferred to die than to lie. What holiness did Muhammad have, knowing fifteen wives in one hour; a killer of citizens, a striker of brothers, a perjurer, a robber, and more wicked than other wicked men? With how many infinite miracles was the Gospel confirmed! Yet Muhammad was never seen to have performed any miracle, and what he said he performed is ridiculous. Moreover, countless external witnesses—excellent men—gave their names to Jesus Christ and his followers; no one ever (except followers conscious of the fable and people captured by trifles) failed to call Muhammad the most cruel of all tyrants. 

Furthermore, since God wants the salvation of men to come through the Gospel, if He approved of those things which are against it and against nature, He would not be God. He waits for you to repent, and He uses you as torturers against our crimes. By these reasons you can recognize how far truth differs from falsehood. Even if Muhammad had not been forced to attribute to Christ and the Gospel what he did attribute, natural judgment suggests that it ought to be preferred to every doctrine in the world.

# THE HARMONY OF THE UNIVERSE AND OF ALL THINGS
### placed in the quaternary, from which the greatest light for knowing the Trinity arises.

Just as we recognized the image of God and of the most holy Trinity—the cause of all things—within the material parts of the world, so we shall recognize that the image of the Trinity is seen everywhere in the harmony of the four things that must necessarily be understood within God.

1. There is, as we saw at the beginning, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: one God. The Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God; not three, but one. These are power, wisdom, benevolence, and divinity: abundance, the progress of acting, choice, and eternity—the end and the cause of all things.

2. Apprehension, consideration, and remembrance: one entire mind, one in the three, and one in each individual; the knowledge of all things and the method of knowing the First Cause through its effects.

3. In created nature, there is the spiritual world, the celestial world, and the lowest world: the world. There is the world in the angelic mind and care (as in a most perfect subject), the world in the power of the active heavens, and the world in the lower nature: not three worlds, but one, in each part and in the whole. It is the preservation and growth <note>original: "uegetatio"</note> of all things, the hand of the Creator, and the blessedness of matter.

4. In the lesser world <term>Microcosm: the human being seen as a miniature representation of the entire universe</term>, which is man, there exists for his perfection whatever exists in the whole of created nature: to be, to live, to feel (along with the lower beings), and to understand (along with the higher substances). Although the nature of the intellect or mind is not entangled with lower, corruptible things in the manner of a harmony, it is nevertheless never here without them; truly, that perfection is preserved for the state of the resurrected bodies. Then it will be true to say: the intellect exists, the intellect lives, the intellect feels. This is indeed true now, but the terms are not interchangeable <note>In logic, "not converted" means the statement doesn't work the same way in reverse; currently, while the intellect "feels" through the body, the "feeling" is not the same as the "intellect" itself</note>. For after the resurrection, there will be no "being" that is not entwined with the intellect. Likewise, nothing will be "life" or "sense" alone, for to be will be the intellect, and the intellect will be to be; likewise the life of the intellect and the intellect’s life, the sense of the intellect and vice-versa. Through this it is clear that while other living things have received their fulfillment, that fulfillment is currently lacking in man. The "well-being" of man is imperfect, and the blessedness of the "form" <note>Aristotelian term for the soul or organizing principle</note> thrust down into the lowest parts consists in this.

5. In all sentient living beings, there is a vital, natural, and animal force: one life in three, and only one in all, which is the well-being of living things.

6. The natural faculties in any life—even the vegetative life—and in every individual part of a living being, consist of the <term>attractive, concoctive, retentive, and expulsive</term> powers. And although the last one (expulsive) does not seem to be entangled with the others, and Galen <note>A famous Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> does not teach it as such, nevertheless, to those considering it deeply, it is present in all. For just as if by a certain discernment of the soul, nourishment is attracted from the earth (or wherever it is mixed together—the useful with the useless), and the desirable part is drawn in while the harmful part is rejected and pushed out; once that useful part is "concocted" <note>Digested or processed by heat</note>, there is a need for purging. For otherwise it would not be concocted if it were already entirely perfect. While it is retained and assimilated, the same law applies; for these faculties do not take place in isolation. This is the means of preserving life, impressed by God upon the principles of things.

7. In the works of nature improved by cultivation: the seed, the plant, the grafting (or any other cultivation), and the fruit. For although these seem to exist through themselves, yet the fruit is in them in potential. For in the seed, the fruit is potential; in the wild or grafted plant, it is in act. In the use of that fruit lies the happiness of the present life.

8. In the sharing of fruits: origin, progress, perception, and use; everywhere the second is in potential from the first, and the third from both.

9. Time—past, present, and future: the whole in each part and in all. Nor was there any moment since the world was created that lacked a "past," without having the rest within itself in potential. For there is no "past" that was not "present" and "future," but they do not convert from the latter. For since every "past" had the "future" within itself in potential...

...and present; however, the present has no past, and no future can be present or past. Thus, there is a future rest for it—I mean for time and motion—so that the last two correspond to harmony, when it will be one and all things in actuality.

10. In the act of moving, there is the **mover**, the **moved**, the **moving**, and the **motion**. The whole motion is in the agent, the whole in the patient <note>The "patient" is the person or thing receiving the action.</note> or the moved thing, and the whole in the moving, since it is only one thing.

11. In all things, there is **abundance or power**, **progression**, **love of acting**, and **choice**; one property entirely in each part, and one in the whole.

12. In the world, there is **generation**, **duration**, **corruption**, and **continuous action and passion**. For it is the arrangement of matter as it rests in form.

13. In the dimension of bodies, there is **length**, **breadth**, **depth**, and **measure**; the whole in each, and only one in all.

14. Certain disciplines: **music**, **geometry**, **astronomy**, and **arithmetic**. <note>These four subjects formed the "Quadrivium," the advanced half of the seven liberal arts in medieval education.</note> The last, which I have placed in the final spot because of harmony, is so entwined with the others that they cannot exist without it.

15. In nature, which has matter joined to form, there is **form**, **matter**, **the composite**, and **essence**. This is entirely in all, and entirely in each, being only one.

16. In human works, there is **action**, **material**, **the work**, and **use**. This last one is primarily only in potential; for before use stands firm, those other things must have preceded it.

17. In the action of loving, there is the **lover**, the **beloved**, and the **love**; a single affection, entirely in the lover, entirely in the beloved, and entirely in the love itself. I mean perfect and reciprocal love, such as is the charity of perfect and holy beings.

18. **Peace** is sought and preserved by the **priest**, the **prince**, and the **judge**. For peace ought to be entirely in the sacred state, entirely in the military state, and entirely in the judicial state, since only one peace is required in the republic, suitable for minds, bodies, and things; this is the good and the goal of human society.

19. The **causes of things**: **efficient**, **formal**, **material**, and **final**. The final cause is primarily in potential; for if it were not first in the mind of the agent, he would not wish to join matter in vain. Thus, in every action, one asks: for what, to what end, and for what use? The end is entirely in the efficient, the material, and the formal causes.

20. **Innocence**, **sin**, **redemption**, and the **status of human nature**; a perfect condition so different, though it exists fully under any state. **Innocence** was in the highest man, and the first created; for God created all things perfect. **Sin** began in that same man, for it infected all people so that they—wretched as they are—delight in their miseries; though they know what is good, they are not accustomed to doing it unless aided by God. Because all are truly in sin, and because God wants to make everyone blessed (while yet preserving free will), this cannot be achieved through man alone. Therefore, through His Son—who is both God and man—God saves the pious and perfect believers, such as the true followers of Christ. Thus we say there was an **innocent humanity** supported by God in Adam; then a **sinning humanity** departing from God, using a dark knowledge represented by natural law (such as those people who heard nothing of Moses or the Gospel); and finally a **redeemed humanity**, such as that which has embraced Jesus Christ.

21. Whatever a great or powerful lord does, he does either by himself, through a servant or friend, or through a son. **By himself**, for those things done without a mediator. God created human nature with the gifts of the soul; when man perished of his own accord, about two thousand years later He sent Moses with the law—a light to which others could approach—and the promises to Abraham and his legitimate descendants. When this had been turned to abuse, after fifteen hundred years, He sent the ultimate remedy after Himself: Jesus his
Son...

<margin>n</margin>
22. **The written law of nature and of grace; the Law.** In corrupt nature <note>Postel refers here to the state of humanity after the Fall of Adam.</note>, an imperfect law is handed down; in the written law, which is the Law of Moses, a more perfect one is given; but in grace <note>The Christian era of the Gospel.</note>, the most perfect law is found, to which nothing can be added. For these laws encompass everything necessary for salvation. Whatever contradicts them cannot be from God; it follows that whatever has been introduced besides them is from the devil, such as the Quran <note>original: "Alcoranum"</note> and the books of heretics. Therefore, just as someone who naturally knows they are acting against their conscience and does not amend or repent is condemned by their own judgment and accusing conscience; so too, he who hears of the Gospel—which corrects our corrupted nature—and yet refuses to believe it, is devoted to a curse. For just as a person acting in the past could use the memory of a certain present and future; and one in the present uses the present and future; and one in the future uses the future alone; so under the law of nature long ago, Moses and Christ could be expected; under Moses, Christ alone; under Christ, only Christ is in use. From this it follows that whoever has heard of the Gospel from which Jesus came, and did not believe in it at all, is outside all expectation of salvation unless they repent.

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
## BOOK THREE.
### CONCERNING RELIGION AND THE LAW COMMON TO THE WHOLE
#### WORLD, OR THE METHOD OF LAW. CHAPTER I.

<margin>m</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial 'Q' containing a circular portrait of a bearded man's head, surrounded by ornate scrollwork and floral designs.</image-desc>
WHILE I was reading the Pandects <note>The *Pandects* (or Digest) are a massive collection of Roman legal writings compiled by order of Emperor Justinian in the 6th century, forming the basis of much of European law.</note> of Roman law, I saw in them many things written whose use among foreign nations was either unknown or obsolete. Yet I observed that those nations enjoyed their own peace no differently than if they had subscribed to Roman civil law in all things. Since there is one truth in all of nature, but innumerable opinions, I began to think to myself that the cause for all peoples to come together legally and civilly cannot be from a trivial or light cause. Rather, it must proceed from that most certain principle by which human affairs are born, progress, and endure; I judged that to be the principle which serves as the proof for all men of all nations. Therefore, withdrawing myself from those so confusedly organized opinions of Roman law—by which the world is usually overwhelmed rather than truly helped—and turning to the precepts of inner philosophy, I began to elicit from all peoples approved principles and the conclusions drawn from them, so that I might weigh in what matter the whole world agrees. Since, however, the book I had observed on this matter was waiting for its guides and supporting parts at home, this seemed the most suitable place for it: so that after the truth known by a few and proved by philosophy, and after false persuasion was refuted by a true guide, the community of the whole world should follow. Finally, by what art it might be possible that, just as the world agrees in these principles, it might also join those things to them without which it cannot attain absolute happiness. And because the nature of generation and birth cannot be known without considering corruption, I shall speak in the first place about the corruption, restoration, and origin of law, taking my starting point from the contemplation of all nature.

<summary>Postel transitions from universal philosophical principles to the specifics of world law, arguing that while Roman law is flawed and localized, there exists a universal "inner philosophy" and a progression of divine law (Nature to Moses to Grace) that should unite all humanity.</summary>
<keywords>Roman law, Pandects, Law of Nature, Law of Moses, Gospel, universal justice, legal philosophy, religious harmony</keywords>

--- Page 274 ---
<meta>Continuity: This page continues the argument from the previous section where Postel discussed the progression from the law of nature to the law of Moses and finally to the law of grace. Here, he begins to explain how even divinely inspired institutions can become overburdened by human traditions and lose their original "measure" or balance.</meta>

### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

Human affairs struggle under their own weight when they reach a state where they can barely accept further growth, or where they can only retain their established greatness (which spreads wider than their strength and wisdom) with great difficulty. This is proven above all by the industry of whoever has, to this day, devised human laws, religions, empires, and magistracies, or received them by divine inspiration. For in things either devised by prudence or produced by nature—though this mortal life is governed by them and cannot be without them without falling or threatening immediate ruin—if they exceed their proper measure, it happens to them just as it does to lamps: if they are deprived of oil, they cannot even stand or provide light; yet if the oil flows in too abundantly, it kills the flame just as surely as if it were lacking. It is certain that this happens not through a fault of the oil or the light, but because the measure was not applied carefully enough according to the requirements of both.

Therefore, by more diligently examining the inventions of prudence through the parts of nature and art, anyone will easily judge that the fault lies in the "measure" of things. This terrestrial globe—which the sun warms and recreates in its cycles, which winters fill with seeds, which the springtime rouses by embracing new growth in its bosom, which summer nourishes, and autumn returns when ready for use—if any one of these seasons increases slightly beyond its measure, it not only fails to increase what it usually provides so kindly, but also leaves great defects behind. For a greater force of cold, if it holds the seeds too long in the womb and moistens them too much, causes them to be cast out as if by a miscarriage. For those well-born, a heat that is too burning or poorly timed takes away their sap, so that they either never reach maturity or come forth empty and withered. What is more useful or more necessary than rain? Yet a heavy and long-lasting rain does not nourish, but rather rots. Heat, without which nothing reaches maturity, burns the crops if it lasts too long and kills the new growth. Thus, if the cycle and measure are lacking in these things subject to corruption, undoubtedly whatever helps will instead bring harm.

Now, if we look to the sun itself, the parent of nature, and see how it accomplishes its annual cycles for the greatest health and preservation of all things, we will sense that nothing in nature is born, grows, or lives without its pleasant gaze. Conversely, if it were to shine steadily with its rays without the variety of the seasons, it would bring not health to the fields, but plague and fire. From these examples, it will be most clear that human inventions are similar, because if **virtue** <note>original: "virtus"</note> exceeds its measure, it must lose its name and degenerate into **vice**. Gentleness will give birth to abjection of spirit, fortitude to audacity, and compliance to flattery.

Indeed, it would have been little, or at least far less troublesome, if nature itself (to which we cannot give prescriptions) were so inconsistent, or if virtues (which pertain to individuals and the few rather than to everyone) brought loss by exceeding their measure—were it not that even that which is most excellent in this mortal life, namely **laws**, both divine and human, also felt this plague. This is a matter all the more bitter to lament because the disease escapes our senses. In other things, a vice immediately shows itself, which can be healed by remedies or by fleeing; here, the more things are added to more things, the deeper the wound penetrates and the wider the disease creeps. Thus, it seems that a greater effort is needed to clean out that **Augean stable** <note>original: "Augiæ stabulũ." In Greek mythology, cleaning the stables of King Augeas was an impossible task performed by Hercules; Postel uses it here to describe the massive effort needed to reform corrupt and overburdened legal systems.</note>.

If anyone doubts that this is the case, they can recognize it most clearly by this reasoning. The **Mosaic Law** <note>original: "Lex Mosaica." The religious law of the Israelites, attributed to Moses.</note>, far the most celebrated for its opinion of holiness and miracles and given by divine inspiration—did it not almost collapse under the weight of opinions and the variety of traditions? It so affected those devoted to that persuasion that it was by far the most difficult thing to observe. Because of that mass of opinions, the far greater part of the Jews themselves, even when their affairs were flourishing, so feared it that they never even wanted to approve those books that follow the Mosaic ones; others hissed at the commentaries and traditions as if they were a plague. Of this disease, **Christ** <note>original: "Christus"</note> is both the physician and the most ample witness.

<summary>Postel argues that all human and divine institutions fail when they lack moderation or "measure," using analogies from nature and physics. He specifically critiques how the Mosaic Law became overburdened by human traditions, a situation he believes only Christ can remedy.</summary>

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK III.

...stus <note>original: "Christus" (Christ). The sentence begins mid-word from the previous page.</note>, who more than once reproached the magistrates, warned that the law of God, undermined by this mass of opinions, had departed from the minds of men. For it happens by some unknown fate that, just when we think we have provided most for this mortal life, we add medicines upon medicines to a disease that is spreading wider and springing up daily, so that we wander very far from the path of healing. Thus, in place of the ancient and genuine, the spurious and new slip in; in place of the true, the fabricated. Consequently, laws no longer protect justice itself. But while each person fashions whatever they wish concerning the law, justice is utterly overturned by "law." I would not dare to fully disclose what human industry has fashioned out of the most perfect religion of Christ through various interpretations; yet it is so <term>notorious even to the bleary-eyed and to barbers<note>The Latin idiom "lippis et tonsoribus" refers to something so obvious that even people waiting in a common barber shop would know it.</note></term> that no one would deny that the law which has flowed from various interpretations down to our own times stands far apart from the Gospel. This is all the more true the further it has receded from the beginning.

The most holy precepts of Christ were increased and illustrated by Apostolic men through canons and rules, as they were neither undermined nor enticed by any notion of human greed. The first councils followed, and these too—convened not by apparent ambition or factions but by the inspiration of the divine spirit—judged that not a few things should be added. That mass of councils and interpreters was not entirely consistent with itself, but was adapted to the logic of times, places, persons, and affairs. Posterity then condensed this into commonplaces, digested <note>original: "προβληματικῶς" (problematically / as matters for debate)</note> as if for inquiry, so that people began not to assert the truth of those matters, but to doubt them as if they rested merely on opinion. For things had already reached the point where more was established for the sake of specific persons than for the sake of the office itself.

Indeed, once wealth had sprung up, fraud began to creep in through tunnels and gradually immerse itself in sacred affairs; thus, the things established five hundred years ago can no longer even use piety as a pretext. For that faction of great wealth demands its own protection—and a far greater protection than the sacred matters themselves which had produced that wealth. Yet the things established first by decrees, decretal letters, <term>paleae<note>Latin for "chaff"; refers to later additions or marginal notes inserted into Gratian's Decree, the foundational text of Canon Law.</note></term>, and <term>extravagantes<note>Refers to papal decretals "circulating outside" the original collections of Canon Law.</note></term> could still have been tolerable, had not the greatest plague of all crept into this harvest of opinion: the innumerable crowd of interpreters. While this crowd dreams up its own ideas, it takes pleasure in its own opinion, contradicts others, approves some, and disapproves others. Preferring to defend opinion rather than truth, it has brought the matter to such a state that, in this law devised by human industry and commentary, it is most certain that nothing is certain. No law is so unjust that it cannot find "equity" for itself through these opinions. Thus, it has become a <term>bird-hunt<note>original: "aucupium"; a metaphor for a legal trap or a way to ensnare the unwary.</note></term> for advocates, judges, and crafty men rather than actual law, since we rely on opinions rather than equity, and we follow the foul streams rather than the original springs.

Thus, without this dull mortality even noticing, it happens that the use and nature of things handled by human whim degenerate. What once helped many now harms many—and all the more so the more innocent they are. For what would wickedness not pervert once it has obtained a handle for covering crimes under the appearance of piety? Thus it becomes <note>original: "summum ius summa iniuria"</note> **the height of law is the height of injustice.** This would have been more tolerable if that variety of opinions had only pervaded the public administration of affairs. But it has even attacked the foundation itself. Men have begun to argue on both sides concerning divine matters, about which it is a sin to doubt, so that an equal opportunity for anyone to defend anything is seen to be created, if one once prefers human reason to divine authority. I leave this for consideration. It shall suffice to have said that, unless we return to the head and the principle itself—exploding the opinion of doubting and depraving, however widely accepted it may be—not only private affairs but also public ones will be most gravely endangered and will soon collapse. As for proposing an example concerning accidental things and those pertaining to wealth, it seems plainly superfluous, since the matter reveals itself sufficiently on its own...

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

...to judge. Roman opulence, built from the spoils and plunder of the entire world, provides the proof; all types of republics confirm this, being undermined by excessive riches and the factions of powerful citizens. Indeed, it was not so surprising that wealth, which is usually driven up and down at the whim of fortune, should have caused harm through its abundance. Even religions themselves—which, except for the one true faith, are primarily born, increased, and maintained by authority and opinions—have so grown through human arts, or rather through lazy negligence, that a huge heap of opinions has risen up from the freedom of personal judgment, just as excessive light dulls the sharpness of one's vision. 

But it is certainly most remarkable and to be deplored that this disease labors most specifically within civil or public laws, where not mere authority, but the highest prudence, reason, and equity ought to be the governors. Such is the condition of human affairs: just as the deprivation of light takes away the sight of things themselves, so a light that is brighter than is proper—if I should call it clarity and not rather most dangerous lightning—brings a defect not to the things themselves, but to the sharp edge of the eyes when it flashes around us. It makes us unable to judge things without corruption, since their condition appears to be equal or very similar to our own clouded state. 

However, we must also briefly explain how this vice crept into that "citadel of truth." I do not wish to start the origin <term>from the twin egg<note>original: "gemino... ab ouo." This is a reference to the Roman poet Horace, meaning to start a story from the very beginning (the birth of Helen of Troy from an egg).</note></term>, as the saying goes, but rather to take up <term>Roman Law</term> now that it has matured to its full size and bring it into the light. I will reveal by what means it grew into this massive weight under which it began to labor long ago, so that it may appear from this example: even among other peoples who are inferior in prudence, the same thing would happen if they used the same written law for a long time. 

For who among mortals was ever of greater prudence than the Romans? Where was there a more august Senate, a greater abundance of legal experts, a more distinguished cultivation of all branches of learning, or a people more fit and inclined toward performing brilliant deeds—unless they had contaminated such brilliant affairs with slaughters, robberies, and finally such a great <term>lust for domination<note>original: "dominandi libidine." A common critique by Renaissance humanists regarding the Roman Empire's shift from a Republic to an autocracy.</note></term>? Indeed, since their law is now undermined by the commentaries of interpreters and made <term>vapid<note>original: "uapidum." Postel uses a metaphor of wine that has lost its flavor or "zing" from being poured from one container to another too many times.</note></term> by the constant habit of transferring it, it is obvious to everyone what should be judged concerning the law of the Athenians, Carthaginians, or other peoples. 

Even in the times of Cicero, when Roman affairs were flourishing the most, there was already a great abundance of opinions in civil law—the kind that demanded a systematic art rather than further increase. This is best testified by the fact that those who were in charge of <term>issuing legal opinions<note>original: "iuri responfitando." This refers to the Roman "Jurisconsults" who gave authoritative legal advice.</note></term> did not take up the whole body of law, which was already immense in its bulk, but selected specific themes in which they wished to excel and spend their whole lives. They could not master that entire doctrine contained in many volumes; thus, even the unskillful could see that the most serious men sometimes tripped over the smallest details. 

For any of the ancient jurists was allowed to propose entire books concerning various parts of the law as if they were the law itself, according to their own wish. While this was necessary at the beginning of the republic and was observed and established in almost all democracies and aristocracies, it soon resulted in a huge multitude of opinions. Different people treated different things, and it was not rare for the same argument to be treated by different authors who, following their own judgment (as we are frequently inclined to do), handed down various things that were not only contrary to others but even to themselves. 

When <term>Justinian<note>The Byzantine Emperor (reigned 527–565 AD) who sought to codify the chaotic mess of Roman legal history into the "Corpus Juris Civilis."</note></term> wished to free students of law from the burden of running through all these contradictions, he saw to it that—out of that great number of 60,000 volumes—those which the republic was then using were selected, following the advice of <term>Tribonian<note>The legal official who oversaw Justinian’s massive project of condensing the law books.</note></term>. He cut away what seemed either obsolete, superfluous, or contradictory. If only this had been done as effectively in reality as it was in the edict and assertion, so that a legal expert could be trained in at least five years! He decreed, indeed, that the republic should not fall back into that previously known state of confusion, and that the things he had approved should be sacred and inviolable; and that no one should add to or diminish them in any...

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK III

...anyone would dare to touch; would that posterity had seen to it that this was done. For although many things perished from the labors of those most excellent philosophers—things which were useful to the Republic—it would still have gone well for posterity if we had preserved those remaining things with as much religious devotion as that most wise emperor <note>Likely referring to Justinian I, who sought to codify and preserve Roman Law in the 6th century.</note> desired. But just as a specific plague necessarily rises against every individual thing, lest this part of the Republic be lacking its own, there arose six hundred years ago a new breed of interpreters. These men were contaminated by every kind of barbarity and an ignorance of philosophy; while they compared laws to laws, they poured darkness over what was already obscure. Relying on opinion rather than truth, they incited such a mob of similar followers that in no other art or doctrine has there ever been a greater lust for writing, or a greater ineptitude. 

A single law, a single assumption, a simple word—which by itself ought to rely only on a single truth—began to be translated into six hundred different understandings. Each man brought forth and thrust forward whatever he thought of, or rather whatever he dreamed up, as the true sense. They fitted the truth itself to the circumstances, and not the circumstances to the truth and the rule, in the manner of a **Lesbian rule** <note>original: "Lesbiæ regulæ." A classical metaphor for a flexible leaden ruler used in Lesbos that could be bent to fit the shape of a stone; Postel uses it here to describe jurists who twist the law to fit their own desires.</note>. From this, judgments began to be made based on opinions rather than equity. Hence, counterfeit things took the place of the genuine, the false for the true, and the doubtful for the certain. Thus, in an art that is by far the most beautiful, the matter began to be handed down with a much greater license for doubting and for proving anything at all than if it had fallen among the **Stoics** or the **Academics** <note>Ancient philosophical schools known for rigorous logic and, in the case of the Academics, skepticism.</note> themselves. 

Even a man of no small authority, **Baldus** <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a highly influential Italian jurist whose prolific commentaries often contained internal contradictions due to the sheer volume of his work.</note>, put forward and left in writing ten different and entirely contrary opinions on the same matter, and recorded them as judged, even though only a single truth lay beneath it. Such is the cost, naturally, of receding from equity and relying on opinions, of dragging authorities to fit circumstances rather than bringing circumstances to the authority of the law. Indeed, nothing is written so diligently that it cannot be violated and dragged into perversity, or converted into a contrary or at least a different sense by an opinion and a biased feeling of judgment. Thus it happens that **extreme law** <term>Summum ius: From the Roman proverb "Summum ius, summa iniuria"—the rigour of the law is the height of oppression.</term> possesses plainly no justice at all, and brings a fuel for litigation rather than an end to it. 

Therefore, we see that nowhere among the nations is there a greater crowd of litigants and of those who make a profit from the law, nor a larger supply of lawsuits, than where Roman Law has been received. Truly, these wretched men, depraved by craftiness, are either enticed by the false solicitations of their patrons and "bloodsuckers" to seek a lawsuit for anything at all, or they are driven to cover up any execrable crime. I remain silent regarding the royal laws and rights, the edicts of the courts, and the judgments of the high senate—which have also increased to an immense degree and fight amongst themselves—and the civil laws, whether written or unwritten, that are customarily observed. By these "furies" <note>original: "erinnybus," referring to the Erinyes or Furies of Greek myth who torment the guilty.</note> they meanwhile torture this wretched mortality. To slay and finish off this monster today, it seems that not just one Hercules, nor any of the greatest power, prudence, or authority among mortals is required, but the highest and most heavenly force. Although such a plague cannot be helped by a few words or a single remedy, it must not be entirely neglected, for it devours the blood, the muscles, and finally the very spirit of the Republic. 

When a body is badly affected and its constitution is so disposed toward ill health that it either cannot recover through the work of doctors or can do so only with great difficulty, the doctor must still not neglect that work by which he might turn away the increase of the disease or preserve a poorly affected life a little longer. He should even apply those remedies by which the disease might be removed in a similar or related condition, leaving nothing untried. For it frequently happens, beyond the hope of the doctor, that those medicines he hoped would be least healthy, by some unexpected chance of fortune or providence, bring health to desperate matters. 

The art of medicine exists for bodies in this order: to retain and preserve bodies in prosperous health insofar as it can be achieved by the benefit of the art, to restore those that are affected, and to look out for those that have been restored. Philosophy is in exactly the same position regarding the preservation of the Republic, while it either puts to flight present vices, or cautions and looks out for those that are imminent, or considers the future by comparison with the past, so that it may dispel the many miseries of this life. Thus, there can be no end to writing, nor should there be, in these matters—not concerning those things which drag the matter into diverse opinions, but those which lead to...

...they might draw back the **principal elements**, so that they may come to the aid of the almost eternal forgetfulness of mortals. For the condition of things—by a certain common disease and error of nature—the further it stands from its beginning and the more its cultivation is neglected, begins to gather moss like trees, whether by its own accord, by luxury, or by the poor quality of the soil. It happens that it either turns more quickly toward destruction or degenerates into an adulterated kind, the less it returns to its principles. Art is indeed one thing; cultivation must be renewed according to things and ages, and new shoots must be brought to bear against new evils. For it happens that while those things which were handled more frequently and by many before are renewed, and new remedies are applied to new diseases, they move people far more vehemently than the old ones. Hence we are usually more moved by a friend's new letter or a new consolation than by one far more ornate and handled long ago. 

For one must always strive so that the things themselves, which are the further from their principles the more they age, are reduced to those very principles and to a disposition not abhorrent to nature; just as health cannot be restored to bodies unless the temperament of the primary elements of the physical body, suited to it, receives itself back into the body, toward which one end the entire utility of the art of healing tends. But just as the goal proposed to a doctor is not always health itself, but only insofar as he can achieve it by his art; so it is not the goal proposed to the moderator of a Republic, or to him who desires to bring help himself, to entirely eliminate and as if proscribe all kinds of vices (for then men would have to be removed, who can never be free from the pressure of vices), but a way must gradually be opened for principles and for those who hold the reins of affairs, by which they may meet such a great crowd of vices even creeping openly. 

Therefore, just as he who wished to purge persuasions themselves from the vices that have arisen could do so by no other art than if—having neglected and universally abolished those vicious constitutions attached like appendages, by which vices are covered under the pretext of virtue—the Prince should strive to preserve "safe and sound" <note>original: "sartam tectamque." A Roman legal phrase literally meaning "patched and roofed," used to describe property kept in excellent repair; here Postel applies it to the fundamental laws of living.</note> that norm of living which the legislator exhibited, and to recall it into use. In the same way, no method of reforming the law can be sought from anywhere else than by putting to flight the crowd of interpreters dragging the laws themselves into contrary directions, and by abolishing superfluous laws, to recall the students of law themselves to a few elements of the **just and equitable**, which are most closely joined with equity. 

For just as philosophy gave the beginning to all human laws, and equity—sprinkled throughout the law in various places—flows from that source as if from a spring; so when vice or ambiguity has crept in there, it cannot seek a remedy from anywhere else than from where the principle flowed. I hear indeed that many have undertaken that task <term>provinciae: literally 'province,' but here meaning a duty or sphere of responsibility</term>, so that they might reduce civil law into an art; of whom some works have already appeared, while others are expected. But they all follow the method of Roman Law. From this, it cannot happen that they can follow equity itself through all things, since there are many things in any civil law that are not only disapproved by others but even ridiculous; others are harmful and pernicious. 

For that reason, I shall collect the elements of law from the treasury of philosophy and embrace them in very few words. For I did not think it necessary in this discourse to inquire about the law of "water-drippings" <note>original: "stillicidiorum." A specific area of Roman property law regarding eaves-drip and drainage between neighboring buildings.</note> or of walls or lights—although we have been involved in these and the matter is useful—but I think the discipline of law should be drawn deep from the innermost parts of philosophy. The whole cause of universal law and statutes must be treated here, so that this law, a taste of which we have decided to sip drawn from the sources, may be confined within a certain small and narrow place. For although some may be able to attain a scattered knowledge of duty in the received laws through long and tireless labors, nevertheless it can be revealed far more happily from philosophy itself: what has been granted to man by nature, for the sake of what duty he was born to perform and cultivate, what the conjunction of men is, what natural society is, what the origin of equity and wickedness is, and finally what the source and spring of law itself is. Thus invited by these principles, to whom both knowledge of things and greater eloquence [are given], as if...

### THERE ARE CERTAIN ELEMENTS OF ALL ARTS,
### *by which, once perceived, any discipline can be easily both taught and grasped.* CHAPTER II.

That there are certain elements of all things set either in nature or in art—in which they agree and by which those who have successfully used things anywhere among nations are admitted to the inner secrets of the things themselves—is not obvious to everyone, but it is certainly confessed by many and by the wise. And if anyone should doubt this very thing, it can be demonstrated in this way. The arts, which antiquity especially honored with that name, consist of their own elements or principles because of a certain trust that is proven to anyone (provided they are of sound judgment and not stubborn). 

For who is so stupid as to deny that things distinct in their very bodies or substances are also given numbers and separated? In these elements—namely, numbers—it is certain that whoever has exercised himself more diligently can pass on the art of **Arithmetic**, from which innumerable benefits for human life arise. For since the primary principle of equity among men is weighed by arithmetic equality, nothing can be taught without the reasoning of numbers. This reasoning will be passed on far more diligently and certainly by one who has been versed in the elements than by one who has conceived it only by natural diligence and common usage. 

The ratios of sounds, which the Greeks called **Music** <note>original: *Musicam*</note> from the act of investigating, were born from arithmetical elements combined with the comparison of sounds. **Geometry**, or the measurer of any matter, has its own principles, from whose mutual composition and relationship it draws out whatever truth there is in the measurement of continuous and solid things. 

The **Astronomer** attains the magnitude of the heavens and the dimension of time, and the varieties of seasons and days, by the benefit of elements known and diligently contemplated. The admirer of all nature, whom the Greeks call a **Philosopher**, necessarily admits (unless he denies that reason is in himself) certain principles known through themselves to all; these, once admitted, demonstrate that the primary part of nature's obscurity can fall under the scope of reason. Hence philosophy, when it is complete, has come forth ignorant of almost no art. 

The **Logician** must confess that names are given to things and actions in all languages, as well as affirmation and negation, and to these the quality of actions, which they call *synkategorema* <note>original: συγκατηγόρημα – a technical term in logic for words like "all," "none," or "not" that have meaning only when joined with other terms</note>; when these are joined together, the most certain art arises, most closely joined to reason, called *Logike* <note>original: λογική – Logic</note>. 

From the philosopher, who has diligently handed down the knowledge of words and things, the **Physician** takes the means by which he may both teach and practice the art of preserving and restoring good health to human bodies. Since this one truth is evident in the whole circle of disciplines, which they call *Enkyklopaideia* <note>original: ἐγκυκλοπαιδείαν – the "well-rounded" or "encyclopedic" education</note>, it is certain that **Jurisprudence**, which is as it were the *Pragmatike* <note>original: πραγματική – the practical or active application</note> of all philosophy, also has its principles proven to all men now cultivated by human reason, from which it is certain the fountains of Law descend. In following and teaching these, although many wise men among almost all nations have toiled, yet all of them immediately from being wise men (I except only Plato in his imaginary republic) became "prudent" <note>Postel here plays on the distinction between *sapientes* (those with theoretical wisdom) and *prudentes* (those with practical legal expertise/jurisprudence)</note> and bound and accommodated themselves to the state in which they lived. ...in individual republics, there are certain occasions and matters adapted to the specific situation, place, person, time, and customs; because of these, wise leaders often depart from natural law and from that law which is generally accepted by all learned peoples. For this reason, it has happened that Roman law <note>original: *ius Romanorum*</note>, although full of equity, never suits the French, Germans, Athenians, Carthaginians, or any other states <term>polities (ordered political communities)</term> in every respect. Nevertheless, it is certain that there is something foundational which all nations approve, even those whose writing, names, and customs were once unknown to us. For the highest principle of establishing law was born in all ages before any written law existed or any city-state <term>city-state (Latin: *civitas*)</term> was ever established. 

In our own time, another world has been opened, and the vastness of Africa and Asia has become known; yet the records of literature—ours, the Greeks', and those of foreign nations <note>original: *Barbarorum*</note>—hardly encompass even a sixth part of the world's memory with any precision. Yet it is certain that those peoples, because they survived (provided they received instruction from wise men or did not lose what they once received—for even among them are those who live in herds like beasts without a fixed place), must have agreed upon certain elements of law to ward off mutual injury; otherwise, they would have been each other's destruction. For no one can deny that as many cities or specific inhabited places as have endured for a long time have done so by the benefit of law. 

I shall therefore endeavor—though it is an arduous task—to present and encompass those principles, partly from philosophy and partly from the histories of nations, which no nation would fail to approve—whether it is one that has long been established or one that will eventually listen to the reason of the wise. I will specifically adapt myself to either Roman or French law where they are such that it would be beneficial for all people of the entire world to use them, and where they are furthest removed from personal passions. The goal of my labor is that anyone who wishes to diligently learn and weigh these very elements may do so here, before they look too deeply into the massive heap of opinions that usually grows alongside expanding and enduring republics. 

For such a person will experience what happens to those skilled in reading: whatever is written in the type of characters they know well, they immediately have it at hand and can read it. Thus, whoever does this will have already succeeded; even if he does not grasp the specific words of a different institution, nor its customs or civil laws, he will still have the doors open to him. He will be far more prepared for the matter than one ignorant of the elements themselves; for once the words and facts are applied, he will immediately grasp the meaning and will judge what is fair and good <note>original: *æquum & bonum*; a classical legal concept of equity</note> in any case. 

In this matter, it is well known that those philosophers who traveled among any nations were most effective and successful, and were held in great admiration and use everywhere, because they gave laws and rules for living to those republics from the highest memory of literature. But if someone should object that we already have more carefully presented elements of law in the Imperial Institutes <note>referring to the *Institutiones* of the Emperor Justinian, the standard textbook for Roman Law</note> of the Romans, I will not deny that the elements of Roman civil law have been handed down even more diligently than I myself could manage. However, Roman Law is only such that it contains many things specifically adapted for the use of that particular republic, and thus seems tied to specific opinions, unable to apply to any other system except that of its own state. But I am going to present those things which suit everyone. 

Furthermore, I have seen fit to imitate the first of the philosophers, and those who were never accustomed to teaching anything without a method. For what would it profit to present even those things which were in themselves perfect in every detail <note>original: *numeris omnibus absoluta*</note>, unless you observe and pass on the art—the highest good fortune—by which they can be grasped and held in the mind? And because nothing is more common or more suited to the knowledge of things in either religion or reason than the number three <term>ternary number (the number three, often seen as a symbol of divine or natural perfection)</term>, I have decided to use it as a model as often as the nature of the matter **will permit**...

He intends to present these universal principles using a systematic method, often employing the "ternary number" (three) as an organizing principle.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Postel’s philosophical justification for his work. Having previously argued that all nations share a common "natural law," he now moves to explain the structural logic of his book, which is rooted in the "ternary" or threefold patterns he sees throughout the created universe, reflecting the Holy Trinity.</meta>

->### BOOK III OF GUILLAUME POSTEL<-

...the condition will permit, to follow a threefold division <note>Postel is obsessed with the number three (the triad or ternary division) as a reflection of the Trinity in all aspects of existence.</note> everywhere, once it has been established that the matter exists. For we see—to begin from the highest level of all things—that the power of the highest, middle, and lowest spheres produces one and the same effect in these lower things. Namely, that God, or the first cause, has established through the various movements of the heavens and planets that whatever is born naturally on land or sea is born through their apparent labor. Power is hidden in the first cause, manifest in the second, and partly hidden and partly manifest in the third. 

All academic disciplines are found in physics, ethics, and logic: they contemplate, they speak, and they act. All things consist of a beginning, a middle, and an end; of increase, consistency, and decrease; of matter, form, and the resulting composite. Bodily things consist of length, breadth, and depth. Time consists of the past, the present, and the future. All actions consist of the agent, the patient, and the action in which either participates. The artisan is made by nature, instruction, and practice; the first brings talent, the second knowledge, and the third brings fruit. The sun is luminous by its body, its ray, and its power. 

In short, there is almost nothing that the most holy Trinity itself does not touch. For this reason, that number has always been held as a symbol of sacred things by philosophers and the more prudent religions, as the father of nature, or as being most in agreement or annexed to it—or to say it with the Greeks, *of the same nature* <note>original: *homophyēs*</note>. 

First, the origin and consistency of things—which others call substance—shall be handed down, whether it exists or not; then, division will indicate how manifold it is; by definition, what or of what sort it is will be opened up; finally, the use for which things are prepared will be made clear. Lastly, I shall declare how things act or are acted upon, and by what reason they are composed. For, as I might say partly with Aristotle, the philosopher of truth, *the "that" (the fact) and the "why" (the cause) must first be sought* <note>original Greek: *to gar hoti... kai to di' hoti prōton zētēteon*</note>. First "what," second "wherefore," must be sought. 

But since it seems to me that no one can well define the source from which the substance of things becomes known unless he knows how manifold that is of which the discourse is proposed, I have seen fit to hand down the division and the effects for the sake of the unlearned. Although he who knows the "why"—that is, the primary and final causes—would also know the division. 

I would have studied to hand down this art in books without chapters and in long-extended discussions, in the manner of the leading men in philosophy, had I not been led by the certain methods usually handled in the chapters of the "elements" <term>Elements: foundational principles of a subject</term> and the art, so that I might propose the things themselves with frequent and distinct arguments. For if the Pythagorean authors, the most famous of all philosophy in both parts of Greece, did not want books to exceed three cubes of the number six <note>The "cube of six" is 216. Three such cubes would be 648. Pythagoreans believed certain numbers governed the limits of human memory and the harmony of the cosmos.</note> (which comprises the ratio of the universe in itself) so that the memory of readers and listeners might be consulted, I must rightly take care in this argument of mine lest even one chapter be of excessive length. I do this not so much for the sake of Pythagorean dogma—which nevertheless does not seem to me to lack reason, if only for its authority alone—but so that I might satisfy the delicate readers or listeners of our age. 

For in this great crowd of authors and those itching to write, and in such an inconstant gamble of judgments which must necessarily be undergone, you see almost nothing that is not extremely long-winded, unless it is already proven by antiquity, that satisfies the palate of many. So prone are people to judge their own age harshly, and to approve ancient follies simply because they are old, rather than to agree with modern thinkers <term>neoterics (modern scholars)</term> in any matter. In this regard, those people seem to me to have deserved poorly of nature, who contend that she concentrated all her powers into those first ages in such a way that she seems a "stepmother" to posterity, but a "mother" to antiquity <note>Postel is arguing against "declinism"—the idea that the world is getting worse and that modern people are less capable than the ancients.</note>. 

He who does not wish to run through whole books will at least be able to taste one or two chapters for the sake of approving or disapproving, even with the "tips of his lips," and to pass judgment on what he touches. I will certainly never be reluctant to agree with such a judgment, provided that, having looked at the whole work, he judges not from a "disease of the mind" <note>i.e., prejudice or malice</note> but from candor. For by this labor, I desire others to be excited toward handling greater things in this same subject, rather than being left behind me. For he who studies for the sake of posterity is a student of utility, not likewise of glory...

unless it follows of its own accord, it must follow reason. Therefore, to use the words of Crassus in Cicero <note>Marcus Licinius Crassus, a character in Cicero’s dialogue *De Oratore* (On the Orator).</note>, I shall say nothing hidden, nothing worthy of the expectation of great or more learned men, nothing unheard of by the prudent, nor anything new. For the basic elements which I have now decided to treat are proposed either for the young in age or in education, and for those who are still practicing at the training post <note>original: "ad palum exercentur." A metaphor for soldiers or gladiators practicing with a wooden post before entering real combat.</note> but do not yet demand the prize of virtue in the line of battle or the gymnasium. Indeed, there is a need for the path to greater things to be paved with small beginnings. For frequently, the greatest matters have emerged from the smallest occasion. Who can judge whether our labor, since it was undertaken by us for the sake of helping the Republic, will one day incite leading men in oratory to pass down more perfectly what we have attempted? 

Certainly, my authority was Cicero, a man placed almost beyond the risk of judgment, who promised this very argument. But, prevented by death, he either could not finish it, or (as is fitting for more prudent men endowed with great authority) he was perhaps unwilling to provide it, lest he be forced to write many things for the sake of favor (as he certainly often did) or for the use of his own State, which would have been little in agreement with natural law. These indeed are his words: "For if," he says under the name of Scaevola <note>Quintus Mucius Scaevola, a famous Roman legal expert.</note>, "I am permitted to do what I have been thinking of for a long time, or if someone else, should I be hindered or die, completes it—namely, to first arrange civil law <term>ius civile: the body of laws applicable to Roman citizens, which Postel seeks to expand into a universal law</term> into categories, which are very few; then to divide those categories into their constituent parts; then to declare the specific force of each by definition—you will have a perfect art of civil law, more great and fruitful than difficult and obscure. And yet, in the meantime, while these things which are scattered are being gathered, one may be filled with that knowledge of civil law by plucking and collecting from everywhere." And a little later: "For all things are placed before our eyes, located in daily use, in the gatherings of men and in the forum; nor are they contained in so many letters or great volumes. For the same things were first brought forth by many, and then written repeatedly even by the same writers with only a few words changed." 

Thus far Cicero. He gave me the courage for daring, after I had somehow grasped the sense of the *Pandects* <note>The *Pandects*, or Digest, a vast collection of Roman legal writings compiled under Emperor Justinian.</note> and had more diligently inspected in person the three Republics that are easily the leaders in our memory: the French, the Turkish <note>Referring to the Ottoman Empire, which Postel visited and studied extensively.</note>, and the Venetian. I also weighed the religion of many nations. In addition to these, I wished to examine more diligently the Republics of all the ancients, whatever rituals and memory have been handed down by our people, or the Greeks, or even the Barbarians, and how they were restored to the people to keep them in their duty—which anyone may easily see in my work *On the Magistrates of the Athenians*. Furthermore, I did not neglect the political institutions of Aristotle, Plato, and Xenophon. If anything is written here with more care, I wish it to be credited to them because of their antiquity and authority. However, I would also dare to assert that through our own reasoning and refinement, some things have been made no worse; which the fair reader, skilled in antiquity and the experience of things, will not deny, provided he follows the things themselves rather than the words.

### CHAPTER III. FROM WHERE LAW FLOWED FORTH AMONG MEN.

Since by their own nature humans alone of all living creatures—having forgotten themselves and the providence of reason implanted in them from the beginning—began to deviate from the law of nature as soon as they started to congregate, and turned fiercely against their own kind, far more cruelly than the animals that are themselves destitute of judgment and reasoning. At first, indeed, having experienced the greater strength of someone and fearing the punishment inflicted on them and the greater forces of an attacker, not a few abstained from the one by whom they had been endangered. But they continued to be no less troublesome to others whose strength they did not fear, and they undermined the species—that animal especially endowed with memory and capable of reason when it is reminded. Furthermore, feeling mutual disadvantages, often not without danger, and loathing these discomforts, the human race, led by the reasons of those who possessed a more sharp wit among the rest, obeyed...

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK III

it indeed rushed headlong, and for some time it refrained from that injury which leads to the ruin and loss of its own species—following the example of wild beasts who spare their own kind and gather together for the sake of preserving it. But because man is born by nature needy of all things, and is entirely stitched together from shrewdness, craftiness, fraud, and deceit due to a perpetual necessity that is either a constant companion or a constant fear (for his character is prone to evil even from the cradle), and being forgetful of both danger and utility, as well as of any warning, he immediately returned to his natural disposition. For before laws were born, the first and only method of possessing and of preserving things for fear of necessity was in occupation <note>original: "occupatione." The legal concept of "right of first possession," where property belongs to the first person to claim it.</note>. All people held an equal right to things and faced a similar necessity; from this, both necessity and lust and vengeance increased the level of cruelty, and injury grew along with age. When wise men saw this and took pity, they did not wish to heal this disease only with warnings and examples, which would immediately vanish, but decided that men must be restrained by a certain bond—one in which they would easily allow themselves to be caught. For equity itself could easily be persuaded by even a thin thread of eloquence to those whom the same nature had produced as similar in body, corresponding in limbs, not unlike in their use of them, equal in necessity, and, as it were, brothers. 

The gathering and nature of other living creatures—which spare their own kind as much as possible, unless for the sake of lust or hunger—was persuasive. Indeed, they were so studious in preservation that many would be incited by cries, as if by a trumpet blast, for their own protection and the banishment of others. Repeated mutual disadvantages, constant fear, love of oneself and one's kind, the similarity of all people, and even the example of those destitute of reasoning <note>Postel refers here to animals, who lack "ratio" or human reason but still act for the survival of their species.</note>, not only persuaded but compelled people to swear into a certain law. If anyone acted against this law, they would be restrained either by everyone else or by someone authorized by the others, and would be affected by a penalty equal to the one they had dared to inflict on the other. This, therefore, was the **first refinement of the law**: *Whatever anyone committed against another against the natural good, they themselves should be forced to endure the same.* For man is not the only creature skilled by nature in seeking bodily good; all kinds of living beings must be judged by the same skill. This first element, placed partly by nature and partly by human prudence, gave the first place to possessions and the first security and tranquility among men. This was the first principle of human gathering and confederation.

¶ However, since men were still semi-wild, with uncultivated minds, great ferocity, and constant necessity—and especially a singular envy regarding necessary things—and were moreover prone to inflicting injury, they forgot the law established in reason. They immediately returned to their natural disposition unless they yielded to the desires of those they attacked, and they would break out in thefts, plundering, and slaughter. Thus, as vices were being born and growing, new remedies had to be established. Therefore, so that the established laws would not be endangered by ignorance, or sit idle, or be hidden by the trickery of certain people, it seemed best to translate them into **letters** <note>original: "in literas." Meaning written language or written statutes.</note>—which, like other human inventions, were devised for human use. When I say that everything was devised by man gradually, I believe this is so certain and proven to all that there is no need to bring many arguments to confirm it. From the highest memory of literature (without which it is not known whether deeds actually happened or not), everything must be traced back. Pits, tree coverings, and huts made of tree branches were the first rudiments of even the greatest buildings. Through constant cultivation, wild things were tamed; the acorn nourished the first farmers. From shepherds, plunderers, and farmers, citizens were born or made, as were magistrates, princes, and judges. All things were led forth from the lowest to the highest; and even those placed at the very summit of affairs were not ashamed to admit this, so much so that the most excellent peoples placed these arguments in honor to be kept among them for a long time—such as the senatorial house covered in thatch <note>original: "Culmo tectam domum senatoriam." A reference to the *Casa Romuli* (Hut of Romulus) on the Palatine Hill in Rome, preserved by the Romans as a sacred memorial of their humble origins.</note>,
