### ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

[It] even wanted [it] preserved for many years in the <term>Areopagus</term> <note>The Areopagus was the "Hill of Ares" in Athens, serving as the city’s most prestigious and ancient deliberative court.</note> by the most holy senate of the Areopagites, so that the city might remember its own origin. The same was done by the Romans regarding the house of <term>Romulus</term> <note>Romulus was the legendary founder of Rome; his supposed hut on the Palatine Hill was maintained as a sacred relic for centuries.</note>, even though it was roofed with thatch; this was done with that same purpose, for it was preserved for many years for the sake of memory. What else did the times of <term>Saturn</term> <note>In classical mythology, the "reign of Saturn" refers to the Golden Age, a lost era of primordial peace and equality.</note> and the Golden Age—ignorant of gold—wish to indicate? You might also prove that both languages and characters (except for the Hebrew ones) were devised by a similar reasoning, although some are persuaded otherwise on this matter. 

For while a son listens to a father, a neighbor to a neighbor, and a servant to a master, they began to express through memory what they heard and to apply it to the use of conversation. From this, they also began to invent "natural letters" to paint the perceptions of the mind with natural signs. Hence the <term>Hieroglyphics</term> <note>original: "Hieroglyphicæ"</note> of the Egyptians and the Western Indians <note>Postel is likely referring to the pictorial writing systems of the Aztecs or Mayans, which 16th-century scholars frequently compared to Egyptian writing.</note>. As the world grew a little more mature, it devised many scripts—some that have perished and others that have endured to our time—arranged according to the parts of the mouth and tongue, the various articulations, and "semi-perfect" characters, such as those of the Phoenicians, Chaldeans, Arabs, Indians, and Africans. For they had devised no vowel pronunciations <note>Postel notes that these Semitic and related scripts are "abjads," primarily recording consonants rather than vowels.</note>. The Greeks, receiving these from the Phoenicians, enriched them with order, shapes, vowels, and declensions, from which the Latins took their own many centuries later. Thus, the journey began from small beginnings toward great achievements.

It was primarily by the benefit of these letters that the memory of the ages, the opinions of the wise, and the principles of Law began to be handed down and preserved. From this, posterity was increased by the riches of its ancestors, and from this, the arts were refined. It therefore seemed good to those wise men (to return to the point from which I digressed)—those to whom we owe either our happiness or the youth, cultivation, and endurance of our intellect and the Commonwealth—to transfer into writing those precepts by which human madness is usually mitigated. This was done so that they might be preserved both by the benefit of memory and as a monument of literature, and placed in a location that was sacrosanct. From there, they could be taken up by judges or those endowed with any other authority, and brought forward like "living voices" both to restrain the deeds of the wicked and to settle disputes. For they would have been set down in vain unless they were also diligently preserved and, with a vigorous magistrate as their champion and protector, applied like a medicine to a disease. From this, praise and certain rewards were promised and bestowed upon good men, while punishments and rebukes were inflicted upon the wicked.

But humanity, always striving for the forbidden, teems with a vast crowd of the wicked. When these wicked people saw that they could not safely commit injury against anyone because of those who held the highest authority in restraining crimes, they rose up against them so that they might never be restrained; not infrequently, they attacked them of their own accord so they could creep into their positions. Others, truly more cunning, committed no crimes openly for fear of punishment, but were accustomed to perpetrating many dire deeds in secret. This disease also had to be cured. 

And since those who were in charge of the highest affairs were not strong enough in power—being weak and as yet destitute of guards—to repel the injuries inflicted upon them, nor could they easily obtain a bodyguard from the rest of the common people given the extreme scarcity of resources—and since they recognized that human thoughts, frauds, and crimes were hidden from them—they judged that a remedy greater than human was necessary. Truly, they observed that man is easily captured by admiration of unusual things and is not reluctantly drawn toward a probable and true opinion (though he not infrequently gives credit to false things); and they saw that he was not entirely averse to returning gratitude, the image of which he might see even in dogs and many tamed animals. Therefore, they persuaded men that there is some divinity above the nature of visible things—of whom men had long since become forgetful—to whom these so ample and varied benefits must be credited, as they had arisen neither by chance nor from themselves: a God <note>original: "Deum"</note> who sees and hears all things, even those that are hidden and obscure, who is the <term>founder</term> <note>original: "conditor"</note> of the universe,

<meta>This page continues Postel’s philosophical investigation into the foundations of human society. Having previously discussed the physical and cultural origins of nations, he now moves into the metaphysical and legal structures—specifically how the universal belief in a divine overseer and the development of two types of law (human and divine) maintain social order.</meta>

GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK III.

[He] is believed, anywhere in the world, to be present everywhere and to take vengeance on all the wicked and criminal; nor should the wicked, who refuse to do what is commanded, think it will be to their profit that He does not immediately take vengeance: there is another life for souls after these ages, in which He exercises the powers of both punishment and reward. This fact easily kept both the good—who indeed need no laws—and many of the more unrefined people in their duty. But because wickedness was never accustomed to be restrained by any laws without force, it was necessary to be held back by a guard, either of judges, or kings, or leaders (which things were once the same). But how this power was acquired will be spoken of in its proper place. 

Necessity, therefore, the primary origin of all things, produced two fountains of law. The first arose from the necessity of nature and wisdom, and was prepared and approved by reason and the right judgment of men. Its springs, like elements, are placed in the contemplation of lower nature, immediately presented to the senses, so that this reason, implanted in the minds of men by nature, can be restored by even a slight persuasion: namely, through <term>equity</term> <note>Latin: "aequitas." Postel views equity as a natural sense of fairness that precedes written law.</note>, the living roots of which God seems to have mixed into the minds of all so they may be perceived. 

The second fountain proceeds from religion and the recognition of God approved in the State; when the true God is unknown, it proceeds from wonder, fear, or love. By this, either hidden things come to light while men, driven by <term>sacraments</term> <note>original: "sacramentis." In this context, it refers to sacred oaths or religious obligations that compel a person to speak the truth.</note>, confess about themselves; or fear is struck into the erring of losing that good which they might enjoy by His benefit; or even of losing the happiness which is believed to be either promised or given by the divine power. Fear also, lest we be destitute of either present happiness or future happiness after death, not rarely terrifies. When I speak of religions, I understand only those which have already faded away, or are believed to be false by our people: not of our Christian religion, which, as Christ himself asserted, will not be in danger. 

Human law is—to make the definition clearer—the knowledge of the equitable and the inequitable according to <term>arithmetic or geometric equality</term> <note>Postel uses Aristotelian categories: Arithmetic equality treats everyone the same (1:1), while Geometric equality distributes rewards based on merit or proportion (ranking).</note>, and the distribution, assignment, and preservation for each person according to merits and accepted rights. I call it **arithmetic equality**, following Aristotle’s opinion, when things themselves are weighed and assigned by an estimation of money, or some thing which is in the place of money. I call it **Geometric equality** when we consider and assign a solid thing for a solid thing, or a favor, or anything else. For you would judge in vain unless you also assigned the judgment. Truly, divine law is the establishment of equity to be observed for anyone, beginning exactly where the strength of human law fails; its observation was accustomed to being done through fear or love, either of the supreme God or of the gods accepted in the State.

### ON THE REASONS AND ENDS OF ALL
->persuasions. CHAPTER IIII.<-

Before I speak of law approved by human senses and falling under reason, since without fear of God or the gods and religion no one could be kept in duty for very long except by violence; furthermore, since God and all heavenly things are both prior to and more worthy than man, it seemed best to discuss the religions of all nations from their origin. For these were introduced either before empires, or along with power, or to strengthen it, or even by themselves without any concern for authority. Not rarely, religion was devised only for the sake of mortal lust, for a longer-lasting memory of men. Truly, the end [purpose] of religion is either in the happiness of the common people using it, or in the utility of the one instituting it, or in both: or in preserving for a longer time the memory of someone who [deified...]

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

[The soul] is believed to enter [heaven] immediately after death and to fly upward in the manner of eagles. It seems necessary to speak here of the primary cause, which first creeps into the mind and serves as the chief occasion for establishing things. For when anything is done by the prudent, it is established that it is done for the sake of some necessity, pleasure, utility, happiness, or opinion.

The first religions of mortals, once the knowledge of God was lost, were indeed instituted for utility alone, following necessity, and were approved by men. For they followed mostly those things which are <term>according to nature</term> <note>Latin: "secundum naturam." A philosophical concept referring to living in harmony with the inherent physical and moral order of the world.</note>. Since humans and other living creatures naturally seek what leads to their preservation and flee what leads to their corruption, both fear and desire are present in everyone: a desire for good things and a fear of evil things, which others have called "things to be sought" and "things to be avoided."

Therefore, it is likely that the first cause (namely, the **Highest God**) was presented for worship—though the eyes grow dim and the mind falters in attempting to perceive Him—as the one who supplies being, life, sense, and all things necessary for human life in such abundance. Conversely, He would send evil and the deprivation of things upon bad and negligent worshippers who were ignorant of Him. To ensure that sacred rites might last longer, they were strengthened by those who wished them to endure through sacrifices, as if the divinity could be captured by them. This allowed those who presided over the oracles, expiations, sacrifices, and—to put it in one word—the preservation of this <term>persuasion</term> <note>Latin: "persuasioni." Postel uses this term to describe a foundational set of religious beliefs that bind a society together.</note> to live. Indeed, that fear or desire, being most deeply in accordance with nature, usefully held peoples under the power of a divinity.

This was a most useful end, the first, and most in accord with natural necessity. This is truly the target and the primary reasoning not only of ancient religions but also of the <term>more mature world</term> <note>Latin: "adultioris orbis." This refers to civilizations that have moved past the "infancy" of early survival.</note> (not yet corrupted by mere opinion): that man is kept in his duty by the fear of evil or the love of good. Both of these are believed to be given and sent by the benefit of a divinity divinely received into religion.

The **Hebrew** religion, divinely revealed to **Moses** and confirmed by innumerable miracles, at first held it sufficient to promise an abundance of things and a long life—witnessed by divine miracles—to the peoples who were to reach a greater perfection of things through those basic elements. For we are all easily captured by the sense of things that serve the duties of this life. Therefore, it was demonstrated to them by many signs that God is perpetually present, endowing His worshippers with great rewards and avenging Himself upon the impious and wicked with the greatest misfortunes.

But since the inconstancy of all things is supreme, and the nature of men—who use prosperity according to their own desires—is prone to all vices, the Jews soon forgot their persuasion and began to follow diverse religions. From then on, the **Prophets**, a race of men divinely inspired, affirmed that all the precepts of the received religion must be observed—not only out of a desire for temporary happiness or fear of evils (the greatest of which were imminent through wars and captivities) but also out of fear of eternal punishment or hope for an eternal reward which God would exercise upon eternal souls. They taught that lower places <note>The underworld or Hell.</note> awaited the impious, while places full of light and pleasantness awaited the religious.

However, when the **Greeks**—who during their travels had drunk from the **Indians, Persians, Syrians,** and **Egyptians**—approved of these methods of keeping peoples in their duty (especially that persuasion regarding the underworld and the **Elysian Fields** <note>The mythological resting place for virtuous souls.</note>), they filled the heavens, the underworld, and the world itself with so many fables (with which they intended to cover religion), and increased them with such absurdities and follies abhorrent to the senses through their own talkativeness, that the fear of the gods vanished. Even the common people began to laugh at the underworld and the Elysian Fields. From here came the source of the world’s weakening; from here came the ruins that not only infected what was healthy but also cast unhealthy things upon the world. The ancient religion of the **Romans** was not unlike this, as they had drawn it from the **Egyptians** when they saw those...

He traces its evolution from the material promises made to Moses to the eternal rewards and punishments taught by the Prophets, eventually criticizing the Greeks for undermining religious authority with absurd myths.</summary>

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK III

[279]

<meta>catchword: hopes</meta>

Hopes of the **Elysian Fields** <note>original: "camporum Elisiorum." In classical mythology, the paradise reserved for the virtuous.</note> and the fears of the underworld were held in mockery, and the minds of the multitude could no longer be restrained by those religions (for they had grown old, as all things do), they established a certain punishment which could terrify both the highest and the lowest. For according to their ancestral religion, they held a supreme observance for burying or—to put it better—**embalming** <note>original: "condiendorum." This refers specifically to the Egyptian practice of mummification, which Postel views as a precursor to legalistic religious structures.</note> their own. Since it was considered a great disgrace to the entire family to have an unburied parent, it was decreed that immediately after death, anyone (except the prince) could be accused by anyone else. If the accuser could prove his case, the judge would condemn the deceased to remain unburied until satisfaction was made by the parents; otherwise, he remained unburied, a perpetual disgrace to his lineage. This invention did not restrain the common people—from whom anyone could seek their rights without fear of accusation—as much as it was formidable to the **magnates** <note>The nobility or ruling class.</note> and those who are accustomed to oppressing the weaker through tyranny. For *a living dog is better than a dead lion*, as the **Wise Man** says <note>A reference to King Solomon in Ecclesiastes 9:4.</note>. For just as the commoners are easily kept in their duty by laws or religions, so those who are led by glory and reputation—and who strive for it so much that they wish to leave a glorious memory of their name to themselves and their kin—fear above all else that they might undergo some mark of infamy even many centuries later. This is true even though they themselves commit almost all popular injuries unless they are restrained. Therefore, the end of this religion was the fear of infamy. They thus compelled parents, kinsmen, and relations, if they belonged to them, to live by the prescription of the laws, lest after death they should happen to have to make satisfaction in their name or be touched by ignominy. Yet that noble invention was not very firm. For it relied upon the superstitious and ridiculous burial and guarding of the dead body, which was immediately exploded; once that was cast down, that fear collapsed. Hence the fable of the underworld was invented by the Greeks: that the shades of unburied bodies could not be ferried across by **Charon** <note>The mythological ferryman of the dead across the river Styx.</note>. Although this was discussed in the first and second books on true and false religion, the main point must be repeated here in a few words for the sake of comparison.

The one religion of Christ—beyond the fact that it encompasses the peaks of all laws based on reason (which are satisfied with keeping a man in his duty so that he does no harm)—also persuades and commands us, by the example of the **Highest God**, who is nonetheless exceedingly beneficent toward all (even ungrateful and lost men), that we should pursue with benefits not only friends but enemies, and that we should forgive their injuries. It does this through the fear of our eternal perdition, or the desire for perpetual happiness; or, what is most excellent, it desires this to be done solely by the example of God and the love of virtue. Nothing greater than this can be devised or given for the preservation of nature. But **atheists** <note>original: "athei." In the 16th century, this term was often used for anyone whose religious views were considered dangerously heterodox or materialistic.</note>, full of madness and opinion, clamor against this prescription. They say it cannot be performed by anyone, and therefore it is set down in vain and established as a law. Let us see first if he who is once evil is always evil; and if he commits a crime against you or another, whether he does the same to someone else; and if he who has erred once is always worthy of punishment. If this were true, since by the consensus of all nations no mortal is without sin—and that most frequently—**Jupiter** <note>Postel uses the name of the Roman king of gods here as a humanist synonym for the Divine Judge or God.</note> would kill everyone and would hold his empire for himself alone. Surely **Divine Providence** would be either unjust, having immediately exposed man to the necessity of all things (from which the occasion for sinning flowed into opinion), and yet taking vengeance immediately for individual faults; or it would be foolish, having brought man forth to the present executioner’s block, and while wishing to rule, would remove from the midst those whom it would rule. Therefore, it wisely tolerates the wicked so that they may return to fruitfulness, acting more wisely than if it killed them immediately. It is no different than how the laws more easily endure the boiling-over vices of youth, until they return to their senses in a more mature age. If therefore...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
### BOOK III

[276]

Therefore, we ought to be moved especially by the example of the highest deity. How can we, though we are wicked sons, be of such a savage mind toward our brothers (who are all those whom nature, our parent, has brought forth)? Furthermore, he who returns an injury proves in himself that which he condemns in another. I will not mention with what heat, what madness, what **Furies** <note>original: "erinnybus." In Greek mythology, the Erinyes (Furies) were deities of vengeance who hounded those who committed crimes against the natural order.</note>, and what torches he is tortured and burned by, who thinks of nothing but revenge; indeed, there is no clearer example of hell. I will not mention that at the very least two men are endangered, and discords are sown among parents, friends, and citizens, leading to seditions in cities or human gatherings; there is no matter of greater danger or more toil than retaliation and revenge. 

It is therefore far better, and more useful for both public and private peace, to both forgive injuries and to conquer an enemy with kindness, drawing him over to our own way of thinking. But some say the wicked will become insolent and commit every crime if they once injure someone with impunity. There are laws and there are judges to punish such outrages; leave it to them. "But," one might say, "unless I avenge the injury immediately, I will not be considered noble." Oh, what a foolish opinion! Oh, what madness to be lamented by all ages! You will be far nobler by settling peace and being useful to man, moderating the impulse of madness with counsel and timing, than you would be by slaughtering a man and being satiated with blood. If someone becomes insolent, he must certainly be restrained, but only when there is no longer any room for repentance or leniency. That anger, that ferocity, should be directed against the enemies of the **republic** <note>original: "reipub." Referring generally to the "commonwealth" or the public good.</note>, not against its own children. 

Certainly, this precept—that an enemy must be reconciled through gentleness and kindness—surpasses all other laws and all constitutions of religions, just as its author, the <term>theanthropos</term> <note>original: "θεάνθρωπος," meaning the "God-Man" (Christ).</note>, surpasses mere men. Other persuasions had scarcely revealed the primary cause of things with light arguments and judgments, and had scarcely persuaded anyone. The Christian religion shows so clearly to the eye both that God exists and that He cares for mortal deeds, that whatever nature (God’s instrument) had previously produced, He has done the same in restoring man or his parts, as an argument of His present divinity. 

Nor did He keep that power of divinity only for Himself; as many as lived with distinguished innocence according to His precept held that same power of divinity as a companion. This continued until pretense, deceit, and greed—under the guise of piety—accumulated wealth even unto **Sybaritic luxury** <note>original: "luxum usq; Sybariticum." Referring to the ancient city of Sybaris, famous for its extreme hedonism and decadence.</note>, forcing these divine spectacles to go into exile from human society. No nation passes over into our persuasion without the gift of an unusual deed or a miracle. Once these became known to everyone, there was no need for them to be constant. For any miracles, if done too frequently, become cheapened; they are not unlike the common things of nature, which, though they are in themselves a very great miracle, are so common that we do not even deign to consider them. 

But especially when the affairs of mortals were afflicted and all but ruined—and when those things which are thought most excellent in human judgment had been found wanting by those in power, by tyrants, and by the destroyers of the world—He came, contrary to human judgment, to teach that the things which men, enticed by opinions, thought were glory and honors, were in fact the height of vanity, calamity, and misery. Therefore, in these slippery matters placed in the rashness of fortune, He asserted (in the manner of the most excellent **Philosophers**) that there is nothing of the "good," but rather much of "evil," when such things exceed the use of private and public necessity. The lust of mortals learns and experiences this every day at its own peril, after many hardships and risks entered into voluntarily. The sole author of religions wished His own authority to be outside the reach of worldly power. He decreed that all things ought to be directed toward the true goods of the soul. Yet, since He knew that the world, once grown and placed in the very vigor of its age, would never be without princes to deal with the condition of things, the care of the republic, the accumulation of wealth, and jurisdiction, He decreed that a Christian man—where reason allows and authority demands—should be obedient.

...which one ought to do for the sake of public peace. Therefore, the goal of this persuasion is to make a person happy not through the body or the gifts of fortune, but through the soul alone—both in this life and in the eternal life of souls—even when the body is one day raised again. But enough regarding our own faith. Now, with a slightly higher overview, we must speak of the origin of all things. In this way, it will become clear to everyone by what reasoning religions were established and confirmed by the fear or credulity of common people.

### WHENCE THE VARIOUS PERSUASIONS CONCERNING THE GODS 
### VARIOUSLY FLOWED FORTH. CHAPTER V.

Necessity or utility (for I do not think those are very distinct) and the desire for various religions were the primary causes for wise men. From these, a third cause arose, resting partly on the desire of the founder and partly on the utility of the people. All things progress in this manner from small and necessary beginnings toward a useful and not strictly necessary freedom, and from there they pass even into desire, luxury, and mockery. For it was enough for the raw and youthful world to have those things sufficient for covering the skin and filling the belly, using whatever material satisfied nature. 

The slightly more learned joined "utility" to it; indeed, once utility takes the place of necessity, it is undoubtedly regarded as necessary—no differently than with sheep or any other tamed animals, where the fodder usually provided by man, though it seems only "useful," is actually so necessary that if they are deprived of it, they will be in danger. For they cannot return to their ancient nature; likewise, men educated with a certain elegance or cleanliness of living cannot return to the **Ages of Saturn** <note>The "Ages of Saturn" refers to the mythical Golden Age of peace and simplicity, before the onset of civilization, private property, and greed.</note>, except very gradually over many centuries. For the method of education, once turned into habit, becomes a second nature. Hence, even if an abundance of acorns from oaks, beech masts, chestnuts, and other fruits, roots, and vegetables—on which the ancients used to live—is readily available, yet unless there is an abundance of useful wheat, legumes, and meat to satisfy our usage, we immediately suffer from hunger and even plague. 

After the necessary use of things, the plague of opinion and glory arose, as everyone began to set the measure of their affairs not just by what is useful and necessary, but according to the example of others. From this comes a **race of monkeys** <note>original: "simiarum genus." Postel uses this metaphor to describe people who mindlessly imitate the status-seeking behaviors of others.</note>, not seeking what is beneficial to themselves, but throwing themselves into infinite miseries for the sake of rivalry, while one man strives to surpass another in luxury, glory, honors, and follies. 

In the same way, Necessity—for all things have had similar growth, progress, stability, and ends—devised the primary religions for men (as we have already shown) solely to keep them in their duty for their own benefit. It planted them in the minds of the wiser sort and explained them through their words and eloquence. This is clear among any nation, but most especially in those cities that were never subject to tyrants; yet, that they were held by some religious opinion is evident from the histories of all nations. 

Indeed, the youthful world was guided not by the work of a tyrant—who by his ferocity would make wild beasts out of tamed animals and overturn established peace with cruelty—but by a certain providence and modesty of men instructed in wisdom (for I do not count novices among the truly wise), through their counsel and labor. For it was necessary that human ferocity be tamed not by ferocity—as is true for other animals—for they would have slaughtered each other more savagely than before if ferocity and monstrous barbarism had been immediately met with ferocity. Among men settled and tempered by modesty, who might have played among free men, there was a need for a "novitiate of wisdom," and for frequent signs, voices, and eloquence, through which...

->**PAGE 278**<-

...they might use them to bend and admonish more unrefined minds. Softness acting upon softness becomes sluggish and sags; a hard thing crushes the soft. But if the soft acts upon the hard, it can press gradually and impress a form upon it, without shattering or crushing it. <note>Postel uses this physical metaphor to describe the "art of persuasion": a teacher must be gentle enough to shape a "hard" or stubborn mind without breaking it.</note> This was the prudence of **Orpheus** (or whoever was the **Pythagorean** who, under his name, brought the religions of Greece and Thrace out of their savage monstrosity). For when he saw that those peoples—among whom he is said to have traveled abroad for a long time—were held by religions that were for the most part utterly false, yet were not easily persuaded by the work of the wise, he instilled his own teachings in such a way that he is said to have drawn after him with his lyre not only men, but even animals and all vegetation.

**Pythagoras** has certainly always been considered the chief author of persuasions among the Greeks: hence his religious authority began to be held as the equivalent of reason. Even the smallest details were admitted by the common people, since the instructors themselves, still unrefined, did not sufficiently know the nature of the supreme deity and were led by weak reasoning and examples. And for this reason, religious dogmas were approved by everyone: the wise approved them strongly after perceiving their practical use, and the commoners believed them easily.

By such examples, religion began to be propagated. From there it was carried into all of Greece, and from there among the Romans, as we may recognize. Hence both the necessary and the false arose among all nations. Since man is naturally inclined to show gratitude and is an admirer of unusual things, nothing can be more easily persuaded to him than that there is some divinity by whose beneficence he has obtained some gift useful for life, or through whom he possesses this great abundance of all things; and who can either grant these things to our ancestors or equals, or deprive those currently living, and inflict many calamities.

For all these things that are placed in this "temple of nature" appear to have been created neither by themselves (since they lack reason and appetite on their own) nor by men; thus they were very easily believed to have a hidden cause. This is because almost all men, being without letters and lacking great experience, are ignorant of the obscurity of celestial things, separated substances, and the whole of nature. 

Those who do not grasp God <note>Those who lack a philosophical understanding of the Divine.</note> defend the dogmas of their fathers "with their teeth" <note>original: "mordicus" — meaning to hold on doggedly or tenaciously.</note>. Those who know by what reasoning these things were introduced—even if they are themselves wise—leave no stone unturned to ensure the opinion of the received religion is preserved in its most whole and holy state. Otherwise, they would overturn both themselves and the entire <term>Republic</term> <note>Latin: "Rempublicam" — the state or organized society.</note>, unless they introduce another religion before they remove the first.

Indeed, through fixed days, sacred rites, ceremonies, sacrifices, and games, the matter began to be maintained—not so much to keep the commoners and the plebeians in their religious duty, as to ensure that while the multitude (which is prone to forgetfulness) frequently gathers, they might hear the answers given by the priests and authors of religions. Thus they recognize the things established by reason for the public utility, frequently recalling and preserving them. For where some divinity was believed to have given an answer, the people were far more obedient than if a man like themselves had been the author. For no rational explanation ought to be sought for a response or an <term>oracle</term>, though one is usually sought from a man.

Thus a useful, though little-scrutinized, religion was introduced—useful, indeed, as long as both the ignorant and the experts strove to keep it. However, it either grew old or, being gradually corrupted and neglected, it faded away. But when crafty men, seized by ambition and the love of amassing wealth and glory, saw that the raw and ignorant multitude was so easily captured and held by any religion, and that they were not slowly bound by the persuasions of those who seemed to possess something not human, but unusually great, they were not satisfied to use the received persuasion and to introduce that which was beneficial for the people: but rather that which [would make] those very men [superior to] the others... <note>The text breaks off here at the catchword "cæteris" (the others/the rest).</note>

...set him over the others, so that he could command his fellow countrymen, and thus from those very small beginnings, inaugurate those kingdoms which later became both great and long-lasting. Furthermore, they wanted this belief in a divine power to be instilled either from the very cradle or through the habit of an entire lifetime of persuasion.

**Jupiter**, the son of **Saturn** (to start from the head), was "exposed" <note>In antiquity, "exposure" was the practice of abandoning an infant in the wild to die, a common trope in the origins of legendary kings.</note> because of an oracle sought and devised by his uncle. It was claimed that he would be the heir to drive his father from the kingdom and would both seek and achieve tyranny over **Crete** unless he was killed or abandoned. Finally, having been raised by a goat—not without divine care (as it was believed)—he drew the hearts of the Cretans (who were very much like him) to himself by this miracle of his infancy. He drove his father and his uncle **Titan** from their ancestral possession and joined his rule to religious persuasion so effectively that he not only convinced mortals of his own divinity while alive, but even after death he held and maintained a place nearly first among the gods. 

The father [Saturn], however, under whom the "Golden Ages" were believed to have existed, was deemed more unworthy of the kingdom than his lying son. Forced into exile from Crete, he sought **Italy**, which he held in submission through the arts of religion (following his son’s example) to such an extent that he was easily considered the first and highest of the "mortal gods." 

This is where that famous and holy (if it please the gods) <term>apotheosis</term> <note>original: "ἀποθέωσις"; the process of a human being being transformed into or recognized as a god.</note> took place. Then, by the license of the Greeks, the heavens were filled with fables—which I certainly believe the barbarians (or those whose writings have not reached us, or whose commentaries were destroyed and suppressed by the work of those same Greeks) had practiced before. For without example or teaching, the Greeks hardly ever thought of anything great on their own—if, indeed, it was "great" to deceive the world and hunt for kingdoms under the pretext of religion. Hence not only men, but goats, rams, lions, bulls, bears—and even ships, javelins, lyres, and arrows—occupied the sky by that same license <note>Postel is referring to "catasterism," the mythological practice of placing heroes or objects among the stars as constellations.</note>. 

For the bastard **Hercules**, worthy of his father Jupiter, the sign of his present divinity was being cast before a serpent; after the son of **Amphitryon** was killed, Hercules, when he was less than two years old (if it is worthy of belief), finished it off. This presence of divinity and victory over the serpent gave him the kingdom of Africa, and the conquered Spains, Gauls, and Britains, who became obedient not only to his laws but to his religions. By this reputation of a divine power protecting even his infant age, he was believed to have finished so many monsters and conquered so many tyrants. This is true unless, however, we believe that the Greeks—with their license for lying—ascribed to one man what many had actually performed. 

The history of the **Egyptian** is certain, while the Greeks may be doubted. **Osiris** the Egyptian too (for from there comes whatever false persuasion exists), although the Greeks contend he was an Argive because of the man’s remarkable prudence and that he ruled the kingdom of **Achaia**—it matters not where he was from: he was believed to be the son of Jupiter. (For to be fated by the gods was always a great thing.) By that fame of divinity, he not only conquered the more famous parts of Asia, Africa, and Europe, but shaped them with laws and customs, taught agriculture, and left such a reputation of himself for everyone that he was held as a God, of whom more shortly. 

For I return to those who were "exposed," who truly seem to have applied themselves all the more ardently to virtue the greater the stain they received from their parents' injury. They did this either to wash away the stain of their parents, or to confirm religions, or to take vengeance on those who, for the sake of plundering, saw to it that legitimate heirs were exposed. 

There were, besides **Cyrus** alone, perhaps all "children of the people" <note>Postel implies they were of illegitimate or common birth, despite their later royal status.</note>. **Semiramis**, born to an unchaste mother and thus exposed, was raised by doves (which gave her that name in the Syrian language); this gave her the most famous kingdom of all Asia. It incited her to acquire and complete such vast wealth, victories, and buildings that she left behind admiration mixed with envy even for the Caesars and Alexanders. So the nurses...

...in the name of goats, she-wolves, birds, and dogs, antiquity easily believed those had been actual animals, though they shared only the name. <note>Postel is suggesting that nicknames or metaphors were later taken literally as animal-nurturers.</note> **Cyrus** would not have so easily added his grandfather’s kingdom to his neighbor’s if he had not been "exposed" as an infant and then persuaded his countrymen—who were perhaps oppressed by excessive tyranny—of the opinion that a divinity accompanied him. I do not wish to bring up **Romulus** here with his she-wolf; for it was fitting that one born of incest should be raised by a harlot "she-wolf." <note>original: "meretrice lupa." In Latin, *lupa* can mean both a literal she-wolf and a prostitute.</note> From such a progenitor of shepherds, thieves, and robbers was born first a kingdom, then a republic, and finally an empire most highly adorned with every title of wisdom, power, and also of injustice and pride: concerning which it is better to be silent, whether in a good or bad light, than to write too little. I will not bring up **Aegisthus** raised by a goat, **Pelias** by a mare, or **Paris** by a bear, since they were said to have been exposed. 

For this example was emended from the divine law by countless others, after the likeness of **Moses**. For however many have imitated this, even if they were able to draw certain peoples to their own way of thinking, they did so in an attempt to rule over them. Who would not believe that the opinion received among the simpler folk concerning **Jupiter Ammon** being the father of **Alexander** gave him easier victories than if he had immediately been held as the son of Philip? Suppose they never thought about religion until after they heard they were "exposed" or born of gods. That opinion certainly lifts their own spirits and depresses and casts down those of the common people. 

For not all things are to be judged false immediately just because some things of that kind have seemed false. Not infrequently, portents, miracles, and omens have happened from uncertain causes—not without the command or will of the supreme divinity—which frequently were heralds of either great evils or of monumental changes, so that mortality itself might take heed. For as it frequently happens that a wise physician, skilled in the temperament of bodies, predicts diseases so they can be prevented, likewise that supremely beneficial divinity, to whom we must attribute whatever we obtain in this life, frequently signals to these republics and assemblies of men those things of which mortals are for the most part ignorant. For while we consider the age, growth, progress, and ends of individuals as things that pertain most to us, we are not so able, nor so accustomed, to weigh the condition of the republic or of universal affairs. 

And because knowing these things is of great importance regarding the state of human affairs, therefore God, the Most Good and Great, frequently helps such a multitude in danger, and finally takes up the duty of a father where human remedies fail. Histories teem with such miracles, so that if anyone were so shameless as to assert they are all false, he would deny that reason exists in himself; yet no one but a fool would fail to recognize that many things have also been fabricated by clever men, especially where they are similar to true miracles. 

But which are true and which are false, let God see to that. Unusual events have also been omens of kingdoms and of great affairs. For **Hiero**, the tyrant of Sicily, bees piling honey into his mouth while he slept, and for **Midas**, ants stacking grains of wheat, were great omens of the power they later acquired and increased. The Persian King **Sophis** <note>Referring to the Safavid Shah Ismail I (r. 1501–1524), the "Sofi," whose rise followed a period of hiding.</note>, father of the brothers now reigning, hiding for a long time in the woods without any human support, although already grown, nevertheless recovered his father’s kingdom, not without evidence of divinity. The same is reported to have happened to **Habis**, king of the Tartessians, who lived for a long time with a doe. 

What of the fact that some born through the work of incubi <term>Incubus: In folklore, a demon in male form believed to have intercourse with women; Postel uses it here to explain the "supernatural" origins of legendary figures.</term> were later great men? Such as **Ulam** in Tartary, the **Hungarians** in Germany, and **Merlin** in Britain. Who would not believe that those "personal spirits" <term>Genius: In the classical sense, a protective spirit or divine spark assigned to a person at birth, like the *daimon* of Socrates.</term> gave courage to **Socrates**, **Girolamo Savonarola**, **Apollonius of Tyana**, and many others to reach the height of affairs, had they not been oppressed or hindered? With his own spirit <note>original: "dæmone," referring to a guiding spirit or supernatural companion.</note>, **Pythagoras** [held] the tyranny of the Thurians...

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK III. 281

...did not blush to affect [divinity]. <note>The Latin text here is a fragment, likely completing a word like *divinitatem* (divinity) from the previous page.</note> The cunning of those who introduced religions—not for the benefit of the people or out of necessity, but primarily for their own profit and often for the sake of their reputation—is clear enough. For even **Romulus** was seen as a god by **Proculus** at the price of his blood. <note>original: "à Proculo deus visus est." Postel refers to the legend where Proculus Julius claimed to have seen the murdered or vanished Romulus as the god Quirinus, thereby pacifying the Roman people.</note> Nor should we only call "religion" that which is struck into someone by fear or love of a deity; it is also that which a leader desires the common people to believe about his own person.

Now it seems we must speak of those who introduced their own opinions about the gods to the world for the benefit of both the people and themselves. When prudence is joined with justice, those endowed with such virtues are not only held in the highest admiration by everyone, but they also easily persuade others to believe whatever they say. For wherever we see in any man a supreme integrity connected to equity, and see that he is held by no ambition that might force him to speak against his faith or his true feelings, we undoubtedly accept all his words as if from an oracle. We take care to observe them no differently than if they were brought forth by a deity. For in that position, a good and prudent man is to other men what God is even above the wise; he is as if privy to divine counsel, since he is highly skilled in both divine and human reason.

Through this reputation for justice and prudence, many were voluntarily called upon and chosen by the people to take the reins of government (I am speaking now of the world as it was coming of age in its religious worship). Some offered themselves to this duty out of care for the people, while others were moved by glory and ambition. Some stabilized a power they had already acquired and refined it through religions and laws. Not a few, seized by a greater desire for glory, were satisfied simply to have established the laws. 

However, all these leaders realized that even if they were currently well-loved, many who had founded laws and republics eventually perished due to the outrages and seditions of the people. Furthermore, because they knew that human minds are prone to change and ingratitude, they sought to avoid danger by persuading the people that they had a relationship with a certain divinity. They did this so that their authority would be greater—a double authority, both human and divine. They affirmed that whatever they did, decided, or advised, they did by the counsel and work of this deity. The people believed them all the more easily because the outcomes usually seemed to be useful for the state.

**Numa Pompilius**, who was quite knowledgeable in **Pythagorean** dogma, was called to govern the city founded by Romulus through the interpretation of omens. He saw that the city had perhaps destroyed its own founder <note>A reference to the theory that the Roman Senate assassinated Romulus.</note> because the people's minds were moderated by either no religion at all or by a very weak fear of the gods. Therefore, he primarily wanted the people to be persuaded that he followed the authority of a divinity—whom he called the nymph **Egeria**—in all things. He did this so that if anything displeased the people, or if a prudent action did not turn out successfully, he himself would not suffer the penalty as the author of the plan. In this way, he both looked out for the people and retained the dignity and grandeur worthy of a kingdom. 

I will not dwell here on **Lycurgus**, **Solon**, **Charondas**, **Zamolxis**, and the others who are remembered as authors or restorers of laws for the great benefit and shared glory of their people. They all made their constitutions stable and firm by claiming a divinity as the author and using oracles. For it was necessary, in the first place, to begin the work with religion and the help of gods or "familiars" <note>original: "geniorum... familiares." Spirits or guardian deities thought to be personal companions to great men.</note> whom they asserted they knew intimately. But **Muhammad the Arab** easily surpassed the arts and genius of them all; I have described him in the preceding pages. In my own judgment, just as men can never exist or be kept to their duty without a belief in religions, so belief can hardly be increased or preserved without arms. Therefore, ancient kings held the office of sacrificing priests, keeping both powers joined under the name of sovereignty.

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

The King of the Indian Africans <note>Postel is likely referring to the Emperor of Ethiopia, often called "Prester John" in this era, who was frequently described as having supreme authority over both church and state.</note> is accustomed to give answers concerning religion and to select the high priests to whom he gives instructions. King **David**, by virtue of his prophecy, was more beneficial to his people than he was through his royal power. Each of these powers—the religious and the secular—ought to be tempered by the other. The one who holds the resources without which neither power can stand must moderate the judgment of all things, at least regarding external matters. For everyone knows that one part of the Republic is like the **soul**, and the other like the **body**. If these are disjointed or scattered, the state must necessarily collapse. If one is placed entirely apart, it withers in idleness unless it is stirred by proper observation, or unless the "bridle" of the other puts a limit on greed. 

The strongest evidence for this is that all religions first perished in the very places where they were first established. Unless the diligence of princes restrains luxury, religions are eventually destroyed by those very people who were for too long the guardians of those faiths at their own whim. In matters of the soul, however, sacred power should be absolute. Yet, when the <term>mystae</term> <note>Priests or initiates into sacred mysteries.</note> favor themselves more than is right, or consult only their own interests, they do not sufficiently weigh the utility of the common good; instead, they naturally tend to look after their own livelihood (since that is how they are supported). Although this income is intended for the longevity and preservation of their order, no one should consider it a miracle if it is consumed by someone else. For they do not set limits for themselves; rather, a fairer judge and a most excellent arbiter of the Republic must do so. 

We shall discuss later the primary reasons why all persuasions have perished or are destined to perish. For now, we must briefly explain how the various forms of worship crept into the world.

## THE ORIGINS OF ABSURD RELIGION AND
### Idolatry. <note>original Greek: εἰδωλολατρείας (*eidololatreias*)</note> CHAPTER VI.

Since this "temple of nature" and the immensity of its blessings draw men into stupor and admiration, they desire to direct their gratitude toward some unknown cause. But the ignorant man does not know to whom he should return thanks (for blind mortality cannot conceive the true form of divinity). Therefore, out of both fear and gratitude, he directs his thanks toward whatever thing is introduced or offered to him by priests and "wise men." The priests—who are appointed to preserve these things—then increase and confirm this received opinion through divinations, riddles, difficulties, and craft. 

Thus, it was enough for tyrants and those who once held the reins of power to restrain the minds of the people using even the most false religious opinions. Regarding the decrees, responses, or oracles of the gods (or of the priests teaching their worship), no one was allowed or accustomed to demand a reason. The "wise," who understand how things actually work, pretend to approve for the sake of the ignorant common folk; they become the authors of the accepted opinion about the gods so that it may be maintained. The prince, for the sake of public peace, compels this through fear. 

Driven by the credulity of the masses back when the world was "less-nosed" <note>original: *parum nasutus*, a Latin idiom meaning "lacking discernment" or "not sharp-witted."</note>, those crafty princes and rogues—who sought to make their memory last through rare deeds, glory, or trickery—wanted to persuade the unskilled crowd that after death they would become immortal gods and migrate to heaven. There, they claimed, they would take care of mortal affairs—but only if all mortals (especially those they had benefited or ruled) busied themselves with frequent sacrifices in their honor. In truth, this was done so that their memory would be preserved longer and so that their priests would be fed. For without a yearly memory held by men, and without a "collection" <note>original: *stipe*, referring to a small coin or donation given to temples.</note> established for that memory, nothing lasts very long. Time obliterates all things, but these things it obliterates more slowly. This is the origin of <term>apotheosis</term> <note>The process of a human being being recognized as a god.</note> and the practice of releasing an eagle from the funeral pyre toward heaven... <note>Postel refers to the Roman imperial funeral rite where an eagle was released from the pyre to symbolize the emperor’s soul ascending to the gods.</note>

<summary>Postel argues that the stability of a state requires a balance between secular power (the body) and religious authority (the soul). He then explains that idolatry and the deification of rulers (apotheosis) originated from a mixture of human wonder at nature, priestly greed, and the desire of rulers to be remembered after death.</summary>

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK 3

...seeking heaven, as if by carrying away souls. This fraud had become so well known to both the Romans and the Greeks in their more mature years that even those who were most powerful among them could not "creep into heaven" once the people had become more refined. From this comes the stain and the origin of evil; from this comes every kind of sacrifice and game; from this comes the various forms of funerals intended to "reach the heavens." From that source, sacred rites arose, which were then increased and confirmed by lies. From this point, he began to be considered a **God** who did not even deserve the name of a man, but rather the title of a most savage beast. 

Hence **Mars** became a robber and destroyer of cities; hence **Jupiter** a pederast <note>original: "pæderastes"</note> and a potter <note>The Latin "figulus" (potter) here likely refers to the mythic role of the gods as creators of mankind from clay, or perhaps a disparaging remark on Jupiter's "shaping" of mortals.</note>; **Mercury** an impostor and a wit; **Venus** a harlot; the **Lemnian** <note>Vulcan/Hephaestus, who was famously cast down to the island of Lemnos.</note> a blacksmith; **Neptune** a pirate; **Bacchus** and **Ceres** farmers; all of whom ascended into heaven through the tongues and favors of their fellow countrymen. But as if that were not enough, even male prostitutes <term>cynaedi</term> <note>Men who performed passive roles in same-sex acts, often associated with the cults of Cybele or Roman decadence.</note> and harlots were granted Roman sacred honors. 

Lest they should immediately perish from the memory of men and fall from their "heaven," besides being worshipped with fixed and certain rites and sacrifices, they also left behind for posterity certain animals whose species would always be among men, as if these animals were sacred to themselves. **Apollo**—the flute-player, physician, and traveling pharmacist—left the serpent; **Jupiter** the eagle, **Venus** the doves, **Juno** the peacock, and others left other things. There are also trees and herbs consecrated to them, arising from the imaginations of priests and the natural properties of the planets.

**Egypt** was the inventor of this artifice. **Isis**, the Queen of Egypt, is said to have devised this in the name of her husband **Osiris**. When he was deprived of life by his brother and torn into twenty-five pieces <note>While many myths say fourteen pieces, Postel specifies twenty-five, perhaps to align with the number of Egyptian provinces or "nomes" he mentions later.</note> under the pretext of tyranny, Isis recovered the parts after the brother was defeated. To ensure that the people did not cast off or strip away the opinion of divinity they had conceived regarding Osiris—both because of the magnitude of his deeds and the belief in his divine origin—she took those twenty-five parts of her husband’s body (which the brother had intended to send to the governors of as many provinces as a sign of his deed) and enclosed each part in statues larger than human form. She then took care to have them consecrated in twenty-five different temples in various provinces, as if the entire body of her husband lay hidden in each one. 

She established a fund of money for the annual income of the priests who would promote this belief; for without the use of money, neither religion, nor laws, nor even the most useful arts can survive in the slightest degree in the developed world. Furthermore, although she wanted him to be believed to be in any province whatsoever (as one who was said to be alone in heaven), in order to generate competition and a longer-lasting memory among the common people—who strive to surpass one another in the display of pomps and ceremonies—she also willed that as many different animals as there were parts of the body be held as sacred. Once an animal was consecrated anywhere, it was to be sacrosanct, not to be harmed even by chance, but to be worshiped with excellence and shown religious devotion—and this was to be done neither frequently nor without ceremonies or the vows of the people. 

For even sacrosanct mysteries become cheap through constant use, but are held in high regard through rarity. Thus, as if Osiris were alive again in each of those animals, he offered himself daily and of his own accord to the remembrance of the Egyptians. Nature has produced men with such a great sense and desire for glory that they are spurred on to illustrious deeds as if by a sting. However, wickedness, translating this desire for glory only into fame and notoriety rather than into virtue, has left behind far more men like **Paris**, **Cambyses**, **Herostratus**, **Dionysius**, **Claudius**, **Nero**, and **Heliogabalus** than like **Saturn**, **Janus**, and **Augustus**. The more shameless these men were, the more ardently they attempted to seize "heaven" to wash away the stain of their wicked lives. 

This was the fountain of **idolatry** <note>original Greek: "εἰδωλολατρείας"</note> and the nursery of false persuasion. From here came the bow, the arrow, the sacred shield; from here, anything at all was forced into religion. Thence, it was believed that divinity was absent from nothing. From this came the ruin and strife of the world, and the variety of burial rites, which seems to be the door to divinity...

...were born from there. Sacrifice was made to the gods themselves—if indeed they survive, happy and lacking nothing—by men, using their own slaves, or even children, horses, weapons, and wax figures <note>original: "cerarijs"</note>, as if sacrificing to virtues. Man himself was offered up like a most pleasing victim: the guilty, the innocent, the slave, the free, the guest, the native, the stranger, and even the parent. Nor was this enough; just as they held certain animals sacred for the sake of a longer memory, so too were certain cursed things usually sacrificed to each of those scoundrels (I meant to say gods): a sow to Minerva, a goat to Bacchus, a donkey to Priapus, and so on. Thus, the Egyptian fabrication <note>original: "Aegyptiacum commentum"</note> prepared a foul destruction for almost the entire race of living creatures. 

Finally, the **Veioves** <note>Sinister or "little" Jupiters, often associated with ill-fortune or the underworld.</note> and the <term>averters of evil</term> <note>original Greek: ἀποτρόπαιοι (apotropaioi); gods invoked to turn away bad luck or divine wrath.</note> gods were devised. Sacred rites began to be performed for the spirits of the underworld. Terrestrial gods were cultivated according to the teachings of **Pythagoras** <note>The famous Greek philosopher and mathematician whose followers practiced specific rituals to appease local spirits.</note>, lest they do harm; and celestial gods, so that they might be of benefit. A crowd of gods from the entire conquered world was brought into the city by the Romans—those overthrowers of human peace—so that wherever men might flock from, they would find and worship their ancestral gods in Rome. 

**Vacinna** <note>An ancient Sabine goddess often identified with leisure or victory.</note>, **Pales** <note>Goddess of shepherds and livestock.</note>, **Rubigo** <note>The god of agricultural blight or mildew.</note>, **Pomona** <note>Goddess of fruit trees.</note>, **Pylumnus**, **Vertunus**, **Cupid**, **Pleasure**, **Lubentina**, **Venus**, **Fever**, **Fortune**, and **Roman Fortune** were all gods dedicated with temples. Temples and images were also erected to **Faith**, **Mind**, **Virtue**, **Wealth**, **Liberty**, and **Victory**. The names of the heavens, the planets, the elements, virtues, vices, men, and demons were transformed by clever and crafty men and drawn into the service of religion. The First Cause, or Providence, began to be held in the greatest ignorance by all men, until it became known again under the leadership of **Christ**. 

Furthermore, lest the authority of a religion once approved be diminished, or the mark of impiety be burned into the tyrants themselves, the victors always spared the temples, as long as they could cover and disguise their thefts. Indeed, one can hardly find in the records of literature, out of such a great number of kings, tyrants, or emperors (except for a few Persians or Romans), those who dared to despoil religious places and shrines. This was true even though they knew that almost all types of religions were false and devised by human cleverness, primarily for this reason: they knew that men who are seen as religious—the authors and preservers of religions—are believed in more than the gods themselves. 

Moreover, if you take away the ancestral gods, or if you overturn or despoil their temples, how will those whom you wish to obey your commands be able to come together for sacred rites? Certainly, he who diminishes the authority of the gods breaks the union of society, unless, once all matters are settled and the empire is strengthened, and the falsehood of the previous system is demonstrated, he strives to provide something better. A new prince certainly ought not to attempt this unless he is far superior. Therefore, all princes, or those who held power, were very busy adorning and building temples, either to leave an opinion of their own piety among the common people, or to confirm the religions, or for both reasons. They sought to decorate those temples with booty taken from human blood or even stolen from other temples, so that the common folk might be held in their allegiance much more easily. These are the causes and origins of false religion. Now we must speak of its progress, growth, and hierarchies.

# ON THE GROWTH AND STABILITY
## of Religions. CHAPTER VII.

**I**n all things that have received order and cultivation through human wisdom and diligence, since they held all things within themselves potentially but not yet in actuality, the same individuals were at first both the magistrates and those who carried out orders, before authority was occupied, attained, or given. Just as before a house is built, there is no distinction in the forest between a post, a beam, a rafter, or a roof-ridge; and in the stone quarry, the stone is the same and similar from which the foundations, corners, pilasters, columns, architraves, and bases <meta>catchword: basesq</meta>

He concludes by transitioning into a discussion on the structural growth of religious institutions, using an architectural metaphor to describe social hierarchy.</summary>

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK III

...and if you make bases, everything is owed to the craftsman’s hand. For all things, as if heaped together in a kind of chaos, have been gradually polished and arranged into their proper orders by human prudence—driven by necessity, utility, hope, and glory, and through the greatest labor of mind and body—mirroring the divine providence that adorned the mass of this world. Principles of all things, which are crude in themselves, certainly receive refinement through learning and, as it were, a smoothing out <note>original: "exaſciatione," a term from carpentry meaning to hew or smooth with an ax; here used metaphorically for refining raw ideas</note>. This is no different than how divine providence, using natural power and arrangement, organized both the celestial and elemental order from the primary and confused mass (which could not rightly be called either matter or form, nor be grasped by the human mind, which did not yet exist). It matched heavy things with light, the highest with the lowest, the incorruptible with the fleeting, and motion with rest through balance. This order is preserved eternally by the celestial element, which some call the **fifth element** <note>The "quintessence" or aether, which ancient and medieval science believed made up the heavens, being distinct from the four earthly elements</note>, because it depends on the pure command of providence and does not contain within itself diverse or conflicting parts that could infect it with decay.

In the beginning of human social life, before vice and greed demanded laws for their restraint, the prince, the people, and the priest were the same and equal. From there, the authority of the father over his children began; then the head of the family over the household, the master or lord over servants, the judge over the province, the prince over his domain, and the priest over souls began to hold rights, following a gradual example and the common consent of men. Both the prince (or judge) and the priest, before affairs matured and empires grew, fulfilled the roles of all magistrates of that kind. For there is no need for a different order where one person can suffice. 

Once an opinion is born and flourishes for a long time, as things become known and demand it, something is added daily to the small foundations of things and the beginnings of sacred laws, arising from the doubts or vices that crop up every day. Furthermore, there is the worship of the common people, though rarely (where matters of substance are concerned) is it done without a small offering. For when religion, propagating itself naturally, has spread a certain belief in holiness, a miracle, or some unusual and useful thing or deity among any people, wealth—either thin or non-existent at the start—gradually grows and flows in from every side through vows. Thus, things that are small at the beginning mature and grow immensely, creeping along in both reputation and riches. 

For there are many who would offer gifts and believe the stories being told. There are few who would reveal the secrets of miracles and sacred rites—lest they become cheapened by being too common—or who would receive such great gifts which (as priests assert) the common people believe are most pleasing to the gods. This is the condition of religion and the growth of persuasion. This "art" constructed immense temples out of small shrines and groves, and it forced people to swear by the words of persuasion through the splendor of wealth. From here arose secondary laws, born from vices and doubts, which explain and confirm the primary ones. From there came the solicitation of gifts in the name of buildings, ceremonies, processions, games, ornaments, rituals, and revenues. 

The people, enticed by the splendor of all sacred things, are even accustomed to offer gifts voluntarily, partly out of religious devotion and partly for a share of the glory and to preserve the memory of their name. Princes, and those who excel in resources, build shrines at their own expense and establish numerous **guardians of persuasion** <note>Postel likely refers here to the clergy or religious officials who maintain and protect the "persuasion" (the established faith or doctrine) of the public</note> to leave behind a glorious memory of their name, to keep the gods favorable, to surpass the zeal of the commoners, and to incite them further toward amplifying religion. To this is added the industry and management of the priests who increase these riches, which brings in by far the greatest offspring of wealth. 

So it happens (as the affairs of mortals can never stand still, and if anyone abuses them, they cause both ruin and change) that sacred wealth immediately grows to an immense degree according to the wishes and resources of the common people; and if there is any luxury anywhere, since it is [fed] by no one... <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "peſcuntur" suggests the next page begins with a verb related to feeding or grazing.</note>

# ABOUT THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

[...they] are sustained, this seems to be most evident in priests or pontiffs. For this reason, religious persuasions <note>original: "persuasiones"; Postel uses this term to refer to organized systems of belief or religions</note> that arose from the first beginnings and were preserved for a long time have grown immensely. In the splendor of their wealth, there is almost no religion of significant duration that has not easily surpassed the Epicureans in luxury and the public treasury in resources. Finally, it even stabs itself with its own sword, and through the allurements of pleasure and depraved morals, it destroys itself. 

Nor does this happen only in our own religion. Although Christians profess a contempt for all worldly things—which certainly cannot be practiced or observed in a fully grown religion—this was different in the beginning. A few people, holy in reputation and not corrupted by depraved opinions, lacked for little during the time when the nascent persuasion of the Church was growing; now, many people lack many things, and those at the highest levels lack the greatest things. It was certainly proper for religion to be meager and bare of all things—and additionally to urge contempt for wealth—when its followers were very few and most abstinent, before vices, opinions, doubts, and a large assembly (to which rules must be given) had yet arisen. But as the orders increased and became distinct, it became necessary for resources to be available that would be sufficient for the necessity of affairs. 

Hence, in my judgment, those who wish to forbid Christian priests <note>original: "sacrificulis," literally "little sacrificers," a term Postel often uses for lower-ranking clergy</note> from having their own resources are completely mistaken <note>original: "toto coelo errant," literally "err by the whole sky"</note>, since if those critics had anything themselves, they would shamefully waste it on luxury. Certainly, the perverse use of wealth, not the wealth itself, ought to be blamed. For who but a fool would refuse gifts, which are the most excellent way of acquiring? Who would forbid great buildings to be constructed in the divine name, or condemn industry, especially when these things are done by the grace of the Deity, and it is permitted for the one to whom they are entrusted to use them either well or badly? 

Thus temples and priests grow rich; thus dead gods are richer than the living. Furthermore, as the ownership of property increased over time, one person could not be sufficient for handling, correcting, and preserving all sacred matters. Yet, several people equal in dignity could not exist together without doubts, lawsuits, and crimes arising. It was necessary for a primary order to be established at some point, and it was necessary for a first arbiter of religion to give laws to those who were absent, and to prescribe rules for those more distant whose care was entrusted to him. 

Whether he is chosen by the one who is the author or preserver of the religion, or by a prince, or by popular consent, or by a great council, it makes no difference. It is necessary for one to be over many, to whom the highest authority <note>original: "rerum summa," the sum of affairs or supreme power</note> is deferred. For just as no one can be a judge for himself (except in conscience and hidden matters), so without a certain supreme authority, one cannot declare the law among equals in dignity, punish crimes, or give answers concerning doubts. 

In the religions of all nations that have spread widely, there have been high priests <note>original: "summi pontifices"</note>, and there will be in the future, to prescribe for others—whether by the authority of the Prince, the consent of the Republic <note>original: "Reipublicae," referring to the state or commonwealth</note>, or the authority of a supreme council. Otherwise, there would be no order in human affairs, but a kind of Chaos, since the matters of this mortal life are always tied to corruption, doubts, lawsuits, and vices. For truth, friendship, and virtue are held here more in name than in reality, except by those whom God has entirely changed through Christ. 

Finally, when the regions subject to the same persuasion spread too widely for the high priest to be conveniently approached by everyone, a third order must arise. Men of middle authority must be appointed according to the nature of the places, to whom the high priest may both prescribe and impart his authority in certain matters. Antiquity called these men "pontiffs" <note>original: "pontifices"</note> for this reason: because they make a bridge <note>Latin: "pontem faciant." Postel refers to the traditional etymology of *pontifex* as a "bridge-builder" between the human and the divine</note> for the religion that flourishes through them, and as it were, they carry it across by handing it down to others, and they keep it so that it is not endangered by being submerged in political cares. 

There are, therefore, three orders of the preservers and explainers of a persuasion: the highest, the middle, and the lowest—high priests, pontiffs, and petty priests. No civilized nation reigning for any length of time under the same persuasion has lacked these names and duties, even if it called them by terms different from ours. For the diversity of words, which differs in almost every people, does not prevent the realities from being the same. That the middle [orders] are sometimes...
