# BOOK II OF GUILLAUME POSTEL

Nothing prevents the existence of various orders. For although archbishops preside in dignity and by a certain right over bishops, and assemblies over assemblies, nevertheless all are intermediaries in that they obey the supreme pontiff or the supreme power. The Greeks had Patriarchs, over whom—when they disagreed, as was the case with the Apostles themselves—not one supreme man but sacred councils presided; would that this practice had been preserved in all Churches. For from the power of a single man—who not infrequently follows his own emotional whims and the personal advantage of his affairs rather than reason—many laws might emerge which, even if they were once useful, do not seem sufficiently suited to the use and nature of all people according to the circumstances of the times.

But yet, for a mature world, it is far more useful and expedient in private matters for one supreme leader to be set in charge and to prescribe rules, since that crowd of prelates and learned men can hardly be gathered so frequently—they should not come together except when the highest matters of state are at stake. For neither for princes nor for pontiffs (whom it most concerns) would that expense of assembly be tolerable. Therefore, the use and constitution of intermediaries is usually established according to the necessity of affairs and times, and even according to personal opinion. 

If the practice of that same persuasion <note>original: "persuasionis"; Postel uses this term to refer to a religious system or organized belief</note> were restricted only to one city or municipality, the same person could be the highest, middle, and lowest authority. Such were the ancient and adolescent religions, when any city, village, or municipality used its own sacred rites, distinct from others. For a crude antiquity (as has been demonstrated before), after losing the knowledge of the "First Cause" <note>original: "caussæ primæ"; a philosophical term referring to God as the origin of all things</note>—which had initially offered itself freely to the first humans—gave names to any deity that presented itself. Nor did a single province know only one God, just as it had not sworn its loyalty to the words of only one prince. 

But when the propagation of religions followed, not even the most powerful emperor could encompass all kinds of duties in one man. Assemblies of equals in the first and second order had to be granted a head, and those more remote from the first origin and place had to be granted a present authority; this was to prevent either doubts or vices from spreading more widely and passing into law by long use before remedies sought from afar could be applied. Whence Paul—the supreme prelate of our persuasion after Christ—said not without merit that "Orders are from God" <note>original: "Ordines esse à Deo"; a reference to Romans 13:1</note>: speaking not only about the authority of princes governing these fleeting worldly things, but about the orders of religions. Thus both wealth and authority were distributed at the same time in sacred matters. By what right they are preserved must now be seen.

### CHAPTER VIII. ON CONSISTENCY.

No one, except by common consent, a sacred assembly, or a Prince, is allowed to be over the supreme pontiff; nor should anyone divert things once dedicated to sacred use, as if they were assigned to the inheritance of a perpetual religion. The supreme pontiff gives the primary laws to the intermediaries (as many as there are), and likewise to the lowest. The intermediaries obey him, and they prescribe rules to the lowest orders within the law entrusted to them. Those in the lowest order are accustomed only to obey, and they do not prescribe to men of their own order by their own authority. 

If an inferior behaves too negligently in his duty, the right of correction belongs to the intermediary; if the intermediary is lacking, it belongs to the supreme leader. By these [priests] especially, the people are led by the hand to religion, sacred things are explained, and mysteries are tasted. In short, almost whatever care is committed to the other orders is usually cast upon them (unless religion is accompanied by a desire for profit). For they are like the powers and parts of the elements, subject to heaven and the "First Cause," acting like the hands and limbs of the other orders—though truly very different from both natural comparisons. That order follows the example of nature most closely so long as it performs its duty diligently and strives to imitate the perpetual action of nature. For heaven obeys sacred providence, as do its powers, and all the lowest things consisting of elements. The world itself

the middle rank, bearing the image of our own overseers <term>Antistitum</term> <note>From the Latin 'antistes', referring to a high-ranking priest or bishop who stands at the forefront</note>, acts only upon lower things, and exercises and impresses upon them the powers entrusted to it by the First Cause. The lower part of the world obeys partly nature, partly art, and partly both. This is the image of the most holy Trinity, which, **diffused through all the limbs, as a mind moves the mass, and mingles itself with the great body** <note>original: "mens agitat molem, & magno se corpore miscet"; a famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid describing the world-soul</note>: if it were to depart, all things would be in peril. The heavens belong to God; the elements are open to both God and the heavens, administered and produced—by both hidden and manifest causes—through a most holy mystery. This system of ranks, as far as it pertains to the intermediaries, can vary. For some, by right and without an intermediary, can immediately recognize the supreme Arbiter of the law, such as those who turn themselves toward the First Cause without the contemplation of intermediate nature; such are the many sacred gatherings and monasteries, which a flourishing **persuasion** <note>Postel uses the term "persuasio" to describe a structured religious system or faith tradition</note> has never lacked. Furthermore, since the reasoning of a religion is usually only rendered within a chosen assembly, opinions are daily joined to opinions, from which many private individuals (provided there is a cause for *persuasion*) even create religious gatherings. But this has nothing to do with the established orders, nor is that crowd necessary if the Commonwealth <term>Respublica</term> could do without them; indeed, a province is far more happily consistent when it obeys a single persuasion before so many different rites and assemblies disturb and increase the number of orders, unless they are introduced by necessity. The law of sacred matters is usually handed down first by the supreme pontiffs, then by the intermediaries, and is pronounced either by them or by those to whom they have given the power of pronouncing the law. It is necessary for them to have vicars who are accustomed to pronounce the law to the multitude concerning sacred matters. For even if they themselves were **Briareus** <note>A hundred-handed giant from Greek mythology; Postel means that even with immense capacity, a leader cannot do everything alone</note>, they would not be sufficient for themselves. They have, therefore, their own judges, who—by the authority granted to them—decide on sacred matters or those pertaining to the sacred, not without the appendages of the courts; this will be revealed most closely in the final book, where we shall deal with the judges of Princes or of secular law.

### ON THE TREATMENT, USE, AND CORRU-
### ption of persuasions. CHAPTER IX.

IT must first be carefully noted that all religious decrees have the force of law, and all those subject to the jurisdiction of any bishop are bound by them. For it is far less expedient for the tranquility of the Commonwealth to infringe upon divine matters than human ones, except in cases of rare and not lazy negligence. Indeed, it is not for a private man to contradict the words [of the law], unless it is commanded by God, or by the supreme prince and a greater power. The authority of the supreme pontiff, or whatever stands in his place, binds everyone with laws. The authority of bishops is like a civil law, and does not reach everyone. For there are many things approved by the use or decrees of pontiffs anywhere in the world (as far as rites and ceremonies are concerned) which are neither cautioned by the highest pontifical law, nor are they usually observed by others, yet they obtain the force of law, provided they do not oppose human law. For since not only every province, but even every sacred place has, as it were, its own **tutelary gods** <note>original: "tutelareis deos"; Postel uses this classical term to refer to patron saints or local spiritual protectors</note>, it is right that they be worshiped by their own accepted rite. Laws of this kind affect those subject to those places, but not others. Divine law treats—after the handing down of customs and the persuasion of piety and worship toward the gods (which is the first source of *persuasion*)—the likes of civil law, concerning only sacred things and persons dedicated to them, or things held in the opinion of being sacred. The first principle concerns divine worship, so that it may be done on certain fixed days, with prayers and ceremonies; it urges probity and duty, suggests the law of reason, and preaches virtue (unless it labors under follies, as many ancient ones once did) by the example, love, or fear of the gods. It prescribes for the sacred orders the manner in which all things held in the place of sacred objects ought to be observed. In the second place, the dignity and duty of persons must be touched upon,

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK III.

namely, what duty each person performs, how they are initiated, by what source of income they are sustained, what their character is, and their style of dress and sacred vestments. For since the uneducated masses are easily struck with wonder and look up to things that are rare and ritualistic <note>original: "personata," literally meaning "masked" or "theatrical," referring to the performative nature of religious ritual</note>, the ministers of religion wear ornate dress so that they are immediately recognized without question and are set apart from the profane crowd by these very ornaments. A good portion of religions is therefore placed in varied attire; this is even proven by their own interpretations to be necessary and essential, as if the divinity had commanded that his sacred rites must be performed with such a ritual, otherwise he would not hear mortal prayers. That outward appearance in a person dedicated to sacred things has always been the greatest part of **persuasion**. If there are any who are to be initiated into the mysteries, or who are to give their names to a religion, it ought to be handed down in this place. For some mysteries pertain to all, some to a few, and some to none except the supreme pontiffs. But because it is a matter of opinion how many or to whom these are owed, it shall be enough to know that this law and the knowledge of it must be sought from the pontifical sanctions <term>sanctionibus</term> <note>Official decrees or laws issued by religious authorities</note>, and the reasoning for what is entrusted, or the decision of a doubt, must be obtained from the same source whence the authority flowed.

The next place after the mysteries in mature **persuasions** must be given to providing for the minor priests <term>sacrificulis</term> <note>A term for lower-ranking priests, often those specifically tasked with performing the physical rites of sacrifice</note> from those resources which are added to, or are already dedicated to, sacred use. These laws themselves cannot be published in their entirety at the very birth of religions before wealth has been acquired. For it is necessary for property to exist, and for there to be disputes about it, before a law can be established concerning it. Therefore, religious laws at their birth are as unrefined as they are close to equity, because they either follow the offered goal of divinity, or at first they pretend to aim for it, and they do not immediately mix the factions of wealth with piety. For this reason, princes comply with a nascent religion and support it for a very long time while it is content with modest means, until it begins to use the right granted to it pervasively.

But when either their faction, their behavior, or their resources begin to be greater than is fair, they become an object of hatred or envy to princes, and not infrequently formidable and a hindrance to the state. Then the rights of choosing dignities begin to be taken from them, and their wealth diminished. For you would sooner break than correct those things which have hardened into depravity. Truly, no one—unless compelled, or driven by a rare religious conviction—can easily abandon the pleasures and advantages which he both possesses in abundance through his resources and which nature has taught him to seek. Therefore, they creep into the place of piety, and occupy the place by the use of virtue, and <insert>then</insert> pass beyond it. Thus, the law is gradually accustomed to being either removed or diminished by the authority of the prince; wealth likewise, otherwise in the progress of time a large part of the state treasury <term>fisci</term> <note>The 'fiscus' was the private or state treasury of a ruler</note> would creep into the sacred realm, and a luxury more than Sybaritic <note>An ancient Greek city famous for its extreme luxury and decadence</note> would infect the sacred order.

And since there are almost no priests among any nation who are not for the most part immune from war and the physical protection of the state (for they are born and instituted for the sake of retaining, moving, and settling souls), and since they are the wealthiest, they would undoubtedly exhaust the treasury, never helping except through sacred rites but always receiving; hence the envy of the treasury comes forth against them. A thin **persuasion** is gradually increased by both laws and wealth; once increased, it stands at its maturity; from there, as if gasping for wealth and choked by it, it perishes in old age, its rights first being diminished and its resources gradually reduced back to the state treasury. If princes could, in their own name, wipe away the place of the saints, there would not be such ample or such long-lasting sacred possession. But because they see that the state of affairs would be endangered if the authority of the **persuasion** is disparaged (for the common people listen to complaints), certain princes and magistrates of the more mature world have devised a certain mixed law from the sacred and the profane, and a power joined to king-priests. For to have kings accompanied by gods is the highest way to strike terror among mortals. But if the sacred order is allowed to grow in wealth without restraint and at its own will, it undoubtedly brings destruction upon itself, the state, and religion. And since resources can never exist without the pleasures and crimes of which they are the providers, they overflow all the more because they lack censors.

Then finally, when the priests <term>sacrifices</term> <note>Postel uses the term "sacrifices" here to refer to those who perform the sacred rites, essentially meaning the high clergy or sacrificial priests</note> are most wealthy—those who ought to approach the gods purely and live more holily than the rest—they betray themselves to the common people. Even if the ruler is absent, they (as the saying goes) bear witness against the gods. From this arise the open deceptions of the common rabble <term>plebeculæ</term>, who believe they have been cheated; they develop a mindset not only of refusing to pay, but of wanting to reclaim what has already been paid out, if possible. Thus, the right and authority of the priest perishes. Thus, all types of **persuasions** perish. This is the outcome and end of all things: while the institutions themselves labor under their own massive weight, and while no one wishes to look into themselves and return to moderation: *Great things collapse upon themselves, and heavy falls happen under excessive weight.* <note>Postel quotes the Roman poet Lucan, referring to how empires and institutions fall due to their own unmanaged growth.</note> I do not wish to add here the violent ends of religions which occur through external power. For necessity sometimes puts an end not only to sacred laws, but also to secular ones; yet this rarely happens anywhere without the great wickedness of those falling, when Providence seeks punishment for a shattered order and a shameful life—or perhaps some cause unknown to us, usually attributed to Providence. 

There were once many, and there are even now other magistrates among certain foreign peoples, whose responses and decrees were customarily observed with superstition in the early stages of their affairs: such as Augurs, Soothsayers <term>Aruspices</term>, Prophets, Sibyls, and any other kind that once restrained and held the minds of unlearned men. But these were ridiculous to other nations and relied only on opinion. For beyond the social ranks and the law itself, by which the common people are usually kept in their duty, nothing at all is usually approved by the decrees of all religions and by natural consensus. Now, however, in a few brief sayings <term>apophthegmatis</term>, religion itself must be summarized in aphorisms <term>aphorismois</term> <note>original Greek: $\dot{\alpha}\phi o\rho\iota\sigma\mu o\tilde{\iota}\varsigma$</note>, insofar as it is agreeable to all, or ever will be. # THE COMMON CANONS OF ALL PERSUASIONS
## Chapter X.

Let it be a conviction for all that there is a God, the author of all things, from whom we should fear dire things and hope for the opposite.

Let it be believed that all things are made by God from a hidden cause.

By all those enrolled in the Republic, or inhabitants of a place where a **persuasion** has been approved, let it be cautioned by sacred laws that the ancestral deities must be both accepted and worshipped; or, if one worships his own, let no one contradict the accepted religion with words.

He who has been initiated, let him not turn back.

Let everyone rest satisfied with the accepted sacred rites.

For the sake of public peace, let everyone observe the things established by sacred laws.

Let no private person possess his own gods.

Family shrines <term>Lararia</term> <note>Shrines to the "Lares," the protective spirits of a Roman household</note> shall be permitted.

Public temples shall be held in suitable places.

Deities shall be depicted by statues.

Let it be cautioned that priests preside over all the sacred rites of the divine beings.

The Pontiffs <term>Pontifices</term> shall take care of this.

Let no private or profane person preside as a leader of the mysteries <term>mystes</term> <note>A priest or initiate into secret religious rites</note> without the supreme consent of the Republic.

Let them reveal the hidden secrets <term>mysteria</term> of the **persuasion** to only a few.

Let no one be an inquisitive meddler, a publicizer, or a despiser.

A certain portion of the year’s harvest shall be given to the ministers of the sacred rites.

They shall use and distribute the gifts, expiations, and vows.

There shall be a right to receive offerings from anyone.

Law concerning all sacred matters is to be prescribed by the high priest, or the supreme power, or by intermediaries; those who are endowed with authority by them shall declare that law, if they [the higher powers] are unwilling [or unable to do so themselves].

They shall follow the customs of the fathers.

Whoever violates the statutes or steals sacred objects shall be excluded from the rites and punished most severely.
There shall be mutual cooperation between religion and secular laws.
Let the High Priests <note>original: *Pontifices*; while this can mean the Roman Catholic Pope, in Postel’s universalist framework, it refers to the highest religious authorities of the Commonwealth.</note> be chosen by the consensus of the Commonwealth.
The authority for deciding on religious matters shall belong to the High Priests, or to those to whom they have delegated it.
In matters pertaining to all people, let the supreme council be available to them.
They shall keep out the opinions of the profane.
They shall remove the common agitators.

These sentences encompass, in a few words, whatever is most useful in religion: so that almost nothing anywhere in the world can be established that cannot be referred back to one of these aphorisms <note>original: *Aphorismorum*; a concise statement of a principle.</note>. But I pass on to the other part of the law, which deals with profane <note>original: *profana*; here meaning secular or non-religious matters.</note> affairs.

### ON THE LAW OF NATIONS AND CI-
### vil Law. CHAPTER XI.

Secular law <note>original: *IVs profanum*</note> consists of nature, the law of all nations, or the law of specific ones. Natural law encompasses everything that nature has taught animals to seek or to avoid. But since law is spoken of in respect to what is equitable and inequitable (matters where nature, being devoid of reason, cannot err, and which power does not reach), we should not dwell on it now; instead, we shall translate whatever is in it for human use—namely, into the law of nations. Therefore, the law of humans, or of nations (which is the same thing), is that which is approved by almost all mortals by nature, reason, or necessity, in which the practice of public peace is established.

Nature indeed suggests in this law that good should be sought and evil avoided: "good" being what pertains to the body, the soul, or the movement of fortune (which they call "external good"). "Evil," however, is what can undermine any of these. Reason is accustomed to suggest many things which prudent men judge should be observed or changed based on time, place, person, or status—even if it is not immediately obvious in the first promptings of nature. Such are those things known to work for the preservation of commonwealths, the status of cities, or their dignity. For although cities and human gatherings are not from nature, but rather established by art and prudence, they still seek their own preservation just like natural things: since all change is contrary to nature and stability. 

And thus they often do many things against nature by the authority of natural law. Indeed, it frequently happens that something is done following "nature joined with opinion" as a guide, which may seem to contravene the very actions of nature itself. If two cities, or any assembly of men, sought something that seemed to work for the preservation of both, without doubt each ought to strive for its own protection to obtain it. In that desire for its own safety, one city can and must leave the other behind, unless the object of desire is enough to satisfy both; in that case, equity <note>original: *æquitate*; the principle of fairness that goes beyond the literal letter of the law.</note> should be used. For it is better for one to be cheated of his desire than for one to serve the other and be deprived of natural liberty against nature. Therefore, that law is usually joined to violence if the rights of both are equal, and it takes its origin from force itself. Necessity <note>original: *Necessitati*</note> naturally has its place in the Commonwealth when we arm ourselves against the nature of others to keep ourselves and our own people safe, and we hold others as captives and slaves (against nature) so they do not harm us and instead might be useful. This part of the law is by far the most violent.

...most solid basis <note>original: *tissima*; completing the word from the previous page, likely *firmissima* or *sanctissima*</note> of natural law, which I am not sure everyone would approve of, unless it took its origin from a law even stronger than nature itself. For since man is born destitute of all the aids which a more kindly parent [Nature] has granted to other living creatures, he has his whole life joined to both natural anxiety and the necessity to protect himself and his possessions. From this "necessity of evil" (as it is commonly called), so that we might not grow sluggish in idleness, there arose whatever exists of the arts, of higher learning, and of our human condition. 

From this came the variety of foods, replacing the acorn. From this, in place of garments made of bark and the inner layers of trees, came linen, wool, and silk. In place of huts and hovels, came spacious houses, palaces, fortresses, and cities. In place of things growing wild, came things produced by industry and art—which, though acquired through necessity, have seen their growth increased by luxury. It can therefore be said that the thing we most greatly dread is and has been most useful to nature: namely, Necessity itself, which daily impels us to magnificent deeds. 

Its daughter is **Opinion** <note>In this context, Postel refers to *reputation* or the desire for the esteem of others.</note>, which usually incites us to all the greatest things through the desire for glory. It forces us to learn the arts that produce wealth and which are, or can be, a source of profit and fame. It causes us to recommend ourselves to posterity through brilliant exploits; and in short, it makes mortals attempt and complete the greatest things, those closest to the gods. From Necessity were established laws, cities encircled by walls, paved and cleared roads, constructed bridges, channeled aqueducts, and temples erected for the observance of religions and the admiration of the people—along with many other such things, without which the life of mortals is usually able to persist only with great difficulty.

But something must be said about that law which applies to a specific group of people, which is therefore called **Civil Law** <note>original: *ius civile*; the internal law of a city or state, as opposed to the universal Law of Nations.</note>. As I reflect on where this law took its origin, it does not seem clear whether it should be attributed to nature, or to its sister, **Custom**, or to both, or to chance and local reasoning. For it is common knowledge that individual peoples use certain laws of their own, and that these are joined to nature. This is indeed the very thing in which we showed a little earlier—in the principles and teachings of nature or wisdom—that all nations agree. 

Yet, beyond that, according to the reason of the place, the nation, the accepted morals, and the practice of custom, almost all peoples have something written in the place of law, or accepted through morals by silent consent, which others not only do not observe, but even despise and mock. Such laws are commonly called **Usages and Customs**, or **Local Law** <term>original: *ius locale*; laws specific to a particular territory or town rather than a whole kingdom.</term>. This example is evident not only among various peoples, regions, and places in secular affairs, but especially in religions accepted through long usage. For the Jew <note>original: *Hebraeus*</note> mocks the Christian and disapproves of his morals as sanctioned by law (as has always been the practice in matters of persuasion). The Christian mocks the Muslims <note>original: *Muhamedicos*</note>, and the Muslims mock both; thus they are affected by an implacable discord. 

Finally, every religion, even when distracted into various sects, is known to have far more factions than civil governments do. This indeed takes away the ability to converse, to travel, and to visit many regions. However, for individual peoples, this conflict and difference with their neighbor brings no small degree of persistence <note>original: *contumaciam*; here used to mean a stubborn steadfastness in maintaining one's own faith.</note> in retaining their religion—a quality than which nothing can be greater or more useful in a Commonwealth. Therefore, custom—whether confirmed by the silent judgment of men or even written down—is usually and ought to be observed according to the reason of the place. Where it has endured for a number of years (which should be more or fewer depending on the practice of the affairs and the fatherland), then at last it receives the force of law. It is therefore right that what differs from common law should stand by reason of its location. Otherwise, by chance, it often

->ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

it happens that many peoples, before they were held by any written prescription of laws, created **civil law** for themselves while they assented to certain things through a kind of silent consent. Therefore, **natural law** <note>original: *ius naturale*</note> ought to follow nature in all things; however, the **law of nations** <note>original: *gentium [ius]*; the laws common to all civilized peoples, distinct from the specific laws of one city</note> follows nature first, to be sure, but a nature joined to necessity and arranged by human reason, which itself not infrequently differs diametrically from natural law for the sake of the utility and preservation of the State <term>Respublica: The "commonwealth" or political community</term>. For a "good man" and a "good citizen" are usually very different, just as a "prudent man" and a "wise man" differ. Civil law follows customs received by whatever reasoning and approved only by those among whom they are in use; yet it does this most effectively when it has received the force of law through time or official sanction. For without custom, approval, or power, no law is ever accepted.

### ON THE CAUSES OF ANY 
### LAW WHATSOEVER. CHAPTER XII.

When we take up anything to be treated and taught through demonstration, we are accustomed, after the manner of the Philosophers, to ask whether it exists, what it is, for what ends it is prepared, or by what causes it arises. It is well established that there is some form of law among those humans who live an ordered life; and we have seen what it is. It remains to weigh those final and primary causes. The **end** <note>The "final cause" or ultimate goal</note> toward which the constitution of law tends is the peace of the entire State and its parts, so that each person may be kept to their duty, and whatever that duty may be that proceeds from them, it may be contributed to the use and preservation of the State; or (as Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and philosopher</note> says) the preservation of a legitimate and customary equality in things and legal cases. The **primary cause** is reason itself, partly implanted in the minds of men by providence, and partly revealed by the experience of things and the order of nature itself. This reason invites men toward the preservation of order and, as much as possible, toward a likeness of God (who is the highest approved being in religion); it prescribed the law to be used by posterity, either in writing or through custom without writing. And because no mortal could provide for all the errors of all people through legislation, laws gradually took their occasion from vices, ambiguities, or disputes; and someone might not undeservedly call them the "daughters and indicators of sin or error." To be sure, error was the cause for the most part, but an accidental one; prudent and just men were the primary cause. For unless those men had provided suitable remedies for vices through noble and just opinions—offering certainties for doubts—their decrees would undoubtedly never have obtained the status of law. For the interests of all, or of the majority of men, must be consulted by laws before they can be received.

Truly, laws are established for everyone to obey by the consent and authority of all, or of some, or of one, into whose words <note>original: *in cuius uerba iurare*; to swear an oath of allegiance to a leader's dictates</note> everyone must swear. Laws are established by the consent of all when a law is usually proposed over a three-market-day period <note>original: *trinundino die*; a Roman legal requirement that a proposed law be announced for three market days before being voted upon</note>, or on any fixed days, with the people called together in any known and public place—such as before the Rostra <note>The speaker's platform in the Roman Forum</note> in Rome, or before certain other statues (as was the custom in Athens to post them by the Eponymous Heroes <note>original: *eponymis*; the monument of the ten heroes representing the tribes of Athens, used as a public notice board</note>). All the common people then discern whether something is useful or useless; nor is it considered ratified, nor ought it be, until all or the greater part have consented to it. It was in this way that laws were introduced in a popular state (which the Greeks usually call a **democracy** or **polity**); so they were established wherever there was any measure of liberty under any administration. But the first method of establishing laws, gathered from the usage of all, came forth first either from everyone, or from a few, or from one. Whether the many or the few held a law to be proposed and examined, it was still necessary that it be done by a magistrate requesting it in the name of all, who would both post the proposal and collect the opinions given on the law. Sometimes eloquent private individuals were able to involve themselves, such as the orators <note>original: *rhetores*</note> in Athens; on the other hand...

He describes how laws are legitimate only when they serve the common good and are ratified through public consent, citing Roman and Athenian democratic practices.</summary>

To prevent these men from imposing false persuasions upon the common people, or passing a law without a popular vote, very heavy penalties were established. For what might **eloquence** not subvert, if the reins of affairs were yielded to it? Suppose eloquence is joined to the best of men. Truly, the opportunity for increasing one's wealth, or for capturing glory, or for factiously gratifying certain people, can indeed turn the best man into the most wicked, the simple man into the craftiest, and (to finish at once) a private citizen into a tyrant. These things have been seen quite often in those cities or provinces which a more long-winded eloquence has led astray. For just as we owe the benefit of every more humane constitution, the better parts of our deliberations, and the drawing of neighboring peoples into our own opinion and utility to the **skill of speaking** <note>original: *dicendi peritia*</note> when it is joined with **prudence**; so, once things are established, when eloquence continues to be excessively abundant while destitute of justice and equity, it undoubtedly brings not safety, but the blight of the State. 

Therefore, when many approve of a law, let a proclamation be made by the magistrates themselves, or by men received for that purpose—a process which they call **signification**. For not everyone, everywhere, is admitted to such an approval. To admit the plebeians and the more unrefined, the rustics, and the craftsmen <term>sellularios: literally "those who sit at a bench"; artisans or manual laborers</term>—who are generally devoid of common judgment—would surely be superfluous and turbulent. It is enough for there to be present from individual neighborhoods, villages, and municipalities either the single more eloquent men, or a few who will speak their opinion in the name of all and bring forth arguments back and forth; and this only in secular matters. For it is never permitted to waver or dispute concerning **religious matters**, except among the Pontiffs, the priests, and those who ought to preserve them. 

Laws are set down by a few, which the whole body recognizes, when the entire people is subject to an **aristocracy** or a **democracy**, and approves the judgments of some more sacred senate or order. Or, on the other hand, it occurs when the common people <note>original: *plebs*</note> hold such authority that even men of great power and the leading citizens obey their decrees. Such were the Roman **plebiscites**, passed during the reign of the tribunes of the people, enacted either for the favor or by the necessity of the commons, so they would not be oppressed by the [noble] citizens and the aristocracy. Because the administration of the **Optimates** <term>Optimatum: Rule by the "best" or the aristocratic elite</term> is full of equity, its edicts are easily approved by all as being most just, without even calling upon the common people. 

But when those leaders begin to turn the state to their own advantage, the people are conveniently bound by the ancient chain of laws; then they are miserably despoiled by the laws passed, the State which should have been preserved is undermined, and it hastens its own ruin. **Senate decrees**, the sanctions of the courts, and **judicial rulings** <note>original: *aresta*; referring to the French *arrêts* or final court decisions</note> also impose law upon those who approve of their judgments, because of an outstanding observance of the **just and the good** <note>original: *aequi bonique*; a legal principle of fairness</note> which is usually found either nowhere else or only among them. 

One person has the right of bringing laws, either by his own authority, or by granted or mixed authority. For he is either appointed, or he appoints himself, or both. Any **Prince**, being powerful enough to use his own and pure power over his subjects—since they, for the sake of public peace and by right or rather by injury, find it more useful to obey than to reject the yoke of empire—is accustomed to prescribe to them what condition of affairs he wishes to be held in the name of all and for the public utility. Indeed, he would rather remove from the midst or compel those who refuse to do what is commanded, than suffer his authority to be easily diminished—unless he is granting **privileges** (which do not serve as a general example) or is venting his rage against everyone. 

Hence the edicts of Princes are usually called **pleasures** <note>original: *placita*; from the legal maxim "What pleases the prince has the force of law"</note>, because they are for the most part proposed by absolute will. No private individual is permitted to oppose or resist these, just as laws took their names from the "counsel and prudence" of the **Senate**, or from the "decrees" <note>original: *scitis*; referring to *plebiscita*</note> of the **common people** (that is, from things known and recognized). For this reason, the most excellent of the governments of states, when it is well and holily preserved, is the **royal** or **imperial power**. For if you remove the names from the midst—leaders, kings, emperors, and men of any other dignity—[they are the same].

<meta>This page continues Postel’s discussion on the origins of legal authority. Having examined popular assemblies, he now moves to the authority of the Prince (the Monarch) and the role of legal experts in shaping the law.</meta>

<page-num>296</page-num>
<header>ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD</header>

Those who are able to exercise absolute power over certain people hold that right not by nature, but through the customs of nations or the ambition of Princes. Therefore, that one individual who holds power is like a **living law** <note>original: *lex uiua*</note>; he ensures that established laws are kept, and he either amends those that are failing or proposes new ones himself. No private citizen can or should demand an accounting for these actions, except in cases where the Prince receives his moderation from a senate. For it is likely that—unless the Prince be, to use the Greek term, **most tyrannical** <note>original: *τυραννικώτατοϛ*</note>—those things he wishes to be ratified have been examined in a council of wise men and those who preside over the administration of affairs for the safety of all. If this has been done, it is not for anyone of private status to debate or scrutinize it. For the **Principate** is a sacrosanct thing, very close to religion: it is not without danger to wish to demand a reason for its decisions, just as one does not demand a reason for religion. For since the affairs of mortals have need of stability, and because the very life and duration of those affairs depends on constancy, undoubtedly whatever things serve to preserve peace and integrity must be maintained at all costs, even if they are partly unfair. For it is certain that if the head of the State is overturned (which must happen if the Prince’s command is rejected), the members will also collapse, be separated from one another, and be mutually forsaken. Indeed, if a Prince is destroyed (unless another more just ruler were already taking power), not only do those laws he himself brought or could bring perish, but all those laws received from the ancients under his rule are usually shattered and cut down—especially if a new ruler is introduced by some violent movement or sedition; otherwise, they are changed daily. 

Furthermore, the origin of Princes who exercise absolute power arose in the past from **virtue**. Because of their merit, the reins of all affairs were permitted to them by their subjects, so that what was once granted by authority now stands by its own right. Thus, new principalities are for the most part granted by authority; over the course of time, they draw this into absolute power, and the descendants then use their own pleasure, being confirmed by the long duration of time. **Mixed principalities** are those where they partly impose and partly receive laws, such as Princes moderated by aristocracies, who are chosen by election rather than by hereditary succession; one must abide by the decisions of all these. In an altogether different category are **praetors** <note>In ancient Rome, these were high-ranking magistrates</note> who have received power from elsewhere; their edicts, supported by the authority of the Princes or the powers to whom they are subject, pass into law. This is the kind the Romans call **honorary law** <term>ius honorarium: law based on the authority of magistrates rather than traditional statutes</term>. But because it is necessary for the one who establishes laws to be most wise, as we have said, Princes and magistrates have granted the power of responding on points of law to wise and prudent men, imparting their own authority to them. This part of the law is by far the most excellent, as it is entirely destitute of personal passions. For this reason, a good portion of the **written law** among all nations consists of the responses of these wise men. Through them, and through the decrees of the High Priests, not only did the Roman state grow, but also all states that have lasted for a long time. For that reason, everyone who uses the Latin language still uses that law today. For the **Pandects** <term>the Digest; a vast collection of Roman legal opinions</term> are nothing other than the responses of wise men who were either clarifying the edicts of the praetors or bringing forth their own. The **Muftis** <note>original: *Muphtij*</note> among the Arabs hold that same legal standing. Formerly, among the Hebrews, the **seventy elders** chosen by Moses and Jethro <note>Referring to the Sanhedrin; Jethro was Moses' father-in-law who advised him to appoint judges</note> held it. Their responses were never made open until **CHRIST**, the restorer of that religion and the founder of the new one, revealed and made public the **crafty justice** <note>original: *ἀκεβοδικαίαν* (akebodikaian); likely referring to deceptive or overly legalistic judgment</note> and guile hidden within them, and rejected it. For all things, however excellent, if they do not grow worse through long use, they are certainly prone to being subverted by sharp-witted men. Truly, it is not rare for these legal responses—when they are joined to opinions, religions, and personal affections—to also possess their own share of unfairness...

reason. Therefore, those laws which are connected to the preservation of religion or of a greater power tend to weigh equity and reason less than those which are rendered by private individuals without any personal bias. For those who hold the reins of power, or who strive to favor someone based on their own authority, accommodate many things to personal favor. On the other hand, those who propose nothing for themselves except what is fair and good are usually far more equitable in providing for the needs of posterity than a Prince or a Magistrate; for the latter, while often looking out too much for their own profit, or looking to the customs of their own age and State, tend to establish many things that are neither favorable nor useful to posterity. 

There is also another certain origin and cause of law which does not pertain to everyone living under a single Prince. Its utility is nonetheless directed toward the good of the State (for otherwise it would not be considered law), but this type of law must be prescribed and approved according to the various conditions of men. For every assembly of mortals, whether in secular or religious matters, possesses—in addition to laws either received by long usage or recently passed, and based on religious, natural, civil, or international law—customs specific to their own conditions or crafts, which do not exceed their own status or manner of life. Regarding these, neither judges can rule nor craftsmen of other arts can speak, owing to their ignorance of them. Hence the sailor has maritime laws; the stonemason and the blacksmith have theirs; the goldsmith has his regarding golden objects according to the usage received in his craft. He explains to the judge the matters belonging to the craft, and this is done not only by the logic of the craft or the material usually handled in it, but also by the usage of specific places and people. 

Indeed, that part is by far the most difficult to know, as it cannot be handled by common law because it is so closely tied to the varying opinions of different men. However, once the utility to the fatherland is proved by a judge, it gives strength to those laws approved by **tacit consent** <note>original: *tacito consensu*; this refers to laws that are accepted through practice and silence rather than being formally written down</note>, through which the Prince also seems to approve them indirectly. Laws are never formally published regarding those crafts, because that **sacrosanct struggle** <note>original: *sacrosancta illa lis*; Postel views professional competition as a "holy" or healthy rivalry that maintains standards</note> and competition, by which one man strives to outdo another in his craft, usually preserves those laws diligently enough—not through malicious means, but through better skills. For everyone strives to be the best in his own craft: a surveyor <note>original: *mensor*</note> measures as best he can; but if he declares a false measurement, it is necessary for the error to be detected by a more skilled surveyor and proved to the judge. Only then does the judge discern whether the error should be punished. For although there is no "consent" from one who errs, nevertheless, when someone professes a craft of which he is ignorant, he ought to pay for the loss caused by the error he committed. 

But this topic is more extensive than can be covered in a few words. Therefore, the judgments and knowledge of all crafts must be referred to those skilled in the art <note>original: *artis peritos*</note>, who, according to the laws received among the most excellent practitioners, may decide on the nature of the sin, error, vice, or virtue committed, and refer these to the judge. We may call this "unwritten law," just as there are many such things in the civil law of individual places. As for written law, we see it everywhere among nations, proceeding from religion and the command of the Prince, and ignorance of it should excuse no one. For if ignorance of the law were admitted even once, it would be the same as if the law were not written at all. For any litigant would pretend not to know that part of the law which seemed to work against him. But the law and custom of particular assemblies

## CONCERNING THE MATTERS TREATED
### in Civil Law, Chapter XIII.

<meta>catchword: All</meta>

<summary>Postel explains that specialized professional customs (like those of sailors or smiths) function as a form of unwritten law that requires expert testimony, contrasting this with the written laws of the Sovereign which no citizen is permitted to ignore.</summary>
<keywords>customary law, unwritten law, professional ethics, legal equity, guilds, expert testimony, civil law, William Postel</keywords>

--- Page 310 ---
<meta>This page continues Postel’s legal taxonomy. Having previously discussed the origins of law from authority and custom, he now moves into the categorization of law based on its subjects: persons and things.</meta>

-># ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

Every law deals with persons, or with things that are sacred, profane, or mixed. Regarding sacred things, pontifical laws <note>original: *iura pontificia*; referring here to ecclesiastical or church law</note> and the primary prescriptions of all religions are concerned. Civil laws do indeed give instructions regarding sacred matters, but only insofar as they relate to their preservation, rather than to their institution, restoration, management, or usage. Civil law deals with profane things. These are either public or private: that is, they concern the property of the entire body of the State, or of individuals. Mixed things are matters of religion, such as whatever land or movable goods are assigned and granted for the use and preservation of religion. For the right itself <note>the legal claim to the property</note> pertains to the sacred, while the physical objects themselves are profane. Yet, since they can never be separated (for if the object did not exist, the right would not exist, and vice versa), one might rightly say they belong to a "mixed law." It is with this category that the volume of our law which they call the *Decretals* <note>The *Decretales*: a major collection of Canon Law forming part of the *Corpus Iuris Canonici*</note> primarily deals. For 그 book was published when religion had already increased in wealth and piety was afflicted; whereas otherwise, the decrees of the holy fathers had dealt copiously with piety itself, ceremonies, and spiritual matters. Thus, the condition of the times changes the laws. Likewise, some things are corporeal, others incorporeal. Corporeal things are men, or their objects subject to the senses. Incorporeal things are the rights themselves to things: such as an action, a sale, a hiring, a leasing, or an inheritance. Furthermore, some things are public, others private. The latter are among the goods of individuals; the former belong to no one, but are for everyone. However, since all laws are established for the sake of man, we shall treat him first, as if he were the prince of all things. First, we will discuss his condition; then his possession; and finally, the mutual relationship of all men must be addressed.

### THE DIVISION OF THE CONDITION OF MEN. Chapter XIV.

All men are either free and freeborn, or slaves, or of a mixed condition. By "free," we mean those who clearly exercise their own will in conducting their affairs (provided they commit nothing against equity and the good, or against received laws). For nature willed that all men be produced as such for the most part. Necessity introduced the condition of slaves <term>servitus: slavery; historically derived by Roman jurists from *servare*, "to preserve," because captives were saved rather than killed</term> against nature, when it became customary for men to be preserved by other men who had been their adversaries. For in ancient times, it was the custom to kill all enemies in war. Eventually, partly out of utility and partly out of piety, they began to preserve them for the use of labor, and to deprive them of their natural liberty so they might not cause harm, and so that their work might be beneficial. Thus, they entirely lost their rights of nature by the consent of their masters, and they began to count for nothing in the State. They were permitted to do nothing unless it yielded to the benefit of their masters. No legal actions and no contracts were permitted to them, because they held no legal standing—not even in sacred matters, which nevertheless usually belong to everyone. They procreate, acquire, and live for their master, not for themselves. Nevertheless, they are held by natural law as long as they are human beings. 

When this slavery exists in a man of very great talent and great resources, it is certainly most contrary to nature, because a most worthy person is sometimes made subordinate to a most unworthy one. But if a man is somewhat duller and less fit for managing affairs, and serves a wiser master by whom he is, as it were, guided by the hand, the prince of philosophers, Aristotle, asserted and demonstrated in his *Politics* <note>Aristotle’s *Politics*, Book I, where he discusses "natural slavery"</note> that such a state is indeed slavery, but it is both for the practical use of things and according to nature. For it goes well for such a person when that which nature had given as crippled and unfit is corrected by a master and rendered suitable for conducting affairs for the use of the State. Those of "mixed" condition are they who, although they can now use the prescriptions of the laws according to the custom of the State, nevertheless...

->### BOOK III OF GUILLAUME POSTEL<-

...they also recognize both patrons <note>original: *patronos*; in Roman law, a former owner who remains a legal protector of a freed slave</note> and those to whom they are indebted, either in all things or in certain matters in which they are physically subject. Such duties are personal, subjecting humans to other humans. The freedmen <note>original: *libertini*</note> of the Romans were under this mixed legal status. For that reason, it was strictly forbidden—out of reverence—to bring a lawsuit involving an "infamous name" <note>a legal action that would damage the defendant's reputation and civil standing</note> against a patron or the patron's immediate parents, just as it is forbidden for a slave to sue a master.

The law differs between these two groups in this way: a master holds power of life and death over slaves, though the Prince <note>the sovereign or head of state</note> ensures that this power is not exercised too severely by private citizens; however, patrons no longer hold that same legal right over freedmen. Liberty is restored in any number of ways, provided the master is willing and consenting, unless it is done either to defraud creditors or by a master of "imperfect judgment," whom a slave might easily manipulate—such as those who are minors, the "furious" <note>original: *furiosi*; those suffering from active insanity</note>, or those whose minds are otherwise impaired. For if sound judgment is present, every manumission <note>original: *manumissio*; the formal act of freeing a slave</note> is usually permitted in favor of liberty. It makes no difference whether one was born a slave or became one, since all are of similar legal status once that condition prevails.

Furthermore, free people either live solely by their own right <note>original: *suo iure*</note>, or partly by their own and partly by another’s. A father, master, tutor, or curator acts by his own right, provided he improves the affairs of the ward or the person of unsound mind. Those who live partly by their own and partly by another’s right include a son, a minor, or an insane person. Because these individuals are incautious and inexperienced in affairs, they are restrained by parents or tutors to prevent them from ruining the household estate or abusing their youth through recklessness or heat. Therefore, they are allowed to improve their condition without the authority of tutors or fathers, but they are by no means allowed to make it worse. Those who are insane can, while they possess "lucid and clear intervals" <note>original: *lucida & clara interualla*; periods of temporary sanity</note>, enter into contracts both for and against their own interests; otherwise, neither is permitted without a curator.

There is also a certain imitation of nature introduced among many people, such as when someone seeks children for themselves through adoption from elsewhere. In this matter, it was decided to imitate nature: for a younger person cannot adopt an older one. Furthermore, the first degrees of affinity are usually preserved among brothers, sisters, twins, and adoptees; they cannot contract a marriage unless an emancipation <note>original: *emancipatio*; the legal release from paternal power</note> precedes it, and this is according to Roman law. For these matters are based on opinion, and are therefore matters of "arbitrary law" <note>original: *iuris arbitrarij*; law based on human decision or convention rather than natural necessity</note>. Yet it was seen as most important to follow nature when handing down the law.

There is another division of humans: all people are either for the purpose of judging the law, explaining it, or simply hearing it. In this, all indeed agree: when their own affairs are at stake, every individual (even the greatest magistrates or princes) must "hear" the law <note>submit to legal authority</note>. However, it is accepted everywhere among nations that two types of people "speak" the law <note>original: *dicere ius*; to exercise judicial authority</note>. These are judges appointed either by princes or by the litigants themselves. Since the duty of princes, who were recently established among men, was to speak the law, and there arose daily a greater abundance of lawsuits than any one man could suffice to terminate, the princes granted their authority to judges. This allowed the judges to settle disputes between litigants with equity, and their sentences were to be upheld no differently than the decrees of princes. Later, more cautious times discovered the benefit of appeal <note>original: *appellationis beneficium*</note>, through which it is not permitted to resist the law for the sake of the peace of the Republic.

Simple or "compromised" arbitrators are also judges in any Republic; the plaintiff and defendant usually agree and swear to their sentence, either by a pact of not withdrawing or otherwise. This was indeed invented as a support for the judges and for the convenience of the litigants. There are truly many types of these judges. For every Prince reserves for himself the judicial investigation of certain matters, and the highest magistrates take cognizance of all business, or only of some. But more on that shortly. Those who explain the law, or set forth cases to the judges according to the law, are either advocates or procurators <note>legal representatives or agents</note>, since the litigants themselves are frequently ignorant of the law. People of private condition only "hear" the law, unless perhaps they are occasionally appointed as arbitrators to "speak" it. All others, besides private citizens, besides the fact that they "speak" the law, also fulfill their duty by hearing and obeying...

->### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

...are subject to the law. The final division of men is this: all men are either nobles, commoners, or are dedicated to religion. Among all nations, virtue—especially military virtue or that which preserves the commonwealth—has brought a reward to its possessor by the consensus of those who perceived or recognized it. This reward is a certain renown and the memory of a benefit once conferred upon the state, from which the families of the "illustrious" <note>original: *illustrium*; a specific rank in late Roman and Renaissance social hierarchy</note> arise among every people. Not infrequently, a great force of wealth has achieved this, leading to authority, force, and power, so that a person was believed to be greater than ordinary men. From this public opinion, they acquired confirmation and authority, and even tyranny. Thus, some nations have allowed this greatness to continue in posterity; others only in those who acquired virtue through their own industry, lest a descendant take pride in a false name without having their father's virtue and glory. Indeed, this latter opinion usually incites more people to virtue every day. Those who lift up the Commonwealth either by wisdom or by wealth are deservedly to be held in that same number. These are the origins of nobility. Commoners <note>original: *ignobiles*; literally "not-noble," referring to those without inherited or granted rank</note> are those who have performed no distinguished deed in the state; or if they did, they were abandoned by an ungrateful multitude or by a prince (who tends to fear or envy those who are somewhat more famous), or were stripped of their status through the perishing memory of their ancestors. For nature produced all men with a similar origin, body, and soul; it is virtue and opinion that elevate them. Those dedicated to religion are those upon whom the care of increasing and preserving religion rests. And these types of men preserve the condition of souls, bodies, or external things. Religion and philosophy care for souls; the soldier, the judge, and the doctor care for bodies; and both the judge and the soldier care for the goods of fortune—unless the proper use of things is overturned. For "who will guard the guardians themselves?" <note>original: *quis custodiet ipsos custodes*; a quote from the Roman satirist Juvenal</note> Truly, though these officials may be wicked, they are to be tolerated rather than removed,

### WHAT RIGHTS HUMANS POSSESS 
### by benefit of law, and how rights are lost or conditions are changed. Chapter XV.

In the affairs of individual humans, there tend to be rights of nature—that is, liberty; rights of the place in which one was born or received, which the Romans call citizenship <note>original: *civitatem*</note>; and rights of blood, which we call family. For any human is born free, and is usually born in a specific place and from specific people. Therefore, one has the right of using one's own judgment from nature: the right of self-preservation and of possessing things for one's own protection usually follows from the benefit of the law used by the people where one is born; and one is necessarily assigned to a certain family, from which one was born as if from a branch. The rights of nature are lost either by one's own fault or by the act of another. When someone allows themselves to be sold for a price, or is obligated by their own deed to serve with their body—such as when it arises from a debt of their property or labor to be provided by them—then they strip themselves of their natural right. Such a person also contracts infamy <note>a loss of legal standing and reputation</note> along with their loss, while perishing by their own will. By the act of another, rights are lost when someone is captured by any enemy and led into slavery; when they have freed themselves from this, they return to their own rights by the "right of return" <term>Postliminium: a Roman legal concept where a person recaptured from an enemy resumes all their former rights and status</term>. For misfortune brought about by necessity does not usually, nor should it, obstruct one’s birthright or natural right. Regarding the law of the city, we possess either public things only, or both public and private things (that is, our own). Although public things are "in the goods of no one" <note>original: *in nullius bonis*; a legal term for property that has no private owner, like a graveyard or a public road</note>, they are nevertheless for the use of all; a person stripped of all means is no less able than a rich man to approach sacred sites anywhere in the world, to walk on a public road, or to frequent the forum and places dedicated to public utility, and to enjoy the use of air, water, and fire. Furthermore, laws are established for his preservation just as much as for the rich man. For laws follow nature, not fortune, and whatever they deal with regarding property, they do so in order to study the preservation of nature. Moreover, since by the benefit of those laws it is permitted to possess one’s own goods anywhere in the world, we also [owe] the preservation of our affairs to them.

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK III.

...we owe. For either our things and our works have become our own, or we make the things of others our own through purchase, exchange, or occupation. From the works of others come donations and inheritances; by accepting these or entering into them, we make them ours, a right which we owe to the laws themselves. For unless the laws and the will of the magistrate made contracts valid, kept us in our possessions, and established the heir as a "living possessor" immediately upon the death of the owner—whom we therefore call an heir (whether he be a legal heir, an "own" heir, or a "necessary" heir <note>original: *legitimus, suus, seu necessarius*; these are technical categories in Roman inheritance law regarding who is required or entitled to inherit</note>)—and unless the laws willed that a thing should belong to the recipient of a gift, we would undoubtedly possess nothing certain. We would be tossed about, and everything would be acquired by the stronger; everything would happen which usually occurs during the total overthrow of society. Therefore, the legal expert Paulus <note>original: *Paulus iurisconsultus*; Julius Paulus, a prominent 3rd-century Roman jurist</note> rightly ascribed everything we own to the State, so that we might understand the State to be the force and majesty of the laws approved in any given place. 

For men come together under laws: those who come together are either citizens, or like citizens. Citizens are those who can perform the duties of a magistrate under the laws; those who are "like citizens" are those who only find it necessary to obey. These relationships exist within the state. We either hold a family, or are held by a family, or both, or neither. It was the custom of the Romans that all people born from male children—whether they were sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, or great-great-grandsons—remained in that family as long as the founder and father of that family survived. It was necessary for that family (both male and female) to obey whatever the parent prescribed as proper in the first place. That entire family always fell back under the power of the elder, except when the young women were married. For then, as if they had been released from power <note>original: *manumissæ*; the legal act of releasing someone from a superior's control</note>, they passed from their father's power <note>original: *patria potestas*; the absolute authority a Roman father held over his descendants</note> into another's power, where they bore children—not for the power of the father from whom they came, but for the husband or the husband's father. This was said to be a "diminution of status" <note>original: *capite minui*; a legal term for a change or loss of civil rights or family standing</note> and a loss of family. Unless a release from power <note>original: *manumissio*</note> or a transition to another power (such as adoption) exempted the males, or unless they were deprived of paternal goods through ingratitude, they never left the family. 

Lastly, those who have not yet fathered children are merely "held" in the family. Only he "holds" a family whose elder parents have died, or who has entirely withdrawn from their location, region, and laws, and has fathered children in another Republic. He who is "of his own right" <note>original: *suo iure*; a person not under the legal power of another, such as a father</note> even among parents both holds a family and is held; he who is in the middle between these extremes neither holds nor is held. This is also true for one who is a stranger anywhere among nations where he has not fathered children; in such places, out of reverence and the honor of marriage, those born out of wedlock <note>original: *spurij, & uulgo concepti*</note> were held as such before they fathered children, unless the law or the Prince comes to their aid and enrolls them in the family of a specific father. Slaves are such that if they father children, they father them for their masters. Because of the status of their birth, they have perished by the "greatest diminution of status" <note>original: *capitis maxima diminutione*; the total loss of liberty, citizenship, and family rights</note>. For they are entirely nothing as far as Roman rights are concerned, except in the interest of the master. 

The common usage of mortals attributes a family to a father only until the children have taken wives or have reached an age fit for managing an inheritance; then they usually become clearly "of their own right," just as the emancipated do. But these things are matters of opinion. It is enough that the natural father presides over his own with authority as long as they are healthy in body and sound in judgment, so that they may rule the family themselves and look well to their own affairs. For this is proved by the example of all nations and living creatures: that there may be greater liberty. Roman law <note>original: *Ius Romanum*</note> provided for the position of a parent until the twenty-fifth year, because human judgment seems weak and insufficiently trained before that age, and no one ought to be destitute of a father's guidance. Otherwise, various opinions are to be followed regarding the proper age for managing affairs. For reason and a more perfect judgment must be prepared by experience of things, not by nature alone. Therefore, when a father has left surviving children before that age, it ought to be established by law that guardians and curators <note>original: *tutores & curatores*; two distinct types of legal guardians in Roman law for different age groups</note> should perform the role of the father. For unless the dying father has appointed a guardian for the children, the nearest relatives ought to take care of them; otherwise, by the authority of the praetor...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

[A] guardian or curator is appointed, both for those who suffer in mind <note>The mentally ill or "insane" in legal terms.</note>—since it is in the interest of the State that no one should misuse their own property—and especially to help those in certain human conditions where they might commit something to the detriment of their affairs, even if done by contract. Whoever is cast out from a family, or departs willingly, if they are able to do so, is considered to have undergone the least <term>decrease of status</term> <note>original: *minima capitis minutio*; a Roman legal term for a change in family status, such as adoption or emancipation, that does not affect citizenship or freedom.</note>. If we lose the right of citizenship without having committed a crime, it is also necessary to lose our status in the family: such as those who are deported, relegated, or foreigners. There is also a middle decrease of status; and when we are slaves, stripped of every right, we are afflicted with the maximum decrease of status. For even that which nature had given is lost.

Indeed, antiquity recognized a twofold kind of slaves. One was common, born without a crime, and usually captured because they wanted their homeland or faction preserved; these were allowed to recover everything by the <term>right of postliminy</term> <note>original: *postliminii iure*; the legal fiction that a person captured by the enemy, upon returning home, is restored to all their former rights as if they had never been captured.</note>. The other kind resulted from a crime, whom the Romans used to call <term>slaves of punishment</term> <note>original: *servos poenae*; individuals sentenced to life at hard labor or the mines, who were legally considered "dead" and had no heirs or property.</note>. For however atrocious the crimes were, antiquity spared human life as much as it could. He who took up arms or secretly conspired against the State in which he was born, raised, and preserved; he who attempted to overturn religion; or he who plotted against the life of a man (for whose mutual protection nature created us to be dutiful); he who killed a man willingly and with premeditation (unless while defending himself); he who plundered the property of others; or he who rose up against the laws and the master's will to the destruction of nature and public peace—such a person is deservedly deprived of the help of human society and ought to be cut off like a rotten limb. 

Yet the wisdom of the ancients knew that men could return to fruitfulness [reform] just as they could sin. For that reason, in place of the death which the offenders deserved, they devised various kinds of punishments. A judge had the power to establish these according to the prescription of the laws, moderated by equity and the "living law." Those afflicted with the most severe punishment were usually relegated to dig in the mines for the use of the State—where a man, even with a very healthy body, can scarcely last for five years. Others were punished with exile, either perpetual or temporary relegation to islands, or others to certain foreign provinces. They attempted everything to keep a man alive, even though he deservedly ought to be deprived of laws, family, and nature. For life is the highest thing; death is the lowest and yet most useful, and to be desired by the wretched. A longer punishment is heavier than death among any nation. He who contravenes the laws is usually deprived of them, either by death or the penalty of exile, proscription, or any other punishment. But let these things be said concerning the possession of men and the change of their condition.

### WHAT MEN CAN MUTUALLY PROVIDE TO ONE
->ANOTHER, OR HOW THEY CAN HARM. Cap. XVI.<-

It is clear that whatever right exists is placed in <term>duty</term> <note>original: *officio*; referring to the moral and social obligations individuals owe to one another to maintain a functioning society.</note>, if men would observe it mutually under the guidance of nature. But that part of duty which brings advantage to us or our affairs, we all easily receive, seek, and solicit; yet we frequently neglect to repay it, unless compelled by shame or the force of the laws. For since nature brought us forth naked, she also left us with a certain desire, not only for accumulating things for the present, but as if we were to live forever, without any limit to greed. To this necessity was added the ruin of the world—opinion—so that we desire future things not only for use, but for glory. Care for posterity, lest they fall into miseries before our eyes, has increased the desire for possessing and has forced equity and gratitude to go into exile among men. With equity driven out, men began to deal in repayments, with faith and reality [deeds] being tied not to the man, nor to his word (which nonetheless was always the greatest bond among good men), but to the things themselves, which on both sides consist of three parts, whatever...
