<meta>This page continues Postel’s legal and philosophical examination of human society. Having previously discussed the status of persons and the nature of slavery, he now transitions into the law of things (property), the origins of currency, and the legal definitions of usage and profit.</meta>

->GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK III<-

For one human can provide to another either in presenting a thing, or in its use, or in an action. We give property that is moveable, or self-moving, or immovable, or the rights to obtain them. A moveable thing is whatever is apart from the soil and lacks life; a self-moving thing includes all living creatures. Immovable property includes the soil, water, and buildings. These things are usually transferred either simply in the hope of receiving gratitude, or for the preservation of nature, or by a specific vow of the giver: such as gifts, inheritances, legacies, and other types of donation. For he who gives receives nothing except the goodwill which he hopes for rather than possesses; if anything is done against this, or against the agreements made in the gift, the recipient is rightly noted for ingratitude, and as an ungrateful person, he can be deprived of the thing given, unless it was a simple gift. For if a heinous crime is committed against the one who gave, the laws rightly moderate such attempts with their severity. For the laws live in the place of both the deceased and the absent: and for that reason, they ratify the things established by them.

Property can be exchanged for property (now I set aside money from "things" for a little while) when solid objects are given for objects without any external valuation, which was the method by which crude antiquity used to conduct its trade. Since there was much labor involved in this—in driving and carrying things back and forth—mortals devised something for the greatest good of all. First (though it eventually turned to their own destruction), they sought something that could easily be exchanged in the place and name of all things and would be of the smallest mass: namely, money <note>original: *pecuniam*</note>, which takes its name from the primary possession of the ancients, which was in cattle <note>original: *pecunia* derives from *pecus*, meaning livestock or cattle, the earliest form of wealth.</note>. Whether it be of iron, lead, leather, wood, gold, or silver, or from any other material (as it certainly was in the past), it mattered not, provided that by the consensus of laws and the people, or by the command of princes, it was valued as much as the things themselves were. 

But when, after the world’s youth, other materials were recognized as being liable to adulteration (as with wood), or to greater bulk, or to corruption, gold and silver began to be approved by the consensus of almost all the peoples of the world. It is established that this was also done by necessity. For when many provinces were not self-sufficient and were forced to seek necessary supports from neighboring regions, and that force of law which had given a price to money elsewhere was unknown, almost all mortals were forced to embrace gold, both for its tiny mass and because it is minimally or hardly at all subject to corruption, and its weight is equal everywhere; its power, like that of a God, would be the same everywhere. Whereas before its frequent use, it was neglected in many regions and was used no differently than iron for making chains for criminals; a good part of the recently opened world <note>A reference to the Americas or "New World" discovered in Postel's era.</note> was even ignorant of its use before the plague of the corrupt world, avarice, arrived there. Now, therefore, gold is sought after in the whole world, in whose dominion is placed whatever the earth brings forth or hides; in its name, one may obtain the property, the use, and the action from any man. Because of this, the ancient fictions of the poets rightly called him Dis and Pluto <note>In mythology, Pluto (or Dis Pater) was the god of the underworld and of the mineral wealth found within the earth.</note>, the king of the infernal regions: because whatever was dug out even from the innermost bowels of the sea and the earth would be under his jurisdiction. 

Sometimes one or more things are given for the use of another or of many. Furthermore, what "use" is, is clear enough: it is the right of using the property of another for a certain time, whether continuous or separated by intervals, while the substance of the things themselves remains intact. When this extends more broadly, namely to every product of the things, then it is called not use, but <term>usufruct</term> <note>original: *ususfructus*; the legal right to use and enjoy the profits/fruits of another's property without destroying it.</note>. For in "use," the necessity of the user is considered; in "usufruct," both convenience and whatever is placed in the profit of the thing are considered. Although use and usufruct are themselves things, insofar as they are rights, nevertheless in law we more properly call "things" those objects for the sake of which, or from which, utility can be drawn. <meta>This page continues Postel’s discussion on the exchange of goods and services. ->ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

...may receive the use, or the usufruct <note>original: "usum fructum"; the legal right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property without destroying it</note>, or vice versa. The logic of an "action" <note>original: "facti ratio"; referring to a legal deed or performance</note> is applied very widely. For it can exist in duty, in obligation, in negligence, and even in a "damage not yet committed" <note>original: "infecto"; a legal term for potential future harm, like a crumbling wall that might fall on a neighbor's house</note>. It is also very frequent for a physical thing to be given as payment in place of an action: for instance, if I give you that field or that object so that you may do this for me. In that case, you owe me the performance of the action, just as I provided the object to you. From this, innumerable types of contracts arise; although they consist only of things, uses, or actions exchanged individually or together, they are all usually measured by money. When the question of "how much it matters" <note>the value of the interest or damages</note> arises, it is measured by arithmetic equality <note>equal value for equal value</note> or by an appraisal of what that thing was worth. In the manifold bond of obligations, humans owe and are accustomed to provide these three things to one another—if they follow the law. 

But if they continue to be unjust and unfair toward those to whom they are indebted—doing so because they act against the law itself, while the law preserves the actions of mortals in the place of "exiled faith" <note>meaning that legal action replaces the trust or "good faith" that has vanished from the relationship</note>—then they do more than just neglect the faith pledged by themselves, or by those whose rights they use, or faith born from the condition of things. They even go against the contracts, pacts, and agreements that ought to be kept among all mortals. From this, legal actions were born to pursue justice. 

For the Commonwealth <note>original: "Respublica"</note>, like a most devoted mother, since she has taken us up to be nurtured in her bosom, also takes care that we obtain through her power whatever is our right. This ensures that we are never left destitute of the duties useful and necessary for living, and that "contempt for one's own"—which is to say, injury—does not reign among men. From such injury comes the ruin of both nature and human affairs. Therefore, even if we are unable to pursue our things, uses, actions, or rights, or if we neglect them, or if an injury is done to us in our property or our person, the Commonwealth herself takes it upon herself to avenge or help us by a specific name <note>legal standing</note>, wherever her citizens may be in the world. She places the unborn child into possession <note>original: "ventrem in possessionem mittit"; a Roman legal protection for the inheritance rights of an unborn child</note>, she gives tutors to orphans, guardians to adults and the mentally ill, she avenges the wronged, and punishes the guilty, even when no one demands it. We are compelled to confess that we owe this much to nature, to prudence, to reason, and to well-established laws—and thereby to God, the Best and Greatest, the author of them all. Thus, humans are harmed when they are forced by the power of laws to seek from one another what reason and right should have persuaded them to do, give, or avoid doing of their own accord.

## ON THE ORIGIN OF INJURY,
### CHAPTER XVII.

It can be clearly seen by anyone looking closely that necessity, ambition, and greed are the causes of injury. For he who inflicts an injury upon the body is led by a desire for revenge or for glory, wanting to be or appear superior to the other; he who sins against property is surely tormented by greed, necessity, or ambition. Furthermore, there are three species of injury: impiety, greed, and outrage <note>original: "contumelia"</note>. Impiety despises the gods, religion, and the things assigned to religion and the gods—such as sacred objects, persons, or the deceased—and it treats them with insults, eventually extending to parents and the fatherland. For these things ought to be sacrosanct not only by profane laws, but by sacred ones. Therefore, he who sins against these things sins most seriously at least twice: for he commits a crime against humans and against the prescriptions of both types of law <note>civil and religious law</note>. Greed specifically, along with necessity, makes people hanker after and snatch what belongs to others. This happens regarding things obtained for the duties of life. We inflict injury on another either by words, by slander, or by blows. Words and outrage sin against reputation; blows sin against bodies. Truly, the cause of inflicting injury arises in a human either from necessity, or opinion, or will, or through stubbornness and fraud. Opinion persuades one that things are different than they are; humans are generally more prone to follow opinion than the truth.

...truth. From this arises the destruction of the world; "mine" and "thine," when they are confused, produce lawsuits for us. For while I believe your things are mine, and you believe the opposite, we feed the crows remarkably well—I meant to say the **advocates** <note>original: "patronos"; Postel is using a common satirical trope comparing lawyers to scavenging crows (coruos) who feast on the carcasses of their clients' estates</note>—and we prefer to fight to the "utmost right" <note>original: "summo iure"; a reference to the legal maxim *summum ius, summa iniuria*, or "the extreme of the law is the extreme of injustice," meaning that applying law too strictly results in unfairness</note> based on our own opinions, rather than living peacefully by allowing arbitrators to extract the truth from our conflicting claims. The mere desire to possess things, whether by right or by wrong, even openly shatters the law, seizes the goods of others through sheer whim, undermines, and overthrows; for most people, this desire stands in for reason.

The third type of corruption is the most ruinous: it is when a large part of humanity uses the law itself, not for the safety of the **Commonwealth** <note>original: "Reipublicæ"; referring to the state or the collective public good</note> as it was intended, but for the destruction of justice. This is the ultimate fate of even the most excellent things: those laws which were once established for the health and safety of the people anywhere in the world, tend to be twisted into a perverse sense through the constant handling of men—especially the wicked—unless you completely renew them every century. Indeed, nothing can be more wretched than this. For when the law becomes clear to someone who was held back by a false opinion, he usually yields, and is not so unwilling to obey the judge. When violence is done openly, it can hardly happen except by a tyrant or in a place where there is no law and nothing is sacred. But who can endure those who, under the most sacred prescription of the laws, immediately cover their frauds so their cunning is not seen, and strive to commit the greatest injustice through the law itself?

Indeed, such is the condition and the misfortune of laws, both divine and human, which is similar to that of **pavements** <note>original: "pauimentorum"; Postel uses this metaphor to describe how a legal system, like a stone floor, becomes dangerous when the individual "stones" or laws become loose and uneven</note>. For if they are new, level, and on a well-placed road, no one can easily say how much benefit those who walk upon them receive. But if they are once overturned and mixed with heaps and pits, no one makes the journey safely; everyone receives the greatest harm, and it is more desirable for everyone to walk through a muddy path than on such a pavement. Therefore, when laws begin to be born and placed among men, they keep if not all, then certainly as many as possible, in their duty. But when their meaning begins to be bypassed by crafty men, then deceit takes the place of good faith, falsehood replaces truth, and injustice replaces justice, all prepared against the heads of innocent men under the cover of the law. **Religions**, through the trickery of cunning men, turn from piety into a hunt for wealth, and from innocence into a thousand arts of doing harm safely. This is not quite so permitted in secular laws, except for the more powerful and those who can supply payment to their advocates. These things happen partly through the wickedness of men, and partly through the excessive mass of opinions that have been attached to the law. From this, it happens that no one's legal case is so bad that they cannot pluck something from that heap of opinions: with which, if they do not win, they may at least remarkably torment their adversary.

## IN HOW MANY WAYS, AND BY WHOM, AND AGAINST WHOM
### sin is committed. Chapter XVIII.

The word "**sin**" <note>original: "Peccati"</note> has a broader meaning than "**injury**" <note>original: "iniuria"; in a legal sense, a wrong done to another's rights or a "tort"</note>. For many sins are not injuries, but all injuries are sins. For since an injury is not done to a person who is willing <note>referring to the legal principle *volenti non fit iniuria*, "to one who is willing, no harm is done"</note> when a man sins against himself or his own property—because he does and suffers it willingly—he indeed sins, but he does not commit a legal "injury." Truly, all sins are committed either against religion, against nature, or against men. He acts against **religion** who neglects to observe it through outward signs and accepted customs; and he does so all the more if, as a private citizen, he strives to tear it down with words, or acts contrary to and differently from what usage requires or has received. For all these things lead to its destruction. Likewise, those who violate things assigned to religion—such as one who violates tombs, who defiles sacred virgins, who affects persons dedicated to sacred duties with any injury, or who [handles] things...

### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...plunders sacrosanct things by theft. Nor indeed are there only sacred things of religion, but also those things which contribute to the **safety of all** <note>original: "omnium incolumitatem"</note>, such as whatever serves the public convenience—roads, the forum, or the walls—and are assigned to them; all these ought to be treated as if they were among sacred things. If anyone, willingly and knowingly, should overturn, scatter, steal, or violate these, it is established that he has sinned greatly. For in these and similar matters, beyond the crime committed, which would be punished even if inflicted upon a private individual, satisfaction must also be made for the damage done to the entire body of the **Commonwealth** <note>original: "Reipublicæ"</note>. Nor is there, nor has there ever been, any nation that has not placed these among the most serious crimes.

To be sure, opinions regarding **tombs** <note>original: "sepulchris"</note> have certainly varied. Some preserved them with spices and glass; others with spices alone; some with the bodies of their parents, like the "parent-eating" Scythians <note>original: "Scythæ parentinori"; a reference to ancient accounts of Scythian tribes who practiced ritual cannibalism of their deceased elders</note>; some with dogs, others with fire, and many with the earth. Yet this was indeed common to all nations: to make the place in which either the solid body or the ashes were laid a "religious" site. It is so much a matter of custom in certain regions that they even create a road where the dead were carried, even if none existed before and it was private property. Nor is it a wonder that, by the consensus of all nations, the law wished those from whom we received our existence and the laws themselves to be **sacrosanct** <note>original: "sacrofanctos"</note> to us. Only Christians make a place religious *before* they bring in the dead; in other religions, the body itself brings the "religion" or sanctity to the spot.

Therefore, although the accepted rites of any religion may seem ridiculous to neighbors, one must nevertheless take care not to do anything against them in the places where they are approved. For that is to disturb and overturn the head of the Commonwealth, and to diminish the respect for religion—unless it be done with such great modesty that you are able to introduce a better way before the accepted one is overthrown, and you are capable of doing so, prevailing chiefly through authority. For it is through these religions especially that peoples grow together, and are held under laws and Princes by **terrors** <note>original: "terroribus"; Postel suggests that religious awe or fear of divine justice is a primary tool for maintaining social order</note>; this is the primary utility of the Commonwealth.

Whoever plots something that brings ruin to one or many men sins against nature; this is a crime full of the highest inhumanity in a private person. For the sake of retaining or obtaining peace, any Commonwealth can (after the misery of desires and opinions has been reached) either slaughter neighboring cities or regions to the point of extinction if they are harmful, unless they surrender. For it is better, when all things are done for the sake of peace, for a few to live in quiet than for many to live in constant misery and conflict.

Furthermore, by a certain use of nature—hidden indeed from men, and for that reason religious—when human affairs have reached their peak and overflowed into pleasures, and there are more people everywhere on earth than can be supported in one place, it is necessary that destruction be prepared either by themselves for themselves, or for others, or from the opposite side. In this matter, since **fate** <note>original: "fatum"</note> and the lust of Princes can do so much, I do not know if anyone sins greatly. But no private individual is permitted to harm another. Therefore, he who kills or attempts to kill a human being—whom Nature is most studious in bringing forth and preserving, and for whose use all laws and other things are prepared—is said to have sinned against nature for this reason: that he has removed from the midst of us the **summit and apex of nature** <note>original: "rerum naturæ fummam & apicem"</note>, namely an innocent man and a brother. For this reason, in all Commonwealths, there are magistrates who are the avengers of this injury.

Truly, he who plots ruin for many—such as one who takes care to infect the water or air which many use, who sets snares, or creates danger by whatever means that tends toward the destruction of the lives of many—is by far the most wicked, and must be removed from our midst. Therefore, he who creates a present danger to the life of a man...

### WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK III. 307

Indeed, such a person offends against nature and humanity. For he sins against nature in that he strips himself of it, while he despoils himself of the **humanity** <note>original: "humanitate"; here referring to the kindness and rational nature that defines a human being</note> which nature had given. He sins against the man who had been preserved by the laws for mutual protection and service, when he not only defrauds him of his duty but deprives him of life. But he who commits any offense against the reputation of a man or men, or against his property, is said to sin against the man, but not against nature—unless, perhaps, the person who suffered the injury is likely to perish as a direct result of the crime committed; in that case, the crime is seen to be committed against nature as well. Truly, a man sins either against one, against many, or against all. Against one, meaning either himself or another. Anyone can offend against himself through negligence or action, and this in matters of the soul, the body, or **fortune** <note>original: "fortunae"; referring to external wealth and status</note>, which are called "external goods."

We are negligent if we do not frequently care for our souls, adorn them with virtues, and exercise them with great contemplations of things; from this neglect, whatever error exists begins to creep in. We busy ourselves with infecting them with vices, and we never cease to undermine our thoughts with unjust actions. Because the danger of these matters pertains to us alone, and because human thought cannot be seized by other men, there is no punishment by the avenger of laws; instead, the expiation of the fault is referred to religion and the **fear of God** <note>original: "Deique timorem"</note>. He will be the punisher of those who have neglected to cultivate and preserve the reason assigned to them by divine power within this harmony of the body.

If anyone should carelessly neglect the health of their body, or encounter danger, and bring evil upon themselves by chance or by will, they must undoubtedly ascribe it to themselves; nor is there any law to avenge that sin. For nature has given such a great care for preserving life, not only to man but to all living creatures, that there is no need for any law in this matter. Hence, death is the greatest fear, and life—and the things that sustain it—is the greatest joy; nature has persuaded us that all things should be held secondary to it. To be sure, there are remedies for the vices of the body, but no one should approach them against their will. For nature has sufficiently taught what should be sought or avoided, without anyone else prescribing it. If a person who suffers in body does not wish to be cured, since **no injury is done to the willing** <note>original: "uolenti non fit iniuria"; a fundamental legal maxim suggesting that if someone consents to a harm, they cannot later claim it was a legal injury</note>, he ought to enjoy his own insanity—unless he suffers from a defect of judgment, age, disease, or nature. For in those cases, the laws ought to stand in the place of a father if parents are missing, as is customary in well-constituted **Republics** <note>original: "Rebuspublicis"</note>.

When someone recklessly squanders and consumes the external goods and supports of life which he possesses on uses that are useless to himself or the Commonwealth, he certainly sins against himself. However, because it is in the interest of the Commonwealth that no one makes bad use of their property, he ought to be restrained by the laws. For the Commonwealth receives damage when those who have squandered their resources or wasted their estate in any other way are forced to beg, to abandon their family, and thus to die while still living. Nor should the judgment of a private individual over his own property be so broad that he may abuse it. For he ought to live for the Commonwealth, not for himself. The majesty of the laws, almost everywhere among nations, has provided that this should not happen; it has given curators, tutors, or administrators to certain people. These guardians are permitted to make the condition of the things committed to them better, but they are not allowed to make it worse. This is especially evident in the **nerves** <note>original: "neruis"; used metaphorically for the essential strength or sinews of the state</note> of the Commonwealth. I call the "nerves" the powers of both laws, the secular and the sacred. Since men must necessarily preside over the administration of these, as well as the places and the property acquired or supplied for them, it is permitted to anyone who wishes to increase these and make them better; but to diminish them is by no means allowed. For these resources are prepared so that they may grow, stand firm, and endure as much as the work of the Commonwealth can achieve. Therefore, no one should be allowed so much power over their own property, especially an inherited estate...

### ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD ###

...and could be restrained by the censors. But for the most part, the laws prefer to permit such things, so that **the Phrygians may be wise too late** <note>original: "ut serò sapiant Phryges"; a classical proverb referring to those who only learn through their own misfortune, specifically the Trojans who realized their folly only after their city was destroyed</note>, and thus serve as an example to others, rather than have the state be hindered by so many preoccupations. Indeed, there would be a need for countless magistrates for such a task. Therefore, those people must be permitted to enjoy their own madness. In so many ways do men sin against themselves and their own interests. They also commit offenses against another, whether a superior, an equal, or an inferior.

The equality or inequality of men consists in two things: **authority** <note>original: "autoritate"</note> or **wealth** <note>original: "opibus"</note>. Usually, wealth without authority and power is not held in such high regard; only if both are joined together is it finally weighed with care. Authority destitute of wealth both should be and usually is considered sacred. An injury is done to a superior even by disparaging his command, if he be a Prince, or his judgment, if he be a judge. Nor do the laws, or the defenders of the laws, weigh so much which *person* was resisted as much as which *dignity*. For what place would there be for the exercise of justice in that **Commonwealth** <note>original: "Republica"</note> if any private citizen dared to oppose its sanctions? It would be the same as having no justice at all. Therefore, we seek out greater crimes when we commit something against the law—either against the authority, the person, or the property of one who is usually sacred because of their dignity (this must be understood as being beyond the rights of others).

When one sins against authority, it is certain that one also sins against the Commonwealth. Therefore, since even the lowliest ministers of justice hold their right not from themselves but from the Commonwealth, it is most certain that we offend most gravely when we inflict any injury upon them by reason of the office committed to them. Thus, **messengers** <note>original: "viatores"</note>, **bailiffs** <note>original: "apparitores"</note>, **summoners** <note>original: "citatores"</note>, and the like, since they are ministers of the Commonwealth, are sacred in the exercise of their duty; their authority ought to be equal to the power of those by whom they are delegated. Nor should the consideration of their persons—who are often of low birth by nature—make us more inclined to inflict injury. For they have their power not from themselves, but from the sovereign magistrate.

Therefore, we must take care above all else that we do not diminish the authority of the laws. If people are equals by reason of their office, we can indeed—without inflicting injury (which is allowed to no one)—contend with them or with anyone else by right, provided we commit nothing by violence. On the other hand, since we have more power over inferiors, far less should be permitted to us against them. For otherwise, it would be easy for one powerful in authority and wealth to overcome an inferior. Truly, in the commission of these offenses, the consideration of the person and their dignity is usually most carefully weighed. For if he who offends is placed in a position of authority, he sins far more gravely than a private citizen—even if he cannot be restrained by the laws—because he turns that authority, which was established for the preservation of men, toward their destruction.

Plainly the same must be judged if a **guild** <note>original: "collegium"</note>, a **corporation** <note>original: "corpus"</note>, a **court** <note>original: "curia"</note>, or any assembly of all parts commits an offense by its common consent against the authority, person, or property of a higher dignity. In my judgment, if all have consented, those who so sin are to be punished more severely than those who sin alone. To put it in a single word: just as virtues conceive strength in themselves and become greater, so do vices. For those who are greater or stronger harm both by the sin itself and by the example they set; while lesser men harm by the sin alone—and that a most grave one indeed, if they act to disparage the command of the Prince or of nature. Thus, either a private citizen sins, or one endowed with authority; the former less so, the latter more. We have seen in how many ways one may sin against a single individual (whoever he may be). One sins against many if he offends in part against a municipality, a village, a city, a corporation, a guild, or an assembly; or if he commits something that harms many people, even of different kinds, places, or professions. Such is the case of one who infects, seizes, or ruins the bodies, souls, or property of a community, a profession, a craft, or a corporate body; or one who substitutes **counterfeit goods** <note>original: "adulterinas merces"</note> and sees to it that they are corrupted, and six hundred things of this sort, the stain of which does not creep over everyone, but over the...

Having previously discussed offenses against individuals and the dignity of offices, he now turns to crimes against the "Commonwealth" (the public good) and the complexities of collective guilt versus individual responsibility.</meta>

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK III ###

...those who make a profit out of things, using them more out of personal opinion than necessity. For such people, their money or their labor is wasted and diminished. Furthermore, a person undermines everyone when he infects the minds of all with false opinions—opinions that tend toward the subversion of the **Commonwealth** <note>original: "Reipublicæ"</note>—and turns them away from their devotion to the state. This also applies to one who consumes cities with fire, or poisons the air or water, which everyone must necessarily use. Though not all bodies perish through his actions, it is not for lack of trying on his part that everyone did not die.

In the same category of vice is the one who diverts or redirects the **grain supply** <note>original: "annonam"; refers to the state-controlled food supply, particularly wheat</note> and those resources without which this life cannot persist. He gives them to enemies or drives the price to an immense height through **monopolies** <term>monopolium: the exclusive control of a commodity to manipulate prices</term>. So too the person who, beyond what is fair and good, persuades others that men should be tortured by decrees, taxes, and levies; or who coins false and adulterated money; and, to embrace all crimes at once, the one who betrays his fatherland for his own gain. For these matters affect everyone, and they tend toward the ruin and expense of nature, religion, the laws, men, and their property; for this reason, they must be punished with the harshest penalties.

Likewise, many people—either from one place or of one profession—can commit a crime together, whether against one person, several, or everyone. They act against one, for instance, if those from a **municipality** <note>original: "municipio"; a self-governing town or district</note> rise up against a Prince or an exceptionally powerful man. They act against others if they commit an offense against another district, city, place, art, or profession. If they commit those acts against the destruction of everyone which I just described regarding private individuals, judgment is indeed difficult when many are investigated. For generally (unless it is proven that everyone from the same district or place conspired together), the innocent can be punished for the guilty, and the **wheat may be cut down with the tares** <note>original: "triticum cum lolio"; a reference to the Biblical parable in Matthew 13:24–30 regarding the difficulty of separating good from evil in a community</note>.

The definition of "everyone" is very broad. For we use the word "everyone" equally to mean all people in the world, in a city, in regions, kingdoms, provinces, and all places. But the term "everyone" should ultimately be understood as those who are joined by the same laws. Certainly, if these people sin against the Prince, they sin more frequently. Yet it hardly ever happens that an act done by the consent of everyone is called a "sin," provided they are superior in the execution of the matter. For a "sin" is defined as whatever breaks unity and duration, and whatever is done against laws approved by the consent of all. But when they remain whole and surviving, they seem to have done better rather than worse.

The same must be clearly understood regarding the Prince, who is, as it were, the condensed and shorthand body of the entire Commonwealth, and who moves the whole world upward and forward at his will. For to believe that he is merely a private person and only a king is not without **sacrilege** <note>original: "piaculo"</note>. Therefore, when everyone attacks and carries out something that contributes to the preservation of all, even if we believe an injury is being done to some man or people—and it is certainly a very great one—nevertheless, because nature has taught even in artificial things to do this for one's own preservation and increase, it is not believed to be a sin by the one who committed it. This is because he lacks a forbidding law and possesses a reason and a pretext for why he does it.

Therefore, that "sin" is only passive, and is said to be non-existent in the agent. It is called a "fault lacking a fault," in which this mortality plays, and permits everything to itself according to nature, even to the detriment of nature. Thus, "everyone" is said not to sin as long as they cannot be punished. Indeed, those punishments that cannot be obtained from human laws are usually referred to religion; just as each man is conscious of his own deeds, so shall he one day feel his deserts. This happens as often as the aid of human laws ceases. Yet it is certain that they cease when those who have power over them commit offenses, and create "reason" and "necessity" out of their own will. And whereas all things ought to be referred to what is good, honest, necessary, and useful, they look only to utility, joined with a lust that frequently subverts it. This usually arises even from the nature of things themselves, since all things are necessarily driven by a certain motion and agitation. For a long-lasting peace, for the sake of which all things are sought, makes men soft and...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s discussion on the nature of human vice and the necessity of governance. Having described various crimes against the public good on the previous page, he now argues that because most people are driven by impulse rather than reason, the "Commonwealth" requires a formal system of judges and magistrates to maintain order and resolve conflicts. The catchword "inq;" from the previous page connects to the opening word "luxum" (luxury), completing the thought that certain conditions breed instability.</meta>

...makes men effeminate, and prone to luxury and sedition—at least those who lack prudence (who make up by far the greater part) and who are accustomed to being kept to their duty by laws rather than by their own reason. It is more useful to treat such people as wild beasts to be restrained than as subjects to be corrected. For he who seeks to remove all wicked people will soon rule over very few, or perhaps none at all. 

Hence, it is necessary that while we are incited by the vices of either the people or ourselves, we rush headlong into wars and deaths. We do this either to attack others, to repel injuries, to seek the goods of others, or to defend our own; not infrequently, we even undermine our own position while seeking gains that lead to even greater expenses. Celestial virtue and hidden causes also play a significant role in this matter. Necessity and the shared nature of physical things incite us as well. For no one desires to eat who has not been tormented by hunger, nor to drink if not thirsty, nor to rest if not weary from labor. Nature has placed all things in a cycle of change <note>original: "uicissitudine," referring to the constant flux or "ups and downs" of the material world</note> joined to necessity, so that while we maintain the middle path between extremes, we might be endowed with virtue.

Truly, it is enough to know this: that everyone—or a Prince acting in the name of everyone—does not sin when he procures those things which lead to the preservation and growth of the state, even if it involves injury to one or many, or even to all the people of another Commonwealth through wars, slaughter, and plundering. The only exception is that he must satisfy the requirements of religion, to which a Prince is just as bound as a commoner. For, as the Lyric Poet <note>Postel refers to the Roman poet Horace; the quote is from Odes 3.6.5</note> says: *You rule because you carry yourself as lesser than the Gods.* <note>original: "Dijs te minorem quod geris, imperas."</note> It has never been done otherwise by the laws and power accepted among men, nor will it ever be otherwise in this mortal life so long as our existence is joined to the necessity of these cycles—unless nature should grant us another order of life. 

I would discuss the many ways in which both injuries and sins might be redressed if the authority of all men (and especially that described by the dignity of orators) were sufficiently established. But it is necessary first to deal diligently with *persons* before we come to the *things* and *actions* by which injuries are punished. Before we can act to pursue or preserve our property, or initiate an action for injuries—and to include everything, whether the legal action is **against a thing** <term>in rem: a legal action directed against property rather than a specific person</term> or **against a person** <term>in personam: a legal action directed against a specific individual</term>—there is a need for a judge appointed for that matter to exist in the Commonwealth. This judge must be the one to value the matter for me, or to claim it, or to take it away. Therefore, we must speak of magistrates and their jurisdiction.

### ON JUDGES AND MAGISTRA-
->tes.<-
### CHAPTER XIX.

<margin>and</margin>
Since every kind of Commonwealth tends toward the same ends—namely, toward peace, duration, and stability—and is nourished, preserved, increased, and flourishes by the same things, and is endangered by similar things; it is nonetheless strange that the very mode of administration in the constitution of magistrates differs so much. Indeed, except in their number and order, almost no state agrees with another. But since it would seem to be an infinite and unnecessary task to report the institutions of every state that exists or is recorded in literature (unless they are excellent examples, as we showed in our work on the *Athenian Magistrates* <note>Postel refers to his own 1541 treatise, *De magistratibus Atheniensium*</note>), we shall instead describe those kinds of magistrates that exist in any Commonwealth based on necessity and utility—whether they hold a specific office or one combined with another. 

It is clear that magistrates were primarily established out of an imitation of nature and arose gradually out of necessity. For nature taught all living creatures to care for their offspring only until the young can provide for themselves and seek their own food. At that point, nature removes that affection in brute animals so they may move on to the procreation of other offspring. But for man, she willed that a perpetual care and knowledge of his own kind remain. This ensures that what a father has acquired through long experience for the support of life, he might always instill in his children and gradually instruct them...

### WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK III.

...and might lead them to that perfection which would also be of assistance to the future family and posterity. Therefore, the father first began to rule over his children in those things which were necessary, prescribing what was to be sought and what was to be avoided—either through signs (before languages were even devised) or by words. When the children obeyed his command, they began to live far more happily than those destitute of all such guidance. And that was the first mode of governing.

However, as men grew into adulthood and increased into a greater multitude, they were oppressed by injustice. Families rose up against other families, either for the sake of lust or necessity, and they afflicted one another with mutual injuries. It then seemed wise to imitate nature: by the consensus of a group, they would choose one man from the entire assembly who excelled in virtue or reputation. To him, in the name of all, was given the power to punish crimes and to decree that whoever committed such acts in the future should be afflicted with specific punishments or penalties. From this, it is established that not only the defense of individuals but the protection and care of all was both entrusted and received.

Thus, municipalities, villages, cities, nations, and provinces were created, as mortals—by imitating nature—chose for themselves a single head and, as it were, a parent. This leader would seek out what was desirable and, being granted the authority of everyone in his own name, would provide for the avoidance of what was harmful. 

I do not deny that princes immediately degenerated into tyrants. When these tyrants were removed, power was permitted to several good men, which is called <term>aristocracy</term> <note>Rule by the "best" or most virtuous citizens</note>. As this passed into a tyrannical <term>oligarchy</term> <note>Rule by a small, often corrupt elite</note>, it gave birth to <term>democracy</term> <note>Rule by the people</note>, and from there into an unjust <term>ochlocracy</term> <note>original: "ochlocratiam," meaning mob rule or the chaotic dominance of the masses</note>, or confused governance. 

For although there are three corrupt types of administration and three desirable types, it is still better to be ruled even by evil and unjust men than by none at all, and to rave in mutual slaughter. If a Prince, or whoever holds the authority of the laws, is absent, we feel every person we meet is a tyrant. Through the desire for vengeance, ambition, and glory—passions implanted in our souls by nature—and even through necessity itself, we become tyrants to others and rave and act cruelly toward one another. 

This is evident in the peoples recently discovered across the whole world <note>Postel refers here to the indigenous peoples of the Americas and other lands reached during the Age of Discovery</note>. Although they are far more numerous than those who inhabit all of Europe, and they know nothing of a more refined nature, having neither written laws nor letters, they nevertheless have Princes as punishers of injury or leaders for seeking vengeance. There is no nation so barbarous that it lacks some leader. This is even evident in almost the smallest of all living creatures: specifically, in the bees. Therefore, that power should be religiously observed as something sacred, for without it, no human social interaction would be safe. This is most clear when you see men roaming about in mutual slaughter and even devouring one another.

One must not immediately think that the "humanity" we possess is entirely from nature; rather, it is gradually instilled in us by the authority of parents, laws, and Princes. For it is enough that nature has produced us as <italic>teachable</italic>, not as already <italic>taught</italic>. If it were otherwise, all people, wherever they are in the world, would be possessed of the same skill and humanity, as if produced by the same nature. Yet there are many who neither speak, nor have laws, nor are guided by any sense of shame (which we believe to be most natural), nor do they know laws or religions, nor do they sow or reap. 

From this, it is clear that these things were discovered by prudence, infused into our teachable nature, and offered to that tender age of childhood which is capable of absorbing all opinions. This can become known to us when we look more diligently into our own origins and consider the records handed down to us. For there was once hardly any nation that did not consider human flesh a delicacy—so much so that they would give their dearest possession as a victim most pleasing to the gods. Among developed <term>commonwealths</term> <note>original: "resp." (republica)</note> today, who would not shudder at this? Every <term>Scythian</term> <note>A classical term used to describe nomadic or "barbaric" peoples from the Eurasian Steppe</note> nation held the bodies of their enemies as the most pleasing food, as is still evident today in many places. They even considered the bodies of their elderly parents a delicacy, whom they would consume at a mature age...

the fear of death was not instilled, so that they voluntarily and joyfully offered themselves to be slaughtered and devoured at feasts by their parents <note>Postel refers here to a "state of nature" without laws, where he believes humans acted with barbaric cruelty, even cannibalism, lacking the natural instinct for self-preservation found in other animals</note>. We owe so much, therefore, not to nature—which created us destitute of all things and the most miserable of all living creatures (unless hope, the knowledge of God’s religion, and the desire for life and glory raised us up)—but to God, to religion, to prudence, to laws, and to princes. These are what keep us within the bounds of humanity, lead us daily toward the cultivation of the mind, and refine nature itself, which is otherwise crippled within us. Indeed, as needs grew, not only did individuals rage against one another, but many against many, moved by vengeance, necessity, or the pursuit of glory; they were either seized by a particular passion or sought to possess what their neighbors held. 

To repel that multitude rising against another, the Prince prepares for war. For the sake of defending liberty, he spends—at his own discretion—the resources that have been prepared and collected from everyone, acting as the shortcut <note>original: "compendiarium," meaning an efficient or direct means</note> body of the Republic to strike down the enemy. I wish to take an example from a victorious people and their Prince, since the defeated usually accept the laws of the victor. In a war—whether arising, ongoing, or concluded—at least three types of magistrates must emerge: those who repel injury at home, those who repel it abroad, and those who collect the strength from every individual in the Republic for both tasks. Before a war, one person acting in the name of all might have been enough. These were the kings or Princes (for the difference is in the name, not the reality), who were both judges and priests of the divinity under whose protection the cities or assemblies were administered—provided that a system of religion had already been devised and established. 

Therefore, when a leader has two locations to govern—unless he compels both peoples to live together in one place—he can only conveniently perform the office of prince in one; in the other, he will necessarily be absent. I am speaking of places that show the world has already reached adulthood. Suppose the Prince acts in one place; in the other, there must be one magistrate to speak the law <term>ius dicere: the formal power of a judge to interpret and apply the law</term> among litigants and to restrain those who act against the laws. Another must also be appointed to gather power for the Prince from the individual members of society—namely a Quaestor <term>Quaestor: a treasurer or financial officer, modeled on the Roman office</term>, for collecting taxes and perhaps managing the recruitment of soldiers.

# THE PARTITION OF THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE REPUBLIC,
## and its exposition. Chapter 20.

Every magistrate, therefore, either drives away domestic injury or external injury; or he collects the power by which both can be done; or he is an assistant to those who handle these matters. Thus, there are three primary elements: the Judge, the Quaestor, and the Prince. The first governs internal affairs, the second gathers power, and the third places himself in the way of violence, both internal and external. The Prince provides the salaries for the judge so that he may better perform his services for the Republic; he supplies the expenses for the soldier, and creates for himself and the state the "sinews" of wealth and resources. 

For although the Prince has been granted authority by the consensus of all, unless he were wealthier than a private citizen—so that he might show favor to his friends and remain formidable to enemies and lawbreakers—his authority would undoubtedly be in vain. The Republic, however well-disposed toward him, cannot provide on the spot or through begging what is immediately required to correct crimes or avoid dangers. The Prince imparts his own authority to the judge, so that the judge may use it—not according to his own whim, but according to the laws of equity and goodness and the Prince’s command. For the Prince alone ought to possess absolute power <term>merum imperium: the highest legal authority, including the power of life and death</term>, lest any private citizen gifted with it think he is allowed more than is proper. Truly, our empire must be increased, and through victories, our Prince must be raised to the highest peak, and our simple magistracies must finally be multiplied. Let us grant, if it could be done, one single Prince for the whole world. For that is most closely modeled after the single Divinity, upon whom the entire order of nature depends.

it hangs, and it lasts forever, so that the sentiment of Homer may be preserved: **The rule of many is not good; let there be one ruler.** <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη, εἷς κοίρανος ἔστω</note> Or if it is not possible for one to rule the whole world—as certainly no king has ever been able, or ever could, hold even a tenth of it—let his domain be as large as it can be for the preservation of his own people. For there is no less virtue in protecting what has been acquired than in seeking it out; yet he who possesses too much can hardly do this, since he can scarcely restrain those who revolt in his presence, especially if he reigns for a long time. For this reason, no empires that attempted to grow larger than their own strength could endure, while smaller ones lasted the longest. This is because the first and primary cause for the institution of <term>Princes</term> <note>Postel uses "Prince" as a general term for a sovereign ruler</note> was to settle and avenge domestic injuries and complaints; the second was for repelling external danger. First, I shall speak of the judges: how many types there ought to be, and how they should exist in a well-constituted <term>Polity</term> <note>The organized government or constitution of a state</note>. All judges, as I said regarding religion, are either supreme, middle, or lowest. The supreme judge, in certain cases, is truly the Prince himself, who rightly reserves such knowledge for his own consideration. In the second place after him are the supreme magistrates, who usually dispense justice in matters the Prince does not wish to be terminated by inferiors, or matters poorly decided, or those that fall into dispute—especially between middle officials—and, to put it in a word, they preside over everyone.

In our France, so that matters may be more precise, there are two magistrates of this kind. First is the <term>Sacrosanct Council</term>, in which the Prince is frequently present. The great nobles, whoever are distinguished by wisdom and experience in affairs and to whom the Prince has granted this honor because of their merits, are usually admitted into such a holy assembly. Otherwise, only a few and the most distinguished enter, especially if the matter is secret or confidential. They therefore call it the **Private Council**, because matters are settled or established by the Prince privately, partly by reason and partly by his own judgment. To fail to obey this decree is a crime and a sacrilege. But because anyone who has been wronged could not easily gain access there, Princes have always kept certain men of distinguished experience and knowledge, the <term>Masters of Petitions</term> <note>original: "libellorum supplicum magistros," today known in France as the Maîtres des Requêtes, who filter legal requests to the council</note>, to offer prayers to the Prince in that assembly and to make themselves available everywhere to those seeking remedies.

The other assembly of judges is called the **Great Council**, where they primarily deal with matters that the Prince, by special privilege, wants them to examine, or where they debate the law, jurisdiction, appeals, and disputes of inferior officials. And since those things done in both the Supreme and the Great Council require singular examination and weighing—and it must be seen everywhere if the decision is based on truth and the utility of the State, and if the petitions rely on truth—a man is appointed by the Prince. This man must possess the greatest prudence, knowledge, long experience in affairs, and a mind refined in all things. He inspects whether the decrees should be ratified (for often Princes are persuaded toward false or useless things), and then finally confirms them with the seal of royal authority (without which nothing receives the force of law in public). He joins the acts to the power of the laws, provided they are fair and good; otherwise, he is accustomed to **cancel** and break the instruments. For this reason, in French, he is called the **Chancellor**. <note>Postel derives "Cancellarius" from "cancellare," meaning to cross out or "cancel" a document by drawing a lattice-like pattern of lines over it</note> When there is doubt regarding jurisdiction or when people complain, his decision is held as ratified.

Although my purpose is not to hand down the civil law of the Romans or of any other specific people, but rather that which is either approved, to be approved, or probable by the consensus of all nations, I nevertheless wanted to take this example from our own Republic, as something no man could easily disparage. For institutions established by the wise, proven by long use, confirmed by the consensus of all, and constant in both war and peace, are certainly to be sought by any mortal. There are also other supreme magistrates, usually appointed daily by any Prince, not for the care of the entire State, but for the knowledge of a specific business or case; these can decide and establish matters with an absolute sentence just like the Prince. But I come now to the **Middle Magistrates**, whom the Greeks call **subordinate** <note>original Greek: ὑπαλλήλους</note> and the French call **subalterns**; these will certainly be much clearer once the lowest ones have been declared. Therefore, all the lowest judges, both <term>petty judges</term> <note>original Latin: *iudices pedanei*; these were lower-level judges who handled minor or local cases, historically named because they often sat on low benches or stood while hearing cases</note> and municipal ones, are those appointed by the prince in specific locations. These are conveniently arranged so they can be easily accessed by all, and they administer justice to the citizens or the common people; below them, no one else has the power to grant a legal ruling. These men are like a council of six judges, though they are not always experts in all matters. Because of this, they are permitted to hear cases only up to a certain financial sum, and they are not allowed to decide capital cases (those involving the death penalty) on their own, unless a larger assembly of judges is called or consulted. Alternatively, once the merits of a case have been exhibited and explained, if any error is made in their judgments, the victims are usually helped through the benefit of an appeal.

The middle judges are those who acknowledge a superior above them and have inferiors below them from whom cases may be appealed. These are of three types. Some depend directly on the prince without any other legal middleman; some are assigned to religious assemblies; and some are granted to men of merit, virtue, and good faith who have been endowed with nobility. These latter ones act not only as middle judges but also as the lowest ones. Indeed, the Prince wishes all—whether religious communities or men who have served the state well—to be granted power for the sake of preserving and increasing religion and for promoting and stirring up virtue in men. This is done not just through material wealth, but through the authority to defend their affairs and to help the <term>State</term> <note>original Latin: *Respublica*; referring to the "public thing" or the common good of the governed society</note> within their own jurisdiction. For when these men recognize the benefit they have received from the Prince and strive to be like him, they act as the hands and supports by which he moves other men and by which he can more easily exercise his power.

Such is the nobility of which I have already spoken. Whether it is better for this status to be hereditary—lasting through one's children—or to exist only for those who personally earned it, is a question you could hardly judge. It is more certain than certainty itself that we undertake far more for the sake of our descendants than for ourselves. We are held by a greater zeal for increasing and preserving something that will benefit our posterity than if we were merely looking after our own interests. For this reason, we cultivate and defend the State with greater zeal than if we were merely temporary inhabitants here, keeping the glory of virtue for ourselves alone and not leaving it to our children. Therefore, he reigns far more securely who possesses an ancestral nobility (even if it uses the father's glory under a false name) than he who has a true nobility sought from the lowest rank. For that "true" nobility has scarcely taken root when it is uprooted. The ancestral kind, however, has grown and stands firm through the immense benefit of industry and through private and ancestral wealth, which is the sinew of the State.

Therefore, this nobility also possesses the license to appoint a judge, distinguished into three types of jurisdiction. First, some can restrain the guilty so they may be handed over to other judges, but they cannot punish them with beatings or fines. Second, others can both restrain and impose fines—either predefined or discretionary—or inflict corporal punishment. Third, others can both restrain and punish with death, or proscribe someone from their jurisdiction, either through permanent or temporary exile. In all these judgments, there must always be the remedy of an appeal. Truly, great care must be taken lest a noble abuse the authority given by the prince according to his own whim, believing that to be his own which is not his, but which depends on the power of the prince. For all men, and especially those endowed with authority, easily become insolent and permit themselves much license, unless continuous virtue and the love of justice restrain them, or the fear of the law and an immediate penalty coerces them.

Among our middle judges, there must be some who are supreme, established in the highest dignity, authority, and fellowship, presided over by someone most worthy of the highest authority. These men should judge and decide specifically on appeals and on the errors of lower judges. From their sentence, no further appeal should be allowed, lest lawsuits be eternal—unless something is decided to the contrary by the pleasure of the prince (which ought to happen only rarely and for the sake of some public utility). For a prince overthrows his own State when he diminishes the dignity and authority of the courts and creates eternal lawsuits, while seeking to help those similar to himself with great...

However many intermediate judges there may be between the lowest and the highest, it matters very little, since an appeal can be made from the former to the latter, whether in the first, second, or third instance; it makes no difference. The first of the middle judges could be called "supreme," because no appeal can be made from them unless their sentences are occasionally retracted, and they hear the law regarding conflicts between courts in the Private and Great Council. This does not diminish their authority, since no one can be a judge in their own case. One point must be noted: in matters of religion, there is also an appeal to the highest prelates of religion, except in cases of sects that cast doubt on the received religion. Because such a thing tends toward the disturbance of the **State**, once it is proven by even slight evidence or by witnesses who would otherwise be considered untrustworthy, a judge of civil causes delivers the law concerning it.

### ANOTHER DIVISION OF JUDGES. CHAPTER XXI.

All judges are established or appointed either for punishing **capital injuries**, or for ending **civil controversies**, or for both; they have jurisdiction either in a single place and matter, or in all of them. They are either "ordinary" judges or those sent as reinforcements, and they take cognizance of either private matters, public matters, or matters of the treasury. The primary concern is the prosecution of crime or the punishment of public injury. For this reason, princes were first chosen and supported by the public: so that justice might be rendered if any injury were done by one man to another. Indeed, a sin involving property is far lighter than one against the body; it was not considered a <term>capital offense</term> <note>meaning a crime punishable by death</note> to sin against property, except in cases of theft or intentional damage, which some were accustomed to punish at various times with death, others with a fourfold penalty, and others with various other fines. Among the **Spartans**, it was once considered a matter of glory—provided one was not caught—to be more cautious in plundering the goods of enemies and more attentive in preserving domestic ones. 

But a capital crime is certain to be committed not only against the person it happens to, but also against all their kin. Many injuries are defined by the opinions of various nations, some of which consider them of no account, while others even hold them in honor. However, it is permitted by no nation anywhere to have slain any human being (except for enemies, or those whom the received law allows to be killed with impunity) whether by poison, or a weapon, or by a plot, or to have killed or sought to kill them by any fraud whatsoever. Furthermore, a judge, in seeking penalties, ought to follow the prescription of the laws and the opinion received for the sake of public peace, acting severely against those accustomed to sin, especially while the benefit of appeal remains. Otherwise, for the supreme judge, equity is to be preferred to the strict letter of the law, and the case must be moderated **by equity** <note>original Greek: *tē epieikeia*; the Aristotelian concept of fairness that corrects or supplements the written law</note>. 

In the second place are those who settle controversies held regarding property. A judge can also be appointed for both types of trials at fixed hours, when there is either a scarcity of cases or a shortage of judges. Lest judges allow themselves too much freedom, contaminating their office through license or negligence, guardians with the highest authority are given to them by the prince, or ought to be given. These act as judges, advocates, or "procurators" of those matters which pertain to the preservation of the State, having care for them; they are, so to speak, the "guardians of the guardians," without whose authority nothing can be established that tends toward the loss of the treasury or of nature. When these guardians request or object to something, they must be obeyed as the prince himself; otherwise, they may refer the matter to the prince. For this duty, many Republics had **censors**. Some permitted anyone who wished to accuse those who had served in magistracies. All these things were invented to keep judges in their duty, serving as the eyes of the highest authority. However, where there are not many lawsuits or where injuries are rarer, a judge can indeed administer justice in many places; but if matters are more complex, lest one man...

<meta>catchword: num (from "numerus")</meta>

In order that nothing hinders or disturbs <term>authority</term><note>Latin: *authoritas*. In this context, it refers to the legal power or right to command and judge.</note>, it is necessary that the seats of all judges be established and fixed. It is essential for justice to be spoken and rendered in specific, predefined places and times; otherwise, the state of affairs would be in utter confusion. Therefore, they have their seats throughout the lands, which they must not exit (unless permission is obtained from a neighbor) nor abandon. In these seats, no one may perform the office of a <term>judge</term><note>Latin: *iudex*.</note> unless they have been granted the authority to speak the law there by the supreme magistrate or the prince. 

But since a judge himself may be hindered by illness or by certain necessary business—so that he cannot frequently attend to more important judgments—it is necessary to provide for the seat so it does not remain vacant. Therefore, someone must be appointed by the prince, or chosen by him for his integrity, to speak the law in the judge's absence. Truly, a grave sin has been committed in this matter by the **French State**<note>Latin: *Gallica Republica*. Postel uses "Republic" in the classical sense of the "commonwealth" or "public affairs" of France.</note>. For those who were once granted very large stipends for the sake of performing their duty, now the <term>praetors</term><note>High-ranking provincial officials or judges.</note> in individual provinces receive those funds while being completely unskilled in judging; they reject the duty entirely, passing it onto sub-prefects—men who are indeed learned and good, but of humbler means and with a smaller salary than is sufficient to maintain a judge's integrity and avoid corruption. This is certainly something that ought to be avoided at all costs. For from this, the first "stain of evil" and the cause of crimes arises within the very arbiters of judgment.

Furthermore, since there are usually certain scoundrels, robbers, and bandits in individual provinces who infest entire regions and fly here and there without fixed homes like nomads, they cause the greatest injury to the common people. Such men cannot easily be restrained or caught by the <term>stationary judges</term><note>Latin: *statarijs iudicibus*. These are judges fixed to a specific location or courthouse.</note>. Therefore, there is a need for a second kind of judge—**itinerant judges**—who can pursue and apprehend these wanderers anywhere in the land. Once captured, and in whatever place they are caught, these judges (having called upon the provincial judge or several prudent men) should be able to determine and carry out capital punishment, or whatever penalty the crimes deserve, <term>without appeal</term><note>Latin: *sine provocatione*. This means the sentence was final and could not be challenged in a higher court.</note>. These itinerant judges do not touch private matters, except perhaps to ensure cases do not stagnate; they sometimes prepare <term>lawsuits</term><note>Latin: *lites*.</note> for the stationary judges, or, at the request of the parties, they might elicit the truth of a particular deed to be presented to the judge.

Furthermore, new remedies must be sought for emerging new diseases. For it often happens through the cunning of men, or even the negligence of judges, or both causes (for the more you try to restrain men, the more they strive to slip away like eels), that an immense number of punishments arise from both criminal and private or civil lawsuits. Additionally, wicked men tend to be all the more stubborn the more they are investigated to give an account of their lives; being conscious of their own guilt, they are less obedient to judgments. 

To heal this vice, the Prince or the supreme power of speaking the law ought to choose the best men from the Great Assembly of the Estates. If he cannot choose from the courts of the judges due to their number, he should grant authority to certain individuals to go and purge those regions of evil men and put an end to the multitude of lawsuits as quickly as possible. Depending on the circumstances, they should do this every second, third, or fourth year in each province. In this way, they will heal the world through terror, punishments, and remedies. 

Moreover, factionalism and a certain personal bias are not uncommon among the judges themselves, or among the various provinces, locations, and offices. The more these judges prevail in authority and wealth, the more they tend to be favored. Therefore, no wise State is accustomed to allowing them to speak the law in their own interest or that of their kin; it permits no jurisdiction from which a judge might benefit. Thus, by the favor of the prince, many people are exempted from a <term>jurisdiction</term><note>Latin: *iuriſdictio*.</note> to which they are subject, or in which they are litigating, because of the hostile bias of the judges. Instead, they receive **delegated judges**, as they are called, who can speak the law there only for that specific case. Regarding all crimes or disturbances of the State and lawsuits which occur among men...

<summary>Postel argues for the necessity of fixed judicial seats and criticizes the French legal system for allowing unskilled, wealthy officials to delegate their duties to underpaid subordinates. He proposes the use of itinerant judges to catch mobile criminals and special delegated judges to ensure impartiality in cases of judicial bias.</summary>

...whether of private individuals or those granted <term>authority</term><note>Latin: *authoritas*. Legal power or official standing.</note>, disputes often arise even concerning the affairs of the assemblies themselves; in such cases, judges are or can be so appointed. Those who handle the affairs of the **treasury**<note>Latin: *fiscus*. The state or royal purse.</note> and prosecute remain for us to discuss; however, we shall speak of them only after we have described the appendages of the courts.

## ON THE APPENDAGES OF THE COURTS.
### CHAPTER XXII.

By **appendages**, I mean those magistrates, ranks, or duties without which an expanded and long-lasting **State**<note>Latin: *Respublica*. Postel uses this to mean any organized political community or commonwealth.</note> can hardly stand. For new States—not yet shaped by long use—or even older ones that remain ignorant of crimes, could do without them, either because vices were not yet known or emerging, or because the remedies were ignored. Indeed, greater knowledge of things, greater prudence, and a more flowing abundance of goods—whether of the mind, the body, or of fortune—are considered the "highest good" in this life according to the pursuit of virtue, and are therefore sought after by everyone. However, if the use of external things is stripped of justice and moderation, these goods undoubtedly become the fuel for all vices. 

Thus, in the old days, young States erred very little due to their ignorance and the meager nature of their affairs. Their concern tended only toward necessity, not toward glory or reputation; lacking such examples, they used to proceed simply. For *man is the imitator of man*<note>Latin: *Homo enim hominis simia est*. Literally: "Man is the ape of man." This refers to the human tendency to mimic both the virtues and vices of others.</note>. Nevertheless, this moderate desire is of the greatest use if there is a limit in things—a limit which ought to be placed in the soul, not in the abundance of possessions.

Now, judges require three types of men. For some are usually appointed for the beginning of cases, others for the middle, and others for the end, in order to carry out those tasks in which a judge can hardly expend his own labor. There are, or ought to be, those who can apprehend—even without a judge’s order—wicked men caught in the act, or those marked as guilty through investigation, witnesses, judgments, or conjectures, and bring them before the tribunal. Because they make the accused **appear** before the judge, the Romans called them **apparitors**<note>Latin: *apparitores*. Public servants or officers who attended magistrates to execute their orders.</note>; otherwise they are called **messengers**<note>Latin: *viatores*. Literally "travelers," these were lower-level officers who summoned citizens to court.</note>, or in the **French courts**, **sergeants**<note>Latin: *seruientes*. Officers of the court responsible for making arrests and serving summons.</note>, because they are the ministers of justice. 

Under the same law are the **watchmen**<note>Latin: *vigiles*. The night-watch or police force of a city.</note> among any nation. Because the greatest power for doing harm exists at night, the law allows them to restrain with chains and present to a judge anyone wandering at unusual or forbidden hours, or those caught in a crime, or those approaching the watchposts without the password, or anyone committing an act considered a vice in any State. 

There are also **investigators**<note>Latin: *quaestores*. Not to be confused with financial quaestors, these are "inquirers" or "investigators" of crimes.</note>—not only for parricide, but for any more serious crime committed—who visit the scenes and hold an inquiry, either at the request of the injured party, or by order of the judge, or even by virtue of their office; they prepare the lawsuits and investigations for the judge. Once the merits of the case are known, the judge decides whether the accused should be summoned or seized (though a summons is permitted unless it is a grave crime or there is a danger of flight). If the accused does not obey on the appointed day or within the prescribed time (or a time extended for legal reasons), he is ordered to be shut in chains, or a sentence is pronounced in his absence; for he is then guilty of **contumacy**<note>Latin: *contumacia*. Contempt of court or stubborn refusal to appear.</note>. 

In the past, it was permitted in all States for anyone to seize criminals caught in the very act and bring them to the tribunal. Now, under **French law**, that power is granted only to certain people, so that there is no room for mutual false accusations and injury. Yet, in cases of public injury, this right ought to be more widely open, so that anyone may be an avenger. The Romans permitted this not only in crimes, but in civil matters as well; the power was given to anyone to call his opponent into court in the presence of one witness, and no one was allowed to release him. This was so that they would not be forced by the apparitors, who performed that service for the State only so that those who refused to come when called into court would be compelled by...

<meta>This page continues Postel's Chapter XXII concerning the "appendages" or supporting staff of the legal system. Having previously introduced the necessity of these roles in more complex societies, he now details the specific functions of bailiffs, legal representatives, and clerks.</meta>
