...and they would be presented to them. Truly, almost everyone has their own custom. For **Bailiffs**<note>Latin: *Viatores*. Literally "travelers," these were messengers or summoners who served the court.</note> can be appointed as either permanent or temporary officials, and for specific predetermined matters. At the request of the litigants, they may summon people to court and restrain those who are lawless, whether the parties obey voluntarily or by the judge's command. For the sake of public peace, this should be common to all: that their authority should not extend further—whether they are summoning someone to court, seizing property as security, or searching for criminals—than the jurisdiction of the judges to whom they are subject. Indeed, they cannot perform these duties in another's domain without obtaining permission, unless they possess authority either previously granted by the prince or specifically permitted for that task so that they may perform their duty anywhere. Therefore, once the defendant is presented and ordered to come into court—either by a legal petition, at the request of the plaintiff, or by the judge's command—the judge learns the main points of the case there through the report of the **Bailiff**, and from there he requests that the supporting evidence be presented to him by the litigants.

From this, due to "human inexperience" (as they say), the use of **Patrons**<note>Latin: *patroni*. Legal protectors or high-ranking lawyers.</note> and **Procurators**<note>Latin: *procuratores*. Legal representatives or attorneys who manage a case on behalf of another.</note> has become common; they explain the facts and merits of the case to the judge and are employed in the midst of the litigation. This occurs in **Republics**<note>Latin: *Rebuspub.* (Respublicis). Organized states or political communities.</note> that have already become corrupted. Since the judge himself ought to necessarily grasp whatever pertains to the law—either by himself, from the recorded instruments and acts, or from the words of the litigants—which contribute to the knowledge of the case, he could certainly do without those aids and hear anyone speaking for themselves. For this reason, many nations do without such men and leave those matters to be weighed by the judge, since the patrons themselves can add nothing to the case beyond a certain order and a clarity of words. 

But in truth, in that court, help ought to be given through such men to those who are absent, as well as to those hindered by language, women, orphans, the unsuited, the mentally impaired, and those who suffer from a defect such that they cannot explain their own rights or the feelings of their mind, or what legal standing they have. I believe **Advocates**<note>Latin: *aduocatos*. Legal representatives called upon to plead a case.</note> were first established for their sake, just as there are even now in many states those who speak the law for defendants even of the greatest crimes. Thus, the **Procurator** reveals to the **Advocate** those things that must be done according to the use of <term>Civil Law</term><note>Latin: *ius civile*. The laws specific to a city or state.</note>; the advocate then explains them to the judge by writing or by voice, adding the reasons which are usually sought from the <term>Law of Nations</term><note>Latin: *ius gentium*. Universal principles of justice thought to be common to all people.</note>. 

Not infrequently, judges also prepare lawsuits for other judges. According to **Roman Law**, all may be admitted to the duty of a procurator except for minors, women, the insane, those marked by infamy, and those enrolled in religious orders (who, in sacred matters, may be either procurators or **Syndics**<note>Latin: *syndicí*. Legal representatives for a corporation or religious community.</note>). Also included are any who are usually exempted anywhere by the opinions of civil laws. They can be appointed for a single matter or for all things, and for any length of time. If, however, someone manages another's affairs without a mandate, he is usually called a "manager of affairs" (*geſtor negotiorum*) rather than a procurator. If he acts by a mandate—enjoined by word, letter, or formal notice—he is not usually approached by the judge as a procurator, which seems to have been established quite unfairly. For it is right for everyone to be heard either in person or through a friend, or one appointed by mandate. Yet many would be endangered by "crows gasping for the wealth of others" <note>A metaphorical reference to greedy legal opportunists or "vultures."</note>. For that reason, it is better to maintain them at the Republic's expense than to remove them.

Those who assist the judges after the case is decided remain for us to discuss, such as those who record what is dictated. The **Clerk**<note>Latin: *scriba*. A secretary or court recorder.</note> is in charge of this: first while the parties are interrogated or the merits of the case are reported in criminal matters; in civil matters, however, while the judge speaks the sentence, the clerk transcribes it and makes, as it were, notebooks. Afterward, showing these to the judge and conferring with him, he polishes them, and from there he issues the petition or the **record of judgment**<note>Latin: *instrumentum iudicati*.</note> and gives it to the one for whom the judgment was made. So that this instrument may have the strength of laws, it must be protected by the **seal of the prince** or of the one under whom that jurisdiction is administered; finally, the effects of this must follow. For the law would be spoken in vain unless the effects were also accustomed to follow in actual affairs. Therefore, nothing should be determined or judged by any judge without it being immediately taken down by a clerk, at least into a diary or into a formal record or petition, if the matter requires it. When someone, having been warned, does not obey the judge...

...cannot be free from deceit. Therefore, either the one who commands the party to appear in court, or another who is called by our people either a **Bailiff**<note>Latin: *hostiarius*. Literally a "door-keeper" or usher, responsible for maintaining order and serving summons.</note> or a **Commissioner**, compels the defendant to obey. Goods or property taken as a guarantee that the defendant will comply with the court's judgment.</note> equal to the estimated value of the matter. For wherever in the world people contend in court over their affairs, matters are usually settled in such a way that it is expedient for the judgment to be paid or carried out; otherwise, both princes and judges would be established in vain. But these matters concern the judges and their ministers. Other things are based on custom and public opinion.

## ON THE MILITARY ORDER AND 
## AUTHORITY. CHAPTER XXIII.

Now we must briefly treat those who were established to repel external injuries—since they do not contribute to the knowledge of the law itself, but frequently contribute to its overthrow. As long as affairs were quite small, and ambition had not yet increased through various opinions, and when the beginning or dominion of republics did not extend far, the prince undoubtedly presided over sacred rites, the administration of the law, and the repelling of external injury. For at that time, lawsuits and injuries were rare, religious rituals were few, and the attacks of enemies were not so frequent nor so formidable. But when that power had to be divided, the peak of religion—as far as supreme power is concerned—could be retained by the prince. However, because of more frequent lawsuits, the judgments had to be permitted to others, as we have taught. The force and power of arms were conferred upon the single prince. 

That power ought to be divided three ways: into internal, external, or mixed. For civil seditions and the movements of the common people must be restrained by a force greater than that of the law, lest they rise up against those administering justice or against the prince. Forces must also be prepared against enemies. And officials must be established for both uses, since a prince cannot be everywhere at once—for example, on the borders of regions where, because of various rumors from neighboring princes, the common people tend to be of inconsistent spirit and loyalty. Therefore, this **Guardian**<note>Postel refers here to Plato's *Republic*, where the "Guardians" are a specific class of citizens trained to protect the state.</note> (for so Plato calls the soldiers established for guarding the republic) must be most faithful to the prince, most loving of the republic, and most prudent. He must be someone who can lead minds through eloquence just as he leads bodies through arms, drawing them to his own opinion and retaining them in loyalty to his prince, and taking up powerful arms for the prince against any enemy, however neighboring or friendly they may be. 

To ensure he does this more from the heart, and so that he is not tempted by the adversary with the allurements of fortune (toward which both nature, necessity, and opinion have made you inclined), the prince ought to grant him wealth located in the heart of the kingdom, or establish him as a wealthy inland resident, so that he does not easily follow the loyalty of enemies. For wealth and already-acquired property keep a man in loyalty, if anything does; nor has any loyalty ever been long-lasting without property. Thus, no one will easily break their word by merely following someone else's hope and seeking uncertainties while leaving behind certainties. He who is poor, unless he is held strongly by the love of his own people and of what is right, is truly for sale. It is common to all those dedicated to military service that, once the **Oath**<note>Latin: *sacramentum*. In the Roman tradition, this was a sacred oath of allegiance taken by soldiers, which carried both legal and religious weight.</note> has been offered for the use of the fatherland and religion, they swear to the loyalty of the prince and the safety of the republic. If they commit anything against this oath, they are to be discharged and removed from the oath as becomes wicked and shameful men—both because of their punishment and disgrace as those who have most gravely offended against the republic, and as an example of shame, the nature and reputation of which strikes fear into us. Therefore, in the highest matters, he must offer that oath of loyalty; for it is like a sacred marriage of both laws. For while the soldier is asked the oath...

...some **divine name**<note>Latin: *numen*. Refers to a deity or a divine power invoked during an oath.</note>, or power, or matter of public opinion (whose authority is sacred and which ought to, and usually does, strike fear into anyone neglecting the sacraments taken in its name) must be asserted and interposed. We affirm that our **faith**<note>Latin: *fides*. In this context, it means one's word, trust, or credit.</note> will endure just as we believe and desire that that through which we swear is true and lasting. But if it should happen that this is neglected—because an injury is done not only to men as witnesses but to the gods, and furthermore a crime has been committed—those who commit perjury are deservedly either punished as **treaty-breakers**<note>Latin: *fœdifragi*. Those who break a formal league or covenant.</note> or marked with infamy. For there is no nation that has received a religion and approves and receives laws that does not keep the faith which it believes and desires to be kept toward itself. He who breaks his word, therefore, ought to feel the vengeance of both God and men. 

But I return to the prince, who, since he is but one man, cannot be sufficient to be present in all places (except by his authority). He therefore needs to appoint **magistrates**, **leaders**, and **military tribunes** over those armies, who may command them to carry out orders, see that they are done, and administer justice among them. For it is necessary that that fierce race of men, dedicated to **Mars**<note>The Roman god of war; Postel uses this to characterize the inherently violent nature of soldiers.</note> and born for the inflicting of injury, be coerced—not by the mildness of laws, judges, and provincial officials (unless you keep a constant watch)—but be immediately warned, terrified, punished, or discharged by their own officers. For otherwise, all things would turn into license; they would undermine everything and hold nothing holy or sacred. 

There must also be established—besides the leaders, who frequently neglect what is just—**judges** who may punish the guilty, not only in the army but also in the courts. For those who are powerful in strength could not otherwise be coerced except by those equal in dignity, but supported by a greater authority or greater forces. 

In this matter, it is a marvel how prudent and severe the **Turks**<note>The Ottoman Empire. Renaissance writers often cited the Ottoman military as a model of strict discipline and meritocracy.</note> are, who are currently the most extensive masters of affairs, on account of their one well-constituted military system. For if a **decurion**<note>A leader of ten men.</note> neglects to punish a crime in war, or neglects to keep order or the duties of his office, and it becomes known to the **centurion**<note>A leader of one hundred men.</note> that he either neglected it or was unwilling to punish it, the decurion is immediately punished in place of the criminal. Likewise, if the centurion fails, he answers to the **Chiliarch**<note>From the Greek *chiliarkhos*, a commander of a thousand men (roughly equivalent to a colonel).</note> (for each has their own jurisdictions); similarly, if the chiliarch fails his own leader, they are all accustomed to pay the penalties according to the military law in place of the guilty, for the sake of military utility. Nor is the criminal soldier punished any less if he is caught afterward. Indeed, a punishment in war is ten times more severe, because where the opportunity for delinquency is greatest, there the punishment ought to be greater and more heavy. 

In the inland regions, where there are stationary soldiers, there is a need for judges rather than leaders, and for both in the other two orders. But since all are either horsemen or footmen, they are usually assigned to a duty at the will of the princes. But this is by far the most certain method: ten men to a **decurion**, ten decurions to a **centurion**, ten centurions to a **chiliarch**, and ten chiliarchs to a **leader**. Finally, all leaders are subject to him who has the care of the whole army. It matters little if they are organized by another number, provided they can be easily managed by one man. Thus it happens that if anything must be done or decided, the commands reach from the highest to the lowest immediately; they come to assemblies at once and do what is commanded. 

Therefore, these men—as much because of their intractable nature as because the duties of military service are little known to civil judges, and because one class usually hates the other—ought to have their own **special courts**; otherwise, vengeance rather than equity would be observed. For this reason, princes are also accustomed to assign their own household servants to certain tribunals, lest they be hindered elsewhere (as they say) and be absent from the prince's service. But these are matters of human opinion. For a single order of judges ought to investigate every crime without distinction or regard for persons, and have the strength to coerce even the greatest crowd and...

...supported by authority, to have them at the ready anywhere in the world. In royal courts and military camps, however—which are essentially cities without restraints, always on the move—there is a need for the kind of men we have previously described.

### ON THE MILITARY EXPEDITION, CHAPTER 24.

Furthermore, provision must be made for the soldiers themselves, so they have what is necessary for the requirements of life and the use of arms, as well as what is required for the journey and the expedition. First, therefore, there is a need for a magistrate, appointed for that specific time during which the expedition lasts, upon whom the care of all (or at least the more important) duties should fall. He should possess such authority that no one would dare resist his command with impunity. He should have primary care of preparing necessities, both for the sustenance of men and for the horses. **Provisions**<term>Latin: *annona*. Originally referring to the Roman goddess of the grain supply, this term describes the yearly produce and the regulation of food prices for the public or the military.</term>, wine, and fodder must be brought in from the neighboring fields, and care must be taken so that they can be sold at a lower price. For when a soldier is forced to buy food at a huge price, he immediately refuses his duties while he is occupied with seeking out necessities, or is forced to spend more than he receives in pay. For it is especially important to note that this class of men—seeking profit and a more splendid fortune by risking their lives for gain—never performs their duties with a generous spirit unless they believe they can obtain some profit. Therefore, care must be taken so that the price of food is as low as possible. For there is no prince who can include in the soldier's pay those things which can commonly be spent outside of military craft; and even if he did, no soldier would want to expend the full sweat of his life for it.

Supplies are gathered either in one place or along one route. If along a route, it is for transit. If in one place, that requires great diligence. If we are attacking and need current crops, only the quantity is required; if we are besieged, there is a need for those things which can be preserved for a very long time, such as rice, millet, wheat flour, rye, and barley. For when they are ground down, they do not rot easily because they do not trap air within the body of the grain. In the second place are all salted things: cheese, meat, and fish. In the third place are wheat, barley, and oats, kept in a place where they may be frequently moved so they do not perish from trapped air. Living animals should not be kept alive for long during a **siege**<note>Latin: *obsidione*. A military operation where an army surrounds a town or fortress to cut off supplies and force a surrender.</note>, so they do not consume the food that horses and men might use to sustain life longer. Furthermore, they can be best preserved and hardened with salt. For unless fodder is supplied in abundance, the animals are killed at home and usually cost no small amount to feed.

So much for the siege. Regarding the instruments for the road and the **machines**<note>Latin: *machinis*. This refers to siege engines and artillery, such as catapults, rams, or early cannons.</note> for attacking or defending, care must be taken so that nothing is lacking when the time comes. For while the soldier is stuck in the narrows of the road, or cannot move the machines, or waits for a bridge, or is delayed for any other reason, he incurs expenses; eventually, what should have been foreseen and done long ago must be done in a great rush. Thus, a great loss occurs in that matter. To ensure the roads are level for driving machines and transporting soldiers, the first care is that a supply of road-levelers is present. Military roads fit for moving troops and **bridges**<note>Latin: *pontes*.</note> (if they are missing) ought to be built in the Roman fashion by commoners and chosen men. Material must be brought from elsewhere long beforehand and prepared in suitable places; for which reason it is necessary to have a skilled surveyor of the regions. Otherwise, if wood is lacking, **skins**<note>Latin: *utres*. Animal skins inflated with air to serve as personal flotation devices or components of a raft.</note> must be prepared and inflated, on which the soldier may swim across. If these are not enough, they can be sent back to comrades by a rope. Beams, jars, planks, and so on can serve as a bridge in summer, but this skill ought to be present in the recruits. But when we are near the enemy...

...there ought to be such diligence in the commander <note>Original: *præfecto*. This refers to the officer in charge of the expedition's logistics.</note> that he grasps all the plans of the enemy and employs the most faithful scouts, so that he may provide aid by foreseeing the necessary remedies. For we easily "drive out one nail with another" <note>A Latin proverb (*clauum clauo*) meaning to solve one problem with another, or to replace one preoccupation with another.</note> if there is foresight. Even a blade of grass terrifies the man who is unprepared. Since every region has its own methods of defense and attack, there is no need to go through each one individually. One thing is primary in any leader: that the effects of mature plans be as swift as possible. If he senses that the adversary is guarding against his usual tactics, he should know he must immediately fly to another strategy. For he ought to be like Proteus <note>A sea god in Greek mythology who could change his shape at will. The author uses this to emphasize the need for tactical flexibility.</note>. But we must return to the overseer, who must have three ranks of men, just like other orders of magistrates. For he must place some in charge of a larger province, whom several inferiors shall obey. First, let him ensure that the sinews of war <note>Original: *neruum belli*. A classical metaphor for the money and resources (like food and weapons) required to sustain a conflict.</note> are reported to the leader. He must have roads cleared of wicked men; second, he must see to the food for the men; third, food for the horses; and fourth, the baggage, including the arms required for both men and horses as well as the entire army. Nothing forbids there being various magistrates for various duties. But no one would deny that they should be in the order I have described; for in human affairs, there is a certain plan that depends on a single head and is distributed into many parts in an orderly way. He will choose individuals faithful to himself, and by their faith, he will be answerable to the prince. If any fault is committed by them, he must compensate for it; therefore, he must have the highest authority over them to restrain them. After he has restrained them, if they are at fault, they should be fined; if he himself chose bad men, he can be punished or pay the penalty. For when many are in the same office, a certain envy inherent in human affairs arises, such that they betray one another, introduce injuries, accuse one another, and instead of the public business, they look after themselves and follow their own factions. Truly, resources must now be prepared for both duties: namely, for the salary of the judges and for military duties.

### ON THE FIRST ELEMENTS OF WEALTH,
->and on the distinction of things. CHAPTER XXV.<-

There has been a great and immense variety among men in gathering that power which the consensus of people wishes to be granted to the head of the state <note>Original: *reipub. capiti*. Referring to the sovereign or central governing authority of a republic or commonwealth.</note>. For after resources were first granted to princes so they could look after themselves while caring for the state, the ancients were accustomed to give them only to a magistrate created for that purpose, who would demand from everyone what was fair. Then the municipalities themselves used to choose either one or several men fit for military service and provide for their expenses by public consent. Others collected both types of money—their own and the military funds—but the judges were paid at home. Some collected the judges' pay, their own, and the military funds all together; once this was drawn into use, taxes <term>Latin: *vectigalia*. These were originally revenues from public lands, but here refers to general state taxes or customs duties.</term> began to be extended by one and the same effort, and the judgment of demanding them rested with the prince. Thus, some grew accustomed to receiving impositions <note>Original: *inditiones*. Taxes or levies imposed by authority.</note> from persons, some from things, and some from both; and gradually, whatever exists from which some utility can be had began to be observed and made subject to the treasury <term>Latin: *fiscus*. The Roman term for the public purse or the emperor's private treasury.</term>. Truly, whatever the custom may have been, those three types mentioned just before encompass everything. For if you seek from persons, the persons possess everything; if from things, all things are subject to the eyes and senses; if from both, the law will be the same. The first republics assessed "heads" <note>Original: *capita*. A poll tax or head tax.</note>, and payments were made to the treasury according to the ratio of the census <note>An official count or survey of a population, typically recording details of individuals and their property for taxation.</note>, which many republics in Germany still do today by a simple oath without any description of the census. For you can hardly know what is in the goods of individuals unless there is some man so honest that he immediately reveals how much he possesses—which is surely a "rare bird" <note>Original: *rara auis*. A reference to the Roman poet Juvenal's description of a "rare bird on earth, very much like a black swan"—meaning something almost impossible to find.</note>. No...

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK III.

...for no one willingly says anything that might contradict himself. As for what is possessed from physical things, it is manifold. For wealth is situated either in the land or in the water. In the waters, resources are movable, immovable, or a mixture of both. On land, they are movable, immovable, or self-moving. The Roman Republic, and many others, regarding the utility of water—without the use of which one cannot live—wished for no tax <term>uectigalis; a tax or tribute paid to the state</term> to be taken. For they wanted the use of seawater, fishing, the seashores, and wild animals to be common to all, and to become the property of the one occupying them for as long as he possessed them. The banks of rivers, however, have always been private property. From the sea come merchandise <term>mercimonia; goods for trade</term>, fishing, and salt. Merchandise is a movable thing. Regarding the right of fishing: if it exists everywhere equally, it is movable; if it is restricted to a certain place, such as a specific occupied and private shore, those resources from which utility is sought are considered immovable. If a thing cannot be produced without the use of a certain fixed shore—as is the case with salt, which is produced partly by art and partly by nature—it holds a middle condition. For insofar as the thing is in the soil, it is immovable; insofar as it is removed and carried elsewhere, it is movable. The right of rivers is like a road, and governed by the same law, except for what pertains to fishing; in the more refined and shrewd parts of the world, fishing rights are now usually held as private property, though otherwise they belong to common law. Waters enclosed within certain limits of the soil, such as lakes and ponds, are either public or private according to the custom of the region. If someone has them enclosed on his own land, it is certain they belong to him. The logic of shores and banks, unless otherwise accepted by law, gives rights to the neighbors. Flowing water can also be subject to a perpetual tax, for instance, if a channel is diverted from its natural course and led into a region which it renders far better through irrigation. In that case, the person by whose labor it was done can, as long as the water flows usefully there, exact a tax from individual owners, with the water granted by "inch-measures" <note>Original: *unciales mensuras*. An early method of regulating water rights by the diameter of the pipe or channel opening.</note> at established hours and days. This type of revenue exists in many places, but it is by far the most abundant in Cisalpine Gaul, which they call Lombardy <note>A region in Northern Italy famous since the Middle Ages for its sophisticated irrigation systems and canals.</note>. For more diligent republics or princes have drawn "Niles" and "Euripuses" <note>Postel uses the names of the Nile river and the Strait of Euripus as generic terms for major canals or artificial waterworks.</note>, either collecting water from the mountains into lower regions, or digging channels from the Po, the Adige, and other rivers into flat and level plains. Among the things usually possessed through the convenience of water, because the prince defends and protects merchandise no less than the things born from the soil—even if they are brought from elsewhere or must be carried away—he can nevertheless take a tax from them, and especially from salt. Truly, these matters are placed at the discretion of princes.

In the soil are crops, trees, meadows, pastures, and woods. By "crops," we mean any kind of legumes and grains, and things usually sown and harvested annually. Of trees, some are fruit-bearing, others are sterile; some are in forests, others in "coppiced" woods <note>Woods managed by periodically cutting back trees to ground level to stimulate growth for fuel or fencing.</note>. Although meadows and pastures can be aided by industry, they are nonetheless chiefly placed in the benefit of nature. There are many uses for forests, for they are usually preserved for domestic use for fire, tools, building, grazing, and hunting. Hence arise the goods born from the surface of the earth: wood, legumes, hay, fruit, and herds. There are also metals, which cannot be rendered pure without the benefit of forests; for this reason, we place their origin in the bowels of the earth, but their perfection in the use of wood for smelting. These are gold, silver, tin, copper <note>Original: *Cyprium æs*, literally "ore from Cyprus," whence the word copper derives.</note>, brass <note>Original: *aurichalcum*, a golden-colored alloy highly valued in antiquity.</note>, lead, iron, quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, and other minerals, stones, pebbles, gems, and whatever else nature produces for us who look more curiously. There remains the class of self-moving animals, which, when accounted for by head or by flock and driven elsewhere as merchandise rather than staying on their native soil, also constitute great wealth. We can therefore very easily teach another division of those things held on land and sea. For everything is either below the surface, or on the surface, or partly inside and partly outside. On the surface of the earth are all living creatures of land and air; partly above and partly below is whatever vegetable the earth produces. Below are all metals, or medicinal...

...ornaments, gems, and whatever is of value. In the sea, there are fisheries, navigations, and salts. There remains for us a very large portion of wealth, by far the most abundant, yet the most difficult to understand. For arising from necessity, if any other thing has been entirely led into the realm of public opinion, it is this: that industrious men, sensing in advance which things a particular region might especially delight in, and having no concern for utility or necessity so long as they make a profit, bring foreign goods there, and if it may be said, they often cause the world to stumble. For man, by nature—besides the unique gift of speech by which he differs from other living creatures—also has this trait: he admires all foreign things, stands agape at the unusual, and is captivated by useless external things rather than domestic and proven ones. Wealth is also gathered by other arts, yet still from some of those things we have mentioned. A good portion of the first men lived by hunting; others by theft committed on land or sea; some by pastures or animals; others by agriculture; others by opinion, such as those who increased their wealth through religions; others by the labors of the body; and others by the benefit of their intellect, who alone among mortals are usually the most beloved in the state and least indebted to the <term>fiscus; the state treasury</term>. For the gifts of the mind usually procure true nobility almost anywhere in the world, provided they are turned to the use of the republic. From all or many of these elements of things, the treasury can pluck something for the preservation and protection of the state. Also, things that cease to belong to any owner, or which return to the treasury as if by <term>postliminio; a legal right where property or status is restored to its original state</term>, should belong to the prince, such as the goods of the proscribed or those marked by a capital crime. Some place under the same law the goods of those who, born elsewhere, die while possessing or acquiring property on foreign soil without having obtained the prince's favor to become citizens or inhabitants of the land—a law used by the King of the French. For he joins the goods of those born elsewhere and dying in his jurisdiction to the treasury, lest more unknown foreigners gradually creep into the region. Indeed, these are the primary headings of wealth.

## ON THE TREASURERS OF THE TREASURY,
### CHAPTER XXVI.

When taxes began to be extended, and were the concern of only one or another city or municipality, there was no need for a great or numerous magistracy to collect them, since the wealth of any private individual could easily be known to the prince, the arbiter of equity. But as wealth and dominions increased—whether things were to be viewed individually, or by the valuation of the soil, or by the power of men—there was first a need for an arbiter of the census, of resources, and of things. This official, once the sum was declared by the prince and commanded for any province, would divide it, and having diligently considered the resources of all places, distribute the portions of the larger required sum according to cities, villages, assemblies of men, and districts, by assessing them for what they are able to provide. Once this is declared, there is a need for a municipal magistrate who, having summoned those more skilled in particular matters, imposes a fair portion of the payments according to the strengths they have disclosed. In this matter, it is amazing how much those whom the French call <term>electos; 'élus', or tax assessors</term> permit themselves. With the greatest inequity, they exempt some who have corrupted them with gifts, and heavily oppress others, unless they have received from both. The municipal treasurers, once the sum is collected from private individuals, present it to the provincial treasurer, who acknowledges it with signatures and witnesses; he then presents it to the high treasurer, who returns it to the treasury or spends it on those uses the prince has established. In these matters, it can hardly be seen whether fraud lies beneath. Nevertheless, an <term>antigrapharius; a counter-accountant or scribe who keeps a duplicate record to prevent forgery or fraud</term> ought to be everywhere and record in a diary whatever is received from the treasurers themselves. And lest the treasurers and accountants commit any wrongdoing together, there is a need for masters of accounts (whom it is proper to have everywhere), who [oversee] what has been received...

...and discuss the accounts of expenses, and record them in the public ledgers. But when the King or Prince gives as a gift something that had been acquired by the <term>fiscus; the state treasury</term>—such as confiscations or anything else—it is necessary that this also be inscribed in the accounts by those in charge of the treasury, which many republics lack. For it is enough for the accounting that everyone who owes the treasury, or who receives from it, be held accountable. Indeed, this matter is so slippery that it can hardly be restrained by any bonds. Therefore, whether the assessments—which they commonly call <term>taleas; tax-tally sticks or levies</term>—are personal (that is, following the valuation of even hidden assets) or real (that is, based only on the land and visible things), the same order must be maintained as in military affairs. 

Because wealth is the "food" of the republic, and because no private person is permitted to question the judgment of the prince, these matters do not tolerate delay, just as the stomach does not. For when pledges are seized, everyone is immediately compelled to pay; and if a fine is involved, one is usually physically constrained, so that he either perishes or is freed from payment by friends. Therefore, these <term>quaestors; treasury officials</term> are the overseers of fixed assets. The same order applies if anything is demanded from other ranks, which has always been done with religious orders when they have become immensely wealthy. For wealth, however it is held, is still wealth; it is useful to the republic and liable to the treasury if it is in need. Otherwise, one could label everything as "sacred" and leave the republic destitute. 

For these things that fall to the treasury by chance, there must also be a specific treasurer, just as when fines—which have their own treasurer—are to be received. Those lucrative offices that are not mixed with judicial duties return to the state fund upon the death of the holder and are usually sold again. There are also <term>vectigalia; taxes or tolls</term> when any merchandise is driven or carried through fixed locations. From these, the republic that protects them can take a toll, excluding those things without which one cannot live comfortably. For everyone pays what the treasury takes; nor does the profitable merchant really pay it, since he immediately recovers it from the buyer; for that reason, that part of the tax is a burden on the public. Do not drive the merchant away, provided he brings things useful to the republic. Let him sell freely. If he sells useless things, penalize them with a tax. When he necessarily takes from you what he needs, then tax him—not so much that he is deprived of his profit (for then he would not come), but so that you become a partner in it. 

Furthermore, "the smell of profit is good from any source" <note>original: "lucri bonus odor." This refers to the Roman Emperor Vespasian's famous justification for taxing public latrines: "Pecunia non olet" (Money does not smell).</note>, and various types of exactions are devised daily according to the whim and tyranny of princes. For some, like the Turk <note>Referring to the Ottoman Sultan.</note>, have even willed that the bodies of the poorest men—those devoted to the faith of <term>Christ and Moses; Christians and Jews</term>—be subject to a tax <note>Postel is describing the *jizya*, the head tax levied on non-Muslim subjects in Islamic states.</note>. Because they cannot pay this, either their bodies are detained or they are ransomed by their fellow townspeople, if it is a fixed or annual sum. Thousands upon thousands of coins are to be collected for his own use, under the pretext of maintaining roads and supporting the military. 

But because this wretched condition of life removes some from our midst daily and creates others, it is necessary that magistrates be so constituted that some are supreme, some middle, and some lowest. The greatest depend on the prince, the middle on the greatest, and the lowest on the middle, in matters of judging and in preparing and commanding the military. Among the treasurers, they work by distributing what is commanded, and by collecting and reporting what has been distributed. For unless you report back, you achieve nothing. These are the accounts of persons, the ranks, and the duties that are necessary in well-constituted republics, upon whose authority depends—or is handled—whatever cases may arise in law. There is one law among all nations for pursuing one's right and keeping one's property. But because every region is accustomed to using its own formulas for legal actions, those things pertaining to practice cannot be handed down with as certain a method as those looking toward theory. Therefore, that discussion should be left to common usage. It was enough to have explained these basic elements.

# ON THE UNIVERSAL HARMONY OF THE WORLD
## BOOK IV: ON THE CONVERSION OF FALSE PERSUASIONS TO THE TRUE [FAITH]
### ON THE ARTS NEEDED BY A PRINCE WHO INTENDS TO CHANGE RELIGION AND SUBSTITUTE THE TRUE FAITH FOR THE FALSE.

---

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial E featuring a man's profile in a medallion with the name AGRIPPA inscribed around it.</image-desc>

Among all the notions that move our minds, none is usually accepted more reluctantly, or abandoned with greater difficulty, than the opinion held concerning religion. It hardly ever happens—unless by extreme force or by the long-term work of instilling different ideas—that it can be altered at all without bloodshed or a total upheaval of affairs. Therefore, Plato advises in his *Laws* that the conviction regarding the God received in any <term>republic; state or commonwealth</term> should not be rashly disturbed. For it happens that if a prince, or anyone else, unwisely loosens the bonds of old beliefs from the mind before binding them with a new religion, the harmony of the people and the common bond is undermined; a people released from their old ways will hardly admit another, even a most excellent one. 

This happens for many reasons, which we must carefully consider before we proceed further into treating how to drive out adulterated beliefs and substitute the truth. In the previous book, it was demonstrated that it is common to all men that, even if they are ignorant of what kind of God they ought to have, they all nevertheless judge that one must be held. This itself proceeds from the opportunity to give thanks, which nature has given to everyone. For it is impossible that this "wise animal," full of reason—though born by nature lacking all things and exposed, as it were, to every kind of misery—should not desire to acknowledge the giver of such a great gift when he recognizes that this entire machinery of the world was prepared for him to compensate for and drive away those miseries. Thus, he worships whatever he has heard from his parents to be held in the place of God. 

Added to this gratitude and compensation is that most tenacious age of childhood, which, as the saying goes, "preserves for a very long time the scent with which it was once imbued." Childhood, handing itself over to custom as if to a "second nature," most stubbornly retains and defends false things just as well as true ones once it has received them; so that a person believes nothing is truer than what he received from his parents. Indeed, the more false the opinion of the gods is anywhere among the nations, the more ardently the <term>sacrificuli; minor priests or keepers of sacrifices</term> strive—at the persuasion of Satan, the author of false persuasion and evil opinions—to ensure it is retained and approved by everyone. 

This is evident from these arguments: A good man, conscious of his own virtue and content with his conscience, is not usually inclined to "sell" his own merits or care much for the judgment of others. He knows that nothing in the nature of things is changed by the words of men, and he knows that true praise is to be expected only from the good and should be pursued so that a solid foundation is reached. A villainous man, however, conscious of his own malice, thinks everyone is talking about him; he puffs himself up, boasts, and pushes himself forward so that he may cover the "fox" he carries in his breast <note>This is a classical metaphor for hidden cunning or a guilty conscience.</note> with the reputation of integrity begged from the votes of others. Hence, you may daily see the most vain men selling their own reputations and belittling those of others. In false religions, it is exactly the same. Therefore, they used to elude people with ambiguous responses and seemed to satisfy everyone. For when antiquity called Apollo "Loxias" <note>original: "λοξίαν" (loxian) – an epithet of Apollo meaning 'the ambiguous one' or 'the slanting one,' referring to his cryptic oracles.</note> and the father of the gods, Saturn, "crooked-counselled" <note>original: "ἀγκυλομήτην" (ankylometen) – meaning 'devious' or 'of twisted mind.'</note>, it meant to suggest...

He warns that a ruler must replace old beliefs carefully to avoid social collapse, noting that false religions often rely on ambiguity and vanity to maintain their power.</summary>

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK IV

...willed it. To these were added the most solemn bird-omens <note>original: *tripudia solistima*; an ancient Roman form of divination where the movements of sacred chickens while eating were interpreted as divine signs</note>, auguries, the inspection of sacrificial entrails <note>original: *extispicia*; the practice of looking for divine messages in the organs of sacrificed animals</note>, divinations, and those deceptive riddles by which both the wise and the common people were fooled. If anyone, however, had dared to even whisper against these things, they were punished with death. For this is the nature of false beliefs: no matter how poorly they were first persuaded, they wish to force themselves upon everyone. They must be proven by the presence of the sword; no one dares to argue against them under penalty of death, so that at least through fear and silence, a person—who out of fear of death does not even dare to mutter against them—might seem to approve. Therefore, those who are unskilled in discerning the false from the true are bound to false religions all the more vehemently the more they are pressured by <term>sacrificulis; "petty priests" or those who perform sacrifices for profit</term> and their ministers, making them harder to cure. For they share the same principles of belief with good men, but age is added to it, custom compels it, and falsehood persists. It follows—since no one cares for or considers such things—that the truth is spread very narrowly, while the false inserts itself everywhere, flourishes, and is approved. For any prince considers it enough to keep the people at peace and to spend those funds belonging to the treasury on his own legal and military affairs. <margin>di</margin> A soldier is hardly restrained by any laws, whether profane or sacred. <margin>10</margin> A judge punishes injuries and resolves doubts, lawsuits, and quarrels. <margin>1</margin> The common people do not grasp mysteries. <margin>1</margin> Only the sacred magistrate has the care of religion; <margin>0</margin> even if it is a most corrupt religion, because he derives profit from it, he never allows it to be changed. <margin>0</margin> He stirs up the common people, threatens them with a plague that is soon to come, and predicts disasters—by which <margin>0</margin> things he strikes the minds of almost everyone. In the midst of such mental consternation, however, hardly any <margin>0</margin> free judgment regarding affairs remains for anyone. And if someone, judging matters freely and incorruptibly, should then wish to be heard, he must necessarily rush into danger and willingly undergo immediate death. Truly, since nature has taught that death is to be feared, no one willingly undergoes it unless they are driven by the divine spirit and entirely transformed—the kind of witnesses Jesus Christ had. Therefore, having carefully weighed these matters, the moderator of the <term>republic; the state or commonwealth</term> ought to communicate, gradually and without a great assembly of men, the changes he wishes for the state to the leading nobles. He should persuade them through reasoning and gentle enticement as to what he thinks should be changed in religious matters. When they have approved it (for if it should displease everyone, he must either wait while continuing to persuade them, or use force—the latter of which is hardly safe for a ruler who governs by the will of others), then the high judges in the various provinces must also be compelled: so that, when preachers advocate for such things as the prince desires, the judges permit those who are willing to be gradually persuaded. In the third place—once the power of both the nobles and the judges has been won over, so that they do not join factions to oppose his efforts—the high priests must be called, and the supreme leader must be compelled, whether he wills it or not, to advocate for (or permit the advocacy for) those things which the prince has approved as best and examined by the consensus of the most learned men. Nor should the high priest dare to oppose even by a word those who have been sent by the prince for the sake of teaching. Moreover, the prince ought to select men suitable for persuading others of the true faith, men who are highly practiced in all arts as much as possible, but especially in the doctrines of the true religion. To resolve the objections of the false religion, they should be most highly instructed in philosophy. Since such men are few, they should travel through entire regions as most holy and inviolable men (guarded, if need be, by a vigilant watch), and they should initiate those willing to approve the doctrines of the true religion; but for the rest, they should leave the freedom of belief to each individual. For what is done by force hardly ever yields good fruit. Therefore, the true religion forbids force being used against anyone of sound and constant judgment, and it disapproves if someone is driven toward the truth by force without understanding. For God wants free souls. It is possible, however, if there are a few infidels among many and a stain spreads from them into the multitude, that a day be set for them: they must either willingly come over to the new persuasion or, if unwilling, be forced to leave the region, lest from a few rotten members the rot creeps into the whole body and brings ruin. These are...

ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...the arts of the prince, by which, with absolutely no loss and with the greatest efficiency and ease, he can persuade his subjects of the truth without uproar or bloodshed. Truly, the visions and dreams of princes—where they agree with the truth—are to be held by the people as revelations; false things must be shown for what they are, and the truth must be confirmed. For even though the truth was already true and the false was false before then, nevertheless, when it is repeated through the benefit of a man placed in authority, it is believed by the common people (who depend on authority) as if it were something new. Indeed, a falsehood is far more easily approved by authority than the truth is when demonstrated by reason from a man of humble status. Why then should we think a prince would not succeed in persuading people of the truth, when he can persuade them of a falsehood by his authority alone? 

Truly, before all else, once a number of the most excellent men of the true religion have been assembled, he ought to have their conclusions reduced into brief <term>axioms; self-evident principles or starting points for an argument</term>. If it can be done, he should even know these and commit them to memory, so that from his own mouth, with great authority—be it sacred or secular—men might hear the very things that the learned men and professors are going to advise, persuade, and confirm. I have provided, argued for, and confirmed those conclusions very extensively in my first book, as they are necessary for anyone intending to persuade others of the true religion. They may be sought from there.

### IN WHAT WAYS THE TRUE FAITH IS TO BE PREACHED WITHOUT OFFENSE 
### *to anyone: and concerning the duty of the one who undertakes the task of correcting,*
### *or entirely overturning, a false persuasion.*

It is necessary that he who receives the task of persuading others of the truth from the prince be no less skilled in those things which the adversaries of truth approve than in the truth itself. For the truth must not only be taught and confirmed, but false objections must be resolved and arguments diluted. This cannot be done except by a <note>original: *collisione locorum*; a rhetorical technique of "colliding" or comparing different topics and arguments against one another to find the truth</note> comparison of the points of falsehood. 

In addition to this, one must see that they "become all things to all men" <note>A reference to the Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 9:22</note>; that is, they should accommodate themselves to those they desire to teach in such a way that they seem to begin from the approval of the people's own laws. Then, once their attention is secured and conclusions are drawn out, we may either confirm our own views or show the views of others to be insufficiently firm. 

Most importantly, however, this must be observed: that which the people find hateful or which they disapprove of should not be named until its description has been carefully delivered. For naming it would make us suspect from the beginning, and would turn the minds of the listeners away from goodwill and attention—without which (unless by a miracle of the Holy Spirit) you can persuade no one of anything. Therefore, so that the minds of the people may be held for the sake of their salvation, one must consult their infirmity at the beginning. They should be praised and approved as if they were good, though they may be "half-impious and half-evil" <note>original: *semiimpij & semimali*; Postel views people in false religions as misguided rather than entirely wicked</note>. Thus, while they partly acquiesce and begin to frequent the company of those who teach the truth and prove it by their deeds, they may be gradually corrected and changed by constant social interaction. For conversation and constant association over a long period of time will bring about what you could never obtain at first sight. 

It was in this way that Moses took up the sons of Israel. In this way, Paul became "all things to all men" regarding social interaction. Because of this, Jesus Christ, being about to fulfill the Law, willed even to be subject to the ceremonies of the Law. Furthermore, the one who teaches must always keep his mind focused on three things. He must always place these before his eyes: 
1. The primary power of teaching comes from the **person** of the speaker.
2. The power of advising comes from the **mind** of the listener.
3. The power of persuading comes from the **matter** itself. 

Therefore, let the herald of truth be of the highest innocence of life and, as far as is possible among men, beyond reproach. He should know the mind of the listener—what intensely pleases or displeases them. Thirdly, he should possess such erudition that, whatever subject he must speak upon, he deserves silence and a listening ear by his own merit. But if the mind of the people is not clearly seen by him, or how easily they might acquiesce to the truth, he should bring forward common principles known to everyone; and having captured the audience by these, when they are already attentive...

...once the people are held <note>In the sense of being attentive or under the prince's influence</note>, he should instill gradually and step-by-step those things which contribute to the particular proof of the truth. In this way, it will happen that the people will easily receive what the prince desires to be accomplished and what is beneficial for the salvation of all. However, one must abstain from specific terms—unless we seem to be tending toward the praise of a false dogma—lest even well-presented points be seized upon with hostility. But once these matters have been brought forward and weighed—matters with which both the prince and the preacher of the word of God ought to be equipped—we must proceed with examples, and we must treat how the practice of these precepts is to be exercised within each of the religious persuasions that are foreign to the truth. First, therefore, we shall hand down the art with which one must deal with the **Muslims** <note>original: "Muhamedicis"</note>, who creep most widely and across almost the entire world. Second, we will discuss how we might approach any kind of pagan or idolater. Finally, it must be seen if it can be brought about through persuasion to rescue any of the **Jews** from the unhappiness with which they have been burdened since the killing of Christ. For that entire nation will never approach God through the Messiah until, after the coming of the supreme Antichrist, the remnants are made safe and numbered among the elect. Thus, when we have provided persuasions accommodated to all those nations, we shall place an end to this book and work.

### A DIVINELY INSPIRED FORMULA FOR PERSUADING THE MUSLIMS.

In the second book, it was seen what we have in common with the Muslims and where we differ. For they confess whatever we hold concerning divine matters, though in their own way—except for those things concerning the divinity of Jesus Christ and his death, which are most certain to us. Because they are violently offended if they hear Christ called God—since that deceitful and lying impostor **Mohammed** <note>original: "Muhamedes"</note> wished to persuade them of the contrary throughout the entire **Quran** <note>original: "Alcorano"</note>—therefore, nothing should be dealt with concerning Christ's divinity at the very start of the persuasion. This is true even though He is the aim of the entire true religion, as are His death and resurrection. If anything is said of Christ, it ought not to exceed those things handed down about him in the Quran, lest the **religious leaders** <note>original: "sacrifices." Postel likely refers to imams or Islamic scholars here</note>, noticing this, secretly call the people away from listening where it is not permitted openly. 

One must, therefore, declaim about divine benefits as ornately as possible. For although the Arabic and Turkish languages are capable of their own eloquence, nothing is more inept than those persuasions made by their **legal scholars** <note>original: "Alphachijs," from the Arabic "al-faqih," meaning a jurist or scholar of Islamic law</note>. The variety of the world, fruits, animals, and kingdoms should be added in a specific order, so that, captured by the light of that order and enticed by a new kind of teaching, the listeners may become most attentive and frequent. Once a larger audience is gathered, one must deal with the power and benefits of the Creator, but with a higher method than before. For the mystery of the most holy **Trinity** must be touched upon with simpler demonstrations. Indeed, those Muslims who excel in any kind of doctrine are most eager to hear of it. 

The first example, which is most familiar, is drawn from the intellect, introducing it thus: whatever things are perfect, good, and just, and whatever is of absolute perfection, they possess that from God. That which comes from a certain principle most abundantly into certain effects and particulars must necessarily be far more perfect, more abundant, and greater in the cause than in the effect. For instance, if many beautiful houses are made from the conception of a most excellent craftsman, no one will deny that in his mind there is an infinite power of designing infinite similar or even more beautiful houses. Thus, it is certain that what is most excellent in us, and established in all things, also has an image in God. Yet nothing in things or in their actions, however simple, lacks a **trinity**; for nothing can be done without a threefold power. For though you may have however much power to do anything, unless there is present the knowledge of how to do it, and of those parts which **to**... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "ad" (to)</note>

## ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
### BOOK IV

...for any work, knowledge and the highest and most powerful wisdom are required; and to these two properties, the will to create and the love of preserving must be added, otherwise no thing at all can exist or be made. Since this exists in the most excellent part of ourselves—namely, in the soul—certainly God possesses that <term>trinity</term> <note>Postel uses 'trinity' here to refer to the triad of Power, Wisdom, and Love as a reflection of the divine nature.</note> in the most excellent degree. For even though He is powerful, unless He had possessed wisdom from eternity, along with the will and the love for creating when it seemed good to Him, He could not have brought anything into existence. God is therefore <term>trine</term> and one. For the same divinity is in power, the same in wisdom, and the same in love; and yet there are not three divinities, but one divinity. Just as when I think, express, and act, these are different actions; and yet they are not three things, but only one. I conceive of the form of a building, I explain it with words, or writings, or a <term>floor plan</term> <note>original: "ichnographia"</note>, and finally I see that it is built. Thus there are three considerations of a building: first as it is in the mind, second as it is in the explanation, third as it is in the actual work; and yet they are not three buildings, but one. In the same way, God the Father is as Power, the Son as Wisdom, and the Holy Spirit as Love and Effect. These points must be confirmed and driven home with many examples, and we must speak out against those misguided Christians who claimed before the prophets that there were three gods; for there are not three gods, but one God. Yet while these things are frequently repeated, they seem to work in their favor. It will be necessary to confirm what has seemed necessary through the likeness of all things, and especially the most excellent ones.

The Sun can do absolutely nothing without this threefold nature; for it consists of a body, light or rays, and power. For the luminous body is not the ray, nor vice-versa, but the ray proceeding from the body differs from its source, and the effect of heat is distinct from both. Nevertheless, they are not three actions, or powers, or heats. So it is in all things. In the arts, there is a most familiar example. For a potter can never form a single jar, or any other vessel, unless power, knowledge, and the will proceeding from both are present. For one can only make that which is placed within his art when he possesses the knowledge and the will to form it. Since this is most excellent in man, it must be far more excellent in the <term>archetype</term> <note>The 'archetype' refers to the original divine model or God Himself, from which all earthly things are copied.</note> by as much as God is greater than man. For just as the whole art is in the power of the craftsman, so also the whole art is in his knowledge, and the whole art is in his will and effect; and yet they are not three things or three arts, but one art. And likewise: nothing can be done by art or nature unless there is in the action an abundance, a process, and a will; or as I have said, a fruitfulness, a birth, and love. For if from that power of art which one possesses, there could be no progression or generated offspring, he would clearly do nothing. And unless he took delight in the action and made a choice of the material in which he acts, undoubtedly nothing could be made by the craftsman.

In natural things, the example is even easier. Unless pepper or ginger possessed a perpetual and inexhaustible abundance of heat and stinging from which the biting and burning always proceeded, and unless nature delighted in it and wished to always act in that way after its own fashion, it could certainly not exist. Moreover, that even inanimate things seem to have a kind of choice is proven by the fact that they direct all their actions toward the most suitable subject. Pepper indeed burns, but not everywhere. When the pores of the body are opened by sweat or exercise, it acts but little; it acts most vehemently on skinned flesh, but in the most excellent way on the tongue, because that member is suited for tasting and sensing things. If fire is placed next to sulfur, tow <note>coarse flax or hemp fibers</note>, straw, dry twigs, or finally solid and thick wood in the middle of a forest, it will never err in choosing or acting upon its object. So too a stone, whose nature (besides its hidden properties) is to tend downward; it sinks very little upon an earthy body, more in mud, greatly in water, and through the air until it touches the earth. Thus all things choose.

...the vegetative faculty itself seeks its own peculiar nourishment from all the surrounding humors. 
Furthermore, we must come to actions, none of which can occur without the <term>ternary</term> <note>Postel uses "ternary" to describe a three-part structure inherent in all things, mirroring the Trinity.</note> principle. No one can love unless some beloved object is proposed to them; nor can any friendship exist without a middle love proceeding from both sides. We must also discuss matter and form even with the learned and those skilled in natural things. Since the hinge of the matter turns on this—that they may know God as He is—one must insist upon this above all. For once this is demonstrated and persuaded, many most excellent things will follow: namely, that God has a Son, and generates Him from eternity from Himself, without whom nothing can be made; and that from both proceed Will, Love, and Effect, which we call the Holy Spirit. It will also follow that it is false and a lie, written perhaps two hundred times in the <term>Alcoranus</term> <note>original: "Alcorano"; the Quran</note>, where it is so often repeated: "God neither generates nor is generated, He has no son, He is not a trinity," etc. If some <term>Imamim</term> <note>original: "Imamim"; Imams or Islamic religious leaders</note> object to these sentences from the <term>Alcoranus</term>, and they must be satisfied (while the work is not yet refuted) lest they stir up troubles or seem to press the Evangelist <note>The "Evangelist" here refers to the Christian missionary or teacher using Postel's methods.</note> when he does not respond, he ought to satisfy them thus: that these sentences are indeed written in their prophet’s book, but they ought to weigh them against other sentences of the law. It is written in two places that no one ought to or can deliver the interpretation of the sentences of the <term>Alcoranus</term> except the prophet himself. Furthermore, it is written in the traditions received from his mouth that out of twelve thousand <term>Aiet</term> <note>original: "Aiet"; verses or "signs" (Ayat) of the Quran</note>, that is, words or miracles, only three thousand are true, while the rest are false. However, so that they might freely call all things either true or false, he did not distinguish them. Therefore, the Evangelist must say that those words which are contrary to natural reason are false and should not be followed, while the rest are true.

### Another instance from man.

When they have now begun to think correctly about God and that opinion is confirmed, man and his gifts, both of mind and body, are to be extolled. In addition, virtue itself, of which man alone is capable, must be extolled with every kind of praise; and among other things, chastity and humanity, and the preservation of human life, must be placed most urgently and frequently before their eyes. [We should say] that the angels and God are most excellent because they are never polluted by the stain of Venus <note>original: "Veneris labe"; a classical metaphor for lust or sexual desire</note>, and they always attend to the preservation of men; whoever does the opposite is wicked and takes up arms against nature. For Nature willed man to be created so that he might be as similar to God as possible. And because they very gladly hear the lives of the saints of the primitive Church, the Evangelist must have a supreme knowledge of them, so that the power of the Gospel and the ornament of all virtues may be seen in them. For we are more easily incited to noble deeds by examples than by words. We should begin with the miracles of the Old Testament, and God should be praised in His saints. But it must always be noted that all miracles performed before Christ were issued by invoking the name of God, by pouring out prayers, or by a command received from God. Christ, however, performed every kind of miracle in His own name, as the true God. The Gospel must be used as testimony in these matters. For the <term>Muhamedici</term> <note>original: "Muhamedici"; Muslims</note> are more studious of the Gospel the more learned they are and the more they are liberated from the captivity of trifles. Noticing this very thing, the <term>Chaliphæ</term> <note>original: "Chaliphæ"; Caliphs</note>, as much as they can, keep them away from the reading of philosophy and the Gospel. For as many as are erudite either become Christians in opinion or die entirely without any religion. For they cannot conceive in their minds the kind of God <term>Muhamedes</term> <note>original: "Muhamedes"; Muhammad</note> wrote of. For besides the fact that he seems to be the author of evil, he also seems to be the author of homicide, idolatry, crime, robbery, luxury, pleasure, and pederasty...

...pederasty <note>original: "pæderastiæ"; the first letters are completed from the previous page's context</note>, the principle and precept of brutal intercourse is attributed to him—things you would shudder to believe even in a man most contaminated by every kind of crime. A preacher must first take care to have with him countless copies of the Gospel printed in Arabic <note>original: "Arabicè excusa"</note>, so that he may share, give, or distribute them to anyone who wishes. Once the Gospel has been introduced and the life of Jesus Christ seen, those things concerning Christ found in the <term>Alcoranus</term> <note>original: "Alcorano"; the Quran</note>, its interpreters, and the <term>Suneh</term> <note>original: "Suneh"; the Sunnah, the body of traditional social and legal custom and practice of the Islamic community</note> must be gathered together and placed before their eyes. He [Christ] is to be exalted as much as possible. Indeed, it should be added to his praises that the Sunnah affirms Jesus Christ will be the future judge of the living and the dead—from which it must be confessed that he is God. For judgment belongs to God alone, who knows all things. Therefore, God the Father would never permit the judgment—in which everything that has ever existed from eternity and the creation of the world must be known and weighed—to Jesus Christ, unless he himself were the all-knowing God. Furthermore, since he was truthful and said he was God (as he truly was), he must be believed. For prophets illuminated by God could never lie. Otherwise, they would not be prophets, just as our Evangelists would not be endowed with the grace of the Holy Spirit. 

<term>Augustine</term> <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian of Western Christianity.</note> used to say that if a single lie were found in the entire Gospel, it should be believed in no way at all. But since Muhammad <note>original: "Muhamedes"</note> wrote nine thousand lies, he could not be a prophet; for the all-knowing God cannot deceive. Therefore, if this law had come from God and his angel (to whom neither forgetfulness nor ignorance applies), it could not have contained anything contradictory, superfluous, or false. 

But one must not yet act against the prophet or the law until God is made known and Christ is accepted through ancient testimonies, his own words and works, the confirmation of his adversaries, and the deeds of his followers. Once we have obtained this, it will immediately be clear to everyone—without any specific pointing or offensive dragging of his name through the mud—what kind of man Muhammad is. For light will both put to flight and expose the darkness. One must therefore proceed with these kinds of logical inductions. No one will doubt that whatever things are more excellent ought to be chosen. Which is more excellent: he who lives chastely, or he who is totally awash in <term>Venereal</term> <note>original: "Venereis"; referring to Venus, the goddess of love; here meaning sexual lust or debauchery.</note> pleasures? He who gives, or he who snatches? He who heals, or he who harms, crushes, and kills? He who brings nature's peace, or he who brings war? The choice is easy. 

And yet, though many have been perfect as far as a human is permitted, no prophet was ever greater, holier, or more divine than <term>Hissa</term> <note>original: "Hissa"; the Arabic name for Jesus, 'Isa.</note> himself, that is, Jesus. Therefore, nothing is holier than his law, his precepts, and the imitation of him. Thus the law of Christ is more excellent than all other laws. And likewise: If there were a man conceived of the Holy Spirit and a virgin, famous for miracles from his very birth, gifted with divine wisdom, most innocent in life, most kind, who restored life and health to many, who never wished to possess any earthly things, and who taught his followers to live in the same way—and, on the other hand, there were a man conceived in the manner of all others, raised in idolatry, practiced in trade, famous for no miracles, suffering from disease of mind and body, who plundered the goods of others, killed, harmed, and oppressed countless people, who turned everything toward profit, and taught his followers to draw the sword against other mortals—which of these would be judged more excellent? Who is more useful to nature? Whose laws would you think should rather be obeyed? Do not laws reflect the character of their authors? The former dictates laws friendly to nature, the latter, laws hostile to it. One nurtures nature, the other is armed against it. One brings salvation, the other destruction. 

I say nothing of the specific gifts of each. For if I grant divinity to Christ, and a resurrection performed without the prayer of any holy person, and to Muhammad those titles which I blush even to think of—who will not see whose examples we should follow? Thus, with many such comparisons <note>original: "exaggerationibus"; in a rhetorical sense, the weighing or heightening of points of comparison.</note> taken from the lives of both, Christ must be named and Muhammad suppressed, until [his] divinity...

...let [the person] be fully persuaded in Christ, and let Him be clearly depicted in His true colors to all. Furthermore, those words which are in the <term>Alcoranus</term> <note>the Quran</note> regarding the Trinity, the divinity of Christ, and His death, are not <term>muhchemat</term> <note>original: "muhchemat"; from the Arabic *muhkamat*, referring to the clear or decisive verses of the Quran</note>, that is, they are not authoritative or true. Now, therefore, having spoken of virtue and of all men, and having made frequent inductions against those vices with which the false prophet teemed (as I have already said), Muhammad will betray himself by signs, and by the same work, Christ and the apostles shall be exalted. Therefore, so that there may be an abundance of evidence with which we may persuade men that the followers of Christ provided testimony of His divinity through both words and deeds, I have decided to subjoin, as a compendium, the lives of certain apostles and several other saints for the sake of example.

# THE LIVES OF CERTAIN DISCIPLES OF JESUS
## CHRIST, in brief.
### PETER.

No one ought to precede him who was first called to the apostolic office. Therefore, in the first place, Peter must be described, who was also called <term>Bar Jona</term> <note>Aramaic: "Son of Jonah"</note>, and <term>Cephas</term> <note>Aramaic: "Rock"</note>, and <term>Simhon</term> <note>Hebrew: "Simeon" or "Simon"</note>. Born in the city of Bethsaida by the Lake of Tiberias (which the scriptures call a sea), Peter followed Christ for three years. He shared this miracle with Him: while Christ provided proof of His divinity during the Transfiguration, Peter walked upon the seas or the lake with dry feet without a boat, just as his teacher Christ had done before. 

But because Jesus was present with him then, that act might be attributed to Him, rather than to the events that occurred after the death of Jesus Christ—although all things were done in His name. The miracle on the fiftieth day from the Resurrection, and the tenth from the Ascension, when all the disciples were gathered together, was the receiving of the Holy Spirit in the appearance of a fiery tongue. This grace was conferred upon them all, so that by the laying on of hands, they could give it to all who came to the faith, either with a sign or without a sign. By that gift, they obtained the knowledge of all languages, than which nothing in all of nature is more wonderful. 

Indeed, they performed such innumerable miracles wherever on earth they traveled that they could not be encompassed in writing. In the presence of the entire city of Jerusalem at the gate of the temple, a man lame from his mother’s womb was healed by Peter in the name of Jesus Christ. From that time, Ananias and his wife Sapphira were struck dead by the mere word and nod of Peter because they had dared to lie to God before the apostle. After the fellowship was scattered into various parts, Peter was divinely freed from prison by an angel and led outside the city, even while he himself did not quite believe it until he realized he was outside the city walls. While staying in Lydda, he restored the paralytic Aeneas to health. In Joppa, he raised a girl named <term>Thabitha</term> <note>Tabitha, also known as Dorcas</note> from the dead to life. He performed miracles in every single city. 

But never was there such a great abundance as in Antioch. For as many sick people as could be found in the city and the neighborhood were collected into one place, and Peter healed them all in the name of Jesus Christ. Indeed, the multitude was so great that ten thousand believers came to the true faith on that day. And so it happened that the church in Antioch first received its place, its seat, and the name "Christian." A certain Theophilus, a leading man of the city, gave his own house as a seat for the bishop. I do not wish here—
