...among these events, the first remarkable thing occurred: they used to keep serpents at home as if they were the most delicate pets, nourishing them in soft bedding. However, when the people brought them out to the middle of the marketplace to be burned, one serpent of unusual size was so protected by its "princely demon" that it remained unharmed in the midst of a great fire while the others were consumed. It could not be destroyed until the sign of the cross was made and the name of Christ invoked, at which point the crowd beat it to pieces. 

Furthermore, there were forests that had been untouched and held as "sacred" by the multitude for countless centuries. In these woods, if anyone had previously violated them, they would immediately suffer harm from a demon. When **Hieronymus** <note>This likely refers to Jerome of Prague (c. 1379–1416), a missionary who worked to convert Lithuania, rather than the famous Saint Jerome who translated the Bible.</note> himself took up an axe and began to cut them down, the crowd followed his lead and began felling innumerable trees. This continued until they came to an ancient oak of extraordinary thickness, which was the most celebrated object of their religious devotion. While everyone else was afraid to touch it, one man, bolder than the rest, swung for the first blow; however, he missed and struck his own leg with the axe. Falling with a great cry, the common people began to accuse **Hieronymus**, wailing that the most holy grove and the home of the gods had been violated. They were terrified and began to stir up a riot. 

After demanding silence, **Hieronymus** showed them that these were merely the illusions of a wicked demon and that the man had actually suffered no real evil. Taking the man by the hand, he raised him up completely healed. Astonished by this, everyone turned against the "sacred" oak and cut down the entire grove. So present is Christ whenever his glory is at stake. Such are the strengths of the true faith. This history is treated at greater length by **Aeneas Sylvius** <note>Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini (1405–1464), who later became Pope Pius II and was a prolific historian.</note> in his treatise *Europe*. 

But a far more celebrated and recent miracle must be set before your eyes, so that we may show that the presence of the divine Virgin Mother of Jesus Christ is also near to her devotees. **Peter Martyr** <note>Petrus Martyr d’Anghiera (1457–1526), the first historian of the Spanish explorations in the Americas.</note> writes of this; he is a man not at all given to superstition, but of singular reliability in delivering his description of the New World. I know that some will laugh and mock this narrative of mine because I am so simple as to believe such things; but in truth, I am persuaded of these and far greater things regarding the holy Virgin. But let them listen and weigh whether all miracles are performed by the authority of a demon. 

When a certain sailor, seized by ill health, was left behind by his companions on the shores of **Euboea** <note>Though the text says "Eubae" (Euboea), the context of Peter Martyr and the Caribbean makes it certain this refers to the island of Cuba.</note>, he went searching for someone he might meet whose house he could recover in. He happened upon a certain <term>Cacicus<note>original Latinized: "regulum"; glossed later as "Cacicus." This refers to a Cacique, a traditional tribal chief or leader among the Taíno people of the Caribbean.</note></term> who took pity on him and nursed him at his home until his health was restored.

Mindful of this kindness, the sailor began to diligently look after the prince's affairs, eventually being placed in charge of his army. Indeed, he fought on the prince's behalf very often and most fortunately, for he always brought back a victory. Once the sailor had gained skill in the language of that region, the ruler asked by what divinity or power he was always so successful. The sailor (as commoners are usually simpler in matters of religion) replied that the holy Virgin Mary—whom he worshipped daily and whose image he wore hanging around his neck—granted him those victories. He told the ruler that the <term>Zemes<note>original: "Zemes." These are the zemís, the ancestral spirits, deities, or physical idols of the Taíno people.</note></term>, those whom they falsely believed to be gods, were actually most destructive demons who distracted men from the knowledge of the true God and eventually plunged them into destruction and the abyss. 

He told the ruler that if he wished to accept the Virgin and her son and be baptized in the name of Jesus, it would surely come to pass that no enemy would ever harm him. Immediately the <term>Cacique<note>original: "Cacicus"</note></term> believed. He built an altar to the Virgin and was given the image by the sailor. The sailor recited the **Hail Mary** <note>original: "Aue Maria"</note>, and his subjects followed. They took the same ceremonies they had established for the **Zemi spirits** and applied them to the image of the Virgin set up on high. Around the circuit of the image are various pots filled with meat, along with vessels full of water and various necklaces, which they are convinced their **Zemes**—that is, their ghosts or spirits—take and use. 

Thus, the places sacred to the **Zemi spirits** were cleared out, and the ruler asked that he be allowed to receive baptism. A priest was summoned from **Hispaniola** <note>The island comprising modern Haiti and the Dominican Republic.</note>; the ruler professed Christ and was called **Commander** <note>original: "Comendator." A title likely referring to the military orders of Spain, such as the Order of Santiago.</note>, because certain knights in **Hispaniola**...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD #

the people of Hispaniola <note>original: "spaniola"; referring to the island of Hispaniola, modern-day Haiti and the Dominican Republic</note> were so called. Once they had been formed and instructed in religion, the sailor departed with his crew for Hispaniola, leaving them no other instruction than that they should recite:
> Hail Mary <note>original: "Aue Maria"</note>
and that in times of danger they should cry out in the Spanish tongue:
> Holy Mary, help us. <note>original: "Santa Maria auida [ayudanos] nos"</note>

The magistrate Anciso <note>Martin Fernández de Enciso (c. 1470–1528), a Spanish explorer and geographer</note>, who was assigned to the shores of Cuba, recounted these and the following miracles to Peter Martyr <note>Peter Martyr d'Anghiera (1457–1526), the first historian of the Spanish explorations in the Americas</note>, confirming them with countless witnesses. Since this commander <note>original: "commendator"; referring to a leader of a Spanish military-religious order</note> was so successful in his victories, he began to be formidable to his neighbors. Therefore, worn down by wars, they made a pact to test without bloodshed which "Zemes" <term>Zemes (or Cemí): spirits or deities worshipped by the Taíno people of the Caribbean, often represented by physical idols</term> was superior: the one (for so they called the Virgin) whom the commander had recently received, or their ancestral ones. They agreed that from the opposing forces, individual youths should be bound with very tight knots, and whoever was freed first, the adversaries would adopt the sacred rites of that youth's Zemi.

Once the youths were bound and prayers were poured out on both sides, immediately as the youth called out and said, 
> Holy Mary, help me,
the Virgin appeared, visible to the eyes of all, carrying a wand in her hand. Driving away a foul demon that was present even in the form of a specter (a sight familiar to them), she touched the bonds of the baptized youth. Immediately, before everyone's eyes, those bonds tightened around the other youth. Thus it happened that not only was the first youth freed, but his adversary was bound with a double knot.

According to the pact, the defeated parties wanted to hand over the "herb" <note>likely a symbolic gesture of surrender or ritual tribute</note>, but certain elders, claiming this was done by human trickery rather than the excellence of the opposing deity, refused to stand by the agreement unless it were done in their presence. Therefore, after eight of the most prudent men were chosen (as is their custom), the same pacts and deeds were performed as before. While they called out, the Virgin appeared before the eyes of the first group, while a most terrifying demon, in the form commonly depicted, appeared before the eyes of the others. After the Virgin drove the demon away with her wand so he could not free his own man, she touched the commander's youth's bonds as before and transferred them to the adversary.

Seeing this, everyone—both young and old—hastened to profess the holy religion. Thus, when Anciso reached that region, they asked him for priests to initiate them. Indeed, one hundred and thirty of the commander's enemies were baptized in a single day. They reported not only that they had seen those two miracles, but that every time they had fought against the commander (since he was a Christian), they had seen the same Virgin before the battle line, holding a scepter and terrifying them with a threatening countenance. Compelled by this, they had converted to the true religion even more than by the later miracles.

In this way, God willed an angel to go before the children of Israel in visible form; thus the angel stood before Joshua at Jericho; thus Sennacherib was struck down and put to flight. The hand of the Lord is not shortened, so that He cannot save. 

When the French, under the leadership of Godfrey <note>Godfrey of Bouillon (c. 1060–1100), a leader of the First Crusade</note>, set out to liberate the Holy Land from the followers of Muhammad, they were in Asia Minor. Their forces were not yet gathered and were exhausted by the long journey, and even the Emperor of Constantinople was plotting treachery against our men. They were met by Kilij Arslan <note>original: "Solimanus"; the Sultan of Rum</note>, leader of the Turks, with three hundred thousand men. Against these, thirty thousand Christians from their own regions routed, killed, and put them to flight. 

A most admirable thing happened there: although our men had followed the enemy for barely a day’s journey in their retreat, a massive slaughter continued for the space of three days. By whom this was done was never known, except that certain captured Turks reported the slaughter was carried out by three knights in white armor and on white horses. Certain men of the Greek religion <note>Eastern Orthodox Christians</note>, held in high reputation for holiness, said these were Saint George, Saint Theodore, and Saint Demetrius. Whoever they were, it is certain they were not mortal men. A certain noble and primary man, whose name is suppressed, wrote these things; he was always a companion to Baldwin <note>Baldwin I (c. 1058–1118), brother of Godfrey and first King of Jerusalem</note> on that expedition and wrote that whole history—though in such Latin,

neither in Latin, nor in French, nor even with proper grammar, yet it is with such integrity that I would not grant greater credit even to Thucydides <note>An ancient Greek historian known for his strict standards of evidence-gathering and analysis</note>. For truth is found in simplicity, whereas in eloquence there is a freedom to amplify, which must be watched for mixing many falsehoods with the truth. By these examples, and by the deeds of the apostles and martyrs, the Evangelist <note>The missionary or preacher of the Gospel</note>—raised up in hope, armed with faith, relying on innocence, burning with charity, glowing with divine love, intent upon fasts and prayers, and trembling with humility—ought to promise himself nothing that is not from God. God will always be present with him and will confirm his efforts. For if He was present not only to the most excellent apostles and martyrs, but even sent an angel to a soldier who was hardly just; if even the wicked and those estranged from Him have performed miracles in the name of Christ; if the Virgin Mary was present to a sailor and to semi-pagans who called upon her, for the sake of confirming the religion of her son; if she shines with miracles daily in countless places, then surely she will not be absent from the prayers of a good man who calls upon her from the heart and with faith. 

I know that no one is so just that they can deserve divine favor on account of their own righteousness, which is like "filthy rags" <note>original: "pannus menstruatæ"; a common biblical metaphor from Isaiah 64:6 for human works compared to divine holiness</note> if compared to divine goodness. This is a gift of God; no one can "command" miracles. Yet, because no one can be considered just when compared to God, one should not live after the manner of certain people who evilly abuse the liberty of the Gospel—I had almost said after the manner of the *Epicureans* <note>Followers of Epicurus, often stereotyped in this era as atheistic pleasure-seekers</note>. One must fast and pray at fixed days and hours. It is something to advance that far, even if it is not granted to go further. But what does it pertain to say of these people in general? The best of them never drink unless they are thirsty; they do not eat unless driven by hunger; they do not become angry unless you inflict an injury; they do not engage in sexual acts unless they are aroused. Is this not living according to the Gospel? Certainly, although this practice of the Gospel does not differ from that of the impious, it would nevertheless be tolerable, were it not that the Law of Christ had been made so broad by the interpretations given to a people very prone to their bellies, so that among those "Evangelists," nothing is more certain than that nothing is certain. Indeed, the Evangelist must certainly not live in an *Epicurean* fashion, however much he may possess a most free faith.

But I return to the point. The Indians <note>A general term used here for the Indigenous peoples of the Americas and Asia</note>, who confess and acknowledge a supreme God, will be refuted by the arguments I have mentioned. Because these people very often enjoy the presence of demons, they must also be warned of the unhappiness they experience from that plague. Finally, if those plagues oppose themselves, they must be routed by the sign of the cross and the invocation of Christ and His saints. These people pass over into the prescription of truth far more easily than a Jew or a Muslim. Already, almost the whole of New Spain <note>original: "Hispania noua"; the Spanish colonial territory primarily in modern-day Mexico</note> has crossed over to the truth. For an innumerable multitude daily approaches Christ. In the kingdom of Narsinga <note>The Vijayanagara Empire in Southern India, frequently called Narsinga by 16th-century European writers</note>, not a few also hear of Christ most willingly. I say nothing of other superstitions, since they destroy themselves. When these men have crossed over into the true knowledge of God, they should be burdened with rituals only moderately. They should be invited to the truth of worship and holy institutions by persuasion, not by force. If they wish to keep the ancient ceremonies of their false worship, that vanity is to be gradually driven out, unless it contains sin within itself. It should be permitted that the worship which was once offered to an idol—if it can be done without loss to nature—be ascribed to Christ, so that, having been nourished on the milk of infancy <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 3:2, where "milk" represents basic spiritual teachings for new converts</note> and confirmed in the true religion, they may become capable of solid food, seek God from heaven, and become like the best of men. Thus, in a few days, religion will have matured. Against their nefarious sacrifices, those who sacrifice their own children to the Zemes <term>Zemes (or Cemí): spiritual beings or deities of the Taíno people, often represented by idols of wood or stone</term> or to whatever idols, one must begin from the dignity of nature and the monstrosity of the crime. They must first be persuaded not to commit such things against their own: that children, parents, friends, servants, and finally all men must be exempt from nefarious sacrifices. Indeed, by the benefit of Spanish navigation, almost all have received

They acknowledge Christ as the founder of both heaven and earth. It is a wonder that this entire nation is circumcised <term>recutita</term> <note>literally "re-skinned," a common 16th-century Latin term for the Jewish people or those who practiced circumcision</note>, even though there is none among them that is not devoted to the worship of idols and ghosts <term>lemures</term> <note>In Roman mythology, restless or malicious spirits of the dead; here used to describe pagan superstitions</note>. We can judge how powerful Satan is from this one fact: that he has persuaded men across the whole world to sacrifice one human for another, and more often for the sake of lust or the most vain opinion. For there has been no nation in the whole world that has not, at some time, slaughtered a human for idols. This is established by the histories of all peoples. We first banished that rite in the Gauls by a law passed by Claudius Caesar. That ruinous Hercules <note>Postel likely refers here to a mythological or historical figure he associates with the spread of Egyptian "heresy" or paganism</note> had brought that wicked religion to us, to the Britons, the Spanish, and the Moors from Egypt. It will easily come to pass that it is also banished from those regions. There is no need for great industry to eliminate that wicked worship. Therefore, I turn myself to Jewish affairs.

### THE METHOD OF BRINGING THE JEWS TO THE KNOWLEDGE
### and faith of Jesus Christ.

**So many** brilliant minds, so many learned men, so many men equipped with every kind of art and discipline, have occupied themselves with this stiff-necked <note>original: "cervicosa"; a common biblical metaphor for stubbornness</note> nation in vain, and so many things have been written against its perfidy, that even I—most infantile in eloquence and stammering, ignorant in knowledge, confused in method, and to finish in one word, barely commendable in anything—might think I am wasting my effort. I should not hope that where the wisest men have profited nothing, I might achieve anything. I certainly do not think, indeed I do not think it will ever happen, that the Jews can be persuaded by any art, however perfect in every part, and led to the truth, since it was predicted by the Holy Spirit through the prophets, and by Jesus Christ—blessed man and God—that the race of Israel will not feel a universal liberation from the captivity in which it now is, before Jesus himself comes a second time, terrible to the whole world for judging.

Although the most excellent men have accomplished almost nothing against the stubbornness of this hardened people through their writings, I do not judge that I should desist from this province of duty. For it happens very often that a city which could not be captured by the art and industry of a most excellent leader, though often attacked, is finally conquered by the work of a common soldier. Not rarely has a recruit <term>tyro</term> <note>A beginner or novice soldier</note> shown an example of himself that a veteran could admire rather than imitate. Before Christ’s terrible arrival, the whole nation will not be gathered. However, what has been said about their dispersion does not imply a loss of truth, nor does it take away the choice of salvation, but it removes their status and the administration of their affairs, which they have now experienced for 1,460 years <note>Counting from the destruction of the Temple in 70 AD, this would place Postel's writing around 1530 AD</note>.

For although that nation is most spirited in protecting its salvation and liberty, and most ready to obey any prophecy or name of an Israelite leader, yet from the time they put their Savior Christ on the cross, they have always been wretchedly oppressed in all their attempts. What is more wondrous—and a greater confirmation of the faith of Jesus Christ—is that the Jew is in a worse condition among pagans <term>ethnicos</term> <note>Non-Christians, specifically heathens</note> and those entirely foreign to our religion, than where the followers of Christ dwell. Nor yet are they ever free from afflictions, fasts, prayers, Sabbath-keeping, and other rites. From this it becomes clear that they have committed a more serious sin than the idolaters themselves, and have offended incredibly against God, the parent of all nature. For they know for certain that they perform sacred rites to Almighty God, and they venerate Him with the same worship as when God was present to all their vows; and yet He does not permit that their sacrifices (once so pleasing), their fasts (so accepted), their prayers (so grateful), and their people (so pious) should protect themselves with any liberty or administration of affairs, while the impious and idolaters enjoy festive peace...

...they enjoy very vast empires and rule over the Jewish people, and they torture them with the heaviest taxes and physical distress, so that it is scarcely allowed even for the priests to think about such a distinguished worship established by God.

### The First Approach.

I will not deal with you through the Scriptures in the beginning, O *Jews*, because by your interpretation of them—which is indeed alien to the truth and the sense of the authors, yet approved by the authority of your rabbis—you elude all things that are brought forward for your benefit and for the confirmation of the truth. Reason, common to us, to you, and to all other men, shall be brought into the middle, so that if you dare to deny those things which are consistent with it, at least the consensus of the whole world may be a witness to your *perfidy* <note>original: "perfidia," here meaning a failure of faith or "unbelief" in the Christian sense</note>. For I do not think it will happen that you subscribe to it, as perfidy and stubbornness contend within you for greatness, such that even when truths are confessed, if not in words, at least in deeds or failures to act, you resist. We will begin, therefore, first from the principles and ends of the parts of this world, so that from demonstrations drawn from there, we may finally complete those syllogisms which are not alien to the truth. 

You admit, along with the philosophers, that God established this entire temple of nature for the sake of man, and man for the sake of God, to be worshiped, honored, and loved above all things on account of these benefits. In the knowledge of God, I think you do not wander. For whatever that highest, eternal, infinite, incomprehensible thing is, above all matter and form, I judge that it is called God by you, as it is by the consensus of all wise men. It is clear, therefore, that all things were made mediately for the sake of God, and immediately for the sake of man. Moreover, just as God is *pure act* <note>original: "actus purus," a philosophical concept describing God as a being of complete reality with no unfulfilled potential</note>, always attentive to the three parts of the world—the highest, the middle, and the lowest—so also man, for whose sake those parts exist, ought to have a certain goal. 

For man, made for the sake of the knowledge and praise of God, ought not to be idle. Therefore, man, created in the image of God—that is, possessing reason which is akin to divinity and endowed with free will—ought also to be always attentive to three things: namely, that he should refer everything he does to the glory of God, his own innocence, and the utility of his neighbor; and whatever he wishes to do, he should weigh most diligently, so that if he should sin in any of these three, he may flee from it entirely; but if he understands it to tend toward any of these, he should not doubt it to be conducive to all three. 

Yet the chief care should be that he strives most greatly to prove himself to God by helping another man, his brother. For both sacred and profane matters must be neglected when it comes to preserving a man's life. Thus, the name of religion is falsely used as a pretext when the need of a brother, who can be helped, is neglected. This logic of a man helping a man is by far the most approved by the philosophers, although for your sake and your stubbornness, Moses, by God's command, wrote that not all men immediately, but only your friends, were to be held by you in the place of brothers. He knew you to be so *stiff-necked* <term>cervicosus</term> <note>a biblical metaphor for stubbornness or pride, often used in the Vulgate to describe the Israelites</note> and refractory that he could scarcely give you even half-just precepts, which is clear in many places of the Holy Scripture. For those precepts were later explained more broadly and humanely, and frequent mention of your stubbornness was made. Is it not clear enough that even while Moses was still living you already practiced that stubbornness and abused circumcision? For in Deuteronomy 10 it is written: *Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and stiffen your neck no more. For God, etc.* But since there are very many testimonies of your hard neck, it is clear enough from your deeds: When Moses wanted to be your avenger, you drove him away; after seeing miracles in Egypt, you murmured at the Red Sea; and when the sea was divinely divided, you judged that God was unable to feed you in the desert. If I should wish to speak of all...

<page-num>356</page-num>
<header>ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD</header>

...to run through [sacred history], nothing is encountered more frequently than your **perfidy** <note>original: "perfidia," referring here to a lack of faith or stubbornness toward God's will</note> toward God.

Indeed, it is most evident that those precepts which God gave you at first glance were adapted to your weakness and wickedness, and were not absolute. This is seen especially in those things handed down to you in many places concerning the love of one's neighbor. For in the first place, Moses says: *You shall love your friend as yourself.* <note>Leviticus 19:18</note> God was adapting Himself to you in such a way that He did not give you a greater commandment than that which the gentiles and those lacking the Law already practiced. For there is no man so impious that he does not have some friend whom he loves vehemently. Indeed, many living creatures devoid of reason possess a sense and fellowship of friendship.

Why then was such a meager commandment given? The reason, O *Jews*, is because you were the worst of mortals; although you preserved some memory and the ceremonies of the Law of Abraham, you were hostile even to your friends. You loved in word and tongue, **in the manner of the court** <note>original: "more aulico," meaning with the superficial or insincere politeness found in royal palaces</note>; but as for those friends following your same faith, you so abused them with impostures and treachery that there was plainly no faith among you. By pleasing yourselves with certain ceremonies, you were even far worse than many brute beasts, and indeed more wicked than all other pretenders. For otherwise, if sin had not been committed in that regard, that law would not have needed to be given to you—just as it is not found in civil laws because it would be superfluous. For no one, of his own accord, fails to love a friend.

From this, one may also derive the contrary law. For in order that God might encourage you to kill those peoples who had lived in the Holy Land before you—who were, as it were, declared enemies—and so that their stain might not creep into you (which later happened extensively), He wished to arm you with hatred against them, as if He had said: *You shall love your friend, and you shall hate your enemy.* For you know better than anyone that almost all precepts imply their opposite. By the same reasoning, Moses wished to adapt himself to your weakness in that same verse when he says: *You shall not take revenge, nor shall you bear a grudge against the citizens of your people.* 

For in all the cities of the heathens, that same law held a place. By that law, the judges themselves were "living laws" everywhere, taking punishment upon wicked men in the name of all. Conversely, He wanted you to be motivated against the enemies of true religion, but not to rage with eternal hatred against nature itself. For in his song, which is like the **catastrophe** <note>original: "catastrophe," used here in the classical sense of a final resolution or summary</note> of the entire Law, He says that vengeance belongs to God, so that He might eventually destroy you fundamentally on account of the iniquities you were accustomed to committing under the cover of the Holy Law. 

He wished you, therefore, to use vengeance only insofar as you had established the commonwealth and driven out the unworthy inhabitants; but He did not want men to be armed hereafter under any pretext of religion. For **vengeance** <term>vindicata: the act of exacting punishment or retribution</term> properly belongs to Him who knows the gravity of the crime and has weighed the spirit in which things were done. This cannot happen for a private individual, who is weighed down by either emotion or ignorance. Therefore, true vengeance belongs to God alone; otherwise, the matter must be sent to a judge, lest we immediately kill those neighbors we hold as enemies under the pretext of injury. For unless our lust for it were bridled by laws, there is no one who, in the heat of passion, would not wish to take a brother's life for the smallest injury. This is seen daily: for the slightest harm to body or reputation, or for the vainest opinion, we see a man slaughtered, and the reckless or the plotters pay the penalty.

But regarding the friendship of a brother—that is, of another man—what the prophets felt after Moses is evident in many places, and appears most clearly in one passage of Micah, chapter 6: *With what,* he asks, *shall I offer a worthy thing to the Lord? Shall I bow my knee before the God on high? Shall I offer Him burnt offerings and calves a year old? Will the Lord be pleased with thousands of rams, or with many rivers of oil? Shall I give my firstborn for my crime, the fruit of my womb for the sin of my soul? I will show you, O man, what is good, and what the Lord...*

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK IV

<page-num>357</page-num>

...[lest He] should require less of you. Specifically: *to do justice, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with God.* <note>Postel is quoting Micah 6:8, a famous summary of biblical ethics</note> This is the aim of man regarding his fellow man: to deal justly with him—meaning, whatever you wish to be done for you, you do the same for him—to have mercy on the sinner, and to feed the hungry.

Although Moses did not explicitly say this regarding *all* people, he showed clearly enough where the perfection of the law would eventually lead when he left it written: *If you encounter the ox of your enemy or a stray donkey, lead it back to him. If you see the donkey of one who hates you lying under its burden, do not pass by without helping to lift it.* <note>Exodus 23:4-5</note> These duties show that even enemies should be loved, or at least that they should be won over through service as if they were friends. For it is impossible for a commonwealth <note>original: "respublica"</note> to ever be happy if there is room for fostering rivalries and hatreds.

Indeed, lest this reasoning of duty be thought to apply only among one's own people, Moses added: *You shall not bother the stranger. For you know the condition of strangers, since you were strangers in the land of Egypt.* <note>Exodus 22:21</note> He intends that no injury be inflicted on anyone even on account of a false religion, nor should anyone be considered an enemy on that name alone (unless they use violence). From this it is clear that, although Moses accommodated himself to the nature of the people he led, he nevertheless felt and judged that no one should be considered an enemy, since he believed all people should be won over by service.

I would wish these points were well urged and persuaded upon the Jews, because they currently busy themselves with overturning the true aim of man through the narrow prescriptions of their law. It is certain—truly certain—that man is born for the sake of other men. Toward everyone (placing those close to us and those of true persuasion in the first rank), one ought to feel an equal affection. Just as all people share and possess one God, one nature, and one common condition of being born, living, and dying, so they should help each other through mutual duties like brothers.

Certainly, a man is more perfect the more he is like God. And yet God is equally beneficent toward all; the more He shares a benefit, the more He acts in a way worthy of God. He cherishes enemies just as He does friends—and not rarely more mercifully—so that, burdened with His benefits, they might recognize the Giver; or, if they remain infamous for ingratitude, they might deservedly pay the penalty of eternal punishment for failing to acknowledge such great blessings.

If, therefore, you grant me, O *Jews*, that the man who is most like God is by far the most excellent—the one who busies himself with proving his worth to God the Father by bestowing benefits on everyone, who preserves himself in the highest innocence as a child of God, and who places his "highest good" in the contemplation of God the Father (that is, of Truth) and in the admiration of His creation—then we are already in agreement. 

But if you dare to deny this, I shall refer the matter to the most holy reason of the divine majesty, with the consensus of the whole world as a witness. Since you have reached such a point of impudence that you prefer to cast off reason rather than agree with the truth, may the divine majesty justly bind your **perfidy**—which allows itself to be directed neither by law nor conquered by reason—under the laws of stubbornness and damnation, and judge you to eternal punishments with your eyes wide open.

But I believe you will acquiesce to such clear principles, known to all. For if you resisted, you would be conquered by this single argument already known to you: for you confess that the visible and sensible world was made for the sake of man, that is, the **macrocosm** <term>original Greek: "κόσμον" (kosmon), the great world</term> for the sake of the **microcosm** <term>original Greek: "μικροκόσμου" (mikrokosmou), the 'little world' or man</term>; and that the world itself, both small and large, visible and invisible, exists for the sake of God. 

If therefore all lower things are for the sake of man, and since man exists within this lower world, it is necessary that he also exists for the sake of man. If he exists for the sake of man, then he exists for both himself and for others. Therefore, he who was made for the "final cause" by the grace of God, exists both for himself and for the sake of other men. 

From this, it is clear that my assumption is true. I insist that you subscribe to this opinion not without reason, for it contributes greatly to the treatment of what follows. Let us proceed. God, therefore, since He wished all things to be referred to Himself as the supreme end, and [appointed] man [master] of all things...

### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
## BOOK IV

<page-num>358</page-num>

...lest he [man] should fail to represent for the whole world that glory which God deserves for His created works. To ensure man could not claim any ignorance regarding this purpose, God willed to create him in His own image and likeness—that is, adorned with the guidance of reason. He did this so that as often as man recalled the form of his Model, he would strive to become as much like Him as possible (so far as our human fragility allows). From this, the axiom I assumed earlier becomes clear: namely, that men are more excellent the more they are like God.

Now, so that we may see and more diligently observe what constitutes the duty of a good man, we must look at what God is like, and how and what He does. Because I am dealing with a stiff-necked people <note>original: "cervicosa gente" — a common biblical idiom for the Israelites, used here to acknowledge the difficulty of the theological debate</note>, I wish to bring here a brief summary of those points from the first book which demonstrated that God is both three and one. 

The Jews agree with us that God is most simple, infinite, most just, most powerful, most wise, and most benevolent. They grant He is most highly adorned with all other titles of goodness and virtue, or—if I could express anything worthily of Him—that He is the most endowed and absolute Being. However, we must pay very close attention when we ascribe these qualities to Him based on His effects (even though, as "qualities," He is technically free of them). These are properties He possesses as Creator, without which a Creator cannot be understood. 

Although He is most powerful, if He did not possess within Himself the wisdom for creating all things and an absolute knowledge of every particular part, and if He had not been moved by benevolence and love to create what He was able and knew how to make, He could never have created anything at all. For any power, unless it knows what it is going to do, does nothing; and even if it knows, but does not will it, the result is the same. Therefore, God is three and one. 

For as the powerful Father and Author, there is a Power from which Wisdom (which is the Son) is eternally generated; and from both proceeds the Love of acting (which is the Holy Spirit). Power is omnipotent, Wisdom is omnipotent, and Love is omnipotent; yet there are not three "omnipotents," but one. Furthermore, the Holy Spirit is not the Father or the Son, nor is the Son the Father or the Spirit; rather, the Persons are co-equal to one another, distinguished by their properties, while remaining only one divinity.

This must be understood, as far as it can be conceived, through a familiar daily example. When I think of anything that needs to be done—for example, a castle to be built—I must have it entirely in my mind and knowledge before any firm notion of it exists. Yet I do nothing unless I reveal the form through a voice or a drawing I have conceived in my spirit. Nor do I make any progress unless the conception, the diagram, the explanation, or the description is applied to the work itself. Therefore, the whole castle was in the mind, the whole in the diagram, and the whole in the work. 

Yet there are not three castles, but one castle. The castle in the finished work is not the same as the castle in the diagram, the voice, or the writing; nor is the castle in the voice the castle in the mind or the work. Instead, they differ from one another by certain properties, even though the thing itself is one, and it is "most simple" within its own category. 

It would be impossible for there to be anything in the natural world in which all things agree, unless it proceeded from a common principle in which that thing was most perfect. There is no thing, however simple it may be, that does not require a ternary number <note>The number three, which Postel views as the "number of completion" found throughout nature</note> for the completion of its essence. For example, take any grain of seed: from the time it reaches completion until it ceases to be, unless it possesses fertility (the power of acting), progress, and the love or will of acting, nothing can be produced from it. Let us take an acorn: when it has been buried in the earth, unless it possesses the fertility and power to produce a tree from itself, it will not produce anything. If the "progress" resulting from that power is lacking, it will do nothing. If it did not "love" to nourish its tree in such soil and form, the tree would never be produced or sustained. Yet the whole tree, and the seed...

### GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK IV

...[the seed] is power, and likewise process, and love or natural delight: and yet there are not three trees, but one tree. So it is in all of nature. Therefore God, who is the cause of all things, is most perfectly three and one. Since God is the highest unity, there is nevertheless in all of nature a unity before number, an eternal equality before the differentiation and inequality of things, and a connection before separation. Unity is the Father, equality is the Son, and the connection <note>original: "nexus"</note> is the Holy Spirit; and yet there are not three gods, but one God. In the soul, which is one and is the image of God, there is a powerful reasoning that, by apprehending, hands over everything to comprehension—or perfect knowledge and discernment. It commits things to memory so that they can be recalled through remembrance; the whole intellect comprehends, the whole knows, the whole remembers; yet there are not three intellects, but one. The souls of brute animals possess fantasy, thought, and memory. Sensation consists in essence, life, and sense. All things arise from matter, form, and the composite proceeding from both. In artificial things, they arise from thought, explanation, and art; or art, the artisan, the instrument, and the material, etc., as was handed down in the first book. Nor is God only simple, three, and one, but His action always regards a triple world: the highest, the middle, and the lowest. 

Whatever He does, He does for the sake of use and an end; wherefore He wishes to be the author of good equally to all, and of evil to no one. For it is a wicked thing to believe He is the author of evil. If He places His gifts in the midst of everyone, He also wishes them to be distributed with the highest justice. Therefore, whatever things could be devised to protect this fragile mortality—and far more than anyone could ever comprehend in their mind—He willed to create for the sake of man. As He is considered the father and author of all, He would propose things in common <note>original: "in medium," meaning for the public good</note> worthy of such a father, from which comes that philosophical maxim: *The more common a good is, the more divine it is.* God willed that the Jewish nation—so often addicted to greed—learn this very thing from the natural use of things, and He confirmed it in the desert for forty years so that the nation should have no deeper conviction. 

For when the manna <note>the miraculous food provided to the Israelites in the desert</note> rained down upon them in a far greater abundance than was sufficient to feed such a great army, anyone who was disobedient to the divine precepts and gathered more out of greed <note>original: "πλεονεξία" (pleonexia) — Greek for insatiable desire or "graspingness"</note> or for the sake of a single person (except on the day before the Sabbath), found that they had no more than the others. Furthermore, while the manna remaining on the surface of the ground stayed uncorrupted, that which was kept at home bred worms and rot. By this matter, God willed to prove the futile efforts of mortals in accumulating wealth beyond what is necessary for use. One cannot see what else a person achieves or feels—when they burn with a total desire for possessing—other than their own miseries, while they scrape together from everywhere for the sake of children, relatives, or even luxury. 

Certainly, many are accustomed to leave behind to those they wish to see enriched by their wealth the instruments of sluggishness, idleness, pride, luxury, and all pleasures; yet no one ever provided virtue through riches. As for that part of virtue usually practiced with the help of wealth, no one is at fault who, being destitute of it, does not practice it. However, he who has the support of wealth can be in the gravest guilt, and a double one at that. For if he does not give as much as he ought, he is already liable to give an account; and if he seeks and ascribes to himself the glory for those things he bestows, it would have been better to have given nothing. Therefore, since the Creator placed all things in common, He willed that they be distributed by those who have obtained more, so that they keep nothing for themselves beyond their necessities. For the administration of wealth <note>original: "dispensatio"</note> has been entrusted to the rich. 

We must now come to our "Human." He is most like God who is always most intent upon a tripartite goal: who refers all things to the honor of God, to his own innocence and the cultivation of his soul, and to the charity and use of his neighbor; who would never do an injury to anyone; who would rather die than act against the right judgment of his soul; and who desires and holds whatever is placed within him as ready for his brothers—that is, for all other men...

...one who seeks no glory from his own deeds. For glory and honor are the peculiar gifts of God; therefore, a person is better and more useful to nature the closer they approach this condition. Furthermore, those precepts are holier which more strongly command, persuade, and teach these things. Therefore, Christ is better, more just, holier, more useful to nature, and more like God in the flesh than Moses. The Gospel is more excellent than the ancient law, and Christians are far more excellent than the Jews. From this, it is certain that salvation and the true way of salvation are found in our religion. You must either deny the first principles or concede the final conclusions, for there is no room for evasion in this argument. The Evangelical precept <note>The "Golden Rule" found in Matthew 7:12</note> is entirely in harmony with God and nature: **"Whatsoever you would that men should do to you, do you even so to them."** This is far more extensive than the version written as: **"Do not do to others what you do not want done to yourself."** <note>Postel is comparing the positive command of Christ with the negative formulation often associated with earlier traditions, such as the Book of Tobit or the teachings of Hillel.</note> For the latter is as if you were saying, "cease from evil"; but the former is as if you were adding, "and do good." For just as no one wants injury to be inflicted upon themselves, so they ought not to inflict it on anyone; but so that you may be most like God, you must do for others whatever you would wish to be done for you by them.

But a certain Rabbi will object to me that the law of Christ does not seem good because it has removed the greatest part of the ceremonies of the Old Testament, even though not one stroke of a pen <note>original: "unus apex," referring to the smallest mark in Hebrew script</note> from the law ought to be omitted. I shall satisfy this. The Jews approve of the Prophets and the <term>Hagiographa</term> <note>The "Holy Writings" or Ketuvim, the third section of the Hebrew Bible</note>; although because there are weightier and more urgent testimonies in David and Daniel, the recent <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud; Postel implies they rearranged the biblical canon to downplay messianic prophecies</note> rejected them among the Hagiographa so they might seem to have lesser authority. "Hear," he says, "the word of the Lord, you princes of Sodom; give ear to the law of our God, you people of Gomorrah." <note>Isaiah 1:10; Isaiah uses these names as metaphors for the corruption of the leadership in Jerusalem.</note>

> To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices to me, says the Lord? I am full of the burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of fatlings; and I do not desire the blood of calves, or of lambs, or of he-goats. When you come to appear before me to sacrifice in my courts, who has required this at your hands? Offer sacrifice in vain no longer; incense is an abomination to me. The New Moons and the Sabbath and the other festivals I will not abide; your synagogues are iniquitous. My soul hates your appointed months and your solemnities; I bear them with difficulty. When you stretch forth your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply prayer, I will not hear, for your hands are full of blood. Wash yourselves, be clean, take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes. Cease to act perversely, learn to do well. Seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge for the fatherless, defend the widow, and come, and let us reason together, etc. <note>A translation of Isaiah 1:11–18</note>

If the worship of the law had made people holy, and if that number of sacrifices and ceremonies were intended to last forever, how is it that the holiest prophet, having rejected them entirely, refers the whole of religion to the piety of the heart and interior goodness? Would it not have been enough either to rebuke those vices committed under the pretext of sacred rites, or to commend virtue without attacking the rites—which, since they were instituted by Moses, could not be the cause of vice? Certainly, the prophets knew entirely that these things were to be abolished, because not only Isaiah, but Jeremiah also dared to diminish them. In the seventh chapter <note>Postel notes "chapter six," but the quote is from Jeremiah 7</note> he says: **"Do not trust in the words of the Lord, saying 'The Temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is this,' for if you truly amend your ways and your doings, if you execute judgment, etc."** Was not the most holy Temple of Solomon the cause of what was committed? Not at all. And yet it is disapproved of because it had become a **"den of thieves."** <note>original: "spelunca latronum"</note> And therefore the prophet forbids praying for the people because the Lord will not hear; which surely cannot be understood regarding the Babylonian captivity, since you were led back from it and were heard. ...to those who long for the day of the Lord, what is it to you?
> That day of the Lord is darkness, and not light; as if a man fled from the face of a lion and a bear met him, or went into the house and leaned his hand against the wall, and a serpent bit him. Shall not the day of the Lord be darkness and not light, even very dark and no brightness in it? I hate and I have rejected your feast days, and I will not take the scent of your solemn assemblies. Though you offer me burnt offerings and your meat offerings, I will not accept them; I will not regard the peace offerings of your fat beasts. Take away from me the noise of your songs, and so forth. <note>original: "desiderantibus diem Domini..." — This is a quotation from the prophet Amos 5:18-23.</note>

These words do not merely predict the setting aside of sacred rituals at the coming of Christ, but they assert that the arrival of the "Day of the Lord" would bring ruin, darkness, and gloom upon you. All things were meant to be removed when the light of the Gospel arrived. But it is also pleasing to hear David’s opinion on this removal. In Psalm 50, he writes:

> Hear, O my people, and I will speak; O Israel, and I will testify to you that I am your God. I will not reprove you for your sacrifices or your burnt offerings, which are continually before me. I will take no bullock out of your house, nor he-goats out of your folds, etc. Offer to God the sacrifice of praise. <note>original: "Audi populus meus..." — Psalm 50:7-9, 14.</note>

Do these words not overturn animal sacrifices and convert them into a pious form of worship? If these rituals were not intended to eventually cease, why would the holy prophets have attacked them? All external things were required to cease—even circumcision itself—at the arrival of Jesus Christ. Moses himself says in Deuteronomy 30:

> If any of yours be driven out unto the outmost parts of heaven, from there the Lord your God will gather you, and from there he will fetch you and bring you into the land which your fathers possessed, and you shall possess it; and he will do you good, and multiply you above your fathers. And the Lord your God will circumcise your heart, to love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live, etc. <note>original: "Si ad cardines coeli..." — Deuteronomy 30:4-6.</note>

We cited the same thing previously in Chapter 10. Jeremiah says the same in Chapter 4:

> Circumcise yourselves to the Lord, and take away the foreskins of your heart, you men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem. <note>original: "Circuncidimini Domino..." — Jeremiah 4:4.</note>

From these passages, it is clear that not only were the ceremonies to be removed when Christ came, but the circumcision of the foreskin was to be changed into the circumcision of the heart. However, in the meantime, one must not pass over the opinion of Moses "with a dry foot" (as the saying goes) <note>term: <term>with a dry foot</term> (Latin: *sicco pede*) is a common scholarly idiom meaning to pass over a subject quickly or without getting "wet" by its complexities.</note>; it must be examined diligently, because the Jews use it to defend their position. They believe it will come to pass that God, with the Messiah as leader, will bring them back and settle them again in the Holy Land. That this "return" cannot be understood as the return from Babylon is clear enough, because physical circumcision continued for nearly five hundred years after that. It must, therefore, be understood as the return in the time of the Messiah, from which point circumcision was to be abolished. 

When he speaks of the "land" to which they shall return, it cannot be understood as Palestine or Judea. For it is entirely impossible that greater wealth or a larger population could exist there than when things were flourishing under Solomon. That region simply could not support such a multitude of people. He calls it "the land of the fathers," in the manner of David; though David was most wealthy, happy, and a blessed prince in every respect, he nevertheless said he would see the "good things of the Lord in the land of the living." <note>A reference to Psalm 27:13.</note> For in this life, however happy we may be, we are entirely in the "land of the dying." Thus, while God seems to promise you one thing, He intends another. Just as when He promised you Palestine—which, aside from a few fertile valleys, is an entirely sterile region—He said He would give you a "land flowing with milk and honey" in order to draw you toward hope and the evidence of heavenly things. For never were springs of milk or honey seen there. 

"But if Christ has come," they say, "how was he not the King of Israel? Why did he not lead the Jews, gathered from the whole world, back into some region which they might cultivate far more happily than before? How could it be that he whom you call Christ had no attendants, no power, and lived in the deepest poverty and contempt?" Many points have been proposed here, and each one must be satisfied individually. Certainly, around the time of Christ’s coming, the Jews from the whole world—

...almost everyone flocked to Judea, for the time predicted by the prophets had come to a head, in which the Messiah was to come. But because Christ was no tyrant; because he was (as I have said, and as is clear from his life) most like God even according to the flesh; because he claimed no power for himself, but spent everything on the comfort of the afflicted and the miserable; and because he trampled the honors of the world and openly rebuked the vices of wicked magistrates and priests—the leaders of the people not only refused to follow him as a leader, but even put him to death. 

Indeed, that the Jews had flocked from the whole world into Syria <note>In the Roman era, Judea was often administratively linked to the province of Syria.</note> in the hope of some bloody Messiah—one who would destroy other men by overturning the world and acquire a vast dominion for them—is proven by the incredible multitude of people who perished under **Titus** and **Hadrian**. For shortly before, under the **Maccabees** <note>The Jewish dynasty that led a successful revolt against the Seleucid Empire in the 2nd century BCE.</note> (who immediately preceded the foreigner **Herod**, under whom Christ came), the maximum Jewish strength could scarcely reach ten thousand men, as their resources were frequently worn down by daily unrest. Yet, within sixty years, such a multitude had gathered there that eleven hundred thousand <note>1.1 million</note> were shut up in Jerusalem while **Titus** was besieging it. 

Furthermore, according to **Hegesippus** <note>A 2nd-century Christian chronicler who wrote a history of the Jewish Wars.</note>, a man of the Jewish race, two million people in total were lost in that war. Fifty years later, under the second **Bar Kokhba** <note>original: "Barchoziba." Simon bar Kokhba led the second major Jewish revolt against Rome (132–136 CE).</note>, your own authors report that four million people were killed when **Betora** <note>Beitar, the final fortress of the Bar Kokhba revolt.</note> was overthrown. They add that within the borders of Alexandria, 700,000 <note>original: "70 myriadas"</note> were killed by him; some even say that forty million <note>original: "quater mille myriadas"</note> were destroyed in or around **Bittera**. From this slaughter, such an onslaught of blood flowed that massive stones were swept away by the crimson torrents—on one side toward the sea, and on the other toward the **Lake of Gennesaret** <note>The Sea of Galilee.</note>.

Mention is made of the first Bar Kokhba by **Rabbi Moses the Egyptian** <note>The famous philosopher and jurist Maimonides (Rambam).</note>, whom they call **Ben Maimon**, in his *Laws of Kings* <note>original: "sententijs regum"</note>, where he speaks of **Rabbi Akiva** <note>original: "Alziba," a likely transcription error for Akiba.</note> as a supporter of Bar Kokhba and a Talmudic authority. Further mention is found in the book of the **Sanhedrin** <note>original: "συνεδρίῳ" (synedriō)</note>, in the chapter *Helek*, and in the **Lamentations Rabbah** <note>original: "Echa rabati," a midrashic commentary on the Book of Lamentations.</note>, where it is said: *Her enemies have become the head,* etc. Truly, there is much about these things in the book **Megillah**. Regarding the second Bar Kokhba, he is mentioned in many places, but especially in the **Genesis Rabbah** <note>original: "Bereſſit Raba."</note>. Let **Rabbi Johanan** be read there regarding that verse: *The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau,* etc. <note>Genesis 27:22.</note> Likewise in the book *Lamentations Rabbah* and in the **Tractate Gittin** <note>original: "Maſchet haghittim"</note>, in the chapter *Hammazikhin*. 

But meanwhile, we must not omit what they themselves hand down concerning their second Bar Kokhba, for it strongly confirms what I brought forward earlier. They record that such a multitude flocked from all sides to Judea in the hope of a future Messiah, that four hundred thousand devoted men joined him as a trial of their strength—each having cut off one of his fingers and uprooted a cedar. Relying on this multitude, Bar Kokhba broke out into these words: 

> "Lord of the world, do not support or help us, but neither should you discourage us. Are you not the one who rejected us? Do not go out with our armies." <note>Postel highlights this legendary prayer to show Bar Kokhba’s arrogance in wanting to win without divine aid.</note>

However, after **Hadrian** had besieged the city for three months and captured it, a certain soldier brought the severed head of Bar Kokhba to the Emperor. The Emperor commanded him to ensure the headless body was brought to him. The soldier returned immediately and found a serpent of unusual size coiled around the torso. When Hadrian heard this, he said: "Truly, unless his God had killed this man, no mortal could have overcome him." 

These things are found in *Lamentations Rabbah* and *Genesis Rabbah*. Certainly, the Jews were gathered from the whole world, not so that they might reign or obey bloody Messiahs, but so that the entire nation might truly pay the penalty for the crime committed against Jesus Christ, and that the survivors might serve a perpetual and harsh servitude among all nations, alongside the dire memory of that slaughter. It was necessary, O Jews, that the prophecies be fulfilled in you.

He specifically targets the figure of Bar Kokhba as a "bloody" and arrogant false messiah whose failure led to the perpetual exile of the Jewish people.</summary>

WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK IV.

## ON THE REJECTION OF THE JEWS.

**F**irst, I will set forth those passages in which the rejection of the Israelite nation is evident; second, I will resolve their objections; third, I will show what kind of Messiah and what state of affairs they were to have under him; and finally, I will gather from the prophets the evangelical prophecy, so that it may be clear whether our Christ is such as the prophets described. That the entire nation was not to be gathered, but only a remnant <note>The "remnant" (Latin: *reliquiae*) is a recurring biblical theme suggesting that while a nation may be judged, a small, faithful group will survive.</note>, is evident from these places. **Isaiah 10**, after speaking of Assyria, also writes of the second punishment: *The light of Israel shall become a fire, and his Holy One a flame; and his thorns and briars shall be kindled and devoured in one day.* Shortly after: *And the remnant of the trees of his forest shall be so few in number that a child could write them down.* <note>original: "Et relíquíæ lígní faltus eíus præ paucítate numerabuntur, ut puer fcríberet eas"</note> These things must be understood as referring to a certain false prince and to a total slaughter. For from the Babylonian captivity, many thousands of captives remained. Therefore, these words were spoken not concerning that captivity, but concerning the slaughter of lost men under a lost prince whom they considered to be the "light," as was the case with **Bar Kokhba** <note>Postel uses the name "Bachoziba," a derogatory pun on Simon bar Kokhba’s name meaning "Son of Lies." He was the leader of the Jewish revolt against Rome in 132–135 CE.</note>. Indeed, those who remained after the slaughter at Jerusalem and **Bether** <note>The fortress of Betar (or Bether) was the final stronghold of the Bar Kokhba revolt.</note> could have been counted by a child. 

The prophet continues: *And it shall come to pass in that day, the remnant of Israel, and those who have escaped from the house of Jacob, shall no longer lean upon him who struck them, but shall lean upon the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, in truth.* All these things are consistent. For before the factions arose under **Titus** and **Hadrian** <note>Roman Emperors who oversaw the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE and the suppression of the Bar Kokhba revolt in 135 CE, respectively.</note>, they leaned upon the Romans—who eventually struck them—until many were converted to the faith of Christ after the slaughter at Betar. *The remnant,* says the prophet, *shall return; I say, the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God. For though your people Israel be as the sand of the sea, yet only a remnant of them shall return,* etc. He does not say the whole multitude, but that its remnant is to be saved. For the few to be saved were the Apostles, the disciples of Christ, and the great number in our primitive church. Thus, by far the greater part was to perish in the slaughter, and the smaller part to be saved; the rest were to be kept in their obstinacy as a perpetual mockery among all nations. 

Indeed, the Spirit spoke through **Jeremiah** that the remnant would be so small in respect to the whole that nothing would remain. He says in chapter 11: *Therefore thus says the Lord God of hosts* (precisely because they had rejected and killed Christ), *Behold, I will visit them: the young men shall die by the sword, their sons and their daughters shall die by famine, and there shall be no remnant of them.* Although Jeremiah is speaking of **Anathoth** <note>Jeremiah's hometown.</note>, nevertheless, under that name, he speaks of the whole race of Israel. Truly, there was no long-lasting siege by the Assyrians where they suffered from famine in Jerusalem; therefore, this must be referred to the second destructions <note>Postel argues that prophecies traditionally linked to the Babylonian era actually find their full realization in the Roman-Jewish Wars.</note>. 

In **Ezekiel 9**, is it not clearly evident that those who were not marked with the **sign of the Tau** <note>The Hebrew letter Tau. In ancient scripts, it was written as a cross (+ or X). Postel, following a long tradition of Christian interpretation, views this as a prophecy of the Cross of Christ.</note>—that is, the sign of the holy cross—were to be utterly removed and exterminated? Is it not true that when **Titus** came to the siege of Jerusalem, a voice was heard in heaven, repeating this several times: *Let us depart from here, let us depart from here*? <note>Postel cites a famous legend, also recorded by the historian Josephus, that the angelic protectors of the Temple were heard leaving before its destruction.</note> The Jews were so blinded that none could leave, yet all the Christians—who were marked with the sign of the Tau—went out. Thus says the prophet: *And he cried in my ears with a loud voice, saying: The overseers of the city have drawn near, and each one had a weapon in his hand. And behold, six men came from the way of the upper gate, which faces the north, each having a weapon of destruction in his hand.* And a little later: *And the Lord said to the man clothed in white garments* (for Christ took vengeance upon you by the instrument of the Romans) *who was in the midst of the others: Go through, and mark the foreheads of the men who are grieved by these abominations. And he said to the others: Go through the city following him, and strike; let your eye not spare, nor have pity...*

### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...slay <note>This continues the sentence from the previous page: "interficite" (slay).</note> the old men, the young men, and the maidens, the little children, and the women unto utter destruction. But do not kill anyone upon whom you see the **Thau** <note>The Hebrew letter *Taw*, which in its ancient form resembled a cross; Postel interprets this as a mark of divine protection for Christians.</note>, and begin from my sanctuary. So they began with the elder men, etc. And a little later: *The iniquity of the house of Israel is so great that it cannot be greater, and the land is filled with blood, and the city is filled with perversity; for they said, "The Lord has forsaken the land, and the Lord does not see." Therefore, my eye shall not spare, nor will I have mercy; I will bring their way upon their own heads.* And behold, the man who was clothed in linen, who had an inkhorn at his waist, responded with these words: *I have done as you commanded me.*

I will show you that all these things clearly fit the destruction by Titus, according to the literal sense. Vespasian was the overseer of the city’s visitation. The five men with him, who made the sixth, are: his son Titus, and with him four leaders—the leader of Arabia, the leader of Phoenicia, the leader of Alexandria, and the leader of Palestine (this is recorded in the *Echah Rabbati* <note>original: "Echa rabeti," referring to *Lamentations Rabbah*, a Jewish midrashic text.</note>). They came from the northern route, for Vespasian made his way by land through Asia Minor and Seleucia, which is to the north, and led his army while Titus gathered forces in Egypt.

He who was in their midst was Christ: they had come to avenge him (for so Providence willed it) even while they appeared to be managing the affairs of the Empire. For he who is the cause of an undertaking is understood to be in the midst of those who carry it out, so long as the business is done in his name. He marked his own with the sign **Thau**, that is, of the holy cross, whom he removed from the crowd of the wicked. 

The work began at the Sanctuary, because the chief priests and the priests had been the primary cause of the death of Jesus Christ; otherwise, they were no more guilty than the others. The cause was not idolatry, but the killing of the righteous; for the prophet says of the elders: *Defile the house, fill the courts with the slain, go out!* This is said concerning the death of Jesus Christ and of James the Just. For they wounded James most severely in the Temple, and finally the high priest Ananus, despite the opposition of the synagogue, handed him over to the people to be stoned in the courtyard along with other followers of Christ. For this reason, Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the Jewish-Roman historian.</note> believes the disaster of Jerusalem occurred. For James was most holy, and his holiness was more clearly seen because he had been the first to receive the task of governing the Church in Jerusalem from Christ.

Furthermore, Vespasian did not even spare the remnants in Jerusalem; at that time, God poured out his fury upon you. The Jews said, "God does not see," when they had sold their most innocent brother, Christ. For this reason, Hadrian also killed those who were in **Betar** <note>original: "Bitter," the final fortress in the Bar Kokhba revolt.</note> and the ten primary men of the synagogue, as you testify in your annual fast <note>Refers to the Fast of the Ninth of Av and the "Ten Martyrs" commemorated in Jewish liturgy.</note>. Therefore, God will not have mercy on you—that is, on the nation as a whole. 

When the slaughter of Jerusalem was finished, Christ said to the Father: *I have done as you commanded me.* These things are not distorted; this is not some vain interpretation by Gabriel or **Kimchi** <note>original: "Chimahi," referring to David Kimchi, a famous medieval Jewish commentator.</note> regarding the Babylonians and Assyrians. None of that commentary fits at all. For that previous destruction happened because of idolatry, but this one happened because of the shedding of blood. Therefore, the word fits the history of the prophecy word for word, whereas not even one minimum conjecture fits the Babylonian captivity. From this one passage, distorted by your Rabbis, it can be clear even to the "blind and the barbers" <note>A Latin idiom (*lippis et tonsoribus*) meaning something is so obvious it is common knowledge even among the simplest people.</note> that they have gone astray and led you into a reprobate sense, just as the prophets had predicted would happen. 

But first, we must see what kind of "remnant" was to be preserved from Israel. **Zephaniah**, in chapter 3, says after speaking of the final coming: *In that day*—after the coming of Christ, of course—*you shall not be confounded because of all your inventions by which you have transgressed against me; for then I will take away from your midst your exulting pride, and you shall no longer be exalted on my holy mountain. And I will leave in your midst a poor and needy people, and they shall hope in the name of the Lord. The remnant of Israel shall not do iniquity...*

...iniquity <note>original: "tem" – completing "iniquitatem" (iniquity) from the previous page.</note>, nor shall they speak lies, and there shall not be found in their mouth a deceitful tongue; for they shall feed and lie down, and there shall be no one to terrify them. Praise, O daughter of Zion; shout, O Israel; be glad and rejoice with all your heart, O daughter of Jerusalem. The Lord has taken away your judgment, he has turned away your enemies: the king of Israel, the Lord, is in the midst of you, and you shall fear evil no more.

These are the true remnants of Israel, and they are to be the poor, the humble, lovers of truth, haters of lies, who—because they have a heart addicted to no human thing—fear nothing at all, because in the midst of those poor people dwells their king, Christ God, acting with his own until the end of the age.

It is a true kingdom, and true rest, where no greed reigns, no vice dominates; it takes away every occasion of injury from robbers and tyrants, since it possesses nothing that it might place before the unwilling <note>The idea is that a person who owns nothing cannot be coerced or robbed by force.</note>. That person is always secure; he does everything for the benefit of others no differently than for his own; he accumulates nothing, is always poor, and always abundant: such is the condition of the most excellent things, O Jews.

For justice and the resolution <note>original: "catastrophe," here used in the classical Greek sense of a "turning point" or "conclusion" of a story.</note> of human happiness consist in this: that one should be most like God—that is, doing all things for the sake of mankind.

If the wicked, most ambitious, and most greedy life—deplorable in almost every part—by which many live under the law of Christ should be thrown in my face: those vices belong to the men and the time, not to the order <note>Postel argues that the failures of Christians do not invalidate the Christian faith itself, just as corrupt priests did not invalidate the Law of Moses.</note>. For because more than eight hundred years before Christ, there was such greed in your priests and princes that none could be greater, the law of Moses was not therefore bad. For it always performed the duty of forbidding such things from happening; the fault was in the men who would not listen, and so we are, until God visits us, as he has already done long ago and more often in the churches of the East.

Through long duration and abuse, any gold is turned into dross. Few are good. Many most excellent demonstrations can be drawn for you from this passage of the prophet, O sons of Israel.

First, that Jehovah <note>The Hebrew name of God, often used by Postel to appeal to Jewish readers.</note> will dwell in the midst of those who fear Him and the true remnants of Israel, and He will be as a perpetual king among the good.

Furthermore, for those who truly profess that poverty and rule of life, God has taken away judgment, because they are so preserved by Him that they cannot sin unto death. For as long as someone is of such great spirit that he despises all these inferior things for the sake of God, without doubt it will rarely happen that he ever wishes to sin from the heart.

"Mine" and "Thine" (he says) have brought the seedbed of iniquity among mortals. Care for the body and pleasure have made man a slave to himself. Therefore, he who cares for nothing corruptible will fear evil no more. For he who has the supreme Prince as a friend ought to fear none of the inferiors.

But since divine providence, to whom the present and future are equally known, knew that very few of you would embrace this poverty, He therefore inspired the prophets to reveal what the condition of the greater part of the Jewish nation would be. Isaiah 6 says:

> And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" and I said, "Here am I, send me, Lord." And he said, "Go, and you shall say to this people: Hear, you who hear, and do not understand; and see the vision, and do not know. Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and be converted, and I heal them." And I said, "How long, Lord?" And he said, "Until the cities be desolated without inhabitant, and the houses without man, and the land shall be left a desert. And God shall move men far away, and He shall again restore the days, and He shall increase those things which had been left in the midst of the earth. And a tenth part shall yet remain, and it shall be converted, but it shall be grazed upon like a lime tree and an oak, whose leaves have fallen and the trunk remains:"

So the holy seed of Israel, just as... <note>catchword: "ti" - continues as "veluti" (just as).</note>
