<meta>This page continues Postel’s analysis of the Messiah, moving from the pedagogical nature of the Mosaic Law to a specific linguistic and mystical breakdown of the prophecy of Shiloh from Genesis 49, emphasizing the dual nature (human and divine) of Christ and his voluntary poverty and suffering.</meta>

-># GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK 4.<-

...in a body he might atone for all men; as God, that he might be powerful enough to save all. But a great mystery lies hidden in the word **Shiloh** <note>original: "שילה"—a term from Genesis 49:10, historically interpreted as a title for the Messiah</note>. Ancient interpreters seem to have read it as **Sheloh** <note>original: "שלה"</note> with the letter *he* instead of *cheth*, and therefore they translated it as "he who is to be sent." Or perhaps, wishing to deliberately hide this holy mystery from the Gentiles, they translated it that way. In truth, that word signifies **his son**. The exposition, says **David Kimhi** <note>A famous 12th-13th century Jewish biblical commentator and grammarian</note>, is **Ben-o** <note>original: "בנו"</note>, that is, "his son," and David hints that it refers to the Messiah. That this should not be understood as referring to King David is shown by the fact that the scepter actually *began* under him; it did not depart. Furthermore, King David was so wealthy, and so far removed from the poverty of riding upon an ass, that no king (except for his son Solomon) was ever richer in proportion to the size of his kingdom. 

But to the mystery: That relative letter **he** <note>The Hebrew letter ה</note> encompasses both generations of Jesus Christ. For it is written and read with a *he*, but it is understood with a **vau** <note>The Hebrew letter ו, often used as a masculine suffix meaning "his"</note>. For this reason, it remains silent regarding the name of either parent. When one reads the *he*, it is of the feminine gender, and it denotes **her son**, that is, the son of the Virgin Mary. When it is understood with the *vau*, it is of the masculine gender, and signifies the eternal progression and generation from the Father, which is the first thing understood when speaking of him. Just as when we speak of a man, we understand his reason before his body. For just as thought is prior to knowledge, the soul prior to the body, and eternal generation prior to the temporal—and yet we understand nothing except from what comes after—so the prophet wished to subject to the senses what we have seen, and did not write what we must necessarily think of first. He expressed **humanity** through the *he*; he kept **divinity** silent in the *vau*. Nor is there anything else like it in the whole of Scripture, just as no man is like the Messiah in his birth. 

As he was meant to differ infinitely in his most excellent condition, even from the most perfect man, so too in his manner of being born. For if he had been born as a corporeal being outside the vessels of nature without a woman, by the operation of God the Father and the Holy Spirit, he would have had Adam as a companion. If he had been born in our manner, he would have been like all other men. Therefore, he ought to have had nothing in common except in part, so that by differing from both, he might nevertheless join both together. He had a Father without a mother, and a mother without a father; therefore, Moses wished to comprehend both generations in a single syllable. This syllable, which God had inspired, He also preserved from the impious corruption of the scribes. 

Truly, that good old man <note>Referring to the patriarch Jacob, who gave the prophecy</note> was not content to have said that the Messiah would come when the kingdom and the senate were perishing and the priests were stripped of authority, unless he also noted two most excellent qualities in the Messiah: **poverty** and **passion**. While he ties his ass to the vine-stock <note>A reference to Genesis 49:11</note>, it is for lack of a place, since he had nowhere to lay his head. He notes that the Messiah willingly embraced remarkable humility and poverty. Otherwise, he who had raised so many men from the dead, and had aided centurions, leaders of the synagogue, and men established in the highest authorities and the wealthiest positions in their greatest hour of need—what riches could he not have obtained if he had wished to sell his services? There is no one who would not gladly acknowledge as heir and lord the man who had restored him to life. 

Jesus Christ was, and was by profession, most poor; he did not wish to be richer than he was. When he was about to enter Jerusalem, he arranged for a little donkey, suited for the use of the poor by local custom, to be untied from a post for him. As a gentle and poor king, he entered Jerusalem, that most pleasing city, which because of his benefits and humility made him its king—though it would forever pay the penalty for neglecting the Just One. 

He speaks of another quality when he says: **"He shall wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape."** <note>Genesis 49:11</note> For this denotes the magnitude of his torments, and the bloody pouring out of blood from his whole body. Wishing to hint at this through the mouth of Isaiah in chapter 63, the Holy Spirit says: **"Who is this who comes with dyed red garments, etc.?"** The Messiah responds: **"It is I, who speak justice, and lead captive Israel back to salvation."** **"Why is your garment red, and your clothing like those who tread in the winepress?"** Answer: **"The winepress I have trodden alone, and of all the nations there was no man with me, etc."** <note>Isaiah 63:1-3</note> This is the dipping of his clothes in his own blood. You cannot deny that those things are said of the Messiah, since he is the one who speaks justice, and who alone can save captive Israel. But after he spoke of his own blood, he immediately added words about yours—of which, as you know, there was such a great pouring out, that its rivers from here...

He further links Jacob's prophecy to Jesus's voluntary poverty and his sacrificial suffering, as symbolized by the "winepress" in Isaiah 63.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument regarding the Messiah's nature, transitioning from the linguistic analysis of the "Shiloh" prophecy in Genesis to a broader discussion of "types" (symbolic foreshadowing) found in the life of Moses and the explicit promise of a future Prophet in Deuteronomy.</meta>

-># ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD<-

...[should] flow from the rising of the sun even to its setting in the sea; and yet you are not wise. Otherwise I ask you, what benefit would there be in washing and dipping clothes in wine? <note>This refers to Genesis 49:11, "He washes his garments in wine," which Postel argues is a metaphor for Christ's blood rather than literal laundry.</note> For garments cannot be cleansed by wine, nor does any scent or instrument of luxury (toward which you drag every interpretation) proceed from a garment submerged in wine; rather, it produces a stain. Therefore, that dipping must be understood as referring to the blood of Jesus Christ, as will be discussed more extensively regarding the Passion. 

I come now to those revelations which Moses had and brought forth concerning the Messiah. In many places—indeed, almost everywhere—there are figures looking toward Christ. For example:
* The rejection of Moses by his own people matches Christ being rejected and killed.
* The selling of Joseph <note>Joseph’s brothers sold him into slavery in Egypt, a common Christian "type" for Judas selling Christ.</note> matches the selling of this man.
* The crossing of the Red Sea and the sprinkling of blood matches baptism.
* The eating of the paschal lamb matches the offering of his body for the salvation of all.
* The raising of the serpent—which those who gazed upon were healed—matches how those trusting in Christ crucified and raised on high are saved. <note>Refers to the Bronze Serpent in Numbers 21:9.</note>
* The leading of Isaac to death, though he was innocent, etc.

However, since you hardly believe even these explicit passages, I do not wish to argue with you using them; I have decided to propose the most manifest proofs. In **Deuteronomy 18**, God says to Moses: *I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers like you, and I will put my words in his mouth, and he will speak to them all that I command him. But whoever will not hear my words which he speaks in my name, I will stand as an avenger.* <note>Postel translates Deuteronomy 18:18–19 here.</note> Moreover, so that a true prophet might be known from a false one, God adds: *If what he predicted happens, he is a true prophet; otherwise he is false.* 

These things must also be examined. For I do not think the stubborn Rabbis will easily admit these points about the Messiah, because they seem to work against what we believe about Jesus Christ. "He says 'prophet,'" they will say, "therefore he is not God." They admit the future Messiah must be a most perfect man. But no quality in man greater than prophecy can be given; therefore it was necessary for him to have possessed it so excellently that even the greatest men placed alongside him were as nothing. The four major and twelve minor prophets; David, Solomon, Nathan, Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, and many others, such as the disciples of Hillel <note>A famous Jewish sage from the 1st century BCE.</note>, and up to **Simeon the Just** <note>A High Priest during the Second Temple period.</note>, there were innumerable most holy men; and yet this one is called "the Prophet" by way of excellence <note>original: "per antonomasiam"—a rhetorical term for using a title as a proper name, like calling Christ "The Prophet" as his primary identity.</note>, as if those others were nothing. 

It is also necessary to concede divinity in him from those things which Moses wrote. For when he says, "Whoever does not hear his words," he exempts no one from his law. If he includes all—as he certainly does—then he teaches that all who keep that law are saved by it. But we have shown that by a law of bodies alone (that is, civil law), it is not possible to rule the entire world. Therefore, he was speaking of one who would be God, otherwise he could not give a saving law to the whole world; he would only have authority over souls throughout the whole world, for physical bodies and men follow the movement of their souls. 

But you will say: "If he were to be both prophet and God, why did the prophets not say so?" If you had once thought that God could dwell in the person of a prophet, there is plainly no prophet who would not have been your Messiah and God. For you sought gods so close to you that you preferred to choose a single calf <note>The Golden Calf from Exodus 32.</note> by popular consensus rather than the God before whose eyes so great a fire turned that you could not bear it. Whoever had shown you even the smallest bit of prophecy would have immediately been regarded as a God; since even the serpent, raised as a sign on account of the damage from serpents, was impiously preferred by you over the God of heaven, whose present power was in the holier temple. 

However, Christ possessed the most excellent signs of a true prophet. For he predicted so many things that they can scarcely be numbered. He predicted the overturning of your city with tears; he said your captivity would soon come; that there would be happy women in Judea who had not given birth <note>Refers to Luke 23:29.</note>; he predicted his own resurrection and proved it by the deed, likewise his ascension, the sending of the Holy Spirit, the deaths of his own followers, the miracles to come in his name, etc.—innumerable things which brought nothing other than bitterness to a wicked nation. All nations had believed in him, when hardly a few Jews had come to the truth; he is truly Christ, the supreme man...

<meta>This page continues Postel’s argument for the divinity and unique nature of the Messiah. Having established the "types" of Christ in the Old Testament figures like Moses and Isaac on the previous page, he now transitions into the prophetic necessity of the Virgin Birth and the superiority of the "Law of Love" over the complex legalism he associates with the Talmud.</meta>

-># WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK 4<-

...the highest prophet, the highest God, most like unto God through every proof of a good mind, obedient in all things to his father according to the flesh, and equal in divinity. But the patriarchs have sufficiently revealed to us what the Messiah was to be. We must now move to the treatment of his birth. I have already taught—through many reasons, and repeated frequently so that I might instill them in you—that Christ ought to have been born in a certain excellent manner, different from other men. Adam was made without a woman; the propagation of his kind occurs through a woman; but Christ willed and ought to have been born of a virgin. I have already brought forward the passages in which the prophets predicted it would happen: that a virgin would carry in her womb and give birth, or that "a woman would encompass a man" <note>This refers to a famous and difficult passage in Jeremiah 31:22, which Christian theologians like Postel interpreted as a prophecy of the Virgin Birth (Mary encompassing Jesus in her womb).</note> (already called a "man" while still in the womb). These are the greatest signs, and they are not suited to the common practice of procreation. 

I believe the first point is sufficiently explained. Indeed, I have strengthened my arguments above against the idolaters: that nothing among men is purer than virginity, and nothing was more worthy of God than that the God-man, the highest of prophets, should take on flesh like ours. For although he could have conceived no stain from the choice of any woman, it was nevertheless most worthy of God to choose what is closest to divinity. The prophets, wishing to hint at this, always and frequently called the **Israelite Synagogue** the "virgin" bride of God as long as God was present with her; conversely, whenever they wanted to set her idolatry and crimes before her eyes, they compared her to a harlot and a fornicator. 

But so that it may appear more clearly that **Jeremiah in chapter 31** speaks of Christ, we must examine the words that precede and follow that phrase: *A woman shall encompass a man.* After he spoke many things regarding the return from the Babylonian captivity (which was then in the near future), and taught that they must abstain from weeping because God would turn back to them if only they would listen; but because they were persistent and obstinate, he added that the Lord would do this "new thing" upon the earth: *That a woman should encompass a man,* and that the captives might be led back to their cities, whether they believe it or not. 

But explaining himself a little later, he says: *Behold the days are coming, says the Lord*—namely when, after the return, a woman will encompass a man—*and I will strike a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not according to the pact I made with your fathers when I led them out of the land of Egypt (which pact they made void, though I was master over them); but this will be the pact I make with the house of Israel. After those days, says the Lord, I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it on their hearts, and I will be their God,* etc. 

This is that law which that man, whom the **Virgin Mary** encompassed, was bound to teach. It is not according to the law that Moses gave, because that had very many things which cannot naturally be inscribed with letters in the heart—that is, in the judgment of natural equity—such as that great heap of ceremonies and rituals. Even the most hardworking man could not suffice to learn them in many years, as your <term>Talmud</term> <note>The Talmud is the central text of Rabbinic Judaism, containing records of legal debates and traditions. Postel argues here that its complexity contrasts with the simplicity of Christ’s teaching.</note> teaches. 

The most holy law of Jesus Christ has a single verse for its law: *You shall love God above all things, and your neighbor as yourself.* And whatever you wish men to do to you, do the same to them. Indeed, the purpose of the Gospel can be understood in your language by this word composed of three syllables, <term>אלתאה</term> (*elatah*): <note>original: אלתאה (elatah)</note> **God, you, brother.** This is *meltheha*, that is, the most holy storehouse of an upright man: that he might worship God, keep himself innocent, cherish his brother with charity, and love him as himself. Therefore, one must worship himself as a son of God, God as father, and man as brother. This is the law from which no one ought to seek an excuse; therefore all know it, from the least even to the greatest, and they are helped by Jesus Christ so that they may fulfill it. For it is as much more fertile in deeds as it is shorter in precepts. The same prophet speaks of this elsewhere in chapter 24. This must be understood as the law which the prophet raised up by God was to give—one similar to Moses in the giving of the law and in humanity, but not in grace or prophecy. God will be the avenger against whoever does not obey him...

<meta>This page continues the argument for the necessity of the Messiah’s unique birth. Having established that the Messiah must be born of a virgin to maintain purity, Postel now transitions into specific scriptural proofs from the prophets Micah and Isaiah to demonstrate how Jesus fulfilled these roles and how his arrival replaced the Old Law with a New Law.</meta>

-># ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD, BOOK 4<-

...this law is easy for even children to understand; he would seem unjust who would bind men to impossible things. Therefore, O Jews, you ought not to rise up against us because we do not keep your ceremonies. On the same day that Jesus was conceived by the Virgin and died, the fruit of the ceremonies perished. At that same time, Jesus and his law began, which the Spirit hinted at through the mouth of Isaiah, when he said: "Before the child knows how to refuse evil and choose the good, the land which you detest shall be abandoned." <note>Isaiah 7:16. Postel interprets the "land" as the old religious system that is abandoned in favor of Christ's new law.</note> For when Christ was born, the sentence for the destruction of Jerusalem was passed, since God knew it would come to pass that his own citizens would put him to death, and the new law succeeded the old. Yet his power was clear after his death, when you did not see your [usual] signs. Indeed, around the time of his birth, the power of judgment was taken away by King Herod, who had seized the tyranny after killing those of royal blood.

We must now touch upon the place of birth. Micah, chapter 5: "Now you shall be joined to the army, the city to be destroyed by the army; they have laid siege against us; with a rod they shall strike the cheek of the judge of Israel. And you, Bethlehem Ephrata, are a little one among the thousands of Judah; out of you shall come forth to me he who is to be the ruler in Israel, and his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity. Because of this, he will give them up until the time in which she who is in labor shall bring forth, and the remnant of his brothers shall be converted to the children of Israel, and (a little later) he shall be magnified even to the ends of the earth. And this man shall be peace, etc." <note>Micah 5:1-5. This is a primary text used by Christian scholars to prove the Messiah would be born in Bethlehem and possess an eternal, divine nature.</note>

These things are most clearly said concerning the Messiah, and they mark the place of birth, the divinity, and the office. Since the city was to be destroyed shortly after the Messiah was killed, it began with a threat of punishments which were to come upon Israel in Jerusalem. Then it adds that Bethlehem does not lack its own greatness, since from it would be born a leader for the true Israel—the one remaining after the other [city] was destroyed—whose origin would not be like that of men, but would proceed from eternity from God the Father.

That these things are understood to be about the Messiah is supported by the Targum <term>Targum: Aramaic translations and paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible. Postel cites them to show that even ancient Jewish tradition identified these prophecies as Messianic.</term>, for it says that this one will be the Messiah. Therefore, the Messiah is God and man. And because he is eternal God, he will give them up for a time to their own judgment, until she who is in labor brings forth—that is, until Titus <note>Titus was the Roman general (and later Emperor) who led the siege and destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD.</note> comes to the ruin [of the city]. For we have seen that it ought to be understood this way from the passage in the last chapter of Isaiah. For the interpreters say it is understood of the Messiah: "Before she was in labor, she gave birth, and before the pain of childbirth came, she brought forth a male child." <note>Isaiah 66:7. This was often cited as a prophecy of the Virgin Birth, occurring without the "curse" of labor pains.</note> That is, before Titus was born [to destroy the city], the Messiah, the Son of God, was born. The prophet, understanding this divinely and knowing that some would resist Christ because he called himself the Son of God, added: "Who has ever heard such a thing? And who has seen anything like it?" This must be a great miracle, and certainly, according to the letter, it can be understood of the birth from the Virgin, who brought forth a male child without pain. Since the following words seem to be spoken about the Messiah and his coming in the flesh, namely that God, the author of all generation, also generates the Son from eternity. 

But I prefer, by referring all things to that birth of sorrows, to agree with the Jews. <note>Postel is likely referring to the "birth pangs of the Messiah," a concept in Jewish thought regarding the suffering that precedes the Messianic age.</note> Therefore, God gave seventy-three years from the time he was born in Jerusalem: forty years of truce from his death, so that those remnants whom Isaiah said were to be saved might be joined to the apostles and the true Israel, and so that the rest might fly together to Jerusalem from the whole world as if to a slaughter. 

Furthermore, he fed his own with such strength that neither fire, nor the sword, nor lions, nor any unheard-of torments could conquer them. For in the sublimity of the name of their God, Jesus Christ, they were capable of all things. For it was necessary for the soldiers to be like their leader, with an unbroken spirit, and prepared to receive and endure even evils from everyone after [doing] good deeds. Certainly, just as no man was more humble than Jesus Christ, yet greater in condition, a greater prophet, more powerful in virtue, and more equipped with every perfection, so also it was necessary for him to magnify his followers, equipped with those same weapons, even to the ends of the earth, because he is peace—realy peace, not just a peacemaker,

->## GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK 4.<-

...but peace itself. Therefore Isaiah writes that he is the Prince of Peace, as will soon be seen. Since therefore, O Jews, the Messiah was meant to be born in Bethlehem of Judah, it is impossible that he has not already come. For otherwise he would never come, because Bethlehem was completely destroyed by the Roman army 1,450 years ago; <note>Postel calculates from the destruction of Jerusalem and its surroundings by the Romans (c. 70 AD) to his own time in the 16th century.</note> thus he cannot be born from it, since the city no longer exists. In this place, I cannot help but be deeply angered by the impudence of Rabbi Solomon <note>original: "Rabi Salomonis." This refers to Rashi (1040–1105), the famous medieval French rabbi whose commentaries Postel frequently disputes.</note> and his followers, and say: *My people, those who call you blessed deceive you, and destroy the way of your steps.* <note>Isaiah 3:12.</note> Those impostors place a veil over your eyes for so long so that they may live off your blood, O fellow Jews; since they are lost men, they could not live except from your life-sap. If you became Christians, they would perish. 

This charlatan says in this place that these prophecies are to be understood as referring to David. But why are prophets called prophets? If they merely weave a history and predict nothing, they are not prophets. What is divine about reporting past events? Can anyone not do this? David had already died long ago; Micah wrote during the times of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. They so distort and pervert all the sayings of the prophets that they seem to be spoken of the past. What is this, truly, except to drag you into a depraved mindset? Wretched and unhappy people, who do not suffer enough being afflicted by all nations, unless your own leaders also deceive you and play this trick for so long. 

But let us hear the qualities of our Jesus, predicted 600 years before he was born. Isaiah, chapter 9, says at the beginning: *The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; upon those living in the region of the shadow of death, light has dawned for them.* And a little later: *A child is born to us, and a son is given to us, and the government is placed upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Father of Eternity, Prince of Peace: while his empire is multiplied, there shall be no end of peace. He shall sit upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, to confirm it and strengthen it in judgment and justice from then on forever. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will perform this.* 

These things belong entirely to God alone; meanwhile, our impious Solomon <note>Rashi</note> does not fear to make the most divine prophet a mere historian, and to attribute the divine names of God to a mortal man—to Hezekiah, the son of an impious parent, who was purified by fire by his father. Yet the Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and commentary of the Hebrew Bible.</note> understands all these things as referring to the Messiah. Indeed, Jonathan <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, the attributed author of the Targum on the Prophets.</note> says: *The prophet said to the house of David: because a child-Lord is born to us, and a son is given to us, and he shall receive the government upon his shoulder, and his name was called even from before: Wonderful in counsel, God, Powerful, abiding forever, Messiah of peace; let it be multiplied upon us in his days; the empire has been greatly increased for his servants, and for those hoping in him there is no end of peace. Upon the throne of David himself, etc.* 

Can these things really suit Hezekiah? The empires of the princes of this world depend on the consent of the people, but his [Jesus's] not at all, because he seeks nothing earthly. Therefore, by his own will, he exercises a blessed kingdom over souls, and carries the punishment of the true law upon his shoulders—namely, the cross—by which he broke the power of Satan, redeemed the world, and opened paradise to believers. In the sign of the cross, infinite miracles have been done, are done daily, and will be done. The translator explained those names which follow. For who can be called "Mighty God" except God himself? Who is the "Prince of Peace"? Whose empire can be so multiplied that there is no end to his peace? 

However, it must not be overlooked that the prophet, in the word <term>le-marbeh <note>original Hebrew: למרבה. In the Masoretic text of Isaiah 9:6 (Hebrew 9:7), this word is written with a "closed" or final "mem" (ם) in the middle of the word, which is a grammatical anomaly.</note></term>, that is "to multiply," placed a "closed mem" contrary to the usual order of writing, for two reasons. First, to show that the beginning of the Messiah’s empire would be 600 years later, according to the numerical value of the letter; <note>In Hebrew gematria, the final "mem" (ם) has the numerical value of 600.</note> second, to signify the integrity of his virgin mother, which was the first proof of his divine empire. <note>The "closed" letter symbolizes the "closed" (virginal) womb.</note> Indeed, who can sit forever up—

### ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

...through the throne of David, who else could this be but the God-man Jesus Christ? I have already shown from various passages that the "eternal throne of David" is the congregation of the faithful, over which he reigned in the time of Moses, and now Jesus reigns forever under the Gospel. All these things rightly indicate that he is called *Emmanuel*, which means "God with us." <note>Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23.</note> For in him, redemption was completed. For he was, as Isaiah says, <term>goel male</term> <note>original: "goel malē." Hebrew for a "perfect" or "full redeemer."</note>, that is, a redeemer who is absolute and complete. That he was born to redeem all people is evident from the fact that he is a perfect redeemer, and that in him all nations are blessed. For all people since Adam have been infected by sin, and they could not be led back except by the one who had formed the first man, as I taught in the first book. But I also wish to confirm with one specific passage, which I have often cited, that Christ was sent to all nations.

> It is a small thing (says Isaiah in chapter forty-nine), O Messiah, that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to gather the dregs of Israel. I have given you as a light to the nations, so that you may be my salvation even to the ends of the earth.

But I come now to other things to be noted concerning his birth. When he was in Bethlehem—a very small city with a great shortage of lodgings—a great multitude had gathered there for the registration of names under Governor Quirinius in Syria. <note>Postel refers to the census of Quirinius mentioned in Luke 2:1–2.</note> Mary arrived there with Joseph, who was of the family of David, though they were very poor. (For you know that it was customary to publicly keep the <term>diaries</term> <note>original: "diaría." Here referring to genealogical records or public registers of lineage.</note> of all tribes and generations, until Herod destroyed many of them.) They were forced to come there by the imperial command on the prescribed day. There, while they were staying in a stable that was open on all sides, Mary gave birth to Jesus—so named by the angel before he was conceived by the virgin. 

Thus, in his first cradle, he gave proof of the life of poverty he was to embrace. For no poverty was ever greater than that into which the Savior of the world was born; and yet that very humility stirred three kings from the regions of the East, from the borders of Persia, and from the domain of the Magi. They arrived at that place on the thirteenth day after his birth and began to ask the wise men and scribes where the King of the Jews had been born. When they learned he was in Bethlehem, they visited this most impoverished king, guided by a star, and honored him with gifts, so that the saying of the prophet might be fulfilled:

> The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts, the kings of the Arabs and Sheba shall bring presents, and all kings shall adore him; all nations shall serve him. <note>Psalm 72:10–11.</note>

That region is to the east, a thirteen-day journey from Judea; it is a maritime land having dominion over both land and sea, as well as the islands of the Persian Gulf. These are the lands of the Magi on the borders of the Arabs and Sheba—that is, of Arabia Deserta and Arabia Felix. <note>"Arabia Felix" (Happy/Fertile Arabia) and "Arabia Deserta" (Desert Arabia) were standard Roman geographical terms for the Arabian Peninsula.</note> There, the princes use dromedary camels; the path from that place goes through the borders of Midian and Ephah, which are in the western part of Arabia Deserta. Thus, another prophecy from Isaiah 60 fits perfectly:

> Arise, he says, be enlightened, Israel, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you. For behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and a thick fog the peoples, but upon you the Lord shall arise, and his glory shall be seen in you, and nations shall walk in your light, and kings in the brightness of your rising.

And a little later:

> A multitude of camels shall cover you, dromedaries from Midian and Ephah; all those from Sheba shall come, bringing gold and frankincense, and announcing the praise of the Lord.

Just as these things can be understood of no one else but the Messiah, the God-man, so too they happened to the Savior Jesus at his birth. For the Messiah was meant to bring light to his people: Jesus gave such great light to his followers that the least of his apostles could turn the faces of all princes toward himself, despite being of the lowest status, and could overcome the whole world through greatness of spirit. The glory of the Lord truly rose in Israel when Jesus was born, and then darkness and thick fog covered all other peoples—not because there was no light at all, but by comparison. For those same people were in darkness before the birth of Jesus Christ; but since the Great Light was not yet present, their darkness seemed to be luminous...

### WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK IV

...which a great light removed, just as the sun removes the stars. The Lord then arose over Judah, that is, over the faithful and those who confess. For these things cannot be understood in any other way than concerning God born and incarnate. Therefore, the interpreter in this passage calls him the "Wisdom of God," where it is written "the Lord." <note>Postel likely refers to a specific translation or commentary where the divine name is glossed as *Sapientia Dei*.</note> Indeed, the Wisdom of God is Jesus Christ. Kings walked in the splendor of his rising. For in the borders of Persia and Chaldea, a star appeared to them—contrary to nature, in the lower region of the air—with a voice saying that they should go to Judea and adore the newly born King of the Jews. 

That splendor of yours, O Messiah, brought kings to you, and it always accompanied them until, out of a curiosity to see the primary city and to ask the leaders about whom they were seeking, they had left it behind. <note>The star disappeared when the Magi entered Jerusalem to consult with Herod’s experts.</note> But once they had left Jerusalem, it immediately shone for them again and led them all the way to Bethlehem, to the very place where the boy was, and then it disappeared. Then, having entered without hesitation, these kings adored the most poor infant king and presented him with gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh, with which their region abounded. 

The gold was for travel expenses <note>original: "uiatico."</note> while the very poor parents fled into Egypt to avoid the fury of the impious and most iniquitous tyrant Herod. For Herod had been informed of the birth of the boy and the birth of the King Messiah. Since these Magi kings had come with a very large troop (as is fitting) of camels and attendants, their arrival could not have remained hidden, even if they had not visited Jerusalem to explain why they had come. Because Herod did not wish to openly reveal his wicked intent against the royal blood to them (as he had already shown his character), he dismissed them, but asked that they return to him after they found the child, so that he too might adore him. He said this not with the intention of adoring, but of killing. 

A few months later, when he realized he had been deceived by the Magi—who had promised they would return to report what they found about the boy (for after their adoration, an angel had forbidden them to return to Herod)—he took care to have all those born within the borders of Bethlehem who were two years old and younger put to death, so that this boy could not escape death. He even killed one of his own sons, lest perhaps he be the Messiah, because he was in Bethlehem. <note>Herod the Great executed several of his sons (Antipater, Alexander, and Aristobulus) for treason, though the "Holy Innocents" narrative is distinct in the Gospels.</note> So great was the man's madness, so great his ferocity, that whatever he heard was of royal blood, he immediately punished with death. For this reason, he wished not only to destroy all royal blood entirely but to kill every single senator, and he spared only one of the priests. 

The history of Herod's impious cruelty is well known in the Roman annals. Macrobius, a pagan <note>original: "ethnicus."</note>, as I have already mentioned twice, reports that when Augustus heard of that crime—that Herod had ordered all boys from the age of two to be killed, and one of his own sons among them—he said: "I would rather be Herod’s pig than his son." <note>original: "Mallem esse Herodis porcus, quàm filius." This is a famous pun attributed to Augustus; in Greek, the words for pig (*hys*) and son (*hyios*) sound similar. Since Herod followed Jewish law and would not eat pork, his pig was safer than his children.</note> For he who had killed his son was sparing the life of a pig. 

The prophet Jeremiah mentions this cruelty in chapter 31, where God speaks of the rejection and the calling back of his people, and among other things says: "A voice was heard in Ramah of lamentation, mourning, and weeping: Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more." <note>Jeremiah 31:15; quoted in Matthew 2:18.</note> They are called the "children of Rachel" because she seems to have been the mother of the whole race, since she bore Joseph, from whom all Jewish happiness proceeded. Some write that Ramah is a city, while others say it is a "high place" (which it is), where Bethlehem is located, in the tribe of Benjamin in the borders of the Gibeonites. 

However, once Herod was dead, Jesus returned from Egypt and went back to the place of his mother's birth. This was also spoken by the prophet when he said: "Out of Egypt I have called my son." <note>Hosea 11:1; Matthew 2:15.</note> If you do not believe these things were said of Jesus, ask even today the Moors and Muslims; they will point out the place where the Blessed Virgin stayed with the boy. As a miracle of the event, they even show an image of the Virgin and Child in the place where balsam used to be collected, because from that time the place was watered by the water which the Virgin Mary used for her own needs and those of the boy Jesus.

But we must now turn to the precursor of Jesus Christ. I believe no Jew, unless by choice, is ignorant of what kind of man John the Baptist was. For mention of him is made by a Jewish man, one who is a stranger to us <note>Postel refers to the historian Flavius Josephus as a "stranger" because he was a non-Christian Jew.</note>, in a statement of this kind: "To some of the Jews," says Josephus, "it seemed that Herod’s army perished for this reason: because he had killed John the Baptist." That man was exceedingly good; he commanded the Jews to strive for virtue, to cultivate justice and piety, and to come together in baptism—for then at last would baptism be life-giving, provided it was observed with the greatest innocence of soul. Because he had many followers due to these words, Herod, fearing his integrity and lest he expose his own crimes, thrust him into prison at Machaerus. Thus, out of suspicion alone, he killed this excellent man. 

The Gospel <note>Referencing Matthew 14 and Mark 6.</note> adds that Herodias was the cause, whom he had joined to himself in unlawful marriage when she was his brother’s wife, because the prophet had freely rebuked him for such a nefarious crime. For Herodias—to whom marriage with Herod the Tetrarch was more pleasing than marriage to the private citizen Herod <note>Herodias was originally married to Herod Philip I (the "private Herod") before marrying his brother Herod Antipas (the Tetrarch).</note>—feared that the prophet might dissuade her husband’s brother from what she desired to be done. Immediately upon the return of Herod from Rome (whose marriage she sought and had already bargained for), she saw to it that the prophet was removed from the scene. Josephus pursues this history more extensively in the preceding chapter.

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK IV.

...the temple was owed to the Messiah. But no greater, more majestic, or worthier temple can be given than the very soul of holy men. Therefore, that Lord whom you seek, and the messenger of the Covenant <note>original: "nuncius Testamenti"</note> whom you expect, was to come into his own temple—the soul—and into his church. 

Since there were actually two comings of the Messiah, the prophet mingles one with the other, as happens in many places concerning both the coming and other matters. For since our soul is unequal to the comprehension of divine things and signs, and being occupied by this mass of the body, it does not judge as freely as when it is separated, it cannot distinctly receive, bear, or bring forth the divine impulse. Before it reaches the organs of the body, it is far removed from that highest concept; therefore, there is the greatest obscurity in all prophecies, and various interpositions that are often not fully understood even by the one who brings them forth. 

This happens by divine providence: so that under a constant fear of God, we may have peace by subscribing to those prescriptions of divine goodness—whatever pious, holy, and just things we have known—while the wicked and villainous men draw poison from what is actually most healthy. 

As I was saying, the prophet comprehends the two comings of the Messiah as one. The first period in the sequence, therefore, concerns the final coming. For no mortal will be able to endure the day of the second coming of Jesus Christ, for it will be so terrible that no one can stand when he appears. But what follows pertains to both; for he says, he is **"like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap, and he will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver."** 

When he is said to be like the herb *borith* <note>original: "herba borith," a Hebrew term referring to a cleansing vegetable alkali or soapwort.</note>, which fullers use to clean and thicken raw cloth to make it fit for use, then this must be referred to the first coming. In this coming, he gradually purifies men and makes them fit for the use of the divine will, even though he appears as the lowest of men. From the power of his rejection, such great force flows into men who are filthy with sins and devoted to worldly cares, that it becomes far better than cloth, without which there would be no good use. 

It truly matters little what *borith* signifies in this place: whether it be soap, or the soapwort herb, or anything else fit for scouring. For by its very appearance (whatever it is), it is lower than the cloth; just as Jesus Christ was even humbler and more rejected than any man in his first coming. Yet without him, no one—not even the greatest prince of the world—ever was or will be pleasing to God the Father. 

When he is called a **"refiner's fire,"** it must be judged as referring to his second and tremendous coming, of which David said: *Fire shall go before him, and shall burn up his enemies on every side. His lightnings enlightened the world: the earth saw, and trembled,* etc. <note>Postel is quoting Psalm 97 (96 in the Vulgate numbering).</note> Those things which follow, **"And he shall sit refining and cleansing,"** etc., pertain to both. For here he purifies the man who believes in him; there, there will no longer be a place for individual purification, but a universal one, so that when his whole flock is gathered and united, he may deliver the wicked—separated and destined for fire—to eternal punishments, and the good to perpetual joys. 

He makes mention especially of the sons of Levi, upon whose example the people depend. For since they ought to be the holiest, and to lead others by their most holy deeds and words, their virtue or vice creeps into those below them. A vice that proceeds from their example becomes all the more detestable the greater the dignity they hold over others. Therefore Ezekiel says in chapter 9, when dealing with great vengeance: *Begin at my sanctuary.* Here certainly are the first to be corrected, and the first to be condemned in judgment. Wherever the order was purified, those who followed Christ were most just, until they stained the order with wealth and pride. Certainly, Jesus Chri-

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
### BOOK IV

[Chri]st <note>Completing "stus" from the previous page's catchword</note> is never going to despise sacrifices established in his name. For the order of things is not the cause of sin. I come now to another prophetic testimony concerning John the Precursor. Isaiah says in chapter 40: *Comfort, comfort my people, says your God. Speak tenderly to Jerusalem, and call out to her: for her time is completed, her iniquity is forgiven. She has received from the hand of the Lord double for all her sins. The voice of one crying in the wilderness: clear the way of the Lord, make straight in the desert the paths of our God.* 

Here the prophet mixes rewards with punishments; for when "her time was completed"—that is, when the Messiah came—he brought the remission of sins to all believers, but by the same works he signaled punishments, even doubled ones, for the wicked and the unfaithful. For such a great slaughter of the Jews was carried out in their jurisdiction that none has ever been greater, nor shall be in the future; and their captivity among all nations has been so long-lasting that none is more memorable. 

But, lest they should say they were unable to recognize Jesus Christ, there came before him *the voice of one crying in the wilderness*, so that they might clear the ways of their souls for the coming grace of God, and make straight the paths of their God. John the Baptist preached repentance in the name of Jesus Christ in the wilderness, and showed him to those who came to him, saying: *This is the Lamb of God; this is he who was made before me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to undo; he must increase, but I must decrease.*

The impostor **Rabbi Solomon** <note>original: "R. Selomoh"; referring to the famous medieval Jewish commentator Rashi (Solomon ben Isaac)</note> breaks out into certain trifles, referring these things to the Babylonian captivity. That pestilence has burned remarkably with the zeal for overturning the truth. From the beginning, he has dared to attack the true sense in order to overturn all sacred things, because while he lived in France—the nurturer of the most brilliant minds—he was attacked by Christians and could not respond to the arguments brought forth from the prophets. Therefore, so that he might be to all Jews like a **Theseus** or an **Achilles** <note>Postel uses these mythological heroes to describe Rashi as a "champion" or "defender" for the Jewish community against Christian arguments</note>, he referred all the oracles of the prophets to the past. He acted so that if the Jews believe him (which they mostly do), there would be clearly no prophet in the entire Old Testament. 

For prophets are named from the Greek *ek tou prophanai* <note>original: "ἐκ τοῦ προφάναι"; to speak forth or manifest</note> or *phanai*, because they foresaw and foretold things long before they happened. If they are only prophets in an allegorical or anagogical <note>spiritual or mystical interpretation</note> sense, then even the histories of the Judges, the Kings, and Genesis will be "prophecies." He does not say this in words, but he proves it by his very deeds. For I ask you: what else is it to drag the literal sense of a prophet entirely to the letter of the past, other than to turn him into a mere historian? 

John the Baptist was also called **Elijah**, because he preceded the first coming of Jesus, just as **Enoch** and **Elijah** will truly precede the second. **Malachi**, speaking of both comings mixed together in the last chapter, called him so, with Jesus Christ acting as the interpreter of the passage and giving the name of Elijah to John the Baptist. Indeed, names are often borrowed in the sacred scriptures. For the Messiah is called by the names of many who were before him. 

In the first place, even as a man in a body, he preserved the name **Jehovah**, which he had from eternity. Jeremiah shows this in chapter 23: *Behold the days are coming, says God, and I will raise up for David a righteous branch, and a King shall reign, and he shall understand and perform judgment and justice on the earth. In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell confidently, and this is his name by which they shall call him:* **THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS** <note>original Hebrew: "יהוה צדקנו" (Jehovah Tsidkenu)</note>. 

If any doubt that these things are said of Christ, the **Targum of Jonathan** <note>An ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible used to support traditional interpretations</note> confirms it: *and I will establish for David a righteous branch.* Jeremiah confirms this himself in chapter 33: *Behold the days are coming, says the Lord, etc.* and a little later: *And this is he who shall call her* (that is, the synagogue or the church) *the Lord...*

**The Lord our righteousness** <note>original: "Iehouah iustitia nostra" from Jeremiah 23:6</note>, Jonathan understands this as referring to the Messiah. This is also how Rabbi David Kimchi <note>A famous medieval biblical commentator from Spain, often called the Radak (1160–1235).</note> interprets it. But he says it should be so called because in his time God will justify Israel. They have wandered so far into a reprobate sense that they wish to strip away from the Messiah what is most excellent in Jesus Christ, so that he might not agree with their own views in any point; they ought not to have feared this so greatly. For their Messiah will be the Antichrist, diametrically opposed to Christ, and most distantly removed from divinity. Some overturn this passage and attempt to invert the reading. Others, in order to deceive our people who are ignorant of the Hebrew language, say that Moses, Israel, and Jerusalem are called God <note>original: "Elohim"</note>, but that they are not actually God. 

But they lie with impunity. For they will never show in the sacred scriptures that the name **יהוה** <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter holy name of God, usually rendered as "LORD" or "Jehovah".</note> is attributed to anyone else but the Messiah and God. From this, it is evident that Jesus is God. But I cannot cover in silence the impiety of these wicked Rabbis, nor fail to show their zeal in corrupting the sacred texts. To show that the Messiah is not God simply because he is called "Jehovah," they corrupt the final word of the prophecy of Ezekiel <note>original: "Iechezchelis"</note>, so that they might attempt to attribute the sacred name to a city; where it is read: *And the city shall be called from that day, THE LORD IS THERE*, they want it to be read: *The Lord is his name*, by changing a vowel point and adding a letter. For where it is written **שמּה** <note>shammah</note>, that is, "there," which is the legitimate writing, they place **שמו** <note>shemo</note>, that is, "his name." 

This is done by Rabbi David Kimchi and Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi (Solomon ben Isaac), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note>, following Jonathan, the author of this corruption, who in the book *Bava Batra*, in the chapter *Moker HaSefina* <note>meaning: "the one selling the ship," a specific section of the Talmudic tractate Bava Batra.</note>, judges that it should be read this way. Even if this reading were to prevail, since the prophet describes the heavenly Jerusalem in that chapter, nothing prevents it from being called "Jehovah," because then God will be all in all, according to presence and substance, whereas in lower and corruptible things He is present only through power and knowledge. If anyone else committed such acts against the sacred texts, they would rightly be hunted down. But because they are now adulterers and estranged from the truth, they feel permitted to rage against their mother <note>The "mother" here likely refers to the Truth or the Church.</note>.

In the 28th and 8th chapters of Isaiah, the same name is given to the Messiah, as the Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> agrees. In some places, Jesus the Messiah is called "David," as in Jeremiah 30, with the Targum’s agreement; he is also called "Solomon" in Hosea 3. In 1 Chronicles 17, he is called both a stone and a rock, and by innumerable names due to properties related to the facts of his life. When Christ was manifested by the voice of John the Herald <note>John the Baptist</note>, beginning then to gather the dregs and remnants of Israel, and setting aside the pride and haughtiness of the world, he took fishermen into his fellowship, addressing them thus:

> Come, I will make you fishers of men.

The Holy Spirit had not held back persons of that condition for many years before, for he said through the mouth of Jeremiah:

> Therefore behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and it shall no longer be said, "The Lord lives who brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt," but "The Lord lives who brought the children of Israel out of the land of the north, and from all the lands to which I cast them out; and I will lead them back into their own land, which I gave to their fathers." Behold, I will send many fishers, says the Lord, and they shall fish for them, and after this, etc.

These things concern the advent of the Messiah and the gathering of Israel. But we have already seen in many places and arguments that Christ would give salvation to all nations. Therefore, when he speaks of gathering Israel, he understands it to mean all the faithful, both from the nations and the peoples: but specifically those subjected to the "north," that is, those liable to the power of the demon. For from the north proceeds all evil. Indeed, in the book of the *Zohar* <note>The foundational work of Jewish mystical thought, the Kabbalah.</note>, Rabbi Eleazar writes that the northern part of the world was made imperfect by God: so that whoever would be God, or would call himself God, might come and complete it, and then they would know that he is God. Indeed, Rabbi Recanati <note>Menahem Recanati (1250–1310), a prominent Italian Kabbalist.</note> says, in that passage taken from the 8th chapter of Ezekiel, that the wisdom of God, which is called *Attah* <note>original: "אתה" - Hebrew for "You," here used as a mystical name.</note>, will dominate the angel of death, that is, the devil. Ezekiel also mentions these same fishermen in a shadowed description of the power of the Gospel and of baptism in chapter 47. For it is impossible for all living creatures to have life from the power of water alone; but through baptism, taking its origin from Jesus Christ who receives every kind of human being without any favoritism <note>original: "sine ulla personarum acceptione," a reference to Acts 10:34</note>, one receives life. For He becomes for them a fountain of water leading into eternal life. Indicating more clearly that He translated the power of the Law proceeding from the Temple into the Gospel, He demonstrates even more expressly the origin of this water’s vigor. For he said that the waters which would heal the others would go out from eastern Galilee, situated near the Lake of Gennesaret. For Christ proceeded from Galilee, and from its eastern borders He chose the chief of the apostles—Peter, Andrew, Philip, and others—who were the first fishermen. Therefore, after we have agreed on this, the individual points must be examined. *It shall be in the last days*: The Jews say this means in the final days of the world, but we say it means in the last days of the Mosaic Law. We must see who speaks better, by bringing forth arguments from both sides. The word <term>אחרית</term> <note>original Hebrew: "acharit"</note> *acharit*, that is, "last" or "afterward," does not signify the absolute extremity of a thing. For Joel 2 says, "its extremity even to the last sea." Similarly, Ezekiel 26 says, "When I shall place solitudes in the last land." But since the earth and water form one round globe, there is simply no "extreme" part there. For in any point of a circle, a beginning and an end can be assigned; therefore, "last" in that context is necessarily said in relation to something else. So too in Isaiah, "last" is said in relation to the Mosaic Law. For in the final constitution of the world, there will be an end to action and corruption. Nor will there be a need for law when time stands still. For a law is not usually given except for long-term observation. It would therefore be useless to establish a law so holy unless it were for the sake of the longest possible observation. Therefore, it ought to be given at least two thousand years before the end of the world, since you see that the saying of Elijah has already occurred in two parts: nature and law. For each lasted roughly two thousand years <note>Postel refers to the "House of Elias" tradition, which divided world history into 2,000 years of Chaos/Nature, 2,000 years of the Torah, and 2,000 years of the Messiah</note>. Therefore, the Law of Grace, being much more excellent than the two preceding it, ought to last longer rather than shorter. The "last days," therefore, in this place, are the end of the Law of Moses. They were the last days when the scepter was taken away from Judah, as Jacob had predicted. When Jesus came, the power...

...the scepter was twice [taken] from Judah, and these were the last days. <note>original: "novissimi dies"</note> But the "Mountain" is understood as that sublime power, higher than all other powers, which should be preferred above all others: namely, the state of the religion and the church of Jesus Christ. For this is the mountain that grew to a great height, being the "stone cut from the mountain without hands" which surpassed all others, as Daniel says. To this mountain, therefore (whether we understand Christ or the church depending on Him, it makes no difference), all the nations were to flock, and be called by the name of **Jacob** or **Israel**. They flowed toward this supreme power, than which none is greater, because the word of God—that is, the Gospel of Jesus Christ—went out from **Zion**. This means Christ was born from the Jewish lineage and taught the word in Judea and Jerusalem, from whence it spread into the whole world. He therefore judges the nations, because that law was given to everyone, and no one can complain of its difficulty; even little children can (as far as salvation is concerned) become most perfect in the knowledge of it.

But here it is a wonder how much the blind nation <note>A common Renaissance polemic referring to the Jewish people of that time who did not accept Jesus as the Messiah.</note> clamors. They ask: "How can Christ have come, as you say, when wars have not yet ceased? When have swords been made into plowshares? <note>A reference to the prophecy in Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3.</note> Nation rises against nation, and everything burns with war, even among Christians." 

Listen: Was the law given by **Moses** not from God and true? It was. But when were springs found in it literally flowing with milk and honey? Therefore, either he spoke falsely, or it must be understood that for one living well under that law, everything ought to succeed so fortunately that he would be no less abundant than if he had springs of milk and honey at home. Promises are therefore made to those who *observe* the commands, not to all those who merely gave their names to circumcision or baptism. For how many Jews were impious and wicked? Yet they were under the holy law and circumcised. And the priests, who among the rest were most observant of ceremonies—what crimes did they not commit? Scarcely against any others were more threats issued. They left no greed untried, they gnawed the people to the very bone, and they suffered most powerlessly from gluttony and lust. Vengeance began with them. Is the law of Moses therefore evil? It does not follow. 

For humans possess <term>free will</term> <note>original: "liberi arbitrii"</note>, and will until the end of the world. Since nothing is more noble than freedom given by God to the human soul, it will always be permitted to act freely, or not to act; for he who does good unwillingly is neither free nor a good man. Since humans will be free until the end of the world, and "the heart of man is prone to evil from youth" and is so deceitful and perverse above all things that no one knows it, there will be far more wicked people than good until the end of the world. Otherwise, laws would be in vain if everyone were either good or bad. For the just have no need of law, and the wicked are held by none. There were, therefore, perhaps even few to be saved under the law of the Messiah, as with **Joshua** and **Caleb**. 

But those who truly and from the soul profess Christ—among them there is no war, no sword, no spear. For what use is a spear or sword to him who loves all men from the soul? Against whom would he wage war, who neither possesses anything nor desires what belongs to others? If he does possess something, let him be as one who possesses nothing; against whom will he rise up for these fleeting goods of fortune? He who regards all men as brothers, how can he wish them ill? These are the prescriptions of the most holy religion: to be in all things most like God, to deserve well of everyone after His fashion, and to expect no repayment in return. For glory belongs to Him alone, and he who demands repayment gives nothing. To be born for other men and not for oneself—the greatest philosophers judged this to be the highest thing in this life. No one has achieved this except the Christian, instructed and aided by his Leader. That the prophet wished to be understood in this way is proved by the fact that he spoke indefinitely.

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
## BOOK IV

For if everyone who was to take the name of Christ had been foreknown to use this divine precept, he would have said, "all shall beat their swords," <note>original: "conflabunt gladios suos," a reference to Isaiah 2:4</note> and so forth. But since he knew that depraved man would, for the most part, act wrongly even until the day of judgment, he said, "They shall beat," etc. That is to say, those who will truly be Christians from the heart shall never have any strife or hatred among themselves; they shall enjoy a festive and eternal peace both in this life and in the life to come. For if everyone were to be without swords, then that great Messiah expected by you—who would bring it about that he leads you back without sword and spears and war—certainly, you Hebrews are in error. The world will never be without its plague; never in this life will vice, the opposite of virtue, be lacking. No law more holy or greater can be given in this life than that which was given by Christ, because it renders a man who obeys his precepts (as far as he is able) most similar to God. The Apostles spread this law, which takes its origin from Judea, throughout the entire world; they taught by most holy deeds that it is impossible for war to be born among the truly good. 

This was evident in Egypt, where at one time for 400 years, nearly 300,000 men lived with absolutely no distinction of fortune, food, or drink, in almost continuous successions—many such people are found even today. But they are not gathered together as they once were. Neither judge nor soldier had a place among them; a holy magistrate was revered not for wealth or clothing, but for the sake of order. 

I need not labor much over the miracles, since even the Jews agree with us regarding them; however, they say they were performed by employing the name of **Jehovah**, <note>original: "יהוה"</note> not understanding how truly they speak. For in the name of **Yahweh**, <note>original: "יהוה"</note> which is common to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, Jesus the Son of God performed all his miracles. Of these, indeed, the prophet **Micah** mentions in chapter 7: *Feed your people,* he says, *with your rod, the flock of your inheritance, that they may rest in the forest as in the midst of the fields, that they may feed in Bashan and Gilead, as in the days of old. According to the day of your coming out of the land of Egypt, I will show him wonders. The nations shall see and be confounded at all their might.* <note>Postel is quoting Micah 7:14-16.</note> 

God speaks in this place through the prophetic mouth to someone who, by the works enjoined upon him, must necessarily be like God. For it belongs to God alone, who sees and governs all things, to be able to keep his own safe equally in any forest—whether of trees or of the impious—as in the midst of the fields. This, after God, Jesus alone was able to do. Indeed, he showed that he knew hidden things from this, that he laid open the thoughts of many. Therefore, since these things concern the Messiah, whom God commands as if he were a man, the royal prophet <note>Refers to King David.</note> also taught with these same words: *I have set,* (says David from the mouth of God) *my king (against whom the princes of the world had risen) upon Zion, my holy mountain.* And soon: *I will give the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession.* The conclusion, *unto the ends of the earth,* shows that all these things are to be understood regarding the Messiah. For no man can rule in such a way, nor even God himself over bodies of free will. 

But wonders according to the day of the exit from Egypt were performed by Christ, as much greater as God was greater than man. The sea receded at the command of **Moses** by the power of God; but the solid waters, like land, bore Christ, and in his name they bore **Peter** as well. The sun, the greatest of sensible creatures, felt compassion for the dying humanity of its creator, with an eclipse contrary to nature. I pass over the innumerable miracles which he performed in individual places. 

But even at this point the Jews mutter, <note>original: "ogganiunt," literally to snarl or bark like a dog, a common polemical term in this era.</note> saying that **Moses**, **Joshua**, **Hezekiah**, **Elijah**, and **Elisha** performed miracles. This is true, but it was by the name of God being frequently invoked and by prayers poured out at length. But Christ, by his own command, restored sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, speech to the mute, liberation to the <term>energumenis: those possessed by demons</term>, health to the paralytics, life to the dead, and calm to the turbulent sea. So that there might be no room to doubt this matter, his Apostles performed such great things in his name, or by the sign of his cross alone,

# WILLIAM POSTEL, BOOK IV

...to such an extent that no one could count them. Seeing this, the pagans—perceiving people who were invincible against every kind of torture—were confounded in their own strength; they saw that their strength, though equipped with every art of doing harm, achieved nothing against that class of men. Countless girls and even boys under the age of ten rendered their torturers exhausted by their endurance. From this, it is clear that they were strengthened by the Supreme Power and depended upon God, especially since tortures applied to other men usually draw out the very things that bring about death. Seeing these things, the pagans abandoned their idols and approached the true God through Christ. You, however, never wished to follow their example, even though salvation had been sent to you; you were worse than the Gentiles, whom you ought to have fled under Moses, but should have followed under Christ. But because you did not do so, God has demonstrated in you a "precedent lacking precedent" <note>original: "exemplum exemplo carens," a rhetorical way of saying a unique or ultimate punishment</note>—one that will always remain, as I have already noted quite often. 

The innumerable multitude of benefits bestowed upon you stirred up such envy in the pride and arrogance of the wealthy and the chief priests against Jesus Christ that they judged this most innocent man should be led to the cross. You miserable people—alas, you miserable Jews!—place your glory in this, and you are accustomed to insultingly call Jesus *Talui* <note>original Hebrew: תלוי (*talui*), meaning "the hanged one," a derogatory term used in medieval Jewish-Christian polemics</note>, that is, "the suspended one," though the world is saved by his cross. Now, the prophets foresaw all these things, which I shall touch upon lightly one by one, since you recognize this horrendous crime. 

But the triumph and pomp of Jesus Christ, when he entered his primary city with a royal title, must be seen just as it was described by the prophet six hundred years earlier. Zechariah says (in chapter 9): "Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your king comes to you, the just one and the savior; he is dejected and poor, sitting upon an ass, and upon the foal of an ass. And I will destroy the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem, and the battle bow shall be scattered, and he shall speak peace to the nations; and his power shall be from sea to sea, and from the rivers even to the ends of the earth. You also, by the blood of your covenant, I have sent forth your prisoners out of the pit in which there is no water," etc. 

In this passage, Rabbi Shelomo <note>The famous commentator Rashi (1040–1105)</note> was compelled to confess that these things are understood to be about the Messiah. Rabbi Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167)</note> also wished to confess that it refers to one or the other Messiah—for as I said, you expect two: because there are two advents of the one Messiah—either the Son of David or the Son of Joseph. He says that a certain Rabbi Moses the Priest understood it to refer to Nehemiah, but the others reject that opinion, and the Targum <note>The Aramaic translation and commentary of the Hebrew Bible</note> supports the Messianic view. Therefore, in whomever all these things occurred, he was the Messiah. 

Now, let us examine everything through interpretation. The daughter of Zion ought to rejoice greatly, because the Church could obtain nothing greater than such a prince. "King," "Just," and "Savior": these are three qualities of God, for He is the King of Kings. But the Messiah ought to be the highest of all kings; therefore, he is God. Furthermore, "no living man shall be justified in the sight of God." "The just man falls seven times a day," and "our righteousness is like a menstrual cloth" <note>A common biblical metaphor for ritual impurity/filth</note>; there is no one, not even one, who does good. Therefore, the Messiah was God. The word "Savior" belongs to God alone; therefore, the Messiah was God. These are the supreme qualities of the Messiah. 

The name *Hu* <note>Hebrew: הוא, literally "He"</note>, although it is also attributed to creatures, is nevertheless a peculiar name of God, as the Commentaries testify, always calling God himself *Ha-Kadosh Barukh Hu* <note>original Hebrew abbreviation: הקבה, "The Holy One, Blessed be He"</note>. How can one who is humble, dejected, and poor be called a King? If he is greater than worldly kings, where are his attendants, where are his bodyguards <note>original Greek: σωματοφυλακές (*somatophylakes*)</note>, where is his treasury, where are his ranks, where are his governors, where is his army? Therefore, so great a kingdom is not of this world. For if his kingdom had been of this world, his ministers (as he said) would have fought so that he would not be delivered to the Jews. Therefore, he exercises his kingdom over happy souls and those whom he has made free. For otherwise, kingship and poverty could not meet in one person. But let the triumphal chariot proceed! "Sitting," he says, "or riding upon an ass"—and not even an ass fit for labor, but...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
<meta>catchword: ape- (referring to "aperte," meaning clearly/openly)</meta>

...still a colt, not yet receiving burdens on its back. These are the Messiah’s ornaments, these are his processions. So great was the poverty of Jesus Christ that he did not even possess a sturdy donkey—he whose smallest miracle could not have been compensated by all the gold in the world. It is established that he did this as an example rather than out of dire necessity, so that he might trample upon the pride, arrogance, riches, glory, and vanity by which the world is brought to ruin, ensuring that his deeds spoke no less clearly than his words. Meanwhile, the synagogue of Satan <note>original: "synagoga satanae"; a harsh polemical term used by Postel to describe the Jewish leadership who rejected Jesus</note> seethes with rage while it sees these things. Children and the innocent (since their fathers were unable to stop them) cry out "Hail the triumph!" and "Hosanna in the highest!" <note>original: "hosiana baramoth," a Latinized transliteration of the Hebrew *hosanna b'marom*</note>, that is, "Save us in the highest." From the mouths of infants and nursing babes proceeds the praise denied by the pride of the world, while the leadership of the supercilious synagogue gnashes its teeth in envy. 

For this reason, the prophet adds what would happen because of that extreme wickedness: namely, that among the ten tribes of Israel, because they had many chariots in which they abounded, and in Jerusalem, the horses would perish. For it was destined that those who, having scorned the truth and neglected God and his commands, placed their hope in the multitude and heap of their riches, would be utterly cut off for neglecting their salvation. Others, however, who were faithful, as we have said, would stir up no war, because they desired nothing beyond necessities, which can very easily be supplied by nature. He shall speak peace to the nations—He who was and is Peace, the Prince of Peace; He urged peace, He removed the fuel of wars, and He wished to cut away all worldly desires from his followers. For unless the lust for dominating and possessing is removed, no mortal can be happy or have a quiet mind. And although many know and say this, no one has ever achieved it except those whom Christ has helped and instructed. His power is most evident in what he says: that he would rule over the whole world. For this, as I said, belongs to God alone. But how will that empire of a poor man be established over the whole world? The prophet reveals it:

-> "Even by the blood of your covenant," says God, "I have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water." <note>Zechariah 9:11</note> <-

By the blood of his covenant this empire is prepared. Nor does it look only to those in the future, but also to those who were held bound in the pit where there is no water: that is, those who had been held in the underworld and in Limbo <term>Limbo: traditionally the "Limbus Patrum," where the righteous of the Old Testament waited for Christ’s redemption</term> since the time of Adam; he redeemed them even from the time of Adam. It is the blood of Jesus Christ that has prepared salvation for the whole world, both for those in the past and those in the future. Therefore, the Messiah had to be killed and his blood shed, in which he would establish this Testament. Daniel also noted this:

-> "And Christ shall be killed and cut off, but not for himself or for his own sake." <note>Daniel 9:26; original: "Et occidetur, abscindeturque Christus nec sibi"</note> <-

Truly, there was no deceit in him; he died for the salvation of all, and through the service of envy. The prophet adds the punishment:

-> "Once Christ is killed, the people of the leader who is to come shall destroy the city." <-

Zechariah does the same in this place:

-> "Turn back" (he says, after the Just One has been killed) "to the stronghold, you prisoners of hope" <note>original: "devincti expectatione"; literally those bound by waiting for the Messiah</note> "(of another Messiah, understand); today also announcing this, I will render double to you." <-

I have already explained in two places what that "double" refers to: two destructions and the present exile. Isaiah repeats the same thing. For after he had spoken of Christ in chapter 40, he repeats it again in chapter 61, also speaking of Christ; having mixed in the blessings of the faithful, he speaks of the punishments of the treacherous:

-> "For your confusion you shall receive double," he says, "and for your shame they shall praise him in their fields. Because of this, they shall possess double in their own land; he has given them everlasting joy." <-

The first part of the sentence refers to the treacherous, who are to be punished with a double penalty in the body and a double penalty in the soul. For, as I said, they feel the penalty of ruin and captivity in the body, and the penalty of anguish and doubt in this life, and in the future they will experience eternal damnation in their souls. Others, however, will also receive "double," but in the soul: they will receive rest and tranquility in this life, and eternal joy in the future. This injury committed by a wicked nation against its savior is mentioned in many places...
