# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
### PAGE 426

...and they diminish human sins so that it is permissible to sin abundantly in the hope of God's abundant mercy, so that it might seem there was no need for a mediator to wash away the stain admitted into nature. Although they have far more teachers of the opposite opinion, I do not wish to refute this except by natural argument. For they fight among themselves and mutually cut each other's throats with various authorities. When God created all things, they were "very good," and such that nothing more perfect could be given. For the philosophers affirm this along with Moses, for God is not the author of evil. 

Truly, all men are born from ADAM; if his sin was a small thing, as the *Nizahon* <note>original: "Nizahon." This refers to the *Sefer Nizzahon* (Book of Victory), a famous medieval Jewish polemic used to challenge Christian interpretations of the Bible.</note> says, how can it be that the heart of man proceeding from the seed of ADAM is "prone to evil from youth"? That all our righteousnesses are like a "menstrual cloth"? That there is none who does good? That no one is justified in the sight of God? Why does God "repent" having made man? All are sinners; in sin all agree, as if from a common principle innate to all from the first parent. This has not only been handed down in sacred scripture but has also been proven by the authors of humanity <note>Postel refers here to classical Greco-Roman philosophers and poets who observed the fallen state of human nature.</note>. For all are so affected that there is no one who does not delight in his own miseries; all desire the good, but they do not achieve it. Therefore, it cannot be that this occurs in everyone unless it proceeds from the first source. 

No one born from ADAM was created more perfect than he; yet a sin is considered more serious the greater the person who sins. Therefore, no one ever sinned more seriously than he, because no one was nobler. Thus, his sin infected the whole "mass" <term>massa</term> <note>Postel uses the Augustinian concept of *massa perditionis*, the idea that all humanity is a single "lump" or mass corrupted by the original sin of Adam.</note>. Nor could this damage, poured into all men, be repaired except by the Author of nature, who would reform that mass by taking it upon Himself. Therefore, Jesus the Messiah saves His people—that is, those who wish to believe in Him—from their sins. 

Otherwise, if God seemed unjust for raging for eternity by inflicting punishment for one transgression, let them see how, by the same reasoning, they might wish the devil—who committed one crime of thought—to be saved by God and to be punished unjustly. For it is established from the scriptures that there are devils and evil spirits bound by perpetual punishments. Truly, God is rightly hostile forever to that foul nature [the devil], because he sinned all the more seriously as he was far more excellent than man; therefore, having been cast down into the lower world, he became the most harmful of all plagues. He leaves no stone unturned here to prevent man from returning to his original happiness. 

To the objection concerning the virgin and the word *Almah* <note>original: "עלמה" (Almah). A central point of debate; Christian tradition translates the Hebrew *Almah* in Isaiah 7:14 as "Virgin," while Jewish scholars generally translate it as "Young Woman."</note>, I say nothing other than what the prophet himself said: that it is a sign and a miracle that a virgin shall conceive, and it would be no miracle if it were something common. Furthermore, it was fitting that the highest of men—as He was both God and man (for otherwise one greater than He could exist)—should be born of a virgin, with a chastity held in common with the angels.

## ON THE SECOND CHAPTER

As for the objection regarding the ruler from Bethlehem, that he is not the Messiah because he saves only Israel, it carries no weight against us. For as many as were to give their names to Christ, from whatever tribe, nation, or region, were to be the true Israel—that is, they were to truly see God in a man, who is otherwise invisible in His essence. For the Messiah was to reign for eternity and over the whole world, and over the Israel of God. This, however, cannot be done by a mere man; it follows that it must be done by a Man-God. 

That objection—that God performing a miracle in a thirteen-year-old virgin was not so great as if He had shown His power in a three or four-year-old girl—what does it reveal but a mind purely intent on slandering? God, who made things exist out of nothing, could make the forms of things change every day; must He therefore do so just so the circumcised <term>recutiti</term> <note>A Latin term for Jews, literally meaning "re-skinned," used here in a polemical context regarding circumcision.</note> might believe? God performs miracles, but not absurdities. God could have shown a greater force of divinity if when...

# BOOK IV OF GUILLAUME POSTEL

...when he granted to Elisha that a child be raised by his prayers, had it been not the body that had died, but had it taken on any other matter, both would have been possible for God: therefore he ought to have done it.

Who could believe that Christ learned magic in Egypt, seeing that he spent only four years of his infancy there? What child at that age is capable of any discipline—let alone that highest [magic], which contains within itself the peak and sphere of all sciences? These are trifles <note>original: "Nugæ." Postel dismisses the *Toledot Yeshu*—a medieval Jewish text—which claimed Jesus stole secret magical names from the Temple or learned sorcery in Egypt.</note>. Until his thirtieth year, Christ practiced nothing else but the craft of a carpenter with his father Joseph, which was used as a reproach against him. For everyone wondered, 
<margin>Matthew 13. Mark 6. John 6.</margin>
saying: "How does this man know letters, when he has not learned?" and "Is this not the carpenter, the son of the carpenter?" and "Where does this man get wisdom and virtues?" Christ ought to have been like himself in all things. Born in humility, he was Lord of all; though instructed in no disciplines or letters, he was knowledgeable in all things. Living in the lowliest condition, he showed, when it seemed right, how great he was—he whom the sea, winds, demons, and all nature obeyed. Indeed, nothing is more excellent or rarer than when that which is thought abject, ignorant, and humble appears, beyond everyone’s expectation, sublime, most wise, and supreme. This is the consistent tenor of Christ’s life.

### ON CHAPTER III.

<margin>I</margin>
Regarding the baptism instituted by Christ, and that infants also must necessarily be dipped <note>original: "intingendis," referring to immersion or baptism.</note>, there is nothing in these things that they <note>The Jewish interlocutors/critics Postel is addressing.</note> can disapprove of. As the Messiah was to be the most excellent of mortals, possessing an excellence common to no one else, he ought not to have claimed his followers or ruled them in any way common to other men or preceding prophets. Therefore, he was to be famous neither through the empty noise of the princes of this world, nor through pride, pomp, ruins, or slaughter, but rather he was to exercise his right over the most noble possession of men. But nothing is greater than the soul; therefore, he ought to exercise his rule over souls. Since, however, he was to be a King of Peace, not of war, and since—after the manner of other princes—he was to receive the names of those who would swear by his words, he ought also to do this by a sign and <term>sacrament</term> <note>A sacred rite or "holy secret" that acts as a visible sign of an inward grace.</note> unlike all others. 

<margin>II</margin>
Thus he was to institute a new law and also sacraments, not according to that law which was given in Egypt <note>The Mosaic Law given after the Exodus.</note>, but entirely new and different. Indeed, those signs which the Messiah was to give as the sacrament of faith were to be similar to their effects. Just as he was going to wash souls by the power of death and the flesh he assumed, so he wished the bodies to be sprinkled with water as a proximate sign in the name of God the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit: who, as we have seen before, is one God, one person of whom the Messiah was to possess within himself. For unless the man were God, a greater than he could be given. 

<margin>III</margin>
Therefore, since even small children are subject to the sin of Adam from the moment their soul is conceived, they must also be washed, so that through the faith of their parents they may "swear by the words of the leader" <note>A Roman military metaphor for the *sacramentum*, the oath of allegiance sworn by soldiers.</note>; no differently than circumcision, given to boys on the eighth day, was for them a cause of salvation. As for the fact that Christ was circumcised, that was done for a twofold reason: to prove that the Law was from God and was good; and so that he might become subject in all things to that Law, which he had given to bodies rather than to souls; finally, so that he who was to be the God-Man might receive the sacraments of both Laws in one man, just as he joined his entirely spiritual Law to the corporal Law, and the New Testament to the Old. 

<margin>IIII</margin>
I do not wish to recount here how God wished the Jews to act in the rudiments of baptism, when he willed those who were fallen to be purified by frequent washings <note>original: "ablutionibus." Postel connects the Jewish ritual baths (Mikvah) to the origin of Christian baptism.</note>. No element is more suitable for purging than water itself, nor one in which God has shown more miracles, or shows in the creation of things, as can be seen in the first book. Therefore, the Messiah, about to give a new law, willed that supreme instrument of washing to be the sign of the supreme washing of souls.

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD, REGARDING CHAPTER IV

How truly it is said that nothing can be more unjust than an ignorant man! The Jews, in their lust for slander, do not fear to diminish the credibility of Christ’s fasting—though they accept such a thing in Moses and Elijah. "If he fasted for forty days," they say, "why was he hungry afterward?" For they claim he could not have fasted so long as a man; it follows, then, that he abstained only insofar as he was God. O, empty-headed ones! Was Moses then a god for forty-eight days? <note>Postel likely calculates forty-eight days by combining various biblical accounts of Moses on the mountain, or perhaps includes travel time, though the standard biblical duration is forty.</note> Was Elijah a god for the same number, or Daniel for twenty-one days? See how they fall into error. Christ willed to be hungry, and he willed to experience in himself whatever imperfections belong to our bodies, sin excepted. There is no reason to doubt the power of the Word of God. 

Christ certainly could have shown his divinity to the demon (which is what the demon was fishing for), but he did not wish to. For as to what the Jews say—that the demon, possessing great intelligence, was able to recognize Christ—that must be steadfastly denied. No "separated substance" <note>A technical scholastic term referring to beings without physical bodies, such as angels or demons.</note>, whether good or evil, is able to know the essence of God and comprehend Him as He is. For God would be finite if He could be comprehended by a finite power. Therefore, the demon could not know the divinity in Christ unless Christ himself permitted it; but Christ did not wish to give him any sign of himself, nor to proceed to miracles when there was a place for the order of nature. Bread could have been obtained from elsewhere than a miracle, and the matter to be turned into bread from elsewhere than the devil. Therefore, that objection is hollow. 

Furthermore, although Münster <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a famous German Hebraist and cartographer whose works Postel often critiqued or expanded upon.</note> responded learnedly to the question the Jews ask—namely, why God did not reveal His Son in the Law if He indeed has a Son—nevertheless, something must be added to his response. Münster responds as follows: God did not want to manifest His Son to the children of Israel because they were prone to idolatry. They had already given examples of idolatry in worshipping the [Golden] Calf and later Baal-Peor. <note>A reference to the apostasy in the wilderness described in Numbers 25.</note> Thus, they would have said there were two gods and two first principles, and they would have perverted the Law by ascribing individual precepts now to the Father, now to the Son, according to their own whims. 

Truly, however, these points do not fully satisfy the question. For we must not admit to them that nothing was written in the Law concerning the Son of God, since in many places in the Law God speaks to God, mention is made of the Wisdom of God, and He who makes all animals capable of giving birth is certainly able to give birth Himself. But the knot of the problem is this: why was it written so obscurely and hiddenly that the matter was not most clearly explained, seeing as it pertained to everyone? 

That which is most excellent in man is the use of the mind—specifically, free will. If this were taken away, the world would have been created in vain, and God would not be God. Therefore, holy religion—in order to exercise the faith of the good and condemn the wicked who do not acquiesce to good and just things—does not open up the things it promises in a completely manifest way. If, therefore, the Holy Spirit had wished to clearly reveal through the prophets all the qualities and times of the Messiah, the merit of believing would have been taken away; for he would have been so obvious from his birth that no one but a madman could have refused him. And if they had spoken openly without a specific time or description, saying that the Son of God would act among men in human form, then undoubtedly anyone who saw even the smallest sign of divinity, or rather, a sign of a miracle in the prophets, would have immediately accepted as many "Messiahs" as there were men famous for rare miracles. 

Thus, for the sake of hope, faith, and the stubbornness of the people, God willed to reveal His Son to the world through slight indications, so that before his coming he might be sketched out by the pious conjectures of the godly; but after he had come, all the things written about him would appear clearly.

It is a wonder that a man so learned and well-versed in every kind of discipline as Münster was rendered so perplexed that he had nothing to answer the Jews when they reproach us with the cult of the saints, claiming we act even against our own Gospel. For in it is written: *You shall worship your Lord...* <note>original: "Dominũ tuum adorabis." A reference to Matthew 4:10, quoting Deuteronomy: "Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve."</note>

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK III

...and you shall serve Him alone <note>original: "illii soli feruies." A reference to Matthew 4:10, where Jesus rebukes the devil.</note>. Was it really so difficult for a man educated in the primary study of sacred matters—and even raised in the stricter profession of the Gospel—to respond to the Jewish objection? He should have said that the Church celebrates the memories of the martyrs and holy men in honor of Him who bestowed His gifts upon them, but that the Church does not worship them <term>with the honors of latreia</term> <note>original: "εἰς τὸ λατρεύειν." Latreia is a Greek term used in theology to denote the supreme worship offered to God alone, as opposed to "dulia," the veneration given to saints.</note>, nor adore them as gods. If Münster is unaware that this has been the established practice since the times of the Apostles, it is a case of gross and lazy ignorance. For as many as wrote within the first three hundred years after the birth of Christ record that this was the custom in the Church. If the men closest to Christ did not understand the Scriptures and they all erred universally, then there was never a Church of Christ at all.

That holy men can obtain more from God through their prayers than those who are still living is something the Holy Spirit says and implies through the Prophet, when He says: *Even if Moses and Samuel stood before me...* <note>Jeremiah 15:1. Postel uses this to argue that if God singles out deceased prophets as powerful intercessors, the concept of the "intercession of saints" is biblical.</note> This shows that they had more influence with God than other mortals. Why is it a wonder, then, that one can call upon the name of a saint—through Jesus Christ who blessed that saint—for one's needs? Or that healings are performed in their name, even through their relics or their mere memory? Countless miracles have been performed in this way, and even the "handkerchiefs of Paul" performed healings <note>A reference to Acts 19:12.</note>. Furthermore, if God is to be praised with frequent remembrance of His benefits, what greater or more pleasing thing can be proposed and repeated to Him than the great things He has done in man, than whom nothing is greater? Thus, in all commemorations of the saints, the Church refers everything back to Christ and God, beginning from Him and ending in Him.

It is true that one might wish a limit had been set on images, so that the **deification** <note>original: "ἀποθέωσις" (apotheosis).</note> of many was not done rashly, and that no fictitious miracles were read. But what can you do? Nothing is so good that men will not abuse it. The tares must be left with the wheat until the harvest. Nothing—not even God Himself—fails to become poison to ruinous men. But things are not "evil" simply because certain people abuse them. Certainly, holy men are to be held in memory above the rest of this corruptible world, second only to God. God is to be praised in them, and He is to be entreated through His benefits toward them—even if this is equally displeasing to the Jews and Muslims who currently live in false religion.

The laws observed for so long ought not to be set aside for us. If it were only this one issue that prevented them from accepting the truth, images could be removed and their veneration paused for a time. But they propose these objections with a spirit of contradiction, not a spirit of learning. Why does this man <note>Referring to Sebastian Münster.</note>, who is so highly skilled in <term>Talmudic traditions</term>, not object (along with many others) to the "Fast of the Ten Wicked Teachers" <note>Postel refers to the "Ten Martyrs" of Jewish tradition, though he provocatively calls them "wicked" because they favored the rebel leader Bar Kokhba.</note> who supported the apostate Bar Kokhba? What does the memory of the Prophets, of Moses, David, and the Maccabees mean to them, if it is not a commemoration of those to whom God was favorable?

I cannot judge this matter in any other way than to say it affects Münster poorly: that Christ granted to those while living the power to perform all kinds of miracles in His name—even greater than He Himself performed—and yet he denies that these same things happen after death to confirm their faith, blessedness, and eternal life. Such ideas savor of that "sleep of the soul" <note>A controversial belief that the soul sleeps between death and the final judgment, which Postel links to a denial of the saints' power.</note> from which our own impious people have derived the notion of the mortality of souls. Surely, a miracle is a greater sign of divine piety toward us when it is manifest and necessary after death, than when it occurred during this present and doubtful life. Therefore, although there are many saints who are not recorded in the daily calendar of saints, the holy congregation never included any among the "divine" except for martyrs or those clearly proven after death by miracles done in the sight of many. Even if some have ambitiously crept into an opinion of holiness, are all the others like them? The veneration of holy men must not be abandoned to the Jews, who—even while God was present and terrifying them—preferred a calf to Him, and worshipped every kind of idol amidst frequent miracles, even sacrificing their own children.

Regarding the entry into Paradise before death and the redemption by the Messiah: Münster answered well that no one ought to enter Paradise before the coming of the Messiah. For since it is confessed that Adam was exiled from both <note>Likely referring to the physical and spiritual Paradise.</note> through sin, and since there is no greater joy or happiness of which a man can be a partaker...

...to become human, than the contemplation of God and the First Cause: it remains that the supreme man, the Messiah, revealed it to his own people, and that through love, or in a manner like no other, namely through death. For men save through life, but Christ saves through death. For if any man besides him could have obtained such a great inheritance for his subjects, he would have had him as a superior or a companion: which is inconsistent with the majesty of such a great man. The Gospel text is a parable; it is not a historical event. The pious were in a certain place unknown to mortals before Christ, in a pit in which there is no water <note>original: "in lacu in quo non est aqua." A reference to Zechariah 9:11.</note>, as Zechariah says. For he, by the blood of his covenant, led out the prisoners from the pit in which there is no water, that is, from a certain place outside of paradise. But as for those wicked corruptors who refer these things in their commentaries to the departure from Egypt, I read of no blood shed there by the lawgiver <note>Postel is arguing against Jewish interpretations that link Zechariah's "pit" to the Exodus from Egypt.</note>. Furthermore, there is a promise asserting immediate joy because of the king who is to come, for it says: *Behold, your king comes,* or *is coming,* etc. Indeed, they also say in the traditions of the Kabbalah <note>The Kabbalah is a school of thought in Jewish mysticism.</note> that Abraham, with his servant Eliezer, and the souls of the righteous are under the throne of majesty: which contradicts the wicked opinion of the Talmud <note>The Talmud is the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> which says that Abraham holds the right over hell and paradise.

As to why Christ did not wish to become known through miracles and the Gospel before his thirtieth year of age, that was placed within his power, since he willed it so. That age is a mature one, which he wished to adorn with miracles. Furthermore, so that he—who had already for a long time practiced, as he said, the craft of a carpenter <note>original: "fabrilem artem." Postel notes that Jesus lived a humble life of manual labor before his divinity was revealed.</note>, and had not previously been engaged in letters or disciplines—might immediately bring forth the works of his latent divinity, even while he was believed to be the lowest of mortals. I have already said before: if he had arrived with human power and glory, and known to all, he undoubtedly would not have lived three years under that stubborn nation without them declaring war on the whole world by exalting him through seditions, when he was meant to be the Prince of Peace.

### ON CHAPTER V.

I have already abundantly satisfied the objection of this chapter, when I taught from the prophets that the ceremonies were to be removed from the Law of Moses so that they might be joined to the Law of the Messiah. Furthermore, Münster <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552) was a German cartographer and Hebraist whose works Postel is critiquing or referencing.</note> recites almost the same things. Let the passages concerning the abrogation of ceremonies and circumcision be seen in Deuteronomy, Isaiah, David, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, etc. In the sixth chapter, Münster brings forward nothing, and I follow his example for the reason that those objections might offend certain people. For otherwise there is no need to know these things, except when they are objected to, in order to refute them and satisfy the Jews. In the seventh chapter there are no objections, but the example Münster brought from the Hebrews is not without error when he discusses the nature of evil; namely, how we are evil, whether in body, or in soul, or in both. I understand from the adversaries themselves in this passage that the whole of nature is badly affected. The parable is of this sort:

If, they say, the flesh sins without the spirit, why is the spirit afflicted? Since, therefore, one sins and the other is punished, it follows that they sin together; this is clear from the following example. A certain king had constructed a garden in which there were the most excellent fruits of all kinds; however, he could not appoint guards over them without the fruits being plucked by stealth. Therefore, having entered into a plan, he appointed to the guarding of the garden one blind man who could not see, and one lame man who was unable to climb the trees themselves. But even they committed a fraud together. For the blind man, supporting the lame man on his shoulders, stretched him up to the fruits, so that the theft became common to both. In this way, they wish to imply that the principle of evil is in both natures <note>the physical and the spiritual</note>, which should not be asserted rashly. Therefore, the souls and the parts of the mind must be distinguished. For it is confessed that there is vice in the flesh. Truly, it has a vital soul, an animal soul, and a sensitive soul: which three are one thing, resulting together and depending on the nature and temperament of the body. If, therefore, the Jews say that this spirit is corrupted together with the body, we do not deny it. But if they mean that highest mind, which comes into the human body from heaven—which the prince of philosophers <note>Aristotle</note> in the third part of his book *On the Soul* calls the abstract and immortal intellect—

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK I.

...to understand, that assertion carries danger. For if evil proceeded even from the abstract intellect, without a doubt free will <term>liberum arbitrium: the capacity of humans to choose between good and evil</term> would completely perish in man. For if those two wills, by which we are driven in different directions, were both corrupted, there would certainly be no accusation of conscience to resist evil. Therefore, since we do the evil that we do not want to do, it is clear that reason perceives things differently from the corporeal spirit. Since, therefore, that intellect, so full of life, allows itself to be conquered within the body and dragged toward the pleasures of the corporeal soul, it is rightly punished: not as the author of the sin, but as an accomplice and one who has complied. Therefore, the comparison of the blind man and the lame man <note>A common medieval allegory where the soul is a lame man who can see and the body is a blind man who can walk; together they commit a crime.</note> is a poor one if it is understood as being about the soul, the immortal part, and the body.

In chapter 8, they object in this way: Why did he send the leper who had been cleansed to the priest after the cleansing? Christ made both into one, and he joined the works of his divinity to the observation of the Law for this reason: to show that its precepts were holy. For it was not necessary for the sake of health, but for the sake of the distinction between one kind of leprosy and another <note>original: "inter lepram & lepram." A reference to the priestly duty in Leviticus to judge different skin diseases.</note>. For he himself never violated the Law, except when necessity compelled him: as when he approved the rubbing of the ears of grain on the Sabbath, or healed on the same day; he neglected the washings of the traditions, but the rest are unworthy of a response.

It follows: Since Jesus calls himself the "Son of Man" in many places, it is indicated to us there that we should not worship the Son of Man, because Balaam said: *God is not man, that he should lie, nor like a son of man, that he should change* <note>Numbers 23:19</note>. *Do not put your hope in the generous, nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation,* says David <note>Psalm 146:3</note>, and even more: *Cursed is he who trusts in man, and makes flesh his arm* <note>Jeremiah 17:5</note>. Christ frequently calls himself the Son of Man, we admit. Therefore, is he not to be hoped in? This we deny. If the Messiah had been a mere man, he was not to be worshiped. But because he is the supreme of all men, that is, the God-man <note>original: "homo Deus"</note>, he was to be worshiped. Nor is it an evil thing to hope in him. For the Scripture says, *the nations shall hope in him,* when it speaks of the Messiah. Therefore, even if he had only been a man, he was to be hoped in: which is what your fathers did. For since you Jews trust in a man, and expect a butcher and a tyrant most unlike God for a Messiah, you are all cursed. You cut your own throats, you circumcised ones <note>original: "recutiti." A pejorative term for those who are circumcised.</note>. By embracing the supreme of men, God and man as one, we follow the truth. Your butcher-Messiah, or rather Antimessiah, will be the blight and ruin of the world. And since God is eager to preserve nature, your Messiah is going to overturn the world for the sake of the pleasure of a few men.

---

### CHAPTER X.

I would truly wish that the occasion of this perplexity had not been presented to me: because I do not know well enough whether I am refuting the opinion of the Jews, or the interpreter. Therefore, since Münster <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a German cartographer and Hebraist whose translations of Hebrew texts Postel often found problematic.</note> harms the accepted faith concerning good works more than the Jews do, both must be criticized. The Jews disapprove of our fasts because we eat during the day; they are not accustomed to take food before evening, which the ancient Church used to do. Furthermore, they say we do not begin the day of fasting well, because we eat meat on the night preceding the day of the fast. But they do not minimize the thing itself, but the manner of doing it. For them, the day begins from evening to evening; for us, from midnight <note>original: "mesonyctio"</note> to midnight; for others from sunrise to sunrise; for some from midday to midday. But since there is a lack in things, eternal night seems to have preceded the light; yet if we take night as a state of being, the day precedes it in dignity. But these things are irrelevant to the matter. For it matters little at what starting point you begin to act well, provided that you act well. As for what they add ironically—that we fast unworthily on the sixth day <note>Friday</note> in memory of the Passion of Christ, when we ought rather to be joyful because of our liberation—this is a matter unworthy of a response. For because of his pains, and our misery which crucified him through the work of Jewish torturers, one must weep and fast, both daily and especially on that day: and one must rejoice because of the certain hope of salvation: which one may do together with the pious and holy.

# ON THE CONCORD OF THE WORLD

...it is possible, for a true Christian must always weep, and always rejoice. By the knowledge of misery the flesh and the **old man** <note>A Pauline theological term referring to the unregenerate human nature before conversion.</note> are depressed and die; yet joy is invited through the certain hope of salvation. Thus, true hope in God first leans upon his own humility.

Furthermore, I wonder greatly what came into the mind of **Münster** <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a prominent German Hebraist and cartographer whose annotations on the Hebrew Bible and Matthew were widely read and often critiqued by Postel.</note>, a man otherwise prudent and wise, that he should affirm that we and the Jews **falsely** believed fasting to be a good work. If fasting is not a good work, Münster, then God is unwise and empty, who commanded it and approved it in innumerable places. Certainly, no greater impiety could be brought forward regarding good works. But he pretends that one ought to fast *always*: as if indeed the apostles and their successors, who prefixed certain days for greater abstinence, did not understand that in this age one must live soberly, justly, and piously. Indeed, Christ—who says, *When you fast*, etc.—did not understand that one must always fast equally, nor did he understand the Gospel in that way. It is indeed true that one must always live soberly, but on certain days more than soberly, so that you barely even assist the laws of necessity. I do not wish to recount the praises of fasting here, nor how often the Lord turned away his anger because of fasting, nor how demons and wild beasts are conquered by it, etc.; for that would be another work. Therefore the Jews write poorly when they observe a fast on Friday <note>original: "die Veneris." While Monday and Thursday were traditional Jewish fasts, Postel may be referencing a specific contemporary debate or conflating customs.</note>; but you, Münster, act impiously because you desire nothing to be prescribed for men except their own lust. For if things were better done without a prescription than with one, God would be a fool to have given laws to men. Certainly, the modern faction <note>Likely referring to the Protestant Reformers who moved away from mandatory ecclesiastical fasts.</note> seems more plausible to you than the Apostolic life, and you prefer to call Christ a liar rather than anyone else similar to yourself.

In the response to the following objection, he **hit the nail on the head** <note>original: "rem acu tetigit" — a Latin idiom meaning to touch the matter with a needle, i.e., to describe something exactly.</note> against the Jews affirming that whatever miracles Christ produced had been produced by the ancients. For in this they differ: that Christ alone did what all the saints did, but he did it in his own name, while they did it by invoking God. Moreover, many things were produced by him that were not done before him: the Transfiguration, the resurrection, the conversation after the resurrection, the sending of the Holy Spirit, and the granting of similar miracles to his true followers, in which matter his divinity is most clearly seen.

I have already responded to the objection regarding eternal peace among true Christians, which Münster also satisfies well in his annotations on chapter 10. It is impossible, while human **will** <term>arbitrium: the power of choice or judgment</term> remains, for evil people to ever be lacking in the world, by whose occasion war arises daily. For if there were to be no future evil people under the Messiah, he would give the Law in vain. But since he was going to give the Law, and that a most perfect one, it is necessary that there be evil and wicked people under it to whom he might prescribe it. Therefore, that peace is understood to be not of bodies, but of souls, and that only among the good. Thus the Gospel does not fight with the Law when Christ says he would send a sword into the world. For as many as are good, the better they are, the more they are afflicted by the impious; and the more they are harassed, the greater the peace they exercise toward all men. For virtue, the more it is exercised—even though it is undertaken for the sake of rest—the less it enjoys its goal [in this life]. For if it wished to enjoy rest in this life, it would cease to be virtue. For the present life consists in the action of good, while the future life consists in the perception of the reward.

Who does not see the impudent calumny of the Jews regarding chapter 12, where the **Sabbath** is treated? For they say that it is stated in our exposition of the Sabbath that one should primarily cease from sin [on that day]; suggesting that we persuade others that on the remaining days one should persist in sin. Who is so impious that he ever even thought this? A Christian must always guard against all sins more than against death, but most attentively on a feast day or the Lord's day, so that we may labor to wash away the sins committed on other days before God with tears, confession, good works, and every kind of expiation. There cannot be a single common tenor of human life in the same order [at all times], and yet a good man must never act wickedly.

...for good. Thus, although one should strive for good works throughout the whole course of life, nevertheless on certain prescribed days one ought most attentively either to resist sins or to persist in good works. Regarding their objection against Christ’s response to the Pharisees—that people are accustomed to succoring both men and beasts in danger of their lives on the Sabbath—nothing else needs to be brought forward than this: if bodily action violates the Sabbath, then it is violated most of all by its guardians, the Levites, who on that day work most with their hands. Whence it follows that the violation of the Sabbath does not consist in necessary work, but in the neglect of the commandment. For otherwise God would not have "hated your Sabbaths" <note>A reference to Isaiah 1:13, where God rejects ritual observance devoid of heart.</note>, O circumcised ones <note>original: "recutiti," a term Postel uses for the Jewish people, referring to circumcision</note>, if you had performed all works of mercy in them through every duty of the body. 

As for the story **Münster** <note>Sebastian Münster, the Hebraist mentioned on the previous page.</note> brings up about the Saxon Jew—although it seems to suggest the customs of everyone, in that he stayed in the latrine on a Saturday when it coincided with the Lord's Day <note>A reference to a popular medieval anecdote where a Jew falls into a latrine on Saturday and refuses to be rescued because it is the Sabbath, and the Christians refuse to rescue him on Sunday because it is their holy day.</note>—nevertheless, the customs of Sabbath observance are not like that in Africa and Asia, especially among the **Karaites** <note>A Jewish movement that recognizes the Tanakh (Hebrew Bible) as its supreme authority, rejecting the oral traditions of the Talmud.</note>, who reject the traditions and the Talmud. They are always snarling and saying that we do not observe the Law, even though Christ came to fulfill it and said that not one "tittle" <note>original: "apex," referring to the smallest stroke or dot in Hebrew writing</note> of it would perish until all things are accomplished. This part has now been abundantly satisfied. For the New Law was not to be like the old one, except in those things pertaining to morals.

But a difficult question follows. "If he is God," they say, "why did he hide himself in the flesh? And why did he not come with boldness to proclaim his law and to explain it in public, so that the people of that age would not be seduced, nor mortals stumble because of him? He should have performed his works in the open, to the known and unknown alike, so that all might believe in him. For the loss of those who perished because of this concealment is greater than the redemption, since they hesitate to believe in one who is hidden." These things have been translated word-for-word so they may be understood. I have already answered these points in many places, yet I will repeat it briefly. 

God wishes to exercise our free will in all things, so that just as he performs all the miracles by which people are stirred to obedience and virtue, so too he allows us the power and will to carry things out, so that those who are proven and upright may be revealed. For although under Moses, God could have—no less easily than he showed power above nature before Pharaoh, in the sea, in the desert, in the river, in the sun, among the Philistines, against Sennacherib, in Habakkuk, in Daniel, and the youths—transferred you all from Egypt in the blink of an eye to the Holy Land without any effort of trusting him, nevertheless he willed that the faithful be tested by human labor in reaching that place. 

Likewise, when the Messiah came, whose law was most excellent, he wished to leave the choice of believing to us; as the preserver of nature, he did not wish to join his power with bloodshed in the manner of tyrants, lest he should force everyone, even the unwilling, to swear by his words. For he would have been most unlike God if he had acted in that way. The power of believing through the freedom of faith was given to all; this merit would have been taken away if it had been more manifest at the beginning. Furthermore, if Christ had been known immediately from his birth, you would have immediately driven him—even against his will—into wars and the ruin of the world. Certainly, if he had come with physical power, he would have either brought destruction to the whole world (which he came to save) or he would have had many equals. He could scarcely have been equal to **Ninus** <note>The legendary founder of Nineveh and the Assyrian Empire.</note>, who led hundreds of thousands of men into war; to **Semiramis** <note>The legendary Queen of Babylon.</note>, who led one million eight hundred thousand; or to **Xerxes**, who led one million. Nor could he have been richer or more splendid than Solomon. 

Thus, it is not his fault that many perished and stumbled, just as it is not the fault of water if many die of thirst because they refuse to approach the spring. That more are lost than saved is no surprise. For few are good; and as you have it in the **Talmud**, what will happen at the coming of the Messiah is like what happened at the entry into the Holy Land. For only two out of at least fifteen hundred thousand men entered the Holy Land—**Joshua** and **Caleb**—which was not the fault of God, nor of Moses, nor of the Holy Land. So it happened that very few were to be saved when Christ came. He was sent for the salvation of Israel in the whole world, yet so...

...me, so that he might leave the judgment of belief without any force among any nations. It also serves the matter that he gave an example, lest we sell ourselves because of divine benefits. In chapter 13 <note>Likely referring to Matthew 13 or a specific chapter in a Jewish polemical work like the *Toledot Yeshu*.</note>, they stir up the parables of Christ based on the similarity to **Aaron’s rod**, which we apply to the **Virgin Mother**, as if every similar thing must agree in all respects with its counterpart—a point that even secular authors never concede. I would ask those people: if parables must be fitted to their likenesses in all things, then when **Hosea** compares his unfaithful wife to the **Synagogue** <note>Hosea 1:2. Postel is arguing against a literalist interpretation of metaphors.</note>, it would follow that the Synagogue must have worshiped all the gods of the entire world, just as a prostitute admits all men. It would follow that they ought to be rooted and implanted into the body like hair, since the Jews are compared to hairs by **Ezekiel** <note>Ezekiel 5:1-5, where the prophet is told to shave his head and beard to symbolize the fate of Jerusalem.</note>; and six hundred such examples exist. For everything is full of parables; yet among the prophets, there is none that fits perfectly in every single comparison.

I do not bother to refute the futility of the Jews regarding the fire of **Hell**, since it refutes itself. For they say that the bodies of the impious are to be consumed by fire like chaff, so that no memory of their name remains. But for what purpose will the **Resurrection** be, if the corruption of those rising again remains possible? Why should those perish entirely, whose name and body ought to endure eternally for their disgrace, so that the action of divine justice may be made known? There will be no consumption of bodies in the future age. Only the matter of the human body will be able to suffer, but not be destroyed, as an eternal bond holds the bodies themselves together. Thus, just as through a stubborn lust for sinning they thought either that there was no God, or that He did not care for human affairs or possess justice, so they may feel forever that He is a Judge, whom they believed did not exist.

The objection of the Jews is false when they say Christ had brothers and sisters because the Jews of his time said: *Is not this the carpenter, the son of the carpenter? Is not his mother called Mary, and his brothers James, Joseph, Simon, and Judah?* <note>original: "nonne hic est faber filius fabri? Nonne mater eius vocatur Maria, & fratres eius Iacobus, & Ioseph, Simon, & Iudah?" See Matthew 13:55-56.</note> For they speak partly the truth—that he was the carpenter’s son (as he was believed to be) and born of Mary—but as for him truly having a father, or brothers and sisters, they were speaking falsely. Nor is this written in the **Gospel** as something true and proven, but as an objection. But suppose they spoke from their hearts: it is the custom of Scripture that a kinsman is placed in the stead of a "brother" by that very name. This is also common in all languages for the sake of friendship, to say of those most closely joined (even outside of kinship) that they are "brothers" of this sort.

Indeed, if they would do such violence to things based on words—if these modern thinkers believe the ancient Jews who scarcely recognized Christ before his miracles—much more should they believe Christ himself. He said that his mother, brother, and sister were those who do the will of his Father; thus he asserted they were his kin. Christ became "all things to all people" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 9:22.</note> so that he might win all; therefore, he affirmed that happy souls were bound to him by every kind of kinship. Thus, he called these people "brothers" under a double name: both by reason of kinship <note>referring to cousins or relatives</note> and by reason of goodness. Truly, he calls his disciples and the poor his "brothers," not by reason of the flesh (to which the miserable Jews refer everything). They are therefore driven into a perverse sense because they twist the force of words to the literal letter even in the prophets, which overturns the truth.

Although I have already spoken of the excellence of the **Messiah**, nevertheless, for the sake of this objection, those things that were said must be recounted briefly and enriched. We said at the beginning that all the highest things—and those common to none but a human body—ought to belong to the Messiah. All those things truly happened to **Jesus Christ**. For as he was God and man (than whom nothing greater can be given), so also he ought to be conceived, born, and have kinship differently from all other men in the world. Nothing is more separate than man and God; he has both in his one self. Nothing is more different than seed and the lack of it; in his conception, both were present. A "Virgin Mother" does not exist in nature; above nature, Mary is a perpetual virgin and a mother. She married and did not marry, so that she might satisfy civil law and hide so great a mystery until the appointed time. **Joseph** was called her husband and Christ’s father, but he was never truly a father nor a husband. Other men are accustomed to and able to have brothers; Christ ought not to agree with them in any respect; therefore, she who is his mother was a perpetual virgin. It is a sign...

This is the **eastern gate** of the mystical temple (which is human nature) described by **Ezekiel**, which shall not be opened, nor shall any mortal enter through it, but only God, who can pass through closed places against the dimensions of bodies, no differently than through open ones <note>Ezekiel 44:1–3. Christian theologians traditionally interpreted this "closed gate" as a prophecy of the perpetual virginity of Mary.</note>. If, indeed, God is understood there in His own nature, without a body, what need is there for the opening of a gate? If He has a body, and enters through a closed gate which shall never be opened, then that gate through which the Redeemer first came among men is the eastern one, and the foremost **Virgin Mary**. For otherwise the prophet would have lied—which is a wicked thing to say—if he had intended this to refer to any other gate of either the first or the second Temple. For there was none that was not opened. Indeed, there is no third material Temple. Therefore, the eastern gate of this temple of humanity is **Mary**, virgin and mother of God alone, and daughter and sister of man, mother and daughter of her own offspring, free from every stain.

If, therefore, Jesus possessed that most excellent quality which the Messiah ought to have, there is no doubt that he is the very one promised in the Law, since a greater cannot be given. Thus, Christ had no brothers and no father according to the flesh.

I pass over the insane opinion concerning demons and traditions, and I address you briefly, my friend **Münster** <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a famous German Hebraist and reformer. I entreat you by the holy name of Jesus Christ: do you think that no mortal until this very day has understood the Sacred Scriptures, and left in writing what their true sense was?

If you say "none," I will not argue with you; but if you say "some," then where all have agreed, it is certain and prescribed that they held to the reason of the Gospel and of pious instruction.

Regarding the **choice of foods** <note>Dietary laws (kashrut).</note> discussed by you in chapter 15: when it was introduced (which was immediately from the time of the Apostles), did the Fathers not understand it in such a way that they did not think there was any inherent evil in the foods? Did they believe—as the Jews do regarding pork, blood, and strangled meat—that there was a vice that defiles the soul? Far be it from us even to suspect this of their piety. Therefore, the choice of foods was not approved by the Church or prescribed on certain days for the same reason it was for the Jews. Rather, it was so that the **wanton flesh**, accustomed to its usual foods, would not resist the spirit.

Therefore, the sacred institutions do not conflict with that passage in **Matthew**, "This people," etc. <note>Matthew 15:8, quoting Isaiah, regarding those who honor God with lips but whose hearts are far away.</note> Tell me, has the **Lord's Day** <note>Sunday observance.</note> not been piously introduced? But where do you find it in the Sacred Scriptures? Do you not believe that John the Baptist and the Apostles and the disciples of Christ were baptized? Yet this is not found in the Sacred Scriptures <note>Postel is arguing that many essential Christian practices rely on Tradition rather than explicit Biblical text.</note>. How many and varied are the things to be held and kept as most holy which consist only of traditions?

What is this madness and childish assertion of one's own wisdom, to prefer one’s own judgment to the whole world? Therefore, the sacred statutes introduced by the observers of the Gospel do not collapse. Let there be hypocrites under them; they would exist even if there were no traditions. Pious statutes that bring perfection to the saints are not the cause of the problem. Otherwise the Gospel—which through distorted interpretation has produced almost as many **Epicureans** <note>In this context, a term for those who deny the immortality of the soul or live only for worldly pleasure.</note> and impious men as it has followers—would be an evil. The Gospel is good; it is the interpretation of certain people that is bad and impious—those most wretched and impious men who twist it for the sake of their bellies, their lusts, and their glory.

You should have been satisfied to bring forward the objections of the **Jews**, with whom you often seem closely aligned. You should never have postponed Christ and His Church—already confirmed in these matters for 1,540 years—for the sake of a new opinion and <term>φιλαυτίᾳ</term> <note>original: "philautia," meaning self-love or vanity.</note>.

It was not Christ who made those who crucified and rejected him sin and stumble against him, but rather their own faithless mind, which did not rest in the truth it had recognized.

For God left man in the hand of his own counsel. Thus it was decreed by God that while some were the authors of His death, they brought death upon themselves and the cause of free life to others. Thus in the death of Jesus, all things were unlike the deaths of other men. Men receive benefits from their own people; He was destroyed. By the death of others, the State suffers a loss; salvation hangs upon His death. The generation of the dead is entirely cut off, but because Jesus laid down his life for his brothers, he sees a **long-lived seed** <note>Alluding to Isaiah 53:10.</note>. # ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

### Chapter 16
On the comparison of Jonah and the resurrection of Christ, which do not align in all details, since Jonah was in the belly of the fish for three days and three nights, whereas Christ was in the heart of the earth for only three days and two nights. Certainly, in one place **Münster** <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a German cartographer and Hebraist whose biblical commentaries Postel frequently critiqued.</note> demonstrated entirely that they falsely cast these slanders, since there are many similar things in scripture that hardly match the thing being compared. As when God said, "Let us make man in our image and likeness." Man has absolutely nothing in common with God except for the invisible spirit—unless the Jews are **anthropomorphites** <note>Those who attribute human form or emotions to God.</note> and thus think the parable must fit in every single detail. 

The Scriptures are full of such comparisons. The three-day period of Christ's resurrection, lasting one full day and parts of two others along with two nights, is calculated in the manner of **tertian fevers** <term>tertian fevers: a medical term for fevers that recur every third day by inclusive counting—meaning there is only one full day of health in between</term>, which no language fails to call "third-day" fevers, specifically those ignited by yellow bile in the veins. For it is enough that they skip an entire day, from the end of one attack to the start of the next paroxysm, for them to be said to recur on the "third day." 

But as for the literal truth of the statement that Christ would be in the heart of the earth for "three days and three nights," it should be understood through **anticipation** <note>A rhetorical or chronological device where an event is counted as starting from the moment it is decided or set in motion.</note>, starting namely from the decree of his death made by the scribes and Pharisees before he was captured on the day of the Last Supper. For it is commonly said, "He is a dead man," from the moment the sentence is passed against him. Although Pilate issued the formal decree, they had prepared their slanders for his death on Thursday. Therefore, he was dead on Thursday night, Friday night, and the Sabbath night—either truly dead, or as if dead, according to the common naming of death. Regarding the days, there is no controversy. For neither full days nor full nights are required, but rather certain hours of them. 

If, however, the Jews should say that this style of writing is unusual in the Sacred Scriptures—that a space of time should be spoken of by anticipation—I will bring forward one passage where there is a far longer preoccupation of time. It is written in **Exodus 12**: *Now the residence of the children of Israel, during which they stayed in Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years.* And yet it is clearly evident through the ages of the patriarchs that the Israelites were in the land of Egypt for only two hundred and thirty years. From this, it is necessary to refer two hundred years back to the times of Abraham so that the number remains consistent. 

In that passage, we shall take "Egypt" to mean a region and a state of affliction. For from the time Abraham was chosen and left all his resources for the sake of God, he was certainly afflicted <gloss>Hebrew: *ben mezarim*, meaning "between the straits" or "in distress"</gloss>, though not literally in the land of Egypt. For that word, if you remove the vowel points, can signify both equally: one is pronounced *mezzarim* [distresses], the other *mizraim* [Egypt]. Truly, God corrects every son whom He loves. In respect to the happiness he left behind, Abraham was never so wealthy that he was not in distress—in Egypt with Pharaoh, in Gerar with Abimelech, and with the servants of his brother Lot. For the entire life of the righteous must be a continuous affliction, either voluntary or in patient endurance, so that he may always remember God, whom prosperity leads one to forget. 

Therefore, there are 400 years from the departure of Israel back to the birth of Isaac, and 30 years from that to the calling of Abraham. That this ought to be understood as the affliction of the pious immediately from the calling of Abraham was indicated by **Stephen the Protomartyr** in the **Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 7**. For thus Luke records his sermon: *But God spoke to Abraham himself, saying that his seed would be a sojourner in a foreign land, and they would bring them into bondage and afflict them for four hundred years,* etc. I believe that error in interpretation arose from which all things have been added to the sacred texts shortly after the time of **Ezra**. Therefore, there is a "preoccupation" [anticipation] based on the power and effect of Christ’s death, just as there is here from the calling of Abraham. **Rabbi Aben Ezra** <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and biblical commentator.</note> collects many such numbers in this place, lest the Jews say that this is merely a groundless invention of my own.

I cannot pass over with a "dry foot" <note>original: *sicco pede*; a Latin idiom meaning to pass over something quickly or without due attention.</note> the insanity—not to say the impiety—of our interpreter. For who could hide such remarkable slanders? As if he has persuaded people that in the sacred constitutions of the Church (for that is what he calls them) laws and works are profitable without faith and without Christ. Produce one writer of any kind you wish in whom that impiety is held, and I will submit.

# WILLIAM POSTEL BOOK 4

<sig>oo 3</sig>

The Church knows that we can do nothing good without faith, without Christ, hope, and charity. But even so, the Church knows that man is so obligated to God—both because of the benefits he has received and because of the sins he has committed—that there is absolutely no good work he should not be doing continually, and he must repent for his whole life. But who are those who are supposedly accustomed to selling their own good works, in which they abound, to others? There is plainly no one. Certainly, it has been accepted since the times of the Apostles that the prayer of a saint is beneficial, that the members of the Church help one another with mutual prayers, and that what one person cannot do, many can. Otherwise, if it were not permitted to be helped by mutual prayers, what is the use of a congregation? Even if some are extremely poor, as the Apostles were, is it not a great thing if they reap "carnal" things <note>A reference to material support (1 Corinthians 9:11), implying that spiritual workers deserve material sustenance.</note> for the common prayers and good works they perform for themselves and others? There are wicked men everywhere, and those unworthy of their rank: but should everyone be held in the same regard because of them? 

If this reasoning holds ground, then all these "fellow-evangelists" are godless <note>original: $\alpha \theta \varepsilon o \iota$ (*atheoi*)</note>. For the greatest part of them, under the pretext of Gospel liberty, has preferred **Epicurus** and **Lucretius** <note>Ancient philosophers associated with materialism and the pursuit of pleasure rather than spiritual duty.</note> to Christ. You <note>Referring to the Reformers like Münster.</note> ought not to defame an entire order just because some are seen to be wicked; that is a "great liberty" indeed—to preach that you and yours are the only good ones while you wish to suppress everyone else. There are no longer any Pharisees; Jewish affairs were cut down long ago. It is necessary that the weeds and the darnel grow with the grain; God will choose from the dragnet those fish which He Himself will approve. From where does that arrogance of yours come? That in matters which can be interpreted for good rather than for evil, you alone—acting like a second **Aristarchus** <note>An ancient grammarian known for his severe and rigorous criticism of poetry.</note>—should snatch away the judgment belonging to God? Why do you judge another’s servant? He stands or falls to his own master. 

If your cowl, your celibacy, your fasts, and the pious works which God prepared for us to walk in, displeased you so much that you bid farewell to them all, supposedly so as not to do an injustice to the merit of Christ: well, not everyone is of the same temperament. And even if they believe they can do nothing worthy of God, and even if they are "useless servants" as Christians, they nevertheless strive to prove themselves to God in those things which they *can* do. He <note>Sebastian Münster.</note> is consistent with himself in his interpretation of the "keys." He says that "binding and loosing" is nothing else than believing or not believing in the remission of sins. How then did Peter "abuse" this power when he bound **Ananias and Sapphira** <note>A couple in the Book of Acts who were struck dead after Peter rebuked them for lying.</note> who were believers? How did Paul, who delivered the Corinthian believer to Satan? Furthermore, since all Christians are equal in authority according to Münster, who shall be the president in the councils? To whom shall we refer the doubtful matters arising daily between two councils? Those who are of equal authority are not obliged to yield to one another. Therefore, everyone will have to feel whatever they please, for that is where such ideas lead. Under an arbitrary interpretation of the Gospel, live as you wish: all things are "free."

I return to the Jews. They say in their exposition of the passage in Genesis: *It is written, "Behold, Adam has become like one of us, etc., so that he may live forever."* <note>Genesis 3:22.</note> You shall question the heretic thus: *Does God not care if man lives forever? Is it not customary for any author to wish the thing he created to last as long as possible? But because God saw it would happen that Jesus would seduce the world and say he was God, He ordained it as a better thing that men should die and that Jesus should be hung on a single piece of wood, so that he would not eat from the tree of life. Whence it is clear to all that he is not God.* 

These are the words of the impious Jews: excellent theologians indeed, who attribute fear to their God! They claim that death was brought upon everyone, and upon Christ himself, so that they might not live forever. In truth, death had already been imposed because of the crime committed <note>The Fall of Adam.</note>, but God expelled man so that they would not persist in doing evil. Therefore, death is not from God, but from sin. As for the claim that Jesus himself seduced the world, they cannot prove this with a single wicked word. Let one take whatever precepts or examples there are in the Gospel; if there is anything that is not most just, we shall concede the point <term>concede the point: literally "reach out the grass," a Roman idiom (herbam porrigere) for admitting defeat</term>. Christ certainly caused many to "err," not as the Jews write, but in the manner of a law being established: for before the law, there is no sin. Therefore, before Christ was incarnate, he did not "err" who did not believe in him while he was unknown; but after he arrived, as many as heard of him and did not believe are in error, and in the far greater sin of infidelity—especially the Jews, to whom he was sent. Let the Jews believe in Jesus as whatever kind of person they wish...

<header>ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD</header>

He certainly possessed all the qualities owed to the most perfect man, the Messiah, as attributed to him by the prophets. Nor can they [the Jews] cast any reproach upon him with their insults. It happened to the Jews regarding Jesus as it does to those with night-blindness <note>Postel uses the term *nyctilopes* to describe those who cannot see in bright light.</note> when they behold the greatest light: because it serves others so that they see nothing without it, it deprives these others of their sight. There is no need for a defense when they object that God cannot be seen, and therefore claim we falsely say that Christ saw God. No Christian has ever asserted that they saw the divinity itself, whether of Christ or of God; for it is so invisible that even the glorified <note>Referring to the saints in heaven.</note> rather wonder at it than are able to comprehend it. Insofar as His appearance <note>original: *spectrum*</note> can be conceived, Moses, Isaiah, and Micah saw Him. But truly, "no one has seen God and lived." Divinity is sought by the mind alone, and can scarcely be conceived—even by a faint image—except by the most perfect. As for their objection that the saints have not moved mountains: Christians are not traveling performers, rope-walkers, or acrobats <note>original: *petauristæ*</note> who turn the eyes of all toward themselves with miracles, unless it concerns the salvation of men. Innumerable dead have been raised by them in the name of Jesus, which is certainly a greater thing than moving a mountain from its place. It is necessary for faith to be at its greatest, and to proceed from a most innocent and purified heart. Indeed, the apostles had their own imperfections while Christ was alive.

It is certainly shameful to say that Münster <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a famous Hebraist and Reformer whom Postel often accuses of "Judaizing."</note> agrees with the Jew in many opinions, since the facts themselves force this conclusion. Since the monastic and eremitic life is, and has always been since the times of the apostles, a most holy institution from which the greatest lights of the world have come forth—men and women of exceptional holiness—yet, as if all were most wicked and as if you admit no judgment on them, they are all criticized by the Jews with a single word, with Münster’s support. It was certainly to be lamented that not a few parents, unworthy of their offspring and wealth, force young people to undertake that kind of life before they have experienced the vanity of the world (from which a certain constancy usually arises), simply so that the family inheritance remains intact. Nevertheless, not a few of them come to a fruitful life even from those coerced beginnings. For Christ also compels those lingering on the road to come to his feast which is already prepared. No form of life lacks its own plagues, and they are more serious the greater the dignity of mind or body they profess. But truly, the world has had far more good than evil in those orders of monks; otherwise, Germany alone would not feel the sense of this evil. The Templars taught Christians not to be held by superstitions whenever the Republic receives more damage than profit from a single order. It would do the same in the rest, if things were as the Jews—or I should say, the "new-evangelists" <note>Postel uses the pejorative *cæneuangelistæ*, a pun on "new" (*kainos*) and "empty" (*kenos*) gospels, referring to the Reformers.</note>—mutter. We all know that chastity is a gift of God, but because it is most pleasing to God, it is likely that He grants it to many, since He can do all things in us. It is the custom of wicked men to begin their agitation against religious orders by focusing on the vices of men, and thus persuade the unrefined common people to rise up against the sacred orders. If the matter is weighed more carefully, scarcely one in twenty will seem unworthy of his order. If the wickedness of some infects the whole flock, then all the angels are treacherous, from whose company the spirits of demons <note>original: $\kappa\alpha\kappa o\delta\alpha\iota\mu o\nu o\nu$ (*kakodaimonon*)</note> fell; the law of the Jews was wicked, under which so many evil men perished for their crimes; the apostles must be called worthless, among whom one was a treacherous betrayer of the Lord; and Christians are impious, who have many impious people among them. All those things which pertain to the duty of a good man, and not to ancient rites, the Christians observe more diligently than the Jews. Nor should they object to our neglect of circumcision, since it held its place only until the New Law, along with other external rituals. In Chapter 21, they say our Messiah, if he is God, should not have mounted a donkey, because it is an unclean animal. He could make all things clean. The prophet had predicted it would happen that he who was to be king would ride a donkey for the sake of humility, in which no one can be his equal. I have already addressed this above in the prophetic gospel. Regarding temples also, that there is none...

<sig>oo 4</sig>

I have already shown above regarding the third [temple], for after the first and second, no other is read about—except for what Josephus writes, that **Herod of Ascalon** <note>Herod the Great, whom Postel identifies by his ancestral city of Ascalon.</note> constructed a most beautiful temple to capture the favor of the Jewish people. But it did not last, except until the destruction brought about by **Titus**. As for the fact that they add that the third house will be eternal, established by God as incorruptible, that is more true than they themselves may say. For the soul and the **church of the faithful** is the truly eternal house in which God dwells, and it is the image of that which is above, in which there shall be no stain or wrinkle. It shall not be on a mountain or in a field, nor shall it belong specifically to Abraham or Isaac, but truly to all **Israelites**. Indeed, because it is to be eternal, there will be no need for the [Mosaic] law; thus, there will no longer be a difference between nations. For that shall be after the resurrection. **Ezekiel** saw its type in the spirit and wrote of it; **John the Evangelist** also wrote of it in the **Apocalypse** <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>. In this current state of corruption, however, nothing will ever be eternal.

The argument concerning the hunger of Christ has already been resolved by me. For Jesus possessed both natures—namely, the divine and the human—in such a way that although he had made one composite and one subject in himself, nevertheless each nature held its own suitability without the hindrance of the other, whenever he willed it. His divinity did not hinder the imperfections of the body, just as those imperfections did not hinder his divinity. He fasted for forty days, with the divinity supporting the body in that middle state of the composite; finally, the body, as if returning separately to its own functions, became hungry. The external glory of God was not present to him to strengthen him, as the "vision of God" <note>original: *spectrum Dei*</note> was for **Moses**, or the angelic vision for **Elijah**. Since the seventh day of fasting is typically fatal to a mortal man, both of them fasted for forty days. He, therefore, who by his own power had made it so that both fasted in him, taught that he had both given that power which he exercised through himself, and he showed the humanity in himself in such a way that, driven by its necessities, he might create faith in both natures. Otherwise, if he had no needs, he would be believed to be a phantom <note>original: *spectrum*</note>, not a man.

Concerning the **fig tree**, which he struck with a curse as an object of loathing because it was barren: he could have done the same while absent, for his physical approach was not the primary consideration. Just as God’s approach and calling to **Adam** after the sin, the descent to the **Tower of Babel**, the visitation of **Sodom and Gomorrah** <note>original: *Hamorrhæ*</note>, and countless other instances are not signs of God’s ignorance, so too this act of Christ was not. Just as God in those instances accommodates himself to the weakness of our intellect, so Christ in this deed was looking out for the disciples, so that he might show both his omnipotence and that all barren deeds—or the "un-deeds" of men—are to be exterminated and punished with eternal penalties. 

As for the claim that he acted against the precept of love by being angry at an unfeeling tree—who is so mad as to believe that? Love, hatred, and anger are directed from one human toward another. Other things which lack both will and judgment deserve neither hatred, envy, nor anger.

There is another objection. They say: "We Christians claim that you Jews are in captivity because of the death or killing of Christ, but we were in captivity before him." I respond: Before Jesus, no captivity took the lordship of things in **Syria** away from you, except for the **Babylonian** captivity, which was predicted and limited by the prophets before it happened. In that captivity, you were indeed not without <term>mehoccecim</term> <note>original: *mehoccecim*, from the Hebrew *mechoqqum*, meaning "lawgivers" or "scepters," referring to the prophecy in Genesis 49:10.</note> or legislators. For **Jeremiah**, **Daniel**, and many other most holy men were with you, who made you very certain that after 70 years you would be liberated, while observing the highest forms of worship, as I have already said. Now, you have spent 1500 years more hated by the pagans than by the Christians. I have seen the condition of your affairs in **Africa**, in **Asia**, and in the most famous cities of **Europe**. Why do you not raise your head? Why does your **Messiah** cheat you of his presence so greatly? For what reason has he been born and slept for 1500 years? As for your wish to mockingly defend yourselves using Christ's prayer on the cross on your behalf: certainly Christ, the Son of God, God from God, the wisdom of the Father, seriously prayed to the Father for you, and obtained it for the good. Truly, whatever the nature of divine prayers may be, unless a man acquiesces through **free will**, he is not saved. For God does not insert force into our will; it stands with the man, by which...
