...less he be saved. Therefore, Christ says: *How often I wanted to gather you together, as a hen gathers her chicks, and you were not willing* <note>original: "Quoties uolui te cōgregare sicut gallina congregat pullos suos, et noluisti." A reference to Matthew 23:37.</note>. It belongs to Him to will, and to man to be unwilling. God calls all who thirst to the waters and invites them freely; and although all mortals thirst, nevertheless very few are saved. God wanted to lead the people brought out of Egypt safely into the holy land; yet because they did not comply with God, out of countless thousands, only two were saved <note>A reference to Joshua and Caleb, the only two of the original generation from Egypt permitted to enter Canaan.</note>. A forced servant is no better than a wicked one, even if he seems to act well. Therefore, that which God gave as the highest gift to man, He wishes to be in man's own power, nor is He accustomed to use force.

What they <note>Likely referring to Jewish interlocutors or critics.</note> concede mockingly in chapter 22, I embrace and approve in earnest: namely, that He is the Son of God, His very wisdom and word, to whom God spoke as to His own Lord and equal, saying: *Sit at my right hand* <note>original: "sede à dextris meis." From Psalm 110:1.</note>. As for what follows—that these things were said because of the Jews who would hatefully kill the Son—that is not true, even though no nation was ever more hostile to God. That phrase expressed by the prophet is an explanation of the divine nature and condition, to prove the equality of the persons [of the Trinity] and a similar deity that does not lack a place. Although, as I showed in the beginning, this deity is entirely in the Son, entirely in the Father, and entirely in the Holy Spirit—just as a whole thing exists in thought, the whole in the word, and the whole in the effect—nevertheless, they must neither be confused nor separated. Therefore, the Son did not leave the right hand of the Father when He came in the flesh. 

He is also the judge of the whole world; nor was He disobedient or rebellious toward the Father, whose will He performed, since man could not be redeemed without His death. That saying, *Sit at my right hand*, cannot be understood as referring to David or Abraham. For David does not have the kingdom of heaven in his power to give to Abraham, who (according to your traditions) was at the gate of hell <term>inferi</term> <note>Postel is mocking a Rabbinic tradition that Abraham stands at the gates of Gehenna to prevent circumcised Jews from entering.</note> resisting God and preventing the wicked Jews whom God was sending to Gehenna from entering it. Sane interpretations of that passage must be brought forward, for which thanks must certainly be given to **Münster** <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a German cartographer and Hebraist whose works Postel studied.</note>. 

Thus the paraphrast **Jonathan son of Uzziel** <note>The reputed author of the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> translates: *Jehovah said to his Lord, sit at my right hand.* In the book *Kibuzin* <note>Possibly a reference to a collection of Midrashic commentaries.</note> it is written: *God, the Greatest and Best, is to come, establishing the King Messiah at his right hand. Since it was said: The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.* **Rabbi Isaac** <note>Likely Isaac Arama or another prominent medieval commentator.</note> writes thus on Genesis: *Before the creation of the sun, the name of our Messiah was flourishing and subsisting, and he sat at the right hand of God.* And this is what the prophet says: *Sit at my right hand.* That passage is usually explained in this way; thus the ancient doctors understood it.

I have already taught, in the primary refutations of the Jews, how Christ said he was ignorant of the day of judgment. For he said that the Son does not know. Certainly, as he saw Jesus <note>i.e., in his human capacity</note>, he truly did not know of that day, because it is not expedient for any mortal to know about the future. God wishes to keep us in our duty through fear. We should not care if the Jews bark about the imperfection of the nature that was in Christ—in his mother's womb, his birth, and his infancy. For that which is without the fault of the one acting or suffering contains no evil. 

As for their contention that the verse of Psalm 19 is poorly applied—where it is written: *He set his tabernacle in the sun like a bridegroom,* etc.—as if it were unsuitable for Christ: surely it can suit no one better. Even if what God touches were foul, filthy, or stained in any way, He cleanses and sanctifies it, never touching a blemish, just as light illuminates all dark things and conceals no darkness. The "tabernacle" of the Messiah was heaven, and this whole temple of nature, after the world was created. When He wished to become man, the tabernacle was the Virgin; now it is the souls of the faithful. And so, Jews, while you think you defile Christ with words regarding the necessity of nature, you immerse yourselves in the mud. You are no different from one who tries to obstruct the light; he can indeed take the light away from himself, but he cannot infect the nature of light. 

I would not dare to mix Münster further into Jewish impieties, unless he so impiously took away man's free choice <term>arbitrium</term> that he judges man should be held as below the other animals, as if man had no...

# GUILLAUME POSTEL, BOOK 4 #

<page-num>441</page-num>

If man possesses no free choice <note>original: "arbitrij habeat homo"</note>, and does all good and evil works by necessity through predestination, then God is unjust. Therefore, no one who commands something actually wishes it to remain undone. Oh, what blasphemy! I will not hesitate to affirm one thing: certain people fall more foully into this error than Arius, than Eunomius, than Nestorius, and however many impious heretics there have ever been <note>Postel refers to famous early Christian leaders whose teachings on the nature of God and Christ were condemned by the Church.</note>. For whoever denies that free choice exists within man—especially for those initiated into the sacred rites of Jesus Christ—and claims that good works contribute nothing to salvation, denies that God exists. It is no wonder if those so instructed pass daily into impiety, since it matters nothing to them what they shall become. Thus, the impious have this saying in their mouths: "I cannot act otherwise; God compels me."

One can clearly see how violently distorted against Christ is the passage usually cited by the Jews from Deuteronomy, chapter 13. It says: 

> "If your brother, the son of your mother, or your son or your daughter, or the wife who is in your embrace, or your companion who is as dear as your soul, should entice you in secret, saying: 'Let us go and serve foreign gods,' whom neither you nor your fathers have known, etc." and at the end of the sentence: "You shall not yield to him; he shall be put to death, and your hand shall be the first against him to kill him." 

This is the verse. Taking only two words, they say it is understood to be about Christ; they explain "the son of your mother" as meaning one who is said to be born without the seed of a father. Yet the entire passage intended to indicate nothing else than that even those closest to us must not be spared in such a crime. Furthermore, Christ never taught about God in secret, nor did he teach of a foreign god, but of the Creator of the universe whom your fathers worshipped, O Jews. I certainly pity such unheard-of blindness, or perhaps I should call it stubborn obstinacy—I know not which. For nothing is less fitting for such things than Jesus Christ. With equal impudence, they affirm that Christ did not know his own betrayer, whom he nevertheless so often said was destined for this. And again: if he were God, why did he allow himself to be bound? Let them ask Isaiah 53: 

> "Who is he upon whom God laid the iniquities of us all? Who shall be led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer shall be silent, and shall not open his mouth?" 

Was death not pleasing to him? It certainly was. His humanity shuddered and shrank from death in its own way; but his divinity sought it—not for its own sake, but as an instrument against the treacherous—so that by that death, sacrifice might be made for the salvation of the world. And so, Judas did evil by betraying him, and the Jews by destroying him, because they performed this not for the sake of the world’s salvation, but he driven by greed and envy, and they by envy and anger. If Christ had revealed himself more clearly to the world, as he certainly could have, the <term>redemption</term> <note>The theological concept of being "bought back" or saved from sin through Christ's sacrifice.</note> which had to be accomplished through a most violent death could never have been fulfilled. For although it was necessary that the God-man be put to death—as he told everyone, otherwise it would never happen that man would return to favor with God—certainly no one would have wished to be the executioner of so pious and holy a man. Truly, even some of his apostles were in doubt regarding his divinity until he rose again and gave them the Holy Spirit. 

Regarding the Passover lamb, they say that just as there were many lambs to be offered, so it would be necessary, if they hinted at Christ, for him to be born and hanged more often, so that the reality would correspond to the figure <note>A "figure" is an Old Testament event or object believed to prefigure or symbolize a New Testament truth.</note>. I said from the beginning that the Messiah would be so excellent that he would exceed all human excellence and would agree with no one in establishing his laws. For his law was to be new, not according to that which God gave in Egypt or to Moses, but that which would be written in the heart. Therefore, just as expiations were made in the Law through the external blood of many innocent animals, so the sins of all believers are forgiven by the power of the blood of the one Lamb slain once. He was both the Lamb, and was offered once for all, and made parts of his own body when he gave it to his disciples. The Jews do not dispute this matter as much as our own "Supper-evangelists" <note>original: "cœneuangeliſtæ." A derisive term for Protestant Reformers who debated the nature of the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist (the Lord's Supper).</note>, since they judge Christ to be powerless to distribute his body anywhere on earth, and affirm that it is taken only by faith; yet we see...

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD #

<page-num>442</page-num>

In nature, there are even countless bodily things that can be entirely in one place and entirely in others at one and the same moment in time, and yet remain only one in the whole. Who does not know that in any tree suitable for transplanting—from a stake or a small fork—there is only one nature, both in body and soul? Make as many cuttings and willow plants as you wish; each one possesses as much as the first. Should I not bring forth an example from spiritual things? The entire image of a single thing is in the eyes of all in countless mirrors and in every power of sight; smells strike the nostrils of all equally; light is equal in small and large quantities, as far as the nature of the thing is concerned. The nature of Christ’s glorified body can be everywhere, no differently than his divinity. It was in his own hands, no differently than if a willow tree could speak and, embracing branch with branch, should say: "This is my body."

The impiety of the "pseudo-evangelists" <note>original: "ceneuangelistarum"; Postel uses this derogatory term for the Protestant Reformers who held a symbolic view of the Eucharist.</note> does not grasp this, because they believe the Creator to be less powerful than the creation. That impiety which Münster <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a famous German Hebraist and cartographer whose works Postel often critiqued.</note> does not dare to vomit out in Latin, he teaches to the Jews: that the sacrament is nothing other than a memory of Christ’s death. He writes those things in Hebrew—as if, indeed, by affirming the presence of the body of Jesus, the Church denies the memory of his passion.

The objection regarding the hour of the lamb's slaughter is false, when the Jews say the lamb was accustomed to be eaten at evening, while Christ was crucified in the morning. They claim that until the lamb was eaten, no one received the power of the Passover. However, although Jesus was crucified toward noon, he did not expire before the ninth hour, which is three in the afternoon <note>Postel is harmonizing the timing of the crucifixion with the Jewish ritual calendar.</note>. Thus, on the same day the symbolic lamb was eaten by the Jews toward evening, Christ gave himself. For as he gave up his spirit, salvation was restored to the whole world. Therefore, he had wished to eat the symbolic lamb on Thursday, contrary to the custom of the Jews, and had substituted his own most holy body for it. He who takes this unworthily (let us not think it is received only by faith and not in reality) eats and drinks judgment upon himself. For this reason, many in the early church died, and others were most seriously ill, because they did not discern the body of the Lord—that is, they did not believe it differed from other foods.

As for the different manner of the killing of Jesus and the lamb, what is the point of speaking? For a man and a lamb are not the same thing. It is enough that they agree in innocence. "Why," says the circumcised *Nizahon* <note>Referring to the *Sefer Nizzahon Yashar*, a medieval Jewish polemical text written to refute Christian interpretations of the Bible.</note>, "was his soul sorrowful even unto death? If you say that he speaks according to the flesh, which fears—does he not say 'My soul is sorrowful'? In every place you say this 'according to the flesh,' yet no one is ignorant that the flesh neither speaks nor knows, any more than a stone."

See, faithless Jew, where your obstinacy and your vow of blaspheming Christ lead you: that which you can concede and daily see in all men, you wish to deny to Christ alone. At the very least, Christ was a man; but no man exists in whom one cannot, in the same matter, both will and not will, be sorrowful and rejoice. What makes anyone permit a doctor to treat figs, fistulas, cancers, or stones with the harshest iron remedies for the sake of obtaining health? <note>Postel uses the conflict between a patient's fear of surgery and their rational desire for health as an analogy for Christ's agony in Gethsemane.</note> Does not reason judge one way, while the sense of nature wills another? Reason leads to the "butcher shop" most willingly, but the nature of the body recoils—not from health, but from a health bought so dearly. Thus, the same man wills to be cut and wills not to be cut. Meanwhile, he implores the doctor, whom he knows will not spare him; and if the doctor wished to spare him, reason would not allow it. Thus, many rush into death willingly, even when nature is not equal to the torments. With the same mind, for the sake of the fatherland or for profit, the leader and the soldier undergo dangers, willing to prepare peace through torments. Thus virtue struggles laboriously against the "corporeal soul"—that is, the vital, natural, animal part. For that part seeks luxury and pleasure, while virtue, with reason as its guide, seeks the greatest perils. Nor are Christians so foolish as to think that inanimate flesh can feel or speak for itself. Therefore, Christ could—even if he had been a mere man—struggle in soul and reason, his soul being joined to a body and subject to death. For those things differ most widely. But how much more so since in him there was, along with reason, a common...

# THE FOURTH BOOK OF GUILLAUME POSTEL #

<page-num>443</page-num>

...shared divinity, he was able to both desire death with his whole will for the sake of the salvation of all, and to flee from it with his whole will. Through the union of divinity with humanity, he did not wish to remove any corporeal imperfection of our fallen nature, lest he should diminish the full punishment owed to it. Therefore, "his soul was sorrowful even unto death," <note>original: "Tristis igitur erat eius anima usq; ad mortem"; a reference to Matthew 26:38 during the Agony in the Garden.</note> the bitterness of which his divinity had already placed before his eyes. Truly, however, that ardor for saving humanity conquered. The prayer made to the Father pertains to this same point. For the man implores the divinity in his fragility, even though his reason does not wish for the body to be spared; not unlike a man who is to be cut or cauterized, who asks and entreats the <term>surgeon <note>original: "χειροῦργος" (cheirourgos), meaning one who works with their hands, specifically a surgeon.</note></term> if it can be done otherwise, and yet desires not his own will, but that of the doctor and of reason to be done. Nor for that reason are the two perspectives unequal—namely, that of the patient and that of the surgeon. For each has decreed the cutting or the cautery.

Therefore, what that impious Jew says—that Christ is not God, nor has a will equal to God the Father—is false. For the power of the Father, the wisdom of the Son, and the love of the Holy Spirit, which is the sole divinity before the world was established, had determined this remedy for man, who was lost by his own accord: that a body connected to divinity should pay the penalties for a fallen human nature. Thus, that will was carried out, even as the fragile nature of the man fled from it and was driven by sadness even to a sweat of blood. I have taught extensively through human reasons in the first book that nature could be repaired in no other way than by the death of a man joined to God. All other objections have been pierced by our victor with the aforementioned reasons.

As for what he adds—that the flesh could not have fasted for forty days except by the grace of the Holy Spirit—it is certain that such a faculty is not in the flesh to remain fasting for so long. But just as the vision of divinity gave this to Moses (as I have said), and an angelic strengthening gave it to Elijah, so too did the divinity bestow it upon Christ Jesus for as long as it willed, as he possessed the fullness of divinity within himself. But if divinity worked this in him, why did it not act so that he would not fear? I respond: so that absolutely nothing of those imperfections and passions (except for sin) which are placed in the nature of all people should be lacking in the flesh that was paying the penalty for all. Certainly, Christ could have removed feeling and emotions from his flesh before death and died an imaginary death; but he willed to truly suffer and to truly give signs of all human passions. For it would have been a mere stage-play <note>original: "actus personatus"; implying a masked or hypocritical performance.</note> and unworthy of him if, when he had come to suffer, he had suffered only in imagination.

O faithless and lost Jews, how could it be possible—unless Christ were God giving his grace to whom he wills—that infinite thousands of saints have been placed among the blessed in his name, a fact which you cast as a reproach against us? Certainly, one man cannot give holiness and the grace of miracles to another man. Therefore, Jesus was offered because he willed it. By these same reasons, the objection of the Jews concerning the three youths falls; it is read that they were not troubled by sadness on account of the fiery furnace which they entered. <note>A reference to Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in Daniel 3.</note> There are also innumerable martyrs (to grant the Jews more than they might wish) who did not rush into all kinds of unheard-of tortures with sorrow, but with alacrity.

However, as I have already said, the rationale was different for Christ when he was about to suffer. For the three youths, strengthened by God through his angel, were encouraged for their torments; and that which the nature of the body could not bear, divine consolation provided, so that the pains were diminished in those torments which fragile nature is unequal to bearing. But in Christ, whatever can happen that is simply sad and distressing without any supernatural aid, happened for the reason that he was washing away the sins of all in himself. He would have done this less truly if he had been encouraged by the same privilege as the others. Yet, so that there might also be faith in his divinity and his friendship with God, his human nature received consolation in word from an angel; for it would not have been possible for nature, left thus in its sufferable condition, to have endured—a nature which divinity did not wish to relieve with its infinite perfection before death—unless it had been assisted by some breath of relief. The ministers...

He refutes Jewish objections by contrasting Christ's intentional lack of divine comfort with the miraculous endurance of the three youths in the furnace and later Christian martyrs.</summary>

God therefore willed to console his Son through the ministry of a servant <note>original: "ministri... ministerio"; referring to the angel who comforted Christ in Gethsemane.</note> rather than by the direct assistance of his divinity. He did this so that the consolation of the divinity—which had itself ordained that this death would be most bitter—would not diminish the weight of the punishment. Just as the death of the Messiah was prepared for the sake of all humanity, so too it had to be set apart from the common experience of dying. For as we have seen that all his qualities were most excellent, it was entirely just that he should also differ from others in his death. The most outstanding of the best of men bore the most bitter reward of virtue: death in a body afflicted by every kind of calamity, without any privilege of a moderated penalty, as is evident even in his crucifixion.

For, as I have taught above, that a living body was suspended by the piercings of the hands for three hours surpasses whatever tortures can be imagined. But at this point the Jews snarl; although they call Christ <term>Talui <note>original: "talui" (Hebrew: תלוי), meaning "the hanged one," often used in a derogatory sense in medieval Jewish polemics.</note></term> (that is, the hanged one) for the sake of insult, and call his cross "the upright and transverse wood," they actually claim he was not crucified but simply killed. They argue that such a type of punishment was unusual among the Jews, for the High Senate was accustomed to stone, burn, strike, or strangle. They speak as if, at that time, judicial matters were still conducted according to the ancient constitution—even if we grant their claims were true—when in fact sixty years earlier, or thereabouts, the Senate of the <term>Sanhedrin <note>The supreme judicial and ecclesiastical council of ancient Jerusalem.</note></term> had been abolished by Herod. As I have taught before, Herod had "killed three shepherds in one month," <note>A reference to Zechariah 11:8, which Postel interprets as Herod's destruction of the three orders of Jewish leadership: the sacred, the profane, and the mixed.</note> effectively destroying the sacred, profane, and mixed orders, and establishing laws, constitutions, and magistrates according to his own whim.

<margin>example</margin>
Therefore, O Jews, it was not permitted for you to put anyone to death when Christ was captured, though it certainly was permitted under the Leaders, Kings, and Heads of the Captivity when you were a free people. The Cross was a mystery of redemption and a sign of eternal life in <term>hieroglyphic <note>Postel often viewed physical symbols as "hieroglyphs" or sacred ciphers of divine truth.</note></term> markings. Upon it, with arms spread wide in an embrace, he died—he who was destined to embrace all who are willing to believe in him.

Truly, now a heap of insults and slanders presents itself. From the version of the <term>Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, traditionally attributed to seventy-two translators.</note></term> (and the Latin version derived from it), they wish to infer that Jesus was even a sinner, because in the 22nd Psalm he cried out: "Eli, Eli, lama azabtani, rahoc misuathi dibre hatati." <note>original Hebrew: אֵלִי אֵלִי לָמָה עֲזַבְתָּנִי רָחוֹק מִישׁוּעָתִי דִּבְרֵי שַׁאֲגָתִי</note> That is: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? The words of my sins are far from my salvation." This is how the Greek text reads. But the Hebrew text has "dibre saagati," that is, "the words of my roaring." They prefer to pervert their own scriptures to insult the Truth, rather than to embrace it by accepting and defending what is true.

Yet, lest we seem to flee from our own version, since that Psalm is said to be about the Messiah, I even admit that "hatati" (that is, "my sin") might be read there, and that Christ "had" sin. But we must see in what way he had it. We say something is "ours" when it is our own property, such as a body, a soul, a field, or a crime. In that way, Christ never had sin. Alternatively, we call something "ours" when it is committed to our trust or received in another’s name. In this way, Christ did not have a single sin of his own, but he took upon himself the sins of the entire world in their full power.

This is what the prophet said: "For the crime of my people I struck him." And elsewhere: "The Lord placed upon him the iniquities of us all," and, "He was wounded for our iniquities, bruised for our crimes." And: "If he shall lay down his soul for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed." And: "By his knowledge my righteous servant shall justify many, and he himself shall bear their iniquities." You cannot deny that these things are said of some supreme man to whom divinity is joined. For a mere man cannot justify other men.

In that way, therefore, he had the sins of all who believe in God through him—and your sins as well, O Jews, if you would only believe in him and repent of your blasphemies. For he "wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth."

As for the blasphemies they pile up in their usual manner, saying he was not "righteous" because God willed him to be forsaken—citing not Solomon in Ecclesiastes (as they wrongly quote), but David—

<margin>Psalm 36</margin>
in Psalm 36: "I have not seen the righteous man forsaken," etc. I have already provided the reason above why He wished [to experience] that sadness...

[he] was not exempt, because both reason and divinity were opposed to his human petition. This is just as the logic of cutting or cauterizing a sick person, held by a surgeon, opposes the sensory appetite that flees from pain, even if the patient implores his mercy so that, if it can be done otherwise, he might be spared for the sake of his health. Thus, for our salvation, the humanity of Jesus Christ did not cry out so much for its own sake, but rather, through a kind of vow, it asked for the sake of the salvation of all, as if already submitting to the divinity. For when he uttered the aforementioned words, Jesus was very near to death.

Why does our "triumphing circumcised one" <note>original: "triumphator noster apella"; Postel uses 'Apella,' a term from the Roman poet Horace, as a derogatory label for a Jew.</note> insist so frequently: "If he was God, and by his own will and love he wished to suffer, why did he pray in sadness?" I have already answered more than enough: it was to show that the human nature, although it was joined to the divinity, nevertheless suffered neither in a fake nor an imaginary way, but without any protection coming from the divine nature. For as I said, he could have eluded all the torments of the Jews without punishment if he had wished, which he showed more than once before his passion, when they wanted to throw him down or seize him.

Finally, mockery and a plague-like spirit laugh at the sacred mysteries and their interpretation. They say (referring to the *hamimin* <note>original: "hamimín"; a Latinization of the Hebrew 'minim,' meaning heretics or sectarians, often applied by Jews to Christians.</note>, that is, the Christian heretics) that when God said, "Let us make man in our image," the Father was saying to the Son, "Help me to make man," and the Son did not want to obey, and so the Father made Adam alone. Finally, he said to the Son, "You did not want to help me just now; someday I will not help you when you ask me," and that is why he did not wish to hear the Son in death. These are the ravings of old women. The divine goodness is most unified in the Trinity, as we have said before; it cannot have a conflict in its will, nor can anything be done unless power, wisdom, and love concur together. May such plagues perish miserably—men so coarse and lazy that they can conceive of nothing in divine matters.

Indeed, who could bear the impious words with which they overturn all sacred things? "If," they say, "the spirit was united with the body, and the divinity was also united into one, then the divinity died." Are you not ashamed, you beast? Even if Christ had been a mere man, would his soul not have survived? For what purpose are laws and rights, piety and virtue, if the soul perishes with the body? If the soul survives death (as it certainly does), how does the unhappy "Apella" dare to place divinity below it and call it mortal? Let the wretch perish.

They also strive to attack the divinity of Jesus Christ from what is written in the last part of Matthew: "All power is given to me in heaven and on earth." <note>Matthew 28:18</note> What does this mean, says *Nizahon* <note>original: "Nizahon"; referring to the Sefer Nizzahon, a famous medieval Jewish polemical work used to argue against Christian interpretations of the Bible.</note>: who gave it to him, if he is the Son of God? What need was there for a gift? Is not the whole world his? If you say that his Father gave it to him, and that he and the Father are two, then is there not one part to each? One is not greater than the other, neither in dominion, nor in virtue, nor in intelligence.

Listen, you circumcised one: does not wisdom always proceed from the singular power of God, and love from both? If Wisdom, who is called the Son by analogy to lower things, should say, "I have all things from my father," would he not speak the truth, since power and wisdom are one? Thus Christ says, "All things are delivered to me by my Father." If they are delivered, if the power is common to both, what then was "given" in terms of power, asks the follower of Moses? It is not the same thing to be God in Himself as it is to be God joined to a human nature. Therefore, after death was conquered through the glorious resurrection, since Christ is a "new composite" consisting of both natures, it was necessary to claim the inheritance anew by right of dominion. Thus, power in heaven and on earth was "given" to the God-man, so that he might draw there those whom he redeemed, whereas before him they had nothing in heaven.

I give no answer to the nonsense of that scoundrel, in which he says that Christ would be with his own until the end of the age, but would not be in the future age. They feel even to this day that he is in heaven, because wherever the Jew acts, even at the furthest distance from Christian rule, Christ ensures that he is in the harshest servitude. At the very least, he is either God, or he is able to stand in the way of the God of Israel, so that He has not been able or willing to hear the Jews in all their worship and affliction for these fifteen hundred years now—

...worshipping Him through [that] kind of affliction. God has shut His ears to them. I bring nothing regarding the comparison of the partridge, because it is an arbitrary slander <note>original: "comparatione perdicis"; This likely refers to a popular medieval polemic based on Jeremiah 17:11, comparing those who acquire wealth or faith unjustly to a partridge that hatches eggs it did not lay.</note>. That Jesus leaves none of His own is clear enough from the final outcome <note>original: "catastrophæ"; here meaning the final act or conclusion of a life.</note> of the lives of the martyrs. For it is not within human power to not only endure so many and such great torments, but even to seek them out willingly; furthermore, that their remains should shine with miracles after death. 

As for their judgment that we err because of our fewness, they lack judgment. For if fewness makes a law null, then Moses gave a false law, since out of at least fifteen hundred thousand people, only two are read to have reached that place to which God had called them. Once, Christianity occupied the whole world; now it is diminished by our own sin. What does it take away from Christ that the Jews do not confess Him to be God? What do they gain by bringing the Muslims <note>original: "Muhametanos"</note> into the same testimony, since that pestilence <note>original: "pestis"; Postel uses this common 16th-century polemical term to describe Islam, which he viewed as a heresy influenced by Jewish teaching.</note> arose six hundred years after the death of Christ, from Jewish teaching? Or is it because something is rare that it is not good? Beautiful, honorable, and good things are rare. We testify indeed that the law of Moses was good and entirely to be kept before Christ; now we say it is abrogated, except for what pertains to morals. Therefore, two false witnesses are not witnesses, especially against the truth, which they keep suppressed in a lie. These are the things I had to propose to our people who are unskilled in Jewish matters, so that in attacking the Jews they may finish the task and answer them.
